## What leaves the machine

With `--cortheon`, the search queries the model writes from the conversation go to DuckDuckGo, or to Brave when a key is set.
Pages are fetched from this machine, so each site sees its address.
Without the flag, the server makes no searches and reads no web pages.

The instruction filter is a heuristic, and it can miss a page written to steer the model, such as one that splits an order across a line break.
So `cortheon_fetch` reads only URLs the conversation has already shown: search results, links on pages it has read, and URLs in the user's, the system prompt's or a tool's messages.
A URL that appears only in the model's own replies does not count, so a steered model cannot build one that carries conversation text.
The one exception is a package registry's JSON for a single named package: `https://pypi.org/pypi/NAME/json`, `https://registry.npmjs.org/NAME/latest` and `https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/NAME`, with a version allowed in place of `latest`.
A name there is at most 64 characters, so that is the most a registry request could carry.
A refused fetch tells the model to search for the page instead.
Use `--cortheon` where sending search queries off the machine is acceptable for the conversations the server handles.

## Budgets

The model may make 6 web calls in a reply, on top of the research done before it starts.
A reply runs at most 8 generation rounds.
When the web budget runs out, the model is told to answer from what it has and to say what is still unsettled.

## Requests

A request can send `"cortheon": false` to skip it.
Cortheon also leaves these requests as they are: `tool_choice` set to `"none"`, `"required"` or a named function, structured output, `logprobs`, title requests, background requests, and requests with no tools that ask the model to transform text they carry.
Harnesses send those last ones for titles, summaries and routing hints.
Requests to `/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages` get the same treatment as chat completions.

A streamed reply shows Cortheon's progress in `reasoning_content`, for example `Cortheon: searching the web for "zig 0.17 release notes"`.
Whole replies and the last streamed chunk carry a `cortheon` object:

```json
{"task": "research_answer", "research_first": true, "rounds": 1, "searches": 2, "pages_read": 2,
 "sources": ["https://ziglang.org/download/0.17.0/release-notes.html", "https://ziglang.org/news/0.17.0-released/"], "checks": []}
```

## Prompt caching

The research and tool rounds a client never saw stay in the server's memory, up to 512 replies or 32 MiB.
On the next turn the server puts them back in front of the reply they informed.
The prompt then matches what the model read last turn, so the prompt cache still resumes it.

## Cost

Research before building adds one short greedy generation for the queries and a few seconds of network time.
Each web call the model makes adds one generation round.
Decoding is unchanged: every round runs through the same engine, with the same exact output for the prompt it gets.

## Example

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit --cortheon
```

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What changed in the latest Zig release?"}]}'
```

Point any OpenAI-compatible client at `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1` as before.
# Credits

TensorFold's native engine (1.0 and later) grew out of the Python engine (0.2.0 to 0.6.6), and much of the Python
engine was written by people who sent pull requests. This page names whose work each native part carries or follows,
with links to their pull requests and to their files at the `v0.6.6` tag. The Python engine is frozen at that tag and
still installs from it.

Upstream projects whose code TensorFold adapts are named in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
Everyone who sent a pull request, a measurement or a bug report is listed under Contributors in the
[README](../README.md#contributors).

## Prompt reuse

- @nood-co1's [#190](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/190) evicts first a kept state its conversation has
  moved past, and keeps a shared system block and a state a conversation forks back to
  ([streams.py](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/streams.py)). The native prompt
  cache (`zig/src/core/prompt_cache.zig`, `prompt_radix.zig`) evicts by the same rule. @nood-co1's
  [#65](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/65) kept a prompt's end state one token before its end, as the
  native cache does for several families.
- The message starts and history boundaries above (#83, #177) decide where the native cache keeps states.

## EXL3

@vcruz305 wrote the shared EXL3 module in [#42](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/42): the format reader, the
row-invariant linear, grouped experts and the 27B and Flash Next packs
([cuda/exl3](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3),
[exl3.md](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/docs/recipes/exl3.md)). The native EXL3 decoder
(`zig/src/core/exl3_format.zig`, `exl3_projection.zig`) follows the format notes from #42, and the EXLR8 codebook
that serves GLM-5.3 builds on that decoder. The native engine does not serve EXL3 packs yet.

## Fluid Subgraph Residency

TensorFold's exact residency implementation follows published techniques: EdgeMoE's storage-backed weights and memory index, MoE-Infinity and Fiddler's expert locality/popularity caching and prefetch, and Fate's cross-layer gate prefetch. These are re-implementations of proven techniques, with no novelty claim. The frozen TensorFold Python engine provides the implementation ancestry for native expert slots and PLE row streaming. Slotstream is an outside comparison for published SSD streaming memory/speed trade-offs, not the design or code source. See [the exact residency design](design/fluid-subgraph-residency.md) for scope and qualification.
# Per-process CUDA memory receipts

`cuda.usage(reset_peak)` counts live `DeviceBuffer` and `HostBuffer` bytes and their respective high-water marks (`peak`, `host_peak`). Both peaks reset atomically to their live counts when requested. A freed transient still contributes to its interval peak. `cuda.memory.takeUsage()` returns the completed interval and resets both peaks under the same lock, so a diagnostic can retain the peak that a reset would otherwise discard. Counts track requested live buffer lengths; borrowed carveouts are excluded. Arena backing reservations and slack are not measured by these logical buffer counts. They exclude CUDA context, NCCL, driver, library and other allocations outside these wrappers. They are neither global GPU usage nor total physical footprint.

`cuda.memory_receipt.emit(rank, phase, reset)` emits a `TF_MEMORY` JSON line only with `TF_CUDA_MEMORY_RECEIPTS=1`. A family can call it at load_begin (reset=true), load_end, cleanup_begin and cleanup_end. Use `takeUsage()` and `emitUsage(rank, .reset, true, completed_interval)` when another API resets peaks; that reset receipt retains the completed interval, while a load_begin receipt describes the newly reset baseline. Receipts name rank, PID, local monotonic time, reset flag and accounting scope. Calls take no CUDA measurements and perform no device synchronization. The caller must establish the load/cleanup boundary. A failed clock is null and cannot qualify an interval. Without family calls, allocator receipts remain unmeasured.

For each rank and context, run a fresh process under the machine owner's existing lock/admission adapter. The following is an input recipe for a future authorized window, not an instruction to access or stop a shared host:

```sh
OWNER_ADAPTER --exec python3 tools/memory_receipts.py \
  --rank 1 --context-tokens 2048 --output rank1-context2048 -- NATIVE_COMMAND ARGS
```

The context value is an operator label, not proof of native context configuration; retain actual launch settings and request token arrays. Use rank 0 and rank 1 independently on their respective hosts with identical context, checkpoint and runtime settings. The adapter must hold the existing owner lock for the wrapper and child's entire lifetime. The wrapper has no admission, remote access or service control. It launches exactly the supplied command; that command must exec the native rank directly, not leave a launcher parent. A mismatched native PID is unmeasured. Preserve existing signal/cleanup ownership when integrating a launcher; do not reuse a native-PID cleanup receipt for this wrapper PID.

The wrapper starts observation before the child runs, samples `/proc/PID/status` and optional `smaps_rollup`, waits for that owned child with `wait4`, and records exit status and boundaries. Linux `ru_maxrss` is an OS lifetime peak resident set, including peaks between samples; it cannot reset. Each fresh process therefore defines one context interval, including fork/exec and startup overhead, not only model allocations. Sampled RSS/PSS/Locked values retain their own timestamps and do not establish between-sample PSS/locked peaks. Permission failure or unsupported readings remain absent/unmeasured, never zero.

A complete native lifecycle has one initial reset and all four ordered load/cleanup phases. Later resets remain visible as separate intervals; never compare an interval peak to a lifetime peak without naming the boundary. A failed child or missing cleanup is unmeasured. After cleanup, nonzero tracked bytes are reported as residual bytes, not silently declared a leak or zeroed. Borrowed resources or process-global owners need separate explanation.

Linux total unified-memory physical-footprint peaks are explicitly **unsupported** here. RSS/PSS plus owned CUDA buffers cannot safely be added: pages may overlap and driver allocations may be absent. The required full physical-footprint qualification remains held until a platform-qualified method with the same rank/load/context/cleanup boundaries is supplied. No host fixture, zero counter, successful tool invocation or JSON manifest qualifies GB10/model memory.

Run host checks with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m unittest discover -s tools -p test_memory_receipts.py -v` and `zig build test-cuda-host`, plus the repository's full project checks. Tests exercise pinned transient/reset accounting, concurrent reset exclusion, both-rank receipt parsing, missing/invalid evidence and real CPU child RSS/exit collection. They do not allocate CUDA memory or qualify a GPU.
# Fluid Subgraph Residency

Fluid Subgraph Residency (FSR) is TensorFold's implementation of proven techniques for running a mixture-of-experts model larger than memory. It keeps the workload's live expert subgraph in a bounded resident cache and treats the unchanged checkpoint as cold storage. Its goal is resident-class exact serial decode when routing locality permits it. This is a goal to qualify per workload and memory budget, not a speed guarantee.

This design covers Tier-E, the exact path, on Flash Next with Metal. The reference is the same native engine, checkpoint, backend, precision, request and settings with resident weights. Moving expert bytes changes their addresses, never their values, arithmetic, routing or traversal. Peer RAM and other families or backends are separate extensions.

## Physical limits

Storage bandwidth and memory bandwidth are different resources. A cached file read measures memory reuse, not SSD throughput. Qualification must bypass the operating system's page cache and report the effective read bandwidth on the tested hardware. Historical measurements are not constants for another device.

Let B be cold expert bytes read per generated token and S be measured sustained SSD bytes per second. With B greater than zero, storage alone bounds single-stream throughput by S / B tokens per second. Read latency, compute and contention can lower that bound. Prefetch can overlap time with compute but cannot remove mandatory bytes or exceed the sustained bandwidth limit.

The exact path improves this limit through reuse: admit checkpoint bytes once, retain useful experts and avoid reading them again. Faster storage raises S. Changing the checkpoint representation or skipping model computation is outside this design.

## Memory ownership

Resident memory includes non-routed weights, the expert pool, its persistent address map, file metadata, bounded read or forecast storage, PLE row staging when selected, execution scratch, all admitted streams, retained prompt state and the runtime reserve. Admission counts the complete path, including startup construction peaks. A pool budget cannot justify loading the full routed weights beside the pool.

One slot owns every component needed for an expert: gate, up and down code bytes and their stored scales and biases. File offsets, component lengths, shapes, recipes and ranges are validated before use. Prepared layouts may rearrange bytes only through the resident engine's existing exact transforms.

The expert-to-slot map persists across tokens. There is no compact selected-expert weight table rebuilt per token. Slots under GPU consumption or background read ownership cannot be overwritten. A slot becomes visible only after all its component reads succeed. Errors stop the request; stale or partly filled bytes never stand in for a missing expert.

## C0: locality profiler

The profiler consumes complete routing observations, including cache hits, for a declared workload. Each observation identifies its layer, execution window and actual expert union. Decode, prompt chunks, draft windows and concurrent streams must be distinguishable. A miss-only file-load trace is insufficient to measure the live union.

Report the expert union growth curve, its byte cost, the pool budget, observed cache misses and cold bytes. A union that fits the cache makes a warm resident working set possible for the observed workload. It does not establish future routing locality or resident-class speed. A union larger than the cache establishes capacity pressure; measured misses and cold bytes determine its storage cost. Do not infer a compulsory read of the entire union on every token.

An empty, truncated or incomplete trace must not receive a fits verdict. Report forecasts separately from actual routes. Cache-policy simulation is a planning tool, not an inference or performance receipt.

## C1: persistent expert addressing

Only the streaming path reads the expert-to-slot map. The resident path keeps its existing kernels, weight addresses and launch work. Streaming operators use the resident operators' quantization recipe, accumulation, reduction order and output rounding. Slot addressing substitutes an expert's physical location without changing the logical expert ID or its place in the route combination.

A multi-row window protects the union of all its real routes. Prompt work reuses each needed expert within a chunk. Drafts and concurrent streams retain the ordinary shared engine verification and scheduling contracts.

## C2: route-driven residency

The native implementation uses load-before-execute. The real router selects experts. Cache hits acquire a lease; misses reserve evictable slots and read the checkpoint with cache bypass enabled. The layer runs only when its complete required union is available. All available slot capacity is a cache, rather than a permanently split hot and cold partition.

Cold eviction is a CLOCK policy. A hit gives a slot a second chance. Current demand is protected before eviction begins, including hits that occur later in the same union. Slots are released for reuse only after their GPU consumers complete. A failed load leaves its map entry invalid and cannot publish a token or accepted state. Cancellation joins readers and drains consumers before resources are freed.

Pool capacity and temporary allocations are admitted before execution. A configuration that cannot fund its supported active window refuses by name. It must not silently shrink top-k, change context, disable drafts or use different model arithmetic to fit.

## C3: bounded next-layer prefetch

The next layer's own router can forecast routes from the available current hidden state. The actual later router remains authoritative. Background reads reserve only slots that are safe to reuse and yield capacity to demand. Correct forecasts turn later misses into hits. Incorrect forecasts waste reads and may displace cold entries, but cannot change routes, state or tokens.

CPU writers and GPU readers have explicit ownership boundaries. Forecast inputs cannot borrow mutable scratch after it has been reused. Prefetch failure cannot expose partial bytes. Shutdown and cancellation join outstanding reads before closing descriptors or releasing buffers. Compare prefetch enabled and disabled under identical cache budgets to establish whether overlap helps.

## PLE rows on SSD

The separate PLE option retains n-gram ID generation and the resident gather formula. It reads only requested checkpoint rows and their stored metadata into bounded staging, deduplicates repeated IDs and restores request order. It must avoid materializing or pinning the full table. Shard edges, range errors, short reads and cancellation follow the same ownership rules as experts. Report its extra read traffic and latency independently.

## Qualification

Host tests cover CLOCK eviction, whole-window unions, leases, full-budget use, correct and incorrect forecasts, failure before publication, short reads, malformed metadata, truncation and reader shutdown. PLE tests compare exact row bytes across duplicates and shard boundaries. Known file-format errors are detectable; arbitrary same-size content corruption needs an independent integrity reference and must not be claimed otherwise.

A synthetic MoE device gate executes resident and streamed versions of the same native operators with fewer slots than the complete multi-layer expert set. Every logit and token must match. Test cache hits, eviction, repeated experts, forecast misses, prompt cuts, draft/plain, concurrent/solo, resumed/fresh and cancellation/reset seams. Kernel contracts include byte-equality replacements, controls and actual launch bounds.

Real checkpoint qualification uses identical complete token arrays and request settings at 16, 22, 33 and 48 GiB expert-pool budgets. Compare the complete output lengths and token sequences, not a nonempty common prefix. Record cold and warm prefill, serial decode, draft acceptance, concurrent behavior, physical footprint, device allocations, SSD bytes and timings. Use uncached reads, fresh runs and repeated alternating resident/streamed measurements. A budget on a large-memory host does not establish behavior on a smaller-memory machine.

## Prior art

These mechanisms are published techniques. EdgeMoE describes weights on storage with a memory index. MoE-Infinity and Fiddler describe expert caching based on locality or popularity and prefetch. Fate describes cross-layer gate prefetch. TensorFold re-implements these techniques in its native engine and follows its existing exactness contracts. FSR is not a novelty claim.

Slotstream is an outside comparison for SSD expert streaming and published memory/speed trade-offs. It is not the design or code source for TensorFold's implementation. Its published results are not TensorFold qualification receipts.
# Drafter releases

A drafter release is a folder that a server can check against the target it loaded before it drafts a single token.
It says which target the drafter was trained against, how that target turns tokens into rows and rows into logits,
which of the target's rows the drafter reads, and the drafter's own shape. The format is version 1. It describes one
architecture, the block drafter, and is read by `zig/src/core/drafter_release.zig` and `drafter_layout.zig`.

A release holds three files:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `config.json` | the manifest below |
| `model.safetensors` | the drafter's weights, plus the target's embedding and head rows it uses |
| `draft_vocab.json` | the target token ids the drafter can propose, in the order of the head's rows |

The embedding and the head rows ship in the release, so the drafter never reads the target's weights in their stored
format. For Kolibri-1 in bf16 that is the full embedding (128,000 x 2,560, 655 MB) and a 60,614-row head slice (310 MB).

## config.json

Kolibri-1's block drafter in this format:

```json
{
 "format": "tensorfold-drafter",
 "version": 1,
 "architecture": "block-drafter",
 "target": {
  "repo": "Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1",
  "revision": "e52eb4627d11516b0c01de49210ab5a4e4061444",
  "layers": 50,
  "hidden": 2560,
  "vocab": 128000,
  "embed_scale": 1.0,
  "tied": false,
  "softcap": null,
  "head_bias": false
 },
 "taps": {"ids": [45, 48, 50], "stream": "residual", "normed": true, "dtype": "bf16", "row_bytes": 15360},
 "drafter": {
  "hidden": 2560, "heads": 20, "head_dim": 128, "ffn": 6144, "layers": 4, "block": 4, "window": 2048,
  "eps": 1e-06, "theta": 10000.0, "pred_rank": 256, "spine_rank": 256
 },
 "draft_vocab": {"file": "draft_vocab.json", "size": 60614},
 "weights": "model.safetensors",
 "serving": {"depth": 2, "body": "fp8", "head": "nvfp4"}
}
```

Every field is required. An unknown field, a missing one, or a newer `version` is refused, never read in part.

### taps

The rows the drafter reads. They are what the target's `features` gives (`lanes.Features`) and what `--record`
writes to a stream's `.st` file, so a recording and a release can be compared field for field.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ids` | tap k is the stream after k of the target's layers, rising. k = `layers` is past the last layer. |
| `stream` | which residual stream; `residual` for a family with one. A family with several streams adds its merge here. |
| `normed` | true: the row as the next norm reads it (layer k's input norm, or the final norm at k = `layers`) |
| `dtype` | `bf16`, `f16` or `f32` |
| `row_bytes` | the taps in `ids` order, each `target.hidden` wide: `len(ids) x hidden x size(dtype)` |

A recording's `.json` carries `taps`, `row_bytes` and `dtype`. `checkRecording` refuses one whose values differ from
the release's. The `.json` does not say `stream` or `normed`: the family defines both once for its tap ids, and the
release states them.

### target

How the target turns tokens into rows and rows into logits. A drafter that uses the target's embedding and head
does the same, so these values change what it must predict.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `repo`, `revision` | the checkpoint the drafter was trained against |
| `layers`, `hidden`, `vocab` | the target's layer count, row width and vocabulary |
| `embed_scale` | rows = embed[token] x `embed_scale` (1.0 when the target does not scale) |
| `tied` | the head is the embedding. The release then ships no `target.head`. |
| `softcap` | logits = softcap x tanh(logits / softcap); `null` when the target has none |
| `head_bias` | the head adds a bias. The release ships it as `target.head_bias`, one value per draft id. |

`check` compares `layers`, `hidden`, `vocab`, `embed_scale`, `tied`, `softcap` and `head_bias` with the values the
loaded target reports, and refuses the release on the first one that differs, naming it.

### drafter and serving

The block drafter's shape. Row 0 of a block is a chain head on the anchor's own row; rows 1 to `block - 1` are drafted
in the same pass. `pred_rank` and `spine_rank` are 0 when the predecessor head or the spine is absent. `hidden` must
equal `target.hidden`, because the target's head reads the drafter's rows. `serving` holds defaults a server may
override: `depth` (1 to `block`), and the formats the body and the head slice are converted to at load (`bf16`, `fp8`
or `nvfp4`).

## model.safetensors

Every tensor is bf16, f16 or f32. D is `drafter.hidden`, T is `target.hidden`, A is `heads x head_dim`, V is
`draft_vocab.size`. A tensor missing, misshaped, or not in this table is refused.

| Tensor | Shape | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `target.embed` | [target.vocab, T] | always |
| `target.head` | [V, T] | `tied` is false |
| `target.head_bias` | [V] | `head_bias` is true |
| `fuse.weight` | [D, len(taps) x T] | always |
| `fc.weight` | [D, T + D] | always: cat(embedding of the token after the row, fused row) |
| `mask` | [D] | always |
| `layers.i.{q,k,v,ck,cv}.weight` | [A, D] | each layer |
| `layers.i.o.weight` | [D, A] | each layer |
| `layers.i.{gate,up}.weight` | [ffn, D] | each layer |
| `layers.i.down.weight` | [D, ffn] | each layer |
| `layers.i.{n1,n2,nc}.w` | [D] | each layer |
| `out_norm.w` | [D] | always |
| `pred_h.weight`, `pred_e.weight`, `pred_out.weight` | [R, D], [R, T], [D, R] | `pred_rank` R > 0 |
| `spine_n.i.w`, `spine_a.i.weight`, `spine_u.i.weight` | [D], [S, D], [D, S] | `spine_rank` S > 0, i < layers - 1 |

## draft_vocab.json

A JSON array of `draft_vocab.size` distinct ids below `target.vocab`, in any order. Row r of `target.head` is the
target's head row for the id at position r of this array, `target.head[r] = lm_head[draft_vocab[r]]`, so for
`[3, 1, 4, 15, 9]` row 0 is the head row of id 3. `target.head_bias[r]` is the bias of `draft_vocab[r]` in the same
way. With a tied head the drafter's row r is `target.embed[draft_vocab[r]]`. The reader checks the slice's shape, not
which rows it holds, so an exporter that writes them in id order makes a release that opens and drafts wrong tokens.

## Two targets

| | Kolibri-1 | Nemotron 3.5 Lightning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| checkpoint | `Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1` @ `e52eb462` | `TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit` @ `d9d758fb` |
| layers, hidden, vocab | 50, 2,560, 128,000 | 52, 2,688, 131,072 |
| taps | 45, 48, 50; normed; bf16; 15,360 bytes a row | 52 (the final norm's rows); normed; bf16; 5,376 bytes a row |
| `embed_scale` | 1.0: the embedding is gathered as stored | 1.0: the embedding is gathered as stored |
| `tied` | false: `tie_word_embeddings: false`, its own `lm_head.weight` | false: `tie_word_embeddings: false`, its own `lm_head.weight` |
| `softcap` | null: the config names none, the head is one matmul | null: the config names none, the head is one matmul |
| `head_bias` | false: no `lm_head.bias` | false: no `lm_head.bias` (`lm_head.biases` is the 4-bit format's offsets) |

The values come from each checkpoint's `config.json` and tensor index, and from the forward passes that read them.
Nemotron's tap is the one `--record` writes on CUDA, the rows its head and MTP head read. Kolibri's ids count layers
the same way: its drafter reads the outputs of layers 44, 47 and 49 (counted from 0), each normed by the norm after it.

Our Kolibri drafter checkpoint (`josch15366/Kolibri-1-block-drafter`, research only, never shipped) predates this
format. Its `config.json` counts taps from 0 (44, 47, 49), has no adapter, and its weights hold an unused `inp.weight`
and neither target tensor. Re-exported with the embedding and its 60,614 head rows, and without `inp.weight`, its 66
tensors pass the layout check above.

## Not in version 1

- Weights stored as FP8 or NVFP4. The release stores floats; `serving` converts them at load.
- A tap that merges several residual streams. `stream` has one value until a family needs another.
- Drafter architectures other than the block drafter.
# Attested HTTP voices

`tensorfold-native serve MODEL --voices DIR --default-voice NAME` loads the catalog at startup. Without these flags the built-in voice and speech request lowering are unchanged. `--default-voice` defaults to `default`; a configured name must exist. A missing, malformed or unattested catalog file refuses startup rather than silently substituting a voice. Restart to reload files.

`POST /v1/audio/speech` selects a catalog entry with `voice` (or the existing `speaker` alias). An absent, empty or case-insensitive `default` selects the configured default. Other names match exactly. Request-supplied reference arrays and paths remain unsupported. `GET /v1/voices` returns `{"voices": ["default", ...], "details": [{"id": NAME, "description": TEXT}, ...]}` with catalog names sorted, without transcripts, codes or attestation notes; `description` is the file's optional one-line description (at most 200 bytes), else empty. Non-speech models return the existing unknown-route response.

Each regular `NAME.json` file contains:

```json
{
  "format": "drama3-http-voice/1",
  "source": {"kind": "synthetic", "note": "Generated integer codes for a parser example, not recorded speech."},
  "description": "Warm, even narrator.",
  "references": [{"text": "A small cloud passes.", "codes": [[7,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]]}]
}
```

The example codes are synthetic, not an acoustic-quality fixture. Names contain ASCII letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, begin with a letter or digit, and cannot be `default` in any case. Names are bounded by the loader. Symlink catalog entries are refused.

The mandatory `source.kind` is `synthetic` (generated audio), `self` (the operator's own voice), or `consented` (explicit permission from the speaker). `source.note` must be nonempty UTF-8 describing the provenance or consent. This is an operator attestation, not proof of identity or consent. Notes are not returned by the API.

The model's licence, the [Fish Audio Community License Agreement](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3/blob/main/LICENSE) v1.0, section IV(b)(i), forbids using it to "generate speech that imitates the voice of an identifiable natural person without that person's prior consent (or, for a minor, the consent of a parent or legal guardian, and for a deceased person, the consent of the holder of the relevant rights) or another legal right to do so". The attestation records the operator's claim; it does not grant that consent or right.

Reference `text` is the exact transcript. Codes are frame-major signed integers, with the semantic code first and residual codebooks following, in the same order as upstream `drama3-generate --encode` emits. Do not substitute codes from an unrelated codec.

The loader enforces the family's reference count, transcript length, frame count and codebook ranges before serving. It also rejects empty references, structural prompt tokens, malformed speaker tags, oversized files and oversized catalogs. The assembled prompt must still fit the engine's advertised prompt budget. Reference rows go through the same family `prompt.build` used by the generation CLI; only the tokenizer interface is adapted.

## Dialogue speakers

Speech input and reference transcripts accept `<|speaker:N|>` with decimal IDs from `0` through `15`. Tags can change speakers within one request. Untagged text defaults to speaker 0; a leading tag after Unicode whitespace is preserved. Leading zeros, negative IDs, non-ASCII digits, incomplete tags and IDs above 15 are rejected.

For example, send this body to `POST /v1/audio/speech` with your served model name:

```json
{
  "model": "MODEL",
  "input": "<|speaker:0|> Is the gate open? <|speaker:15|> Yes, come through. <|speaker:0|> Thank you.",
  "response_format": "wav"
}
```

For streamed audio, set `"stream": true` and `"response_format": "pcm"`. To condition speakers on reference audio, create a catalog entry whose reference transcripts have matching tags, such as `<|speaker:0|> First reference transcript.` and `<|speaker:15|> Second reference transcript.`, then select its name with `"voice": "conversation"`. The HTTP `speaker` field remains an alias for that catalog name; dialogue speaker IDs belong in the text tags.

One catalog entry still accepts at most **four reference passages**, even though there are sixteen valid speaker IDs. Each passage keeps its own transcript and code rows. Reusing a catalog entry preserves its exact reference prefix; changing a reference speaker tag changes that prefix. Speaker tags specify the prompt's roles; this does not guarantee distinguishable voices without suitable references or establish voice similarity.

The public [Drama 3 MLX prompt implementation](https://github.com/Sogni-AI/drama3-mlx/blob/ecc235039ccd5f982f66a6982184f57432354ab4/drama3_mlx/prompt.py) provides a behavior reference for these speaker markers. TensorFold uses its existing native prompt builder.

## Writing a voice file

`zig build drama3-voice` builds the writer next to `drama3-generate`, which it runs once per reference to encode the audio:

```sh
drama3-voice --codec MODEL/codec.pth --ref-audio tone.wav --ref-text "A small cloud passes." \
  --source-kind synthetic --source-note "A generated test tone." --out voices/tone.json
```

Repeat `--ref-audio` and `--ref-text` in pairs for up to four references. `--generate PATH` names the encoder when `drama3-generate` is not on `PATH`. The writer refuses, before encoding, a missing or invalid attestation, transcripts the speech request would reject, and an output name the catalog cannot load. The encoder writes into a fresh private directory beside the output. The writer replaces `NAME.json` by an atomic rename only after the catalog's own parser accepts the new file.

The operator's encoder binary and processes with the same UID are trusted. The safety boundary covers other users (including shared sticky directories), stale files or symlinks, encoder failures and concurrent tool runs; it does not cover a malicious encoder or same-UID processes renaming the operator's directories during a run. The output parent must not allow other users to rename the operator's entries; a shared sticky directory is suitable.

Each run exclusively creates a randomly named private directory with owner-only access beside the output, retrying name collisions. The encoder receives an ordinary path with a fresh output name for each reference; writing nothing is an error. Directory-relative reads reject code-file symlinks. The validated final file is staged in that directory and renamed over `NAME.json`, replacing a destination symlink rather than following it. No pre-existing file is touched before publication.

Cleanup restores owner access on the private directory and removes its contents and the directory. Before publication, cleanup failures are reported alongside the primary error. After publication, a cleanup failure is a warning on stderr naming the leftover directory, and the command succeeds because the output is correct. Abrupt termination such as SIGKILL can also leave a private directory behind.

Cleanup responsibility starts immediately after directory creation, before allocating its encoder pathname, so allocation failure also removes the private directory.
# Drama 3 CUDA prompt chunks

The CUDA prompt prefill can run in bounded row chunks instead of one row at a time. It is off by default: the stock path prefills one row a chunk, and its output is byte-identical to the path that shipped before this feature. Batching is opt-in, through two settings.

- The serving host reads `TF_DRAMA_PREFILL_ROWS`, which accepts integers from 1 through 1024 and defaults to 1 (the single-row path). `TF_DRAMA_PREFILL_ROWS=N` prefills N rows a chunk.
- The generation tool takes `--max-rows N`, which selects both the engine's row capacity and the rows a chunk, and defaults to 1. `--max-rows N` prefills N rows a chunk.

On a GB10 with the Drama 3 checkpoint, 128-row chunks brought the first audio from 18.2 s to 0.76 s and the whole utterance from 47.5 s to 30.2 s. That is the gain the opt-in buys; the default pays none of it and keeps the stock bytes.

Metal's native host is untouched: it prefills one row a chunk, and its engine's capacity is unchanged. The shared options keep Metal's own values; only the CUDA path asks for a row count of its own.

## The plan

Each prompt starts at offset zero and takes full chunks followed by its remaining rows. Chunk boundaries do not depend on the number of active lanes, request timing or queue order. The last backbone row is retained for decode; the tower consumes only prompt rows with a successor. A shared round still returns to the scheduler after its chunk. Cancellation granularity is therefore a chunk, not a row.

An empty or oversized capacity is refused before any checkpoint or GPU allocation: more than 8192 rows a chunk is `BadPrefillRows`, and an attention query chunk outside 1 through 1024 is `BadAttentionChunk`. The serving host refuses `TF_DRAMA_PREFILL_ROWS` outside 1 through 1024 by name.

## Reference cache

A request in a catalog voice starts with the same reference rows as every other request in that voice. The CUDA host keeps the state after them so a later request prefills only from there, as Metal does. The cache is opt-in: `TF_DRAMA_REFERENCE_CACHE` sets how many voices it keeps, 0 through 16, and the default 0 keeps none. The least recently used entry is dropped first, and all lanes share the entries.

The saved row is Metal's boundary: the last whole chunk of `TF_DRAMA_PREFILL_ROWS` rows that ends before the last reference row. A request that resumes there therefore makes the same chunk cuts an uncached request makes, and each saved tower row's lookahead label is still a reference row. An entry is keyed by its saved rows and that lookahead row, every token and code compared, and holds both recurrent state blocks and the backbone's attention and tower's K and V rows up to the boundary. Restoring it after the prompt's reset leaves the bytes the skipped chunks would have written, so a cached request's audio should equal an uncached one's; that is checked on host against a fake lane, and the copied K and V rows against the kernel's position-major layout, not yet on a GPU. The default voice, and a reference shorter than one chunk, are not cached.

Each entry takes 64389120 + 47104 × saved rows device bytes: the recurrent state (61.4 MiB), plus 46 KiB a saved row for the 10 backbone attention layers' and 13 tower layers' K and V rows. Saved rows stay below the context, so at `--context 8192` an entry is at most 429 MiB, and 16 entries at most 6.7 GiB; a 512-row reference takes 84 MiB an entry. Admission does not reserve entries: they are allocated when made, inside the engine's device cap, from the room the lanes leave. A failed allocation or copy keeps no entry and the request continues uncached; a failed restore drops the entry and the request prefills whole.

## Memory and synchronization

The bounds below are per lane, at context 8192. CUDA's row-dependent buffers in `Engine.allocState` contribute 290832 bytes per row, excluding routing-plan storage. With 128 attention query rows, score storage is 67174400 bytes, and row buffers plus scores total 104400896 bytes per lane. At capacity 1024 the same subtotal is 835207168 bytes. These are allocation formulas, not device measurements; weights, KV, recurrent state, routing plans, codec storage, alignment and library workspaces are additional.

`setPos` still synchronizes its asynchronous upload before its stack-backed scalar expires. It is called for each prompt chunk, not each row within that chunk. Attention may also change position between its bounded query subchunks. The host's completion wait remains at the round boundary. No asynchronous upload lifetime or completion guarantee is removed.

## Arithmetic contract

Chunk size is an arithmetic setting, not a promise of identical hidden bits across sizes. This matters only where a caller opts in: the default's one-row chunks are the stock path.

- Dense projections in `cuda/kernels.zig:linear` use `d3_gemv` for one row and cuBLAS for multiple rows. The former accumulates `dot8` groups per lane and performs a warp reduction; cuBLAS chooses a tiled reduction over the same input dimension. Both consume BF16 inputs and produce BF16 outputs with FP32 accumulation, but their grouping and rounding can differ. This affects backbone attention QKV/output, GDN input/output, router/shared-expert projections, and tower embedding/hidden mixing, QKV/output and feed-forward projections. The sampled-token head remains a one-row GEMV.
- Full attention in `cuda/forward.zig:attention` uses split-key online softmax for one row. Its QK dot products, running softmax denominator and weighted-value sums are merged across warps and key splits. Multiple rows use BF16 QK GEMM into FP32 scores, a block-reduced causal softmax, and FP32 PV GEMM. These regroup the QK, exponential-denominator and weighted-value sums. The retained causal keys are unchanged, but GEMM dimensions and reductions can change with query chunk size and the final partial chunk. Both paths round the attention result and sigmoid gate to BF16 before their product. `cuda/blas.zig` requests FP32 compute, not TF32.
- Routed FP8 experts switch from decode tiles to prompt tiles above two rows. `drama3_fp8.cu` preserves the per-output MMA order inside each input scale group and the ordered FP32 `fmaf` accumulation of scaled groups. The tile changes routing and staging, not that output's sum. Per-row quantization and router reductions remain unchanged for identical inputs.
- The causal convolution and GDN recurrence retain their sequential row order and FP32 state arithmetic. Their inputs can nevertheless differ after a changed dense projection. Row-local normalization, rotary preparation and embedding operations do not introduce a cross-row sum.

Consequently, code selection near a logit tie can differ across capacities. Do not use exact cross-capacity frames or PCM as the fidelity gate. Keep the chosen capacity fixed for a request and record it in receipts. No GPU kernel implementation is changed by this patch.

## Qualification

`--check` reads upstream PyTorch oracle `vectors.safetensors`, including prompt layers, tower layers, decoded hidden states and teacher-forced picks. Prompt probes honor `--max-rows` and use each chunk's actual reference-row offset instead of the reference tail. The existing cosine and greedy-reference checks remain in force. The extra `PREFILL` records carry worst-row cosine and maximum absolute error for each tensor chunk.

Given an existing checkpoint and oracle dump, run both modes against exactly the same vectors:

```sh
"$BIN" --model "$CKPT" --check "$VECTORS" --max-rows 1 2>"$OUT/check-1.log"
"$BIN" --model "$CKPT" --check "$VECTORS" --max-rows 128 2>"$OUT/check-128.log"
python3 tools/zig/drama_prefill_compare.py "$OUT/check-1.log" "$OUT/check-128.log"
```

The comparator requires complete, contiguous coverage of every backbone and tower prompt tensor, both upstream checks passing, no lower worst-row cosine, and no larger maximum absolute error for any tensor. It reports both measurements, without inventing a tolerance for cross-capacity differences. The full oracle-only tower probe still requires scratch for the vector's entire prompt; oracle vectors exceeding the checked allocation capacity are refused.

Run `--replay 1` at each selected capacity to retain the existing exact eager/graph, poison/reset, codec chunking and interleaved-lane checks. Repeat a fixed-seed request with the same capacity and require identical frame and PCM bytes. Compare capacities 64, 128 and the default explicitly; record whether their outputs differ. The default and explicit 1 must have the same partition.

For free-running audio, compare stop reason and length, then word error rate and speaker similarity on the same text and reference. Keep checkpoint and evaluation-model revisions, text normalization and thresholds fixed before the run. Report cross-capacity frame/PCM equality as information, not a rejection criterion. Performance qualification includes first-audio latency, decode rate, peak physical memory and device allocation high-water marks. A host-only test pass does not establish these GPU outcomes.

Host coverage:

```sh
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= zig build test test-kernel-contract test-golden test-cuda-host check-drama-cuda-host
zig build test-drama-prefill-host
python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/zig -p test_drama_prefill_compare.py
```

`test-drama-prefill-host` checks the plan itself: that the serving host's default and the generation tool's default both take the stock single-row plan, and that an opt-in capacity plans N-row chunks with a partial tail.
# Native environment validation

Malformed numeric settings are refused at startup with the variable, supplied value and accepted forms.
The same parser is used by direct CUDA entry points. An unset variable keeps its existing default.
A valid value keeps its existing meaning, including documented caps and clamping.
Diagnostics quote and escape the supplied text so it cannot create another terminal line.

| Variable | Accepted explicit value |
| --- | --- |
| `TENSORFOLD_VIDEO_TOKENS` | Nonnegative whole video-token budget; default 16384; stored as an unsigned 64-bit count |
| `TENSORFOLD_MAX_PDF_PAGES` | Whole count 1 through 4294967295, capped by `--vision-max-images`; default min(16, image limit) |
| `TENSORFOLD_PRESSURE_CACHE_PERCENT` | Whole percentage 0 through 100; default 50 |
| `TENSORFOLD_PREFIX_WAIT_MS` | Whole milliseconds 0 through 4294967295; zero disables waiting; default 60000 |
| `TENSORFOLD_RESTORE_PREFETCH` | Whole unsigned 64-bit count, capped at 65536; zero disables reading ahead; default 2 |
| `TENSORFOLD_RESTORE_PREFETCH_GIB` | Whole unsigned 64-bit GiB count, capped at 16777216; default 16 |
| `TENSORFOLD_RESTORE_PREFETCH_MS` | Whole unsigned 64-bit milliseconds, capped at 1099511627776; default 30000 |
| `TF_CUDA_DEVICE` | Whole ordinal 0 through 4294967295, or empty; default 0 |
| `TF_CUDA_SEGMENTS` | Whole count 1 through 4, or empty; default 1 |
| `TF_CUDA_CARVEOUT` | Exactly `0` or `1`; default off |
| `TF_CUDA_CARVEOUT_MIB` | Positive whole MiB count whose byte size fits the platform, or empty for 1792 MiB |
| `TF_Q27_COPY_ROWS` | Whole u32 count; zero disables copied rows; default 48 |
| `TF_Q27_DRAFT_SLOTS` | Whole u32 count, clamped to 1 through the lane stream limit; default 8. DFlash2 can draft for at most the smaller of this count and the admitted streams, and none without a drafter. |
| `TF_MTP_DRAFTS` | Whole u32 count, clamped to 1 through the drafter's window less one; existing depth when unset |
| `TF_DRAFT_NODES` | Whole native-size nonnegative count, capped by the drafter's window; zero disables trees |
| `TF_QMMF_HALF_BELOW` | Whole native-size nonnegative block count; zero disables half tiles; default 96 |
| `TENSORFOLD_PROMPT_CACHE_KEEP_OTHERS` | Exactly `0` or `1`, checked when the CUDA backend starts; default off ([profiles](profiles.md)) |
| `TF_HEAD_GEOMETRY` | Whole native-size nonnegative geometry count in the head benchmark |
| `TF_ROCE_GID_INDEX` | Whole index 0 through 2147483647; unset searches for a RoCE v2 IPv4 GID |
| `TF_PROMPT_ROWS` | Native serving: a multiple of 16 from 128 through 2048; unset keeps the chip/family default |
| `TF_ANE_COLUMNS` | Whole u32 count; zero disables the experimental share; default zero |
| `XPU_A8_BITS` | Exactly `4` or `8`, for the XPU quantization study; unset keeps the study's existing setting |
| `LFM3_FUSE` | Whole u32 fusion mask; default 7 |
| `TF_SLIDE_POCKET_KEY` | Exactly `auto`, `reply`, `subject` or `both`; default `auto` |
| `TF_SLIDE_FIT_GIB` | Whole native-size nonnegative GiB count; default 4 |
| `TF_SLIDE_FORGET_FAIL` | Whole u32 fact index, zero off; only checked in a slide-test-hooks build |

The video-token reader has no fixed model-independent token ceiling. Its unsigned storage width is not a useful token budget.
The request geometry and model context decide whether a parsed budget fits; zero remains accepted as before.

u32 means 0 through 4294967295. Native-size counts use the platform's unsigned integer size.
Existing numeric spellings accepted by each reader, such as leading zeroes, remain valid.
Pressure, prefix-wait and restore-prefetch values retain trimming of spaces and tabs.
Prefix-wait and restore-prefetch still require the first remaining character to be a digit.
CUDA device/segments and the slide test hook retain their space trimming.
Other numeric readers do not gain whitespace aliases. Empty or whitespace-only text means unset for every variable, as it did before.

An explicit `--device` or `--segments` wins over its environment value, even if the ignored value is malformed.
`--carveout` likewise enables the carveout regardless of its enable variable.
The carveout size is checked only when the carveout is enabled, and still rounds to framebuffer rows.
`TF_NO_TREES` retains precedence over `TF_DRAFT_NODES`.
Backend-specific settings are checked when that backend starts; slide settings require learning to be enabled.
Common server settings are checked before checkpoint resolution, including when no request would use them yet.
Direct family readers also refuse malformed values when called without the server.

## Existing lenient switches

These settings retain their existing boolean policies rather than gaining new aliases or refusals:

- `TF_GRAPH_CACHE`: exact `0` or case-insensitive `off` disables graphs; every other value leaves the family's settings unchanged.
- `TF_QWEN27_SLOT_RESUME`: exact `0` disables resume; every other value keeps it enabled.
- Kolibri pages: exact `TENSORFOLD_KOLIBRI_KV_PAGES=0` disables requested pages; other text keeps the option unchanged.
- Dory pages: unset or exact `TENSORFOLD_DORY_KV_PAGES=0` uses windows; every other present value selects pages.
- `TF_SLIDE_EDIT`, `TF_SLIDE_PROBE` and `TF_SLIDE_ROUTED` select modes by presence, even empty or `0`; probe wins over edit.
- `TF_COOP_SPLIT` retains its first-character `0` disabling rule, `TF_NEMOTRON_TRACE` its first-character `1` trace rule,
  and `TF_SLIDE_FIT_REDUCE` its exact `tree` reduction selection. These developer switches keep their existing semantics.
- The existing tool-grammar, rows-sync, log-time, memory-pressure and XPU-MTP boolean policies are unchanged.

The profile registry reports selected arithmetic/experimental overrides; it does not change their parsing or defaults.
See [profiles](profiles.md) for classes, scopes and grouped slide-learning names.
`capabilities --json` no longer advertises `TENSORFOLD_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` or `HF_HUB_OFFLINE`: the native binary reads neither.
The command-line `--no-update-check` remains an accepted no-op.
# Evaluating TensorFold

This page is for anyone reviewing, testing or benchmarking TensorFold from outside the project.
It covers what to pin, how to check a download, the tests that run without a GPU and the requests worth replaying.

## Pin what you test

Record four things with every result:

- The release, from `tensorfold --version` (on Linux, `tensorfold-native --version`).
- The checkpoint and its revision, as `REPO@revision` in `tensorfold pull`.
- The backend: Metal on a Mac, CUDA on Linux or Windows.
- The recipe you followed from [Pick a model](../README.md#pick-a-model), with its flags.

Releases from 1.0.0 on are the native Zig engine. The Python engine stopped at 0.6.6 and lives only at the `v0.6.6`
tag; its tests need MLX and its results do not describe a 1.x release. `pip install .` at the root stops and says where
to get the native binary.

## Install and check the download

On a Mac, `brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold` checks the archive against the checksum in the formula.

On Linux, the [Quick start](../README.md#linux-with-an-nvidia-gpu) downloads the archive and checks its `.sha256`.
The `.sha256` file is itself signed with the release key. To check that signature too (OpenSSL 3.0 or later):

```sh
A="tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/$A.sha256.sig"
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ashhart/TensorFold/main/packaging/runtime-trust.json \
  | python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["ed25519PublicKey"])' > tensorfold-release.pem
{ printf 'tensorfold-native-checksum-v1\n'; cat "$A.sha256"; } > signed-checksum
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey tensorfold-release.pem -rawin -in signed-checksum -sigfile "$A.sha256.sig"
```

OpenSSL prints `Signature Verified Successfully`. After unpacking, `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` inside the archive's
directory checks every file in it.

## Smoke checks without a model

These need no GPU, driver or checkpoint:

- `tensorfold --version` prints the release.
- `tensorfold capabilities --json` lists the backends, model families, formats, serve flags and
  `optional_libraries`, each with a `found` flag.
- `tensorfold info REPO` prints a pulled checkpoint's family, format, context, weights size and memory floor.

## Container

The root [Dockerfile](../Dockerfile) installs a Linux release archive in an Ubuntu 24.04 image. The build stops unless
the archive's checksum, the release signature over it and every unpacked file's checksum all match.
It runs as the image's `ubuntu` user and keeps the Hugging Face cache in `/huggingface`, the directory to mount.

```sh
docker build -t tensorfold .
docker run --rm tensorfold
docker run --rm tensorfold capabilities --json
```

`--build-arg TENSORFOLD_VERSION=1.2.4` picks the release; Docker picks the `linux-x86_64` or `linux-aarch64`
archive from the build platform. To serve, the host needs NVIDIA driver R580 or newer and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit,
which supplies `libcuda.so.1` to the container. Listen on all addresses inside the container:

```sh
docker run --rm --gpus all -p 8080:8080 \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/huggingface:/huggingface" \
  tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --host 0.0.0.0 --name local-model --context 8192
```

Add `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` when your user ID is not 1000, so the server can write to the mounted cache.
The image holds only the release archive. Features that need cuBLASLt, NCCL or the image decoders (see
[optional shared libraries](../packaging/RUNTIME.md#optional-shared-libraries)) need an image that adds them.

## Tests that run without a GPU

- `python3 -m pytest` from the repository root needs only Python 3 and pytest. Tests that need a GPU, numpy or a
  built test binary skip and say why.
- `zig build test` builds and runs the host tests with the Zig version in `.zig-version`. On a Mac it also runs the
  Metal device checks it can.
- `zig build test-golden` checks frozen parity answers and the HTTP security cases.

[CI](../.github/workflows/no-gpu.yml) runs these on Linux and Windows for every pull request, with the root pytest on
Linux. GPU kernel and served-model checks run on the maintainers' Macs and NVIDIA machines before a change lands;
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) lists those gates.

## Check exactness yourself

Drafting must never change the output. At temperature 0, send the same request twice, once with `"draft": false`,
and compare the text and `usage`. A request repeated against the prompt cache must equal its first run, and
concurrent requests must each equal their solo run. [Exact decoding](../README.md#exact-decoding) states the rule
and what it fixes.

## Requests worth replaying

| Request | What to expect |
| --- | --- |
| A prompt longer than the context window | HTTP 400 with `code` `context_length_exceeded`; no GPU work is spent. |
| `tool_choice: "required"` or a named function | The reply calls a tool. Needs the archive's `lib/`; without it, HTTP 400. |
| `thinking_budget` or `reasoning_effort` | The reasoning stops within the budget; `reasoning_effort: none` turns thinking off. |
| `response_format` with a JSON schema | The reply matches the schema and equals its `"draft": false` reply. Needs `lib/` too. |

The [API reference](api.md) lists every field and refusal.

## Memory

`tensorfold info REPO` prints a checkpoint's memory floor: its weights plus the reserve the server keeps.
Context length, `--parallel`, prompt caches and drafters need memory beyond that floor. Once a model is loaded,
`GET /v1/memory` reports the memory in use: the process footprint on macOS and the backend's device counters
([memory diagnostics](memory-diagnostics.md)).
The machines each model was checked on are in [Pick a model](../README.md#pick-a-model); where no minimum was
measured, none is published.

## Dependencies

Serving installs no Python packages, so `pip-audit` has nothing to scan for the server.
`build.zig.zon` declares no Zig packages, so the Zig code builds from this repository alone; the kernels need
Xcode's Metal compiler or CUDA 13's `nvcc`. The Linux archive adds `libtfgrammar` (xgrammar v0.2.8).
Every bundled licence is in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
Some repository tools, such as checkpoint converters and reference generators, use numpy, PyTorch, MLX or
Transformers. None of them is needed to build, run the host tests or serve, and the root pytest skips the tests that
need them. The Mac app under `app/` has its own dependencies.

## Reporting

Use the issue templates for bugs and performance results, with the four pinned facts above.
Report security problems privately, as [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md) describes.
# Flash Next rotary probe allowances

This is a conditional numerical-contract change, not a kernel change or a passed device gate.
The normalizer, phases and final reference remain independently evaluated in FP64.
The allowance compares the device output with that reference after its FP32-to-BF16 rounding.
The original nonfinite, repeatability, guards, row-count invariance and resource checks remain required.

## Scalar accuracy required before qualification

Let u = 2^-24. The candidate requires relative rsqrt error at most 4u, relative exp2 error at most 8u,
and absolute sine/cosine error at most 8u at the actual FP32 argument.
These are explicit scalar accuracy requirements, not guarantees about Metal fast functions.
For finite normal results, two and four FP32 ulps are no larger than 4u and 8u relative, respectively;
for sine/cosine, four ulps over [-1, 1] are no larger than 8u absolute.
They are chosen independently of any observed output-to-bound ratio.
Device component traces must establish these caps before the candidate can qualify.
If they fail, do not increase them to fit the final output.

The prepared fixture values are multiples of 1/8 in [-1, 1]; their four-row means are multiples of 1/32.
The allowance rejects other input grids, weights outside [0.5, 2] in magnitude, nonnormal/nonpositive epsilon,
and positions outside [0, 1048576), instead of claiming an unchecked universal input bound.
The numerical probe's separate nonfinite gate retains its original exact class checks.

## Normalization and intermediate BF16 values

For this fixture grid, every square is an integer multiple of 1/1024, at most one.
At most 256 such terms total at most 262144 units, requiring only 19 significant bits.
All FP32 products and additions are therefore exact in any order.
This proof does not assume a particular SIMD reduction tree or weaken the accumulator declaration.
The registered generic reduction depth remains unchanged.

Let S be that exact sum and q = S/n + epsilon.
Division by n is a power-of-two scale, so only the epsilon addition contributes to the denominator radius:

    Eq = u |q| + guard(q).

Enclose 1/sqrt(q_device) by evaluating q +/- Eq, then apply the rsqrt accuracy cap.
Multiply each signed input and weight by both inverse endpoints.
Expand them for two FP32 products with gamma(2, u), then round both endpoints through FP32 and BF16.
Monotone rounding encloses midpoint crossings instead of charging their error to a cancelled final result.
This gives the already rounded reference pair a, b and absolute radii Ea, Eb.
Unrotated dimensions need only their own BF16 interval radius.

Both pooling probes use an exact four-row FP32 mean in these fixtures.
The checker verifies every addition and the power-of-two scale is exact before its BF16 store.
An inexact pooling fixture is refused and needs its own propagated mean interval, not an implicit larger tolerance.
The subsequent normalization interval is identical to the preparation probes'.

## FP32 phase construction

The plain reference frequency is f = 2^x with x = -(i/32) log2base.
The device exponent x32 is the FP32 rounding of that exact product; i/32 is exact.
Evaluate 2^x32 independently in FP64 and enclose the exp2 result with its required relative cap.
For YaRN, both sides read the same stored FP32 frequency, so this interval has zero frequency radius.
Supported integer positions are exactly representable in FP32.
Round the position-times-frequency interval endpoints to FP32 and compare them with the ideal angle t = p f.
Let h be the largest resulting absolute angle discrepancy.

Sine and cosine are globally 1-Lipschitz and bounded by one.
Taylor's remainder also gives a local enclosure:

    Dcos = min(2, h, |sin(t)| h + h^2/2)
    Dsin = min(2, h, |cos(t)| h + h^2/2).

Add the absolute trig accuracy cap, multiply by the stored YaRN scale and propagate that FP32 multiply.
This yields coefficient errors EC and ES for C = scale cos(t), S = scale sin(t).
Phase error is weighted by the unrotated inputs; it cannot disappear when a rotated term approaches zero.

## Rotation and the already rounded reference

For each relabelled pair, let r = a C +/- b S.
A pre-output error allowance is

    E = |C| Ea + |S| Eb
      + (|a| + Ea) EC + (|b| + Eb) ES
      + gamma(2,u) [(|a| + Ea)(|C| + EC) + (|b| + Eb)(|S| + ES)].

The depth-two term covers separate products and addition; contraction needs no larger allowance.
The final absolute comparison to w = BF16(FP32(r)) uses

    E + 2^-8 (|r| + E) + |r - w| + guard(r).

The reference's own rounding is explicit. A relative term based only on |w| would miss cancellation.
The implementation adds conservative FP64 evaluation guards and a smallest-normal FP32 floor for underflow/flush.
These guards are independent of measured errors.

The generic kernel bound is unchanged. Only these ten numerical probes provide an absolute-allowance callback;
the mask keeps its exact check. Both the shape and accumulation gates consume the same callback and reject invalid allowances.
CPU witnesses and real callback tests establish the stated arithmetic and wiring only.
All eleven probes, component caps, compiler/resource receipts, model equality and long-context fidelity must be rerun before release.
# GLM-5.3 (EXLR8) on two Macs

TensorFold serves the whole GLM-5.3 model from kindlingai's EXLR8 release on two Macs joined by Thunderbolt. Each Mac
holds half of every expert and every attention head, and rank 0 serves the OpenAI-compatible API while rank 1 runs each
request beside it. The release is
[kindlingai/glm-5.3-exlr8-k2-k3-k4](https://huggingface.co/kindlingai/glm-5.3-exlr8-k2-k3-k4), pinned at revision
`f459f5d0272a529403dd9b3fd32f771f4250a0d4`. We have run its `home` profile on two M5 Ultra Macs with 256 GB each.

## What you need

- Two Macs with 256 GB each. A served Mac holds about 160 GB: 157.2 GB of weights with the MTP layer, and 159.6 GB at
  `--context 8192 --parallel 4`. The server refuses to load past 66% of RAM.
- About 270 GB of free disk on each Mac. A Mac's share is 139.5 GiB of expert halves plus 11 GB of whole files, but the
  expert files keep their full size with only that Mac's halves written, and APFS gave those folders 256 and 264 GB.
- A Thunderbolt 5 cable between the Macs and MCDMA's fabric library, set up as in steps 3 and 4 of the
  [speed-up mode guide](speed-up-mode.md). The settings files are the same.

The weights come under the release's own terms: the GLM-5.3 license, and CC BY 4.0 for the EXLR8 format.

## Pull each Mac's share

`pull --exlr8 PROFILE --node R/2` fetches only what node R of two needs: every whole file, and its half of each
expert's intermediate channels. Run it on each Mac with its own node number:

```sh
tensorfold pull kindlingai/glm-5.3-exlr8-k2-k3-k4@f459f5d0272a529403dd9b3fd32f771f4250a0d4 \
  --exlr8 home --node 0/2 --dir ~/models/glm-5.3-exlr8-home
```

On the second Mac, pass `--node 1/2`. Every whole file must equal the hub's sha256, every expert file's published hash
must equal the hub's, and each expert half must equal its xxhash64 before it is written. A pull that stops resumes:
run the same command again, and it checks what is on disk and fetches only what is missing. Our two Macs took 43
minutes over a shared uplink, at about 55 MiB/s each.

## Serve

Start rank 1, then rank 0 within five minutes. Each Mac loads in three to four minutes.

```sh
tensorfold serve ~/models/glm-5.3-exlr8-home --speed-up rank1.json --context 8192 --parallel 4 --temperature 0
tensorfold serve ~/models/glm-5.3-exlr8-home --speed-up rank0.json --context 8192 --parallel 4 --temperature 0 \
  --name glm-5.3
```

Run each command on its own Mac, and send requests to rank 0. `--context` defaults to 16,384 tokens and takes up to
262,144, and `--parallel` sets the streams, 8 by default and 16 at most. Rank 0 keeps prompt states for later turns in
up to 8 GiB by default, inside the load limit; `--prompt-cache-gib` sets another size and 0 turns them off. The engine
decodes greedily, and it refuses `--learn` and `--slide`.

## Measured

On our two M5 Ultras over one cable, one stream decodes at 21 tokens a second with `"draft": false`, and at 31 to
32 with the MTP layer's drafts, of which 60 to 74% land. Prompts run at about 200 tokens a second, 205 at 837 tokens
and 184 at 3,251, and the first prompt after a load at about 120.

Drafted replies equal `"draft": false`, a resumed conversation equals a fresh one, and concurrent requests equal their
solo replies, idle and with 36 busy threads on each Mac.

## Known limits

- Decode is slow. A one-row round takes about 45 ms of GPU time. At one row, the attention output projection's 48
  trellis jobs fill 48 of the GPU's 80 cores, and the routed experts' short down-projection jobs run unsplit, so part of
  the GPU stays idle.
- No CUDA serving yet. The CUDA kernels decode EXLR8 weights bit for bit as the Metal ones do, but no CUDA engine serves
  GLM-5.3.
- Contexts past 2,048 tokens have not been checked against a whole-model reference. Past 2,048 tokens the sparse
  indexer picks which keys each query reads; the layer checks covered 2,304 tokens, and a 3,251-token prompt served,
  but nothing compared a whole reply at that length.
- Only the `home` profile, two nodes, and M5 Ultras have been run.
# GLM prompt K policy experiment

Fresh prompt batching credits @BobClawblaw's #1014. Its default remains one K slice at every prompt row count.
This separate experiment selects K slices from the weight's N and K dimensions, independent of the number of
prompts, their row count or their position in a batch. It uses the existing tiled kernels in windows of at most
64 rows and the existing ordered fp32 slice reduction. Verify and draft windows keep their previous policy.

Select `TF_GLM_PROMPT_K=shape` on every rank to try it. An absent value or `one` keeps the default.
The experiment requires `TF_GLM_MM=1`; the untiled combination is refused. The selected policy is included in rank
agreement, so different choices refuse before loading weights. Applying this patch does not enable the experiment.

No speed or device qualification is claimed. The different reduction grouping can change near-ties even though
precision is unchanged. Keep the current numerical and quality bars. The default must remain unchanged until
matched device evidence supports another decision.

## Device checks

Run the current kernel contract and measured-resource gate first. This experiment changes no kernel source, ABI,
thread count or shared-memory specialization. Keep the existing GLM launch records; pending resources still need
measurement on the device being qualified.

Run `tf-cuda-test glm-mm-fixed` on a GB10. It compares the default and experimental policies for bf16 weights and
4-, 6- and 8-bit weights, with fp32 and bf16 outputs. Every input row runs alone, then in batches at offsets 0, 1 and
7, across row buckets and partial tails through 129 rows. Input stride includes padding; output prefix and tail
bytes are guarded. Two matrix shapes exercise shape-selected K splits. Results are checked bitwise against each
row alone and an independent fp64 product on exact dyadic fixtures. Packed fixtures use independently assembled
codes and fp16 scales. These synthetic checks do not establish full-checkpoint numerical fidelity.

The shader-free `test-glm-mm-policy-host` checks actual dispatch with recording CUDA calls. The separate
`compile-glm-prompt-gate-host` code-generates the actual device gate with inert images, without executing it.
Neither replaces the device run. The ordinary `compile-cuda-tests` target also includes the gate in the runner.

Then run the existing GLM layer/operator references at all selected checkpoint widths, and the served greedy and
seeded checks: drafted/plain, fresh/resumed and concurrent/solo. Keep prompt caching enabled for resumes. Include
MTP and DFlash2, unequal prompt lengths, several 2048-row passes, an already-live stream, cancelled admissions and
image/resumed prompts alongside fresh text. Repeat both-rank gather/split/ring cases.

## Timing

Use one pinned binary, checkpoint, precision, context, prompt set and cache state. Compare `one` and `shape` on both
ranks in matched A/B/B/A runs with one, eight and sixteen streams. Record prompt time, first-token latency, decode
throughput and whole-run throughput separately. Keep drafting and cache settings equal. Repeat structured-output
and quality checks, including the original IFEval/JSON comparisons. A faster isolated matmul is insufficient to
resolve the reported lone-stream regression or justify a default change.
# Grammar timing

Lane rounds measure grammar work on the host when a constrained stream builds its window. The decision log records `grammar_window` with the step and stream id, then `grammar_round` with that step's sum. Both carry `windows`, `fills`, `window_ns` and `fill_ns`. A stream's round total resets on its first window in a new step.

`fill_ns` covers the rules fill, optional completion-budget mask and dead-end check. `window_ns` covers the whole grammar traversal, including fills, rollback and allocations. It excludes reading held GPU drafts and preparing the window's token and parent arrays. Errors retain work already timed. The windows include their fills, so their durations must not be added.

Finished replies expose lifetime sums as `tensorfold.grammar_windows`, `grammar_fills`, `grammar_window_seconds` and `grammar_fill_seconds`. These fields are absent when no grammar window was measured. They use a separate host clock; planner costs and GPU timings are unchanged. Unconstrained windows perform no timing reads or metric allocations. A clock without a host timing hook leaves these metrics absent.
# Use TensorFold with Hermes Agent

The community [hermes-tensorfold](https://github.com/atakann/hermes-tensorfold) plugin makes TensorFold a model
provider in [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) and adds a TensorFold tab to Hermes' web
dashboard. It implements the Hermes part of [#1399](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/1399), tracked in
[#2109](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/2109).

- **Provider:** "TensorFold" appears in `hermes model` and the in-chat model picker. The models come from the server's
  `/v1/models`, and each model's context window from the same list.
- **Dashboard tab:** the served model, decode and prefill speed, running and waiting streams, token totals, MTP
  acceptance and memory, read from `/health`, `/stats` and `/v1/models` every 2 s. The key stays on the dashboard's
  side; the browser never sees it.

The plugin needs Hermes Agent 0.23.0 or later. It changes nothing in the engine's requests or tokens.

## Start the native server

Use a checkpoint already qualified for your platform, following its [model recipe](recipes/). Keep the server on
loopback with an API key:

```sh
tensorfold serve /path/to/checkpoint --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --api-key-file /path/to/server.keys --dashboard
```

Follow the [key-file format and permissions](api.md#api-keys). A scoped key needs `inference,read`: chat uses the
inference routes, and the dashboard tab reads `/stats`. `--dashboard` serves `/stats`; inference works without it.
Hermes must run on the same host as TensorFold, or reach it through a loopback forward such as
`ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 gpu-box`.

## Install and pick the model

```sh
hermes plugins install atakann/hermes-tensorfold
hermes plugins enable tensorfold
echo 'TENSORFOLD_API_KEY=<a key from server.keys>' >> ~/.hermes/.env
hermes model
```

Choose TensorFold, then the served model. The default endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`; set
`TENSORFOLD_BASE_URL` for another port. `hermes plugins enable` is what loads the dashboard tab: Hermes loads a user
plugin's dashboard routes only when the plugin is in `plugins.enabled`.

## Tool calls

Hermes' agent loop sends no `tool_choice`, so the server's `auto` applies to tool calls. Some auxiliary requests can
ask for `required`, which the server enforces with `libtfgrammar`. The release archives include it in `lib/`; a source
build without it answers such a request with HTTP 400 and names the library.

## Checked

On a DGX Spark (GB10) with TensorFold 1.2.3 serving `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` (`--context 131072
--parallel 2 --dashboard`), and Hermes Agent 0.23.0 on a Mac reaching it through a loopback forward:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `hermes plugins validate` (the catalog's admission check) | passed, security scan safe |
| First run on an empty Hermes home: install, enable, one question | answered |
| Model picker | "TensorFold (1 model)", the served model, a 131,072-token window |
| Streamed tool use: write a file and run it | written, run, the right output |
| A long reply interrupted mid-stream | the server shows no running or waiting stream; the next request answers |
| The server stopped, then started again | Hermes reports the server unavailable after its retries, then answers once it is back |
| Dashboard tab against `/stats` | the same prompt, generated and round totals |

On an M1 Max (64 GB) with the macOS release archive serving `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` on loopback with a
scoped `inference,read` key, the same checks passed, with the endpoint and key only in Hermes' `.env`.

Not run yet: the M3 Ultra run the release checklist asks for.
# Kernel contract

Every GPU kernel, ours or a contributor's, registers with the kernel contract before it lands. One harness
(`zig/src/core/contract/`) runs five gates on Metal, CUDA and HIP, and each gate has a planted control: a kernel built
to break that gate, which the gate must report as failing. A run where a control passes is a failed run, because then
the gate proves nothing.

A kernel's own unit test usually compares a few outputs within one tolerance. The gates ask more: what happens to NaN
and infinities, whether the bytes repeat, whether every tile edge is covered, whether the sums are really fp32, and
whether the launch fits every chip we serve.

## What a kernel registers

The test of a kernel fills a `contract.spec.Spec` and hands the harness a few hooks (`contract.gates.VTable`, or
`gates.hooks(T)` for a test type with `prepare`, `run`, `count` and `reference`).

`runAll` calls each kernel's optional `VTable.release` before moving to the next kernel, including after a failed
gate or planted control. `gates.hooks(T)` supplies `rig.reset()` for value or pointer rigs with a `reset` method.
Direct `one` callers remain responsible for cleanup.

- Its float64 reference: the kernel's own formula in float64. The input families in `zig/src/core/contract/` cover the
  common cases: `affine` (MLX's affine-quantized projections), `dense` (dots against dequantized weights, in K
  slices) and `rows` (RMS norm, softmax, sums, dots, maxima). Each builds inputs for every gate, computes the reference
  and the magnitude of the terms each output sums, and can replay the sums in another accumulator.
- Its served envelope: the shapes the engine calls it at, and for each dimension its tile, the step a valid size
  moves by and the least valid size.
- Its accumulator (`f32` where a kernel sums) and the depth of its longest chain of roundings at a shape, plus any
  fp32 operations after the sums (`ops`), intermediate roundings to the output type (`mids`), and the precision it
  stores at when that is narrower than the output's element (`store`: bf16 values in fp32 words).
- Whether it may write in place. If it replaces another kernel, the kernel whose bits it must equal.
- Its NaN rule: `propagate` (as float64 arithmetic on its formula does), or a stated rule the test checks itself
  (top-k, argmax, sampling and routing kernels state theirs).
- For gate 5, its launch in `zig/src/core/contract/registry.zig`: threads a group and threadgroup bytes (the source's,
  and any its encoder sets) on Metal, or symbol, image, threads a block, dynamic shared bytes and cluster width on CUDA,
  with the limits its compiles recorded. HIP launches are in `zig/src/core/contract/hip_records.zig`: symbol, code
  object, threads a workgroup and dynamic LDS bytes. XPU launches are in `zig/src/core/contract/xpu_records.zig`:
  symbol, image, work-group size, static SLM bytes, sub-group size and GRF mode, with the values ocloc's `.ze_info`
  recorded for the card class. The seam's records are in `metal_pair_records.zig`, which `registry.zig` concatenates.

## The gates

1. Non-finite. NaN, +Inf and -Inf go into the inputs at known places (a row each, one row holding both infinities).
   Every output's class (finite, NaN, +Inf, -Inf) must equal the float64 reference's, tolerance-free. A kernel with a
   stated rule checks the rule instead. Control: a row maximum by `fmax`, which drops a NaN.
2. Repeat and aliasing. Five runs on the same inputs give the same bytes, the inputs are unchanged afterwards, the
   guard bytes around every buffer are intact, and no output overlaps an input unless the spec says in place.
   Controls: a row sum by atomic adds (its order changes from run to run), and a row sum that writes into its input.
3. Shapes. Every served shape, then each tiled dimension at its least size, a tile minus a step, a tile, a tile plus a
   step and the largest served size. Each output must be within `|want| * outputs' half ulp + gamma(depth) * magnitude`
   of float64, or for a replacement kernel bit-equal to the kernel it replaces. Control: a row sum whose partial tail
   loses its last input; it passes at whole tiles and fails at the edges. A kernel with bf16 rounding points between
   its steps (MLX's op-by-op rows) checks each output against float64's value at those points, as a range over the
   spread its fp32 steps allow, and its controls each drop one rounding point, which that check must catch.
4. fp32 sums. The inputs are integers whose partial sums reach about 2^20 in any order and stay below 2^24, so fp32
   sums are exact whatever the kernel's order; the second half of each row mirrors the first, so the result is small.
   Before the kernel runs, the harness replays the sums on the CPU in fp16 and bf16 (one chain, contiguous halves, and
   32 lanes then their halves) and requires each to miss by at least 100 times the exact-sum bound: fp16 overflows,
   bf16 loses thousands. Then the kernel must meet the exact-sum bound, which enforces "no fp16 sums where fp32 is
   used". Where the output's own rounding hides a sum's error (a bf16 softmax of at most 4,096 terms in [0, 1]), the
   spec says so and the run prints the margins it could prove. Control: a dot product summed in half.
