5. Limits. Every registered launch against each chip we serve, from its declaration and recorded compiles, so this part
   runs with no GPU in `zig build test`. Metal: threads a group and threadgroup bytes against M1 to M5; on M1 and M2 a
   pipeline's thread limit falls as its registers rise (simd_qmm_bits' 8-bit tiles compile for 224), so every launch
   records its M1/M2 limit, unless its launcher sizes its groups to the pipeline or its source reserves the threads. A
   tensor-op kernel, which cannot be built for M1/M2 ahead of time, stays at 256 threads. CUDA: registers a thread
   (rounded per warp), static plus dynamic shared bytes, launch bounds and clusters against sm_80, sm_86, sm_89, sm_120
   and sm_121. HIP: VGPRs a wave (a workgroup's waves spread over the WGP's four SIMDs, each rounded to the chip's
   allocation step), static plus dynamic LDS bytes, the kernel's `__launch_bounds__` and its wave size against gfx1030,
   gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1201, one chip a generation. Tools re-derive the records: on a Mac, `tf-kernel-contract
   --offline DIR` compiles each pipeline for M1 and M2 with Xcode's Metal toolchain (native code built for T threads
   equal to the plain build means the plain pipeline runs T); on a CUDA build machine, `tf-cuda-test
   kernel-contract-limits DIR` reads registers, shared bytes and launch bounds from the fatbins' ELF images for every
   SM, counted as the driver counts them (sm_120 and sm_121 images keep registers only in the `.nv.info` register
   records, and add the block's reserved 1 KiB to `.nv.shared`); with hipcc, `tf-hip-kernel-contract limits DIR` reads
   VGPRs, SGPRs, LDS, scratch, the bound and the wave size from the AMDGPU metadata note of each chip's code objects. On
   the GPU itself the runners check the loaded kernels and the device's own limits. Controls: Metal, the row
   projection's pipeline launched at 1,024 threads where M1 and M2 compile it for 512, and 36 KiB of threadgroup memory;
   CUDA, a kernel launched past its `__launch_bounds__`, and one needing more registers than a block has; HIP, a kernel
   launched past its `__launch_bounds__`, and 40 KiB of static LDS launched with 32 KiB more (hipcc fits a kernel's
   VGPRs to its bound, so a register overflow shows as a launch past the bound).

## Running it

On a Mac, `zig build kernel-contract -Dcpu=apple_m1` runs every Metal kernel registered for this GPU, the controls
and gate 5. `zig build tf-kernel-contract` builds the program alone; `--only TEXT` runs the kernels whose name holds
TEXT, `--offline DIR` adds the M1/M2 compiles, and `--repro` prints the smallest input behind each known finding.

On a CUDA machine, build with `-Dnvcc` (the controls are compiled only then), and run `zig build kernel-contract
-Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`. For the limits of every SM, `zig build fatbins kernel-contract-fatbins -Dnvcc=...
-Dsm=80,86,89,120,121`, then `tf-cuda-test kernel-contract-limits zig-out/fatbin`. Its `RECORD` lines are the values
`registry.zig` holds for that build's nvcc (see [CUDA records per nvcc release](#cuda-records-per-nvcc-release)).

For a development sm_110 build, use `-Dsm=110` in the fatbin build and run the same limits command on that set.
The `DIR` must contain `norms.fatbin` and every registered image; the runner reads `norms.fatbin` first to select
the release or sm_110 audit mode. It reads sm_110 registers, static shared bytes and bounds from each cubin and
checks its device limits; the five release SMs retain their pinned `RECORD` entries. This does not enable
`-Dgpu=sm_110`. On sm_110, some 48 KiB dynamic shared-memory kernels carry another 1 KiB of static shared memory.
Only their sm_110 audit uses the opt-in limit already raised by their loaders (`allowDynamicShared`).
For a mixed release and sm_110 set, each planted control must go red on each target separately.

On an AMD machine, run `zig build hip-kernel-contract -Dhip-arch=ARCH -Dhipcc=...` on a GPU of that chip (the
controls are built with the kernels). For the limits of every served chip, `zig build hip-kernel-contract-limits
-Dhipcc=...` compiles every kernel group and the controls for gfx1030, gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1201 and checks each
record against them, no GPU needed; `hip-kernel-contract-objects` installs those code objects into `zig-out/hsaco/`.
Its `RECORD` lines are the values `hip_records.zig` holds for that hipcc. The records hold ROCm 10.1's hipcc (HIP 7.16),
which ROCm 10.1 installs under `core/bin` of its root.

On an Intel GPU host, `zig build -Dxpu-contract=true xpu-kernel-contract-objects -Docloc=... -Dxpu-device=bmg` compiles
every registered XPU kernel and the controls to zebins, and `xpu-kernel-contract-limits` checks each record against the
BMG card's row, no GPU needed. Level Zero does not report a kernel's GRF mode, so the record states it, and the audit
fails a record whose mode is not the zebin's `grf_count`. `tf-xpu-kernel-contract limits DIR` runs that audit on a
directory another host built. The `RECORD` lines are the values `xpu_records.zig` holds for that ocloc.

On an Arc Pro B70, `zig build -Dxpu-contract=true tf-xpu-contract-run` builds `tf-xpu-contract-run` with the zebins
linked in, and `./zig-out/bin/tf-xpu-contract-run [--device N]` runs gates 1 to 4 over ten registrations of the
Qwen3.8-27B glue and decode attention, seven planted controls, and gate 5
live: the card's own properties against the BMG-G31 row and every loaded kernel's against its record. It loads the same
native zebins the audit reads, so the GRF mode the record states is the loaded image's. Its `SUMMARY` line names the PCI
id it ran on. `xpu-contract-run` runs it on this card. On a host without ocloc, `-Dxpu-images=DIR` links zebins that
another host made with the commands the receipt records.

The decode attention registration runs `attn_decode` followed by `attn_merge` as one operator: bf16 query rows,
bf16 K/V cache and a tree table to bf16 attention rows. Gate 3 requires the bytes of the upstream `1a5644892` pair,
whose decode grid is retained in `zig/kernels/xpu/contract_attn_upstream.cl`. It covers single rows and branching
trees of 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 rows (heap-order parents; chains and other topologies are not fixtures), 32-key slice
edges, and 8,193 through 32,770 visible keys at selected root positions. The positions include 32,768 and 32,769
(zero-based). Two planted controls go with it: a merge that drops the last non-empty slice, and the new `attn_decode`
launched on the old `(slices, heads, rows)` grid wherever that grid stays inside the buffers (no more slices than rows),
so the registration also guards the launch order `zig/src/xpu/forward.zig` uses. Gate 4 uses uniform attention with
cancelling integer values; it tests the value and normalization sums, without separately proving the query/key dot
accumulator. The default NaN rule compares
classes with the independent float64 formula. Int8 caches and multi-stream metadata are outside this registration.

On any host, with no device, `zig build cpu-contract` runs the CPU kernels (Qwen3.5-2B's affine projection and RMS
norm on the host's cores) through gates 1 to 4 and their eight controls; a CPU kernel has no launch, so gate 5 has
nothing to check. `zig build test-kernel-contract`, CI's no-device step, runs the same gates as a test, and `zig build
test` the kernels' own test that the bytes are the same at 1 to 16 threads and at column splits every 8 columns to 256 and every 256 beyond (each alignment of the four-tile pass), on x86_64 and arm64.

`--only` filters generic Metal launch labels too; both global launch-limit controls still run.

Every run ends with a `SUMMARY` line: kernels passing gates 1 to 4, known findings, controls red, and limit problems.
The program exits 1 on any failed gate, any control that stayed green, or any limit problem.

## Adding a kernel

1. Write its test type in `zig/tests/contract/` (Metal), `zig/tests/cuda/contract_*.zig` (CUDA),
   `zig/tests/hip/contract_*.zig` (HIP) or `zig/tests/cpu/contract_*.zig` (CPU): `prepare` builds
   the inputs for a shape and a gate's fill (usually through an input family), `run` launches once and waits, `count`
   and `reference` give the outputs and their float64 values, `simulate` replays the sums for gate 4.
2. Add it to the runner's list, with its served shapes and tiles.
3. Add its launches to `registry.zig`, or to a records file it concatenates as the seam's are, and fill them from
   `--offline` (Metal) or `kernel-contract-limits`
   (CUDA: nvcc 13.0's in `cuda`, and each later release's set where that release compiles it differently); a HIP
   kernel's go to `hip_records.zig`, filled from `hip-kernel-contract-limits`, and an XPU kernel's to
   `xpu_records.zig`, filled from `xpu-kernel-contract-limits`. Its test type goes in `zig/tests/xpu/contract_*.zig`
   and, where it needs a planted control, `zig/kernels/xpu/contract_gate_controls.cl`.
4. Post the `SUMMARY` lines from each backend you ran in the pull request, and say which chips you could not run.

A replacement kernel names the kernel it replaces and gives `replaced`, which runs that kernel on the same inputs.

## Known findings

A gate failure on a kernel already shipped is reported, not hidden. Until its fix lands, its spec can carry a
`known` entry naming the gate and what fails. That gate must keep failing (the run prints `KNOWN`); once a fix makes
it pass, the run fails until the entry is removed. Today: affine_mm's 4-bit form gives NaN for an infinite input where
MLX's formula keeps the infinity, because its codes enter the MMAs as q + 128 and its bias as b - 128 s. GLM-5.3-Flash's
`tf_glm_scores` scores a NaN dot as 0 where float64 keeps the NaN: its relu is `fmaxf(x, 0)`, as `tl.maximum` is in the
Python family's Triton glue it was ported from. Nemotron's Metal `tf_xup_w3` gives 0 for a NaN dot where float64 keeps
the NaN: its relu2 is `metal::max(bfloat(acc), 0.0f)`; the other up pipelines give its bytes on the same inputs.
HIP's prompt attention tile (`tf_fa_paged_*`, `tf_fa_wide_*`) writes 0 for a row whose every score is NaN where
float64 gives NaN, as its running max is `fmaxf` and a row at max -inf takes p = 0; and an infinite value at a key
the row sees under fp32's least weight gives NaN where float64 gives inf, as 0 x inf enters its P x V.
Qwen3.8 Flash Next's `tf_sattn_nax` and `tf_attn256_nax` score masked keys -FLT_MAX, the value each row's running
max starts from, so a row whose every score is -Inf weighs its masked keys 1 and gives a finite average where float64
gives NaN. `tf_sattn_nax`'s padding lanes also read key 0 at p = 0, so a non-finite value in key 0's row reaches every
row whose key count is not a multiple of 32 (0 x Inf is NaN where float64 gives the infinity).
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash's `mm_prompt_attention`, Spark-X2.6-4B's `sp_prompt_attention`, Gemma 4's `gemma_prompt_attention`
(31B and 12B, sliding and global), Nemotron's `tf_attention_nax` and Qwen3.8 Flash Next's `tf_attn256_nax` give NaN
for a row whose tile or block reads a non-finite value at a key masked for that row, and Gemma 4's
`gemma_decode_attention` for a decode row whose 32-key step reads one: P = 0 times Inf inside the P x V mma, where
float64 leaves the masked key out. These were seen on the M5, where their cases run. Each kernel has an entry of its own
that plants such a value and carries the finding, so its other entries keep a clean gate 1.

HIP’s MLX stream tile keeps its finite dot2 sums unchanged. A non-finite result with an actual non-finite
operand is recomputed by full quantization groups using the factored float64 formula. The plain tile is
registered at all six supported bit widths and groups of 32, 64 and 128, with no known finding.

The HIP relu^2 replacement retains every non-finite plant and checks both unfused bytes and every
independent float64 output class. No inherited infinity discrepancy is accepted.
The paired launch retains every table plant and checks both members' separate-launch bytes and every
float64 output class, without an inherited exception.

## Isolated masked-value panels

`metal masked-V` entries isolate one hidden +Inf or NaN in otherwise finite Q/K/V. Every output class and every
finite output is checked against binary64 over the actual visible set, including a visible exceptional-value control.
The fixtures cover causal tiles, sliding rings, indexed/padded lists, page mappings and shared-context masks.
Latent MLA treats its shared K/V storage as both key and value; a visible poisoned latent can also make its score NaN.
The tensor kernels' dropped visible NaN scores and zero residual probability parts times visible Inf are separate
known findings from hidden-value leakage. No production kernel is repaired by these registrations.

The source-only focused runner builds without an offline Metal compiler:

```sh
zig build --build-file build.masked-values.zig tf-masked-values test-masked-values-host -Dcpu=apple_m1
./zig-out/bin/tf-masked-values
```

It runs the same entries registered in the main Metal runner. Its equal-score/unit-value panels do not discriminate
accumulator precision, so gate 4 states that limitation instead of claiming a stress proof. The two device controls
plant a hidden NaN leak and erase a visible infinity; each must fail gate 1. A known finding must still reproduce.
LFM3 entries register only on a tree that actually contains its source. DeepSeek CSA2 and H3 are operator checks,
not new native serving paths. Flash Next is excluded. This focused run does not replace the complete backend gates.

## Coverage

Metal: softmax, RMS norm, bf16 top-k, the row projection (3, 4, 6 and 8 bits), affine_mm (4 and 8 bits), simd_qmm (4
bits) and simd_qmm_bits (3, 6 and 8 bits), and the lane projection (6-bit groups of 32 on every chip; 4- and 8-bit
formats on the M5's tensor units, where its reg kernel must equal the cooperative one bit for bit), and tile_qmm's
prompt tiles and their decode twin (4, 6 and 8 bits; the twin bit-equal to the tiles). Gate 5 also holds the rest of
tile_qmm's pipelines and GLM-5.3-Flash's hc_expand_10.
On the M5's tensor units, Metal also checks what nax.h's `mma_16x32` keeps of an fp32 operand
(`metal_mma_operand.zig`): the left, the right and both (attention's fp32 P, `gemm_nax`'s f32 kernels), each output a
single product bit-equal to float64 on operands with their low 13 mantissa bits cleared. That is 10 bits kept, rounded
toward zero, fp32's exponents and subnormals kept, NaN and the infinities passed. Four controls state the operand as
fp32 or as rounded to nearest at 10 bits, on each side, and must go red at `shapes`. The cut was measured on the tensor
units only, so the cases run only there; what M1-M4 keep of an fp32 operand is not measured.
`core/attention_range.zig` names that cut (`operand_cut`, 2^-10) as a form's `p_cut`: one-sided, since each p only
shrinks, so it moves an output down by up to 2^-10 of its positive values' share and up by its negative values'. On the
M5, Nemotron's `tf_attention_nax` states its fp32 P with it, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash's `mm_prompt_attention` does on
every chip (before the M5 that only widens its range); each bf16 output must lie between its range's ends rounded to
bf16. Nemotron's adds a case with P spread over about
[2^-6, 1] and values in [0, 1), where the cut's bias adds up; its control, the same range without the cut, goes red at
`shapes`. Before the M5, `tf_attention_nax` keeps attention_ref's bound.
Qwen3.8 Flash Next's prompt attention on the M5 does too: `tf_sattn_nax` (the indexer's dense and selected rows) and
`tf_attn256_nax` (the causal chunk without the indexer), head dim 256, 24 heads over 2. Each bf16 output,
bf16(bf16(o) * bsig(gate)), must lie between its range's ends rounded to bf16 and through the gate's rounded sigmoid.
Each adds a P-spread case whose cutless range is a planted control, and a source edit gate 3 must catch: `tf_sattn_nax`
counting its padding lane (key 0 again), `tf_attn256_nax` seeing one key past the row. Before the M5 neither is
registered.
On the M5, Nemotron's SSD steps (`prefill_mixers.zig`'s Mamba mixer) run `gemm_nax`'s five f32 kernels with both
operands fp32, so each product enters cut, smaller by up to 1 - (1 - 2^-10)^2. Their entries
(`metal_nemotron_ssd_gemm.zig`, y = sur x dtx and the state dd^T x bh^T a head, at the step's served row counts) state
it as a one-sided range: float64's value less that share of the positive terms and plus that of the negative, beside
the fp32 sums' `mma_step` roundings for every k16 step. Gate 4 runs 11-bit integers times 5-bit ones, which the cut
keeps. Two cases take operands in (0, 1], where the bias adds up; their controls state the operands as fp32 and go red
at `shapes`, as does a source edit dropping the ragged K tail's last column. Before the M5 they are not registered;
their launches are in `nemotron_ssd_records.zig`.
Spark-X2.6-4B's `sp_prompt_attention` registers both pipelines the engine builds (sliding layers over a 512-key window
in a 2,560-slot ring, and full layers), its fp32 P stated with the cut, each with a P spread case
and its cutless control, and one source edit each (a key past the window, a key past the row); before the M5 they are
not registered.
On the M5, Gemma 4's `gemma_prompt_attention` (the 31B's and 12B's sliding and global layers) and
`gemma_decode_attention` with `gemma_attention_merge` (their global layers; the 12B's assistant launches the 12B's)
state their fp32 P with the cut too, each form's counts taken from the kernel's own steps, at the sliding ring, image
rows and decode chunks the engine serves. A P-spread case on the 31B's global prompt and decode has a cutless control
each, red at `shapes`, and a score edit (2 log2e) in each kernel is a control. Their launches are in
`gemma_attention_records.zig`.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B's shared rounds: the greedy pick (`lfm2_argmax`) and the conv and attention kernels that run every
stream's rows in one dispatch, each bit-equal to the per-stream kernels it replaces. Four controls edit the source: a tie
to the highest id, a nonfinite logit not flagged, and every stream reading or writing the first stream's state or cache.
Their launches are in `lfm2_records.zig` with the M1 and M2 limits from `--offline`; `lfm2_attn_segs` reserves its 128
threads in its source, as Metal cannot build it for M1 or M2 at another count.
Metal also checks Nemotron's routed experts on the engine's route tables, one row to 128: `tf_xup_w3` and `tf_xdown_w3`
against float64 at tf_load16's bf16 x sums (up's relu2 as an interval over its two bf16 roundings), and the rows2, rows4
and six geometry pipelines of each projection bit-equal to them (two controls: member rows read from one row, and
w3's x sums without their bf16 steps).
Metal also checks DeepSeek V4.1's routed experts at hidden 5120, width 2304, rows 1 to 16: the gate/up (`tf_dsv41_xp_up`:
fp8 act_quant of the input, bf16 projections, clamped SwiGLU, route weight, bf16, act_quant of the result) against an
oracle in the kernel's fp32 order whose silu may move by exp's error, and the down (`tf_dsv41_xp_down_one`/`_multi`, a
DeepSeek-only copy of Kimi K3's chains with the full E8M0 scale range) against its bytes (also over the release's real
FP4 expert bytes), each with four controls. The copied plan and combine (`tf_dsv41_route_plan`, `tf_dsv41_xp_combine`)
are checked end to end through the GPU's own plan, and every launch is recorded for gate 5.
The row-split seam's four kernels (`pair_rows.metal`, launched by `pair_rows.zig`) move bf16 frames, never sums:
`pair_stage` copies this rank's half of a frame row into the slot the relay sends, and `pair_gather` writes both halves
of every row, its own natively and the peer's from the relayed frame. `pair_argmax` flags a row whose logits are not
finite (its id word carries bit 31, its value word a NaN) and takes the lower id on a tie; `pair_pick` turns a flagged
rank's word into the id sentinel, so both Macs refuse a non-finite round where one Mac does. Six controls edit the
source: a stage reading the peer's half, a gather writing its own half twice, and an argmax or pick tie to the higher
id must go red at `shapes`, and an argmax or pick that does not flag at `nonfinite`.
The Llama family's own kernels (`metal_llama*.zig`): its glue (embedding, the norms at HF's rounding points, the
residual add, RoPE with bf16 cos and sin, the SiLU gate, the decode attention's partials and their merge, the argmax
draw by its stated rule), its row projections (1 to 32 rows) and, on the M5's tensor units, its four GEMM forms and the
prompt attention at both served geometries; gate 5 reads their pipelines on this GPU. Twelve controls edit the
source, one a kernel group: an embedding reading its own row, a norm's mean over the threads, a subtracting add, an
add-norm dropping its residual, a SiLU with gate and up swapped, a rope at the window's first position, a decode that
never rescales, a merge dropping each block's scale, a row projection dropping its tail, a GEMM reading its weights
untransposed and a prompt attention seeing the next key go red at `shapes`, and an argmax never picking a NaN at
`nonfinite`. The INT4 release's row projections and dequantization have two more: every group taking its row's first
zero point, and a word's nibbles read in reverse, both red at `shapes`.
CUDA: the RMS norm rows (16-byte form and the fp32-out tree), the bf16 residual's norm tails (MLX's rounded rows and
the once-rounded ones, each checked on its residual and its output, with four controls each dropping a rounding point), Nemotron's router logits (and their 128-row tiles,
bit-equal to them) and top-k, the latent top-k's decode form (bit-equal to `tf_super_topk`), the latent combine and

epilogues bit-equal to main's kernel (kept in `contract_controls.cu`), and its SwiGLU-OAI (`act_mode` 2,
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash's) against float64 at its rounding points (two controls: the up without its + 1, alpha 1).

CUDA also checks the grouped EXL3 experts (`tf_exl3_grouped_0`, `_1` and `_2`, one a codebook), which on sm_120 and
sm_121 load a warp's next k tile while the current one decodes: each bit-equal to main's loop (kept in
`contract_controls.cu`) at one, two and three k tiles a warp and at GLM-5.3-Flash's, MiMo-V2.6-Flash's and the Qwen3.5
EXL3 pack's widths (two controls: the next load reading tile i + 2, the last tile decoding the words before it).
Older SMs build main's loop, and their records are main's.

CUDA also checks MOSS-Image's glue (`moss_image.cu`: the norm, plain and modulated; q/k norm and rotary into packed
rows; situ; the gated add), each output within float64's range at its torch bf16 points (five controls, each dropping
one point), and `vision_kernel` at head dim 128 against `contract_attn.zig`'s float64 reference (`moss-contract`).

CPU: Qwen3.5-2B's affine projection (4 bits, groups of 64, `cpu_kernels.zig`) at the widths the 2B calls it, one row
to a 128-row prompt chunk, registered once for each chain count of its projection classes (16; 32 for the delta rule's
a and b; 8 for the head), and its RMS norm over 2048-wide rows; each registration's runs take 1 to 8 threads in turn,
so gate 2's five runs are five thread counts (the 16-output a and b projections have two tiles, so all five of theirs
run on two). Eight controls: a projection zeroing a non-finite activation, writing its
activations, skipping the rows past its last block of eight, and summing each group in half; a norm taking a
non-finite input as zero, writing its output over its input, scaling by the next element's weight, and summing its
squares in bf16.

## CUDA records per nvcc release

nvcc allocates registers differently from one release to the next, so the CUDA records are kept per release.
`registry.cuda` holds what nvcc 13.0 compiles, the compiler of the release fatbins. `registry.cuda_sets` lists what
each later release compiles differently from the release before it: nvcc 13.2's set holds `tf_rms_rows`, `lane_gemv`
and its split-K form, prompt16's FP8 tile, qmmf's FP4 32-row cluster tile, five 64-row fused-slice tiles of the MXFP8
and FP32-output paths, FP8G's 32-row cluster tile with FP32 output, the common EXL3 prompt products, Super's
decode-sized latent top-k and NVFP4 up experts, the Mamba scan and Super's NVFP4 prompt down kernels, three of
GLM-5.3-Flash's packed matmuls and three of its DFlash2 launches, and the training launches it compiles differently,
and nvcc 13.3 keeps 13.2's and changes four of GLM-5.3-Flash's KV page launches, its two prompt-indexer launches
and its wide decode select. `kernel-contract` and
`kernel-contract-limits` read the release from each image's `.note.nv.tkinfo`, check the image against the newest set
at or below that release (13.0's when an image names none), and print which set they used. A release with no set of
its own is checked against the one below it, so its differences show as stale records: re-derive them with
`kernel-contract-limits` and add a set for that release rather than loosening the audit. Launch dimensions, dynamic
shared memory, the device's limits and the planted controls are checked the same way under every release.

`-Dnative-fp-decode` (off by default; nvcc 13.2 or later) builds prompt16 and fp8_experts for `sm_<n>a` from sm_120
on and decodes their FP4/FP8 weight pairs with PTX ISA 9.2's `cvt.rn.bf16x2.e2m1x2`/`.e4m3x2`. Known finding: the
hardware decode equals `fp4pair` on all 256 e2m1 bytes and `fp8pair` on every e4m3 pair without a NaN code; the 1,020
pairs holding `0x7F` or `0xFF` decode to NaN, where the software gives ±480 (`tf-cuda-test native-fp`). Those codes
are NaN in e4m3, so only a broken checkpoint can tell the two apart. Default images keep the software decode.

A restored 13.0 receipt can arrive after the later compiler sets. Such records mark `later_pending` so 13.0 and
13.1 use their base usage, while 13.2 and later keep their independently measured or pending selection.
A missing later receipt remains pending; a 13.0 measurement never substitutes for it.

Gemma 4 CUDA tower QKV norms and nine-term pooling register FP32 sums and BF16 outputs.
Their contract keeps the exact FP32 mirror and adds independent FP64 ranges at the BF16 nodes.
The sum fixtures use integers with exact FP32 partials below 2^24, including pooling cancellation near 2^20;
FP16 and BF16 simulations must fail in each of the three accumulator orders. Pooling declares its nine-term
reduction separately from the physical grid width, so the small stress grid remains a valid launch.
NaN and both infinity signs have explicit class controls. These registrations still require the device gates.

## Shared M5 attention products

The shared `attention_nax` defaults to the relaxed tensor P x V: float P is truncated to ten fraction bits.
`TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=1` opts into full float P with FP32 FMA accumulation on M5; unset preserves the old arithmetic.
The cut registration's independent formula includes the operand cut, while the full registration uses the full P.
A third registration executes the real cut kernel against the full FP32 bound and must fail the shapes gate.
The product fixture writes float output so BF16 rounding cannot conceal that control.
Both modes still require exceptional-class, repeat, guard, shape, accumulator and separate launch checks.
See [the mode's scope and device checks](recipes/m5-attention-precision.md); other families' rounding is unchanged.

Flash Next's BF16 shared-down entries `tf_qmmf_shared16_half`, `tf_qmmf_shared16`, `tf_qmmf_shared32` and
`tf_qmmf_shared64` preserve the contiguous projection's FP32 result and store it directly in expert slot 10.
The baseline shared expert has all 640 intermediate channels and runs only on rank 0 at two ranks.
The contract checks all four geometries, nonfinite inputs, output bytes and untouched routed slots.
`moetile_records.zig` holds launch geometry and measured nvcc 13.0 resources on all five served SMs.
Later compiler receipts remain pending. Check each build with `tf-cuda-test kernel-contract-limits zig-out/fatbin`.
`tf-cuda-test moetile` compares the direct slot and the BF16 prompt tile plus scatter with the lane's contiguous
product and scatter at 1, 16, 17, 32, 64, 65, 1536 and 4218 rows, five repeats with guards.
`moetile-contract` runs the replacement gates and planted control.
`moetile-bench` rotates GPU event timings of the three at 64 to 4218 rows; no timing is a gate.

BF16 prompt K32 staging registers two unfused 128x128 entries, one for BF16 output and one for FP32 output.
They read the parent's K64 weight packs in two K32 halves and keep the K16 MMA order and output rounding.
Only unsplit prompt calls select K32; fused slices retain the parent K64 tile.
`qmmf-prompt` compares each new output directly with the parent's 128x128 K64 output, including forced small rows.
`qmmf-prompt-contract` keeps the four parent entries and adds both K32 replacements and their scaled controls.
Each new control launches K32 for its output type at small and production row counts.
`qmmf-prompt-bench` times the 64-row lane, prompt16, the parent K64 tile and K32 on each Flash Next BF16 shape.
Measured nvcc 13.0 resources cover both K32 entries on sm_120 and sm_121; later compiler receipts remain pending.
# Known issues

This is the current list. Each release's notes summarize it and say what changed; an issue leaves the list only when a
release fixes it, and the release notes say which one.

## Models

- GLM-5.3 (EXLR8) decodes slowly next to the other models: a one-row round on two M5 Ultras takes about 45 ms. No CUDA
  engine serves it, and only the `home` profile on M5 Ultras has run. Replies past 2,048 tokens, where the sparse indexer
  starts picking keys, have not been compared with a whole-model reference.
- Kolibri-1 on CUDA with `TF_KV_SHARE=n`: the prompt store keeps whole 512-token pages, so a shared start shorter
  than a page (a chat template's first 45 tokens, say) is not reused, and a prompt is cut at a page boundary. On a GB10,
  cold 2K chat prompts take about 10% longer to the first token than without the store (0.87 against 0.79 s). Decode
  speed and tokens are the same, and prompts with no shared start take the same time.
- Qwen3.5-2B with a JSON schema: on an integer field it wants to write as a decimal, the 2B can keep adding digits until
  `max_tokens`, because the grammar allows no decimal point there. Nemotron writes the same schema correctly.
- Qwen3.8-27B: the drafter's landing counts last for the server's life, so the first greedy code reply after prose lands
  about 5% fewer tokens a round on an M3 Ultra. Its shallower rounds cost less, so decode stays within about 1% of a fresh
  server, even after 40 prose replies. The tokens are the same.
- Qwen3.8-27B on Metal allocates DeltaNet rollback scratch lazily for the verification slots that need it. The bank
  can be resized or released between completed rounds; an idle or newly lone host can release it after the previous
  verification has been kept. A revised physical-memory peak comparison with 1.0.12 remains unmeasured.
- Qwen3.8-27B cold prefill at 64K tokens on RTX 50-series GPUs (sm_120) measures about 2% slower than 1.1.0; 32K and shorter prompts, and GB10, are at parity or faster.
- Flash Next on Metal with explicit --parallel 2 or more ([#1893](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/1893)):
  on an M3 Ultra with the MLX 4-bit checkpoint, in a 12-turn chat of about 15,000 tokens, 8 of the 11 resumed
  turns reused 31 to 350 fewer tokens than the single host, about 0.4 s in all. Replies are the same. On an M5 Ultra
  with the MLX 4-bit checkpoint, two overlapping clients still finish later at `--parallel 2` than at `--parallel 1`
  (47 s against 40 s; 44 s with `--decode-share 0.95`), and so does a 64K prompt beside a reply (21 s against 19 s).
  The default --parallel auto uses the single host.
- The 1.0.12 gfx1151 Qwen receipts leave the 27B cancellation failure open and the 9B/27B drafted/plain comparisons
  unrun. Those receipts do not establish a new 1.1.0 device pass.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a Mac: a turn more than `--keep-warm` seconds after the last request (900 by default) takes
  about 2 s to its first token on an M3 Ultra, even when its prompt is cached, while macOS wires the model again.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on one GB10 reads its n-gram embedding tables (29.8 GiB in the MLX 4-bit MTP checkpoint) from
  the checkpoint files through the page cache, so they compete with the server's own memory. As saved prompt states
  (up to 16 GiB by default) fill, time to first token on a new prompt of about 65,000 tokens rises from 34 s to about
  38 s at 1,536-row passes, and from 27 s to about 32 s at 16,384-row passes, with the tables paging in both. One
  16,384-row run reached 38.9 s. With the prompt cache off, repeats stay within about 1%.
- On a Mac without tensor units (M1 to M4), Flash Next's uniform 6-bit checkpoint decodes different tokens from 1.0.9
  since 1.0.10's faster products. `FZ_M3_LANES=1` keeps the earlier kernels and their tokens.
- @Bizuayeu's regression run on shipped 1.1.0 loaded the whole GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 checkpoint on two GB10s at TP=2 in 302.1 s, kept one token hash per prompt across three runs and found a passphrase in 199,307 tokens; scored prompts and more than two ranks were not covered ([#1040](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/1040)).
- DeepSeek-V4.1 CUDA pieces land in this release, but no release binary serves DeepSeek checkpoints until its whole-model gate ([#827](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/827)) passes.


## HIP builds

- gfx1100 with Ubuntu's clang 21 hipcc fails to compile `affine_dot2_stream_relu2_pair<Dot, 6, 1, 8>` ("branch size
  exceeds simm16"). Build with ROCm 7.13, or pass `-Dhip-relax-branches=true`, which adds
  `-mllvm -amdgpu-s-branch-bits=15` to the gfx1100 code objects. The option is off by default and has not been run on a
  gfx1100 GPU ([#1521](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/1521)).

## Living Weights (`--slide`)

- Living Weights implementation and safety work is in the 1.1.1 tree, including CUDA learners, shared retention
  controls, lesson progress and save/restart work. Model, retention and save/restart qualification remains pending.
  The #1029 lesson-counter repair is excluded and remains held: rejected lessons must not shift the prompts used
  for later training and checks.

- Facts about the same subject can overwrite each other, a later fact about the user can disturb an earlier one's
  answers on a GB10, yes-or-no questions about a changed value are unreliable, facts pile up badly past a few dozen, and
  thinking on brings back fewer answers. 1.0.8's release notes have the measurements.
- Learned facts cost decode speed on a Mac. 1.0.9 took back about 8% on an M3 Ultra with two facts; 1.0.8's M5 Ultra
  figures (213 tok/s after ten facts, 248 before any) have not been measured again.
- A rollback is all or nothing: `tensorfold slide rollback` returns the folder to its snapshot, undoing every lesson
  and delete since the first. One fact can be deleted on its own (`DELETE /v1/slide/fact/{id}`), which silences its
  neurons rather than erasing them. A key keeps other clients from teaching, but anyone with the key can teach a wrong
  fact. Teach a copy of the checkpoint folder.
- On file systems without clones, such as ext4, the snapshot is a full copy of the files a lesson can change, 18.5 GB
  for Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, and the rollback copies them back.
- The folder hold that keeps a server and a rollback apart works between TensorFold processes only: other tools that
  write files ignore it.

## Web research (`--cortheon`)

- The instruction filter that removes orders aimed at the model from web text is a heuristic. It reads each line on its
  own, so an order split across a line break is not seen whole, and a page written to steer the model could still
  make it put conversation text into the path of a URL it fetches. [docs/cortheon.md](cortheon.md) says what leaves the
  machine.
# Living Weights: how to use it

Living Weights teaches a running model new facts. Tell it "I like blue." and a few minutes later it answers "What colour
do I like?" with blue. The fact goes into the model's own weights, so it is still there after a restart, without
`--slide`, and on any TensorFold server you start from the same folder, Mac or NVIDIA.

It is not a prompt cache, a retrieval index or an adapter: each fact it keeps becomes about ten new neurons inside the
model, written into the checkpoint's own safetensors files. Nothing the model already had is changed. It shipped in 1.0.3
as Sliding Weights (experimental), and its flag and API use the name `slide`.

## Repeating a lesson

The same text and supplied questions can take different steps and choose different neurons on separate runs.
The lesson writer generates extra question wordings at temperature 0.9, including when you supply questions.
Sampled requests use a fresh random seed by default. The fitter also shuffles examples, with deterministic seeds
from its round and pass counters; the lesson history affects those counters.

For a repeatability check, start each run from fresh copies of the same checkpoint and graph. Use
`--prompt-seed` to key sampled generations by their rendered prompt. Keep the build, backend, seed salt and settings fixed.
This controls the writer's random seeds; it does not promise identical lessons across devices or builds.
The acceptance checks still decide what is kept on every run.

## What you need

- An Apple-silicon Mac (tested on an M5 Ultra and an M3 Ultra), or an NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark) with the CUDA build,
  with room for the model and a copy of it. On a GB10, `--slide` also keeps GPU memory for its trainer (about 26 GiB
  for Nemotron, 10.6 GiB for Qwen3.8 Flash Next); on a Mac the trainer works on the model's own weights.
- The Nemotron 3.5 Lightning MLX 4-bit checkpoint, or, on a GB10 only, the Qwen3.8 Flash Next MLX 4-bit group-32
  checkpoint with its MTP head. Macs refuse `--slide` for Flash Next.
- A TensorFold build with the pocket learner described here (the release after 1.0.6). A folder taught by 1.0.3 to
  1.0.6 still serves and answers from what it learned, but `--slide` refuses it: those releases saved lessons into
  the shared experts the pocket widens. Teach a fresh copy instead.

A Nemotron folder that learned on either backend serves on the other.

## Quick start

### 1. Install or upgrade TensorFold

```sh
brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold    # or: brew upgrade tensorfold
```

On a GB10, install the `linux-aarch64` archive as the [RUNBOOK](../RUNBOOK.md#linux-and-cuda) shows.

### 2. Get the model and make a copy to teach

Learning rewrites files in the model folder, and so does deleting a fact. The server keeps the folder's original
files before its first lesson or delete, so `tensorfold slide rollback` can undo them all at once
([Undo what it learned](#undo-what-it-learned)), but teach a copy and keep the pulled model as it is.

```sh
tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit
src=$(ls -d ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--TensorFold--NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit/snapshots/* | head -1)
mkdir -p ~/models
cp -cRL "$src" ~/models/nemotron-living
```

Use exactly these `cp` flags. The pulled model lives in the Hugging Face cache, whose folders hold links to shared
files: `-L` copies the real files, so learning can never write into the cached original, and `-c` makes APFS clones, so
the copy takes no extra disk until learning changes it. `--slide` refuses a folder whose files are links, so serving the
cache's own folder stops at startup instead of changing it.

On Linux, copy without `-c` (there are no APFS clones), which takes the checkpoint's full 18.5 GB:

```sh
cp -RL "$src" ~/models/nemotron-living
```

### 3. Make a key and start the server with `--slide`

```sh
(umask 077; openssl rand -hex 24 > ~/models/slide-key)
tensorfold serve ~/models/nemotron-living --slide --api-key-file ~/models/slide-key \
  --slide-graph ~/models/nemotron-living-facts.json
```

`--slide` turns learning on, and it starts only with a key, because any client that reaches the server could otherwise
rewrite the model's weights. Give it `--api-key-file FILE` (one key a line, readable only by you), `--api-key KEY` or
`TENSORFOLD_API_KEY`. The server reads the key before it loads the model. It stops with one line naming the cause when
there is no key, when the key file is missing, empty or readable by other users (`chmod 600` it), or when a key has a
space in it. Every request then sends the key, as the commands below do; [API keys](api.md#api-keys) has the rest.

`--slide-graph` keeps the list of learned facts in a file, so it survives a restart; without it the list lives in
memory, though the weights keep what they learned either way. The server listens on `http://127.0.0.1:8080` unless you
pass `--host` or `--port`.

### 4. Teach it a fact

```sh
curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/learn \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"text": "I like blue."}'
```

The reply streams server-sent events: `fact` when it finds a fact, `learning` when it starts, `progress` during the
lesson, and `learned` when it is done. Progress carries `phase`, `at` and `of`; zero `of` means the total is unknown.
A `progress` event with `heartbeat: true` arrives every five seconds while a long unit is still running. It reports
that the request remains open, without claiming another unit completed.
After the facts finish, `saving` progress continues until `saved` confirms the shard write or `failed` reports its
error with `phase: "saving"`. `[DONE]` follows that result.

`"recalled": true` means it answered its held-out questions with the fact, and its change is kept. `false` means none of it is kept: the lesson is taken out whole before anything is written, and
`message` says why, for example that the fact did not come back on its held-out questions or that it disturbed another
answer. Lesson time depends on the family and device and can take many minutes. The first lesson also keeps the
folder's original files before opening the stream.

New lessons use conversation checks only where the learner reads full conversation prompts through taps. Bounded
readers use standalone held-out questions. Saved graph entries retain their recorded conversation checks.

A body may also carry `"questions": [...]` (at most 16 of up to 300 bytes each; anything but an array of strings is a
400). Each fact's lesson takes them ahead of the questions the model writes, and the model answers each knowing the
fact, so you supply no answers. They are judged as the written ones are: one that does not name the fact's subject, asks
the fact's own value or is not answered from the fact is dropped, and the text-only path is unchanged without the field.
The model-written questions establish the subject before supplied questions are filtered. For example `{"text": "Our warehouse robot is called
Pebble.", "questions": ["What is our warehouse robot called?"]}`.

### 5. Ask

Use the normal chat API, from any client:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What colour do I like?"}]}'
```

## How it works

Every MoE layer's shared expert gets 64 extra neurons, zero until a fact uses them. The first save widens the shared
expert's tensors in the shards (3712 to 3776 neurons) and records `tensorfold_learned_neurons` in `config.json`; any MLX
loader reads the folder as a slightly wider model. A fact takes one neuron at each of about ten layers.

- A fact about you ("I like blue.") fires its neurons at the first row of the reply to a question about it.
- A fact about someone or something ("My sister is called Ana.", "Quillmoor Labs was founded in Sheffield.") fires them
  at the last token of the subject where a question names it, in the middle layers, where models keep what they know of a
  subject. A question has to name the subject: "When does the Quillmoor team deploy?" reaches the fact, "When does the
  team deploy?" does not.
- Each neuron's input weights are fitted to fire on the fact's questions and stay at zero everywhere else. Its output is
  then fitted through the model so the answers come back, with thinking on too, while other answers that name the same
  subject stay as they were.
- The model writes the lesson itself: a dozen questions, its own answers with the fact in front of it, the same answers
  under client system messages and after an unrelated exchange, and near misses it must leave alone.

Before keeping a fact, the server asks held-out wordings it never trained on, with thinking off and on, plus near misses
and unrelated prompts. A fact that does not come back, or changes an answer it should not, is taken out and leaves
nothing behind. An earlier fact's neuron that the new lesson would disturb is refitted only away from its own rows.

## Teaching it more

- Several facts at once: put them in one text, as in `{"text": "I like blue. My sister is called Ana."}`. Each is
  learned in turn.
- A file: send its contents as the text, for example:

  ```sh
  jq -Rs '{text: .}' notes.md | curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/learn \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-
  ```

- A web page: fetch its text first, or use omp's `/learn <url>` below, which does it for you.

The server keeps answering chat requests while it learns: learning runs when no reply is being generated. Short,
distinct facts work best.

## From omp

The omp extension in `packaging/omp/sliding-weights.ts` adds a `/learn` command. Copy it into
`~/.omp/agent/extensions/`, then select your TensorFold model in omp and give that model the server's key as its API
key; `/learn` sends it.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/learn` or `/learn on` | Learn from this session as you work: each finished turn is sent to the model |
| `/learn I like blue.` | Learn the facts you type |
| `/learn @notes.md` | Learn a file |
| `/learn https://example.com/page` | Learn a web page's readable text |
| `/learn graph` | Open the fact graph in your browser |
| `/learn off` | Stop learning from the session |

A panel shows each fact as queued, learning, learned or missed.

## See what it learned

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/slide` in a browser while the server runs. It draws the model in 3D and updates live:

- The model as a tower of its 52 layers. Each MoE layer is a ring carrying its 64 pocket neurons, and a neuron glows in
  the colour of the fact that owns it.
- The checkpoint's shard files beside the tower, each linked to the layers it holds, with how full each pocket is.
  A save shows which files it wrote, how many bytes and how long it took.
- The facts and the people and things they name, as a graph around the tower: queued, learning, learned or missed.
- The lesson running now, phase by phase: writing, reading every layer, fitting the neurons' inputs, fitting their
  outputs (with the loss after each step), checking each question, then kept or taken out.

Drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom, and click a fact for its neurons, the questions it was checked with and its
rounds. Phones get a bottom sheet. Without WebGL2, or with `/slide?flat`, the page draws a flat graph from the same
data. The page asks for the server's key once and keeps it for that browser tab.

- `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/graph`
  returns the same data as JSON: each fact's state, neurons (layer, index and key), questions and rounds, and the
  model's layers, pocket and shards.
- The same with `-X DELETE` clears the graph. The weights keep what they learned. To take one fact out of the weights,
  see [Delete one fact](#delete-one-fact).

## Audit a pocket

`tensorfold slide audit --server http://127.0.0.1:8080 --key-stdin < ~/models/slide-key` explicitly measures what each
learned fact's neurons fire on. Add `--json` for the complete machine-readable audit, or `--threshold 0.02` (a rate
from 0 through 1) to flag an off-subject firing rate above 2% instead of the default 1%. The same request is
`GET /v1/slide/graph?audit=1&threshold=0.02`; its response adds `audit` and keeps the existing graph fields.
Ordinary graph requests do not run an audit, and audits require a pocket learner served with `--slide`.

The four groups are the fact's questions, its subject in eight other contexts, the other learned facts' questions,
and a fixed general bank of 256 prompts over 32 topics. Subject extraction is a heuristic from the fact and its
questions; an empty subject means that group is unavailable. Questions are asked cold, without their saved
conversation. Every group's prompt count and rate are reported, so missing coverage is visible.

A prompt fires a neuron when its largest absolute activation over all rendered prompt rows exceeds `0.0001`.
The audit reconstructs activations with the pocket's host math from a private snapshot of the live weights and the
forward pass's BF16 layer inputs. It lists each neuron's group and overall firing rates, its off-subject rate,
flag, and five strongest off-subject prompts with their activation and row. These are diagnostic flags, not a
verdict that a fact is wrong. The probe bank and thresholds are versioned in the JSON.

The engine reads one prompt per idle step; serving requests can run between prompts. A large audit can take time.
Lessons and deletes wait until it finishes. No weights, lessons or checks change, no graph or shard is written,
and the audit never saves, undoes or refits anything. Unsupported, overlong or incomplete measurements refuse
instead of presenting a partial result as complete. Real-checkpoint activation and serving-parity gates are still
required for a newly supported backend.

## Delete one fact

```sh
curl -N -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/fact/2 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"reason": "my sister changed her name"}'
```

Take the fact's `id` from `GET /v1/slide/graph`. The body is optional; its `reason` goes into the graph. Like a
lesson, the reply streams server-sent events. With a few facts learned it takes seconds; every learned fact's
questions are asked twice, so it grows with them:

1. `fact`: the fact and its state.
2. `checking` with `"when": "before"`: every learned fact's held-out questions are asked as its lesson checked them,
   with thinking off and on, and the wordings its lesson never trained on with thinking off.
3. `zeroed`: the input weights of the fact's neurons are set to zero in the running model, so they never fire, and
   their layers are rounded to the 4-bit values the shards will hold, so the checks after read what will be written.
4. `checking` with `"when": "after"`, then one `checked` event a fact, saying whether it came back before and after.
5. `forgot` with `"deleted": true`: every other fact still comes back, and the deleted fact's questions no longer give
   its answer. The change is written into the shards, the graph marks the fact `deleted` with the time and reason, and
   its neurons at the top of each layer's pocket are free for later lessons.
6. Or `forgot` with `"deleted": false`: the delete did not complete, because a check failed or a write failed (below).
   For a failed check, the neurons are put back exactly as they were, nothing is written, and `message` names the
   fact and question that failed and what the model said.

`forgot` also carries `state`, the fact's state in the graph file when the request ends. A delete writes two things,
the shards and the graph file, in this order, so that together they never claim more than is on disk:

1. The graph file marks the fact `deleting`.
2. The shards are written.
3. The graph file marks the fact `deleted`.

`"deleted": true` means all three were written. When one fails, `forgot` says `"deleted": false` and `message` says
what happened:

| What failed | What is on disk | `state` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The graph file, before the shards | Nothing changed: the delete was put back | `learned` |
| The shards | The delete was put back and the shards written again as they were, so nothing changed | `learned` |
| The shards, and writing them back too | The folder may hold part of the delete | `deleting` |
| The graph file, after the shards | The shards hold the delete; the graph file does not say so yet | `deleting` |

A put-back restores the pocket in memory at once, and on the GPU once every layer's upload succeeds. If one does not
(on CUDA, an upload or a graph capture that fails), the server keeps what it needs to put it back, and refuses every
reply until it lands: a reply says "a Living Weights delete could not be put back on the device" (one that was
already waiting ends with the same words, unanswered), and a learn or delete request answers 503. Each learn or
delete request tries the put-back again first, and replies come back once it lands. A restart reloads the folder,
which a put-back never wrote.

A fact left `deleting`, by one of these or by a crash, is settled by sending the delete again, after a restart too.
If its neurons are silent already, an earlier delete reached the shards, and the graph file now records it. If not,
the delete runs again, checks and all. A fact left `deleting` is not checked as a kept fact meanwhile, and a lesson
placed on one of its neurons takes that neuron over. Without `--slide-graph` the graph lives in memory only, and only
the shards are written.

A kept fact passes when each answer that came back before the delete still does, and at least half of its other
wordings do if they did before. The deleted fact passes when none of its questions gives its answer, or when the model
as shipped gives that answer too (a likely guess, such as a common colour, is no trace of the fact).

To delete a statement learned as several facts, select their IDs explicitly in one request:

```sh
curl -N -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/facts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"ids": [1, 2], "reason": "duplicate statement"}'
```

`ids` must contain 1 to 256 distinct positive integer IDs. Every selected fact must exist and hold neurons; an invalid
selection refuses the entire request before any cut. A fact left `deleting` can also be selected for retry. Graph
links never select another fact: they are not proven dependencies. The selected neurons are silenced in one cut,
then every selected fact must stop answering under the same shipped-model exception, and every retained fact must
pass the same checks as for a single delete. Any regression restores the whole selection, with no shard save.
The graph marks the selection `deleting` in one write, the shards save once, and the graph marks the selection
`deleted` in one write. On a write failure, the same recovery rules above apply to all selected facts; retry with
the same IDs. Each selected ID gets a final `forgot` event. Successful batch events include `selected` and
`total_neurons`, the count for the whole selection. This operation silences the selected facts and does not rebuild
an older value or scrub their unused output columns.
For disjoint additive neurons whose retained weights never moved, silencing gives the same forward values as never
teaching the selected rows. Refitted neighbours, replacements and shared quantization groups can retain history, so
a delete does not promise byte equality to a separately trained folder. The retained-answer checks detect regressions
on their questions; they do not prove equality for every possible prompt.

Host qualification covers duplicate orientations refused one at a time but deleted together, a retained-answer
regression restoring the whole cut, invalid selections, graph allocation/write failures, shard-write restoration,
retry of the pending selection, and both HTTP routes with JSON bodies. Checkpoint qualification must repeat the
duplicate and retained-fact cases on each backend after save and restart.

- A fact a newer one replaced has its neurons at zero already: deleting it answers "nothing to delete" and changes
  nothing. Deleting the newer fact does not bring back the one it replaced.
- A fact learned before this release kept its questions but not their answers: its check holds each question to the
  answer the model gave just before the delete.
- A delete silences a fact; it does not erase it. A deleted neuron's output weights stay in the shards, unused, until
  a later lesson takes the neuron. Zeroing them too would round again the 4-bit groups that other facts' neurons in
  the same layer share, and move their answers.
- A model with a fact deleted is close to the same model never taught it, but not the same: the lessons after it
  were learned with it in place.
- Only freed neurons at the top of a layer's pocket go to the next lesson. One below another fact's neuron stays
  silent, and taken, until that fact is deleted too.
- While a delete runs, chat replies already see the fact gone; a delete that is put back brings it back once the GPU
  takes the put-back (above).
- Before its first write, a delete keeps the folder's original files as a lesson does, so a rollback undoes deletes
  along with lessons.
- A delete changes the weights only. Recall's records and saved conversations (`--recall`, `--learn-conversations`)
  keep what the conversations said, the fact's words included.

## Keep, move or reset what it learned

- Keep: learned facts live in the folder. Restart the server, with or without `--slide`, and they are still there.
- Move: copy the folder to another Mac or to an NVIDIA machine and serve it there. It answers the same way. A copy of
  the whole folder takes its snapshot (`.tensorfold-original/`) along; leave that folder out if you will not roll the
  copy back.
- Delete one fact: `DELETE /v1/slide/fact/{id}`, as [above](#delete-one-fact).
- Reset: stop the server and run `tensorfold slide rollback ~/models/nemotron-living`, below, or delete the copy and
  clone a fresh one from the original (step 2). A rollback undoes every lesson and delete since the snapshot.

## Undo what it learned

Before a folder's first lesson, the server keeps every file a lesson can change in a hidden folder inside it,
`.tensorfold-original/`: each `*.safetensors` file, `model.safetensors.index.json` and `config.json`. On a Mac, and
on Btrfs or XFS, each kept file is a clone that shares the original's blocks, which takes no disk at first. The first
lesson writes new shard files, and from then on the snapshot keeps the original blocks on disk; a copy cloned from the
pulled model with `cp -c`, as in step 2, shares them with the pulled model, so they cost nothing more. On other file
systems, such as ext4, each kept file is a plain copy, so the snapshot takes the model's size again (18.5 GB for
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning); the server checks the disk has room for the copies and the largest file again first, and
refuses the lesson with HTTP 507 and the space it needs when it does not. The snapshot's `SHA256SUMS` lists every kept
file's SHA-256 (`shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS` inside the folder checks it by hand). The server checks the kept files
against it as it makes the snapshot, and removes the snapshot and refuses the lesson if one differs.

Later lessons reuse the snapshot, which is never refreshed. Each server checks it against `SHA256SUMS` at its own
first lesson, and refuses to teach while it does not match ("the way back is broken"). Model loaders read only the
folder's own files, never a hidden folder, and `tensorfold info` leaves it out of the model's size. A folder taught
before it had a snapshot (by 1.0.7 to 1.0.11) gets one at its next lesson, holding the folder as it is then; the log
says so, and a rollback returns there, not to the model as pulled.

To undo every lesson, stop the server and run:

```sh
tensorfold slide rollback ~/models/nemotron-living
```

The rollback:

- refuses while any TensorFold server has the folder open. Each server holds its folder while it runs (shared, or
  exclusive with `--slide`), and a server in turn refuses to start while a `--slide` server or a rollback holds it.
- checks every kept file against `SHA256SUMS` first, and changes nothing when one does not match.
- clones every kept file beside its own where the file system makes clones, and checks the disk has room for the
  largest file it must copy instead, before it changes any file: a refusal for space, or a clone that fails, leaves
  the folder as it was. It then puts each file back (a copy is made beside the file and checked against its SHA-256
  before it is renamed over it) and checks every file's SHA-256 against the manifest.
- only then removes what the lessons added: lesson files (`living-weights-00001.safetensors` and on, or an older
  `living-weights.safetensors`), writes a lesson left cut short (`NAME.tmp` beside a kept or lesson file), and the
  fact graph files that `--slide-graph` named while the folder learned. A fact graph can live outside the folder; the
  rollback removes it all the same, since it describes weights that are gone, and prints every path it removes.
- leaves everything else: files you added after the snapshot, files a lesson never writes (the tokenizer, templates,
  a download's `.cache`), and the snapshot itself, so you can teach the folder again and roll back again.

It prints how many files it put back, their size, how many were clones and how long it took. When a put-back file does
not match, it says so and leaves the lessons' files where they are; run it again.

## Who can teach it

A key stops clients that do not have it from teaching the model. It does not stop someone who has the key from
teaching it something wrong, and a learned fact stays until you delete it or roll the folder back, which undoes every
lesson since the snapshot. Give the key only to clients you trust, and keep the original model. The folder hold works
between TensorFold processes only: other tools that write files (`cp`, `rsync`, an editor) do not take it, so leave
the folder's files alone while a server or a rollback has it.

## When something goes wrong

| You see | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `501 this engine does not learn: serve its model with --slide` | Start the server with `--slide`, on a Mac or a GB10 |
| `503 the engine cannot take a learn request now` | Another learn request is running; send yours when it ends |
| `503 a learn or delete request is running` | A delete does not wait for another learn or delete: send it when that one ends |
| `forgot` with `"deleted": false` | A check or a write failed; `message` says which, and `state` what the graph file holds (see Delete one fact) |
| `a Living Weights delete could not be put back on the device` on a reply | The GPU did not take a delete's put-back: send the delete again to retry it, or restart the server |
| `400 text is required` | The JSON body needs a `"text"` field |
| `learned` with `"recalled": false` | Nothing of the fact was kept (its neurons were taken out), and `message` says why: for example it did not come back on its held-out questions, it kept answering questions about something else, or the model wrote too few clean questions to learn from |
| `--slide rewrites the model's own files, and … is a link to data another file shares` at startup | The folder holds links into the Hugging Face cache (or hard links); make the copy with `cp -cRL` (Linux: `cp -RL`) as in step 2 |
| `--slide learns on a GB10 (sm_121) so far` at startup | CUDA learning is qualified on a GB10 only; serve this GPU without `--slide`, or teach on a Mac or a GB10 |
| `--slide runs a prompt one chunk at a time` at startup | Serve it without `--segments` or `TF_CUDA_SEGMENTS` |
| `--slide trains on Flash Next's own glue` at startup | Serve Flash Next without `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS` |
| `--slide adds learned neurons beside every shared expert, and … is unquantized` at startup | The folder was taught by TensorFold 1.0.3 to 1.0.6; serve it without `--slide`, or teach a fresh copy |
| `--slide lets any client that reaches this server rewrite the weights in …` at startup | Add a key: `--api-key-file FILE`, `--api-key KEY` or `TENSORFOLD_API_KEY` (step 3) |
| `--slide needs a key this server can read, and --api-key-file … gives none: …` at startup | Make the file (one key a line), `chmod 600` it, and check its path; the end of the line gives the reason |
| `--slide needs a key this server accepts, and --api-key or TENSORFOLD_API_KEY gives one it refuses: …` at startup | A key has a space or a control character in it; use one without |
| `` … is held by a --slide server or a `tensorfold slide rollback` … `` at startup | Another server is teaching the folder, or a rollback is running; stop that server or let the rollback finish |
| `--slide rewrites the files in …, and another TensorFold process has that folder open` at startup | Stop the other server, or teach another copy |
| `… cannot be locked, so a rollback could rewrite it while --slide teaches it` at startup | The folder is on a file system without file locks (some network shares); teach a copy on a local disk |
| `… is on a file system without clones, and copying its original files needs … GB free` | At a lesson (HTTP 507), the snapshot does not fit; from `slide rollback`, the copies back do not fit and nothing changed. Free that much space, or teach a copy on APFS, Btrfs or XFS |
| `500 … the way back is broken …` | The snapshot does not match its manifest; move `.tensorfold-original` out of the folder to keep the folder as it is now, then teach again (a new snapshot starts from the folder as it is) |
| `a TensorFold server or another rollback has … open` from `slide rollback` | Stop the server first |
| `… has no .tensorfold-original snapshot …` from `slide rollback` | The folder never learned with a release that keeps one; reset it from the original model |
| `… does not match its line in SHA256SUMS, so … was left as it is` from `slide rollback` | The snapshot is damaged and the folder is unchanged; reset it from the original model |
| The answer has not changed yet | Wait for the `learned` event before asking |

## What to expect

Living Weights is experimental. Measured on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (MLX 4-bit) on an M5 Ultra, an M3 Ultra and a GB10:

- **Facts you tell it.** "I like blue.", "My sister is called Ana." and "My dog is called Ginger.", taught one after
  another, each came back on both test questions on all three machines, with a client system message in front too,
  and after a plain restart. Unrelated questions kept their answers and no fact leaked into questions it does not
  answer. With thinking on, a fact sometimes misses one wording ("Do you remember what colour I like?"): the model
  recalls the fact in its reasoning and stops there without a reply, or says it keeps no memory of past
  conversations.
- **Short documents.** From a three-sentence handbook (six facts) it answered 3 to 6 of 6 questions across six runs on
  both backends, with no drift. In three runs the founder's name also answered a question about another role ("Who is
  the head of marketing?"), and in one the team chat tool answered a question about video calls. A fact it cannot
  learn is left out, and `learned` says why.
- **Long documents about one subject are the weak spot.** From a 21-fact company handbook it kept about half the facts
  and answered 6 of 16 questions, and with ten facts about the company kept, its answers about things the handbook does
  not say got worse, most with thinking on. Teach a few facts per subject, and always teach a copy.
- **Time.** Each fact needs its own generated lesson and checks. The first lesson also writes the keep prompts and
  personal bank. Independent cold prompts share the serving lanes; time still depends on the model and device.
- **Memory.** On a Mac the trainer works on the model's own weights. On a GB10, `--slide` keeps about 26 GiB for its
  trainer, which is ready a few seconds after the server starts.
- **Undo.** On an M3 Ultra, the snapshot of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (7 files, 18.5 GB) took 5.3 s as clones, a new
  server's check of it 2.6 s, and a rollback 5.6 to 5.7 s. On a GB10's ext4, with a build for the GB10's own CPU, the
  snapshot took 35 s as copies and 18.5 GB of disk, a check 2.6 s, and a rollback, which copies one file at a time, 58
  to 91 s; the release's Linux build computes SHA-256 about five times slower (0.39 GB/s against 2.1 GB/s), so expect
  its checks to take longer. Rolled back, the folder matched the untaught copy byte for byte and, served again, gave
  its replies token for token.
- **Serving.** Without learned facts the server gives the same replies, token for token, at the same speed as without
  Living Weights. A folder holding many learned facts decodes slower on a Mac (about 16% with 21 facts in the pocket),
  and drafted replies still equal plain ones.

On Qwen3.8 Flash Next (MLX 4-bit group 32 with its MTP head) on a GB10, five facts about the user were taught one
after another to a fresh copy. Three were kept, in 8.7 to 10.5 minutes each (two and a half to four of them the model writing its
lesson and three to four its trainer's first round, half a minute each round of checks), and each came back right after
its lesson; one was refused at once, the model having written too few clean answers to learn from, and one was not
kept after five rounds in 40 minutes. A later lesson can stop an earlier fact coming back (#870): after the five, two
of the three kept facts still answered. Unrelated questions kept their answers, plain and `--slide` restarts gave the
same replies, drafted replies equal `"draft": false` and four streams at once equal each alone. With three facts in
the pocket, drafted decode was 5% slower (80 against 84 tokens a second on code) and `--no-drafts` 1% slower.

While it learns, near misses and free writing about the fact's subject are trained to stay as they were. Before
keeping a fact, it checks wordings it never trained on, with thinking off and on, near misses and unrelated prompts.
If the fact does not come back, or another answer changes, the whole lesson is taken out before anything is written.
It also asks a few questions about the user that nothing told it, such as a cat's name or the user's own name; a lesson
that makes it answer one with something made up ("Your cat's name is Whiskers.") is taken out too. Keep the original
model for anything that matters.


### Fixed drift and supplied recall

With `--slide --slide-drift-gate`, each candidate that reaches the commit checks is measured against `server/slide_panel.zig`:
115 original unrelated prompts, 15 untold personal controls and 20 fictional neighbour questions.
This is a new fixed panel, not the reporter's unavailable 155-question panel.
The graph records the untaught replies and token SHA-256 hashes once. Every later candidate checks
that the untaught replies still match that baseline. It never substitutes the previous taught reply.
Greedy replies use 64 tokens with thinking off; where supported, a separate bounded thinking pass is recorded.
Changed unrelated replies are classified as byte-equal, alike, judged the same, or changed in meaning.

Supply fixed external recall wordings separately from the writer's `questions`:

```json
{"text":"I like blue.","recall":[{"fact":"I like blue.","question":"Which shade do I favour?","answer":"blue"}]}
```

`fact` must match an extracted fact exactly and `answer` must occur in it. These wordings never go to
the writer. A wording that the generated training plan also reads makes the measurement incomplete.
The graph's `facts[].recall` and `facts[].evaluation` retain the external set and per-lesson receipt;
`drift_baseline` retains the original replies. Early refusals are explicitly `not_measured`.
Measured refusals keep their candidate receipt even after the fitted lesson is taken out.

`--slide --slide-drift-gate` adds an opt-in commit gate, after every existing acceptance check.
Missing external recall, a changed baseline/profile, an incomplete panel or a failed receipt write refuses.
The hard limits are zero invented personal answers, zero leaks, at most two meaning changes before ten
kept facts and at most five from ten onward, plus 90% supplied recall and, from ten facts, 90% earlier-fact retention.
Drift uses the worst of three greedy passes and recall the median. Thinking recall is reported separately.
Byte-equality targets (103/115 after three facts, 92/115 after ten) remain report-only.
Without the flag, `recall` is ignored and no fixed-panel requests, receipt writes or new graph fields are added.
An earlier fact without supplied recall and a complete receipt makes the next measurement incomplete.
To enable the gate over an existing graph, delete facts missing those records, then re-teach them with the gate
and external wordings enabled.

These three passes observe one fitted candidate. They do not replace the release experiment's three
fresh-checkpoint lesson sequences. Full-model results, keep rates and measurement cost on every backend
remain unchecked; no family is qualified by the host fixtures.
# Loaded groups in community-v2

A benchmark measures the group's serving endpoint. Rank count and machine count differ: several ranks can use one node. Managed and attached runs both read `GET /v1/benchmark/manifest` after the server loads. They copy its accepted inventory, never a client rank flag or `TF_NEMOTRON_WORLD` / `TF_BENCHMARK_RANK_COUNT` hint. Missing or invalid inventories stay unranked. Legacy manifests can still supply model and hardware metadata, but their rank hints are not copied into new receipts. Start followers separately and attach to the serving rank when measuring an existing group.

A new v2 receipt may add a root `group` object. The workload suite ID and digest stay unchanged; the topology is an additional comparison dimension, not a new prompt or token budget. V1 retains exactly its previous fields, canonical bytes and rank limit of 1, 2 or null. Legacy v2 receipts without `group` keep that same bound. New grouped v2 receipts accept 1 through 8 loaded ranks; a larger count without a complete group refuses.

```json
{"schema_version":1,"source":"loaded-group","rank_count":2,"category":"multi-node","nodes":[{"id":0,"ranks":[0],"hardware":{"cpu_model":"Example CPU","system_memory_bytes":137438953472,"memory_type":"unified","gpus":[{"name":"Example GPU","memory_bytes":128849018880,"cores":null}],"gpu_count":1,"source":"detected"}},{"id":1,"ranks":[1],"hardware":{"cpu_model":"Example CPU","system_memory_bytes":137438953472,"memory_type":"unified","gpus":[{"name":"Example GPU","memory_bytes":128849018880,"cores":null}],"gpu_count":1,"source":"detected"}}]}
```

The manifest carries the same `group`; `settings.rank_count` in its receipt must equal `group.rank_count`. Node IDs are ordered ordinals. Their sorted rank lists cover every rank from zero through count minus one exactly once. Each node carries its public CPU model, system memory, memory type and GPUs, with the same allowlist as ordinary receipt hardware. GPUs describe devices used by the loaded group, deduplicated within a node. Root `hardware` repeats the node containing serving rank zero for older displays; it must not be mistaken for the whole group.

CUDA groups query the loaded communicator's count and rank, collect each rank's inventory at startup, and publish only the frozen result. Private boot and GPU identities establish node membership and device deduplication but never enter JSON. Paired Metal transports exchange that inventory during their existing startup handshake. An older paired peer can still serve, but its missing inventory leaves the pair unranked. A missing identity, conflicting hardware, unsupported count or incomplete rank cover cannot become a one-rank fallback. HTTP reads copy the snapshot under the unload lock; a parked or draining engine attests no loaded group. Ordinary single-rank engines retain their local hardware probe. ROCm distributed inventory is not yet implemented and remains unranked; ROCm publication is also still disabled.

The receiver should partition on `suite.id`, `suite.sha256` and `group.category`, keeping legacy receipts without a group separate. Within a category, retain `group.rank_count`, `group.nodes[].ranks` and each `group.nodes[].hardware` as comparison filters. `group.category` is `single-node` exactly when `group.nodes.length` is one, otherwise `multi-node`. Do not infer it from rank count or GPU count. In particular, two GPUs on one node belong to `single-node`, while two nodes sharing identical GPU names remain `multi-node`.

The loaded-group source is provenance within the engine, not cryptographic authentication. A saved receipt or an arbitrary attached server can still lie. Validation detects structural inconsistencies such as a changed settings count or duplicate ranks; it cannot authenticate hardware supplied by an untrusted server. Transport and link class, per-rank timing, effective settings, boot agreement, exactness at that world size and process start order still belong in the local run report. A failed launch is not a slow successful measurement.

Community-v2 publication remains disabled until the receiver accepts its routing and topology fields and separates those categories. This engine change does not implement or certify the receiver's ranking. Runs above eight ranks, missing inventories and unsupported transports stay in local reports.
# Runtime memory diagnostics

`GET /memory` and `GET /v1/memory` return a read-only JSON snapshot with `schema_version: 1`.
Both routes require an API key when authentication is enabled, including with `--metrics-open`.
Neither route resets counters; `reset_peak=1` has no effect here. `/health` retains its existing contract.

All sizes are integer **bytes**. Optional objects and fields are omitted when their source is unavailable;
zero means a measured or configured zero. The endpoint publishes no paths, UUIDs, keys, hostnames or prompts.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `context_window` | Loaded engine's prompt-plus-reply token limit; omitted when unspecified. |
| `context_fitted` | Whether startup memory fitting reduced the context. |
| `process.source` | `darwin_rusage_info_v4`; this scope is currently available on macOS. |
| `process.physical_footprint_bytes` | Kernel physical footprint, including charged Metal buffers. |
| `process.lifetime_peak_physical_footprint_bytes` | Kernel lifetime maximum, including peaks between polls. Never reset by TensorFold. |
| `device.active_bytes`, `device.cache_bytes` | Existing backend allocator counters, where implemented. |
| `device.peak_bytes` | Backend peak since startup or the last `/health?reset_peak=1`. |
| `device.peak_scope` | `since_start_or_health_reset`; distinct from the process lifetime peak. |
| `prompt_cache_plan` | Immutable retained-prefix budget applied at startup, reported by Nemotron, Flash Next, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-MoE, Gemma 4, LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B on Macs, and by Qwen3.5-2B with `--prompt-cache-gib`. |

The cache plan contains `source`, `budget_bytes`, and `explicit_budget`. With OS readings,
`source` is `physical_footprint` and the plan also includes the sizing inputs: `ram_bytes`,
