`ready_footprint_bytes`, `cap_bytes`, `room_bytes`, and `margin_bytes`. Qwen3.8-27B's `room_bytes` also leaves out the
memory its stream slots take on first use, which `ready_footprint_bytes` does not count yet; its startup line names
that figure. Without `--prompt-cache-gib`, the budget is
`room_bytes` up to 16 GiB, so `budget_bytes` can sit below `room_bytes`. The cap, margin, refusal and override
behavior are unchanged. `over_cap` records an applied budget above the computed room,
rather than merely the presence of an override flag.

Without both OS readings, the existing fallback uses an explicit budget (`source: explicit`) or the spare
Metal working set up to 16 GiB (`source: metal_working_set`). Its OS inputs and unknown `over_cap` remain omitted.
Nemotron, Flash Next, LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B report a disabled retained-prefix cache as a known `budget_bytes: 0`;
Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-MoE and Gemma 4 omit `prompt_cache_plan` when their budget is 0. GLM-5.3-Flash and the CUDA server
omit it too: GLM keeps `--prompt-cache-gib` or 16 GiB inside its load limit, and the CUDA server keeps `--prompt-cache-gib`
or 16 GiB inside what its streams leave and names that size in its startup line. The 2B keeps prompt states only with
`--prompt-cache-gib`, and then reports the plan, `budget_bytes: 0` included.
This plan is a cache allowance, not a process limit, current cache occupancy, or an admission guarantee.

`/metrics` keeps `tensorfold:process_footprint_bytes` and adds `tensorfold:process_footprint_peak_bytes`
for the same kernel lifetime peak. Both gauges are omitted when the OS reading is unavailable. Existing
device gauges retain their backend scope and reset behavior. Process and device counters overlap on
unified memory: do not add them. RSS, allocator peaks and physical footprint are different measurements.
The Darwin structure follows Apple's `sys/resource.h` `rusage_info_v4` layout; host tests check its size
and both footprint offsets, and exercise the kernel reader on macOS.

Linux has no physical footprint count, so the footprint gauges stay macOS only. On Linux, `/metrics` reads
`/proc/self/status` at scrape time and reports the resident set: `tensorfold:process_resident_bytes` (`VmRSS`),
its parts `tensorfold:process_resident_anon_bytes` (`RssAnon`), `tensorfold:process_resident_file_bytes`
(`RssFile`) and `tensorfold:process_resident_shmem_bytes` (`RssShmem`), and
`tensorfold:process_resident_peak_bytes` (`VmHWM`, the kernel's lifetime peak, never reset by TensorFold).
A count the kernel does not report is omitted. The resident set holds no device or driver memory, so it is
not a physical footprint.

Route/auth regression checks use the CPU-only fake engine:

```sh
python3 zig/tests/server/test_memory_http.py zig-out/server/fake_serve zig/tests/server/fixtures
```

For certification, record startup, prefill, decode and cleanup boundaries; sample current footprint and
retain the kernel peak. A lifetime peak includes startup and all earlier workloads, so start a fresh
process for each independent matrix cell. Record context, concurrency and cache state alongside the
memory data. A constrained run on a larger Mac is budget emulation, not a measurement on a smaller Mac.
The API does not predict a smallest compatible RAM class or certify a workload by itself.
# Measuring a usable memory profile

A checkpoint fitting in memory is the beginning of a serving profile. A useful
profile also names the context, reply reserve, request capacity, cache policy and
exact runtime. Measure those together before recommending a RAM class.

This guide separates the Python/MLX server, frozen at 0.6.6, from the
[native Zig preview](../ZIG-PREVIEW.md). The MLX details below were checked against
[v0.6.6](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6) and describe that engine. They do not qualify the
native engine's models, kernels or memory admission.

## Keep the memory quantities separate

| Quantity | What it establishes |
| --- | --- |
| Checkpoint bytes on disk | Storage and transfer size; packed weights may be transformed at load. |
| Resident model bytes | Loaded weight representation; excludes request state and other runtime allocations. |
| MLX active and cached bytes | Allocator use; excludes the rest of the process. |
| Process physical footprint and lifetime peak | Memory charged to the process, including allocations missed between samples. |
| Installed RAM | Host capacity; shared with macOS and other applications. |
| GPU recommended working set | A separate device limit used by the Python 0.6.6 MLX server's budget ceiling. |

Record the working set from `mlx.core.device_info()` alongside installed RAM.
The Python 0.6.6 server caps `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB` by both values, then reserves
3 GiB for the rest of the process before setting the MLX limit. Read the applied
budget from startup and `/health`; recording only the requested environment
variable can mislabel a silently capped run. This is an allocator/admission budget,
not an OS-enforced physical-footprint cap; measure the process peak independently.
The native engine does not read `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB`. GLM on a Mac reads `GLM_LOAD_LIMIT_GB`, in GB,
and the CUDA build reads `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB`.

An emulated budget on a larger Mac is useful for finding refusal boundaries and
cache tradeoffs. It does not reproduce the smaller Mac's GPU, bandwidth, working
set, background memory pressure or thermal behavior. A recommendation needs
headroom for the host and a check that the target can apply the measured budget.
Do not derive a minimum RAM promise by dividing the budget by a default fraction.

## Freeze one serving profile

Retain the engine commit, Python and package versions, checkpoint repository and
revision, weight format, chip, OS, applied budget and complete launch options.
Pin the rendered prompt tokens too: template and tokenizer revisions affect the
actual context length. Count the encoded rendered string, rather than the number
of fields in a tokenizer result.

State whether thinking, an external drafter, other drafting methods, vision and
tools are enabled. On the Python 0.6.6 MLX server, `--drafter none` disables an external
draft model; it does not disable every drafting method. `--no-drafts` and each
request's `"draft": false` have their own scopes. Use the same precision and
weight representation for serial and concurrent exactness comparisons.

For Ternary Bonsai on M1-M4, the Python 0.6.6 loader can retain packed 2-bit projections,
widen some layers, or widen all layers to 4-bit storage as the budget permits.
Capture the startup representation for every cell. Equal checkpoint revisions
alone do not establish equal runtime representations across budgets or GPU
generations; do not turn within-profile token equality into a cross-profile claim.
See the [Bonsai recipe](recipes/ternary-bonsai-2.md).

## Separate cold, repeated and restarted requests

Give every independent cold run a fresh cache parent. In the Python 0.6.6 server,
`--snapshot-dir` selects the prefix directory, while conversation snapshots use
its sibling `session-snapshots` directory. Emptying only the selected directory
can leave a restarted request warm. Preserve the old parent as evidence and use a
new one; never clear a user's shared cache to make a benchmark cold.

A compact workload matrix contains:

1. Startup, model loading and the first short completion.
2. Cold prompts at several lengths, with a fixed explicit reply reserve.
3. The same prompts repeated, then a follow-up turn; report cached-token counts.
4. Short concurrent requests compared with their solo token hashes.
5. Independent long requests submitted together from an empty cache, each compared
   with its solo hash. Verify that cached-token counts establish the intended cold
   condition.
6. An over-context request and a fresh process restart with the same profile.

Choose a reply reserve that represents the intended application. A short measured
output does not qualify every larger output merely because the context setting
allows it. Report requested capacity separately from simultaneous decode: memory
admission can queue requests within `--parallel`, and queueing changes TTFT.

Measure startup through shutdown. Sample process physical footprint during load,
prefill, decode, cache retention and restart, and retain the kernel's lifetime
high-water mark. Record MLX active/cached/peak bytes separately. Host swap and
compression provide context, but are not attributable to the model alone.

## Publish failures and cache tradeoffs

For each applied budget and context, retain passed, startup-refused and
request-failed cells. A failure after a long prefill is different from rejecting
before loading. Keep the requested context, largest completed prompt, explicit
output length and phase of failure. An estimated context ceiling is not a
completed workload measurement.

Report client-observed time to first generated text, decode throughput, cached
prompt tokens and process peak together. A larger budget may retain more prefixes
and reusable buffers, increasing observed footprint while improving later turns.
Repeating a long prompt can still require prefill at a smaller budget. Do not label
that request a warm-cache speed result just because it is the second request.

Document fan mode, other active workloads and thermal sampling definitions. Named
core averages and raw sensor maxima are different quantities. A fixed fan setting
without an alternating controlled comparison establishes a test condition, not a
cooling-policy speedup. Missing power or temperature data stays missing.

## Backend and preview boundaries

CUDA has separate memory admission and cache support; MLX-only snapshot flags do
not establish disk-spill behavior on CUDA. Check the backend's actual startup and
[API fields](api.md) instead of transferring an MLX command unchanged.

The Zig preview uses its own native Metal allocations and cache policy. In its
Flash Next server, `--prompt-cache-gib` controls retained prompt states, not a
whole-process memory budget. Flash Next serves one reply at a time under the default `auto` and
`--parallel 1`; an explicit `--parallel` above one shares sessions. Nemotron's prompt reuse has a different status. Consult
[the preview's current limitations](../ZIG-PREVIEW.md#known-gaps) before building
a matrix. Python 0.6.6 MLX measurements are not preview performance or exactness results.

A public receipt should contain synthetic or public prompts, generic hardware
specifications and pinned public revisions. Exclude hostnames, account names,
private network addresses, credentials and operator paths. Keep benchmark tables
and retained measurements in the pull request or linked report, rather than
turning a single machine's results into unqualified source defaults.
# Receipts from a group of ranks

A client measures a serving group through the single endpoint on its serving rank. The measured latency and rate
include the exchanges needed to produce its replies. Ranks can share a machine; rank count is not machine count.
Each path places its ranks its own way:

| Path | Places ranks by | Documented by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flash Next on two Macs | `--speed-up FILE`, one file per rank | [Speed-up mode](speed-up-mode.md) |
| Native GLM-5.3-Flash on CUDA | `TF_GLM_RANK` of `TF_GLM_WORLD`, with `NCCL_COMM_ID` on rank 0's address | [Its recipe](recipes/glm-5.3-flash-cuda.md) starts two; [native placement and limits](../zig/src/families/glm/cuda_native.zig): the engine refuses a world past 16 |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super on CUDA | `TF_NEMOTRON_RANK` of `TF_NEMOTRON_WORLD`, with `NCCL_COMM_ID` | [Its recipe](recipes/nemotron-3.5-super-vl.md) starts two; a world must divide the expert shares |
| Legacy Python 0.6.6 engine | `--tp`, `--rank`, `--master` | [The Python GLM recipe](recipes/glm-5.3-flash.md) |
| Native ROCm build | `--tp`, `--rank`, `--master` | [Native ROCm placement](../zig/src/native/hip.zig) |
| The `fabric/tp` transport's harness | `TF_TP_WORLD`, `TF_TP_RANK`, `TF_TP_MASTER` | [The transport's README](../zig/src/fabric/tp/README.md) |

Placement is family-specific; use the selected family's current native recipe. `tensorfold benchmark` accepts no placement hints of its own. Both managed and attached runs read the loaded server's manifest, so inherited rank variables cannot silently become a one-rank label. Start followers separately and attach to the serving rank when measuring an existing group.

## What a receipt can carry

New community-v2 receipts carry an optional `group` object with 1-8 loaded ranks, per-node hardware and a `single-node` or `multi-node` category. The server gathers it at startup and HTTP reads its frozen snapshot. `settings.rank_count` must agree. [Loaded group receipts](loaded-group-receipts.md) defines the fields, validation and receiver partitions. Ranks sharing a node are not multiple nodes; identical hardware names on two nodes do not merge them.

V1 remains byte-for-byte unchanged, accepting 1, 2 or null as before. Legacy v2 receipts without `group` keep that bound. Missing, unsupported or inconsistent inventories remain unranked. No client or environment rank hint can fill them. ROCm distributed inventory remains unavailable. Community-v2 publication stays disabled until the receiver accepts and separates its new fields.

## The settings the ranks agreed on

Boot agreement is path-specific. Native GLM compares a settings/model/build fingerprint and reports the differing
field and rank. Nemotron compares its model, cut, precision and build, reporting a category and rank. ROCm checks a
join identity and coordinates startup values; the `fabric/tp` harness compares a settings digest. These checks do
not establish that every path compares every serving setting. Record each rank's effective settings and the boot
checks that actually ran, together with the start order and any timeout or refusal. A failed launch is not a slow
successful request. A prompt split also fixes how rows reach the other ranks:
on GLM-5.3-Flash, `TF_GLM_PREFILL_REDUCE` defaults to `split`, which sends every rank's rows to every other, and a
world whose ranks reach only their neighbours needs `ring` or `gather` instead, as the collective path supports.

Transport choice changes exchange cost; verify token equality at the same world size rather than assuming it. On
native GLM on CUDA with two ranks, `TF_ROCE` takes the small all-gathers over RDMA writes and `TF_ROCE=0` on either rank keeps NCCL;
`TF_ROCE_HCA` names the devices and
`TF_ROCE_MAX_KB` bounds the largest gather sent that way. Nemotron's serving path opens the NCCL group without
enabling its optional RoCE gather. On the `fabric/tp` harness, `TF_COMM_BACKEND` picks `nccl`, `mailbox` or `roce`, and
`TF_TP_ROCE_FALLBACK` decides what a failed setup or probe does: `nccl` permits fallback to NCCL, while `error`
refuses. A harness run that reports the RoCE path sets `error`, so a silent fallback cannot
pass as the transport it names. The boot line is the evidence for which transport ran, and the harness prints it as
`tp: rank N of M up` beside the transport kind and the library version it opened: keep it with the output.

## Prompt and decode numbers

Both describe the group as served; the work distributed to other ranks differs by path. A cold prompt's
`ttft_s` from `tools/bench_cache.py --require-cold` on a long prompt is the group's first token, not one device's
prefill, and the ranks' own prefill times do not add up to it. Take it with the prompt cache off
(`--prompt-cache-gib 0`, where the family supports it) and a fresh process for an independent cell, as
[cache measurements](cache-benchmarks.md) describe.

`tools/bench_openai.py` warms each cell once and then measures its repetitions. Its rate is the stream's delivery rate
at the client, one fewer than the completion count over the span between the first and last delivery, so it includes
every exchange a round needs; a delivery can carry several tokens, so it is not an engine clock either. Quote that
rate for a group, and do not present it as any single rank's rate.

`tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial` still applies: `--alone` compares each concurrent reply's token hash with
its solo run, and `--serial` compares the solo runs with `"draft": false`. Each rank count has its own serial
reference, so a report says which world size each equality ran at; an equality at one rank count is not one at
another. A family that admits one request at a time turns a level above one into a measure of the queue, so quote the
level and what `--parallel` admitted beside the throughput.

## What stays out

No machine names, addresses or local model paths, as for any receipt. A local model directory cannot be published:
name the checkpoint's public ID and revision, or keep the run local. Add the hardware class of each rank and the class
of the link between them, because the exchange cost is a property of that fabric; two runs at the same rank count on
different links are not comparable at the same numbers. When a change reaches the transport, the before column is the
base commit at the same rank count.

## Reporting an unattested group run

When no complete loaded inventory is available, prose accompanies the local receipt: the rank count, each rank's effective settings and completed boot checks, the start order,
each rank's hardware class and the link's, the client that measured it, which equalities ran, and what it could not
attest. It does not enter a comparison beside rank-1 and rank-2 receipts, whatever it measured.

A contributor reports four GB10 nodes at TP=4 over RoCE, serving a 2.9-bpw EXL3 pack of a DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
model. Their completion-route client, sampled at 0.6 with 512-token replies, reportedly read 37 to 41 tokens a
second from the stream. It is one rank count with no single-rank column beside it, so it is not a speed-up; that
client divides every completion token by the wall time from the first token to the last byte, where `tools/bench_openai.py` divides one
fewer by the delivery span; no `--alone` and no `"draft": false` equality was run; and no public checkpoint ID or
matched revision was supplied for that local pack. This unverified example illustrates a four-rank report; it is
not a measurement of this tree.
# N-link settings for speed-up mode

One logical peer can use one through eight distinct Thunderbolt RDMA devices. The MCDMA N-link build must be
installed by the owner on both ranks before using a bond. Its ABI remains 1; explicit port arrays use new optional
symbols. An older library refuses more than two devices or explicit arrays with `NeedNLinkLibrary` before verbs open.
Both bond endpoints must run the same N-aware wire build, including for a two-device bond.

Rank 0's four-device example uses a single existing meeting interface. Replace the example address and library path
with the peer's address and the owner's local build. Rank 1 uses rank 1, peer 0, and rank 0's meeting address.
Corresponding cable ends must occupy the same device-array position, even when their interface numbers differ.

```json
{"rank":0,"library":"/opt/mcdma/libmcdma-fabric.dylib","links":[
  {"peer":1,"devices":["rdma_en4","rdma_en3","rdma_en2","rdma_en13"],
   "via":"en4/192.0.2.2","ports":[7490,7491,7492,7493],"name":"speedup","gid":-1}
]}
```

`devices` or the existing `device` plus string describes physical members. `vias` supplies one or N strings, or use
`via` with one meeting interface or N plus-separated entries. One common meeting interface must expose an ACTIVE Thunderbolt RDMA device;
the QPs still use each data device's own GID. IPv4 on every data device is unnecessary if those devices expose ACTIVE
ports and usable GIDs. Run the owner's `fabric-check --gids DEVICE` probe to establish that before qualification.

`ports` and `peer_ports` are arrays of N distinct nonzero u16 UDP ports. If arrays are omitted, scalar `port` and
`peer_port` allocate N consecutive ports. Missing peer ports mirror local ports. An explicit array takes precedence
over its scalar. Default `gid` remains 1 for old one/two-device settings; it is -1 for three or more. Specify -1 to
scan each device independently, skipping zero GIDs and preferring IPv6 link-local. Invalid counts, duplicate devices,
port overflow, empty members and conflicting device/via plural and singular fields refuse parsing or endpoint creation.

`mtu` is the RC path MTU: 1024, 2048 or 4096, default 4096. Both ends must give the same value, at most the port's
active MTU; Thunderbolt keeps 4096, and a ConnectX link through a switch may need 1024. `kind` is optional: `tb5` or
`cx5` names the link MCDMA must report and refuses the other; omitted, the endpoint takes whichever connects. Endpoint
creation refuses `cx5` with gid -1 (NeedGidIndex), a bond or port arrays (UnsupportedLink) before anything opens; any
other `mtu` or `kind` value refuses parsing.

```json
{"rank":0,"library":"/opt/mcdma/libmcdma-fabric.dylib","links":[
  {"peer":1,"device":"rdma_mcrdma0","via":"en0/192.0.2.2","port":7490,"name":"speedup","gid":0,"mtu":1024,"kind":"cx5"}
]}
```

On a Mac a ConnectX link needs `gid` 0 (the MCDMA kext exposes only GID index 0) and a window plus both ranks' staging
of at most 63 x 4 MiB, about 252 MiB (the kext registers at most 64 memory regions per context), so flashnext and glm
do not fit a Mac ConnectX link yet.

The existing `tp.zig` path passes the parsed logical link through unchanged to the MCDMA endpoint. Tensor partitioning
and its flags do not depend on the number of physical members. An inactive or missing member refuses initialization;
a member failing later fails the entire logical peer. Qualify prompt first-token time and decode with token equality
before making any performance claim for this build.
# Optimization ledger

This page shows which speed and memory optimization applies to which model family, and where each one stands.
A change proven on one family should be ported to the others, not invented again, so each row names the PR that did
it first and the families still to do. The cross-family parts live in shared helpers, so a port is mostly the family's
own hook on top of them. Update a cell in the same PR that changes it.

Shared helpers that hold the cross-family parts:

- `zig/src/core/kv_pool.zig`: the core KV page pool, its leases and promises. CUDA's plan for it is in
  `zig/src/native/cuda_kv_pool.zig`, and the page reads in `zig/kernels/cuda/common/kv_pages.cuh`.
- `zig/src/core/prompt_radix.zig` and `zig/src/core/kv_prompts.zig`: one prompt store over the pool's pages
  (`TF_KV_SHARE`), with the CUDA adapter in `zig/src/native/cuda_prompt_pages.zig`.
- `zig/src/core/kv_ledger.zig`: the admission ledger the lane host checks for every request.
- `zig/src/core/lane_host.zig` and `zig/src/core/lanes/`: rounds, shared drafts, copy drafts (`context_copy.zig`,
  with the search in `zig/src/core/copy_index.zig`) and `--decode-share`.
- `zig/src/core/checkpoint_prefetch.zig` (`TF_LOAD_PREFETCH`), `zig/src/core/direct_gather.zig` and
  `zig/src/core/direct_io.zig`: load read-ahead and reads past the page cache.
- `zig/src/native/disk_spill.zig` and `zig/src/native/cuda_disk.zig`: kept prompt states on disk.
- `zig/src/cuda/graph_cache.zig`, `zig/src/cuda/grouped.zig` and `zig/src/cuda/experts.zig`: CUDA graphs, the
  expert plan and the grouped expert call.
- `zig/src/cuda/window_attention.zig` `promptRows`: the shared prompt attention over a window.
- `zig/kernels/cuda/common/`: shared CUDA headers (`fp_pairs.cuh`, `cp_async.cuh`, `reduce.cuh`, `vec.cuh` and others).
- `zig/src/core/bf16_round.zig`: the one fp32-to-bf16 rounding every host copy uses.
- `zig/src/core/profile.zig` and [profiles](profiles.md): the `--profile` switch registry.
- `zig/src/core/contract/` and the [kernel contract](kernel-contract.md): the gates a new or ported kernel passes.
- `zig/src/core/prompt_tail.zig`: the last layer's kept tile ([#2229]) and the chunks nothing reads ([#2432]).
- `zig/src/core/state_walk.zig`: one walk for kept prompt states. Not on main yet: it is on [#2215].

## The table

Each cell is one of these:

- `yes`: applies, not done yet.
- `no`: does not apply, with a short reason.
- `done`: on main. A closed PR that the maintainers landed on main counts as done.
- `failed`: tried and measured, with no gain, or rejected.
- `open`: a PR is open.
- `?`: can't tell from the code and the PRs.

`done¹` means the code is on main but no single PR for it was found. `C`, `M`, `H` and `X` name the backend (CUDA,
Metal, HIP, XPU) where it matters; with no letter, the cell is about CUDA. The table is split into parts of five
columns or fewer to keep lines short. The first three parts hold the native families, the most active first. The
last two hold the families with only a Metal, HIP or scoring backend.

the HIP OCR families `dots_mocr` and `glm_ocr`. They are not autoregressive text servers on the lane host, so few rows
apply.

## Rough gain

A rough size of each optimization's effect where it applies, before measuring a family: `low` under 3 %, `medium`
3–15 %, `big` over 15 %, or for memory, what lets a case fit at all. Measured numbers and their PRs are in the list
below; these are estimates for planning a port, not results.

| Optimization | Prefill | Decode | Memory | Where it shows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Prompt tail | low | none | none | a cold prompt, about 1/layers |
| 2. Paged KV | none | none | big | streams take pages as they grow |
| 3. Prompt store | big | none | medium | resumed turns skip their prefix; cold turns 3–6 % |
| 4. iGPU states | low | none | low | integrated GPUs only |
| 5. State walk | none | none | none | shared code; enables pool pages |
| 6. KV ledger | none | none | medium | more streams admitted in the same memory |
| 7. Host KV tier | medium | low (a cost) | big | resumes past the card's memory |
| 8. Disk cache | big | none | big | resumes across restarts and long sessions |
| 9. FP8 KV | low | medium | big | half the KV; decode gains at long context |
| 10. FP4/FP8 decode | low | low | none | 4–5 % of the FP4 prompt kernels |
| 11. Fused proj. | medium | medium | none | +3..+13 % measured |
| 12. Add + norm | low | low | none | one launch and one read fewer per layer |
| 13. MoE grouped | big | medium | none | MoE families only |
| 14. CUDA graphs | none | medium | none | launch time at one to few streams |
| 15. MTP | none | big | low | +30..+70 % one stream, acceptance-bound |
| 16. DFlash(2) | none | big | low | drafter weights; acceptance-bound |
| 17. DSpark | none | big | low | drafter ships with the release |
| 18. Copy drafts | none | medium | none | only where the reply repeats the context |
| 19. Shared drafts | none | big | none | +18..+38 % at 2–8 streams; none at one |
| 20. Solo chunks | medium | none | none | first token −5..−10 % |
| 21. Read-ahead | none | none | none | cold load about −50 % |
| 22. Direct load | none | none | low | cold load; no page-cache copy |
| 23. Page drop | none | none | medium | frees the checkpoint's page cache |
| 24. L2 prefetch | none | low | none | +1..+4 % on GLM TP=3; a cost on Qwen |
| 25. TP ranks | big | big | big | scale-out: models past one box |
| 26. Pipeline | none | none | big | fits models across nodes; adds hops |
| 27. Profiles | none | none | none | names the opt-in switches |

## The optimizations

1. **Prompt tail on the last layer.** A prompt chunk keeps one row's logits, so past the last layer's keys and values
   only the kept row's 128-row tile needs q, attention, o and the MLP ([#2165]). It saves about 1/layers of a cold
   prompt, less the k/v share. A family is blocked where something else reads every row of the last layer: MTP taps,
   drafter taps, hidden readouts, or a fused projection that makes k/v and q in one GEMM. Where only the prompt's last
   chunk has its logits read, the other chunks keep no tile and stop at their last state write.

   | Family | Last layer, layers | Main blocker | Gain | Effort |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | qwen3_5 (27B) | full attention, 64 | MTP taps the last layer | −1.2..−1.6 % TTFT | done [#2229] |
   | qwen3_5 (35B-A3B) | full attention, 40 | MTP taps the last layer | −1.3..−2.9 % TTFT (no drafter) | done [#2229] |
   | gemma4 | global attention, 42–60 | drafter taps copy every row | ~1.5 % | easy |
   | dory | an MLP sublayer, 72 sublayers | none | ~1.3 % | easy |
   | spark25 | full attention, 36 | fused QKVG GEMM | ~2 % | medium |
   | kolibri1 | full attention, 50 | fused QKV; MoE plus shared expert | ~1.7 % | medium |
   | minimax_m3 | sparse attention plus indexer, 60 | `prep` fuses q with k/v; taps; TP gathers | ~1.5 % | medium |
   | nemotron | MoE block, 88 | MTP reads every row's hidden state | ~1.1 % | medium |
   | flashnext | attention plus indexer, 48 | MTP, hyper-connections, `.all` logits | ~2 % | hard |
   | deepseek_v41 | compressed attention, 40 | DSpark taps, mHC, emitted programs | ~2 % | hard |
   | glm | KDA linear layer, 45 | must write the recurrent state for every row | small | hard |
   | qwen4, lfm2 | | | n/a | |

   The qwen3_5 numbers are measured. The others are estimates (`~`): about 1/layers, minus the k/v share.

2. **KV pages from the core pool.** Streams lease KV pages from one `kv_pool` as their rows grow, instead of each
   reserving a whole `--context` window, so more streams fit and a short request holds little ([#1156], [#781]'s
   follow-ups). Sliding layers keep their rings. Qwen's pages are opt-in (`TF_QWEN_KV_PAGES`, `_ALL`); [#2011] keeps
   them opt-in, makes `--parallel` a cap with pages set, and brings them to the window path's speed (2k to 32k prompts
   within +0.3..+0.7 %). Dory's are opt-in
   (`TENSORFOLD_DORY_KV_PAGES=1`), Flash Next's experimental. Metal's port is tracked in [#1293].

3. **Shared paged prompt store.** A kept prompt stays as the pool's own pages in one `prompt_radix` store, so a resume
   copies nothing and the cache and the streams draw on the same memory (`TF_QWEN_KV_SHARE`, and `TF_KV_SHARE` on
   the core adapter, [#1657], which GLM uses). On Qwen3.8-27B a cold first turn is 3–6 % faster with it on, and the
   second turn level ([#1357]). [#2211] moved GLM onto the shared store. It can't be combined with
   `--learn-conversations` today. Flash Next already resumes a prefix from the host store's whole-state copies; on the
   shared store a kept 32k state would stop duplicating about 0.9 GiB of attention rows (27 KiB a token).

   Qwen CUDA's host-copy path can instead opt into message-start cuts with `TF_QWEN_REQUEST_STARTS=1`
   (#2176). Later turns closer than 256 tokens now keep their own history cuts. On a GB10 with Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit and
   its DFlash2 drafter, turns 2 to 6 of a six-turn chat reused 1,450 to 1,635 prompt tokens and took 0.72 to 1.33 s
   against 1.78 to 2.10 s unset. Prompt passes are cut at replies, so one of the six replies differed from the unset
   path; resumed and fresh replies matched with it set. This mode remains incompatible with `TF_QWEN_KV_SHARE`.

4. **Prompt states in device memory on integrated GPUs.** On a GB10 the device and host share memory, so a kept
   state can stay where it is instead of being copied through pinned host memory on every save ([#2043]). On Qwen
   CUDA this takes 1.6–2.1 % off 8k and 32k prompts ([#2113]). Metal is unified already.

5. **Core state walk for kept states.** About 25 snapshot files each had their own loop that splits a state's live
   parts at page ends and copies them. `core/state_walk.zig` holds that loop once, and a family keeps only its parts
   list and a one-copy hook ([#2215], GLM first on CUDA and Metal). It saves code, not time: every later layout change
   is made once.

6. **KV admission ledger.** A request reserves its prompt and reply, not a whole window a `--parallel` stream
   ([#1943]). [#1945] added the core ledger, and [#2127] counts every paged pool's promises in it, with no change in
   behaviour. A stream paid for at load (the engine's own sequence) is a standing lease in it, so the ledger admits the
   window plan's streams and not one fewer; no family on main reaches that yet. The unpaged families still convert one
   by one, as #1943 plans.

7. **KV pages in pinned host memory.** Pages that don't fit on the card live in pinned host memory, so a long
   conversation's next turn still resumes. GLM keeps its latent rows there with `TF_GLM_KV_HOST` ([#1795]) and its kept
   states with `TF_GLM_HOST_CACHE` ([#1736]). [#1501] adds a host tier to the core pool itself.

8. **Prompt cache on disk.** `--learn-conversations` and `--spill-gib` keep prompt states on disk under a probed
   identity, so a conversation resumes after a restart or after its RAM slot was evicted. `--checkpoint-slots` bounds
   what stays in RAM beside it.

9. **FP8 KV cache.** `--kv-cache fp8` stores keys and values as e4m3 with a scale a row, which halves KV memory for
   longer windows or more streams ([#886] on Qwen). GLM has an opt-in FP8 latent cache; its quality qualification is
   pending. DeepSeek-V4.1's compressed attention is FP8 by design.

10. **Native FP4/FP8 pair decode.** nvcc 13.2 (PTX ISA 9.2) decodes an FP4 or FP8 pair to a bf16 pair in one
    instruction on `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`, where TF decodes in software today (`fp4pair`, `fp8pair` in `fp_pairs.cuh`,
    [#1555]). On the 27B's prompt16 FP4 projections it took 4–5 % off the kernel time with bit-equal output ([#1448]).
    The FP8 block experts gained nothing, as decode there is bandwidth-bound, so FP8-only families are `failed`. [#2238]
    lands it behind `-Dnative-fp-decode`, off by default; the release toolchain stays on nvcc 13.0 until its own PR.

11. **Projections that share an input, in one launch.** Projections that read the same input (q/k/v/gate, gate/up)
    run as one grouped launch or one fused GEMM, byte-equal to separate launches. [#1783] does this for affine-4
    decode and verify on GB10; [#1439] runs up to four BF16 prompt projections in one grid on Qwen3.8.

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | nemotron | +5.9 % (2 streams), +13.3 % (8 streams) | [#1783] |
    | qwen3_5 (27B, DFlash2) | +3.5..+5.0 % decode | [#1783] |
    | qwen3_5 (Qwen3.8, BF16) | +9.5 % prefill one stream, +8.2 % at 8 | [#1439] |
    | gemma4 (31B), spark25 | level | [#1783] |

12. **Residual add plus norm in one launch.** The residual add and the next RMS norm run as one kernel, which saves a
    read and a write of the hidden rows a layer. Nemotron's is on the shared norm kernel ([#796]); HIP Qwen3.5's
    prompt does it after the mixer ([#2099]).

13. **MoE grouped plans and expert kernels.** One expert plan sorts a step's rows by expert, and one grouped call runs
    every expert's rows ([#558], [#605], NVFP4 in [#629], EXL3 in [#741]). A family adds only its router and its weight
    format.

14. **CUDA graphs for decode and verify.** Each decode or verify shape is captured once and replayed, which removes the
    host's launch cost from every step. `TENSORFOLD_GEMMA4_GRAPHS=0` (and the same switch for Kolibri, Spark
    and Dory) keeps those eager. GLM's capture is [#2279] (open), for [#1490].

15. **MTP drafts.** The checkpoint's own MTP head drafts tokens that the target verifies in one pass, with the same
    replies as serial decode. `--mtp-drafts` and `--mtp-confidence` size the drafts on Nemotron and GLM.

16. **DFlash and DFlash2 drafters.** An external block drafter reads the target's hidden taps and drafts a block (or a
    tree) a step. It needs a trained drafter for each target; see [training a drafter](recipes/training-a-drafter.md).

17. **DSpark drafters.** A drafter that ships with the release (DeepSeek-V4.1's `mtp.i` blocks, MiniMax-M3.1's, Kimi
    K3's) drafts from the target's taps with a confidence schedule. Applies wherever a DSpark drafter exists for the
    target.

18. **Copy drafts.** Where a reply repeats earlier text, the lane host drafts the continuation from the context
    (`copy_index.zig`) and the target verifies it. It needs no drafter weights; [#2022] brought verified root and
    context copies to five CUDA lane hosts at once (opt-in). GLM's issue is [#1910].

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | nemotron | level from 2K to 64K (−1.4..+1.0 %) on prompts without repeats | [#1974] |

19. **Shared draft rounds.** Several streams' drafts run in one batched pass, and a shared round prices drafts first
    and skips proposals it won't verify ([#1779]).

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | qwen3_5 (Qwen3.6 MTP) | +18 % (2 streams), +32 % (4), +38 % (8) aggregate | [#1562] |
    | nemotron | −3.6..−7.5 % time at 2–8 streams | [#768] |

20. **Prompt chunk size and interleaving.** A prompt pass takes a wider chunk while no other stream decodes, and the
    normal chunk once one does, so a cold prompt is faster without longer decode waits ([#1554] option C).
    `--decode-share` ([#1327]) sizes a filling prompt's chunks beside live replies on every lane family.

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | flashnext (C) | first token −5..−10 % at 2k–32k, decode waits unchanged | [#1733] |
    | glm (C) | cold first token −6..−7 % at TP=2, −7..−8 % at TP=3 | [#1823] |
    | flashnext (M) | 1,024-token reply beside a 64K prompt 48 → 8 s, prompt's first token 90 → 54 s | [#2167] |
    | flashnext (C), one GPU | prompts 15–23 % faster at `--parallel 1`, up to 8,192 rows a pass | [#2246] |
    | glm (C), TP=2 | prompts about 2 % sooner at 8K–128K, two chunks a step, replies unchanged | [#1423] |
    | gemma4 (C) | first token 31B −4..−5 %, E4B −9..−10 %, opt-in with `TF_GEMMA4_CHUNK_SOLO` | [#2391] |

    `TF_GLM_CHUNK_SOLO=4096` is slower with GLM's NVFP4 checkpoint on two GB10s ([#2288]).

21. **Load read-ahead.** Reader threads read a layer's checkpoint into the page cache while the loader packs the
    previous one (`TF_LOAD_PREFETCH`, 16 readers, on by default where it landed). [#2033] ports it to six more
    loaders, opt-in. The readers start only on Linux, so a family on Metal alone is `no`; Metal's shared loader
    reads large tensors on eight threads of its own.

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | glm | cold load −52.6 % (TP=2), −53.9 % (TP=3) | [#1616] |
    | qwen3_5 (27B NVFP4) | cold load 25 / 22 → 15 s | [#1928] |
    | gemma4 (31B) | cold load 18 → 11 s | [#1928] |

22. **Direct load past the page cache.** Weights are read with direct I/O into the loader's buffers, so a cold load
    reads at the disk's speed and leaves no page cache behind ([#1873]).

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | flashnext | cold load 74 → 48 s | [#1901] |
    | flashnext | 50 → 43.5 s, next chunk gathered while one packs | [#1960] |

23. **Page-cache drop after load.** Every CUDA loader drops its checkpoint's pages once the weights are up, so the
    memory goes back to KV and the prompt cache on unified-memory boxes ([#1884]). TP loaders wait for every rank
    ([#1887]). Metal's loaders drop theirs from the file cache ([#1885], [#1888]).

24. **L2 prefetch.** A side stream reads a decode window's next weights into L2 ahead of the kernels that use them.

    | Family | Gain (measured) | Where |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | qwen3_5 (27B), nemotron | −3.5 % (a cost) with exact tokens, closed | [#2014] |
    | glm | decode +3.0..+4.1 % at TP=3, +0.8..+1.9 % at TP=2 | [#2162] |
    | flashnext, gemma4 | null: +0.45 % and +0.15 % at one stream, inside the runs' spread, same replies; not proposed | measured on a GB10, no PR |

    Qwen3.8-27B's decode attention on XPU takes its L2 reuse from launch order instead, with no prefetch: [#2595] is a
    grid-only change. `attn_decode` runs on a (rows, heads, slices) grid, so a key slice's tree rows run back to back;
    each work group's arithmetic and the bits are unchanged ([#2543] keeps wider slices for later, as an opt-in). On
    an Arc Pro B70 at one stream, drafted, with a bf16 cache: +6 % at 8K prompt tokens, +23 % at 32K, +33 % at 131K;
    `"draft": false` is unchanged. With `XPU_KV_INT8=1` it is 2–4 % slower below about 12K tokens and faster past it.
    Not run: sampled decoding, resumed prompts, `QPARTS != 1` builds and any GPU but BMG-G31.

25. **Tensor parallel ranks.** A model splits over two or more GPUs or hosts, so a model that doesn't fit one box
    runs, and decode reads each rank's share of the weights. Mixed Metal and CUDA ranks are tracked in [#1236].

26. **Pipeline stages.** Layer ranges on different nodes, one hidden row a token over Ethernet, so a GB10 and a Mac
    can serve one model ([#2005]). The stage link and its protocol are [#2012] and [#2060]; the 27B as a stage is
    [#2115], logits byte-equal to the whole model at two and three stages.

27. **`--profile` switches.** One registry names each opt-in switch with its backend, families, class and evidence,
    and the startup line prints what differs from the defaults ([#1660], [#1944]). Only `stable` is served;
    `fast-exact` and `fast` are refused by name until switches qualify for them.
