## The ROCm source `fb8eaf85` follows

Read on 19 Oct 2026 at ROCm/ROCR-Runtime `547bc139`, ROCm/clr `dfa6202d` and ROCm/rocm-systems `df181d33`, the `develop`
heads that day. In `rocm-systems`, `projects/clr`'s visible-device block in `rocdevice.cpp` and
`projects/rocr-runtime`'s `amd_filter_device.cpp` are the same as in the other two.

- ROCr applies `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` before anything lists a GPU. `BuildTopology` in
  `runtime/hsa-runtime/core/runtime/amd_topology.cpp` (lines 401-459) ranks the GPUs the variable names in its
  order and creates the others disabled; `RegisterAgent` in `runtime.cpp` (236-245) keeps disabled
  GPUs out of the GPU list, and `IterateAgent` (312-329), which `rocminfo` reaches through `hsa_iterate_agents`, walks
  the CPU, GPU and AIE lists. So `rocminfo` prints only the visible GPUs, renumbered, and the probe must not apply
  the variable again.
- HIP reads `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, else `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (`rocclr/device/rocm/rocdevice.cpp` 390-393), over
  every GPU agent in `hsa_iterate_agents` order (`iterateAgentCallback`, 327-349), the order `rocminfo` prints. An
  entry with `GPU-` in it is matched as a substring of each agent's UUID, first match wins (408-421); an index must
  read back unchanged through `std::to_string(atoi(entry))` and be below the GPU count (422-426); the first invalid
  entry ends the list (428-431), and a repeated index is skipped (433-436).
- clr reads these variables in `rocclr/utils/flags.cpp`: a variable set to nothing is stored as one space (121-124),
  which no entry rule accepts, so HIP sees no GPU; `removeQuotes` (26-61, applied at 187) drops one pair of double
  quotes around the value.
- `rocminfo` prints every agent's UUID on its `Uuid:` line (`projects/rocminfo/rocminfo.cc` 450-453 and 665 in
  `rocm-systems`), the value HIP compares: `GPU-` and 16 lower-case hex digits, or `GPU-XX` for a device with none
  (`amd_gpu_agent.cpp` 2057-2075 in ROCR-Runtime). The probe compares it and never records it.

## Sanitizing

These are copies of the raw files, changed only as follows. `provenance.tsv` lists every file's published sha256 and
which change it had. A file marked `unchanged` (the JSON receipts and manifests among them) is byte-identical to the raw
file, so its raw and published sha256 are the same. For each file that was changed the raw sha256 is withheld
(`withheld: sanitized`): such a file differs from its published copy only in the replaced paths and the stripped
spaces, so its raw hash would let anyone who guesses a replaced path check the guess.

- `/home/<user>` and `/Users/<user>` became `~` (logs and `binary.sha256`).
- Trailing spaces were stripped, so the files pass `git diff --check`: the two `35b-serve.log` files, whose first line
  ended in a space, and five negative-control logs, where the undo diff's blank context lines and the test runner's
  blank lines were only spaces.

The binary sha256 values above are the recorded originals. No file names a hostname (the machine is called only
"Bosgame M5", here), a private address, MAC address, serial number, Wi-Fi name, proxy or credential; the only address
is loopback `127.0.0.1`.
# XPU Qwen3.8-27B decode attention grid order: receipts

The change dispatches `attn_decode` as `(rows, heads, slices)` so the tree rows of one key slice share it in L2.
Per-work-group arithmetic is unchanged; outputs are bit-identical to `1a5644892`. Gate agreed in #2543.

## Machine and builds

- One Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG-G31, PCI id 0xe223, 32 GB), 230 W cap, Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0, xe, oneAPI 2026.1.
- Zig 0.17.0, ocloc 26.05.37020. Both binaries carry one local build change that drops
  `-cl-intel-128-GRF-per-thread` from the Gemma 4 prompt-rows kernels, which this ocloc rejects.
- Checkpoint `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` @ `22d8d538`, drafter `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`, bf16 KV.
- Serving: `--parallel 1 --context 139264 --prompt-cache-gib 0 --no-thinking`, greedy, 512 tokens, one stream.

## Files

- `contract-attention.txt`: the attention lines, the `SUMMARY` and the exit status of `tf-xpu-contract-run --device 0`.
- `token-sha.json`: server `token_sha` per prompt length for main and branch, drafted and `"draft": false`. The kept
  server logs cover 46 of the 54 timed requests: main drafted has n=2 below 130K tokens and n=1 at 130K tokens,
  while its speed medians use n=3 and n=2. The other 8 main requests have text hashes only.
- `decode-depth.json`: streamed decode tokens/s, TTFT and prefill per cell (code and prose prompts).
- `bench-openai.json`: `tools/bench_openai.py --tokens 256 --reps 3 --temperatures 0`, two alternated rounds.

## Results

Contract: 10 kernels pass gates 1 to 4, 6 controls red as planted, 0 limit problems; the attention pair is
bit-equal to `1a5644892` at 20 shapes (tree widths 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16; 33 to 32,770 visible keys).

Token hashes are equal across main and branch, drafted and `"draft": false`, at 52 to 130,856 prompt tokens.

| Prompt tokens (code) | main tok/s | branch tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| 68 | 128.2 | 128.1 |
| 7,976 | 85.1 | 90.1 |
| 32,552 | 37.3 | 45.9 |
| 130,856 | 11.4 | 15.1 |

## Not run

`XPU_KV_INT8=1`, `--parallel` above 1, prompt-cache resumes, sampled decoding, chips other than BMG-G31.
`xpu-qwen27-tests` means-test fails identically on main and branch (worst error 5.12e-5 prompt, 1.86e-5 decode
against a 2e-6 bound, then exit 139); seam and close pass on both.
# XPU Qwen3.8-27B prefix decode attention (`XPU_ATTN_PREF`): receipts

An opt-in, off by default (#2543). With `XPU_ATTN_PREF=256` a round reads the committed prefix once: `attn_pref`
scores chunks of 256 keys on bf16 DPAS for 8 (row, head) queries at a time, `attn_tail` keeps `attn_decode`'s
arithmetic for a row's last keys, and `attn_merge2` merges both in key order. Unset, decode runs `attn_decode` and
`attn_merge` as before and token hashes equal main's.

## Machine and builds

- Two Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG-G31, PCI id 0xe223, 32 GB): #1 at a 230 W cap, #2 at 180 W. Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0,
  xe, oneAPI 2026.1. One server at a time on a card.
- Zig 0.17.0, ocloc 26.05.37020. Every binary carries one local build change that drops
  `-cl-intel-128-GRF-per-thread` from the Gemma 4 prompt-rows kernels, which this ocloc rejects.
- `measured`: `a1d896a88` (#2595 before its two contract commits) with this change's kernels inside `decode.cl`.
  `head`: this pull request, where the same kernels are in `decode_prefix.cl` and `attn_decode` keeps its signature.
- Checkpoint `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` @ `22d8d538`, drafter `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`, bf16 K/V.
- Serving: `--parallel 1 --context 139264 --prompt-cache-gib 0 --no-thinking`, greedy, 512 tokens, one stream.
- Prompts: the code and prose prompts of #2595's receipt (68 / 7,976 / 32,552 / 130,856 and 52 / 7,963 / 32,540 /
  130,846 prompt tokens).

## Files

- `requests.json`: every timed request: path, switch, build, card, prompt tokens, decode tokens/s, TTFT, the
  server's `token_sha`, rounds and accepted drafts, and the sha256 of the answer text.
- `battery.json`: 329 graded items, default path against `XPU_ATTN_PREF=256`, with both text hashes an item.

## Results

Default path (switch unset), `measured` and `head` builds: `token_sha` equals #2595's at every prompt length,
drafted and `"draft": false`.

With the switch, drafted equals `"draft": false` equals a second drafted run at every cell (0, 8K, 32K twice;
131K once), and on the 211 battery items run with `"draft": false` (211 of 211; the other 118 were not run that
way). A second card returns the first card's drafted text on 329 of 329 items. `head` returns the `measured` build's hashes on both paths (8K and
32K, B70 #2).

Decode tokens/s on B70 #1, drafted, code / prose, default against the switch in one session:

| Prompt tokens (code) | default | `XPU_ATTN_PREF=256` | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 68 | 127.4 / 100.7 | 127.4 / 100.7 | 1.00 |
| 7,976 | 90.0 / 71.6 | 114.7 / 91.5 | 1.27 |
| 32,552 | 45.9 / 33.9 | 90.1 / 66.5 | 1.96 |
| 130,856 | 15.1 / 13.6 | 50.7 / 45.6 | 3.35 |

`"draft": false`: 30.4 / 23.7 / 13.0 (default) and 30.4 / 27.3 / 18.8 (switch) at 8K / 32K / 131K. The 68-token row
of the default column is the switch run's: no row there reaches a prefix chunk, so both run the same kernels.
On B70 #2 at 180 W with the `head` build, while the other card served a battery: 85.0 / 67.8 to 109.0 / 87.0 at
8K and 42.3 / 31.2 to 84.5 / 62.5 at 32K.

The switch changes tokens. Against the default path the answer text differs at 4 of 6 depth cells (8K prose, 32K
code and prose, 131K prose) and on 67 of 329 battery items. `XPU_ATTN_PREF=512` against 256 differs again at 3
of 4 cells, so the text follows the order of the sums.

Battery passes, default / switch: HumanEval even 78 / 78 of 82, odd 76 / 76 of 82, knowledge 40 / 42 of 55, JSON
schema 55 / 55 of 55, instruction following 33 / 33 of 55. Two items gained, none lost.

## Update 2026-11-13: status, floor, int8 K/V and 262,144 context

Status: this change is not in upstream TensorFold and is not proposed there. Upstream keeps main's tokens for every
speedup, opt-ins included (#2543, 2026-11-10), and this switch changes tokens. It lives on this branch of the fork.

- **Floor.** Rows below position 1,040 keep the default kernels. B70 #1, 230 W, same binary with the switch unset as
  control: a 68-token prompt gives 128.1 / 102.4 drafted (code / prose) and 32.0 with `"draft": false` on both paths,
  with the default path's text. 8K, 32K and 131K keep the hashes and speeds of the tables above.
- **int8 K/V.** `XPU_KV_INT8=1 XPU_ATTN_PREF=256` runs `attn_pref8`. B70 #1, 230 W, one repeat, drafted, code /
  prose, int8 default against int8 with the switch: 8K 88.8 / 74.3 to 102.6 / 85.0; 32K 43.6 / 35.0 to 65.2 / 53.5;
  131K 30.8 / 24.6 with the switch (int8 default not run). `"draft": false`: 8K 30.4 to 28.0, 32K 24.0 to 26.4.
  Drafted equals `"draft": false` in every cell.
- **262,144 context.** `--context 262144` with both switches served a 249,784-token prompt: 20.7 tokens/s drafted,
  15.3 with `"draft": false`, same text both ways, cold TTFT 330 s.
- `attn_pref8` widens every K and V byte to bf16 before DPAS, so it is slower than `attn_pref` (131K: 30.8 against
  50.7). int8 DPAS for Q.K is the open step.
- Not run on this head: the 329-item battery with the floor or with int8 K/V, repeats of the int8 cells, int8

## Capability floor

The native release includes CUDA kernels for sm_80, sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121. This is a build target list, not
per-card model qualification. Nemotron MLX 4-bit has been checked on GB10, RTX 3090 and RTX PRO 6000.
The A100 (sm_80) has [kernel-check evidence](../../CHANGELOG.md#1012) from #846, but no served checkpoint on record;
it is not model-qualified. See [qualified models](../../README.md#qualified-models) for the measured scope.
`tensorfold info REPO` prints a checkpoint's memory floor: its weights plus a 2 GiB runtime margin. On macOS, a
Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) checkpoint instead prints its startup and cold pack budgets.

| Engine | Floor |
| --- | --- |
| Native CUDA, NVFP4 / FP8 | Nemotron and dense Qwen have non-cluster fallback code for sm_80 to sm_89 (#901, #1470). No NVFP4/FP8 model run on sm_80 to sm_89 is recorded; no A100 model qualification is claimed. Other families keep their own gates. |
| Flash Next, native CUDA | MLX 4-bit served on a GB10; the ModelOpt/two-local-rank path is experimental. Drafting at multiple ranks requires the prompt cache off. No qualification on every release SM is implied. |
| Intel GPU (XPU), Nemotron | Experimental. Weights need 17.3 GiB of device memory (18 to 19.4 GB in use from 4k to 128k context); measured on an Arc Pro B70 (32 GB). Cards below 24 GB are untested and a 16 GB card cannot hold the weights. |
| Python 0.6.6 MLX, Apple Silicon | Historical family-page scopes, not measured minimums: GLM-5.3-Flash is written for a 256 GB Mac, about 151 GiB resident. DeepSeek-V4-Flash is the same, about 151 GiB resident. Flash Next's default command sizes to a 128 GiB M4 Max. Qwen3.8-27B on a 32 GB Mac needs more than the default 22.4 GiB. Machine classes, not measured minimums. |

New families go on the Zig engine: [adding a Zig family](adding-a-zig-family.md) has the steps in order, what each
one gained, and which code owns it. For the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6, the contributor guides cover
[adding an MLX family](adding-a-family.md), [adding a CUDA family](adding-a-cuda-family.md) and
[CUDA implementation rules](cuda.md).
[Training a drafter](training-a-drafter.md) takes a target's `--record` output to a learned block drafter, with
what each step gained on Kolibri-1.
[EXL3 weights](exl3.md) and [universal EXL3 experts](exl3-universal-experts.md) describe the shared EXL3
module @vcruz305 wrote for the Python engine's CUDA families in [#42](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/42):
any codebook, any width per tensor, one grouped launch per MoE projection.

## The contract

Drafted output must equal the same engine's serial output. A resumed prompt must equal that prompt served
fresh, and every concurrent stream must equal its solo run. This contract applies within the same weights,
runtime and settings; another backend or quantization can have different arithmetic.

The sampler keys each draw by seed, absolute position and token ID. A draft is accepted only when it
matches that draw from the target. Each verify row must use the serial row's arithmetic, including
attention boundaries, routing ties and recurrence updates. Rollback must restore all state after the
accepted path, including draft-head state.

Prompt reuse is equally strict. The MLX planner computes chunks from rendered tokens and caches only
compatible boundaries. Its resume points are assistant-message starts and the second message start
when the tokenizer exposes those markers. Chunks skip resume points less than 256 tokens from the
previous start and otherwise end at the first eligible point or after 2,048 tokens. Without recognized
markers, chunks use the 2,048-token grid. Rewriting earlier template text can invalidate reuse.
The chunk scheme and kernel/runtime identity must match before a stored prefix can be reused.

For CUDA checkpoint loading, see [load-time prefetch](cuda-load-prefetch.md).

## Measurements

`tools/bench_openai.py` contains public fixtures: a raw Fibonacci-function prompt and a chat prompt asking
how matrix multiplication uses a GPU. The chat fixture disables thinking. After starting a server with
`--name bench`, run from the repository root:

```bash
python3 tools/bench_openai.py http://127.0.0.1:8080 bench \
  --tokens 64 --reps 5 --temperatures 1.0,0 --output bench.json
```

The client warms each cell, uses seeds 1234 through 1238, and reports the median decode rate after the
first token. Sampled cells use temperature 1, top-k 20 and top-p 0.95. The client sends `ignore_eos: true`;
MLX, GLM CUDA and the Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6 CUDA engines honor it, while the Flash Next and Nemotron CUDA engines can stop
at EOS before the requested limit.
It measures throughput; it does not itself prove token equality. Record checkpoint and tokenizer revisions,
runtime versions, backend, rank count, launch command and output hashes with a result. Compare serial and drafted output separately.

For concurrent MLX workloads, use `tools/bench_concurrent.py` with `--alone --serial` to compare each
concurrent reply with a solo run and check those solo runs against `draft: false`. Long-context and memory
measurements also need a public prompt fixture and its exact rendered-token count. Separate cold, resumed
and post-restart requests.

All 0.3.5 decode, prefill, concurrency and peak-memory results are TBD [release-0.3.5]. Older public-fixture
results in the CUDA family pages are historical measurements, not release qualification.

## Kernel checks

For CUDA refactors that promise unchanged machine code, use the [five-SM SASS identity runner](cuda-sass-identity.md).

Use exact equality for serial versus multi-row kernels and committed caches. Use a separate trusted
forward for model-quality checks; agreement with one's own serial implementation does not establish
model fidelity. Include real head dimensions, sparse-attention boundaries, partial keeps and concurrent
streams at different lengths. After changing a kernel or runtime, regenerate serial references.

Measure dependent operations and complete requests. Independent microbenchmarks can hide launch cost,
weight-cache effects and lost overlap with other work.

# TensorFold contributor

Produce a small, reviewable native contribution with evidence for every affected contract.
This skill defines the conditions a contribution must satisfy; it does not approve a merge, release or hardware qualification.

Before editing, follow the [ATC contributor instructions](../atc/SKILL.md), inspect the public radar and check or claim the issue.
Publish an anonymous session with `atc start <issue> --public https://tensorfold.dev --json` when reporting this work is authorized; show a GitHub name only when the human opts in.
Pulse only while working, review overlaps before a pull request, and land the session when it stops.

## Establish the contribution contract

Find the TensorFold checkout and its Git root before editing.
A native checkout has `build.zig`, `.zig-version`, `zig/src/native/` and `docs/recipes/`.
Read any AGENTS.md in the folders you touch (the app has its own), [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md), [RUNBOOK.md](../../RUNBOOK.md) and the [recipe index](README.md).
For a GPU change, also read the complete [kernel contract](../kernel-contract.md) before choosing an implementation.
Target `main`, the only branch, and preserve unrelated changes; a different local TensorFold checkout may be the frozen Python engine.

Before implementation, write a short contract in the working notes or PR draft:

- The requested behavior, reproducer and existing failure, or the missing capability being added.
- The target commit, family, backend, checkpoint revision, quantization, precision mode, GPU class and rank count.
- The owning modules and existing shared operator or family adapter to extend.
- The applicable correctness checks, performance metric and agreed acceptance threshold, including cold-prefill requirements.
- The hardware available, required checks that cannot run there and the evidence needed from another tester.

New families, backends and arithmetic changes need the maintainer-agreed gate described in CONTRIBUTING.md.
If that gate is missing, identify the missing decision before presenting the work as ready to land.
Do not silently lower a threshold, change its workload or replace an unavailable test with an easier one.
The current `zig/gate.json` may have no entries; that is not permission to invent a release-wide speed target.
Creating an issue, sending a PR, uploading results or changing a shared machine still needs the user's authorization.
Keep one job per pull request; stack dependent ones, say what each sits on, and keep stacks short.
Maintainers rebase at landing, so don't force-push a branch under review just to follow main.

## Read the right recipe and the code it describes

Use [adding a Zig family](adding-a-zig-family.md) for native bring-up and optimization stages.
Read the affected family's page from the recipe index, then trace the actual native loader, backend registration, operator and tests.
For checkpoint arithmetic, also read [quantization](../quantization.md); for transport changes, read [speed-up settings](../speed-up-mode.md).

Separate native instructions from sections explicitly labelled Python 0.6.6, historical measurements or unproven next steps.
The Python engine is frozen; Python clients, fixture builders and trusted references under `tools/` are development tools, not native inference dependencies.
Do not copy a Python-only flag, environment variable, transport or support table into a native port.
Do not require every optimization stage for an unrelated bug fix or documentation change.

Some family-page introductions lag newer native code.
Check the target build's `--version`, `--help` and `capabilities --json`, its native registry and loader, and matching device/model receipts.
A registered family or compiling source proves neither whole-checkpoint support nor qualification on every GPU.
If documentation and implementation disagree, record the discrepancy and proposed correction; do not treat it as permission to relax a precision or exactness requirement.

## Keep ownership in the native architecture

| Responsibility | Inspect and extend |
| --- | --- |
| Request lifetime, events and advertised capabilities | [engine API](../../zig/src/core/engine_api.zig) and [server adapter](../../zig/src/server/engines.zig) |
| Shared scheduling, target verification, sampling and per-stream state | [lane core](../../zig/src/core/lanes/) |
| Backend selection, admission and family registration | [native adapters](../../zig/src/native/), including the relevant Metal, CUDA, HIP or XPU adapter |
| Family config, tensor mapping, layer graph and family-specific mixers | [families](../../zig/src/families/) |
| Reusable projections, layouts, caches and backend operators | [shared core](../../zig/src/core/), [CUDA operators](../../zig/src/cuda/) and [GPU kernels](../../zig/kernels/) |
| Build registration and deployable assets | [build.zig](../../build.zig), [build modules](../../zig/build/) and [packaging](../../packaging/README.md) |

Adapt the family to the existing engine interfaces; do not add a parallel scheduler or a second copy of shared verification/cache machinery.
An unsupported family is a bring-up task, not a reason to route production inference through Python, a CPU substitute or a serial-only workaround.
Plain decoding remains the correctness oracle; disabling drafts must not be required for an advertised drafted path to work.
Concurrent requests share rounds through the lane core, with drafting on for every stream the family admits; a drafts-off or serial fallback at some width or stream count is a bug, not a limit to document.
Test the path the native server will actually call, including capability reporting and intentional refusals.
A checkpoint whose config declares a vision tower needs image input in the engine's own kernels before the family is complete; until then, refuse image parts and `--vision` with a clear message and test that refusal.

Keep stored weights and tokenizer assets unchanged.
Respect each tensor's actual bit width, group size, strides, scales, bias convention and format metadata; mixed projections cannot share an incompatible fused kernel.
Reject unsupported layouts and malformed geometry explicitly, and test those refusals.
Keep scratch and prepared packs in the loader's owned cache, with its existing identity and atomic-publication rules.

## Register and prove a GPU kernel

A new or changed GPU operator must be reachable through its backend contract runner, not merely have a standalone unit test.
The registration types are [Spec](../../zig/src/core/contract/contract.zig) and [Kernel/VTable](../../zig/src/core/contract/gates.zig).
Use the shared affine, dense or rows reference helpers where their formulas match the operator.
Declare real served shapes, tile edges, output type, accumulation and rounding depth, NaN behavior, and permitted aliasing.
A bit-preserving replacement declares `replaces` and supplies the `replaced` hook on identical inputs; its contract requires byte equality.
If an intended reduction reorder changes bytes, stop treating it as that drop-in replacement and resolve the arithmetic/comparison contract with the maintainer before landing it.
An improved FP64 error alone does not waive replacement equality, authorize a new serial baseline or justify renaming the kernel to evade the gate.
Register the operator in [the Metal runner](../../zig/tests/contract/metal_main.zig), [the CUDA runner](../../zig/tests/cuda/contract_tests.zig) or [the HIP runner](../../zig/tests/hip/contract_main.zig), as appropriate.
Register its launch limits and compile records separately in [registry.zig](../../zig/src/core/contract/registry.zig), or [hip_records.zig](../../zig/src/core/contract/hip_records.zig) for HIP.

| Gate | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Non-finite inputs | Every output class matches the FP64 formula or the operator's explicitly tested NaN rule. |
| Repeat and aliasing | Five byte-identical runs; unchanged inputs and guards; no undeclared output/input overlap. |
| Shapes | Served dimensions and valid tile edges meet the derived reference bound, or replacement outputs equal the replaced kernel's bytes. |
| Accumulation | The stress fixture distinguishes reduced-precision sums and proves the required accumulator; report stated limitations or genuine N/A cases. |
| Launch limits | Updated recorded compiles and device checks cover the relevant served chips, threads, registers, shared memory and clusters. |

Use [Metal contract tests](../../zig/tests/contract/) and [CUDA contract tests](../../zig/tests/cuda/contract_tests.zig) as concrete integration examples.
Every planted control must fail its intended gate; a control error, skip or unexpected pass proves nothing.
Attach the backend's complete `SUMMARY`, exit status, known findings and unrun chips.
Diagnostic `--only`, `--no-gates` or `--no-limits` runs are not the full qualification receipt.
Do not add a `known` entry to conceal a new regression; an existing known finding must remain reproducible until its fix removes the entry.
Metal, CUDA or HIP runner coverage does not establish another backend's correctness, nor XPU's; name missing backend coverage and agree its checks separately.

Keep checkpoint activation precision and the required accumulation precision.
Do not add FP8/int8 activations, lossy caches, reduced-precision sums or fast-math changes merely to clear a speed gate.
Checkpoint-defined arithmetic is a separate case: [Nemotron Super VL](nemotron-3.5-super-vl.md) explicitly defines `checkpoint` and `full` modes.
Qualify each claimed mode against its own plain output, label the mode in receipts, and measure fidelity between modes separately.
Do not turn an older recipe's broad precision statement into a ban on an already qualified checkpoint mode.

A changed reduction order also needs an independent FP64 reference for each affected projection class.
Native error must be no worse than the current reference.
Compare prompt and decode rows separately; retain worst-column errors and teacher-forced top-token differences and margins.
Same-engine drafted/plain equality cannot replace this independent model-fidelity evidence.
Do not widen a tolerance or apply a tie policy beyond its documented contenders and margins to manufacture a pass.

### Preserve device ordering and buffer lifetime

Trace the launcher as well as the shader.
For generated or captured kernels, update their owning source or generator and regenerate the matching assets and manifest; patching one generated copy does not update the runtime path.
The [Metal lane projection](../../zig/kernels/metal/core/lane_projection.metal) shares weight reads while preserving each row's sums; [CUDA lane GEMV](../../zig/kernels/cuda/lane_gemv.cu) preserves group and K-slice order.
Keep row arithmetic independent of verify width, grouping, prompt chunking and concurrent stream order wherever the selected contract requires it.
Check real dimensions, tails, sparse-attention boundaries and accepted-path commits, not only convenient full tiles.

GPU resources, borrowed views and per-call metadata must remain valid until their commands complete.
Preserve residency declarations and the existing Metal fence/event ordering when command buffers or queues change.
On CUDA, upload on the stream that consumes the data and preserve graph capture/replay ownership and stable buffers.
Do not introduce host readbacks or synchronizations into the hot path without measuring their dependent and served cost.
A chip-specific fast path must retain a valid capability-gated path for the older chips the contribution claims to support.

## Prove the engine contracts

At the same checkpoint, backend, runtime, rank count, precision and request settings, check every affected case:

- Drafted output equals `"draft": false` token for token at the supported windows/depths.
- Supported resumed, edited, regenerated and post-restart paths equal fresh execution of their full rendered prompts.
- Concurrent replies equal their solo runs, including backends that queue requests.
- Prompt/decode seams preserve required KV, recurrent, convolution, n-gram, drafter and final-logit state.
- Rejection, partial acceptance, cancellation and reset leave the next request valid.
- Advertised thinking, sampling, tools, structured output and media features reach the intended native path and preserve their existing API behavior.

Only claim supported combinations actually exercised; do not equate different backends, quantizations or precision modes by assumption.
Use fresh processes for cold checks and seams vulnerable to uninitialized state.
Retain before/after failures and token hashes or full token arrays, not just plausible text.
For cache changes, verify identity/invalidation, cached-token counts and genuinely cache-off controls.
For multi-host changes, include matching build/checkpoint/precision checks and peer failure/cleanup, using the affected transport's recipe.

## Select checks by the change

Use the exact Zig version in `.zig-version`; do not upgrade the toolchain as a porting shortcut.
The native-code baseline host checks are visible in [no-GPU CI](../../.github/workflows/no-gpu.yml):

```sh
zig build test test-kernel-contract test-golden fuzz-cortheon
git diff --check
python3 tools/zig/lean_check.py
```

Use [lean_new.py](../../tools/zig/lean_new.py) and the CI procedure to compare the same checker against the PR's merge base.
Inherited lean findings must be reported; the acceptance condition is zero new problems, not a fabricated clean exit.
Source modules stay at most 600 lines, with single-line comments/docstrings within 120 columns; put measurements in receipts or recipes.
Run additional family/operator tests selected from the actual build targets and the affected recipe.
CI runs `fuzz-cortheon` unconditionally; a focused local iteration is not the complete no-GPU receipt.
Run a plain `zig build` as well, because the named steps skip some tools and only the plain build compiles every target.
Use the existing packaging checks for changed assets or archives.

Mac builds need Xcode's Metal toolchain (`xcrun metal`); Command Line Tools alone can't build the metallibs.
On a Mac, a native build intended to run across supported Apple chips uses:

```sh
zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig build kernel-contract -Dcpu=apple_m1
```

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar).

The second command runs GPU gates and requires the test device to be available.
For compile-limit records use the Metal contract's `--offline DIR` workflow from the kernel-contract guide.
On an authorized CUDA test machine, with the qualified compiler path adjusted if necessary:

```sh
zig build kernel-contract -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc
zig build fatbins kernel-contract-fatbins -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Dsm=80,86,89,120,121
zig-out/bin/tf-cuda-test kernel-contract-limits zig-out/fatbin
```

On an AMD test machine, on a GPU of the chip named, and for the records of every served RDNA chip without a GPU:

```sh
zig build hip-kernel-contract -Dhip-arch=gfx1100 -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/bin/hipcc
zig build hip-kernel-contract-limits -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/bin/hipcc
```

Inspect [kernel-contract build registration](../../zig/build/kernel_contract.zig) ([HIP's](../../zig/build/hip_contract.zig)) and the target's build options before running a platform command.
Host tests, compile-limit records, a host-only archive and a fake-engine golden corpus do not prove real-model inference on a GPU.
Documentation-only changes need link/claim checks, not an invented model receipt or a new GPU workload.

## Attach a reproducible performance receipt

Use the native server, the issue's agreed workload and the existing [served](../../tools/bench_openai.py), [concurrent](../../tools/bench_concurrent.py) and [cold-cache](../../tools/bench_cache.py) clients.
Match the machine, baseline/candidate binary identities, checkpoint/tokenizer/drafter revisions, exact rendered prompt IDs, output length, seed and generation settings.
Record thinking mode, precision, rank count, cache state, concurrency, warmups and repetitions.
Measure ordinary greedy prose and code, and sampled or feature-specific cells when the changed path requires them.
Check that run's tokens before interpreting its speed.

Report decode rate, cold prefill/TTFT and aggregate concurrency separately.
For prompt processing, retain cold 2k/8k/32k/64k token arrays and request bodies where admitted, with longer model-native windows separately labelled.
Keep `--prompt-cache-gib 0` controls and fresh KV state for cold measurements; a warm prefix is not a cold-prefill improvement.
Alternate baseline/candidate runs for small differences, retain all attempts and explain interruptions or drift.
Do not call a change in output tokens or quantization an isolated kernel improvement.
Independent microbenchmarks supplement dependent operations and whole served requests; they cannot replace them.

Include peak physical process footprint and device/pinned allocations where available, plus the actual RAM class and context.
A configured budget on a bigger machine is not proof of fit on a smaller machine.
Use the existing GPU lock and admission guard, with one model process per test machine.
Do not stop somebody else's server, raise shared memory limits, change drivers or expose a listener merely to complete a receipt.
Keep receipts local unless upload has been explicitly authorized.

## Decide readiness without changing the gate

Follow the existing [PR template](../../.github/pull_request_template.md).
State the changed behavior, issue/gate, owning modules, commands, exit statuses, pass/fail/skip counts, exactness results, kernel summaries, before/after rates, cold-prefill impact and unrun platforms.
Update the relevant recipe or capability documentation only as far as the new evidence supports it.
Write the code for TensorFold rather than copying source, kernels or tables from other inference engines or projects.
If something has to come from elsewhere, name its source and license in the PR and wait for the maintainer's decision.
Preserve contributor authorship, required licenses and third-party notices; exclude private paths, hosts, credentials and confidential data from source, fixtures and public receipts.
Commit under the contributor's GitHub noreply address with no AI-tool co-author or "Generated with" lines; a PR whose commits carry them lands as new commits credited with Co-authored-by and shows as closed, not merged.

A contribution is ready for the claimed scope only when its required checks and agreed performance gates are met.
A result just below a minimum is still below it; a skip or unavailable device is not a pass.
Unqualified support can be presented as a draft or limited experiment, with the remaining gates explicit.
Report blockers and the smallest next check instead of claiming completion or weakening the test.
Do not merge, publish, assign a release version or deploy as a side effect of using this skill.
# Adding a CUDA family

This guide covers the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Its paths are at that tag. New families go on the
Zig engine: see [adding a Zig family](adding-a-zig-family.md).

A family serves CUDA when it exports `cuda_engine`. Keep implementation files under the family's `cuda/`
package and import PyTorch inside backend code, so family discovery also works on an MLX installation.

## Package and engine

```python
MODEL_TYPES = ("mymodel",)
TITLE = "My model"
MODELS = ("example/checkpoint",)

def cuda_engine(model_dir, *, drafter="", tp=1, rank=0, master="", master_port=29551,
                no_drafts=False, mtp_drafts=None, **options):
    from .cuda.engine import MyEngine
    return MyEngine(model_dir, ...)
```

Validate supported weights, context and rank settings before allocating model state.
An optional `CUDA_APP` subclasses `tensorfold.cuda.server.App` for family-specific request handling.

The engine exposes `eos`, `generate(prompt, max_tokens, sampling, on_tokens)` and, for a follower rank,
`follow()`. `generate` receives token IDs and keyed sampling settings, reports newly committed tokens
through the callback, honors its stop result where supported, and returns statistics. A `generate` that also
takes `stop_eos` is passed `stop_eos=False` for an `ignore_eos` request and decodes past end tokens; without it,
an end token ends every reply, unless the family's `CUDA_APP` hands `ignore_eos` to the engine and sets
`reads_ignore_eos`, as GLM's does. Expose cache capacity
so the server can reject oversized prompt-plus-reply requests before streaming.

Use the dense Qwen engine as a starting point. Both ranks must agree on settings, request headers,
prefix identity and forward order. Do not advertise shared requests merely because the CLI accepts
`--parallel`; the HTTP scheduler and engine both need that support.

## Exactness

A row must get exactly the same bits alone and in every supported verify window. Check projections,
attention, routing, recurrent state, accepted-path commits and subsequent decode. Compare eager calls
with CUDA graphs. For two ranks, compare with that same two-rank engine's serial reference.

Keep split-K and attention partitions independent of window width. Use stable routing ties and fixed
reduction order. Where ranks combine fp32 partials, gather and add in rank order. Library matmuls whose
algorithm changes with row count cannot define an unchecked exact verify path.

Use a separate fp32 forward for quality checks and set `TORCH_ALLOW_TF32_CUBLAS_OVERRIDE=0` for that
reference. Exactness against serial and quality against a trusted model are separate checks.

## Memory and packaging

Budget checkpoint storage, cache capacity, workspaces, captured graphs and file-backed tables on every
rank. On unified-memory systems, host allocations and GPU allocations compete for physical memory.
Reject an explicit context that cannot fit and report the estimated fitting capacity.

Declare non-Python kernel sources and data files as package data. Verify the wheel contains them and the
extension compiler is available in the supported container. Keep PyTorch and Triton versions tied to the
qualified toolchain instead of replacing the container's packages implicitly.

## Tests and measurements

Put GPU tests in `tests/cuda/`, with imports and bad-setting checks that can run without weights.
Cover each window width, sparse-attention transitions, partial keeps, resumed versus fresh prompts and
rank synchronization. Add concurrent versus solo checks before exposing concurrent execution.

Use the [public fixture command](README.md#measurements) for server measurements. Keep model/runtime pins,
launch commands and output hashes with results. Time dependent chains and full requests; do not select a
kernel solely from independent microbenchmarks.
# Adding an MLX family

This guide covers the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Its paths are at that tag. New families go on the
Zig engine: see [adding a Zig family](adding-a-zig-family.md).

Create `src/tensorfold/families/<name>/`. The CLI discovers packages by `MODEL_TYPES`, matching
`config.json` or its `text_config`. Keep backend imports inside the loader so discovery does not load a model.

## Package interface

```python
MODEL_TYPES = ("mymodel",)
TITLE = "My model"
LANES = True
MODELS = ("example/checkpoint",)
KERNEL_PACKAGE = "tensorfold.kernels.mymodel.v1"
KERNEL_VERSION = "v1"

def load(model_dir, **options):
    ...  # return model, tokenizer
```

Optional declarations include `DRAFTER`, `MLX_ENV`, `check`, `engine_settings`, `kernel_version` and `setup`.
`check` must reject unsupported configuration before downloading weights, then validate the weight index
when available. List shared kernel modules in `KERNEL_DEPENDENCIES` so snapshot keys include them.

`weight_bytes(model_dir, ple_on_ssd)` can provide a conservative resident-weight estimate for MLX startup
admission. Without it, the CLI counts every safetensors file's size. Read headers only, use the loader's
placement decision, and exclude only tensor bytes kept on the host (file mappings, or the SSD reads of
`--ple-on-ssd`). Runtime cache and workspace admission still applies after loading; this hook does not change
the memory budget.

## Model interface

`load` returns a model with `lane_family = True` and a tokenizer. The complete model protocol is in
[`src/tensorfold/engine/lane_family.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/engine/lane_family.py).

| Member | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `make_cache()` | New state for one stream |
| `hidden(inputs, cache)` | Consecutive hidden rows, advancing the cache |
| `head(hidden)` | Target logits |
| `keep_rows(cache, rows, keep)` | Restore precisely the accepted prefix |
| `exact_width`, `window_costs` | Checked window width and measured cost by width |
| `prefill(inputs, cache)` | Optional prompt path, called on the engine's planned chunks |
| `hidden_rows`, `keep_rows_streams` | Shared forward and independent stream commits |
| `batch_rows`, `max_streams`, `shared_costs` | Shared-forward limits and costs |
| `speculate`, `settle`, `draft_streams` | Optional draft-head operations |
| `adopt_cache(cache)` | Restore family-specific cache classes from snapshots |
| `release_rounds()` | Drop the last forward's rollback buffers when no stream is live, including after startup probes |

Start with `exact_width = 1`. Use one sampler consistently for serial and drafted calls; the host and GPU
implementations can differ at near-ties. Prompt chunks must follow the engine's plan both fresh and resumed.
The CLI finds message markers in the tokenizer's chat template. The plan uses assistant-message starts
and the second message's start as resume points, with chunk starts at least 256 and at most 2,048 tokens
apart. Without usable markers it uses 2,048-token chunks from position zero. A cache lookup must not
choose a different prefill shape for an otherwise identical prompt.

## Verification

Check each projection and attention row alone and in a window using exact equality. Compare recurrent
state after partial keeps, then continue decoding. Check shared forwards against streams run separately,
including unequal stream lengths. Disable an unsupported wider path when a load-time check fails.

Row-dependent matmul dispatch, shape-dependent reductions, attention masks, routing ties and different
rounding points can break exactness. Fix arithmetic order per row. Pass per-step values in buffers instead
of creating a new kernel specialization for each token. Evaluate derived weights on the loading thread.

Compare model quality against a trusted forward on a named public fixture. Use teacher-forced NLL and
top-token agreement, and report the reference's own numerical variation. Tests on small synthetic models
must be supplemented by the real model dimensions.

## Tests and measurements

Use [`tests/lane_fakes.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/tests/lane_fakes.py) and
[`tests/test_family_streams.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/tests/test_family_streams.py) for
model-free engine cases. Add family tests
for forward correctness, row equality, shared streams, rollback, snapshots and context/memory admission.
Exercise thinking on and off, tools, later instructions and templates that rewrite earlier turns.

Measure whole requests with the [public benchmark fixtures](README.md#measurements). Record revisions,
commands, runtime and output hashes. Measure complete dependent chains before promoting a kernel change.
# Adding a Zig family, and taking it to full speed

This is how a model goes onto the Zig engine and gets every speed-up we know. The steps are in order. Each one is a
known win with its measured result, so a new model goes through them without measuring each one again. It comes from
three bring-ups:

- Flash Next 6-bit on an M5 Ultra, 5 Oct 2026. Served decode went from 117-120 tok/s on the Python engine to 134-160,
  and prefill from 2,000-2,500 to 4,000-4,200 tok/s.
- Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on an M5 Max, 3-4 Oct. Prose went to 272-277 tok/s, against about 220 on Python.
- Kimi K3 on four M3 Ultras, 3-4 Oct. One stream went from 2.7 to 11.6 tok/s plain, and 20.3 drafted on prose.

The Python engine's guides, [adding an MLX family](adding-a-family.md) and
[adding a CUDA family](adding-a-cuda-family.md), describe the engine frozen at 0.6.6. New families go here.

## How to use it

1. Do the steps in order, and build each one rather than probing it first. Build it once, in the core, and plug the
   family in (next section).
2. After each step, run that step's exactness check.
3. Before any speed claim, run a served side-by-side against the current release on the same machine. Cover
   generation, prefill and time to first token, 0.5k to 256k tokens, code, prose and edits, all greedy. Check the
   run's tokens.
4. When a new step proves out on a model, add it here with its result. When one loses, add it to "Don't bother".

## Build each step once, in the core

A new model should get every step below by default, not a hand-built engine. So far each family was built as its own
engine, to be exact quickly, and the GPU-side wins stayed inside one family:

- Flash Next replays the Python engine's recorded lane kernels and has its own GPU-side rounds
  (`zig/src/families/flashnext/replay.zig`).
- Kimi K3 and Nemotron have their own rounds.
- Our GLM-5.3 port (not pushed yet) started with MLX-identical row kernels and a host-synchronous round loop.

Some of the host side already lives in core, but so far each piece serves one family, or two:
- the lane round loop, the depth rule and copy proposals (`zig/src/core/lanes`) are Nemotron's;
- prompt reuse (`zig/src/core/prompt_cache.zig`) serves Flash Next, GLM, Nemotron and the Qwen3.8-27B, each with its own `snapshot.zig`;
- staggered segments (`zig/src/core/segments.zig`, and `zig/src/cuda/segments.zig` on CUDA) serve Flash Next on Metal and Nemotron
  on CUDA;
- every host returns the HTTP contract in `zig/src/core/engine_api.zig`, and `zig/src/core/lane_host.zig` serves Nemotron on Metal
  and CUDA, and Flash Next on CUDA. Flash Next on Metal has its own host, one reply at a time, unless an explicit
  `--parallel` above one asks for shared sessions on one Mac: then `zig/src/native/flashnext_batch_host.zig` serves it
  through `lane_host` too (the rule is `shared` in `zig/src/families/flashnext/batch_meta.zig`).

The GPU side is barely shared yet, and that costs time. In the GLM-5.3 port each extra row in a window cost about
4.4 ms of GPU time, against about 2.3 ms for the row's own experts. Row kernels read every replicated weight again for
every row.

**What the core owns.** A family gets all of this by plugging in:

1. Lane kernels by format.
   - Formats: affine 4-, 6- and 8-bit at the checkpoint's group size, and bf16. They run on M5 tensor units and in the
     M1-M4 layout (`zig/src/core/frags.zig`).
   - Ops: dense projections; the expert gather (gate and up fused, then down); the router with its top-k and this Mac's
     expert lists; the head with its argmax; norms.
   - Each kernel reads a weight once per window and keeps every row's own sums, so a row's bits are the same at any
     width.
2. GPU-side rounds (steps 6-9).
   - The accept kernel, the ring, and two rounds in flight.
   - The MTP chain driver and copy drafts.
   - A depth rule set from measured tokens per ms for each model.
3. The prompt path (steps 10-15).
4. Several Macs.
   - Tensor and expert parallel over [MCDMA](https://github.com/ashhart/MCDMA), with exchanges inside the command buffer.
   - Experts split by rows, so both Macs do equal work for every pick.
5. Serving (steps 16-17), and the exactness suite.

**What a family supplies.** Its config, weight map and layer graph, plus kernels only for what is its own: a mixer such
as KDA, GDN or MLA, or a sparse-attention indexer. On day one it's exact against the reference (stage 0). After the
lane kernels go in, check against the engine's own plain output (step 4).

**Where each piece lives today:**

| Piece | Shared now | Family copies or gaps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lane kernels | `zig/kernels/metal/ops/qmv.metal` (affine 4-, 6- and 8-bit row matmuls, MLX's arithmetic) and `zig/src/core/frags.zig` (the prompt layout on M1-M4) | Flash Next: `zig/kernels/metal/decode/fn_lane.metal` (6-bit, groups of 32, tensor ops, up to 16 rows). Kimi K3: MXFP4 experts and bf16 projections. Nemotron: generated per-shape kernels. On CUDA, `zig/kernels/cuda/experts_rows.cu` runs affine 4-bit group-32 experts over a window's rows with the decode kernel's sums, and `route_rows.cu` the router logits and softmax top-k (Flash Next) |
| GPU-side rounds | the host loop, depth rule and copy proposer in `zig/src/core/lanes`, used by Nemotron | Flash Next: its own host loop, plus `fz_accept`, the ring and event chaining (`zig/src/families/flashnext/replay.zig`). Nemotron on Metal: `zig/src/families/nemotron/gpu_round.zig` for a lone stream. Kimi K3: none |
| Several Macs | the MCDMA fabric (`zig/src/fabric`) | Flash Next: `zig/src/families/flashnext/tp.zig` splits rows and holds the whole model on each Mac. Kimi K3: `zig/src/families/kimi_k3/parallel.zig` is a split plan with no link yet |
| Prompt path | segments; the prompt cache, used by Flash Next, GLM, Nemotron and the Qwen3.8-27B | per-family prompt kernels and snapshots |
| Serving | `engine_api` for every host; `lane_host` for Nemotron, Flash Next on CUDA, and Flash Next on Metal under an explicit `--parallel` above one | Flash Next on Metal by default: its own host, one reply at a time |

**The order.**
1. GLM-5.3 builds the core pieces first:
   - the route (router logits, then the pick) and the hyper-connection boundary, each in as few launches as its
     arithmetic allows;
   - 4-bit lane kernels with groups of 64, generalized from `fn_lane.metal`;
   - GPU-side rounds lifted from Flash Next;
   - experts split by rows across two Macs.
2. Flash Next moves onto the core kernels once they give its own bits, and drops its copies.
3. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Kimi K3 and Nemotron follow.

A model is done when the exactness checks pass and the served side-by-side beats the release on the same Mac.

## Tokenizer byte API

`Tokenizer.tokenBytes(allocator, id)` returns an allocator-owned byte slice, or `null` when the decoder
cannot safely decode a token independently of its neighbors. Free a returned slice with the supplied allocator.
Unknown IDs return an empty slice for a supported decoder; special tokens retain their literal spelling.
The bytes may contain incomplete UTF-8, including individual ByteLevel or `<0xNN>` byte-fallback pieces.
Use `Tokenizer.decode` for human-readable text; its existing replacement-character behavior is unchanged.

Supported chains contain ByteLevel or ByteFallback, Fuse, and literal Replace steps before any joining step.
An empty chain or a token-local literal Replace chain is also supported.
Strip, Metaspace, WordPiece, regex replacement, missing decoders, and replacement after joining return `null`.
This API does not enable constrained generation or add a server capability.

## The exactness checks

- **Decode kernels.** Drafted output equals the engine's own one-token-at-a-time output, token for token, at every
  depth and window width. A kernel swap on the target must hold at every width. The MTP head may differ, because its
  drafts are only proposals.
- **Prompt path.** The first token is the same, last-row logits are within bf16 rounding, and the next 48 decoded
  tokens are equal, at 8k and 32k. Run it from a fresh process: an A/B inside one process can hide uninitialized
  state.
- **Precision.** No int8 or fp8 activations, and no lossy cache. A new summation order at equal precision is allowed.

## Stage 0: exact on day one

1. **Record and replay.** Run the reference engine once with a hook on its kernel launches.
   - Record every kernel's source and its launch sites, keyed by role and row count. That covers one-row steps,
     verify windows of 2-16 rows, MTP absorbs and chains, and prompt chunks.
   - Write a pack of prepared weights, reference tokens and fixtures. The Zig engine loads the checkpoint plus the pack
     and replays the kernels natively.
   - Flash Next matched Python bit for bit on its first run: 64/64 tokens, 110/110 window rows, 14/14 drafts.
   - The recorder is `tools/zig/flashnext_dump.py`. Python is only a dev-time oracle here. A model isn't v1 on Zig
     until it runs without a recorded dump.

## Stage 1: the decode round

2. **One command buffer a round.** Drafts stay on the GPU. Flash Next went from 115-118 to 123.2 tok/s at depth 3.
3. **Lane matmuls sum their own groups**, and run on a serial encoder. This removed 99 launches a step: 128.9 tok/s.
4. **Full-width expert kernels at the checkpoint's bit width**, gate and up together, then down: 141.7 tok/s. This
   changes the summation order, so check drafted against the engine's own plain output, not Python's.
5. **A dense matvec for the MTP head only.** The target keeps its lane matmul, because the matvec wins one row and
   loses wide windows: 142.9 tok/s.
6. **GPU-side rounds.**
   - An accept kernel checks drafts against the target's picks on the GPU.
   - It writes the verdict and the next round's positions into a small arena.
   - Two rounds stay in flight, chained by events.
   - The host only reads accepted tokens from a ring (`(round & 511) * 20`), and picks the next draft width from
     rounds two back.
   - 144.8 tok/s, GPU busy 97%.

## Stage 2: fill the lanes

7. **The depth rule.**
   - Three draft levels: 3, 6 and 8 (3 or 7 on a paired Mac).
   - A moving average of drafts landed over drafts offered moves the level: from 3 up to 6 above 0.8, from 6 up to 8
     above 0.74, from 8 back to 6 below 0.62, and from 6 to 3 below 0.65. On a pair, 3 goes to 7 above 0.95.
   - The widest level holds while the moving average stays at 0.62 or above (0.8 on a pair). Metal's MTP chains run
     up to 8 drafts; on CUDA the recipe defaults to 6 (8 for greedy streams), and an explicit depth stops at 15.
   - Flash Next code at depth 6: 6.07 tokens a round, 242.7 tok/s.
8. **Copy drafts on the GPU.** The GPU keeps the token history and finds the longest suffix match, up to 8 tokens.
   - Lenient gate: a match of 3 that reaches 6, or that agrees with the head's first draft.
   - Strict gate: a match of 4 that reaches 9, or that agrees with the first two.
   - Stay lenient while copies land within 0.05 of the head's drafts.
   - Flash Next edits went from 228.6 to 314.1 tok/s, with code and prose unchanged.
9. **Windows of up to 16 rows**, the widest only while copies land.
   - **Routed experts past one row: a 16-group's weight words as the outer loop** (`tf_experts_w`, Nemotron on Metal,
     8 Oct 2026). The lane kernel took its members two at a time with all 16 activations of a chunk live; taking the
     four weight words as the outer loop keeps four activations a member live, so three members a pass at four
     simdgroups fit. Same bits at every width (`tf-nemotron-experts`); the up and down projections of 23 layers went
     from 2.35 to 2.27 ms at 4 rows, 6.68 to 6.48 at 16, 11.93 to 11.24 at 32 and 22.57 to 20.58 at 64, equal at 2.
     Served, cache off, alternated twice: one stream 503 to 513 tok/s on code and 348 to 351 on prose; 8 streams 947
     to 985 and 713 to 731 in all; 32 streams 792 to 802 and 752 to 761. Every reply equal to its solo and plain run.

## Stage 3: the prompt path

On M5 tensor units. Chips before M5 need their own path.

10. **8192-row prompt chunks, and attention on the tensor units.** Each row's query heads go in as one operand over its
    selected keys, so each key is read once for every head. Flash Next went from 2,000-2,500 to 3,300-3,600 tok/s.
11. **Tensor-op matmuls at the checkpoint's bit width** for dense projections and expert gathers, with gate and up
    fused. The router and the split-K hyper-connection projection go on the tensor units too.
12. **Sparse-attention indexer scores on the tensor units**, and block selection past the key budget everywhere:
    decode, prompt chunks and GPU-side rounds.
13. **The MTP head's prompt keys on the tensor units.** With step 11's fused gate-up: 4,000-4,200 tok/s.
14. **The linear-recurrence scan over 16 lanes a row** (DeltaNet). A small gain, kept.
15. **Staggered segments on two queues** (`zig/src/core/segments.zig`, any family).
    - A long prompt's call runs as two segments, each on its own Metal queue with its own prompt buffers.
    - The second segment runs each layer's mixer after the first's, so one segment's scan and glue run beside the
      other's matrix work.
    - The core owns the queues, an MTLFence per segment and an MTLEvent between them. Buffers are untracked, so
      without the fence the encoders overlap and the output breaks.
    - A family supplies hooks: begin, pre, mixer, post and finish. It also supplies `wait` and `handoff`. `wait` says
      which layers wait ahead of their pre-mixer work, such as a convolution tail the segment before writes.
    - Recurrent state slots alternate as serial chunks would.
    - Split only when every segment gets 4,096 rows or more, in even calls (`segments.next`). Each segment re-reads
      nearly every expert's weights, so small segments lose: 2k rows -7%, 3k level. Three queues gave +2%, and four
      timed out.
    - Flash Next served: TTFT -5% to -8% from 8k (32k 7.52 to 6.94 s, 128k 31.5 to 29.1 s), with the same replies.
      The second segment's buffers take about 9 GB. Pushed in c2bede8fd.

## Stage 4: serve

16. **Serve on `tensorfold-native`**, warmed at load, foreground before background, with stop strings and cancel.
17. **A Metal keepalive** for any model that holds a large residency set. That's a one-thread command buffer every
    250-500 ms, on its own queue, inside the engine process. Without it macOS unwires the set after 1-2 s idle, and
    the next request pays a full re-wire: 2.7 s on K3.

Native CUDA families may export `healthy(ctx: *anyopaque) bool`. The native host forwards this callback to
lane health and admission. It must read thread-safe host state without binding a GPU context, waiting on device
work or taking the inference thread's lock. Families without it retain the lane host's normal closing/stale checks.
Unavailable or busy admission returns HTTP 503 before a streaming response opens. Context-window refusals retain
their existing streamed error policy; failures after admission remain stream errors.

## Across several Macs

From Kimi K3 on four Macs:
- Split by tensor parallel and expert parallel over Thunderbolt RDMA, which is two-sided only.
- Send one message per exchange, with a spinning lock instead of a sleeping one. Posting fell from 14-19 us to 2-7 us.
- Put one MTLFence between consecutive round command buffers, or a later buffer's spin wait holds an earlier one's
  work.
- Give each simdgroup one weight tile in one-row dispatches. The rank-to-rank spread came from the threadgroup tail.
  +1.4%.
- Run drafters on other ranks, asked through the round's draft command.
- Send bulk copies between nodes over the Thunderbolt link addresses, not the LAN.

## On CUDA: Nemotron served on a GB10

These wins are on a branch we haven't pushed yet. The Zig CUDA engine replays the Python engine's captured Triton
kernels next to our own .cu kernels, so stage 0 holds from the start: `tensorfold run` gives Python's tokens. These
were the wins, served through `tensorfold-native`, in order. Each kept every check exact.

1. **Graphs on the engine's own sequence.** The first stream takes the sequence the window graphs were captured on
   and replays them. Other streams run eager. Served drafted +0.7-3.5%, serial +4.5%.
2. **lane_gemv and a forked shared expert.**
   - Every projection with K slices runs a column tile's slices in one CTA, summed in order, instead of a cluster per
     tile.
   - The shared expert runs on a forked graph branch while the router and plan run.
   - Byte-equal against the kernels they replace. Serial +6%, drafted +1-4%.
3. **A lone-stream driver.**
   - A lone drafted stream decodes the way `tensorfold run` does, with the depth rule that reads each draft level's
     confidence. The lane core's rule reads acceptance by depth and keeps fewer drafts a round.
   - The driver hands the stream to the lane core when another request arrives.
   - Served drafted +3-7%, 1.05-1.12x the Python engine's one-stream numbers, every rep within 1%.
4. **A graph set per draw mode.** Greedy and sampled each get their own window and head graphs, and the sampled ones
   read the rule from the sequence's buffer. Sampled streams replay graphs and run lone too. Sampled story +8-17%.
5. **Shared rounds.** Several streams' windows run in one forward, 16 rows in all.
   - The dense matmuls, router and experts run once over every row.
   - Each stream's embeds, conv, scan, KV write, attention and draw run on its own row slice, with its own state and
     rule.
   - It stays exact because every 16-row kernel is row-invariant.
   - Aggregate over taking turns, sampled with a seed a stream: 1.17-1.28x at 2 streams, 1.39-1.57x at 4, and
     1.53-1.91x at 8.
   - Greedy cells that send one sequence to every stream go higher, up to 2.91x, and swing by rep.
   - One stream is unchanged.

Next on CUDA: one MTP head forward a level over every stream's row. Each stream drafts on its own today, eagerly, at
0.75 ms a level, which is about 9 ms of a 4-stream round. Graphs for shared windows would save only 1-4.5% of a
forward.

CUDA traps:
- Zig 0.17's `readFileAlloc` reads up to the size `stat` reports, and procfs reports 0. Read /proc files with a
  streaming reader, or the GB10 memory budget silently falls back to MemFree.
- A synchronous copy (`cuMemcpyHtoD`) runs on the legacy stream. A kernel launched right after on a non-blocking
  stream can read the old bytes. Upload on the stream that reads.
- A shared round drafts before it keeps. Commit each window to its kept path at whichever comes first, or the round
  commits twice.
- Two GB10s ran identical code 4-6% apart. Compare engines on the same box.

## What to attack first, by model type

| The model has | Do first |
| --- | --- |
| Routed experts | Step 4 at its bit width, then step 11's fused gate-up. Don't group experts by lane. |
| DeltaNet, Mamba or KDA layers | Step 14, and keep recurrent state fp32. |
| Hyper-connections | Step 3. Split-K hyper-connection projections on the tensor units in prompts. |
| A sparse-attention indexer | Steps 10 and 12. |
| An MTP head | Steps 5 and 13, chains capped at 6. |
| Text that repeats its context, like edits and code | Step 8. |
| A model bigger than one Mac | The section on several Macs. |

## Don't bother: built, run, and lost

- 128-row prompt tiles: same bits, no faster than 64.
- 32-row expert tiles for every size: 4,031 against 4,205 tok/s at 8k.
- A staged DeltaNet prompt scan: slower.
- Coalesced hyper-connection kernels in decode: no change.
- The dense matvec on the target: it wins one row and loses wide windows.
- DeltaNet step and hyper-connection tensor-op kernels at 2-7 rows: exact, slower.
- Split command buffers: no gain, and they need events between them.
- Grouped experts, so each distinct expert is read once for all lanes: bit-identical and slower. The GPU cache already
  shares lanes' expert reads. Packed expert rows: no change.
- Two lane groups at once: the same work as one window of both.
- One launch for all experts: exact, slower.
- Input sums once a threadgroup, and weight prefetch beside short launches: slower.
- A persistent kernel with a GPU-wide barrier: it loses to plain dependent launches on the M5 Ultra.
- A pool of kept prompt-state buffers for Nemotron: a fresh 9.2k-token prompt costs 1.07 s whether the cache is off,
  keeps every state, or evicts and reallocates two 106 MiB states a request (22 evictions in 12 prompts). The GPU copy
  hides a new buffer's cost; Flash Next's pool stays, for its idle pre-touch.
- Nemotron's routed experts, three ways that kept every bit and gained nothing (`tf-nemotron-experts`, M5 Ultra):
  an expert's member blocks spread over grid z instead of looped (the GPU already overlaps a popular expert's loop
  with the other 230 threadgroups a layer); the activations' floats and bf16-rounded group sums prepared once a
  forward instead of remade a member (50 fewer ALU ops a chunk, the same time, so the loop is not ALU-bound);
  8-byte vector loads of the weight words and activations (slower than the compiler's own schedule). Six or eight
  members a pass, or four at two simdgroups, lose 5-40%: only two to four at four simdgroups win.
- Adaptive depth by landed+1: it lost to fixed levels. Full-vocabulary drafts lose too.
- Reshaping the 6-bit expert prompt kernels, all exact, Flash Next on the M5 Ultra at 8k:
  - 128-row paired gate-up tiles lost 25% to register spills.
  - These were all level: 128 rows on 8 simdgroups; mixed 128/32-row heights; 32-column tiles with half the shared
    memory; those tiles double-buffered; and a tile list built once a layer.
  - The paired kernel's gap to the dense projections isn't tiling, occupancy, barrier overlap or the tile search.
- Lanes without a drafter on prose, all measured on K3 and Nemotron:
  - Jacobi self-lanes landed 1.1-1.3 of 32.
  - Recycled lanes landed 0.59 a round, against MTP's 3.01.
  - A phrase store added 2-15%.
  - Logit-lens pruning found the true token in its top 64 at most 6% of the time.
  Lanes land when they're guessed right going in.

## Traps that cost a day each

- Compile Metal kernels at run time with safe math. An offline metallib gives wrong values for bf16 tensor-op inputs.
- Register arrays need full-unroll hints, or kernels run 5-9x slower. A `break` inside an unrolled loop kills the
  unroll.
- `var x: T = undefined` skips Zig field defaults, so set every field. It once gave a wrong first token, and garbage
  replies that only showed in a fresh process.
- The strict tensor-op mode lays out operands differently from our fragments. Use the relaxed mode.
- `half` is a Metal type name. macOS 27 rejects it as a variable name.
- Untracked buffers let command buffers overlap. Separate buffers need an event or fence between them.
- Ordering encoders with a shared event's signal-and-wait works, but it's slow: staggered prefill fell to 2,629 tok/s.
  Use an MTLFence inside a queue and an MTLEvent across queues.
- Per-call metadata buffers must be distinct inside one command buffer, because the GPU reads them when it runs.
- MLX checkpoints put tensors at odd offsets. Load each shard into one Metal buffer; don't mmap typed.
- A binary that leaves the build machine needs `-Dcpu=apple_m1`, or M1-M4 Macs crash on start with SIGILL.
- Check the build's exit status before copying a binary. A failed build piped through grep once shipped the old one.
- Send `"temperature": 0` to the Flash Next host. A missing temperature becomes the model default of 1.0, which the
  host refuses.
- Never quote a speed before checking that run's tokens. A Nemotron build once looked 25% faster because a bug gave
  wrong tokens that were easier to draft.

## Next steps, not yet proven

Try these on Flash Next first, then move each into the stages above with its result:
- Staggered segments for Nemotron and every other family. For Nemotron, the in-projection goes in pre, conv and scan
  are the mixer, and MoE layers need no wait.
- The hyper-connection write fused into its norm in the prompt path.
- Expert inputs read through a row map instead of copied, and the down projection read back through the inverse map.
- Draft trees in one pass per depth, so 16-32 lanes carry the head's best alternatives.
- A drafter trained on the model's own replies.

## Toolchain: Zig is pinned to 0.17.0

Zig 0.17.0 is the release of 1 Oct 2026. 0.18 is in development, and Zig breaks between releases.
- The repo enforces it. `.zig-version` holds 0.17.0, `build.zig.zon` sets it as the minimum, and `build.zig` refuses
  to compile with any other Zig.
- Official builds and their sha256, from ziglang.org's release index:
  - aarch64-macos: zig-aarch64-macos-0.17.0.tar.xz, b607e9b9234790a008116ae5bdb71c6243b84b9fb42a53a9e70fde41c06c536a
  - aarch64-linux: zig-aarch64-linux-0.17.0.tar.xz, 9e8d11661d4ae3bd57702a3832781e23ad151dde5798e16a5ccd503f65234ff8
  - x86_64-linux: zig-x86_64-linux-0.17.0.tar.xz, 1cbe9df9f27e6b78d14ccbca43b6703a404ef79ef1c463de901d7f088d4e2026
- Moving to a newer Zig is a deliberate step: change `.zig-version`, rebuild everything, and rerun every exactness
  check.
# Adding Living Weights to a family

This is how a family on the Zig engine learns facts with `--slide`. [Living Weights](../living-weights.md) is one
learner for every family (`zig/src/living`): it writes lessons, reads the model, fits a pocket of new neurons and saves
them into the checkpoint's own shards. A family describes itself as data, and its host and trainer give the learner a
few hooks. The steps are in order. It comes from three families:

- Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on Metal and CUDA, the first family and the only one whose learning has landed;
  `living/families.zig` also lists Nemotron Omni, Flash Next and the 27B.
  Its relu^2 shared experts carry the pocket at the MoE layers.
- Qwen3.8 Flash Next on CUDA (#895 and #896). A SwiGLU shared expert behind its own gate at every layer, with
  hyper-connections, Gated DeltaNet and gated attention below it.
- Qwen3.8-27B on CUDA, a port on #726's branch that is not a pull request yet. A dense SwiGLU MLP at every layer, with
  no experts at all.

Only Nemotron learns in this tree. Flash Next's and the 27B's learning have not landed, so their file names and
numbers below come from those branches.

Bring the family up on the Zig engine first, exact and at speed ([adding a Zig family](adding-a-zig-family.md)). The
learner trains through the engine's own forward, so everything below assumes that forward is done.

## How to use it

1. Do the steps in order. Each ends in a check that has to pass before the next step means anything.
2. Never teach the original folder. Teach a `cp -RL` copy (`cp -cRL` on a Mac), and check the original's sha256
   after each run.
3. Put the receipts at the end of this page in the PR: an untaught folder serves as before, the trainer's forward is
   the serving forward, lessons are kept, and a taught folder serves.

## 1. Describe the family as data

Add a `Family` to `living/families.zig`. The learner, the shard writer and the server's Living Weights view all read
it, by the checkpoint's `model_type`.

| Field | Nemotron (`nemotron_h`) | Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) | Qwen3.8-27B (`qwen3_5`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `names.layers`, `names.expert` | `backbone.layers.`, `mixer.shared_experts.` | `language_model.model.layers.`, `mlp.shared_expert.` | `language_model.model.layers.`, `mlp.` |
| `names.inputs` | `up_proj` | `gate_proj`, `up_proj` | `gate_proj`, `up_proj` |
| `names.mtp` | its own file, `mtp-4bit.safetensors` | in the index, `language_model.mtp.layers.0.mlp.shared_expert.` | none |
| `neuron` | relu^2, margin 0.25 | SwiGLU, gated, margin 0.5, sharp 16 | SwiGLU, margin 0.5, sharp 16 |
| `quant` | 4-bit, groups of 64 | 4-bit, groups of 32 | 4-bit, groups of 64 |
| `keys` | `moe_shared_expert_intermediate_size` at the top level | `shared_expert_intermediate_size` in `text_config` | `intermediate_size` in `text_config` |
| `experts` | `.pattern`: the MoE layers of `hybrid_override_pattern` | `.every` | `.every` |

**Where the pocket goes.** A pocket is 64 neurons a layer (`Family.neurons`, a whole number of quantization groups),
zero until a fact uses one. Each is one more row of every input projection and one more column of the output
projection, so the first save makes the projection 64 neurons wider and any MLX loader reads a slightly wider model.

- **An MoE layer with a shared expert:** beside the shared expert, as Nemotron and Flash Next do. The routed experts
  are left alone: a pocket there would fire only when its expert is picked.
- **A shared expert behind a gate:** set `neuron.gated`. Flash Next scales its shared expert by
  `sigmoid(shared_expert_gate x)`, so a pocket neuron adds `gate act(x) v` and its output is fitted through the gate.
  The trainer reports the gate at each row (`gateAt`).
- **A dense MLP:** the MLP is the expert (`expert = "mlp."`, `experts = .every`), and the width key is the MLP's
  (the 27B's 17,408 neurons become 17,472).

**The neuron's kind.** A relu^2 neuron is exactly zero below its threshold. A SwiGLU neuron is not: `silu` leaks
below zero. A SwiGLU neuron fitted as `u` is written as gate row `sharp u` and up row `u / sharp`
(`living/neuron.zig`), so at z = u x it fires `z^2 sigmoid(sharp z)`, which is relu(z)^2 only where z is well above
zero: `neuron.zig`'s test checks the two agree within 1e-6, relative, at z = 1, 1.5 and 3 with `sharp` 16, and at
z = 0.1 they differ by about 0.0017. The output fit reads each neuron through its own activation (`Pocket.act`), not
as relu^2. Rows a neuron stays silent on are fitted to z at or below `-margin`, and with margin 0.5 what leaks there
is at most `0.25 sigmoid(-8)`, about 8.4e-5 (the test checks z from -0.5 down to -20). Keep `sharp` a power of two, so
the up row gives `u` back bit for bit in fp32 while `u / sharp` stays a normal number and `sharp u` finite. A save
still rounds every row to the family's affine format, so the checks read the rows as saved (#877).

`Family.check()` refuses a description whose inputs do not match the neuron, whose code width is 0 or does not divide
a 32-bit word, whose group or pocket is empty or not a whole number of groups, or, for SwiGLU, whose `sharp` is not a
whole power of two from 1 up (`living/family.zig`). Add your family to the tests in `families.zig` and `family.zig`:
its model type is found, and a tensor name of its expert gives the layer back while a similar one (a gate, the MTP
head's) does not.

## 2. The pocket in every pass

The engine adds the pocket wherever the model runs: prompt chunks, verify windows and decode rounds. Load it from the
shards as fp32 rows beside the packed weights (Flash Next: `cuda_pocket.zig`; the 27B: its `pocket.zig`), and take
the shard's projection apart at the old width.

- **An untaught folder's bits do not change.** A layer with no neuron in use launches nothing. Flash Next sums a
  pocket layer's MoE output in fp32, adds the pocket and rounds once; every other layer writes back exactly as before.
  Check the untaught folder against the last release: the same replies, drafted and `"draft": false`, and the same
  speed.
- **Row by row.** The pocket's kernels read each row alone, so drafted still equals `"draft": false` and a concurrent
  stream equals its solo run. Flash Next uses the two-kernel form of #787 (`tf_fn_pocket_in`, then `_out`).
- **Untaught streams.** A request with `untaught` set (the lesson writer's and the judge's, in
  `server/slide_ask.zig`) reads the model as shipped. Zero the pocket's output on its rows. The 27B missed this at
  first: the judge then read the lesson's own neurons, called a reworded "I don't know" a changed answer, and took a
  good lesson out.
- **The config check accepts a taught folder.** If the engine checks the checkpoint's widths at load, subtract
  `tensorfold_learned_neurons` from the expert's width first. Flash Next's check refused its own taught folder at the
  first restart.
- **The MTP head.** The first save widens the MTP head's shared expert with zero neurons, so its tensors stay one
  width. Drafts are made without the pocket; the verify rows run it, so drafted replies still equal plain ones.

## 3. The host

The host is a type the learner is generic over (`Learner(H)` in `living/learner.zig`). A family's slide file
(Nemotron's `cuda_slide.zig`, Flash Next's in #896) declares it.

- **Always:** `Trainer`, `max_rows`, `Ctx`, `family`, `layout(ctx)`, `trainer(gpa, io, ctx)`, `free(t, gpa)` and
  `seconds(io)`.
- **The pocket, relu^2:** `pocket(ctx, layer, up, down, used)` hands the forward a layer's neurons;
  `pocketRead(ctx, layer, up, down) usize` gives back the neurons loaded from the shards; and
  `pocketSave(ctx, gpa, io, layers, neurons, up, down) usize` writes every layer and hands the rows back as written.
- **The pocket, SwiGLU:** `pocketSwiglu`, `pocketReadSwiglu` and `pocketSaveSwiglu`, the same three with a `gate`
  beside `up`.
- `up` and `gate` are each neuron's input rows as the forward multiplies them (`[neurons, D]` f32), and `down` is its
  output. A save hands the rows back rounded as the shards hold them (#877 checks every lesson on those).
- **Optional:** `attach`, `write` and `layers` (Nemotron's routed blocks), and `codes`, `commit` and `fold4`
  (weight edits). The learner offers them only when the trainer has `sites`.

`layout(ctx)` is a `Layout`: the hidden size, the expert's own width with any saved pocket left out, the layer count,
the layers whose expert carries the pocket (`widen`) and the ones lessons put neurons in (`learn`).
`Layout.fromExperts` widens every layer that has an expert and learns at all but the last, whose nudge has no
gradient to read. Read the widths from `config.json` at load, as Flash Next's `layoutOf` does.

## 4. The trainer

The trainer runs the learner's passes on the engine: a keys pass (the rows a pocket reads), a loss pass, and a target
pass that runs the loss's gradient back to the lowest nudged layer.

- **What it gives:** `normed(layer, row)` (a row's input to the expert, as the forward normed it), `pass(seqs, mode,
  turn, out)` and `step(ids, start, mode, turn)`, `spans`, `packs()`, `pack`, `count`, `prefixes`,
  `prefixSlots(n)`, `pushAt(i, key, layer)` (the gradient's push at a nudged row), `deltaAt(i, key, layer)`,
  `residual(layer, row)`, `nudge` and `from`. A gated family also gives `gateAt(layer, row)`.
- **Optional:** `tapRows` (#891) reads a question asked after a conversation through the engine's own prompt chunks,
  so a pocket can read it in context. Nemotron's routed blocks, edits and probes also use `sites`, `sketched`,
  `score()`, `projected()`, `key()` and `config()`.
- **Sequences side by side.** A pass packs several sequences into one forward (Flash Next 1,024 rows, the 27B 1,024
  rows over up to 16 sequences). Row-wise launches run over every row; a recurrent mixer or attention runs each
  sequence from position 0. A sequence's loss in a pack equals its loss alone, exactly.
- **What the forward keeps.** The backward reads what the forward computed: each layer's expert input and its routing,
