(the oracle vectors ship beside the test). Its real checkpoint bytes are one 128x128 block from
`UnstableLlama/Qwen3.5-2B-exl3-8.00bpw` (mcg codebook, 8.00 bpw), in `zig/tests/fixtures/exl3_oracle.bin`.

The scalar decoder and its oracle tests do not register an EXL3 model on their own; the native CUDA kernels below
are checked against them.

## Native CUDA (Zig)

The Zig engine carries the same arithmetic as hand-written CUDA, ported from the Python engine's kernels so a
row's bits match it:

- `zig/kernels/cuda/exl3_decode.cuh`, `exl3_linear.cu`, `zig/src/cuda/exl3.zig`: the input rotation and the linear
  for 1 to 128 rows, every codebook and width (the `mul1` half steps included), with the K split planned from the
  layer's shape alone. `exl3.Dense` runs prompt rows in 128-row blocks of the same kernel, so a prompt row's bits
  equal its decode-row bits wherever its chunk starts; `qlinear.Weight` has an `.exl3` arm for both.
  The split counters are zeroed on the calls' stream when they grow, and each block's last program resets its own.
  On sm_90 and newer the input rotations and the linear, alone or grouped, go out as programmatic dependent
  launches: a linear loads its weights while the kernel before it finishes, then waits for its rows.
  `TF_EXL3_PDL=0` makes them plain stream-ordered launches with the same bits, to time a change without them or to
  rule them out when chasing a fault; below sm_90 they are plain already.
- `zig/kernels/cuda/exl3_experts.cu`, `zig/src/cuda/exl3_experts.zig`: grouped routed experts (member lists,
  each expert's rotation, gate and up, GLM's SwiGLU roundings, down and the weighted combine), widths mixed within
  a layer; an expert's member count never changes a row's bits.
- `zig/src/core/exl3_load.zig`: every trellis group of a checkpoint from its safetensors headers;
  `zig/src/cuda/exl3_upload.zig` puts a group, or a layer's experts, on the device.

`tf-cuda-test exl3 DIR` checks them: every width and codebook against float64 references built on
`exl3_format.zig`, row and chunk invariance, and, when `DIR` holds bytes the Python engine recorded on real checkpoint
layers, those layers bit for bit, two whole layers of RED-SNOW-5.3-Flash (a KDA and a DSA layer, all 288 experts
under real routing) included. The program that records them runs the Python engine and is not in this repository;
`none` skips those checks. `tf-cuda-test exl3-tp2 RANK HOST:PORT DIR` runs the GLM split rules on two ranks over
NCCL (output-column cuts, input-row cuts with fp32 partials summed rank 0 first, and the experts' intermediate cut)
and checks every rank's bytes and the sums the same way.

The Metal projection (#681) and these CUDA pieces are what a family's engine takes, through `qlinear` and
`exl3_experts`. On CUDA, `qwen3_5` serves EXL3 packs of the Qwen3.5 MoE models and of the dense
[Qwen3.8-27B](qwen3.8-27b.md#cuda), whose DFlash2 drafter reads the head through column views
(`exl3.Weight.columns`: whole 128-column blocks with the parent's strides).
# Qwen3.8 Flash Next on CUDA

The native CUDA build serves Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) on one NVIDIA GPU from an MLX affine 4-bit, group-32 checkpoint
with its MTP head, on kernels built in this repository. A set of the Python 0.6.1 engine's Triton kernels, captured
and packed, can stand in for its glue to compare against that engine's teacher path. @AdrianBinDC started the port in
[#476](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/476); it is tracked in
[#472](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/472). Its authors ran the model on a GB10 (sm_121); our kernel tests
also pass on an RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120).

## Experimental ModelOpt and two-rank path

The CUDA family also reads ModelOpt NVFP4 routed experts, including CSF-compressed scale planes, with separate
MXFP8 shared experts and dense projections and the checkpoint's BF16 activations. Two local CUDA ranks partition
expert intermediate channels and gather disjoint vocabulary ranges without reducing their BF16 bits. Each rank
owns its recurrent state, and peer failure makes the serving rank unavailable rather than returning partial results.

This path remains experimental pending independent full-model numerical qualification and complete GPU kernel
contract receipts. Compile success and host tests do not establish checkpoint fidelity. Performance and context
limits must be measured with the exact checkpoint, binary, device topology and request settings. Prefix retention
with MTP is outside this path's qualified scope; evaluate with `--prompt-cache-gib 0`.

### NVIDIA's NVFP4 checkpoint on two GB10s

`nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (the checkpoint SGLang's Flash Next recipes serve) loads as stored: NVFP4 routed
experts with plain scales, BF16 attention, DeltaNet and shared-expert projections, its n-gram table as E4M3 rows
times one BF16 scale (`bf16(e4m3 * scale)`, as SGLang computes it), and its MTP head's routed experts as E4M3 with
BF16 128x128 block scales on the block-FP8 expert kernels (BF16 activations). Two ranks, one a host, rank 1 first:

```bash
# on rank 1
tensorfold-native serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --tp 2 --rank 1 --master 192.0.2.1 --context 65536 --prompt-cache-gib 0
# on rank 0 (192.0.2.1), which serves HTTP
tensorfold-native serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --tp 2 --rank 0 --master 192.0.2.1 --context 65536 --prompt-cache-gib 0
```

- Both ranks run the same executable (they compare it) and need NCCL 2.30 or later; set `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` and
  `NCCL_IB_HCA` for the link between the hosts. `--master-port` (default 29551) names rank 0's control port.
- Each rank sends a digest of every checkpoint byte, cached after the first read (about 2 minutes for this
  checkpoint's 124 GiB on a GB10), and both wait up to 30 minutes for the other. `TENSORFOLD_CHECKPOINT_SHA256`, when
  set the same on both ranks, replaces the digest and keeps the wait at a minute.
- `--prompt-cache-gib 0` is required with drafts at `--tp 2`, and `--idle-unload` is refused with `--tp`.
- At `--tp 2` each stream's window verifies alone, so concurrent streams do not yet share a verify pass.

## Experimental K32 prompt experts

`TF_FLASHNEXT_PROMPT_EXPERT_TILE=1` selects the K32 staging pipeline for NVFP4 prompt gate-up;
`2` also selects its FP32 down projection. Unset or `0` keeps the existing kernels. Decode retains its existing
16-pair form. `TF_FLASHNEXT_FACT_ROWS` retains its existing prompt threshold, including `0` to disable prompt tiles.
The pipeline adapts MiaAI-Lab's MIT recipe patch0014 and retains the same packed weights, BF16 activations,
16-term dots, scale-FMA order and epilogue. This is an unqualified opt-in pending the GPU gates.

`tf-cuda-test nvfp4-fact` compares both prompt forms with the decode bytes on skewed routes, row and column tails,
odd K32 groups and shared-expert skips. The normal CUDA kernel contract adds both replacement kernels and their
rounding-order controls. Their compiler resource slots remain pending until measured for each served SM.
Before enabling it for serving, run the full contract and compare main/candidate prompt-cut, resumed/fresh,
drafted/plain and concurrent/solo tokens at the same checkpoint. Measure cold 4k, 16k and 128k prefill with cache
disabled, alternating with the flag off. Host checks and compile-only checks do not establish GPU exactness or speed.

NVFP4 PLE gathers sort requested row IDs, dequantize each distinct row once through the parked worker pool,
and copy duplicate BF16 rows after the readers join. Hash history and FP32 row sums retain their existing order.
On Linux these rows use positional reads by default; `TF_FLASHNEXT_PLE_IO=mmap` retains the mapped reader,
and `pread` selects positional reads explicitly. MLX tables retain the mapped path.
`TF_FLASHNEXT_WARM_AHEAD=1` enables next-chunk file hints; unset or `0` leaves them off. Hints derive IDs from the future token
prefix without changing a sequence history, issue on the caller and leave no borrowed worker after return.
These I/O choices need cold-storage and served-token A/B gates before a performance claim.

Raw completion prompts of at least 16 tokens gain a kept end mark after they have been served once, when the
prompt-cache budget fits it. The first pass is unchanged; a second identical pass keeps near its end; later repeats
resume there. Chat endpoints retain priority. `TF_FLASHNEXT_REPEAT_CACHE=0` disables this Flash Next CUDA policy.
Other families keep their existing cache policy. Full token keys and frame identity still decide every resume.

## Run

```bash
tensorfold-native serve /path/to/checkpoint --temperature 0
```

- `--context N` takes up to the model's 262,144 tokens; the default is the whole window. Past 2,048 keys each attention
  layer reads 512 blocks of 4 keys a row, chosen by the model's block indexer, as the Python engine does.
- `--parallel N` admits N streams. Each stream's caches are its own: about 110 MiB of DeltaNet state and the n-gram
  tail, plus 28 KiB a token of keys, values and indexer keys, and with drafts its MTP head's cache.
- `--no-drafts` serves without the MTP head; `"draft": false` on a request does the same for that request.
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_READOUT_ROWS` (default 64, `0` never) is the rows from which the hyper-connection read-out takes the prompt
  tiles. Same bits either way; `128` keeps 16-stream decode rounds on the row kernels, up to 7% quicker on a GB10.
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK` (1 to 16,384, default 1,536) caps the rows of one prompt pass. Every pass reads the weights
  of every expert its rows route to, so fewer, larger passes cost less a token; but a pass runs to its end, so a
  stream decoding during a pass waits up to the whole pass for its next token. See
  [Prompt chunk size](#prompt-chunk-size).
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK_SOLO` (`TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK` to 16,384) is the chunk a pass takes when no other stream
  is decoding as it starts; with one decoding, the pass takes `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK`. Unset, it's 8,192 at `--parallel 1`
  on one GPU, and every other server's passes take `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK`. See [Prompt chunk size](#prompt-chunk-size).
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_DRAFTS` (1 to 15, default 6) and `TF_FLASHNEXT_CONFIDENCE` (default -0.4) set the head's chain. A
  negative value keeps drafting while the drafts' probabilities multiply to at least its size (0.4 by default), a
  positive value keeps a later draft only at or above it, and 0 keeps every draft.
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_LOAD_THREADS` (1 to 32, default 8) packs the routed NVFP4 experts on that many threads at load, staged
  through at most 192 MiB of pinned memory: every layer on one GPU, and the MTP head's layer on rank 0 at `--tp 2`.
  1 keeps the one-expert loop. Other values are refused.
- The engine uploads 73.3 GiB of the checkpoint: the n-gram tables stay mapped from the shards, and the vision tower is
  not loaded without `--vision`.
- `--vision` (experimental) runs images through the Qwen-VL tower that Qwen's CUDA family runs too
  (`zig/src/vision/qwen_cuda.zig`), on rank zero alone; its rows replace the prompt's image placeholders, M-RoPE
  positions reach attention, the block indexer and the MTP head, and a second rank receives the rows over NCCL. The
  checkpoint's preprocessor and processor files set the image processor. No checkpoint has been checked with images
  yet.
- It refuses another quantization, other shapes, and semantic settings its kernels fix (RMS epsilon, RoPE base, rotated
  share, type and scaling, the gate and activation types, attention bias, the layer roles, the n-gram layer, kernel
  and dilation): config.json is checked at load and the log names the field. It also refuses `--segments`, `--slide`
  and a folder whose shared experts carry Living Weights neurons.
- `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS=DIR` swaps the glue for a captured set (see [A captured set](#a-captured-set)) when the set
  holds every entry point the engine launches; a set without them (Nemotron's, say) is passed over, and the startup
  line says which glue runs. With a set loaded, `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED` (`all`, or Triton names such as
  `_chunks,_merge`) runs those entry points on our kernels and the rest on the set's, to put a difference down to one
  kernel.

## What the core runs and what the family runs

The family plugs into the core's pieces and adds no scheduler:

- The core's round loop and lane host drive every token. Drafted windows, shared rounds of streams without drafts, and
  prompts a chunk at a time between other streams' rounds (`prefill_step`) all go through them.
- The core's prompt cache keeps and resumes a stream's state at the marks it asks for. The family copies the state
  (`cuda_snap.zig`), with the MTP head's cache rows for a drafting stream; the head reads one token past a row, so
  states keep with a lookahead of 1, as Nemotron's do.
- For a last user message of at least 8,192 tokens, the lane cache may also keep one state inside that message.
  It chooses the latest existing cold chunk cut leaving at least 2,048 tokens outside the state's key, for a
  replacement question after the same document. It uses the loaded prompt pass size and adds no chunk split.
  Endpoint, rewind and shared states have priority; the extra copy is skipped if they cannot fit together under
  the byte or snapshot-slot cap. Existing eviction rules still apply. `/metrics` includes it in
  `tensorfold:prompt_cache_states` and `tensorfold:prompt_cache_bytes`; a successful resume counts toward
  `tensorfold:prompt_tokens_cached_total`. The chunk and budget host fixtures exercise this policy; real-model
  resumed/fresh parity and TTFT for this interior state still need the GPU gate.
- Shared row kernels: the token rows (`embed_rows.cu`, groups of 32 and a copy a hyper-connection stream), the MTP
  head's RMS rows with their group sums (`norms.cu`), the router logits and softmax top-k (`route_rows.cu`), and the
  routed experts over a window's or a chunk's rows on the core's plan (`cuda/grouped.zig`, `experts_rows.cu`).

The family supplies its config check, weight loading and packing, the layer graph on one batched pass
(`cuda_batch.zig`), and kernels for what is its own: the hyper-connections and the n-gram gate and conv
(`flashnext_hc.cu`), attention with its gate and the sparse indexer's pooling, scores and block selection
(`flashnext_attn.cu`, `flashnext_batch.cu`), the Gated DeltaNet chain, the n-gram gather and the MTP head.

The text path's kernels keep each row's own sums in a fixed order, so a row's bits are the same at any width; the
authors' text checks below compare drafted, concurrent and resumed replies with their plain, solo and fresh controls.
Images, through the cuBLASLt tower, are not qualified that way yet. The glue kernels round to bf16 where
the Python engine's do, with IEEE division and square root and a within-one-ulp exp; the router and the 4-bit
hyper-connection dots run on mma tiles with K in ascending order.

## Checks

- `tf-cuda-test flashnext-hc`, `flashnext-attn` and `route-rows`, and `norm-rows` for the shared rows: each kernel
  against a float64 chain that rounds where it rounds, and every row count's bits equal (tolerances in the test files).
- `zig build flashnext-prompt -Dflashnext_model=DIR -Dflashnext_kernels=native -Dflashnext_ids=FILE
  -Dflashnext_count=32`: 32 greedy tokens through the batched pass, against the Python engine's teacher path
  (`zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/lr7/results.json`, `results-sparse.json`); a captured set's folder in place of `native`
  runs its glue. `TF_FLASHNEXT_DRAFTS=6` decodes each prompt serially and drafted and compares them token for token
  (`TF_FLASHNEXT_SEED` for keyed sampled draws).
- `zig build flashnext-compare -Dflashnext_model=DIR -Dflashnext_kernels=SET -Dflashnext_ids=FILE`: our glue against a
  captured set on one loaded engine: every prompt row's scores (top-1 agreement, KL, each path's perplexity on the
  prompt's own next tokens, dense rows and rows past 2,048 apart), then each path's greedy reply and where they part.
  With `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED` it compares the set against the set with those entries swapped.
- `zig build flashnext-select -Dflashnext_fixtures=DIR`: the native block selection against Triton's lists.
- `tf-cuda-test experts-rows`: the rows kernel against the decode kernel's one-row launches, byte for byte.
- Served: `tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial` (concurrent equal to solo, drafted equal to `"draft": false`),
  and a prompt sent twice (the second resumed from a kept state, equal to the first).

## A captured set

A set is built from the Python 0.6.1 engine in a container (`IMAGE`, default tag `tensorfold-qwen38:v0.6.1`) with the
scripts in `zig/tests/cuda/flashnext`, then packed with `tools/zig/triton_aot_pack.py`:

```bash
zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/capture.sh WORK/cap /path/to/hf/snapshot          # the model's own run, about 78 GiB of GPU
zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/capture_rows.sh WORK/rows                          # the batched pass's forms, no checkpoint
zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/capture_mtp.sh WORK/mtp                            # the MTP head's own kernels
zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/capture_sparse.sh WORK/sparse                      # the sparse attention's kernels
zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/pack.sh KERNELS WORK/cap/out/cap WORK/rows/out WORK/mtp/out WORK/sparse/out
```

`capture.sh` also writes the prompts and the Python engine's references the checks read. The set has 76 kernels;
`capture_sparse.sh` writes the selection fixtures `flashnext-select` reads.

## Measurements

On a GB10 (DGX Spark, driver 580.178, CUDA 13.0), an MLX 4-bit group-32 Flash Next checkpoint with its MTP head,
greedy unless said, `tools/bench_openai.py` (256 tokens, median of 3) and `tools/bench_concurrent.py` (256 tokens,
aggregate tok/s), on our kernels and, for comparison, on the 76-kernel captured set:

| | ours | captured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One stream, drafted, code / chat | 84.2 / 62.6 | 82.5 / 62.1 |
| One stream, `--no-drafts`, code / chat | 35.1 / 35.1 | 35.2 / 35.2 |
| `--no-drafts`, 1 / 2 / 4 streams, sampled code | 35.0 / 53.1 / 77.9 | 35.2 / 53.0 / 77.1 |
| drafted, 1 / 2 / 4 streams, greedy code | 83.8 / 82.7 / 82.2 | 82.3 / 81.1 / 80.7 |
| Cold first token at 3,001 / 12,001 tokens (s) | 2.67 / 10.40 | 2.67 / 10.30 |
| 45,030-token prompt, no cache (s) | 36.5 | 35.8 |

Every concurrent reply equalled its solo run, and every drafted one its `"draft": false` run. Drafted streams verify
their windows a pass each, so drafted throughput does not grow with streams yet. While a 12,001-token prompt runs,
another stream's decode waits at most 1.3 s between tokens (one prompt chunk). Each stream at a 16,384-token window
takes 0.74 GiB with drafts, 0.54 GiB without.

Our kernels' sums are their own, so tokens part from the captured set's (the Python engine's teacher path) where two
candidates are close: 32 greedy tokens equal it on four of `zig/tests/cuda/flashnext/lr7`'s five prompts and part at
token 15 on the 3,001-token one. Over 4,096 tokens of this repository's documentation, the next-token perplexity is
6.168 on the captured set and 6.178 on ours.

### The ModelOpt checkpoint on one GB10

`nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` (revision `b9ce18a6`) on a GB10 (128 GB, driver 580.178, CUDA 13.3), greedy,
`--prompt-cache-gib 0`, the tools above, three runs of the defaults at a 32,768-token window alternated with other
settings in one session. These are @balancedscorpion's measurements on `beec1aad6`, the #952 branch build before
1.1.0, and have not been remeasured on 1.1.2:

| | defaults |
| --- | --- |
| One stream, drafted, code / chat | 64.1-64.6 / 40.7-41.1 |
| drafted, 1 / 4 / 8 streams, greedy code | 64.1-64.4 / 44.9-45.2 / 66.2-66.8 |
| Cold first token at 2,048 / 8,192 / 32,768 / 65,536 / 131,072 tokens (s) | 1.83 / 7.11 / 29.2 / 60.1 / 131.7 |

Every concurrent reply equalled its solo run and every drafted one its `"draft": false` run. A reply cancelled
mid-stream, or sent again after a restart, equalled a fresh one, and a second conversation turn resumed from the prompt
cache (`--no-drafts`) equalled the same turn computed without it. Prompt rows equal one-token rows bit for bit at seven
fixed histories of 20 to 6,496 tokens. Three streams draft at a time; the rest share plain rounds.

The engine holds 73.2 GiB and keeps a 12.2 GiB reserve. A 32,768-token window then admits 7 or 8 streams of 1.21 GiB
and a 131,136-token window (the cold prompts above) 2 of 4.03 GiB; a 262,144-token stream takes 7.79 GiB, which fitted
in one start of four on this machine. After the 131,072-token prompt the process had peaked at 6.5 GB of host and
83.0 GB of device memory. Absolute speeds on this machine moved by about a tenth between sessions.

### Prompt chunk size

`TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK` sets how many prompt rows one pass takes. A prompt of N rows runs in ceil(N / chunk) passes: a
1,922-row prompt is two passes at the default 1,536 and one at 8,192.

- **For:** every pass reads the gate, up and down weights of each routed expert its rows route to (1.84 MB of gate and
  up weights an expert, 512 experts a layer). Fewer passes read each expert fewer times, so a prompt longer than one
  chunk gets faster as the chunk grows.
- **Against:** a pass is not interrupted, so a stream that is decoding waits up to the whole pass for its next token,
  and a pass's time grows with its rows. The prompt scratch grows with the chunk too, and at 16,384 rows the n-gram
  tables of the MLX 4-bit checkpoint page (see `docs/known-issues.md`).
- One stream at a time (an agent loop, a single user): a larger chunk shortens every prompt longer than the default
  chunk. Several streams that decode while others send long prompts: the default keeps each wait to one short pass.

`TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK_SOLO` takes both: each pass picks its rows when it starts, the solo chunk when no other stream is
decoding and `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK` otherwise. Replies are the same bytes either way, because a pass's rows do not
change the sums. Two costs remain:
- A request that arrives during a solo pass waits for that pass to end before its own prompt runs. After that, the
  passes are short again.
- The prompt scratch is sized for the solo chunk for the whole run.

On one GB10 with `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` and
`--parallel 3 --context 40960 --no-drafts --prompt-cache-gib 0` (two fresh servers for each setting, medians):

| | unset (1,536) | `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK_SOLO=4096` | `=8192` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First token, one stream, at 1,927 / 8,320 / 31,736 tokens | 0.99 / 4.07 / 16.05 s | 0.91 / 3.88 / 14.94 s | 0.89 / 3.86 / 14.78 s |
| Longest wait between a decoding stream's tokens while an 8k prompt runs | 0.81 s | 0.81 s | 0.85 s |
| First token of a short request sent 2 s into a 31,736-token prompt | 0.36 s | 1.91 s | 1.94 s |
| Model and scratch at startup | 71.39 GiB | 73.64 GiB | 77.25 GiB |

4,096 rows took most of 8,192's gain for 2.25 GiB instead of 5.86 GiB. A solo pass lasts about 1.9 s at 4,096 rows
and about 3.8 s at 8,192: that is the longest a request arriving during one waits before its own prompt starts.

At `--parallel 1` no other stream can wait on a pass, so on one GPU the solo chunk defaults to 8,192 rows. On one GB10
with the MLX 4-bit MTP checkpoint, `--parallel 1 --context 73728 --prompt-cache-gib 0`, a 65,536-token prompt, three
fresh servers for each setting:

| `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK_SOLO` | First token | Model and scratch at startup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1,536 | 35.5 s | 75.8 GiB |
| 4,096 | 30.7 s | 77.0 GiB |
| 8,192 | 29.5 s | 79.0 GiB |
| 16,384 | 28.8 s | 82.9 GiB |

Decode speed is level and the replies are the same bytes. What remains is the scratch, and a cancel that arrives during
a pass, which waits for that pass to end. `TF_FLASHNEXT_CHUNK_SOLO=1536` keeps the shorter passes.

### One-launch attention

`TF_FLASHNEXT_ATTN_LANES=1` runs a shared decode round's attention in one launch a kernel: each row finds its stream's
caches and position in a table uploaded once a round, in place of a launch per stream. It applies to two to 32 streams
of up to 16 rows each, text on contiguous caches, on our own glue; page-table KV, media and captured sets keep the
per-stream launches. The bytes equal the per-stream launches': `tf-cuda-test flashnext-attn-lanes` compares them.

## Not yet

- The dense projections run a copy of the Python engine's group-32 lane matmul (`qmm.cu`); the core's `qmm_group` and
  `lane_gemv` are built for groups of 64.
- No CUDA graphs or GPU-side rounds; drafted streams verify their windows one pass each, and the MTP head drafts one
  stream at a time.
- Prompts run slower than the Python engine's: a cold 12,001-token prompt takes about 10 s against its 6.7 s.
- Draws are made on the host from each row's scores.
- Our glue's sums are not the captured kernels' bit for bit, so replies part from the Python engine's teacher path
  after a while, as that engine's own served path does (10 to 36 tokens, from its routed-experts kernel's rounding).
# Flash Next CUDA images

This recipe describes the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). @shantanugoel added Flash Next images on CUDA in
[#146](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/146), adapting @MiaAI-Lab's vision patch. The native binary has no Flash Next CUDA backend and does not read the
`TENSORFOLD_VISION_*` variables below; on a Mac it reads Flash Next images and videos itself (see
[Qwen3.8 Flash Next](../vision.md#qwen38-flash-next)).

Run a complete local Flash Next checkpoint with `--vision --parallel 2` (or more), on one CUDA GPU.
This port supports images, including multiple images within the existing 4096 visual-token budget; video and
large-image extensions are not included. Image rows replace embeddings in every hyperconnection stream.
Multimodal RoPE follows the checkpoint's sections; text decode continues with its image-position offset.
Image prompts always prefill from the start and are never retained in the text-prefix cache, since identical
placeholder IDs can name different pixels. Grammar and ignore-EOS settings remain available.

A floating-point tower in the indexed checkpoint is discovered normally. EXL3 packs whose vision tower is a
quantized sidecar need a one-time CPU conversion, stored outside the original model snapshot:

```bash
python -m tensorfold.vision.exl3_convert /models/vision_k6.safetensors /cache/vision-f16-v3.safetensors
TENSORFOLD_VISION_WEIGHTS=/cache/vision-f16-v3.safetensors tensorfold serve /models --vision --parallel 2
```

The converter decodes represented EXL3 weights, transposes matrices and combines split Q/K/V. It records the
source SHA256 and converter/dtype version; repeat conversions reuse a matching artifact and refuse to
replace a mismatched one. Conversion never runs in the serving loader. The FP16 artifact loads into the
existing BF16 CUDA tower; rounding may differ from native quantized vision execution, so compare image
features and quality for the checkpoint in use. The original weights stay unchanged.

Admission counts an external tower separately, including its expanded resident bytes. It reserves 4 GiB of
image workspace by default; `TENSORFOLD_VISION_WORKSPACE_MIB` sets a measured override from 0 to 16384 MiB.
Image requests cannot use yieldable background lanes. Distributed vision and serial-only Flash Next image
serving are not supported by this port.

The integration is adapted from MiaAI-Lab patch 0008, with its MIT license in `LICENSES/MiaAI-Lab-MIT.txt`.
# Exact Fluid Subgraph Residency

[Fluid Subgraph Residency](../design/fluid-subgraph-residency.md) is TensorFold's implementation of published techniques from EdgeMoE, MoE-Infinity, Fiddler and Fate. Slotstream is an outside comparison only. The native phase covers Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) on one Metal device. Other families, backends and the paired speed-up path refuse these options.

## Serve stored experts from SSD

```sh
tensorfold serve CHECKPOINT --ssd-experts 16 --ple-on-ssd
```

`--ssd-experts GIB` is the routed-expert slot budget, not the whole process budget. Shared experts, non-routed weights, the original execution scratch, admitted sessions, prompt states and the runtime reserve still need memory. The startup plan includes them, all nine stored components per slot, the persistent expert map, source metadata and the bounded reader stack. It reports usable slots and unused budget bytes. A budget must hold one layer's maximum expert union. A shortfall refuses; it never changes top-k, context, drafts or concurrency to fit.

The loader leaves routed target and MTP experts in their original checkpoint files. Demand protects all selected experts before CLOCK eviction, which counts uses: a hit adds one up to three, the hand takes one off as it passes, and a newly read expert starts at none, so one used once leaves before one used again. All nine components load into an exclusive slot before its map entry is published. The existing expert kernels use the persistent map only on this path. Mixed stored widths retain their original formulas and combine order. Missing or malformed spans, short reads, changed file length and a failed cache-bypass setup stop the request before partial data can be used.

Readers require macOS `F_NOCACHE` and use positional reads directly into shared slots. Native PLE streaming can be selected independently with `--ple-on-ssd`. It deduplicates requested rows, coalesces adjacent rows within each shard and feeds staged IDs and unchanged stored bytes through the resident lookup arithmetic. Logical n-gram IDs and history stay unchanged.

Decode prefetch uses the next layer's own router on the current state. One bounded worker reads predictions into unleased slots behind submitted expert compute. The later real router remains authoritative. A wrong prediction wastes reads and cannot change routes or output. Prompt chunks load each layer's complete demand union once per chunk. Streaming chunks use one command stream so host storage cuts cannot wait on an unsubmitted staggered sibling; concurrent request windows and MTP still use the lane core.

Loading doesn't bring the whole expert set into memory: the peak stays about 2 GiB above where memory settles. Flash Next MLX 4-bit MTP on an M3 Ultra, `--context 65536 --parallel 1`, physical footprint sampled every 250 ms through load, a short reply, a 16,000-token prompt and a 512-token reply, one run each, with the same reply bytes in every row:

| Flags | After load | Peak | 16K prompt and 32 tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ssd-experts 8 --ple-on-ssd` | 36.0 GiB | 37.8 GiB | 49.1 s |
| `--ssd-experts 17 --ple-on-ssd` | 45.0 GiB | 46.8 GiB | 47.8 s |
| `--ssd-experts 8` | 65.9 GiB | 67.6 GiB | 44.4 s |
| `--ssd-experts 17` | 74.9 GiB | 76.9 GiB | 34.9 s |
| `--ssd-experts 35` | 92.9 GiB | 94.9 GiB | 35.9 s |
| Everything in memory | 129.7 GiB | 131.6 GiB | 11.2 s |

## Bound read overhead

The demand path deduplicates route IDs and reserves missing experts in logical order. Adjacent stored experts merge only when both the source bytes and their destination slots are contiguous. A request is at most 4 MiB. The reader queues at most nine requests through macOS asynchronous IO, drains every submitted request on errors, and checks each touched file's length before and after the batch. Queue pressure falls back to positional reads after submitted work drains. Cache bypass remains required.

An expert has nine stored components in separate tensor ranges. They cannot become one contiguous read without changing the checkpoint layout. Dense prompt unions can merge neighboring experts within each component; sparse decode routes often still need nine requests per missing expert. Mixed-width slot padding prevents merging across that padding. No gap bytes or unselected expert payloads are read to manufacture larger requests.

A private pending-read index avoids scanning the pool for each route ID. Forecasts consume only cold, unleased slots and do not spend actual demand's use counts. An unused prediction remains cold. When actual demand arrives, the worker stops after its current expert. Predictions it never started give their slots back, so the cold expert each one displaced stays, and demand reads what it needs itself. Demand waits for the current expert only if its union needs that one; otherwise that read finishes beside demand's, and no new forecast starts until it has. The actual router and complete-demand lease remain authoritative. Shutdown reports lifetime bytes, read requests, file checks, reservations, canceled forecasts, raw and unique demand IDs, worker joins and command waits, including startup.

Router readback and storage ownership still require command-buffer boundaries. These changes reduce unnecessary forecast splits when no cold slot exists; they do not remove the real router's dependency or claim resident-class throughput at every budget. The worker remains bounded and is joined before cache publication or teardown.

## Analyze routing locality

```sh
tensorfold serve CHECKPOINT --fsr-route-trace routing.jsonl
python3 tools/fsr_profile.py routing.jsonl --budget-bytes 17179869184
```

Stop the server cleanly before analyzing the trace. The native writer excludes startup warm-up and calibration. It records every actual expert demand, including hits, and distinguishes prompt chunks, solo decode, shared batches and MTP. Rows and stream counts distinguish plain and drafted windows. A kernel that executes an encoded upper bound includes those rows; a gated kernel that skips them excludes them. Forecasts are never actual-route observations. Checkpoint identity is a hash; prompt text is not written.

The `tensorfold-fsr-v1` format has a header, ordered complete layer observations for every window, window ends and a final close/count. The analyzer refuses missing layers, reordered or duplicated observations, forecasts and truncated traces. Repeat `--budget-bytes` to compare pool budgets. `--ssd-bytes-per-second` accepts measured uncached bandwidth and reports a storage-time lower bound. The report includes union growth, usable slots, unused tails and a protected-demand CLOCK simulation without forecast. A fit verdict applies to the observed workload and predicts neither future locality nor native speed.

For an explicitly synthetic planning example at the real 49-layer, 512-expert, top-10 geometry:

```sh
python3 tools/fsr_synthetic.py --locality hot80 --windows 512 > synthetic-routes.jsonl
python3 tools/fsr_profile.py synthetic-routes.jsonl \
  --budget-bytes 17179869184 --budget-bytes 23622320128 \
  --budget-bytes 35433480192 --budget-bytes 51539607552 \
  --tokens 512 --resident-tps 123 --ssd-bytes-per-second MEASURED_BYTES_PER_SECOND
```

The generator offers uniform, skewed and sticky route scenarios, preserves all top-10 IDs per row, and includes target and MTP windows. It does not load weights or predict a real model's routing. `--rows` and `--streams` describe batch width; `--prompt` labels prompt windows. One synthetic step includes one MTP row per target row; measured draft acceptance needs a real trace. `--tokens` is explicit because a trace window is not necessarily one emitted token. The synthetic header declares uniform component widths so the analyzer can estimate contiguous request counts. Native traces without those widths report bytes and locality without inventing read geometry. Use lifetime IO counters for the actual layout and forecasts.

Optional `--read-latency-ns` adds an explicitly uncalibrated latency scenario. The reported serialized estimates add resident compute time, mandatory byte time and per-request or per-nine-request-group latency. They are planning estimates, not measured native speed. Actual queue depth, layout fragmentation, forecasts and overlap can change them. Measure uncached bandwidth at the same request sizes on the tested storage before interpreting any throughput ceiling.

## Qualification

Host steps are `test-fsr-host`, `test-fsr-source-host`, `test-fsr-cli-host` and `test-flashnext-fsr-owner-host`. They check ownership, source transformations, actual native option forwarding, admission, complete multi-row demand, forecast joins, PLE staging and file failures. Run `python3 -m unittest discover -s tools -p test_fsr_profile.py` for the locality tool's controls. `compile-fsr-metal-gate-host` and `compile-fsr-metal-contract-host` compile the real gate bodies without executing a shader compiler or device.

Device qualification requires `zig build test-fsr-metal` on a Mac with the Metal toolchain and GPU. Its nonzero two-layer MoE has 32 experts per layer and four slots. It compares every observed node and all 32 logits with resident execution at four and six bits, repeats five times with uncached reads and requires a wrong-map control to differ. The Metal kernel contract includes exact stored-view replacements, wrong-map controls and the serving variants' source-reserved launch bounds. The address-view contract does not claim to requalify the unchanged resident accumulation precision.

Synthetic and real-device results remain required before advertising a qualified memory tier. Real checkpoint receipts must compare complete token arrays for cold/warm prefill, serial decode, drafted/plain, concurrent/solo, resumed/fresh, prompt cuts and cancellation/reset at 16, 22, 33 and 48 GiB pool budgets. Record actual RAM, physical footprint, device allocations, SSD traffic and timings with cache bypass. A budget on a larger-memory device does not prove operation on a smaller-memory device. Follow the complete [qualification contract](../design/fluid-subgraph-residency.md#qualification).
# Gemma 4 12B, native Metal

This recipe covers text and image input with Google's
[`google/gemma-4-12B-it`](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-12B-it/tree/707f0a3b8a3c7ad586ed01e27eafbad8a27dd0f7),
revision `707f0a3b8a3c7ad586ed01e27eafbad8a27dd0f7` (`gemma4_unified`), its language model converted to MLX affine
4-bit in groups of 64 and its image embedder kept in bf16, with Google's MTP assistant
[`google/gemma-4-12B-it-assistant`](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-12B-it-assistant/tree/46d4c6f13f0ac0ad827b915669b8df9b81c64c51)
(revision `46d4c6f13f0ac0ad827b915669b8df9b81c64c51`) as the drafter. It runs on the native Gemma 4 family that serves
[the 31B](gemma-4-native.md), on M5 tensor-unit GPUs. Build with Zig **0.17.0** and Xcode's Metal toolchain, as
described in [the native preview](../../ZIG-PREVIEW.md#build).

```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --revision 707f0a3b8a3c7ad586ed01e27eafbad8a27dd0f7 --local-dir "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b-hf"
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it-assistant --revision 46d4c6f13f0ac0ad827b915669b8df9b81c64c51 \
  --local-dir "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b-assistant"
python tools/zig/gemma4_12b_convert.py "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b-hf" "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b"   # mlx and mlx-lm installed
zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b" --port 8888 --parallel 4 \
  --drafter "$HOME/models/gemma-4-12b-assistant" --vision
```

`--parallel 4` caps this example at four active requests; additional requests wait for a free slot.

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar).

`gemma4_12b_convert.py` quantizes the language model's tensors with mlx-lm's converter to affine 4-bit in groups of
64 (6.3 GB, 4.5 bits a weight with the scales), writes the image embedder's ten tensors as stored (bf16, 100 MB) to
`model-vision.safetensors`, drops the audio input's, and writes the checkpoint's own `gemma4_unified` config back with
that quantization. Run twice, it writes the same tensors bit for bit.

## The model

The 12B is Gemma 4's dense decoder at another size: 48 layers, five sliding-window layers (window 1,024, head dim 256,
16 query heads over 8 key heads) to each global one (head dim 512 over one key head, keys reused as values,
proportional RoPE), hidden 3,840, GeGLU at 15,360, per-layer scalars, and the tied 262,144-token head with its logit
soft-cap at 30. The family reads both sizes from one geometry the config picks (`zig/src/families/gemma4/config.zig`):
every dimension must match the 31B's or the 12B's exactly, and other layouts (per-layer inputs, shared KV layers, MoE)
are refused by name. The kernels take each size as a define, so the 12B runs the 31B's kernels.

Without `--drafter` the 12B decodes plain at 88 tokens a second for one stream.

## The MTP assistant

`--drafter` reads the drafter's `config.json`: a Gemma 4 assistant type goes to the MTP assistant
(`zig/src/families/gemma4/assistant.zig`), which admits `gemma4_unified_assistant` and refuses others by name, and a
DFlash checkpoint to DFlash (the 31B's), each refused by name on the wrong target. The assistant is four layers 1,024
wide (three sliding, one global) with no keys or values of its own: each layer's queries attend over the target's own
caches, the last sliding layer's and the last global layer's, from the last kept row's position. Its input is the
pending token's scaled embedding beside the target's final-normed row, then its own projected output; its head is tied
to its own 262,144-row embedding. Its bf16 weights are quantized at load to 4-bit groups of 64 by MLX's affine rule. A
round drafts up to six tokens (0.97 ms a draft), every stream's chain in one command buffer, the next step's token
straight from the GPU's picks. Ordered (centroid) embeddings are refused by name.

Served, one stream decodes at 140-248 tokens a second with it (prose 140, code 223, structured 205, list 248;
3.2 accepted tokens a round), 183 against 88 undrafted on the quality suite's draft check, with the same tokens.

## Serving

| Checkpoint / platform | Qualification |
| --- | --- |
| The converted 12B, M5 Ultra, macOS 27 | Greedy and sampled decode, prompts to 252k, shared rounds, MTP drafts, structured output, prompt reuse, the server, below. |
| `google/gemma-4-12B-it-assistant` `46d4c6f1` | The one MTP assistant admitted for the 12B. |
| M1 to M4 | Served through the row path (the fused lane projection needs M5 tensor units); the drafters refuse. |
| Images | `--vision`: PNG and JPEG, 256 to 280 tokens an image, [below](#images). |
| Audio | Not read: the converter drops the audio input, and the server takes no audio. |
| Other widths | MLX affine 2-6 or 8 bits in groups of 64, uniform or per module: [other widths](#other-widths). |

Structured output (`response_format`, `guided_*`) works with drafts on: the harness's structured check obeys 18 of 18
(each field greedy, sampled and with thinking), and a bad regex gets HTTP 400. Thinking is on with
`chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true}`; replies carry it in `reasoning_content`.

Prompts are reused between requests as for the 31B: an 11,481-token conversation took 3.0 s to its first token fresh
and 0.09 s asked again (11,264 tokens resumed). A 1-token request after 2 to 120 idle seconds took 57-74 ms, where a
busy server takes 37 ms.

Thinking replies fill the window: at `--context 32768`, three greedy prompts (a proof with a checked list, a
tested red-black tree, a question on a 25,801-token document) thought until the window was full (32,705, 32,714 and
6,959 tokens), each drafted reply equal to the same request with `"draft": false`.

## Images

`serve --vision` loads the image embedder (`vision_embedder.`, `embed_vision.`) and reads images as for
[the 31B](gemma-4-native.md#images): PNG and JPEG data URLs in user messages and tool results (public HTTPS URLs with
`--vision-urls`), decoded to Pillow's pixels by core's picture decoder (JPEG needs libjpeg-turbo 3.1.4.1, as
[image input](../vision.md#the-native-server) says). An image is sized as for the 31B (the largest aspect-preserving
size whose sides are multiples of 48 and whose 16-pixel patches fit 280 tokens, PIL's bicubic resize, then 1/255),
and `zig/src/families/gemma4/image.zig` cuts it into 48-pixel patches, the order transformers'
`Gemma4UnifiedImageProcessor` gives with `patches_merge`, one token each: 256 to 280 tokens (70 or 140 with
`detail: low` or a smaller `--vision-image-tokens`).

The 12B has no image encoder: `zig/src/families/gemma4/vision_unified.zig` follows `Gemma4UnifiedVisionEmbedder`,
LayerNorm, the 6,912 to 3,840 Linear and LayerNorm on each patch, the x and y position rows and LayerNorm, then
the unscaled RMS norm and the 3,840 x 3,840 projection, in bf16 at torch's rounding on gemm_nax's tensor-unit
GEMMs (about 2 ms an image). The language model does the rest: the image's rows replace its tokens' embeddings, and on
the 40 sliding layers they see one another both ways (`use_bidirectional_attention: "vision"`, as for the 31B).

Checked with `tools/zig/gemma4_vision_fixtures.py` (transformers 5.17 and torch, bf16 and fp32 runs of the embedder)
and `tf-gemma4-vision` on the 31B's five drawn images: the patches equal those of the PIL processor's resize through
`patches_merge` bit for bit, and each stage is as close to the fp32 run as torch's own bf16 run (the projected rows
0.30% relative error averaged over the images, torch's 0.31%). The checkpoint's own processor resizes with
torchvision, 0 to 2 levels of 255 from PIL's. Served with the assistant, `tools/zig/vision_served.py` passes its 19
checks (drafted equal to `"draft": false`, concurrent image requests equal to their runs alone, a later turn resuming
past its image, the refusals), and questions about the images answer right (the circle red and the rectangle blue,
the circle on the left, the text "GEMMA 4", the tall image taller than wide). mlx-vlm 0.7.2 on the same checkpoint
gives the same pixels and the same five short answers; an 80-token description parts from it at its third token, on
a near-tie in mlx-vlm's own logits ("design" -1.625, "illustration" -1.75).

## Other widths

The family reads each linear's MLX affine width from the checkpoint's `quantization` table
(`zig/src/families/gemma4/widths.zig`, on core's `core/quant/mlx.zig`): 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 8 bits in groups of 64,
uniform or per module, the embedding and the image projection included. A tensor stored at another width than its
entry, groups of 32 or 128, 7 bits, other modes (mxfp4, nvfp4) and a module declared unquantized are refused by name,
never guessed from the shapes. A q|k|v or gate|up stack whose members differ runs one lane projection for each run of
equal widths, each writing its own columns of the stack's rows, as gilby's runs do. 4-bit groups of 64 keep the reg
kernel and, when every linear has that width, the fused one-row pipelines; other widths take the lane kernel's general
unpack, unfused, so they decode slower than their bytes alone would say.

| Checkpoint | Checked |
| --- | --- |
| [`unigilby/gemma-4-12B-it-oQ8e`](https://huggingface.co/unigilby/gemma-4-12B-it-oQ8e/tree/a47ebf1a53598bb9ebe474724b20b2c0cd2e3b73) `a47ebf1a`, oMLX oQ uniform 8-bit | Decode equal to gilby's oracle on the four prompts x 128 tokens; long prompts against mlx-lm: 32k and 128k equal, 8k parts at a near-tie (23.375 / 23.125); `tf-gemma4-lanes` plain, copy and assistant drafts equal at one, four and eight streams, seeded at one and four; images: the embedder's rows 0.31% from fp32 (torch bf16 0.31%), `vision_served.py` passes. |
| `gemma4_12b_convert.py --recipe mixed_4_6` (v_proj 6-bit in 16 layers, down_proj in 24) | Decode: two of four prompts equal, two part at near-ties (22.875 / 22.75, 19.375 / 19.25); long prompts: 8k and 32k equal, 128k parts at a near-tie (27.375 / 27.25); lanes as above, all equal. |

Served (harness target `gemma4-12b-oq8e-m5`), the oQ8e pack with the assistant: one stream 93, 142, 146 and 158
tokens a second (prose, code, structured, list; 4-bit: 140, 223, 205, 248), four streams 262-340 together; the draft
check 137 against 46 undrafted (4-bit: 183 against 88); structured output 18 of 18, concurrent 12 of 12.

## Verification

The references are gilby's `gemma4_unified` Python engine (`6b0ead7a`, MLX 0.32.3, mlx-lm 0.32.0, lane kernels) for
decode and mlx-lm for long prompts (the gate script on #975's branch, with `--family gemma4_unified`).

  token on a near-tie (18.25 against 17.875 there, 18.125 for both here). As for the 31B since its speed work
  (decode attention and the projections' K splits), the logits are not the reference's bit for bit, and the last

- Long prompts, 49 tokens after each, against mlx-lm in 2,048-token steps: 8k and 128k equal; 32k, 64k and 252k part

  into a loop).
- `tf-gemma4-lanes`: plain and copy drafts at one, four and eight streams, and the MTP assistant greedy at one, four
  and eight and seeded sampled at one and four streams, all equal to their references.
- The 31B's decode, long-prompt, lanes, DFlash and image receipts are byte-identical to `21e8040e`'s.

# Gemma 4 31B, native Metal

This recipe covers text generation with
[`mlx-community/gemma-4-31B-it-4bit`](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/gemma-4-31B-it-4bit/tree/696d436c404745a59f30e4939a658162b0a9e57f),
revision `696d436c404745a59f30e4939a658162b0a9e57f`, the dense 31B in MLX affine 4-bit, groups of 64.
Build from `main` with Zig **0.17.0** and Xcode's Metal toolchain, as described in
[the native preview](../../ZIG-PREVIEW.md#build).

```bash
hf download mlx-community/gemma-4-31B-it-4bit --revision 696d436c404745a59f30e4939a658162b0a9e57f \
  --local-dir "$HOME/models/gemma-4-31b"
hf download z-lab/gemma-4-31B-it-DFlash --revision eabd648301ce28583cc14757912e5e0f84e152e1 \
  --local-dir "$HOME/models/gemma-4-31b-dflash"
zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve "$HOME/models/gemma-4-31b" --port 8888 --parallel 4 \
  --drafter "$HOME/models/gemma-4-31b-dflash"
```

`--parallel 4` caps this example at four active requests; additional requests wait for a free slot.

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar).

Without `--drafter` the model decodes plain, at about 51 tokens a second for one stream at short context (mlx-lm 46)
and 40 at 32k. With z-lab's DFlash drafter
a stream decodes at 150-190 tokens a second (6-7 accepted tokens a round on chat and code, 10 on copying replies,
2 on open-ended prose), with the same tokens.

For the 31B the loader admits its dense geometry exactly: 60 layers, five sliding-window layers (window 1,024, head dim
256) to each global one (head dim 512, keys reused as values, proportional RoPE), GeGLU, the tied 262,144-token head
with its logit soft-cap, MLX affine weights at the widths [other widths](#other-widths) lists. It refuses the 26B-A4B
MoE, per-layer inputs and shared KV layers, each by name. With `--vision` it also loads the image tower
([images](#images)). The 12B (`gemma4_unified`) runs on the same family with its MTP assistant: [Gemma 4 12B, native
Metal](gemma-4-12b-native.md).

Every linear, the tied head included, runs on the core lane projection (`zig/src/core/lane_projection.zig`) on M5
tensor units; the rest of a layer is `zig/kernels/metal/gemma4/glue.metal`. The glue ports the Python reference's
decode kernels (gilby's `gemma4-dense` branch, #360, built on cshintov's Gemma kernels from #10) with their rounding
points, and MLX's own ops where that reference calls them: the looped RMS norm, the 4-bit embedding times its bf16
scale, `geglu` and the soft-cap as bf16 ops, and the global layers' RoPE frequencies from MLX's precise `pow`.
Each output equals the reference's bit for bit at 1, 2 and 16 rows (`tf-gemma4-kernels`, `tf-gemma4-glue`, on
fixtures dumped from that reference) at the reference's K split. Decode takes each shape's fastest split instead
(`weights.splitK`: 4 for o and down, 8 for the gate/up stack and the head), another fp32 summation order: at one row a
handful of outputs a linear move by one bf16 step (5 of 43,008 on gate_up, 99 of 262,144 on the head, none on qkv).

A stream keeps a ring of window + 512 slots for each sliding layer and a buffer for each global one; rolling back is
moving the cache's length. A decode forward takes up to 16 rows of one stream and 128 of several, and every row keeps
its bits. A one-row window runs five or six dispatches a sliding layer rather than ten, and seven a global one: the
previous layer's dense tail is the qkv projection's prologue, the attention tail the gate/up projection's with geglu as
its epilogue (the stack's rows interleaved in 16-row blocks, so a lane holds a gate column and its up column), and the
down projection sums its own input (`zig/kernels/metal/gemma4/fused.metal` on the lane core's `Fused` hook); a sliding
layer's attention kernel preps its own query heads and writes the row's key and value, and with one key chunk writes
the merged output itself. The same bits as the kernels apart.
Prompts run in chunks of 512 rows on Gemma's private `families/gemma4/affine_mm` and a tensor-unit attention kernel, at about 1,360
tokens a second at 8k, 1,200 at 32k and 560 at 252k.

The drafter is z-lab's DFlash (`zig/src/families/gemma4/dflash.zig`): five Qwen3-style layers reading six of the
target's layer outputs (1, 12, 23, 35, 46, 57) through `fc` and a norm, drafting a block of the pending token and up
to 15 mask tokens with the target's own embedding and tied head. Its bf16 weights are quantized at load to 4-bit
groups of 64 by MLX's affine rule and run on the same lane projection; the context keys and values of each stream
live in a 2,047-slot ring for the four sliding layers and a growing buffer for the full one, as in z-lab's MLX model.
It sits in front of the engine as the lane core's `Drafted` wrapper (chains, no trees): the target hands it each
prompt chunk's and each verify's tapped rows, and the depth rule prices its drafts against the forward's cost by rows
timed at load. A round's streams draft in one block forward (3.4 ms for one stream, 9 for eight) and absorb in one
pass, whose command buffer the block settles.

The context defaults to 32,768 tokens; `--context` raises it to the checkpoint's 262,144, at the cost of attention
scratch that grows with it.

Prompts are reused between requests (`zig/src/families/gemma4/snapshot.zig`). A kept state is each sliding layer's
last 1,024 keys and values, every global layer's keys and values so far, and the DFlash drafter's own context for the
same stream (4 KB a token in its full layer, 34 MB of sliding rings), so a resumed stream drafts as a fresh one does. A
prompt chunk's rows are their own arithmetic, so states are kept and resumed only where the request's planned chunks
start, as Step-5's are; a drafting stream does not resume a state kept without the drafter's context, and none is
resumed inside an image. The budget is what 70% of RAM leaves beside every stream's caches, 16 GiB by default
(`--prompt-cache-gib`, 0 for none). A later turn of a 3,336-token conversation resumed 3,329 tokens and answered as the
first pass did; one with an image after 2,300 tokens of system prompt resumed 3,584 of 3,607 tokens, alike. Served
with the drafter and `--vision`, an 11,481-token conversation took 7.8 s to its first token fresh and 0.23 s asked
again (11,264 tokens resumed); with an image in it, 8.1 s and 0.13 s.

Structured output (`response_format`, `guided_json`, `guided_regex`, `guided_choice`, `guided_grammar`) is enforced
through `libtfgrammar`, as [structured output](../api.md#structured-output) describes, with drafts on: before each
verify the `Drafted` wrapper hands the drafter's held drafts to the host, where the grammar cuts the ones it rejects.
The recipe harness's structured check obeys 18 of 18 (each field greedy, sampled and with thinking), and a bad regex
gets HTTP 400. Tools are called with `tool_choice: "auto"`; `"required"` and a named function are enforced through
the token grammar, which writes Gemma's `<|tool_call>call:NAME{...}<tool_call|>` markup. The
weights, both scratches and the drafter's and tower's buffers stay in one residency set, which the idle keepalive's
tick keeps wired: a 1-token request after 2 to 120 idle seconds took 0.10-0.12 s to its first token, where a busy
server took 0.07 s (ten idle gaps, none slower).

| Checkpoint / platform | Qualification |
| --- | --- |
| The pinned 31B 4-bit, M5 Ultra, macOS 27 | Greedy decode, prompts, shared rounds, copy and DFlash drafts and the server, below. |
| `z-lab/gemma-4-31B-it-DFlash` `eabd6483` | The one drafter admitted: DFlash v1, block 16, six taps, head dim 128. |
| M1 to M4 | Served through the row path (the fused lane projection needs M5 tensor units); the drafters refuse. |
| Images (`--vision`) | PNG and JPEG data URLs, and public HTTPS URLs with `--vision-urls`, below. |
| Structured output | `response_format` and the `guided_*` fields, drafts on and off, below. |
| Other widths | MLX affine 2-6 or 8 bits in groups of 64, uniform or per module: [other widths](#other-widths). |

## Images

`serve --vision` loads the checkpoint's image tower (`vision_tower.`, `embed_vision.`; 1.1 GB, bf16 but for the 4-bit
projection) and reads PNG and JPEG data URLs in user messages and tool results (with `--vision-urls`, public HTTPS URLs
too), decoded to Pillow's pixels by core's picture decoder, as [image input](../vision.md#the-native-server) describes.
`zig/src/families/gemma4/image.zig` prepares an image as transformers' `Gemma4ImageProcessorPil` does: the
largest aspect-preserving size whose sides are multiples of 48 and whose 16-pixel patches fit 280 tokens (PIL's bicubic
resize, then 1/255), so an image becomes 256 to 280 tokens (70 or 140 with `detail: low` or a smaller
`--vision-image-tokens`). The template's `<|image|>` expands to `boi`, the image's rows, `eoi`.

`zig/src/families/gemma4/vision.zig` runs the 27-layer encoder on gemm_nax's tensor-unit GEMMs at torch's per-op bf16
rounding: the patch projection and the x and y position rows, RMS norms in fp32 times their weights, per-head q, k and
v norms, the axial 2D RoPE (theta 100, x on dims 0-35 and y on 36-71), attention with scale 1 as two batched GEMMs and
a softmax, GELU-tanh gating, the 3 x 3 pooler, the standardization and the projection on Gemma's private affine_mm. An image takes
about 90 ms, and adds about 270 ms to a request's first token (a 290-token prompt with an image 365 ms, the text
alone 92 ms). In the language model the image's rows replace its tokens' embeddings, and on the 50 sliding layers they
see one another both ways, as `use_bidirectional_attention: "vision"` asks (the prompt attention kernel takes each
row's last key; global layers stay causal); a prompt chunk never cuts an image.

Checked with `tools/zig/gemma4_vision_fixtures.py` (transformers 5.17 and torch, bf16 and fp32 runs of
`Gemma4VisionModel`) and `tf-gemma4-vision` on five drawn images, from 20 x 15 to 1200 x 800 and 180 x 1400: the patches
equal the PIL processor's bit for bit, and the tower's rows are as close to the fp32 run as torch's own bf16 run (7.6%
relative error averaged over the images, torch's 7.8%). AutoProcessor with torch installed picks the torchvision
processor instead, whose resize differs from PIL's by a level at a few pixels in a thousand. Served with the drafter,
a described image answers token for token as mlx-vlm 0.7.2 does (80 greedy tokens, the same 287-token prompt), with
drafts on and off; `tools/zig/vision_served.py` passes its 19 checks, concurrent image requests equal their runs
alone, and text-only prompts keep their bits (the receipts above, unchanged).

## Other widths

The family reads each linear's width from the checkpoint's `quantization` table, as [the 12B
recipe](gemma-4-12b-native.md#other-widths) describes: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 8 bits in groups of 64, uniform or per module,
stacks of mixed widths in runs, every other width or mode refused by name. 4-bit groups of 64 keep the reg kernel and
the fused one-row pipelines: the 4-bit decode, 512-row prompt and 8k and 32k receipts are the same bytes as before
other widths were read. Other widths run the lane kernel's general unpack, unfused.

[`unigilby/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-oQ8e`](https://huggingface.co/unigilby/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-oQ8e/tree/53dc2af091c166c8cefe5f670e744864f964ad47)
(`53dc2af0`, oMLX oQ uniform 8-bit from Google's QAT checkpoint, 33.8 GB): decode against gilby's oracle, the four
prompts x 128 tokens, two equal and two parting at near-ties (24.625 / 24.5, 21.25 / 21.125); `tf-gemma4-lanes`
plain, copy and DFlash drafts equal at one, four and eight streams, seeded at one and four; images: the tower's rows
7.6% from fp32 (torch bf16 7.8%), the 8-bit projection included, and `vision_served.py` passes.

Served with DFlash (harness target `gemma4-31b-oq8e-m5`): one stream 40, 63, 52 and 55 tokens a second (prose, code,
structured, list), four streams 110-180 together; the draft check 50 against 22 undrafted; structured output 18 of 18,
concurrent 12 of 12. On the four prompts DFlash accepts 1.6-4.1 tokens a round on this pack against 2.0-5.8 on the 4-bit
one (`tf-gemma4-lanes`), whose unfused path accepts as many as its fused one.

## Verification

The oracle is gilby's `gemma4-dense` Python engine (`a6ff795e`, MLX 0.32.3, mlx-lm 0.32.0) with lane kernels. The
scripts that run it and compare (`tools/zig/gemma4_gate.py`, `gemma4_dump.py`) import that Python engine, so they
stay on #879's branch; this tree holds the native side of each step:

```bash
zig-out/bin/tf-gemma4-run M O N 128 16   # O: the oracle's tokens and margins for four chat prompts; N: ours
zig-out/bin/tf-gemma4-lanes M O && GEMMA_DRAFTER=D zig-out/bin/tf-gemma4-lanes M O
zig-out/bin/tf-gemma4-run M O R 128 512
zig-out/bin/tf-gemma4-run M L NL 49 512  # L: the oracle's long prompts (8k to 252k tokens)
```

- Four chat prompts, 128 greedy tokens, prompts fed one row at a time or in windows of 16: three equal the oracle
  token for token; the story prompt parts at token 56, where the native run ties the oracle's top two (24.5 and 24.5,
  the oracle 24.5 and 24.375) and takes the lower id. Every row keeps its bits at any window width and beside other
  streams' rows.
- Long prompts against the oracle's mlx-lm prompt forward (fed in 2048-token chunks, as `mlx_lm.generate` feeds a
  prompt), 49 greedy tokens each: equal at 32k, 64k and 252k. At 8k and 128k the two part at tokens 25 and 30, each
  where mlx-lm's top two logits are equal (28.25 and 26.25); the native run puts them 0.125 and 0.75 apart.
- The lane core: copy-drafted and DFlash-drafted streams, alone and 4 and 8 in shared rounds, equal the engine's
  plain replies token for token, on the four prompts and on two copy-heavy ones.
- Served on an M5 Ultra with the drafter: greedy token SHAs equal the engine's receipts alone, with drafts off and on,
  and four at once; thinking replies keep their reasoning apart, and tool calls parse.

With the drafter, one stream decodes at 150-190 tokens a second (6.4, 6.4, 2.1 and 6.7 tokens a round on the four
prompts; 10.2 and 7.8 on copying replies) and eight streams at about 210 together. Plain decode is 51 tokens a second
for one stream. The drafts match z-lab's own MLX drafter's acceptance. Shared rounds draft shallow on purpose: past 16
rows the forward is bound by tensor-op compute at about 0.8 ms a row (40 ms at 32 rows, 71 at 64, 130 at 128, the
same rate as the prompt path and mlx-lm's), so the depth rule, given those costs, finds deeper shared drafts do not
pay; the drafter's own cost is 9 ms a round for eight streams.

Long prompts, one after the other on the same M5 Ultra: native in 512-row chunks (`tf-gemma4-run ... 49 512`), mlx-lm
0.32.0 in 2048-token steps into a fresh cache. Native decode is the run's 49 tokens after the prompt, timed to 0.1 s.

| Prompt | Native prompt tok/s | mlx-lm prompt tok/s | Native decode tok/s | mlx-lm decode tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8k | 1385 | 1305 | about 38 | 39 |
| 32k | 1241 | 1139 | about 35 | 32 |
| 64k | 1072 | 944 | about 33 | 32 |
| 128k | 882 | 651 | about 27 | 25 |
| 252k | 570 | 440 | about 20 | 16 |

Prompt attention takes 32 query rows of a head a threadgroup: each simdgroup scores 32 keys of a block over the whole
head and accumulates its own 64 output columns, the row maxes and fp32 probabilities crossing threadgroup memory 128
keys at a time. A 512-row chunk's 60 layers spend 138 ms there at 32k and 527 ms at 128k, where 16 rows a threadgroup
spent 194 and 810 (mlx-lm's fused attention about 161 at 32k): the kernel streams keys and values, so what each load
serves decides its rate, and vector loads, fetching a step ahead, and sparing interior blocks the mask and the rescale
moved nothing. The prompt GEMMs use Gemma's private affine_mm, which dequantizes each step's weights to bf16 in its tile (scale
times code plus bias in fp32, rounded once, as mlx-lm's quantized matmul does) and accumulates on the tensor unit over
the whole depth: a 512-row chunk's 60 layers take 284 ms there (mlx-lm's quantized matmuls 302), where the exact-codes
design, its per-group scale and bias epilogue and its row-sums pass took 344. So the prompt path rounds its weights as
mlx-lm does while the decode path's lane kernels keep the codes exact: over 40 tokens their last-row logits part by up
to 0.8.

A plain token at short context is 19.7 ms on the M5 Ultra (mlx-lm 21.6), where it was 23.7: the 241 projections read
17.3 GB in about 18 ms at the decode splits, 20.3 at the reference's (the 168-tile o and down projections ran two
waves of 256-thread groups at a split of 8 and one wave at 4; the gate/up stack and the head streamed 84-group chains
at 1, eight times the simdgroups at 8); the attention's 120 dispatches took 0.9 ms and the glue's 0.7, which running
as the projections' prologues shortens by 0.2 (a prologue costs what the tail kernel cost, and only the dispatch gap
goes) and the attention's prep and merge folded into its kernel by 0.6. `tf-gemma4-bench` prints the stages
(`GEMMA_DSTAGES`), each shape plain and fused (`GEMMA_FUSED`) and the glue kernels alone (`GEMMA_GLUE`).

## Shared arithmetic at landing

The shared affine and lane kernels, their Zig encoders, other-family callers and numerical tests retain the released
implementation. Gemma's rounded-weight dense source is in `zig/kernels/metal/gemma4/affine_mm.metal`. Its fused lane
variant is in `zig/kernels/metal/gemma4/lane_projection.metal`, with host encoding in `families/gemma4/fused_lane.zig`.
Ordinary Gemma lane packing and projections still use the shared lane module. The measurements above are the original
PR's receipts. They do not qualify the isolated landing tree. Re-run numerical, resource, teacher-forced, draft/plain,
resumed/fresh, concurrent/solo, vision and performance gates on that tree.

The host attention adjoint and native learner implementation plan are in
[Gemma Living Weights](gemma4-living-weights.md).
# Gemma 4 26B-A4B (`gemma4`)

This page describes the Python engine's `gemma4` family, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6); the packages, tools and tests it names are at that
tag. @cshintov wrote the family and its fused one-row kernels in [#10](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/10),
and @di37 made its `qkv_rows` kernel launch on M1 and M2 in [#224](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/224).
The native binary serves the dense 31B ([Gemma 4 31B, native Metal](gemma-4-native.md)) and the 12B
([Gemma 4 12B, native Metal](gemma-4-12b-native.md)); it refuses the 26B-A4B.

Measured on an M4 Pro with 64 GB (273 GB/s) and MLX 0.31.2, with `mlx-community/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-4bit`.
Packages: [`src/tensorfold/families/gemma4/`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/families/gemma4)
and [`src/tensorfold/kernels/gemma/v1/`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/kernels/gemma/v1).

## What decides the speed

- 30 layers: 25 sliding-window attention (window 1,024; 16 query heads over 8 KV heads, head dim 256) and 5
  full attention (16 query heads over 2 KV heads, head dim 512, keys reused as values, proportional RoPE).
  Hidden size 2,816.
- Every layer has a dense GeGLU MLP (width 2,112) and a MoE block beside it: 128 experts, top 8, expert width
  704, GeGLU. Three post-feedforward norms and a per-layer scalar join them.
- Vocabulary 262,144, tied to the embedding, logits soft-capped at 30. 4-bit affine weights in groups of 64.
- A token reads about 2.16 GB of weights: 7.9 ms at 273 GB/s. The vocabulary head alone is 415 MB (1.5 ms).
- mlx_lm's step runs about 40 small kernels a layer around the matmuls and takes 14.6 ms synchronous, 13.3
  ms decoded one step ahead.

## Drafts

The checkpoint has no draft head, so a stream drafts copies of its context. With `--drafter
z-lab/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-DFlash --drafter-bits 8` (Apache-2.0; `tensorfold pull` it first), z-lab's DFlash model
drafts a chain of up to 15 tokens a round. It reads the target's hidden rows after layers 1, 6, 11, 17, 22 and 27,
and the engine sets each round's depth from its costs. Replies stay equal to `"draft": false` ones.

Measured on an M3 Ultra (MLX 0.32.2, quick cells, 64 and 256 tokens, thinking off, gemma/mlx_lm's server):

| Cell | No draft model | DFlash |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chat, greedy | 1.31-1.35 | 1.52-1.53 |
| Chat, sampled | 1.12-1.16 | 1.29-1.31 |
| Code, greedy | 1.31-1.35 | 2.03-2.12 |
| Code, sampled | 1.10-1.16 | 1.62-1.84 |

Rounds average 3-5 rows at 13-20 ms, and the draft takes about 4 ms of that. The draft model runs once per stream
in a round, so four streams sharing rounds make 173-179 tok/s together against 196 without it.

## What worked

One-row steps, greedy, median ms a step on a chat prompt (`tools/gemma4_decode_bench.py` for synchronous,
one step ahead as the server's pipelined engine runs it):

| Step | Synchronous | One step ahead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mlx_lm model | 14.62 (68.4 tok/s) | 13.34 (75.0 tok/s) |
| fused glue only (norms, residuals, routing, stacked q/k/v and dense gate/up) | about 14.0 | |
| plus the expert kernels | 12.65 (79.1 tok/s) | 12.34 (81.0 tok/s) |
| plus the expert down loads issued before the reductions | 12.7 | 12.3-12.5 (80-81 tok/s) |
| plus every load of `attn_tail` and `moe_tail` issued before their first reduction | | 11.7-11.9 (84-85 tok/s) |

Through the server (`TF_GEMMA4_PIPELINE=1`, `tools/bench_openai.py`, 512 tokens, 5 reps, back to back on the
same machine), median tok/s:

| Prompt | Temperature | mlx_lm forward (`TF_GEMMA4_FUSED=0`) | fused, first cut | fused, tails fixed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fibonacci-raw | 0 | 70.0 | 76.3 | 81.3 |
| gpu-chat-no-think | 0 | 70.0 | 76.2 | 80.2 |
| fibonacci-raw | 1.0 | 61.8 | 77.5 | |
| gpu-chat-no-think | 1.0 | 69.3 | 75.2 | |

The server runs about 0.6 ms a token slower than a short in-process loop: back-to-back requests keep the GPU
hot (12.05 ms rested against 12.64 ms after a 2,500-token run, same short context), and the step grows with
context (12.6 to 14.3 ms over 2,500 tokens, the sliding-window caches filling to 1,024 keys).

The pieces (`src/tensorfold/kernels/gemma/v1/`), per layer:

- q, k (and v on sliding layers) stacked into one quantized matmul; `qkv_norm` applies the three head norms
  in one kernel. RoPE, the cache update and attention stay mlx_lm's.
- `attn_tail`: post-attention norm, residual add, and the three norms that read the result (dense MLP input,
  expert input, router input) in one kernel.
- The dense MLP's gate and up stacked into one matmul.
- `route`: router logits to the top 8 of 128 (ties to the lower id), softmax over the 8, per-expert scale.
- `expert_gateup`: the 8 experts' gate and up projections and GeGLU in one pass over the input. MLX's gathered
  matmuls read the input once a projection and launch the activation apart.
- `expert_down`: the 8 experts' down projections and their weighted sum.
- `moe_tail`: post-feedforward norms 1 and 2, the joint norm, residual add, layer scalar, and the next layer's
  input norm.
- The work before and after attention compiled with `mx.compile` per layer; the graph goes to the GPU every 8
  layers.

The glue alone saved about 4%: mlx_lm's glue kernels were cheap next to its gathered expert matmuls, which
read the input once a projection. Stubbing parts of the step showed the experts at 4.2 ms of 13.1 before
the expert kernels.

## Where the time goes now

Each op timed over all 30 layers in one chain (each layer's weights read once, as a real step reads them),
best of five:

| Op | ms a token | MB | GB/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| q/k/v (MLX quantized matmul) | 1.72 | 397 | 220-234 |
| o_proj | 1.0 | 227 | 228 |
| dense gate/up + down | 1.45 | 301 | 195-215 |
| expert gate/up + GeGLU | 2.5 | 535 | 210-215 |
| expert down + sum | 1.37 | 268 | 196 |
| head (in the step, with soft-cap and sampling input) | 2.0 | 415 | |

The most this machine read in our runs was 254 GB/s (the head), so the practical floor is about 8.5 ms.

Those rates are for independent calls, which overlap. The step is a dependent chain of about 10 kernels a
layer, so what counts is each kernel's latency in that chain. Removing parts from the real step (medians of
three interleaved rounds, 11.86 ms whole): the head is 1.74 ms, RoPE, the cache update and attention together
0.2 ms, so the 30 layers take about 10.1 ms for 1.74 GB, 173 GB/s. Each matmul reads only 7 to 27 MB a layer,
and its ramp-up and drain sit on the critical path. Dependent-chain latency per call, 30 layers of weights:

| Op | us a call |
| --- | --- |
| trivial elementwise kernel | 9 |
| q/k/v matmul + `qkv_norm` | 93 |
| o_proj | 50 |
| `attn_tail` (before / after issuing loads first) | 54 / 25 |
| router matmul + `route` | 41 to 62 |
| `expert_gateup` | 107 |
| `expert_down` | 80 |
| `moe_tail` (before / after) | 39 / 27 |
| dense MLP (off the critical path, beside routing and experts) | 86 |

## Tried and rejected

- The expert down kernel with every lane busy (704 inputs are 44 chunks of 16, so the committed layout idles
  20 of 32 lanes on the second chunk): 4, 8, 16 or 32 lanes a row. All slower than issuing the 8 rows' loads
  before the reductions, and they change the sum order.
- `expert_gateup` launch shapes (1 to 8 simdgroups, 1 to 8 rows each) and an unrolled K loop: within noise.
- Handing the graph to the GPU every 0, 4, 15 or 30 layers instead of 8: within noise.
- Folding RoPE into `qkv_norm`: removing RoPE from the step saves 0.07 ms, so not attempted.
- The dense MLP as three more expert slots (its width 2,112 is three expert widths; Nemotron folds its shared
  expert the same way): two launches instead of five, correct to bf16, but 12.39 to 12.56 ms. The dense MLP
  used to run beside routing; merged, it waits for the router.
- The 8-bit router matvec and the top-8 selection in one threadgroup: same experts and bit-identical weights
  in 600 of 600 checks, 62 to 46 us in a dependent chain, but 11.69 to 12.13 ms in the step. MLX's matvec
  spreads over the GPU beside the dense MLP; one threadgroup does not.
- `qkv_norm` with its norm weights loaded before the reduction: no change (many threadgroups hide the latency).
- `MLX_MAX_OPS_PER_BUFFER=200` and `MLX_MAX_MB_PER_BUFFER=100000` (Nemotron's and Flash Next's settings):
  within noise.

## Exactness

- One-token steps run the fused kernels; prompts run mlx_lm's forward and fill the same caches. The fused
  arithmetic follows mlx_lm's (fp32 sums, bf16 where mlx_lm stores bf16) with its own sum orders (strategy C
  in the [recipe book](README.md)), so serial decoding through it is its own reference.
- The family does not draft: without `multi_row_exact` the engine runs one row a round. The same limit as
  Flash Next and Nemotron applies to prompts: a one-token suffix after a cache hit goes through the fused
  step, a longer one through mlx_lm's forward.
- Quality, judged against the same 4-bit weights run with fp32 activations (`tools/gemma4_truth_eval.py`), on
  5,742 tokens of the model's own sampled answers to 12 chat prompts:

| Path | KL mean | KL trimmed | KL median | tokens over 1 nat | top-1 = truth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mlx_lm whole-sequence forward | 0.00297 | 0.00228 | 3.6e-6 | 0 | 98.89% |
| mlx_lm decode | 0.00329 | 0.00251 | 4.1e-6 | 0 | 98.61% |
| fused decode | 0.00893 | 0.00245 | 4.0e-6 | 2 | 98.66% |

  The fused mean comes from 2 tokens of 5,742, knife-edge positions where any bf16 rounding flips the answer.
  At one of them every bf16 path disagrees with the fp32 one. At the other, each of the 354 x 30 expert-down
  calls matches mlx_lm within bf16 on identical inputs.
- Tests (`tests/test_gemma4_kernels.py`): every kernel against an MLX reference, each layer against mlx_lm's
  layer on identical inputs with a small quantized model, and the caches advancing as mlx_lm's do.

## Traps

- KL or NLL against mlx_lm's own samples charges any difference from mlx_lm as damage: it called this path 4x
  worse. Compare every path against an fp32 truth, and read the trimmed and median figures beside the mean.
- A chat model's NLL on raw text or on chat templates is 7 to 10 nats a token. The distribution there is too
  flat to rank kernels. Score the model's own answers.
- Timing a kernel by calling it repeatedly on one layer's weights reads them from cache: 402 GB/s on a 273
  GB/s machine. Chain through all layers.
- Single timing runs of the step drifted up to 7% between runs (12.3 to 13.2 ms). Decide with interleaved A/B
  runs in one process and identical output hashes.
- A kernel's latency in an isolated dependent chain did not predict the step twice: the merged dense MLP and
  the one-threadgroup router both won alone and lost in the step, where they gave up overlap with other work.
- The server rebuilds saved system blocks after a kernel change. A request that arrives during that rebuild
  waits (11.8 s behind a 25k-token block here), which looks like a slow first token.

## Next

- The layers read 1.74 GB at 173 GB/s against about 245 possible, 2.9 ms a token. The loss is latency in the
  per-layer chain, so it needs fewer dependent kernels a layer (one kernel per matmul and its tail, or a
  persistent kernel over the layer), not faster matvecs.
- `expert_gateup` from about 215 toward 240 GB/s is worth about 0.3 ms a token.
- A multi-row fused step with a load-time row check would allow copy windows (drafting).
- Prefill through the fused step would remove the cache dependence of prompt bits.
# Gemma 4 Living Weights: host backward and implementation plan

This is the host mathematical first step for #1803. It enables no native learner, pocket, admission flag or save
path. Existing serving sources and all CUDA/Metal shaders remain byte-identical. The new module is reachable only
from a host test target, included in `zig build test` on every host.

`families/gemma4/attention_backward.zig` differentiates prepared attention with scale **1**:

```text
P = softmax(Q K^T) over the captured window
O = P V
dP[j] = dot(dO, V[j])
dS[j] = P[j] * (dP[j] - sum_i P[i] dP[i])
dQ += dS[j] K[j]; dK[j] += dS[j] Q; dV[j] += P[j] dO
```

Gemma's logit softcap of 30 belongs to the LM head. Attention scores have no such softcap or inverse-root-width
factor. The current CUDA forward sets `scale = 1` and `p32 = true` in `gemma4/cuda_forward.zig`; the Metal prompt
kernel likewise takes the prepared dot product. The source of those conventions remains unchanged.
