Run device commands only after device selection and memory admission.
Contract controls must fail at their stated gate. The runner reports
those failures as controls; a passing suite has no missed controls or
production failures.

Capture tools report differences without assigning a pass from an arbitrary
tolerance. Cross-backend logits can differ. Within the native engine,
shared, drafted and resumed execution must preserve the required bytes.

## Current boundaries

Use one GPU and BF16 activations for images. Qwen vision admits at most
4096 merged image tokens, or 16384 encoder patches. LightOn 1B admits
its full 1540-pixel side, including odd patch grids; the learned merger
drops unmatched edges after the encoder.

The 1B host prompt cache compares exact image identities beside compact
cache words. Image states are not written to disk formats that lack that
metadata. Qwen image requests currently keep per-request pages and bypass
cross-request radix reuse; text requests retain the existing cache path.

CUDA, Metal and other AMD GPUs are not qualified. Issue #1927 tracks CUDA.
# Shared M5 attention precision

`TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=1` selects explicit float FMA products for the shared `attention_nax` P x V on M5.
Unset or `0` keeps the existing tensor product, which truncates a float probability to ten fraction bits.
Other values are refused when a library using this attention source is opened.
Set the variable before starting the process and keep it fixed for that process.
The default has not changed. This is an experimental arithmetic mode, not a family qualification.

The full mode retains Q x K, softmax, masks, the normalizer and the final BF16 output.
It preserves every normal FP32 probability bit in its products, with FP32 FMA accumulation.
It does not promise exact real sums or bit equality with the cut mode.
The extra scalar products and lane shuffles can cost throughput; measure the selected checkpoint and prompt size.
Older GPUs keep the previous simdgroup-matrix source even when the switch is set.
Nemotron disk prompt states include the mode in their identity and cannot cross it.

The shared helper serves Nemotron prompt attention, including its paged twin, and Qwen Image/MOSS Image attention.
It does not change the 27B text path's explicit half probabilities, general float GEMM or another family's attention.
The 27B's Qwen-VL tower also uses a separate float GEMM.
A teacher-forced 27B comparison is an unaffected control, not proof of a quality change in that model.
Image denoisers have velocity outputs rather than top tokens; their teacher-forced velocities need their own case.

## Checks

```sh
zig build test-kernel-contract tf-kernel-contract -Dcpu=apple_m1
./zig-out/bin/tf-kernel-contract --only 'attention PV'
```

The contract registers cut operands against a cut-operand binary64 formula and full operands against full binary64.
Both require FP32 sums, guarded buffers, repeats, exceptional classes and matrix tile edges.
The served Nemotron prompt range keeps the measured one-sided operand-cut terms when unset.
Full mode removes that operand cut and counts 32 FMA steps per key tile; its control still compiles the cut product.
The masked-key nonfinite finding remains a separate case in both modes.
Its planted control runs the actual cut helper against the full-operand bound and must fail the shapes gate.
The bound is the FP32 chain length and term magnitude, not a percentage fitted to the observed result.
Separate launch records name both probes and all four production full-mode alignments.
M1/M2 compilation records and an M5 device receipt are distinct evidence; unsupported hardware is not a pass.

The template probe injects exact dyadic probabilities into the real attention source, including a float-output copy.
It checks causal/full visibility, query/key tails, key-tile seams, five repeats, input bytes and guards:

```sh
swiftc -O tools/zig/attention_pv.swift -o attention-pv
TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=0 ./attention-pv . check red
TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=1 ./attention-pv . check
TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=0 ./attention-pv . bench 2048
TF_ATTENTION_PV_FP32=1 ./attention-pv . bench 2048
```

Run device work only on an isolated GPU under the machine's existing queue and lock.
A compile failure cannot stand in for the cut mode's numerical red witness.
Teacher-force identical histories and report every top-token difference and both margins; do not judge diverging replies.
No default should change before the affected family has its own accepted correctness and fidelity receipts.
# MiniMax H3 / FastH3 CUDA blocks, one device

This library contains @drowzeys' #958 BF16 transformer blocks and kernel contracts, with the maintainers' boundary,
shared-context, complete-block and allocation repairs. The later shared copy-source owner protects temporary uploads.
Weights and activations retain BF16 storage and products use the runtime's cuBLASLt Linear with FP32 sums.

The host supplies text encoding, sampling, projections, video/audio encoding and decoding. This is a block library,
not a complete native clip-generation endpoint. No weights are included. Code is Apache-2.0; MiniMax H3 / FastH3
weights have the MiniMax H3 Community License and its territorial limits.

Build the real library on a CUDA build machine:

```sh
zig build tf-h3 -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
```

This stage has no rank inputs, transport source, exchange kernel or libibverbs dependency. The C interface is
zig/src/families/h3/cuda_lib.h. Check tf_h3_abi_version() == 1 before passing its 96-byte tf_h3_inputs.
All tiles and rows belong to one device. The library retains the current primary CUDA context through Context.shared;
a host framework's device addresses must belong to that context. If no context is current, the runtime selects zero.

The same entry points support device addresses (tf_h3_forward), host addresses (tf_h3_forward_host), mapped host
allocation, profiling and BF16 projection replacement. The host owns pointer extents and serialized calls on a model.
The fixed 16,384-row cuBLASLt algorithm-selection shape is retained to preserve the original arithmetic policy.

Host tests and compile-only ABI libraries do not load a GPU image:

```sh
zig build test-h3-boundaries test-cuda-host test-cuda-copy-source compile-h3-library
```

Compile-only artifacts are installed under zig-out/host-checks and contain an empty image. They are verification
artifacts, not runnable inference libraries. The Linux library is cross-compiled and is not executed on this Mac.
The numerical contracts, actual kernels, model fidelity, real context interoperability and performance need CUDA hardware.

The original #958 thread reports one/two/three-GB10 results. Those measurements predate this split and do not qualify
this exact source. Sequence-parallel execution is a separate follow-up with an extended ABI and its own transport gates.

The Linux CUDA runner and all H3 contract adapters also have a compile-only gate:

```sh
zig build compile-cuda-tests -Dtarget=x86_64-linux-gnu
```

This step has no NVCC or Metal compiler dependency and does not execute the resulting binary.
# MiniMax H3 / FastH3 transformer on Metal (M5 tensor units)

This is a video model's denoising transformer, not a token model. It has no lane round and no drafted tokens. It
keeps the checkpoint's precision: bf16 weights read in place from the checkpoint, bf16 activations, fp32 sums. It is
a test tool beside the engine; nothing in the lane core, the server or another family changes.

## What it is

`zig build tf-h3-dit -Dcpu=apple_m1 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` builds `zig-out/bin/tf-h3-dit`. It reads the FastH3
checkpoint's shards and a case file, runs every denoising forward for the packed [text | keyframe | audio | video]
rows, prints the first forward's velocities against the reference velocities the case holds, and writes the final
video and audio rows (and the first forward's velocities) as raw float32.

```sh
zig-out/bin/tf-h3-dit <transformer_dir> <shards> case.safetensors out_prefix [dense | profile | DEFINE, ...]
```

It needs the M5's tensor units and refuses to load without them. `dense` makes every query tile attend to every tile
and leaves the pooled branch out (not how the checkpoint was trained; for kernel work only). `profile` times one more
forward stage by stage.

## Arithmetic

- Block projections: the prefill kernels' `tfp::gemm_nax` (MLX 0.32.3's NAX GEMM), bf16 x w^T as the checkpoint
  stores w, fp32 sums, bf16 out. The SwiGLU's first projection is one product over its stored [value; gate] rows.
- Norms, rotary, the gated adds and the SwiGLU round to bf16 where the reference's bf16 MLX arithmetic rounds.
- Attention is FastH3's video sparse attention over 64-row tiles: a text, keyframe or audio tile attends every
  tile; a video tile attends the prefix tiles and its top 20% of video tiles by pooled score; the pooled branch is
  gated in. Tile means, scores, the top-k and the pooled branch are fp32. The routed attention is bf16 q, k and v
  on the tensor units with fp32 scores and an online softmax across key tiles; its weights are rounded to bf16
  before the value product, as MLX's attention rounds them.

## Kernel contract

Thirteen kernels are registered (`zig/tests/contract/metal_h3*.zig`), each against its formula in float64, and their
launches in `registry.zig`. The two GEMM entry points are the prefill source's own and are registered as launches.
Kernels whose outputs pass through intermediate bf16 roundings declare them as `mids`; their test inputs are of one
sign where a sum could cancel, so no rounding hides behind a small result.

```sh
zig build tf-kernel-contract -Dcpu=apple_m1 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
zig-out/bin/tf-kernel-contract --only h3
```

## The case file

The prompt's rows, the schedule and the tile map come in one safetensors file. The exporter that writes one is not in
this change: it uses the Python 0.6 H3 family, which lives on a fork (`drowzeys/TensorFold`, `tools/zig/h3_case.py` on
branch `h3-1.0.4`).

| Tensor | Holds |
|---|---|
| `text` | The prompt's rows after the condition projection and the token refiner, bf16 |
| `video`, `audio`, `condition` | Starting noise rows; a first frame's rows when the clip starts from an image |
| `cos`, `sin` | Rotary tables for every packed row |
| `adaln`, `times`, `tables.N`, `final` | Each row's line in a block's six modulation tables per step, and the tables |
| `video_step`, `audio_step` | Per step: the sigma the model sees and the Euler ratio |
| `tile_slot`, `tile_sizes`, `geometry` | FastVideo's tile map: each row's padded slot, each tile's rows, the counts |
| `video_in.*`, `audio_in.*`, `video_out.*`, `audio_out.*`, `final_norm.weight` | The small float projections |
| `video_velocity`, `audio_velocity` | The reference's first forward, for the parity line the tool prints |

## Receipt

Mac Studio, Apple M5 Ultra, 256 GB, macOS 27.0.1, Zig 0.17.0. Checkpoint `FastVideo/FastVideo-FastH3-8-Step-V2`,
864x480, 124 frames, 8 steps, 15,435 packed rows (36 text, 414 audio, 14,985 video), 288 tiles. Reference: the
Python 0.6 family in bf16 on MLX 0.32.3 with FastVideo's reference routing; with FastVideo's fp Metal sparse attention
it takes 27.9 s a forward on the same Mac. Peak process footprint 4.3 GB, the checkpoint mapped read-only beside it.
The pull request has the full tables.

| Run | A forward (median) | Video velocity against the reference | Audio velocity against the reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Step 1 of 8 | 10.1 s | cosine 0.98981, relative error 0.143 | cosine 0.99987, relative error 0.017 |
| Step 5 of 8 | 10.1 s | cosine 0.99838, relative error 0.057 | cosine 0.99980, relative error 0.020 |

At step 1 every video tile is noise, so FastH3's top-k among them is decided by differences far below bf16. The same
binary with only the fp32 summation order of the tile scores reversed differs from itself by video cosine 0.99021 at
step 1 and 0.99834 at step 5: the comparison with the reference is at that floor.

## A clip that starts from an image

A case exported with a first frame (`h3_case.py --first-frame IMAGE`) has a seventh geometry count: the keyframe's
rows, between the text (which then also holds the image's vision tokens) and the audio. They enter like video rows
on every pass, at the keyframe noise level the case's tables give them, and are never stepped.

Same Mac, checkpoint and size, a 864x480 first frame: 16,253 packed rows (449 text, 405 keyframe, 414 audio,
14,985 video), 302 tiles (22 prefix).

| Run | Video velocity against the reference, step 1 | Audio velocity against the reference, step 1 |
|---|---|---|
| From a first frame | cosine 0.99711, relative error 0.076 | cosine 0.99986, relative error 0.017 |

Text to video is bit-identical with and without this change (final video and audio rows, 8 steps).

## Other step counts

With `tables` or `steps=N` the tool makes the run's schedule itself instead of reading the case's. The rungs come from
the checkpoint's `fastvideo_inference.json`, or N spread evenly from its first rung, with the video and audio shifts
(a preview checkpoint's from its scheduler folders). Then come every row's timestep at each step and the timestep
embedder (on the host, float64 sums of the checkpoint's float32 values). Each block's and the final layer's AdaLN
tables come from `h3_modulation` on the GPU, bf16 inputs and weights with fp32 sums. `from=K` starts at step K of
a case exported mid-run. The case still supplies the prompt's rows, the noise, the rotary tables and the tile map.

## The released MiniMax-H3, and re-voicing a clip

The tool also loads the released MiniMax-H3 transformer (its FL2VA or Ref2VA folder, `model-*` shards): each head's
fused [q, k, v] rows in one product, the SwiGLU's [gate; value] rows, dense attention with no routing gates, and its
own timestep embedder and AdaLN names. `revoice=N` re-voices a finished picture as the Python sampler's `revoice`
does in its whole-sequence form: every row but the generated audio stays at the keyframe level for every step, the
audio rows go down the released model's grid of N + 1 points (audio shift 3), and the video rows are not moved.
A case for it comes from `h3_revoice_case.py` on the fork's exporter branch, from a finished clip's rows.

## Ref2VA: reference pictures, videos and audio

The released Ref2VA transformer loads like FL2VA. A Ref2VA case (`h3_ref2va_case.py` on the fork's exporter branch,
after `packing.reference_layout`) puts its rows in the engine's order: text, the references' video rows (held at the
keyframe level, as a first frame's are), the audio rows with the references' clean audio first, then the clip's
video. Its geometry has an eighth count, the reference audio rows: they enter on every pass at timestep 1 and are
never stepped. `steps=N` on the released weights makes their own grid of N + 1 points (video shift 12, audio 3).

## Not done

- No exporter in the tree, so the tool cannot be exercised from this repository alone.
- One machine (M5 Ultra). Chips without tensor units are refused.
- No `tensorfold generate`, no text encoder, decoders or sampler: the forward only.

## Host geometry admission

`zig build test-h3-geometry` tests the case reader and schedule without a GPU or the Metal compiler.
On macOS, `zig build compile-h3-host` compiles the actual tool with embedded shader source but does not compile or run
shaders. Device and reference-output checks still need a Mac with the Metal toolchain.

The reader accepts six, seven or eight nonnegative geometry counts. The seventh is held picture/video rows; the eighth
is held audio, from zero through the total audio count. Text and held picture rows may be empty. Both audio and generated
video must have rows for this tool's unconditional buffers and dispatches. Tiles hold one through 64 rows each; their
unique slots must match the prefix/video partition. Keep may be zero through the generated-video tile count.

Malformed counts, tensor shapes, tile maps, table indices, schedule sizes and overflowing byte products return named
`H3` errors before shader compilation or scratch allocation. Integer shader dimensions must fit `i32`; GEMM widths must
be multiples of 256; rotary width must be even and between 2 and 128. The top-k tile map is capped at 32768 tiles for the
32 KiB threadgroup array. These arithmetic limits do not promise that an admitted request fits the available memory.
# MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on CUDA (two DGX Sparks)

The `minimax_m3` family's CUDA backend serves [MiniMax-M3.1-Flash](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash)
at tensor parallel over hosts from a published EXL3 pack read as published: its trellis projections and routed experts
through the shared EXL3 kernels, the rest as stored. The release's DSpark drafter and vision tower (copied verbatim into
the pack), tools, structured output, thinking on or off, kept prompt states and two streams are served. Rank 0 serves
HTTP; the other ranks follow its steps. It shares the family's config, tokenizer handling, chat template and tool-call
markup with the [Metal backend](minimax-m3.1-flash.md).

The model is MiniMax's, under the [MiniMax Community License](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash/blob/main/LICENSE):
free for non-commercial use; commercial use needs a notice to, or above a revenue threshold an authorization from,
MiniMax.

## The checkpoint

Two GB10s (128 GB each) do not hold the release whole (its routed experts are 216.4 GiB NVFP4), so the backend serves
[Mia-AiLab/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-EXL3-EAQ-v1-3.06-bpw](https://huggingface.co/Mia-AiLab/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-EXL3-EAQ-v1-3.06-bpw)
at revision `c33e7a6619f0f12ac99098e07ec5e56acb7eeda9`: exllamav3 1.6.1, the `mul1` codebook, attention q/k/v/o at 6
bits, the dense and shared MLPs at 5, every routed expert at 3, the head at 8; the indexer's projections fp16, the
router fp32, embeddings and norms bf16. This is a lossy third-party quantization of the release, not MiniMax's own
weights: its fidelity against the release is measured below. The release's own MXFP8 and NVFP4 tensors are not served on
CUDA (they need four GB10s; the loader takes EXL3 packs only).

```sh
hf download Mia-AiLab/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-EXL3-EAQ-v1-3.06-bpw --revision c33e7a6619f0f12ac99098e07ec5e56acb7eeda9 \
  --local-dir ~/models/mm-exl3   # on every rank
```

The loader checks `quantization_config` (`quant_method` "exl3", `codebook` "mul1", `version` 1.x) and every projection's
trellis, marker and scales as it reads them. The indexer's fp16 weights load as bf16 exactly (each is a dequantized
e4m3 value times a power of two; the loader refuses one that bf16 does not hold). A rank takes whole key heads, and each
MLP's and expert's intermediate and the vocabulary in 128-column blocks (EXL3 tiles and rotations): at TP=2 85.3 GiB a
rank, the vocabulary split 782 and 781 blocks.

## Run

The family is admitted only as it was run: on GB10 (sm_121) at two ranks. Any other GPU is refused
(`MiniMaxM3RequiresSm121`), and so is one rank or any other world (`MiniMaxM3RequiresTwoRanks`). `TF_MINIMAX_RANK`
(0 or 1) of `TF_MINIMAX_WORLD=2` places each rank, and `NCCL_COMM_ID` names rank 0's address and port on the link
between the hosts. With 192.0.2.1 as rank 0's address on their direct link, the same folder on both:

```bash
export NCCL_RUNTIME_CONNECT=0 NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0 NCCL_CUMEM_HOST_ENABLE=0   # on GB10 pairs
# on rank 1
TF_MINIMAX_RANK=1 TF_MINIMAX_WORLD=2 NCCL_COMM_ID=192.0.2.1:29581 TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB=3 \
  tensorfold serve ~/models/mm-exl3 --context 32768 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 3 --vision
# on rank 0 (192.0.2.1)
TF_MINIMAX_RANK=0 TF_MINIMAX_WORLD=2 NCCL_COMM_ID=192.0.2.1:29581 TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB=3 \
  tensorfold serve ~/models/mm-exl3 --context 32768 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 3 --vision
```

Set `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` and `NCCL_IB_HCA` for the link as NCCL documents them; each rank keeps a TCP line to rank 0
on the port after `NCCL_COMM_ID`'s, so a rank that fails stops the others. On two ranks the layers' small gathers go by
RoCE writes (as GLM's); `TF_ROCE=0` leaves them to NCCL and `TF_ROCE_MAX_KB` caps a rank's bytes.

- The key/value cache is bf16, exact; a token takes 75 KiB a rank at TP=2 across the 60 layers (keys and values of the
  rank's two key heads, the shared index key).
- Drafts: the release's DSpark head (`dspark/`, MXFP8 as released), on unless `--no-drafts`; replies are identical
  with drafts off.
- The vision tower runs on the last rank; the others receive its rows. Its patch embedding is fp32 as stored. An image
  takes at most 576 tokens (672 x 672, the release processor's `max_pixels`); no video.
- Kept prompt states start at 2,048-token chunk boundaries (`--prompt-cache-gib`).

## How it computes

- Projections: `cuda.exl3.Dense` (q, k and v by columns, o by rows; gate and up by columns, down by rows; the head by
  columns), each rank's fp32 partials summed in rank order. The indexer's projections are one bf16 lane weight.
- Routed experts: the shared grouped EXL3 kernels (`cuda.exl3_grouped`), with SwiGLU-OAI as their `act_mode` 2:
  (clamp(up) + 1) g sigmoid(1.702 g), g = min(gate, 7), in bf16 steps as transformers and the Metal backend round it.
  A prompt chunk and a decode window take the same path (every pick's down rows in fp32), so a row's bits do not depend
  on the window it arrives in.
- Attention: each index head selects its key head's blocks (the MSA paper's top-k per GQA group): the block's max of
  index scores in fp32, the row's own block always kept, every block while a row sees at most 16. Index scores and
  attention run on the tensor units for prompt chunks and decode windows alike (`tf_mm3_index_scores_tc`,
  `tf_mm3_attn_prompt_tc`: fp32 online softmax, bf16 probabilities into P.V), so drafted replies equal plain ones and a
  resumed prompt equals a fresh one.
- Drafts: DSpark's block over the anchor's 4,096-key window, the Markov walk kept on the device (one host read a
  block). The lane costs (`cuda_lanes.zig`) were timed on two GB10s, every rank at once after the load: verify windows
  of 1 to 32 rows at positions 1k and 8k (their mean, never less than a narrower window's) and a draft block.
- Rounding follows transformers' and the Metal backend's (Gemma norms rounded once, the residual rounded to bf16 after
  every add, cos and sin rounded to bf16, the rotary frequencies' power rounded once to fp32 as torch and Metal's
  `precise::pow`), with one difference: the MoE sums its weighted picks in fp32 and rounds once, where transformers
  rounds after every pick.

## Checks (two DGX Sparks, GB10)

- Fidelity against the release: 2,406 tokens of a three-turn chat (prose, code, math, German, Chinese, JSON),
  teacher-forced. The served engine's logits for every row (`tf-minimax-cuda ... rows` at TP=2) against the release's
  (`tools/zig/minimax_m3_ref.py --logits`: its MXFP8 and NVFP4 decoded exactly, in transformers' order), compared by
  `tools/zig/minimax_m3_kl.py`: KL(release || served) mean 0.0788, median 0.0076, p99 0.97; top-1 agreement 89.90%
  (243 misses, each listed with both sides' top contenders and margins in the tool's report). Rows past 2,048 keys
  (the indexer selecting): KL 0.0674, top-1 89.66%. For scale, the release itself with the MoE's picks summed in fp32
  (this engine's order, `--fp32-picks`) against transformers' order: KL 0.0120, top-1 97.13%.
- Served (recipe harness, TP=2): soak 60/60, concurrent 12/12, streaming 4/4, multi-turn 8/8, stop 3/3, max-tokens 3/3,
  thinking switch 10/10, copy 2/2; DSpark drafted == plain 12/12; structured output 18/18 (drafted == plain 12/12); tool
  calls 5/5; seeded sampling 9/9; a resumed turn equals the same turn cold after a restart. Images: shapes, text and
  counting read right, and 16 image requests at once equal each alone.
- Decode with DSpark drafts, one stream: prose 24.3-24.4, code 38.1-39.4, structured 27.6-29.7, list 29.8-30.4 tokens a
  second, first token 0.60-0.65 s; two streams 31.0, 44.9, 35.7 and 52.0 in total.
- Kernel contract: gates 1-4 for every MiniMax kernel (`tf-cuda-test minimax-contract`): the attention and indexer forms
  and the glue (norms, q/k preparation, SwiGLU-OAI, router and routing, the MoE partial, picks, DSpark's Markov head, the
  tower's RoPE and patch embedding, the copies), with planted controls red. The shared experts' `act_mode` 2 is checked
  against float64 (also with the gate driven past the clamp) and for row invariance (`tf-cuda-test exl3`), with two
  wrong formulas as controls.
- Shared code: only `tf_exl3_plan_finish` changes in the `exl3_experts` image (SASS of the other 11 symbols identical
  on sm_80, sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121). Qwen3.5-MoE's EXL3 checkpoint (Ornith-1.5-122B, the image's other grouped user) on
  one GB10 gives byte-identical greedy replies before and after, at the same speed.

## Not covered

- Only TP=2 on two GB10s was run (TP=1 needs a GPU holding about 160 GiB; TP=4 was not tried).
- The release's MXFP8 and NVFP4 tensors are not read on CUDA; only EXL3 packs.
- Video is not served. With two images in a prompt, a borderline yellow can be named orange or green (single images read
  it right; an earlier build on a mix of the release's NVFP4 and 3-bit experts did the same).
- Quality suites (thinking off and on) were not run on this build.
# MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on Metal (one 256 GB M5 Ultra)

The `minimax_m3` family serves [MiniMax-M3.1-Flash](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash), a
428B-A23B mixture of experts with block-sparse attention (a lightning indexer picks each row's key blocks) and a
CLIP vision tower, on the lane host: tools, structured output, thinking on or off, images, the prompt cache, two
streams, and drafts from the release's DSpark head or incoai's DFlash2.

MiniMax's release stores its experts in NVFP4 and the rest in MXFP8; as published it takes about 248 GB, more than a
256 GB Mac can give a model. The family reads MLX-style affine groups instead, from two community checkpoints:
lossy conversions of the release, published with its own `config.json` (`minimax_m3_vl`, the language model under
`text_config`), the MLX `quantization` block in place of the release's, and the drafters' weights:

| checkpoint | experts | on disk | window on 256 GB |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| [`BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34`](https://huggingface.co/BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34) | 4-bit (g128) on 26 of 60 layers, 3-bit (g64) on the rest | 203.7 GiB | 32,768 |
| [`BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix256k`](https://huggingface.co/BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix256k) | 4-bit on 3 layers, 3-bit on the rest | 189.2 GiB | 147,456 |

Attention, the shared expert, the dense layers and the head are 8-bit in both; both carry the DSpark and DFlash2
weights. Against the release's own weights (1,024 positions teacher-forced, bf16 cache) the conversion costs a mean KL
of 0.244 (80.7% top-1) on mix34 and 0.295 (78.4%) on mix256k. Everything the engine does from the converted weights on
is exact. The key/value cache is bf16: under the 226 GB limit below its caches fit 150,400 tokens on mix256k and 37,376
on mix34. The
[serving recipe](https://github.com/BobClawblaw/minimax-m31-flash-mlx-m5-ultra) has the conversion's studies.

TensorFold's code is Apache-2.0. MiniMax-M3.1-Flash's weights, and these checkpoints made from them, have the MiniMax
Community License: free for non-commercial use; commercial use must show "Built with MiniMax M3.1-Flash" and notify
MiniMax, with its written authorization above US$20 million yearly revenue; its appendix lists prohibited uses.
incoai's DFlash2 drafter, carried in both checkpoints, is Apache-2.0, as its
[model card](https://huggingface.co/incoai/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-DFlash2/blob/ac07a7c1ecaae26a7ace595756124dca974b432d/README.md)
states at the revision converted (`ac07a7c1`); the release's DSpark head is under MiniMax's licence with the rest.

## Run

```sh
hf download BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34 --revision 9524999057e0d277d26438606e033e2191fb465c \
  --local-dir ~/models/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34
MINIMAX_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=226 tensorfold serve ~/models/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34 \
  --context 32768 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 4 --vision
```

For mix256k (revision `916e7ca1044f1c3e7566163096243c940327224d`), `--context 147456`.

- `MINIMAX_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` bounds weights, scratch and caches together. The default (75% of RAM) holds the weights
  but no caches, so set it; at 226 a 145,203-token prompt on mix256k peaked at 210 GiB wired.
- The cache takes 135 KiB a token across the 60 layers; `--parallel 2` streams share it.
- `MINIMAX_DRAFTER`: `dflash2` (the default) or `dspark`; any other value is refused. `--no-drafts` decodes plainly.
- Thinking off ends the prompt with `</mm:think>`, as the model does when it chooses not to think. Tool calls use
  MiniMax's `]<]minimax[>[` markup, parsed into OpenAI `tool_calls`; `tool_choice: required` or a named tool is
  constrained in that markup (xgrammar's `minimax_m3_xml`).
- Images: at most 576 tokens an image (672 x 672, the release processor's `max_pixels`); larger images are scaled
  down. Each image is its own tower pass. No video.

## Checks (Apple M5 Ultra, 256 GB, macOS 27)

- Four layers against transformers' own model: KL at most 0.005. The full model against an MLX reference at the same
  weights: KL 0.015.
- 1,024 rows teacher-forced against the release's NVFP4 weights: mix34 KL 0.244 (80.7% top-1), mix256k 0.295 (78.4%).
- Drafted replies equal plain ones (DFlash2 and DSpark); windows equal one-row steps bit for bit; two streams'
  replies equal their runs alone; replies are equal with the prompt cache on and off.
- A needle at 145,203 tokens on mix256k (115 s cold; 210 GiB wired at the peak). The tower against transformers':
  relative error 0.030 to fp32 (torch bf16: 0.039).
- Decode with DFlash2, one stream (prose / code / structured / list): mix256k 44.0 / 55.8 / 47.8 / 50.9 tokens a
  second, mix34 41.2 / 61.3 / 49.3 / 55.3. Cold prompts on mix256k: 1,478 tokens a second at 8,403 tokens, 1,486 at
  16,598 and 1,484 at 30,929 (4,096-row chunks); 1,379 at 128k before the kernel fixes.
- The family's 50 Metal kernels are registered with the kernel contract: 50 pass gates 1-4.

## Not covered

- Only the M5's tensor units were checked; nothing smaller than 256 GB holds the weights.
- The release itself: serving it exactly needs native NVFP4/MXFP8 kernels on Metal and a Mac that holds about 248 GB.
- Video input.
# MOSS-Image on CUDA

`zig/src/families/moss_image` also runs MOSS-Image's transformer on the CUDA runtime (`cuda.zig`, `cuda_model.zig`):
the same denoiser as on Metal ([moss-image.md](moss-image.md)), from the same released bf16 checkpoint, driven by the
same `tf-moss-image` tool and checked against the same publisher pipeline.

- A prompt's rows once a prompt: the input projection and the two refiner blocks.
- The image and prompt rows together at each step: every joint block under one shared modulation, full attention
  over both.
- The card's guidance: two passes a step, the prompt and the empty negative prompt with block 22 skipped.

The prompt encoder and the image decoder are not ported; `tools/zig/moss_image_case.py` runs them in torch, as on
Metal. It is a denoiser, not a token family: it does not register with the lane engine, the server or
`families.detect`.

The config, the rotary tables and the timestep's modulation (`config.zig`, `host.zig`) are shared with Metal. The
weights are checked as on Metal: the released geometry only, and no tensor left unread.

It runs on the two GPUs it was checked on, sm_120 (RTX 5090) and sm_121 (GB10): `Model.load` refuses any other.

## Precision

The Metal family's rounding, step for step:

- bf16 activations, rounded where the publisher's torch code rounds them.
- fp32 sums in every projection and in attention. Projections are cuBLASLt bf16 GEMMs with fp32 accumulation
  (`vit.Gemms`, as the vision towers use); the biased ones add the bias to the fp32 sums and round once
  (`vit.linear`).
- fp32 for norms and softmax; the rotary tables in bf16; the time MLP and modulation on the host, once a timestep.
- No int8, no fast math: `moss_image.cu` builds with the glue flags (`--fmad=false`, IEEE division and square root).

Attention is `prefill_attention.cu`'s full (non-causal) `vision_kernel`, which the vision towers use at head dims 72
and 80, here instantiated at 128 (eight warps, 69,632 bytes of shared memory). The new instance leaves the existing
ones as they were: their SASS is identical before and after (sm_80, 86, 89, 120 and 121; nvcc 13.0, 13.2 and 13.3).

`moss_image.cu` holds the family's own steps, each a port of `moss_image.metal`'s kernel:

- `tf_moss_norm`: RMSNorm, then optionally the modulation's scale and shift;
- `tf_moss_qk`: each q and k head's RMSNorm and rotary, q, k and v packed into attention's input rows (both the
  joint blocks' separate projections and the refiner's packed one);
- `tf_moss_situ`: the situ gate, over the MLP's (hidden | gate) rows or two buffers;
- `tf_moss_gate_add`: the gated residual add (ones for the refiner's plain residual).

## Kernel contract

`zig/tests/cuda/contract_moss_image*.zig` registers the four kernels in each form the family launches, and the head-128
attention:

- each output is checked against float64 at the kernel's bf16 points, in the range its fp32 steps allow (IEEE division
  and square root, two ulps for `expf` and `tanhf`);
- shapes are the served ones (4,106 to 4,188 joint rows, 10 to 63 prompt rows, widths 3,072 and 8,192) and the tiles'
  edges; the attention runs all 24 heads at the prompt lengths and two at the joint lengths;
- five controls each drop one bf16 rounding point (the norm's, the modulation's, the rotary's, the sigmoid's and the
  gate's), and gate 3 must catch each;
- the attention is checked against `contract_attn.zig`'s float64 reference; its gate 4 uses P x V sums that fp16 or bf16
  sums would miss.

Gate 5's records are in `moss_image_cuda_records.zig` (sm_80, 86, 89, 120 and 121; the same on nvcc 13.0, 13.2 and
13.3, so no later release needs a set of its own).

`tf-cuda-test moss-contract` on a GB10 (nvcc 13.0 and 13.2) and an RTX 5090 (nvcc 13.3):

```
SUMMARY moss image: 8 kernels, 8 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail; 5 controls: 5 red as planted, 0 missed
```

## Run a case

```sh
hf download OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Image-Base --revision 85975793d8b3d432f1b6e27f352abaa4c2a4c0d3 --local-dir MODEL_DIR
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py case MODEL_DIR case/ --prompt-file prompt.txt --device cuda
zig build install -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Dsm=121   # -Dsm=120 for an RTX 5090
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image MODEL_DIR/transformer case/case.safetensors case/
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py decode MODEL_DIR case/latents.f32 case/zig.png --device cuda
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py compare case/reference.png case/zig.png case/side.png
```

The case tool needs diffusers 0.38 or later: the checkpoint's decoder config names `decoder_block_out_channels`.

`tf-moss-image` gates each whole forward element by element against the case's float32 run, and
`tf-moss-image-blocks` gates each block alone against the farther of torch bf16's two runs, both as on Metal
([moss-image.md](moss-image.md), "Run a case"). The block cases measured below were made on a Mac by
`moss_image_case.py blocks` (torch on MPS and on the CPU); a block case runs the whole transformer in float32, which
does not fit an RTX 5090.

```sh
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image-blocks MODEL_DIR/transformer case/blocks-23-negative.safetensors
```

## Measured

Setup:

- The Metal doc's two cases, their prompts and seeds: a fox at 1024x1024 (4,096 image rows, 34 prompt rows, seed 42)
  and the card's Chinese sticky note at 1200x880 (4,125 image rows, 63 prompt rows, seed 7); the negative prompt has
  10 rows. Each case holds a float32 run of the same transformer at all 50 steps (`--fp32-steps 50`).
- Reference: the checkpoint's `pipeline_moss_image.py` on torch 2.11.0 (CUDA, bf16), diffusers 0.38.0, transformers
  5.12.1, on the same GB10.
- The card's defaults: 50 Euler steps, guidance 3.

Results on a DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, 121 GB unified memory, nvcc 13.2):

- **Velocity**, both branches of each of the 50 steps on the pipeline's own input:
  - Against torch bf16: cosine 0.99972 to 0.99998 (fox) and 0.99981 to 0.99998 (sticky note).
  - Against the float32 run, mean 1 - cosine: fox prompt 1.598e-4 (torch bf16's own 1.596e-4), negative 1.693e-4
    (1.707e-4); sticky note prompt 1.602e-4 (1.602e-4), negative 1.759e-4 (1.748e-4). Ours is the closer of the two at
    23 and 29 of the fox's 50 steps, 24 and 27 of the sticky note's.
- **Image:** our latents through the pipeline's decoder are 45.93 dB PSNR from the pipeline's own picture for the fox
  and 32.76 dB for the sticky note (its handwritten text the same; fine detail such as cabinet handles differs, as on
  Metal: 50 guided steps magnify bf16 rounding).
- **Repeat:** the same step twice, another between, gives identical bytes; two runs of a case give identical latents.
- **Speed**, the GPU otherwise idle, the median of a case's 100 forwards:
  - torch bf16: 1.402 s a forward for the fox, 1.477 s for the sticky note.
  - Ours: 0.690 s and 0.700 s, 2.03x and 2.11x torch's (69.6 s and 70.6 s for 50 guided steps). 0.2 s for both
    prompts' refiner once.

Results on an RTX 5090 (sm_120, 32 GB, driver 615.71, nvcc 13.3), on the same two cases (their inputs, torch bf16
velocities and float32 runs as recorded on the GB10):

- **Velocity:** against torch bf16, cosine 0.99967 to 0.99998 (fox) and 0.99978 to 0.99998 (sticky note). Against the
  float32 run, mean 1 - cosine: fox prompt 1.607e-4, negative 1.694e-4; sticky note prompt 1.612e-4, negative
  1.762e-4 (torch bf16's own as above). Ours is the closer at 23 and 21 of the fox's steps, 25 and 29 of the sticky
  note's.
- **Image:** 44.01 dB PSNR from the pipeline's picture for the fox, 34.51 dB for the sticky note. The latents differ
  from the GB10's in their low bits: cuBLASLt picks different GEMM kernels on each GPU.
- **Repeat:** identical bytes, as on the GB10.
- **Each block alone**, on the Metal doc's seven block cases (made on the Mac: torch bf16 on MPS and on the CPU): all
  305 gates pass, at a mean of 0.50 of the limit and at most 0.60, and a second run repeats the first byte for byte.
  At block 0 of the fox's step 1, negative branch, ours is 5.70e-6 from float32 in cosine error and 0.00960 in its
  worst row (the negative prompt's seventh row), as torch bf16 on the CPU is (6.58e-6, 0.00960); torch on MPS is
  2.28e-6 and 0.00687. Each of our operations there, run from our own inputs, matches torch's bf16 code to within the
  order of its sums; that row turns small rounding differences into larger ones, on torch's devices as on ours.
- **Each whole forward**, over each case's 100: our cosine error from float32 is 1.00 times torch bf16's on average
  for the fox (0.87 to 1.13) and 1.01 times for the sticky note (0.85 to 1.55); our worst row 1.01 times (0.34 to 1.63)
  and 1.02 times (0.66 to 1.98).
- **The teacher gate** (`tf-moss-image`, exit 1, its bound from the GB10's torch bf16 run) fails all 100 branch-steps
  of both cases, as on Metal ([moss-image.md](moss-image.md), Measured, where torch's own bf16 run on the CPU fails it
  too). Worst element over its bound, min / median / max: fox 161 / 432 / 2946, sticky note 115 / 459 / 7921. Two
  runs give identical latents.
- **Speed**, the GPU otherwise idle:
  - torch bf16 (torch 2.13.0, the pipeline's own forward on this card): 0.307 s a forward for the fox, 0.309 s for the
    sticky note.
  - Ours: 0.243 s and 0.245 s, 1.26x torch's (24.6 s and 24.8 s for 50 guided steps).
- **Memory:** the transformer's bf16 weights (9.5 GB) on the device, plus scratch sized at load for one image and the
  longest prompt: 0.51 GB at 1024x1024 with a 34-row prompt (from the allocations, not measured), and cuBLASLt's
  32 MiB workspace.
# MOSS-Image on Metal

MOSS-Image is a text-to-image model. A 5B joint transformer (42 blocks, hidden 3,072, 24 heads of 128, an MLP of
8,192 with the "situ" gate) denoises 128-channel latents by flow matching. `zig/src/families/moss_image` runs that
transformer on the Metal runtime from the released bf16 diffusers checkpoint:

- a prompt's rows once a prompt: the input projection and the two refiner blocks (bidirectional attention, biased
  projections, no modulation);
- the image and prompt rows together at each step: every joint block, one modulation from the timestep shared by all of
  them, full attention over both.

The card's guidance runs two passes a step: the prompt, and the empty negative prompt with block 22 skipped.

The prompt encoder, the checkpoint's Qwen3.5 text model, and the image decoder, FLUX.2's small VAE decoder, run on
Metal too (below): `tf-moss-image --prompt` makes both prompts' rows itself, and `tf-moss-image` turns the final latents
into the picture. `tools/zig/moss_image_case.py` runs the reference pipeline through the publisher's own
`pipeline_moss_image.py` in torch, a development reference.

It is a denoiser, not a token family. It does not register with the lane engine, the server or `families.detect`.

It runs on the M5 alone, the only chip it was checked on: `Model.load` and `Decoder.load` refuse a GPU without tensor
units.

The same transformer runs on CUDA too: [moss-image-cuda.md](moss-image-cuda.md).

## Checkpoint

`OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Image-Base` at `85975793d8b3d432f1b6e27f352abaa4c2a4c0d3`, Apache 2.0. `transformer/config.json`
must be `MOSSImageTransformer` at the released geometry, and `vae/config.json` `AutoencoderKLFlux2` at its released
decoder geometry. Any other config is refused, and so is a checkpoint with tensors this family does not read.

## Precision

- bf16 activations, rounded where the publisher's torch code rounds them: once per elementwise op, as torch's bf16
  tensors do.
- fp32 sums in every projection and in attention. Biased projections add the bias to the fp32 sums and round once, as
  a bf16 GEMM's bias epilogue does: their sums come from the prefill split-K GEMM (one part), then `mi_bias`.
- fp32 for norms, softmax and the time sinusoid's input (the sinusoid itself in float64, as the publisher computes it).
- The rotary tables in bf16, as the pipeline casts them; its frequencies are the checkpoint's `rope.bands`.
- No int8.

The decoder is float32 throughout, as the pipeline decodes: its weights as published (float32), fp32 sums in every
convolution and in its attention, GroupNorm's mean and variance in two fp32 passes, then the pipeline's own 8-bit
conversion (clamp, `* 0.5 + 0.5`, `* 255`, round to even). Its 3x3 convolutions run as Winograd F(2x2, 3x3)
(`md_wino`): the weights' transform G g G^T is computed in float64 at load and rounded once, the input's and the
output's transforms in fp32 in the kernel, 2.25x fewer products than a direct convolution. Its error stays the size
of a direct convolution's (see Measured). Like any Winograd convolution, an infinite input can come out NaN where a
direct one gives an infinity; the contract checks the classes against the Winograd formula's.

The bf16 projections are the Qwen-VL tower's `tfp::gemm_nax`. Attention is the prefill `tfp::attention_nax` template's
full (non-causal) form. The time MLP and both modulation projections run on the host, once a timestep.

## Prompt encoder

`encoder.zig` runs the checkpoint's `text_encoder/` (Qwen3.5's text model: 32 layers, three Gated DeltaNet layers to
each full-attention one, hidden 4,096) as the pipeline's `encode_prompt` does:

- the prompt in the pipeline's chat format (one user turn, then the assistant's turn with thinking on), cut at 4,096
  tokens;
- one causal forward;
- the final norm's rows.

The tokenizer is the native one on the checkpoint's `tokenizer/tokenizer.json`, and its ids equal the publisher's
tokenizer's on every prompt checked. The vision tower is not read.

Precision:

- bf16 weights as published and bf16 activations, rounded where the torch code rounds them;
- fp32 sums in every projection (the tower's `gemm_nax`), norm and attention;
- the DeltaNet's q, k, decay and state in fp32, its state a column a thread over the rows in order (the publisher's
  chunked algorithm computes the same recurrence);
- attention in fp32 throughout, the keys in order.

Its own kernels are in `moss_image_encoder.metal`:

- `me_norm`: the zero-centered RMSNorm;
- `me_head`: the head norms, the 64 rotated channels and the heads' layout;
- `me_attention`;
- `me_gate`;
- `me_silu_mul`;
- `me_conv`: the DeltaNet's 4-tap conv;
- `me_gdn_prep`;
- `me_gdn`: the recurrence;
- `me_gated_norm`.

The residual adds reuse `mi_gate_add`.

`tf-moss-image-encoder` checks a case from `moss_image_case.py encode`:

- the token ids;
- each step alone, every layer and the final norm, on the float32 run's input for that step rounded to bf16: its rows
  against float32 must be within twice torch bf16's distance on the same input (or plain bf16 rounding's, when
  larger) in cosine error and in its worst row;
- the whole prompt, every layer's rows against torch bf16's and the final rows against float32, reported but not
  gated: in bf16 the 32 layers magnify each implementation's rounding differently, so two correct runs part by more
  than any one step's error;
- a second encoding must repeat the first byte for byte.

It fails otherwise, and `reference.zig`'s tests check that a planted mismatch fails even when its repeat is identical.

## Kernel contract

`zig/tests/contract/metal_moss_image*.zig` registers every kernel of `moss_image.metal` and
`moss_image_encoder.metal`:

- `mi_norm`, plain and modulated, and `me_norm`;
- `mi_qk`, in both row layouts: q, k and v in three buffers, and packed in one row;
- `me_head` for q, k and v;
- `mi_situ`, in both layouts: hidden and gate halves of one row, and two buffers;
- `mi_gate_add` (in place), `mi_bias`, `me_gate`, `me_silu_mul`, `me_conv` and `me_gated_norm`;
- `me_gdn_prep` and `me_gdn`;
- the attentions: the transformer's three forms and `me_attention`.

The steps are checked output by output at the bf16 points the publisher's torch code rounds at. Each output must
lie in the range its fp32 steps allow, with Metal's error bounds for the `precise::` calls and fast-math division. Each
of 16 controls drops or adds one rounding point (the last adds bf16 rounding to the DeltaNet's state), and gate 3 must
catch each.

`me_gdn` is checked against the recurrence in float64. Each output's allowance is its two sums' rounding over the
state's magnitude, plus every earlier step's error: a decay and a projection by a unit key never grow it. The
attentions are checked against `attention_ref`'s float64 formula and bf16-P bound.

Gate 4:

- the attentions: equal scores over values whose sums reach about 2^22 and cancel;
- `me_gdn`: one-hot keys writing j, 2^20 and -2^20 to three state rows that its query sums back to j;
- `me_conv`: taps of 256, 1, 1 and -256 over rows that cancel to 2.

Gate 5 holds the 17 launches of the family's source and the two split-K projections.

`zig/tests/contract/metal_moss_image_decoder*.zig` registers every kernel of `moss_image_decoder.metal`:

- `md_unpack` (the latents' batch norm undone, the patches unpacked);
- `md_wino` (64 output channels a threadgroup) and `md_wino_32` (32, for 96 and 3 channels) in the forms the decoder
  launches: 3x3, 3x3 read nearest from half size, and 3x3 with a residual, against the float64 convolution through the
  exact transform, within a bound on the transformed terms' magnitude;
- `md_conv`, the 1x1 convolutions, with and without a residual;
- `md_norm`, with and without SiLU, and GroupNorm's statistics: `md_group_part` (plain and centered) and
  `md_group_finish`;
- `md_attention` and `md_pixels`.

Each fp32 step's output must lie in the range float32 allows about float64. Gate 4 uses integer channels, pixels or
values whose sums pass fp16's range and cancel. `md_pixels` is checked byte for byte against the same fp32 steps, with
every tie between two bytes among its inputs. Nine controls each break one kernel: a swapped patch axis, a 1x1's
inputs staged in half, a Winograd patch staged in half, a term dropped from its output transform, a SiLU in half,
both statistics kernels summing in half, the attention's rescale dropped, and the pixels' halves rounded up. Each is
caught at the gate it names. Gate 5 holds its nine launches.

`tf-kernel-contract --only "moss image"` on the M5 Ultra:

```
SUMMARY 37 kernels: 37 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail, 0 known findings; 25 controls: 25 red as planted, 0 missed; 0 limit problems
```

## Run a case

`moss_image_case.py` imports and runs the checkpoint's own `pipeline_moss_image.py`, the publisher's Python. It does so
only when the file's sha256 is the pinned revision's (`1dac1aca…8b31`) and refuses any other file.

```sh
hf download OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Image-Base --revision 85975793d8b3d432f1b6e27f352abaa4c2a4c0d3 --local-dir MODEL_DIR
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py case MODEL_DIR case/ --prompt-file prompt.txt   # needs torch, diffusers, transformers
zig build tf-moss-image -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image MODEL_DIR/transformer case/case.safetensors case/      # case/picture.png
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py compare case/reference.png case/picture.png case/side.png
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py exact MODEL_DIR case/      # the same schedule with a float32 transformer
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py exact MODEL_DIR case/ --fp32-encoder prompt.txt   # and a float32 encoder

# the prompt encoder alone, and a picture with it
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py encode MODEL_DIR enc/ --prompt-file prompt.txt
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image-encoder MODEL_DIR enc/encoder.safetensors prompt.txt
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py start MODEL_DIR pic/ --no-encoder --seed 42
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image MODEL_DIR/transformer pic/case.safetensors pic/ --prompt prompt.txt
```

The case holds:

- both prompts' encoder rows;
- the timesteps and noise levels;
- the starting latents;
- the publisher's pipeline's input and both velocities at every step;
- a float32 run of the same transformer at every step (`--fp32-steps N` keeps only the first N, which leaves the
  teacher gate below inconclusive).

`tf-moss-image` first runs both branches of each step on the pipeline's own input and compares the velocities with torch
bf16's (max |diff|, cosine, worst row) and with the case's float32 ones. The teacher gate checks every element: its
distance from float32 must be within twice the larger of torch bf16's own distance there and half a bf16 ULP at the
float32 value. A case without float32 velocities for both branches at every step is inconclusive (exit 2), and a step
run twice must repeat byte for byte. On this doc's cases the gate fails every step, as torch's own bf16 run on the CPU
does (see Measured); the bound's form is still being settled in #1529. It then runs the whole guided schedule from the
starting latents, times it, frees the transformer, and decodes the final latents with the checkpoint's `vae/` decoder
into `picture.png`. A case made by `start` holds only the prompts, the schedule and the noise; `tf-moss-image` then just
makes the picture. With `--prompt` (and `--negative`, else the empty negative prompt), it encodes both prompts natively
in place of the case's rows; `start --no-encoder` leaves them out of the case, and torch never loads the encoder.

To check the decoder alone against a float64 decode of the same latents:

```sh
# float64 on the CPU, and float32 on MPS as the pipeline decodes
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py vae MODEL_DIR case/latents.f32 case/decode.f64 case/torch.f32
zig build tf-moss-image-decoder -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image-decoder MODEL_DIR case/latents.f32 1024 1024 case/decode.f64 case/torch.f32 case/decoded.png
```

Ours must be within twice torch float32's distance from float64, in cosine error and in its worst row of pixels, and a
second decode must repeat the first byte for byte; it fails otherwise.

To gate one step's transformer block by block (as the encoder's are), from a `case`:

```sh
python3 tools/zig/moss_image_case.py blocks MODEL_DIR case/ --step 23 --branch negative
zig build tf-moss-image-blocks -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/bin/tf-moss-image-blocks MODEL_DIR/transformer case/blocks-23-negative.safetensors
```

The case tool runs that step's branch in float32, keeping the stream into each block and after the last, then in bf16
with every block and the final layer handed the float32 stream rounded to bf16, on the case's device and again on the
CPU. `Model.steps` runs ours the same way: the embedding, each block but the skipped one alone, and the final layer
alone. Each must be within twice torch bf16's distance from float32 (the farther of its two runs, or bf16 rounding's,
when larger), in cosine error and in its worst row, and a second run must repeat the first byte for byte; it fails
otherwise. Two torch runs set the limit because one device's bf16 can land well inside torch's own spread (see
Measured).

On MPS, which has no float64, the case tool computes the time sinusoid on the host in float64 and moves its float32
result to the GPU; every other step of the publisher's code runs unchanged.

`moss_image.noise` makes the starting latents natively, as the pipeline's `torch.randn` on a seeded CPU generator does.
torch's own bits depend on the CPU. x86 torch (AVX2 or AVX512) computes them with `avx_mathfun.h`'s log and sincos;
ARM torch (a Mac, a GB10) calls its libm instead. For seed 42 at 1024x1024, a Mac's latents differ from x86 torch's in
200,873 of 524,288 values, by at most 2.2e-6. The native generator matches x86 torch byte for byte on any CPU.
`moss_image_case.py noise` records sha256s of x86 torch's latents (torch 2.13.0) for 24 seeds and 9 sizes, and
`zig build test` checks them. A case made on a Mac holds the Mac's noise, not these.

`moss_image.schedule` computes the timesteps and noise levels from `scheduler/scheduler_config.json`, as the
pipeline's `MOSSImageScheduler` does: a float32 grid shifted by `shift`, snapped to the nearest of the
`num_train_timesteps` training levels (shifted by `training_shift`), with repeats dropped. It reads those three
settings. A config that turns on Karras, exponential or beta sigmas, dynamic shifting, `shift_terminal`, inverted
sigmas or stochastic sampling is refused: diffusers warns that it ignores them, but its base scheduler applies them.
`moss_image_case.py schedule` records sha256s of the scheduler's own timesteps and sigmas for 21 step counts (1 to 2000)
and 5 configs. torch gives the same bits on x86, a GB10 and a Mac, and `zig build test` checks all 105. The image size
does not enter, since the released config has no dynamic shifting.

## Measured

Setup:

- Mac Studio M5 Ultra 256 GB, macOS 27; this commit's `tf-moss-image`.
- The card's defaults: 50 Euler steps, guidance 3, the empty negative prompt skipping block 22.
- Reference: the checkpoint's `pipeline_moss_image.py` on torch 2.14.1 (MPS, bf16), diffusers 0.42.0, transformers
  5.21.0.
- Two cases: a fox at 1024x1024 (4,096 image rows, 34 prompt rows, seed 42), and the card's Chinese sticky-note prompt
  at 1200x880 (an odd 55 x 75 grid, 4,125 image rows, 63 prompt rows, seed 7). The negative prompt has 10 rows.

Results:

- **Velocity**, both branches of each of the 50 steps on the pipeline's own input:
  - Against torch bf16: cosine 0.99973 to 0.99998, worst at the last steps.
  - Against a float32 run of the same transformer on the same inputs (the second case, every step): mean 1 - cosine
    1.602e-4 for the prompt branch, as for torch bf16's own (1.602e-4); 1.735e-4 against torch's 1.715e-4 for the
    negative branch. Ours is the closer of the two at 25 and 27 of the 50 steps.
- **Each block alone** (`tf-moss-image-blocks`), on seven steps' branches: the fox's steps 1 and 25 and the sticky
  note's step 23, both branches each, and the sticky note's step 50, the prompt's. Each gives the embedding, every
  block but the skipped one and the final layer the float32 run's stream in bf16; torch bf16 ran each on MPS and on
  the CPU:
  - All 305 gates pass, at a mean of 0.50 of the limit and at most 0.50. Our worst row is 0.99 to 1.00 times the
    farther torch run's on average in each of the seven, and a second run repeats the first byte for byte.
  - torch's two runs are within 0.84 to 1.20 times each other in worst row, and 0.95 to 1.05 in cosine error, at all
    but one step: block 0 of the fox's step 1, negative branch, where the negative prompt's seventh row becomes a
    massive activation (one channel near 16,500). There torch on the CPU is 6.58e-6 from float32 in cosine error and
    0.00960 in that row; torch on MPS 2.28e-6 and 0.00687, and ours on Metal the same as MPS. A gate on one device's
    run alone would fail a result as close as the other device's.
  - A row planted 5% off in block 20's output, in the float32 stream and in both torch runs, fails at blocks 20 and
    21, with an identical repeat.
- **Each whole forward**, over each case's 100: our cosine error from float32 is 1.00 times torch bf16's on average
  for the fox (0.92 to 1.08) and 1.01 times for the sticky note (0.76 to 1.26); our worst row 1.01 times (0.64 to
  1.48) and 1.03 times (0.37 to 2.55). At the sticky note's step 23, negative branch, torch's own bf16 run on the CPU
  has a worst row 1.37 times its MPS run's (0.0664 and 0.0486) and ours 2.55 times (0.1238, row 313): the worst row
  of 42 bf16 blocks in a row moves by more than torch's own bf16 runs agree.
- **The teacher gate** (`tf-moss-image`, exit 1) fails all 100 branch-steps of both cases. Worst element over its
  bound, min / median / max: fox 146 / 509 / 7206, sticky note 168 / 435 / 6018. A step run twice repeats byte for
  byte. #2291's head without this commit gives the same latents and the same worst element at every step. At the
  sticky note's step 23, negative branch, ours is 0.0173 from float32 against a bound of 6.1e-5 there. torch's own
  bf16 run of that step on the CPU, scored against the same bound (from its MPS run), fails too:

  | step 23, negative branch, against float32 | worst error / bound | elements over the bound | median error / bound |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|
  | torch bf16, CPU | 353 | 16.6% | 0.50 |
  | ours, Metal | 284 | 22.3% | 0.50 |

  Each element's bound is twice the MPS run's own error at that element, so it is tight wherever MPS happened to
  round close to float32; any other bf16 run of 42 blocks, torch's on the CPU included, lands outside it at a sizeable
  share of the elements.
- **Image:** our latents through the pipeline's decoder are 48.52 dB PSNR from the pipeline's own picture for the fox
  and 28.93 dB for the sticky note. Fifty guided steps magnify bf16 rounding into different fine detail, so the ruler
  is a float32 run of the whole schedule. There are two rulers, over the same 8 cases (both prompts, 4 seeds each):
  - The transformer in float32 on torch's bf16 encoder rows: our picture is the closer in 6, at a mean of 32.3 dB PSNR
    against torch bf16's 31.4 dB. Those 8 ran on an earlier build of this family (0b69e127); this commit's latents are
    byte for byte its on the two cases above.
  - Everything in float32, the encoder too (`exact --fp32-encoder`): torch bf16's picture averages 32.5 dB, ours 31.2
    dB. Six cases are within 0.5 dB of each other or favor ours (fox seed 1 by 2.9 dB). Two sticky-note seeds favor
    torch's by 4.6 and 8.7 dB, where the schedule settled on different fine detail.
- **Repeat:** the same step run twice, another between, gives identical bytes.
- **Speed**, one session with no other GPU work:
  - torch bf16 on MPS: 0.744 s a forward for the fox, 0.760 s for the sticky note (the median of its 100).
  - Ours: 0.489 s and 0.486 s a forward, 1.52x and 1.56x torch's (the median of three runs of 50 guided steps;
    0.472 to 0.544 s over all six). 0.08 s for both prompts' refiner once.
- **Memory:** 11.3 GB peak process footprint (10.6 GiB), with the transformer's bf16 weights (9.5 GB) in shared Metal
  buffers.
- **Prompt encoder**, both the prompt and the empty negative prompt (10, 34 and 63 tokens):
  - Token ids: equal to the publisher's tokenizer's.
  - Each layer's rows against torch bf16's, given the same token ids: cosine 0.99974 or more, the worst at the last
    layers.
  - The final rows against a float32 run of the encoder, ours beside torch bf16's own:
    - cosine 0.999826 and worst row 0.0261 against 0.999806 and 0.0294 (empty);
    - 0.999931 and 0.0261 against 0.999934 and 0.0259 (fox);
    - 0.999926 and 0.0454 against 0.999938 and 0.0318 (sticky note).
  - Repeat: identical bytes.
  - `tf-moss-image-encoder`'s gates, all 33 steps on these three prompts and six more (31 to 75 tokens): each step's
    distance from float32 is a mean of 0.50 of its limit, torch bf16's own, and at most 0.65 (the fox's layer 13,
    worst row). A row planted 5% off at layer 20, in the float32 rows and torch's, fails there and at layer 21, its
    repeat identical.
  - The whole prompt in bf16 spreads by more than any step: on the 75-token prompt, torch's own runs (MPS or CPU,
    chunks of 8 to 64, or the recurrent form) end 0.86 to 4.97 times its default's cosine error from float32, and
    ours 1.82 times. Against float64, which float32 matches to four places, the sticky note's row 58 is 0.0153 to
    0.0320 across eight of those runs, and 0.0454 in ours.
  - Pictures with our encoder, against the all-float32 ruler over the same 8 cases: a mean of 31.13 dB. Our
    transformer on torch's encoder rows gives 31.20 dB, and each is the closer in 4 of 8. The fox, against the
    pipeline's own picture: 47.07 dB.
  - Speed, one session with no other GPU work: 0.054 to 0.067 s a prompt against torch MPS's 0.158 to 0.165 s
    (warm). Loading takes 0.6 s against 2.60 s.
- **Decoder**, on the transformer's final latents of both cases, against the publisher's decoder in float64 on the CPU:
  - Ours: max |diff| 8.9e-6 (fox) and 5.2e-6 (sticky note) before the clamp; 162 of 3,145,728 and 45 of 3,168,000
    8-bit values differ from float64's, each by 1.
  - torch's own float32 decode on MPS, in the same session: 155 and 34 values differ from float64's, each by 1 (the
    count moves between torch runs). Ours and torch's pictures differ by at most 1 (95.4 and 97.7 dB PSNR).
  - Speed, back to back in one session with no other GPU work, the median of three: ours 0.181 s and 0.188 s on the
    GPU; torch's warm float32 decode on MPS 0.186 s and 0.191 s. Ours loads in 0.3 to 0.4 s. Its scratch is five
    float32 picture tensors at the widest stage: 4.7 GB at peak at 1024x1024, after the transformer is freed, so
    `tf-moss-image` peaks at the transformer's 11.3 GB.
# Nanbeige4.3-33B, native Metal

This recipe covers text generation with [`Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B`](https://huggingface.co/Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B)
(model_type `llama`: a dense 33B Llama-architecture model, 512K context, thinking and tool calls in its chat template)
on the Metal engine, served from the bf16 release as published: no conversion, nothing lost. Nanbeige's own INT4
release, [`Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4), is served as
published too, read in place ([below](#the-int4-release-nanbeige43-33b-int4)). It was brought up on an M5 Ultra
(256 GB); other Macs are untested. The family admits only the checkpoints checked against Hugging Face, by the
geometry and weights their configs name (`qualified` in `zig/src/families/llama/config.zig`: Nanbeige4.3-33B and
Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4); another `llama` checkpoint is refused by name until it has been checked the same way. Prompts
run on Metal 4 tensor units, so it needs an M5 or later: M1 to M4 Macs are refused by name at load.

## Build and serve

```sh
hf download Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B --revision c1093c501cc6460427c0ac634db7223d0450c0ee \
  --local-dir models/nanbeige4.3-33b
zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native
zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=PATH_TO_XGRAMMAR_v0.2.8 -Dcpu=native   # structured output
LLAMA_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=150 zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve models/nanbeige4.3-33b --name nanbeige --port 8888 \
  --context 131072 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 8
# with Nanbeige4.1-3B drafting from its bf16 release (the same replies, faster: see Drafter below)
hf download Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.1-3B --revision 9c4555c37921c0982af8fffeee1e0a6e6b953c4f --local-dir models/nanbeige4.1-3b
LLAMA_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=150 zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve models/nanbeige4.3-33b --name nanbeige --port 8888 \
  --context 131072 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 8 --drafter models/nanbeige4.1-3b
```

`LLAMA_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` caps weights, scratch and caches together (75% of RAM when unset). The weights take 61.7 GiB; a
stream's caches take 208 KiB a position (every one of the 52 layers keeps bf16 keys and values), so a 131,072-token
stream holds 26 GiB and the full 524,288-token context 104 GiB: 150 GB holds two 131,072-token streams, or one of
262,144; the whole context needs a Mac with the weights and 104 GiB free (192 GB, the 75% default on a 256 GB Mac,
holds one 524,288-token stream). Thinking is on by default, as in the chat template; a request sends
`"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}` to turn it off. The server forwards only the thinking switch to
the template: earlier turns' reasoning stays out of the prompt (the template's `preserve_thinking` default) and tool
calls take the template's XML form (its `tool_call_format` default), which the server parses.

## What the family is

`zig/src/families/llama/` follows the Spark-X2.6 Metal family, with HF's `modeling_llama` as the reference:

- The reference's rounding points, its PyTorch code in bf16: the residual stays bf16 and each add rounds to it; the
  norm is `bf16(w * bf16(x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)))` with the mean in fp32; RoPE is `bf16(bf16(x * c) + bf16(o * s))`
  with the fp32 angle's cos and sin rounded to bf16 as HF rounds them, pairs (d, d + 64); the MLP is
  `bf16(bf16(silu(g)) * u)` (`kernels/metal/llama/glue.metal`).
- Projections over the release's bf16 rows, read in place from the mapped shards (no copies, no stacking): prompt
  chunks of up to 2,048 rows on `gemm_nax`'s tensor-unit GEMM (`gemm.metal`); decode windows on `ll_matvec`, a
  simdgroup an output row, fp32 sums rounded once as torch's bf16 linear rounds them. q, k and v write side by side
  into one row, gate and up into another.
- Attention: prompt chunks on the tensor units (Gemma 4's prompt attention over a position-major cache,
  `attention_nax.metal`); decode rows on sdpa_vector lanes over key blocks at absolute positions, so a row's bits
  never depend on the rows beside it.
- The lane host's shared rounds, a lone stream's steps drawn on the GPU a step ahead (argmax, or `tf_sample_full`),
  copy drafts and the prompt cache.
- `--drafter`: a smaller Llama on the same tokenizer (`drafter.zig`) as the lane core's priced copy proposer, its
  drafts verified by the model's windows like any copy, so replies keep the model's bits.

Every kernel is registered with the kernel contract (`zig/tests/contract/metal_llama*.zig`, the roll call in
`contracts.zig`): the glue, the six row-projection forms, the four GEMM forms, the prompt attention at both served
geometries, and the INT4 release's six row-projection forms and its dequantization. Each kernel group has a planted
control (`metal_llama_controls.zig`: one edit of its source, which its gate must report). `tf-kernel-contract --only
llama` on the M5 Ultra:

```
SUMMARY 28 kernels: 28 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail, 0 known findings; 14 controls: 14 red as planted, 0 missed; 0 limit problems; gates 611490 ms, limits 163 ms
```

## Measured (M5 Ultra, the bf16 release, 26 Oct 2026)

Against Hugging Face's `modeling_llama` on the release (transformers 4.57.1, bf16 on the CPU): 1,500 positions
teacher-forced, mean KL 0.0015, top-1 99.1%; 64 positions after a 9,000-token prompt, mean KL 0.0013, top-1 100%. Six
greedy chats of 64 tokens (code, prose, Chinese, a document, with and without thinking): three equal HF's token for
token; the other three part at a position where the engine's two best logits are the same bf16 value. One-row steps
and windows of 7 or 16 rows give the same logits bit for bit after prompts of 64 and 1,500 tokens.

`tools/zig/llama_teacher_judge.py` judges every teacher-forced position by the repository's near-tie rule
(`qwen27_margins.py`: the same two contenders on both sides, each margin within one bf16 step) and exits 1 on anything
else. Against HF's bf16 run, 13 of the 1,500 positions differ and two are red: at 425 and 1370 three tokens sit within
one bf16 step, so the two sides' contenders differ. `tools/zig/llama_f64_reference.py` runs the release in float64
(its bf16 weights cast up exactly, HF's arithmetic, one rounding at the end) and settles them:

- Against the float64 pass, the engine passes the rule: 1,483 of 1,500 positions equal, all 17 differences near-ties.
  HF's bf16 run does not: 1,488 equal, and at 425 it rounds two contenders a step high (red).
- At 1370 the exact logits are `it` 388 38.1266, `no` 754 38.1037 and `the` 269 38.0106: within 0.116 of each other,
  under half a bf16 step (0.25 at 32-64). 388 lies 0.0016 above the rounding midpoint 38.125, so rounded once it is
  38.25 and the others 38.0. HF's bf16 run gives 754 a step too high (38.25); the engine gives 388 a step too low
  (38.0).
- Layer by layer at 1370 (the engine's forward stopped after each layer count by a local probe, not in this PR; HF's
  `output_hidden_states`), the engine's residual and HF's drift from the float64 one alike (0.3% after the first layer,
  1.8% after the 51st; 0.80% and 0.82% on average over the layers). The engine's largest excess, 1.5-1.7 times HF's at
  layers 20-22, is channel 4086, a massive activation near 427 where a bf16 step is 2: both hold 430 after layer 19,
  and at layer 20 HF's add lands on 428 while the engine's stays at 430.

  (auto, required, named, thinking, streamed) 5/5; seeded sampling repeats 9/9.

  alone; streaming 4/4, multi-turn recall 8/8, stop strings 3/3, thinking 10/10, max_tokens 3/3.
