## Performance options

Each keeps the replies' bits.

- **Streams (`--parallel`).** One stream decodes at 16.4 tokens/s, bound by reading the weights each step; two give
  28-32 tokens/s in all (66 ms a round against 61), each reply equal to its run alone. The row kernel holds up to 32
  rows a launch; the caches set the count (26 GiB a 131,072-token stream).
- **Context and memory (`--context`, `LLAMA_LOAD_LIMIT_GB`).** 208 KiB a token. Cold prompts run 1.1-1.3k tokens/s
  to 33k tokens, 866 at 61k and 563 at 131k (attention grows with the prompt).
- **Prompt cache (`--prompt-cache-gib`).** A resumed turn starts in 0.34 s against 4.5 s cold; kept states give way to
  streams that need the room.
- **Copy drafts.** On from the lane core, replies equal to drafts off; they accepted 0-30% of their tokens on the
  harness's prompts and gave no measurable decode gain (drafted 16 tokens/s, undrafted 16).
- **Sampling.** Draws run `tf_sample_full` over the whole 166,912-token vocabulary (the 1,024-candidate kernel is
  compiled for a 131,072-token vocabulary): sampled replies decode at the greedy speed.
- **Weights.** The bf16 release, or Nanbeige's own INT4 release as published (decode 2.6 times as fast; its
  quantization's cost is the publisher's, measured [below](#the-int4-release-nanbeige43-33b-int4)). The engine makes
  no quantized conversion of its own.
- **Not offered.** No int8 or fp8 cache, no fast-math, no reduced-precision sums.

## Drafter: Nanbeige4.1-3B

[`Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.1-3B`](https://huggingface.co/Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.1-3B) (revision
`9c4555c37921c0982af8fffeee1e0a6e6b953c4f`, Apache-2.0; model_type `llama`, 32 layers, hidden 2,560, 20 query and 4 key
heads of 128) shares the 33B's tokenizer: the same 166,100 ids, merges and added tokens, the same bos and eos (its
`vocab_size` pads to 166,144, the 33B's to 166,912). The family admits it as a drafter only, served from its bf16
release as published (7.33 GiB), so the plain `--drafter <dir>` serves it: `--drafter-bits` (which picks Qwen's
DFlash width) is not read for Llama, as for Gemma 4, and quantized drafter checkpoints are refused by name.

- **The proposer.** `--drafter` loads the smaller Llama on the served model's queue and registers it as the lane
  host's copy proposer (`LaneHost.proposers`), priced, so a round takes its drafts as given. The model's window
  verifies them row by row and keeps the prefix its own draws agree with, as it keeps any copy draft: replies are the
  model's whatever the drafter says.
- **One budget.** The streams' caches and the drafter's (64 KiB a token) share one ledger (`budget.Ledger`). A
  stream's admission (`budget.admitStream`) checks its peak first (its caches and its drafter cache's growth, the old
  state's copy included), trims the kept prompt states to what that peak leaves, and only then allocates; a freed
  drafter cache keeps its tokens for the next request sharing its prefix, counted, and gives way first.
- **Drafting.** Before each round the drafter's cache is synced to the stream's context by their longest common
  prefix, the new tokens are fed, and the drafts are greedy steps chained on the GPU. The depth comes from measured
  rates: the stream's decayed acceptance, a chained step's time (8.5-8.9 ms) and a line fitted to the round's time by
  its window's rows. With several streams in a round, each stream drafts the depth with the most tokens a millisecond
  for the whole round (`pricing.depthShared`), nothing only when drafting costs the round more than it lands.

Checked with `tf-llama-run <33B> <tokens> draft <drafter>,<n>`, which decodes greedily through the drafter's windows:
on eight chat prompts (128 tokens, thinking on and off) and after a 1,500-token prompt (256 tokens), the drafted
tokens equal the plain greedy tokens exactly (28 Oct 2026, one model process on the Mac):

| prompt | plain | drafted | tokens a round | drafts kept |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Fibonacci function, thinking off | 15.8 tok/s | 40.7 | 4.54 | 99 of 127 |
| Fibonacci function, thinking on | 15.8 | 22.0 | 1.81 | 57 of 142 |
| why the sky is blue, thinking off | 15.8 | 26.8 | 2.44 | 75 of 151 |
| why the sky is blue, thinking on | 15.9 | 22.8 | 1.88 | 60 of 125 |
| Hangzhou in two sentences (Chinese), thinking off | 15.9 | 21.1 | 1.73 | 54 of 137 |
| Hangzhou in two sentences (Chinese), thinking on | 15.9 | 24.1 | 2.02 | 64 of 130 |
| 9.11 or 9.8, thinking off | 15.8 | 31.1 | 3.31 | 90 of 167 |
| 9.11 or 9.8, thinking on | 15.8 | 25.9 | 2.42 | 75 of 158 |
| 1,500 tokens of Python's json docs, 256 tokens | 16.1 | 27.8 | 2.68 | 160 of 332 |

Served (`--context 32768 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 8 --drafter ... --drafter-bits 0`, fresh servers): eight new
prompts sent two at a time (greedy, 256 tokens, thinking off) decode together at 30.1-40.9 tokens/s (36.1 on average)
against 26.6-30.1 (29.0) without `--drafter`, every reply's token ids equal to the undrafted one. Streams joining,
leaving, queued, refused (HTTP 400) and cancelled each return the token ids of their plain solo run, and a reply alone
after a cancel is unchanged; in rounds shared from the first token to the last, 199 drafts were offered and 125 kept.
The drafter's cache is fed the prompt on the first round, after the model's own prompt pass, so the first token keeps
its time.

## The INT4 release: Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4

[`Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4) (revision
`d834b414cf1c47e42640de33c147b7cf8a9321ef`, Apache-2.0) is Nanbeige's own int4 release of the same model, the
tokenizer files identical to the bf16 release's: a compressed-tensors `pack-quantized` checkpoint, asymmetric int4
weights in groups of 32 along each row with a bf16 scale and a zero point each (packed as 4-bit codes, `zp_dtype`
int8), `lm_head` and the embedding left in bf16; 21.0 GiB. The family serves it as published, read in place from the
mapped shards:

```sh
hf download Nanbeige/Nanbeige4.3-33B-INT4 --revision d834b414cf1c47e42640de33c147b7cf8a9321ef \
  --local-dir models/nanbeige4.3-33b-int4
LLAMA_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=150 zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve models/nanbeige4.3-33b-int4 --name nanbeige \
  --port 8888 --context 131072 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 8 --drafter models/nanbeige4.1-3b
```

- **Admission.** Exactly that scheme is read (`config.zig`'s `packQuantized`: format, 4 bits, asymmetric, groups of
  32, int8 zero points, every Linear but the head and embedding, no activation or cache scheme, no activation
order); any other
  compressed-tensors or MLX quantization is refused by name. Each projection's `weight_shape` must match the config,
  and its packed words, scales and zero points their extents.
- **The weights it means.** compressed-tensors decompresses a weight as `bf16((q - z) * scale)`: the code and zero
  point are exact small integers and their difference times the bf16 scale is rounded once to bf16
  (compressed-tensors 0.20.1's `dequantize`). The kernels compute that same bf16 value, so the model the engine runs
  is the checkpoint's own bf16 model, with the bf16 release's rounding points everywhere else.
- **Decode windows** (up to 32 rows) run `ll_q4_matvec`: a simdgroup an output row, a lane a group of 32 codes,
  each weight made as above and multiplied in fp32, the row's sum rounded once as torch's bf16 linear rounds it.
  One-row steps and 16-row windows give the same logits bit for bit after a 1,500-token prompt (0 of 49 rows differ;
  the planted row is reported).
- **Prompt chunks** first make the projection's bf16 weights in a scratch (`ll_q4_dequant`, a thread a packed word),
  then run the bf16 release's tensor-unit GEMM over them, so a prompt's arithmetic is the bf16 path's on these weights
  (the scratch holds the widest projection, 301 MiB).

Against `llama_f64_reference.py`, which now reads the same checkpoint (its weights decompressed exactly as above,
then float64 throughout, rounded once at the end), over 1,500 teacher-forced positions of a chat asking for a summary
of TensorFold's README (31 Oct 2026, M5 Ultra):

| logits from | mean KL against float64 | top-1 agreement | positions equal | not near-ties by the judge's rule |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| the engine, this checkpoint | 0.0044 | 97.1% | 1,456 | 16 |
| HF transformers 4.57.1, this checkpoint, bf16 on the CPU | 0.0346 | 96.6% | 1,449 | 22 |
| the engine, the bf16 release (against its float64 pass) | 0.0110 | 97.1% | 1,457 | 21 |
| HF transformers, the bf16 release (against its float64 pass) | 0.0234 | 96.5% | 1,447 | 28 |

On this text the judge's strict rule (`llama_teacher_judge.py`: the same two contenders on both sides, each within one
bf16 step) fails every implementation, Hugging Face's included; the engine is the closest to the float64 pass on
both checkpoints. Against HF's own run of this checkpoint, the engine's mean KL is 0.0275 (top-1 96.5%).

**What the release's quantization costs** (the publisher's choice, not the engine's): on the same 1,500 positions,
HF's run of the INT4 release against HF's run of the bf16 release gives mean KL 0.082 and top-1 90.8%, and the
engine's INT4 against HF's bf16 gives 0.087 and 90.8%. The bf16 release stays the exact choice; the INT4 release is
the faster one with its own maker's quantization.

Served through the recipe harness (31 Oct 2026, this branch's build, an idle 4 GB server of another model the only
other one loaded), `--context 131072 --parallel 2 --prompt-cache-gib 8`, greedy 256-token replies:

| | streams | prose | code | structured | list | first token | a round |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| undrafted | 1 | 42.8 | 42.0 | 42.9 | 41.4 | 0.27-0.30 s | 23.8 ms |
| undrafted | 2 | 74.6 | 53.4 | 66.6 | 74.7 | 0.41-0.45 s | 30.4 ms |
| `--drafter` | 1 | 79.4 | 79.6 | 81.0 | 80.5 | 0.27-0.31 s | 24.8 ms, 1.98 tokens |
| `--drafter` | 2 | 74.4 | 74.6 | 73.7 | 74.8 | 0.41-0.46 s | 27.8 ms |

Tokens a second, all streams together: 2.5-2.6 times the bf16 release's one stream undrafted. One stream reads the
21 GiB of weights each step. The ruler's texts repeat themselves, which the drafter continues (92% of drafts kept); on
ordinary chats, where the 33B's step is already short beside the drafter's (24 ms against 11), it about breaks even:
`tf-llama-run ... draft` on the Drafter section's eight chat prompts (128 tokens, thinking on and off) decodes at
35.6-44.5 tokens/s drafted against 37.9-41.8 plain (40.5 and 40.7 on average), the drafted tokens equal to the plain
ones on all eight; the suite's drafted check gives 42 against 39. With two streams the shared rounds mostly run
undrafted, at the plain speed.

| cold prompt | 2,109 | 8,254 | 32,829 | 61,501 tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tokens a second | 1,185 | 1,257 | 1,041 | 846 |
| time to first token | 1.78 s | 6.57 s | 31.6 s | 72.7 s |

A fresh server, undrafted, each prompt starting with words no earlier one did; with thinking on within 4%. With the
drafter loaded the same prompts ran 6-8% slower (thinking on, 4-15%), though the drafter reads the prompt only after
the model's first token; an earlier run of the same INT4 code on the previous base was within 4% of undrafted. Prompt
chunks make each projection's bf16 weights before the GEMM: against the bf16 release's prompt numbers above, 4-6%
slower at 2k-8k tokens and 2-3% at 33k-61k. A multi-turn chat's third turn, resumed from
5,493 of its 5,649 kept tokens, starts in 0.39 s against 4.6 s cold, with the same reply.

- A passphrase at 10%, 50% and 90% of a 128,579-token prompt comes back exactly (3/3, greedy, thinking off) on the
  131,072-token server with the drafter; the cold prompt takes 254 s to the first token (506 tokens/s). The drafter
  reads the prompt only after that first token, so on such a prompt the rest of the reply waits for it: 9-10-token
  replies took 33-47 s after their first token.
- Both servers pass the harness's quick plan in full: structured output 18/18 with drafted == plain 12/12, tool calls
  5/5, seeded sampling 9/9 equal on repeat and undrafted, resumed turns equal to cold ones after a restart, a 60-turn
  soak and 12 concurrent replies each equal to the request alone, streaming 4/4, multi-turn recall 8/8, stop strings
  3/3, thinking 10/10, max_tokens 3/3.

## Not done

No quality suite was run. The family has no draft head of its own: drafts come from `--drafter`'s smaller Llama or
the lane core's copies. Quantized drafters are refused by name: the drafter is served from its bf16 release.
Logprobs are refused by name: the release's tokenizer decodes through a `Strip` step, which the engine's tokenizer does
not count as token-local, so the server cannot give a token's bytes on its own.
The INT4 release was run to the 131,072-token window, not the full 524,288. After a long prompt the drafter reads
it before drafting, which holds the reply's second token (30-47 s at 110k-129k tokens with the INT4 release). Only
the M5's tensor units were checked; M1-M4 Macs are refused at load, and smaller RAM is untested. Other `llama`
checkpoints, tied heads, other head sizes, Llama 3's scaled RoPE and biased projections are refused at load rather
than served untested.

(`d834b414cf1c47e42640de33c147b7cf8a9321ef`).
# Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B (`nemotron_h_omni`) runs on the native CUDA engine from NVIDIA's NVFP4
checkpoint, on one GB10 or split over two. The text model is Nemotron-H with a latent MoE: 88 blocks (40 Mamba-2,
8 attention, 40 MoE), 512 routed experts with 22 picked a token, each reading and writing a 1,024-wide latent between
two bf16 projections, a shared expert on the hidden rows, and one MTP layer. The family is
`zig/src/families/nemotron/` (the latent MoE in `cuda_latent.zig`); images go through the checkpoint's RADIO tower,
described in [vision](../vision.md#nemotron-35-super-vl-on-cuda).

## Checkpoint

`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4` at revision `82d93699acd3be9e4617c53360fe5b3f5dbeb1b3`
(75.1 GB). Its ModelOpt export stores the experts in NVFP4 (e2m1 codes, an e4m3 scale every 16 inputs, one fp32 scale
an expert), the Mamba, attention and output-head projections in FP8 with static input scales, and the router, latent
projections, embeddings and the MTP layer's attention in bf16. The engine reads these tensors as stored; nothing is
converted ahead of time.

## Run on one GB10

```bash
tensorfold serve /models/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 --name super --vision
```

The weights take 70.8 GiB of the GB10's memory (73.2 GiB with the image tower and its rows). At the default
16,384-token window the server admits 8 streams at 0.35 GiB each and keeps a prompt cache of about 8 to 10 GiB, and
about 24 GB of the GB10's memory stays available. Leave the other ranks' variables below unset.

A [community recipe](https://github.com/plotarmordev/Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-Single-DGX-Spark-TensorFold/tree/72ef12b05b0b3d839ff973ff624e8410859dfb8c)
from @plotarmordev sets this up on stock v1.1.3: it downloads the release, checks it and the checkpoint against pinned
sha256 sums, and has start and stop scripts and smoke and benchmark clients.

The MTP draft head can use the embedded draft vocabulary's FP8 output rows or the already-resident full output head.
A stream drafts on the subset while the last 16 tokens of its context, its prompt's tail at first, are all draft ids,
and on the full head otherwise; other streams do not change its choice. Each head has its own captured graphs and
its own measured level cost beside the window costs both share, and shared rounds are priced at the full head's.
The target still verifies proposals with its unchanged full-vocabulary head.
For CUDA MTP streams, `--mtp-drafts` caps MTP depth (at most 31 for Super) and `--mtp-confidence` sets a
cumulative-confidence threshold from 0 to 1 instead of the cost-based cutoff. A zero draft cap disables
drafting. The same controls apply in lone and shared rounds, including resumes and handoff.
Positive MTP caps leave copied continuations and Recall on their existing row limits.

## Run on two GB10s

Use NCCL 2.30.7 or newer, the tested minimum for this setup. The runtime refuses versions below 2.30.0;
2.28.9 can deadlock during startup window-cost timing (#1060).

Rank 0 runs the whole model and serves; rank 1 holds only its share of every MoE layer's experts (the MTP layer's
too) and computes it for rank 0's jobs. The ranks meet over NCCL, which the engine opens at run time from the system
(`libnccl.so.2` on the library path); start rank 1 first, with the same binary and checkpoint on both hosts:

```bash
# on rank 1
TF_NEMOTRON_RANK=1 TF_NEMOTRON_WORLD=2 NCCL_COMM_ID=192.0.2.1:29741 \
  tensorfold serve /models/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4
# on rank 0 (192.0.2.1)
TF_NEMOTRON_RANK=0 TF_NEMOTRON_WORLD=2 NCCL_COMM_ID=192.0.2.1:29741 \
  tensorfold serve /models/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 --name super --vision --host 0.0.0.0
```

Set `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` and `NCCL_IB_HCA` for the link between the hosts as NCCL documents them. Rank 1 keeps a TCP
line to rank 0 on the port after `NCCL_COMM_ID`'s (29742 here), opened before NCCL. Before any weight loads, both ranks
check that they run the same build, model, cut and precision and the same checkpoint layout: config.json, the index,
and each shard's name, size and header. While the weights load, each rank reads and hashes every byte of every shard
it holds (sha256), and checks each file against its Hugging Face blob name, which is its sha256, when the folder is a
Hugging Face snapshot. The ranks exchange those digests before rank 0 serves, so a copy that differs anywhere, by one
bit, stops both ranks before serving, naming it. A GB10 hashes the 70 GiB checkpoint in about 22 s, at the same time as
it loads its weights. If either rank fails, it sends its error's name and the other stops with it; if either process
dies, the other stops within about a second instead of waiting; rank 1 leaves when rank 0's server stops.
Rank 0 takes 40.1 GiB (42.2 GiB with the tower) and rank 1 31.4 GiB. One prompt pass runs at a time at TP=2
(`--segments` above 1 is refused).

## How the experts split

Every expert's width is cut into two shares. A rank sums the shares it holds in share order and the ranks meet in
rank order, so one GB10 and two give the same bits: on the eight release prompts, all 17 replies (greedy, seeded
sampled and one with thinking) were the same tokens at TP=1 and TP=2. A routed pick carries its share in its pair id,
so one grouped launch serves every share a rank holds.

Passes of up to a verify window's rows read shared-expert plans built when the buffers load, one per row count;
longer prompt passes and the other rank's jobs plan the shared expert at their own row count.
On one GPU those passes run the shared expert on the side stream while the router and routed experts run on the main
stream: its activations, quantized rows and plan are its own, and events order its input and the final sum.

## Precision

On Blackwell the engine runs the checkpoint's own math by default (`--precision checkpoint`): e4m3 rows into the FP8
layers and NVFP4 rows into the NVFP4 experts, on the FP8 and block-scaled FP4 tensor cores. `--precision full` keeps
bf16 rows throughout (W4A16 and W8A16). Each is exact on its own terms; they give different tokens from each other.
On one GB10, `checkpoint` teacher-forced on `full`'s greedy 256 tokens after three prompts:

| Prompt | Mean KL(full \|\| checkpoint), nats | Same top token | NLL of the fed tokens, full to checkpoint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Python code | 0.0036 | 255 of 256 | 0.0480 to 0.0482 |
| Long prose | 0.0137 | 246 of 256 | 0.1416 to 0.1514 |
| Repetition | 0.0057 | 255 of 256 | 0.0179 to 0.0252 |
| All 768 tokens | 0.0077 | 98.4% | 0.0692 to 0.0749 |

`checkpoint` read a cold 8,192-token prompt in 4.41 s against `full`'s 7.96 s (1.81x; 1.82x at 2,048 tokens) and
decodes at about the same speed. The [quantization guide](../quantization.md#nvidias-nvfp4-checkpoints-on-cuda)
describes both modes. Both ranks of a two-GB10 setup must run the same precision; they check it before loading.

Checkpoint prompt passes of 128 rows or more run the FP8 layers in 128-row tiles (128 columns where K slices meet in
a cluster) and the NVFP4 experts in blocks of 128 pairs of one expert by 128 columns, their inputs and weights staged
through shared memory; decode keeps its narrow tiles. The per-row MMA steps, split-K summation order and output
rounding are unchanged. The prompt up kernel quantizes its relu^2 rows to down's NVFP4 input in its epilogue, the same
bytes the decode path's bf16 rows and separate quantizer give. On one GPU the prompt down kernel runs both expert width
shares of a pair and adds them in share order before the bf16 rounding the combine applies, so the combine reads one
bf16 row a pick instead of two fp32 rows. `tf-cuda-test checkpoint` compares the prompt kernels and the combine after
them with the decode path byte for byte on synthetic inputs.

Router logits of passes over 32 rows run on 128-row by 128-expert register tiles, each logit still one fma chain over
its slice in input order; `tf-cuda-test glue` compares them with the untiled router and the host reference.

## Exactness and speed

Served on GB10s at a 16,384-token window, the eight release prompts at 256 tokens each, every cell held in both
precisions: drafted replies equal `"draft": false` (greedy, seeded sampled, thinking on), 2 and 4 concurrent streams
equal their solo runs, and three-turn chats with regenerate, edit and delete equal a cache-off server's replies.

| Setup | Precision | MTP drafts (greedy, mean of 8 prompts) | `"draft": false` | Cold 8,192-token prompt |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One GB10 | `checkpoint` (default) | 38.2 tok/s (29.8 to 49.0) | 18.8 tok/s | 4.41 s |
| One GB10 | `full` | 38.7 tok/s (30.2 to 50.8) | 19.4 tok/s | 7.96 s |
| Two GB10s | `checkpoint` (default) | 46.8 tok/s (35.9 to 63.6) | 20.2 tok/s | |
| Two GB10s | `full` | 48.1 tok/s (36.4 to 65.6) | 21.4 tok/s | |

Four concurrent greedy streams on two GB10s took 6.2 s together against 11.8 s one at a time.

## Images

`--vision` loads the checkpoint's RADIO tower and projector (see [vision](../vision.md#nemotron-35-super-vl-on-cuda)).
Super VL's `--vision-image-tokens` defaults to 13,312, so up to four images keep the size NVIDIA's processor gives
them (at most 3,328 tokens each); the flag given explicitly still sets the budget. One request with four full-size
pictures (3000 x 1340, 13,124 prompt tokens) on one GB10 answered its first token in 11.45 s, its drafted reply
equal to `"draft": false`, with device memory at 74.4 GiB and 22.9 GB of the GB10 still available. Four full-size
images take most of the default 16,384-token window, so raise `--context` for long replies after them.

## Not served yet

- `--slide` is refused for this checkpoint, and `--learn-conversations` keeps nothing on disk for it yet (its prompt
  cache stays in memory).
- Video and audio parts are refused; the checkpoint's video embedder and sound encoder stay unloaded.
# Nemotron 3.5 Lightning

The model combines Mamba-2, attention and MoE blocks. The native family is `zig/src/families/nemotron/`, on Metal
and CUDA; the native prompt reuse, routed experts and shared rounds sections below describe it, and the
[README](../../README.md#qualified-models) lists its qualified checkpoints and hardware.

The MLX execution, CUDA, draft vocabulary and measurements sections describe the Python engine,
frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the [`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Its MLX family
is [`src/tensorfold/families/nemotron_h/`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/families/nemotron_h),
with Metal kernels in
[`src/tensorfold/kernels/nemotron/lightning/v1/`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/kernels/nemotron/lightning/v1).

## Run

```bash
tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit
tensorfold serve TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit --name bench
```

The checkpoint includes `mtp-4bit.safetensors`; `pull` and `serve` check that it is available.
`--no-drafts` or request field `"draft": false` selects serial decoding. In the Python engine, MLX supports affine 4-bit
projections and experts in groups of 32 or 64; unsupported formats are refused before weight downloads
and checked again at load. CUDA supports the named 4-bit/group-64 checkpoint. The native engine serves the named
checkpoint on Metal and CUDA, and NVIDIA's NVFP4 export on CUDA.

On Metal the native engine also serves MLX checkpoints at a width per module (2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 8 bits, not 7, in groups
of 32, 64 or 128), such as `TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-oQ4`, `-oQ6` and `-oQ8`, the three
measured. A matrix at 4-bit in groups of 64 runs on the kernels above. Any other width runs on the shared row kernels in
decode. In prompt chunks past 128 rows, dense matrices in groups of 64 run on tiled kernels and the routed experts on
width-general gathers; dense matrices in other groups stay on the row kernels. These checkpoints carry no MTP head. Copy
`mtp-4bit.safetensors` from the 4-bit checkpoint into the folder to draft; without it each round decodes one token. With
the head on an M3 Ultra, greedy prose decodes at 162 tok/s with oQ4, 117 with oQ6 and 111 with oQ8, against 188 with the
4-bit checkpoint, and prompts of 8,192 to 32,768 tokens read at 0.96x to 0.99x mlx_lm's rate on the same checkpoint; a
server's first 2,048-token prompt after it starts reads at 0.78x to 0.90x. For MLX affine checkpoints, CUDA, the Intel
GPU engine and `--slide` refuse widths other than 4-bit group 64 and name the first such module.

## MLX execution and exactness

This section describes the Python 0.6.6 engine's MLX family.

The lane engine verifies MTP drafts and context copies. TensorFold projections use tensor-unit kernels
where available and row-exact kernels elsewhere. Fused routing, Mamba updates and expert kernels keep
serial and window arithmetic consistent. Drafting depends on the load-time row check, not an MLX downgrade.

Rollback retains the accepted Mamba convolution and recurrent states and trims attention caches.
Alternating KV buffers let pipelined decode avoid overwriting state still read by the preceding step.
The lane engine can combine requests after load-time shared-forward checks. Prompt chunks start at
detected assistant-message boundaries and the second message at least 256 tokens after the previous
chunk start, or after 2,048 tokens when no earlier boundary qualifies. Prefix reuse starts only at these
cuts, so cold and resumed prompts use the same chunks; templates without markers use 2,048-token chunks.

## CUDA

This section describes the Python 0.6.6 engine's CUDA family; its `--tp`, `--rank`, `--master` and `--prefill-fp8`
flags are that engine's. The native binary refuses `--tp` above 1 for Nemotron by name, since its CUDA family has
no tensor-parallel ranks, and refuses `--prefill-fp8`. The native CUDA build serves Nemotron on one GPU, from
the MLX 4-bit checkpoint or NVIDIA's NVFP4 export, with concurrent requests sharing each round, and its own
`--mtp-drafts` (at most 15 for this model) and `--mtp-confidence` set MTP drafts in lone and shared rounds; see the
[native CUDA runbook](../../RUNBOOK.md#linux-and-cuda).

CUDA reads this model's MLX 4-bit checkpoint only; NVFP4 and EXL3 exports of it are not read yet. Its prompt matmuls
have no FP8 kernel, so prompt precision does not change and `--prefill-fp8` is refused.

Use the [CUDA container setup](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/RUNBOOK.md#nvidia-gpus). One or two
ranks are supported.
Pull the checkpoint on each rank and start rank 1 first:

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit --tp 2 --rank 1 --master 192.0.2.1
tensorfold serve TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit --tp 2 --rank 0 --master 192.0.2.1 --name bench --host 0.0.0.0
```

The default cap is three MTP drafts. Later drafts stop when their cumulative head confidence falls below
20%; the first draft is retained. `--mtp-drafts N` sets a cap from zero to eight. Context copies can also
supply proposals, and verification uses windows of up to 16 rows.

The shared grouped expert kernel handles routed experts and two half-width shared experts. Mamba
convolution and recurrent state commit by replaying the kept rows before the next window. Attention
uses fixed 512-key chunks and merges them in order. Prefill uses separate prompt-chunk kernels.

Requests take turns. The engine retains prompt and reply states for prefix reuse; `"draft": false`
uses a separate serial engine. The default requested context is 16,384 tokens, subject to startup
memory admission; `--context` sets an explicit window. Inspect the reported capacity before sending
long requests. Both backends use the same public draft list below.

## Native Omni video

The maintained CUDA Bolt family shares RADIO with image input. See the [video recipe](nemotron-omni-video.md)
for checkpoint requirements, request parts, limits and qualification status.

## Draft vocabulary provenance

This section describes the Python 0.6.6 engine's list,
[`src/tensorfold/families/nemotron_h/draft_ids.txt`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/families/nemotron_h/draft_ids.txt).
The native engine embeds its own 49,152-ID list, `zig/src/families/nemotron/draft_ids.txt`, on Metal and CUDA; the
rebuild below does not produce it.

The shipped `draft_ids.txt` contains 32,768 sorted IDs. It can be rebuilt byte for byte from CPython
3.14.5's standard-library Python files, excluding `site-packages`, plus tracked Python and Markdown
files from TensorFold commit `cfea94372391f3761d42d0d8946462adf28a68b4`.
No PyPI package source or working-tree text is part of this corpus.

Tokenizer JSON SHA-256:

```text
623c34567aebb18582765289fbe23d901c62704d6518d71866e0e58db892b5b7
```

Use `tokenizers==0.22.2` and the archived commit's `tools/draft_vocab.py`, whose SHA-256 is
`980f3d0c3520260d49841b85b5298b08109b7148e99fb5d7a03f4011df7b26a4`.
Place the matching tokenizer at `tokenizer.json`. In an empty output directory within a repository clone,
export the tracked corpus and copy a clean CPython 3.14.5 stdlib:

```bash
git archive --format=tar --prefix=corpus/tensorfold/ cfea94372391f3761d42d0d8946462adf28a68b4 | tar -xf -
python3.14 -B - <<'PYTHON'
from pathlib import Path
import shutil
import sys
import sysconfig
assert sys.version_info[:3] == (3, 14, 5)
source = Path(sysconfig.get_path("stdlib")).resolve()
for path in sorted(source.rglob("*.py")):
    rel = path.relative_to(source)
    if "site-packages" in rel.parts or "__pycache__" in rel.parts:
        continue
    path.resolve().relative_to(source)
    dest = Path("corpus/cpython") / rel
    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    shutil.copyfile(path, dest)
PYTHON
TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false python3 -B corpus/tensorfold/tools/draft_vocab.py tokenizer.json draft_ids.txt --size 32768 --min-count 1 'corpus/cpython/**/*.py' 'corpus/tensorfold/**/*.py' 'corpus/tensorfold/**/*.md'
```

The verified stdlib came from Homebrew CPython 3.14.5. The selected corpus contains 1,849 stdlib Python
files and 173 package Python/Markdown files. The generator reads 1,995 nonempty UTF-8 files and
10,172,943 tokens. It skips unreadable files and text over its default 2,000,000-character limit.
It keeps IDs below 1024, then IDs by frequency, then the lowest unused IDs until full.

Expected output SHA-256:

```text
436840405e3507339efe85c410bb87a927ede7eb44eae620c0dda225c392d45f
```

A different stdlib distribution can change the selected files. Check the output hash before adopting a
rebuild. This subset affects draft proposals only; the target still verifies against its full vocabulary.

## Native prompt reuse

The Zig engine keeps a stream's prompt state at each planned chunk end: every Mamba conv and SSM state, the KV rows and
the draft head's KV rows (`zig/src/families/nemotron/snapshot.zig`). A later request whose prompt extends a kept state
resumes there. Both the keep and the resume are copies on the GPU, on the engine's own queue, so neither waits for the
host. `--prompt-cache-gib` sizes the memory as for Flash Next; `0` turns it off.

Measured on an M5 Ultra (256 GB), macOS 27.0.1, Zig 0.17.0, checkpoint revision `d9d758fb`, with
`--context 32768 --temperature 0 --no-thinking`, greedy, 96 reply tokens, a 9.2k-token chat over four turns:

| | Turns 2-4, cache off | Turns 2-4, cache on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prompt time | 1.29-1.36 s | 0.28-0.31 s, 9,213 tokens resumed (turn 4: 9,556) |

A fresh 9.2k-token prompt costs the same with the cache on or off: 1.07 s mean over four prompts each way, alternated,
while the cache keeps two states (106 MiB each) per prompt. Every reply equalled its cache-off reply: one conversation
alone, two conversations at once with `--parallel 4` (each equal to its solo run), and `--no-drafts`; drafted output
equalled `--no-drafts` throughout.

`--learn` keeps the states at shared cuts (a system prompt and its tools) on disk, under an identity made of the
checkpoint's config and tensor index, each shard file's size, inode and change times, the prefill step, the head,
every kernel source, a probe's prompt-pass bits, the OS build and the chip
(`zig/src/families/nemotron/learned_prompts.zig`). Weights that `--slide` writes into the shards start a new identity,
and a live weight change stops the server reading or writing learned states until it restarts. The probe runs a fixed
4,143-token prompt at startup, about a second. A later server with the same identity reads a learned state back and
resumes a fresh conversation from it: with the 9.2k-token system prompt above, a new server's first turn took 0.27 s
instead of 1.30 s, resuming 9,213 tokens from disk, and every reply equalled the cache-off reply. The two learned
states took 213 MB on disk.

## Routed experts past one row

Windows and shared rounds take the routed experts through `tf_experts_w` (`zig/kernels/metal/nemotron_experts.metal`):
a 16-group's four weight words as the outer loop, three member rows a pass, four simdgroups a threadgroup. Each lane
sums in the one-row kernel's order, so every width gives the one-row bits; `zig build tf-nemotron-experts` checks that
and times the shapes. On an M5 Ultra the 23 layers' up and down projections went from 2.35 to 2.27 ms at 4 rows, 6.68
to 6.48 at 16, 11.93 to 11.24 at 32 and 22.57 to 20.58 at 64 (equal at 2). Served with the cache off, alternated twice
against the previous kernel: one stream 503 to 513 tok/s on code and 348 to 351 on prose, 8 streams 947 to 985 and 713
to 731 tok/s in all, 32 streams 792 to 802 and 752 to 761, every reply equal to its solo and its plain run.

## Measurements

Use the [public benchmark command](README.md#measurements) with the server above.
Compare drafted/serial and resumed/fresh output on each backend and rank count, plus concurrent/solo
requests on MLX. Decode rate, cold/resumed first-token latency and peak memory are TBD [release-0.3.5].

On a 64 GB M5 Pro with TensorFold 0.3.5.1 and `TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit@8bbcb5b6`
(#70; setup in the [Qwen3.8-27B recipe](qwen3.8-27b.md#a-64-gb-m5-pro-on-0351)), the fitted context was the full
262,144 tokens and the lifetime peak footprint 42.21 GiB, reached during load and warm-up. A 261,780-token prompt
prefilled in 311.5 s and resumed in 0.63 s with 261,774 tokens cached. Decode medians were 146.0, 123.3, 131.3 and
135.3 tok/s with MTP (code sampled, chat sampled, code greedy, chat greedy) and 107.8, 109.0, 109.5 and 109.0 with
`--no-drafts`. All 180 concurrent replies at 1, 2, 4 and 8 streams equaled their solo runs, and every solo run
equaled `"draft": false`. These are 0.3.5.1 results, not a later release's.

## Shared rounds on the Zig engine

The native server runs every live stream's window in one forward. That forward holds four rows a lane (`--parallel`),
64 at least and 128 at most, so up to `--parallel 16` nothing changes from the 64-row buffers the engine always
allocated, and at 32 or 64 lanes each drafting stream keeps rows for its drafts instead of the round splitting. Each
row past 64 costs one Mamba state slot, 2 MiB a Mamba layer, 47 MiB across Lightning's 23, so `--parallel 64` takes
about 2.9 GiB more than before and `--parallel 8` the same. The startup timing sweep times shared rounds up to that
width, so the planner prices them from measurements rather than a straight line past 32.

Measured on an M5 Ultra (256 GB, macOS 27.0.1) with `--parallel 64 --context 32768 --prompt-cache-gib 0`, 256
tokens a reply, greedy, two alternated rounds, `tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial`:

| Sessions | Code, before | Code, after | Chat, before | Chat, after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 939-944 tok/s | 944-953 | 717-721 | 713-717 |
| 32 | 779-795 | 958-1,019 | 740-755 | 843 |
| 64 | 779-795 | 968-1,006 | 738-753 | 847-849 |

Every concurrent reply equaled its solo run and every solo run equaled `"draft": false` (832 replies checked a
binary). One stream decodes the same as before: 505 and 347 tok/s on the two decode prompts. A 64-row cap alone,
measured on the way, gave most of the 32-session gain and a quarter of the 64-session one.

## Stream memory on CUDA

The native CUDA engine keeps one sequence of its own at the full `--context` window, as before; its captured graphs
and the lone stream's fast path read it. Every other stream takes its key and value rows from one pool of 512-row
pages (`zig/src/core/kv_pool.zig`), which the engine fills from the room its own sequence and the weights leave:
each further stream's fixed part (Mamba states, window scratch, its page table: 64 MiB), the prompt cache's snapshot
slots (48 MiB each, made at load) and its copied rows come first, then pages, never more than every stream could hold
at once. A request reserves `ceil((prompt + max_tokens + 32) / 512)` pages when it is admitted: a 2,048-token prompt
with 4,096 reply tokens takes 13 pages (45.5 MiB) instead of a whole window. A request whose pages do not fit waits
until a stream ends. The attention kernels read the pages through a table at a fixed device address, so the graphs
keep their addresses. The startup line shows the pool. `TF_KV_PAGES=0` gives every stream a window again;
`TF_KV_PAGES=all` puts every stream on pages (for checks).
# Nemotron Omni video on native CUDA

This increment adds video to the maintained Nemotron Bolt family and its shared RADIO tower.
It uses the engine's existing vision kernels and GEMMs. It needs no Python vision process.
The supplied #940 video work is by @MiaAI-Lab, with literal marker shielding by @cwschroeder.
The Bolt family comes from @BobClawblaw's #897 and the maintained lane integration.

Start an admitted Omni checkpoint with `--vision`. Video is offered only when its config declares
`video_temporal_patch_size: 2`, its tokenizer has the reserved video marker, and its checkpoint contains
`vision_model.radio_model.model.patch_generator.video_embedder.weight` with the expected BF16 shape.
Image-only checkpoints keep their image path.

Requests use the chat content part `{"type":"video_url","video_url":{"url":"data:video/mp4;base64,..."}}`.
Public HTTPS URLs require `--vision-urls`. The native decoder library, libtfvideo with FFmpeg, must be
available beside the server. A missing library gives a named refusal. See the server's video build instructions.

`--vision-max-videos` defaults to 2 and accepts 1 through 16. `--vision-video-tokens` defaults to 16384
and accepts 64 through 262144 visual tokens shared by the request's videos. Image tokens have a separate
budget. The engine reserves the checked sum of both budgets in its whole-request visual rows buffer.
A larger budget increases device memory admission and can make a checkpoint too large to load.

Encoded input is bounded to 16 MiB per clip and 20 MiB across the request. Dimensions are bounded to
8192 per side and 16 Mi pixels, with at most 3600 seconds per clip. Source frame counts and rate components
must fit the decoder's signed integer range. At most 256 frames are sampled per clip, or 128 above
720 rows. The visual token budget can lower that count. Frames are sampled at 2 fps, or 1 fps above
720 rows, and paired for the temporal projection. An odd last frame is repeated in its pair.
The prompt includes each pair's timestamp and visual rows. Literal marker text stays ordinary text.

This patch's host checks cover preparation, limits, ownership, prompt marker handling, and row planning.
Real decoder compatibility, tower reference accuracy, model outputs, drafting, concurrency and prompt
reuse across video boundaries still need final-source GPU qualification before release.
# Nemotron 3.5 Parse on native HIP

This port runs `nvidia/Nemotron-3.5-Parse` on one HIP rank. The
validated checkpoint revision is
`4035ffb1d8f8bafcdb867dfaf6f7514f101464f9`. The family is
`nemotron_parse`; it is separate from Nemotron-H and Super VL.

The original FP32 safetensors stay unchanged. The loader validates all
510 tensors, then owns BF16 device copies of the 509 floating tensors.
Activations and KV use BF16 with FP32 sums. The image tower, horizontal
neck, causal mBART decoder and trained one-step proposal run in native HIP
kernels. Python is used only for independent development references.

## Build and serve

Use the repository Zig version. On ROCm installations with a different
layout, give the actual compiler and device-library paths:

```sh
zig build native-hip -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1201 \
  -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/core/bin/hipcc \
  -Dhip-device-lib=/opt/rocm/core/lib/llvm/amdgcn/bitcode

zig-out/native-hip/bin/tensorfold-native serve "$PARSE_MODEL" \
  --backend rocm --device 0 --vision --name parse --parallel 2 --context 4096 \
  --mtp-drafts 1 --prompt-cache-gib 0.25 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

`PARSE_MODEL` names the already cached snapshot. Select the intended
visible device and verify its PCI identity; management and HIP ordinals
can differ. The engine checks driver free memory at load and admission.
The developer checks require at least six GiB free before a bounded
two-lane run.

Send one user message with one PNG `image_url` data URL to
`/v1/chat/completions`. For example, with an ordinary OpenAI client:

```python
import base64
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

image = base64.b64encode(Path("page.png").read_bytes()).decode()
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="local")
reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="parse",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64," + image}}
    ]}],
    temperature=0,
    max_tokens=1024,
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

Use the served model name reported by `/health`, or set `--name` explicitly.
The built-in media template puts the visual prefix before the example's
six task tokens. Optional text parts follow those tokens. Generated OCR,
including its location/class markers, is returned in `content`. A custom
`--chat-template` still overrides the built-in bridge.

The image processor shrinks into 2048-by-1664 without enlargement, pads
bottom/right to 16/64, and preserves the visible content size for RADIO
positions. A full page uses 3329 visual context rows. Visual and text rows
share the 16384-row model context; `--context` may lower this limit. One
image is required. Multi-turn chat, video, tensor parallelism, lossy KV,
Sliding Weights and multiple proposal heads are not part of this port.

Default generation is greedy with repetition penalty 1.1. The shared
sampler widens raw logits to FP32 before applying penalties, and forces
EOS at the configured final output position. `"draft": false` selects
plain target decoding; normal drafted requests use the trained head and
the existing target verifier. Shared rounds batch dense work across all
admitted streams. Prompt snapshots use image content and frame identities.

## Reproduce the checks

Create offline BF16 references from the checkpoint's own example workflow:

```sh
python tools/zig/nemotron_parse_reference.py --model "$PARSE_MODEL" \
  --image page.png --output "$REFERENCE"
python tools/zig/nemotron_parse_reference.py positions --model "$PARSE_MODEL" \
  --output "$POSITION_REFERENCE"

zig build test-nemotron-parse-host -Dparse-model-dir="$PARSE_MODEL" \
  -Dparse-reference-dir="$REFERENCE"

TF_PARSE_DIR="$PARSE_MODEL" TF_PARSE_POSITION_DIR="$POSITION_REFERENCE" \
  zig build hip-parse-ops-test -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1201 \
  -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/core/bin/hipcc \
  -Dhip-device-lib=/opt/rocm/core/lib/llvm/amdgcn/bitcode
```

The reference environment used CPU Torch 2.11.0, TorchVision 0.26.0,
Transformers 5.14.1 and timm 1.0.22. It loads only local assets. The tool
retains NVIDIA's OpenMDW notice; the license is
[LICENSES/NVIDIA-OpenMDW-1.1.txt](../../LICENSES/NVIDIA-OpenMDW-1.1.txt).
Reference directories must be new; large tensors are not checked into Git.
`nemotron_parse_reference.py processor` prints the model-free
`zig/src/families/nemotron_parse/fixtures/processor.json`.

`tf-nemotron-parse-test` builds a developer probe. Give it the model,
reference and output directories. It compares intermediate seams and
teacher-forced logits, then checks full/chunked and solo/shared KV/hidden
bytes and suffix rollback. `nemotron_parse_reference.py compare
--reference "$REFERENCE" --native "$PROBE_OUTPUT"` applies the original HF
logits processor to saved native rows.

The kernel contract registers twelve new operator cases, which
`tf-hip-kernel-contract` runs with no argument, beside the rest of the
contract and its planted controls. `hip-kernel-contract-objects` builds
the code objects for gfx1030, gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1201, and
`hip-kernel-contract-limits` checks every launch record against them
without a GPU.

## Evidence and limits

Native HTTP token arrays matched three PNG references (two 512-by-256
pages, one 1664-by-2048 page), plain/drafted and solo/concurrent. The
full page uses 3335 prompt rows including the six text tokens. Prompt KV
and final-hidden bytes agree across full/chunked and solo/shared forwards
and after suffix rollback. No speed target is claimed.

All twelve new operator cases pass arithmetic gates 1–4, including five
repeat runs, guards, non-finites, tile edges and accumulator stress.
Their seven launch records match the code objects of all four recorded
chips and the live gfx1201 device. The complete contract reports only
the limit problems that main reports too: two stale records on the live
gfx1201 (`tf_sum_partials`, `tf_sum_partials_act`) and 13 across the four
chips' code objects.

BF16 intermediate tensors differ from HF's CPU GEMM rounding; saved
seam errors are diagnostic, while actual output token arrays are checked
separately. Runtime model checks cover gfx1201 only. CUDA, Metal, other
AMD hardware have not been qualified here. Sampled plain/drafted equality
passes at two small-page seeds, one with presence and frequency penalties;
this does not compare TensorFold's keyed sampler with HF's random draws.
PNG is tested. JPEG uses the repository's pinned libjpeg-turbo decoder
and has no qualification receipt yet. Structured output needs the
existing grammar library and has no real-model receipt yet.
# Persisted prompt keys and reviewed profile values

The native disk identities call `zig/src/native/disk_identity.zig`'s profile helper. It visits every registered entry whose class is arithmetic, experimental or debug and whose family/backend scope applies. CUDA passes the loaded Nemotron model_type or the generic registered family name; the Metal owners pass their family and metal backend, with Qwen distinguishing dense and routed configurations. No eligible entries means the helper leaves its input hash unchanged.

Environment values take precedence over the entry's stable default, as in the profile resolver. Exact-one booleans resolve to0 or1, so unset and explicit0 share a key. Counts use their numeric value, including equivalent decimal spellings; absent counts default to0. Auto values default to auto. Entries with special reporting values retain their explicit/default distinction. Malformed counts retain their raw value in a separate hash domain; this helper introduces no new startup refusal.

Names, classes and resolved values are length-framed, with family/backend and a format tag. A changed relevant value gives a new namespace. The old files remain under their old identity; the first long prompt for the new namespace prefills again. State bytes, token matching, kernels and serving defaults are unchanged.

The supplied main has no arithmetic-class entry. The regression therefore supplies a clearly marked fake arithmetic row, with an isolated environment callback, to the actual CUDA identity function and recording driver. It verifies unset=0, unset!=1, a same-key reopen hit and a changed-key persisted-index miss. Other tests cover all non-identical classes, every applicable row, defaults and out-of-scope/identical controls. This is a host contract, not qualification of a real arithmetic switch or device. TF_QWEN_REQUEST_STARTS is a separate contribution (#2176).

## Audit of the supplied main

The table covers the common native disk owners. Numeric token-prefix matching, chunk starts, decoded spans and image identity are shared preconditions, so tokenizer/template filenames need not independently invalidate identical numeric state. A tokenizer or template change that changes those inputs misses through the shared matcher. This is a prompt-state cache, with no stored rendered reply.

| Owner | Source/checkpoint binding already present | Arithmetic and KV form | Tokenizer/template, adapters and learned epoch | Remaining gap or fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CUDA Nemotron and generic kept-state families | Embedded CUDA strings, optional aot.json, device/driver, family facts, fixed probe; checkpoint config/index and safetensors stamps | Family facts/probe plus this helper for every applicable non-identical profile entry | Shared exact numeric prefix/modes/images; loaded-family ownership; learner clear barrier | Profile omission fixed here. Full executable/captured-cubin binding remains in the separate source-binding follow-up #2163. |
| Metal Qwen dense/routed host | Main and drafter config/index/shard stamps, runtime/shared source texts, OS/chip and probe | Tensor-unit/ANE/drafter facts, probe and this helper | Same shared matching and learner barrier; drafter checkpoint included | Profile omission fixed here. Complete executable/layout binding belongs to #2163. |
| Metal Nemotron | Config/index/shard stamps, MTP header, kernel source hash, OS/chip and probe | Chunk/head facts, attention precision, probe and this helper | Same shared matching and learner barrier | Profile omission fixed here. Complete host/shared source binding belongs to #2163. |
| Metal GLM | Config/index model hash, kernel source hash, OS/chip and probe | TP, chunk rows, EP presence, probe and this helper | Same shared matching and learner barrier | Profile omission fixed here. Current supplied main still lacks shard-payload stamp binding at this owner; checkpoint/source follow-up #2163 handles it. |
| Metal Flash Next | Prepared checkpoint identity, selected source hash, OS/chip and probe | Three loaded mode bits, probe and this helper | Same shared matching and learner barrier | Profile omission fixed here. Current main still needs current shard stamps, complete loaded variant/policy and executable binding from #2163. |

The shared matcher is `prompt_imprint.Imprint.best` plus `prompt_cache.Store`'s decoded-span/image checks. The live learned epoch is an invalidation barrier: `lane_host_learn.zig` clears the cache after changed learning steps; `Store.clear` stops disk writes, expires states and detaches both disk stores. It is not a persisted epoch counter. Supported weight commits move checkpoint stamps before a later process opens a store. This change does not introduce an external adapter loader; adapter-specific cross-process reuse remains unqualified.

DeepSeek reference sessions use fresh-start behavior rather than these common disk owners; adapters without a disk attachment have no cross-process store in this scope. The source-binding follow-up is separate from this profile fix. No claim that the supplied main closes every #2131 gap follows from the table.

Host checks: `zig build test-disk-identity-host test-cuda-disk-open-host check-native-cuda-host compile-disk-identity-metal-host -j1`. The Metal step only emits an object for the four real identity bodies and their probes; it has no shader producer or execution step. Actual model/device resume-versus-fresh qualification remains required separately.
# Persisted serving state identities

A resumed state belongs to the loaded model and arithmetic that produced it. The native disk stores bind the
running serving binary with a streamed SHA256 fingerprint. This covers compiled host code, embedded shaders,
compiler options and snapshot layouts. Rebuilding or changing the binary can cold-start the optional disk cache.
Old files remain in their original namespace and follow the existing cache budget and eviction rules.

| Persistence owner | Source and arithmetic | Checkpoint | KV and draft state | Weight learning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nemotron, Metal | Binary, kernel texts, precision mode, probe, OS build and GPU | Config, index, shard stamps and MTP header | Canonical snapshot, head flag and probe | Shared host clears RAM and detaches disk stores when weights move |
| Dense Qwen hybrid, Metal | Binary, shared/family shader texts, tensor/ANE modes, probe, OS build and GPU | Config, index and shard stamps for target and external drafter | Canonical recurrence/KV/tap image and draft end | Unsupported learners refuse; the store remains scoped to its loaded model |
| GLM, Metal | Binary, compiled source hash, rank/chunk modes, probe, OS build and GPU | Config/index identity plus current shard stamps | Canonical KDA/MLA image and checked snapshot header | Unsupported learner on this adapter |
| Flash Next, Metal | Binary, actual loaded shader texts/bindings, rotary/precision policy, probe, OS build and GPU | Pack metadata identity plus current shard stamps | Checked snapshot layout; canonical session image | Unsupported learner on this adapter |
| Nemotron, CUDA | Binary, embedded images, captured manifest and cubin bytes, probe, GPU and driver | Config, index and shard stamps | Head flag and canonical state image | Shared host clears RAM and detaches disk stores when weights move |
| Qwen dense/MoE hybrids, CUDA | Same shared CUDA identity | Same shared checkpoint identity | Explicit BF16/FP8 format, tap flag and prompt-int8 mode; image states stay off disk | Same shared learning barrier |
| Flash Next, CUDA | Same shared CUDA identity | Same shared checkpoint identity | Head flag and canonical recurrence/KV/PLE image; tensor-rank disk persistence is refused | Same shared learning barrier |
| DeepSeek sessions, CUDA reference path | Config/options/mode, checkpoint digest, rank, selected layers and piece layout | Checkpoint digest required | Versioned lossless session pieces and exact token prefix | No learner; the disk tier starts fresh for each process |

Other native family adapters have no attached cross-process serving-state tier. Their snapshots remain owned by one
open model. This includes the other Metal families (Qwen4, Fish, Qwen MoE, LFM2, EXLR8 GLM, Gemma, Step, Spark,
MiniMax and Llama), other CUDA families (Omni, GLM, MiniMax, Kolibri, Gemma, Spark, Dory, LFM2, Fish and Qwen4),
and the HIP and XPU adapters. A family name or a RAM snapshot alone does not imply persistent disk reuse.

Tokenizer and chat-template bytes are covered through the canonical numeric token prefix that the store actually
matches. Changed rendering or tokenization that changes an ID misses. An identical ID prefix has the same target
state under identical weights and arithmetic, so it can remain reusable. Planned stores also compare their chunk
boundaries, while the shared cache compares decoded spans and image identities. These stores do not persist
rendered answer text. No separate hot-swappable LoRA state is admitted by these persistence adapters; checkpoint
changes and supported external drafters use the identities above.

GLM and Flash Next now include safetensors shard names, sizes, inode and modification/change stamps. A weight
write with unchanged config, index, tensor header and size moves their namespace even when a fixed probe does not
visit the changed tensor. Flash Next also hashes the loaded variant text and input/output/meta bindings in sorted
function-name order. Captured CUDA sets hash each cubin named by the parsed manifest, through the same loader
paths and size limit. A missing or changed file fails identity construction instead of opening an old namespace.

The executable and kernel fingerprints use a 32 KiB read buffer and check file stamps across the read. Checkpoints,
executables and kernel assets must remain stable while a model opens and serves. The existing learner owns runtime
weight changes and clears the store before another reply; it does not attach an old disk tier after a lesson.

Host checks:

```sh
zig build test-persistence-identity-host test-cuda-persistence-source-host compile-persistence-host -j1
zig build test-checkpoint-identity test-cuda-disk-open-host test-sessions test-frame-cache-identity-host -j1
```

The first command's Metal consumer compile and checkpoint fixtures require a macOS host but execute no GPU call.
These checks cover stale namespaces, real same-header shard rewrites, binary and captured-cubin mutations, loaded
variant bindings, allocation failures, canonical token matching and whole-file fingerprint coverage. Actual
checkpoint/device qualification still requires exact drafted/plain, resumed/fresh and concurrent/solo token arrays.
# Qwen-Image-2.1 on Metal

Qwen-Image-2.1 is a text-to-image model. A 7B single-stream transformer (32 blocks, hidden 4,096, 32 heads of 128,
SwiGLU width 12,288) denoises 64-channel latents. `zig/src/families/qwen_image` runs that transformer on the Metal
runtime from the released bf16 diffusers checkpoint:

- the prompt rows once a prompt: causal attention, every block's keys and values kept;
- the image rows at each step: attention over the kept prompt keys and the image's own.

The prompt encoder (Qwen3-VL) and the image decoder are not ported. `tools/zig/qwen_image_case.py` runs them through
mflux, a development reference.

It is a denoiser, not a token family. It does not register with the lane engine, the server or `families.detect`.

## Checkpoints

- `Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo`: 8 steps on the `sample_sigmas` saved in `model_index.json`.
- `Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1`: the same transformer shape. It is untested here.

`transformer/config.json` must be `QwenImage21Transformer2DModel` at the released geometry. Any other config is
refused. The weights are under the Qwen Research License (non-commercial); read it before use.

## Precision

- bf16 activations, rounded where the reference rounds them.
- fp32 sums in every projection and in attention.
- fp32 for norms, rotary and softmax.
- No int8.

The projections are the Qwen-VL tower's `tfp::gemm_nax`. Attention is the prefill `tfp::attention_nax` template,
with full (non-causal) entry points added for the image rows.

## Run a case

```sh
python3 tools/zig/qwen_image_case.py case MODEL_DIR case/ --prompt-file prompt.txt   # needs mflux and MLX
zig build tf-qwen-image -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/bin/tf-qwen-image MODEL_DIR/transformer case/case.safetensors case/
python3 tools/zig/qwen_image_case.py decode MODEL_DIR case/latents.f32 case/zig.png
python3 tools/zig/qwen_image_case.py compare case/reference.png case/zig.png case/side.png
```

The case holds:

- the prompt's encoder rows;
- the noise levels;
- the starting latents;
- mflux's input and velocity at every step;
- with `--fp32-steps N`, a float32 run of the same transformer.

`tf-qwen-image` first runs each step on mflux's own input and compares the velocities. It then runs the whole schedule
from the starting latents, times it, and writes the final latents.

## Measured

Setup:

- Mac Studio M5 Ultra 256 GB, macOS 27.
- `Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo` at 1344x768: 4,032 image rows, 44 prompt rows, seed 42, 8 steps.
- Reference: mflux `add5164` on MLX 0.32.3, bf16.

Results:

- **Velocity**, each step on the reference's input:
  - Against mflux bf16: cosine 0.99996 to 0.99999, max |diff| 0.11 to 0.21.
  - Against a float32 run of the same transformer: cosine 0.99997 to 0.99998.
  - mflux bf16's own cosine against that float32 run: 0.99994 to 0.99999.
- **Image:** our latents decoded through mflux's decoder are 43.35 dB PSNR from mflux's own image.
- **Repeat:** the same step run twice gives identical bytes.
- **Speed**, one session with no other GPU work, runs alternated:
  - mflux: 0.702 s a forward, before and after.
  - Ours: 0.740 s a forward (0.730 s on the GPU), and 0.23 s for the prompt rows once.
- **Memory:** 15.1 GB peak process footprint, with the transformer's bf16 weights (about 14 GB) in shared Metal buffers.
# Qwen3-Embedding-8B on native HIP

The native HIP engine serves `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B` as published (BF16
safetensors, revision `1d8ad4ca9b3dd8059ad90a75d4983776a23d44af`) through
`POST /v1/embeddings`. It is qualified on one Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201).
gfx11 builds run the same code; FP16 builds (RDNA2) refuse the checkpoint.

| Responsibility | Files |
| --- | --- |
| Config, BF16 weights, batched prompt pass | `zig/src/families/qwen3/` (`config.zig`, `model.zig`, `forward.zig`) |
| Prompt-only engine, lane backend, embedding head | `zig/src/families/qwen3/` (`engine.zig`, `prompt.zig`, `native.zig`) |
| BF16 dense GEMM (dot2 tile, BF16 weight decoder; gfx12's WMMA tile) | `zig/kernels/hip/quant/bf16_decoder.hpp`, `dense_tiles.hpp`, `zig/kernels/hip/tiles/wmma12_gemm.hpp`, `zig/src/hip/launches/dense.zig` |
| Head-major attention rows | `tf_heads_rows` in `zig/kernels/hip/ops/attention.hpp` |
| Stored-dtype dense weights | `zig/src/core/quant/dense.zig` (`readStored`) |
| Device contracts | `zig/tests/hip/contract_dense.zig`, `contract_dense_wmma12.zig`, `contract_heads_rows.zig` |
| Pinned model-card oracle | `tools/zig/oracle_qwen3_embedding.py` |

The weights stay BF16 on the GPU (14.1 GiB). Activations are BF16 and every
product sums in fp32. The head comes from the sentence-transformers folder:
`1_Pooling/config.json` must pool the last token only, and `modules.json`'s
`Normalize` makes every full-width vector unit length. A folder without
`1_Pooling` is refused.

On gfx12 the BF16 projections can run on a WMMA tile, opt-in with
`--policy matrix=on`. The default `matrix=auto`, `matrix=off` and every other
chip run the dot2 tile and keep its bits. The two tiles sum in different
orders: on Qwen3-8B's layer-0 projections WMMA's fp32 sums sit 8 to 41
times further from float64 than dot2's, while the BF16 outputs the engine
writes are as close (`TF_QWEN3_*` GPU checks below, `projection_test.zig`).
A less exact default output needs an opt-in, so WMMA is not the default.
gfx1200 builds the same tile but is unmeasured: no run, and no gate 5
record (the records cover gfx1201).

## Build and serve

```sh
zig build native-hip -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1201 -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/core/bin/hipcc
zig-out/native-hip/bin/tensorfold-native serve MODEL_DIRECTORY \
  --name Qwen3-Embedding-8B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8090
```

With ROCm 10.1, pass the hipcc under `/opt/rocm/core`: the build takes the
ROCm root from the hipcc path, and `/opt/rocm` lacks the device math headers.

The server sizes one pass to `--context` (32,768 tokens by default, at most
the config's 40,960) and shrinks it by halves to fit the memory budget, down
to 2,048; the startup line names the window. A request holds at most 128
inputs and the window's tokens in all. `dimensions` crops to any width from
32 to 4,096 (the card's MRL range) and renormalizes. The chat and completion
routes are refused.

Queries take the card's instruction prefix; documents are sent as they are:

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "input": ["Instruct: Given a web search query, retrieve relevant passages that answer the query\nQuery:Explain gravity",
            "Gravity is a force that attracts two bodies towards each other."]}'
```

Text inputs end in `<|endoftext|>` through the tokenizer's post-processor,
which last-token pooling reads. Token-ID inputs are used as sent, so a client
must append 151643 itself.

## Gates

The oracle runs the model card's Transformers example in a venv with
Transformers 5.22.1. It refuses a snapshot or a Transformers install whose
files differ from its pins before any model code runs. Its fidelity set is
the card's 4 inputs and 5 long inputs of 2,044 to 32,759 tokens, each the
longest whole-line prefix of a pinned file within 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K or 32K
tokens (the card's `LICENSE` and `README.md`, three Transformers sources);
every input's text and token IDs are pinned by SHA256. The card's inputs run
as the card runs them, one padded batch; each long input runs alone. The
fp32 reference takes about 20 minutes on 32 CPU cores:

```sh
python3 tools/zig/oracle_qwen3_embedding.py sources --model MODEL_DIRECTORY
python3 tools/zig/oracle_qwen3_embedding.py ref --model MODEL_DIRECTORY --dtype float32 --device cpu --out ref32.json
python3 tools/zig/oracle_qwen3_embedding.py ref --model MODEL_DIRECTORY --dtype bfloat16 --device cuda --out ref16.json
python3 tools/zig/oracle_qwen3_embedding.py check --ref ref32.json --bar ref16.json --url http://127.0.0.1:8090
```

`check` sends the inputs in requests that fit the server's window (the card's
and the 2K to 16K inputs together, the 32K one alone). It passes when every
vector lies within transformers' own BF16 distance of the fp32 vector,
rounded up to two digits and at most 0.001 (distance = 1 - cosine), has unit
norm, is the same fp32 bytes alone, in a batch and from token IDs, and the
card's 2 x 2 scores are within 0.01. At MRL widths 32, 1024 and 4096 (`dimensions`) every vector
must have unit norm and lie within the same bound, taken at that width, of
the fp32 vector cropped and renormalized. The full-width gate runs on the
GPU without a server too:

```sh
TF_QWEN3_EMBED_DIR=MODEL_DIRECTORY TF_QWEN3_EMBED_REF=ref32.json TF_QWEN3_EMBED_BAR=ref16.json \
  zig build qwen3-hip-gpu-test -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1201 -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/core/bin/hipcc
```

The GPU checks take `TF_QWEN3_MATRIX=auto|off|on` to run either tile, and `TF_QWEN3_ATTENTION=wide|f32` for the attention path.

The WMMA rows below come from a server started with the WMMA tile:

```sh
zig-out/native-hip/bin/tensorfold-native serve MODEL_DIRECTORY \
  --name Qwen3-Embedding-8B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8090 --policy matrix=on
```

Results on the R9700 (ROCm 10.1); the distance rows are dot2 (the default), the WMMA rows `matrix=on`:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Card example, distance to fp32 (4 inputs) | 1.32e-4, 9.30e-5, 7.76e-5, 9.27e-5 |
| Long inputs, distance to fp32 (2,044, 4,043, 8,177, 16,383, 32,759 tokens) | 1.16e-4, 5.24e-5, 7.00e-5, 9.90e-5, 9.22e-5 |
| Full-width limit (transformers BF16's worst, 1.572e-4, rounded up) | 1.6e-4 |
| MRL width 32, 1024, 4096: worst distance (limit; transformers BF16's worst) | 7.92e-5 (1.9e-4; 1.884e-4), 1.18e-4 (1.7e-4; 1.624e-4), 1.32e-4 (1.6e-4; 1.572e-4) |
| Card 2 x 2 scores | [[0.7479, 0.0759], [0.0886, 0.6324]] (card: [[0.7493, 0.0751], [0.0880, 0.6318]]) |
| Batch, alone and token-ID vectors (all 9 inputs) | identical fp32 bytes |
| `hip-kernel-test`, `dense_gemm_block` | fp32 within the dot2 chain's bound against float64; BF16 out is the fp32 sum rounded once |
| `hip-kernel-contract` | dense GEMM (fp32 and BF16 out) and `tf_heads_rows` pass gates 1 to 4; their gate 5 records are current (gfx1030 does not serve the dense GEMM) |
