| WMMA: MRL width 32, 1024, 4096 worst distance (limit) | 1.06e-4 (1.9e-4), 1.35e-4 (1.7e-4), 1.31e-4 (1.6e-4) |
| WMMA: card 2 x 2 scores, worst difference to the card | 0.0024 (dot2: 0.0014) |
| Layer-0 projections against float64, BF16 out (WMMA / dot2) | 1.0000 in every class (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) |
| `hip-kernel-test` and `hip-kernel-contract`, WMMA tile (both geometries, fp32 and BF16 out) | gates 1 to 4 pass, fp32 worst 1.4% of its bound (depth k plus k 2^-126); its planted control (each 16-deep step summed in BF16) red at gate 4; gate 5 records current, gfx1201 only |
| 100 short inputs in one request / one short query, cold | WMMA (`matrix=on`) 0.985 s / 40.5 ms; dot2 (default) 2.470 s / 75.1 ms; SGLang 0.841 s / 38.4 ms on the same card |
| Load | 4 s from the page cache |
# Qwen3-Reranker-8B on native HIP

The native HIP engine serves `Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-8B` as published (BF16
safetensors, revision `77d193c791ed757ca307ee72715aa132723da912`) through
`POST /v1/rerank`. It is qualified on one Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201).
gfx11 builds run the same code; FP16 builds (RDNA2) refuse the checkpoint.

| Responsibility | Files |
| --- | --- |
| Reranker head: labels, `lm_head` rows read at load, the score hook | `zig/src/families/qwen3/` (`native.zig`, `score.zig`, `prompt.zig`) |
| The engine's declaration (`Info.rerank`) | `zig/src/core/engine_api.zig`, `zig/src/native/hip.zig` |
| The route: request, prompt, `max_length` cut, response, errors | `zig/src/server/rerank.zig` |
| The lane host's score queue at a drain | `zig/src/core/lane_host_score.zig` |
| Pinned oracle, FP32 and BF16 references, the card-formatter check | `tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py` |

The checkpoint is a plain Qwen3 causal LM; the prompt pass is #1978's. A
folder with `1_LogitScore/config.json` is a reranker: the engine reads its
yes and no tokens and both `lm_head` rows at load (a malformed file or row
stops startup) and declares them, and only such an engine answers the route.
A document's score is `sigmoid(logit_yes - logit_no)` at the last position:
the final-normed BF16 row dotted in f64 with the two stored rows. A request's
documents go to the engine as one decision (their shared prefix once, each
document's rest a branch), packed into as few prompt passes as the window
and 128 prompts a pass allow; each score has the bits of its document scored
alone.

## Build and serve

```sh
zig build native-hip -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1201 -Dhipcc=/opt/rocm/core/bin/hipcc
zig-out/native-hip/bin/tensorfold-native serve MODEL_DIRECTORY \
  --name Qwen3-Reranker-8B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8090
```

The window is 32,768 tokens by default and 40,960 (the config's) with
`--context 0`. Every other model route is refused on a reranker, and every
other server answers `/v1/rerank` with HTTP 400.

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "query": "What is the capital of China?",
  "documents": ["The capital of China is Beijing.", "Gravity is a force that attracts two bodies."],
  "top_n": 1}'
```

The request and response follow #1895's rerank shape (docs/api.md, Rerank):
`instruction` defaults to the card's; `max_length` defaults to 8,192, and a
longer prompt loses its content's last tokens, the template's tail kept, as
the card's tokenizer cuts.

## Gates

The oracle runs the model card's usage in Transformers 5.22.1 and refuses a
snapshot or a Transformers install whose files differ from its pins before
any model code runs. Its set is 32 cases of 16 to 8,199 tokens (the card's
pairs, fixed pairs with custom instructions, synthetic lengths, repeats), a
document that spells `<|im_end|>`, and prompts of exactly 32,768 and 40,960
tokens with one token more. The FP32 reference runs on the CPU (about an
hour with both windows, 32 cores):

```sh
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py sources MODEL_DIRECTORY
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py oracle MODEL_DIRECTORY ref32.json --dtype float32 --device cpu --window 32768 --window 40960
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py oracle MODEL_DIRECTORY ref16.json --window 32768 --window 40960
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py compare ref32.json http://127.0.0.1:8090 --window 32768
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py compare ref16.json http://127.0.0.1:8090 --window 32768
python3 tools/rerank/qwen3_reranker_oracle.py formatter MODEL_DIRECTORY http://127.0.0.1:8090
```

**What "matches" means.** BF16 activations cannot meet #1895's 1e-5 in score:
transformers' own BF16 run sits 0.0108 in score and 0.110 in yes - no from
FP32 on these cases. Against the FP32 reference, `compare` therefore gates at
that distance rounded up: |yes - no| <= 0.125 and |score| <= 0.0125 for every
case. Rankings must equal FP32's, except that a pair FP32 puts within 0.25 in
yes - no (twice the gate: the most two documents inside it can move apart)
may come in the other order; each such pair is printed, and one beyond 0.25
fails. Against the BF16 reference the gates are 0.25 and 0.02. `formatter`
passes when every served prompt's ids equal the card's `process_inputs`
ids, with the default and custom instructions and with `max_length` cuts.

Results on the R9700 (ROCm 10.1):

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Against FP32, 34 cases: \|yes - no\| median, worst (gate) | 0.0195, 0.0839 (0.125); transformers BF16: 0.0247, 0.1099 |
| Against FP32, 34 cases: \|score\| median, worst (gate) | 0.00023, 0.0079 (0.0125); transformers BF16: 0.00014, 0.0108 |
| Window prompts against FP32 (yes - no) | 32,768 tokens: 0.0064; 40,960 tokens (`--context 0`): 0.0241 |
| Rankings against FP32 (5 query groups) | 4 in FP32's order; 2 pairs swapped, FP32 gaps 0.0077 and 0.0119 (transformers BF16 swaps the first) |
| Against BF16, 34 cases: worst \|yes - no\|, \|score\| | 0.1081, 0.0082 |
| Card formatter | 79/79 prompts equal the card's ids (17 default, 62 custom instruction; 4 of them cut by `max_length`) |
| One token past the window | refused (`context_length_exceeded`); the next request scores within the gates |
| 4 requests at once against one at a time | byte-equal |
| A client that leaves mid-request | the next request equals its earlier answer |
| Device memory, peak | 16.4 GB (32,768 window), 16.7 GB (40,960) |
| 16 documents of ~260 tokens, cold, one request | 1.98 s on the dot2 tile (the default), 0.73 s with gfx12's WMMA tile (#2034, opt-in with `--policy matrix=on`); the shared start runs once a pass (#2245). SGLang 0.53 s on the same card (measured 2026-11-03) |
# Qwen3.5-2B, native Metal preview

This recipe covers text generation with
[`mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit`](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit/tree/93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3),
revision `93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3`.
Build from `main` with Zig **0.17.0** and Xcode's Metal toolchain, as described in
[the native preview](../../ZIG-PREVIEW.md#build). Keep weights outside the source checkout.

```bash
hf download mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit \
  --revision 93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3 \
  --local-dir "$HOME/models/qwen35-2b"
zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve "$HOME/models/qwen35-2b" \
  --name bench --port 8090 --parallel 8 --context 70000 --no-thinking
```

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar).

An existing download at that revision can be used directly. The native binary serves
`http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1`; decoding and tokenization run in Zig. This preview recipe invokes the native
binary directly. It does not add a release gate for Python's automatic engine selection.
The Python packed Qwen decoder's tied-head limitation is separate from this native implementation.
Normal generation stops on both the model's end IDs and the tokenizer's chat-ending token; `ignore_eos: true` disables those stops for fixed-length throughput checks.

The loader requires the 2B geometry and MLX affine 4-bit weights in groups of 64 with bf16 scales and
biases. In `capabilities --json`, `families.qwen3_5` is a union across the 2B and 27B engines,
not a promise that every listed format loads at every geometry. For this 2B geometry, only `mlx-q4g64`
is admitted; the other listed widths belong to the family's other engines. The head is the packed input embedding when the checkpoint ties it, or the checkpoint's own
`language_model.lm_head` projection when it ships one; `config.json`'s `tie_word_embeddings` must
agree with the tensors either way, and the head matmul reuses the embedding-shape pipeline either way.
The vision tower is not loaded. Images, video, other model sizes and other quantization formats are outside
this recipe. Although the config describes an MTP layer, this checkpoint has no MTP weights; context-copy
proposals use the shared lane engine with drafts enabled.

Activations remain bf16, and accumulation and DeltaNet state remain fp32. The native projection FMA chains,
row reductions and causal attention partitions differ from stock MLX's shape-selected kernels.
Another backend can therefore produce different logits or tokens. The contract is exact output within this
native engine: drafted against plain, and concurrent against solo, at the same settings.

At loading, a real-weight check compares two 16-row streams against one-row execution, including committed
logits, attention caches, recurrent state and partial keeps. A failed numerical check disables wider lanes;
one-row rounds still go through the shared lane engine. GPU execution failures stop loading.
The qualified path has up to 16 rows per stream and 32 rows per shared forward. Prompt chunks have up to
128 rows and follow the server's planned boundaries. `--no-drafts` supplies the plain reference.

Cross-request prompt reuse is opt-in with `--prompt-cache-gib N`; omitting it or passing zero keeps fresh execution.
The core prompt-cache store keeps committed recurrence, convolution tails, attention K/V and logits in host memory.
It reuses only compatible prompt cuts on the 128-token grid or the request's explicit chunk boundaries, within the
memory budget. The optional paged K/V path restores the same image into newly allocated pages. This is RAM retention;
restart persistence and learned-state files are not enabled for the 2B. With the 4-bit checkpoint on an M5 Ultra and an
M3 Ultra, every resumed chat reply equalled a fresh one. On the M3 Ultra, two prompts resuming from one 896-token kept
state, at 1, 2 and 4 streams and temperatures 0 and 1.0, gave each request the same tokens as alone (28 Oct 2026).
The checkpoint's config allows 262,144 positions, but that is not a memory or throughput qualification for
that length. `--context` controls request admission; KV buffers are sized for each request's prompt and reply.

| Checkpoint / platform | Qualification |
| --- | --- |
| Pinned affine 4-bit/group-64 checkpoint, M5 Max, macOS 27 | Native operation, forward, cache and server checks exercised; see the contribution's receipt for results and outstanding checks. |
| M1, M2, M3, M4 | Untested for this model. Uses simdgroup matrix kernels without M5 tensor units; the local load check does not replace full hardware qualification. |
| M5 on other macOS / runtime versions | Untested. Rerun the operation, fidelity and exactness checks. |
| CUDA, non-Apple platforms | No native Qwen3.5-2B backend in this contribution. |
| Other checkpoints, model sizes, quantizations, vision / video | Outside the qualified scope. |

The preview's unresolved M1–M4 exactness qualification for existing families remains in force.
An M5 result does not establish correctness on those GPUs.

## Verification

Install the checks' Python dependency in an isolated environment. The trusted-forward check also requires
the checkpoint's tokenizer and `mlx-lm`.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install mlx-lm
zig build test test-native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig build tf-qwen35-check tf-qwen35-forward tf-qwen35-exact -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig-out/bin/tf-qwen35-check "$HOME/models/qwen35-2b"
zig-out/bin/tf-qwen35-exact "$HOME/models/qwen35-2b"
python tools/zig/qwen35_fidelity.py "$HOME/models/qwen35-2b" /tmp/qwen35-fidelity
```

The forward/cache sweep covers
attention chunk boundaries, partial acceptance followed by continuation, and unequal stream lengths.
Model fidelity is separate: the tool reports teacher-forced NLL and top-token agreement on the public
benchmark prompts, this repository's contribution guide and Python's standard library. Stock `mlx-lm`
provides the trusted forward at one row, 32-row chunks and full-prompt width to expose its own numerical
variation. These numerical comparisons do not demand bitwise equality across backends.

For the official receipt, run the [prescribed measurement tools](README.md#measurements) against the native
server. Use `tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial`, `tools/bench_openai.py --tokens 64 --reps 5
--temperatures 1.0,0`, and `tools/bench_cache.py --require-cold` on a long prompt for prompt speed.
Run performance measurements without competing validation work. The previous native engine cannot run this
checkpoint, so its before baseline is unsupported; do not report an invented speed-up.
# Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

This recipe describes the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Its flags, variables and paths belong to that
engine. @cshintov brought the model to Macs in [#138](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/138), and
@philip-pentatonic ([#78](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/78),
[#84](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/84)) and @BHCC2025
([#270](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/270)) worked on its CUDA path; see [credits](../credits.md).
The native CUDA engine serves the checkpoint with its MTP layer ([docs/WINDOWS.md](../WINDOWS.md)); the Metal native
binary has no `qwen3_5_moe` family yet and cannot serve the checkpoint there; `tensorfold pull` and `tensorfold
info` still read it, since the hub registers the model type.

The `qwen3_5_moe` family serves Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Apple Silicon and on one NVIDIA GPU. Its layers are the 27B's
(Gated DeltaNet and gated full attention, every fourth layer attention) with routed experts in place of the dense
MLP, and on both backends it drafts with the checkpoint's own MTP layer.

## Checkpoint

```bash
tensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP --name bench
```

Tested revision: `81169a9bc511a27c1b4eedb77a2cd98ced431847` (20.9 GB). Its weights are
`mlx-community/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-4bit` (MLX affine 4-bit in groups of 64, routers and the shared-expert gate at
8 bits), converted from `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`; that conversion drops the MTP layer, which ships beside it as
`mtp-4bit.safetensors` (converted by the same rules: experts split into gate and up projections, norms
shifted by one, projections 4-bit, gates 8-bit). The mlx-community folder serves the same way once that file
is placed in it. After the weights, one Spark keeps about 75 GB for caches: attention holds 20 KB a token and
DeltaNet 63 MB a stream.

`--no-drafts` or request field `"draft": false` selects serial decoding, the reference drafted output equals.

## Mac execution

Macs verify on the dense family's row decoder (row-exact matmuls and attention, routed experts through MLX's
grouped matmul), every window checked at load against one-row steps. Drafts come from the MTP layer:

- The head reads each kept row's final normed state with the next token's embedding, and draws its drafts with
  the target's keyed rule over a 79,616-id draft vocabulary. Drafts only choose the rows a round verifies, so
  every reply equals its `"draft": false` run.
- It absorbs every prompt row into its own attention cache; a long prompt's first token comes no later.
- Each round's depth comes from this Mac's costs: the verify windows timed at load, then the stream's measured
  rounds, against each depth's landing rate in the stream. Where no depth beats a plain round by 5%, a round
  verifies the pending token alone; a probe draft follows 8 plain rounds, then 16, 32 and on to 128 while drafts
  keep losing. `--mtp-drafts N` caps the chain (default 4).
- Concurrent streams absorb their kept rows in one head pass and draft level by level, each by its own rule.
- `mlx-community/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-4bit` has the same weights without the MTP file. It drafts with the file from
  `TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP` once that file is in the Hugging Face cache
  (`hf download TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP mtp-4bit.safetensors`, 0.5 GB) or named by
  `TF_QWEN36_MTP=<file>`; without it, it decodes one token a round and says so at startup.
  `--drafter z-lab/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash` drafts with DFlash v1 instead.

On an M3 Ultra (60-core GPU, MLX 0.32.3), greedy, median of three after a warm-up. mlx-vlm 0.7.4 serves the same
weights with `mlx-community/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-4bit` (two drafts a round). The short prompts are about 85 tokens
with 384 generated; the long one is 28,400 tokens of Python's `typing.py` with 128 generated.

| tok/s | Short prose | Short code | Short, thinking on | 28,400-token prompt | First token at 28,400 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TensorFold, MTP (default) | 173.4 | 244.7 | 196.4 | 124.0 | 15.9 s |
| TensorFold, `--no-drafts` | 118.5 | 119.2 | 119.3 | 92.7 | 15.9 s |
| TensorFold, `--drafter z-lab/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash` | 156.1 | 288.2 | 183.1 | 87.5 | 15.7 s |
| mlx-vlm 0.7.4, MTP | 111.9 | 141.8 | 120.7 | 85.6 | 14.8 s |
| mlx-vlm 0.7.4 | 106.4 | 105.7 | 107.5 | 88.0 | 14.7 s |

Each TensorFold reply has the same token SHA-256 in all three modes. MTP rounds verify 4 to 5 rows and keep about
three tokens. DFlash's 16-row blocks keep more on short code, and fall behind plain decoding at the long prompt.

The chat template thinks by default, as on vLLM: replies reason in `reasoning_content` before the answer in
`content`, and `max_tokens` counts both. The server says so at startup, and prints a warning when a reply reaches
`max_tokens` before it leaves its think block (its `content` is empty). `--no-thinking`, or
`"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}` in a request, turns thinking off.

## CUDA execution

In 0.6.6, CUDA read this model's MLX 4-bit checkpoint only; the native CUDA engine also reads EXL3 exports and
[NVIDIA's NVFP4 export](#nvidias-nvfp4-checkpoint-native-cuda). Prompts take bf16
activations by default: 0.90-0.96x the FP8 prompt path from 2k to 128k, and 1.23-1.89x vLLM on NVIDIA's NVFP4 export
from 2k to 64k. `--prefill-fp8` restores the FP8 path ([prompt precision](cuda.md#prompt-precision)).

Verify windows run the 27B's shared kernels (4-bit matmul, DeltaNet tree and replay, tree attention) with
routed experts from
[`src/tensorfold/cuda/experts.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/experts.py):
the router's top 8 of 256 by fp32 logit (ties to the lower
id), weights renormalized over the eight, the shared expert as expert 256 with a sigmoid gate, and the slots
summed in slot order. Each (row, expert) pair gets the same bits in any window, so a drafted row equals the
serial step.

Each round first verifies a copied continuation when the context repeats eight or more tokens, and otherwise
a chain of up to three MTP drafts: the head reads the target's final normed state and the next token's
embedding, drafts with the target's keyed sampling rule over a draft vocabulary, and a chain stops after a
draft it gives under 30%. Decoding runs in buffers the engine keeps between requests, so verify chains and
head steps replay CUDA graphs captured once per width and context bucket.
Prompts prefill in chunks; the head absorbs every prompt row but the last. States are kept at the second
message's start, the last assistant turn's start and prompt ends, so a prompt sharing a system block or
extending a conversation resumes there with a fresh prefill's bits.

### Concurrent requests

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP --parallel 8 --name bench
```

`--parallel N` decodes up to N requests in shared rounds, and every reply equals the same request served alone
and its `"draft": false` run. A round verifies every stream's MTP chain or copied continuation in one forward;
the head absorbs every stream's kept rows in passes of up to 16 rows, then each draft level runs every stream
still drafting in passes of up to 16 rows, with one vocabulary-head read and one synchronization a pass, so a
stream drafts exactly what it drafts alone (`TF_MTP_BATCH=0` drafts one stream at a time, for comparison). A new prompt prefills 1,024 tokens a round
while the others decode, states are kept at message starts and prompt ends, and each stream's caches are sized
once, at admission. Startup admits N full prompt/reply windows, three kept prompt ends and the graph buffers
before loading; an explicit `--context` that does not fit is refused with the window that does. Rounds over
several streams run eagerly, as the 27B's do; a stream decoding alone replays the one-stream CUDA graphs, so a
lone request runs as fast as without `--parallel`.

On one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (NGC 26.07, torch 2.13, `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`,
checkpoint revision 81169a9), with 8 client threads over HTTP:

| | `--parallel 1` | `--parallel 4` | `--parallel 8` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Label JSON: 32 requests, public-domain passages, up to 1,410 tokens, default sampling | 904 tok/s | 1,255 tok/s | 1,476 tok/s |
| p50 / p95 latency | 8.6 / 9.1 s | 5.9 / 8.1 s | 5.1 / 7.7 s |
| Chat: 48 requests, up to 256 tokens, half greedy, half seeded | 427 tok/s | 859 tok/s | 1,094 tok/s |
| p50 / p95 latency | 3.3 / 3.9 s | 1.6 / 2.5 s | 1.2 / 2.0 s |
| Peak memory (nvidia-smi) | 22.3 GiB | 22.1 GiB | 22.9 GiB |

Every reply's token SHA-256 is the same at each N and with `"draft": false`. The label replies repeat their JSON,
so copied continuations keep 9.3 tokens a round per stream; chats keep 2.9. One client at a time gets 912 tok/s
on the label requests at `--parallel 8`, as a lone stream replays the graphs.

On one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0), checkpoint revision f84b054, the fleet benchmark's 4.2K-token prompt
(`bench.py` of spark-sglang-docker, 512 tokens, thinking on) gives 115.7 tok/s single-stream decode and 136.8 /
181.7 / 220.1 tok/s aggregate at 2 / 4 / 8 users, against 112.6 and 115.5 / 137.9 / 159.0 with `TF_MTP_BATCH=0` on
the same binary. The drafter's attention over its ring loads eight slots ahead of the fold, in the same order: a
4,200-slot ring takes 0.24 ms where it took 1.6 ms.

## NVIDIA's NVFP4 checkpoint (native CUDA)

The native CUDA engine serves `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` as downloaded, MTP drafts included:

```bash
tensorfold pull nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4@1355db6a052410cfd62085d94b58866fd0f2c3c5
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --drafter nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4
```

Every target projection runs as stored, with bf16 activations: the routed and shared experts' W4A16 NVFP4 codes and
e4m3 block scales with their global scale, the FP8 attention and DeltaNet projections with their per-tensor scale, the
W4A16 NVFP4 head, and bf16 `in_proj_a`/`in_proj_b`, router and embedding rows. Admission reads every expert
projection's effective recipe, so a checkpoint that quantizes one expert, the shared expert or the router differently
is refused before loading. The shared expert sits last in the routed table, as in the MLX layout. Decode rows run the
grouped NVFP4 expert kernel and prompt tiles its decode-sum form, so an expert pair has the same bits in a prompt
chunk, a verify window and a one-row step.

The checkpoint keeps its MTP layer in bf16 in its own shards. Without `mtp-4bit.safetensors` beside it, the drafter
quantizes that layer to MLX affine-4 at load, as Nemotron's ModelOpt drafter does; this changes only which rows a
round proposes, never a reply, and the startup log says so. With the file present, the file is read instead.

`--drafter` can also name a DFlash2 draft model: a directory whose `config.json` has `dflash_config` drafts with it,
any other with the target's MTP layer. `incoai/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash2` (revision `51ef7b69`, the SGLang DFlash
recipe's draft) reads eight target layers and is quantized to affine-4 at load:

```bash
hf download incoai/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash2 --revision 51ef7b6923ad6c14cb1bb41c37a9041446496ab6
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --drafter incoai/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash2
```

On the fleet benchmark's 4.2K-token prompt (`bench.py`, 512 tokens), one build with either drafter, it decodes 130.3
tok/s at one stream against MTP's 98.6, and gives 131.3 / 161.4 / 198.0 tok/s aggregate at 2 / 4 / 8 users against
124.7 / 170.6 / 208.4: it proposes more rows a round and keeps fewer of them, so it leads at one and two streams and
MTP leads under load. Every drafted reply equals its `"draft": false` run with either drafter.

The rules come from @gilby's Python port ([#345](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/345)): bf16 activations
for the W4A16 layers, the shared expert last in the table, and the MTP layer drafting through the target's head.

One DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, CUDA 13.0), checkpoint revision `1355db6a`, greedy unless noted, thinking off, 256 tokens:

| | Code | Chat |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `--no-drafts` (`tools/bench_openai.py`) | 66.6 tok/s | 66.2 tok/s |
| MTP drafts, one stream (`tools/bench_concurrent.py`) | 124.7 tok/s | 111.8 tok/s |
| MTP drafts, four streams, aggregate | 240.3 tok/s | 236.2 tok/s |

The model takes 20.3 GiB (20.9 GiB with the drafter) and loads in about 30 s. Every drafted reply equals its
`"draft": false` run (6 of 6, greedy and two seeded temperatures), every concurrent reply equals its solo run (40 of
40 at one and four streams, greedy and sampled), and a second turn that resumes from 8,192 cached tokens equals its
run on a server with the prompt cache off.

Cold prefill: a fresh server per size with `--prompt-cache-gib 0 --context 66560`, exact token arrays of Python
standard-library source from the checkpoint's own tokenizer, one request each through `tools/bench_cache.py
--require-cold` (time to first token):

| Prompt tokens | 2,048 | 8,192 | 32,768 | 65,536 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Time to first token | 0.38 s | 1.42 s | 6.59 s | 15.91 s |
| Prompt rate | 5,441 tok/s | 5,757 tok/s | 4,975 tok/s | 4,120 tok/s |

### A 1M-token window (YaRN)

The checkpoint was trained on 262,144 positions. Static YaRN rope with factor 4 serves 1,048,576, as SGLang's Spark
recipe does: either name the factor on the checkpoint as downloaded, or serve a copy whose `config.json` carries the
YaRN block (`rope_type: yarn`, `factor: 4.0`, `original_max_position_embeddings: 262144`,
`max_position_embeddings: 1048576`, the copy SGLang's `extend-qwen3.6-35b-a3b-nvfp4-context-1m` mod stages):

```bash
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --drafter nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --rope-yarn 4 --context 1048576
```

YaRN turns every position, so replies differ from plain rope at any length; without the flag or the block, every
byte is as before. Both ways give the same reply bytes. A 1M window takes 22.2 GiB a stream, so a GB10 admits two;
`--context 0` serves the whole window. The target's and the MTP layer's rope read the YaRN table; the DFlash2 drafter
keeps its own rope over its 2,048-row window, and a scaled rope in a config TensorFold cannot honor (HIP, Metal, the
DFlash2 drafters, another scaling type) is refused rather than read as plain rope.

On one GB10 with `--parallel 2`: drafted replies equal their `"draft": false` runs (6 of 6), concurrent ones their
solo runs, and a resumed second turn its fresh run. A passphrase 5% into a 300,000-token prompt comes back after
173 s of prefill (1,740 tok/s). A prompt of 1,048,512 tokens with the passphrase prefills in 1,546 s (680 tok/s),
returns it, and decodes its 64 tokens to the window's last position at 31 tok/s; one token more is refused with the
server's context-window error. The MTP drafter's cost over a continuation of many thousands of tokens is not measured.

Serial decoding (`--no-drafts`) runs at 86-88 tok/s. A round verifies up to four rows, and each row brings its

# Qwen3.8-27B

The native engine serves `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` on Metal, qualified on M5 Max and M3 Ultra, from
`zig/src/families/qwen27/`. It drafts with DFlash2 (`zig/src/families/qwen27/dflash/`) only when `--drafter` names
the drafter; without it the model decodes plain. On CUDA the native engine serves the MLX affine checkpoints (2, 3,
4, 5, 6 and 8 bits in groups of 64) from `zig/src/families/qwen3_5/cuda_*.zig`, with DFlash2 drafts and
`--kv-cache fp8`. It also reads ModelOpt NVFP4 and FP8 exports, and turboderp's EXL3 packs (`mul1` codebook) with
DFlash2 drafts through the shared EXL3 module, on one GPU.

The Metal dense loader reads aligned hidden, intermediate, layer and head counts from `config.json`.
It retains the existing attention/DeltaNet head layouts and layer schedule. The untied 9B geometry
(4096 hidden, 12288 intermediate, 32 layers) uses the same runtime-shaped projections; full checkpoint
reference, draft, resume, concurrency and performance qualification remains pending. The pinned 2B
continues to open its separate engine. Host header checks do not qualify another checkpoint.

```bash
tensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit
tensorfold pull z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --drafter z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 --name bench
```

A lone Metal DFlash2 stream can verify 16, 32 or 64 rows (`TF_QWEN27_WINDOW`), on tensor units and earlier chips.
Both device classes retain the 16-row default. Startup prices every row count through
the selected width, in a width-tagged cache.
Tensor-unit servers with several slots also measure wider unfused row shapes, through 64 rows when the context fits.
Shared allocation uses those prices beyond the lone window; the lone window retains its own measured prices.
Shared DFlash2 proposals use the allocator's grants before their batched pass, on both projection paths.
Lone, cost-pruned trees keep their learned landing counts; shared requests and their tails use the node log-probability prior.
Wide tensor-unit windows enable context copies by default; earlier chips keep copies opt-in.
A lone lane request may propose up to 15/31/63 tree nodes at 16/32/64 rows, including the drafter's next-most-likely siblings at each depth. It chooses a parent-closed prefix
by expected accepted tokens per measured millisecond in the common lane allocator, using its calibrated landing rates.
The proposal keeps every candidate available until that decision. Copies compete for the same verification window;
`TF_QWEN27_COPIES=0` disables them. The narrow tensor-unit default keeps copies off.
The masked drafter block is unchanged. Both device classes use the lane loop by default, including at 16 rows.
`TF_QWEN27_LANES=0` selects the legacy greedy shortcut; sampled requests retain the shared lane loop.
Startup names the selected lone loop and width beside the lane window and copy policy.
`tf-qwen27-bench --model DIR --widths costs` measures rows 1 through 64, with GPU and wall time including keep.
The wall price excludes the diagnostic's host logit hash and scan.

A greedy single-window lane pass gathers its matching taps with its target picks
in the final verify command buffer. The lane core still chooses
its authoritative keep. A matching prefix publishes its cache keep behind the next drafter frame; other paths
keep synchronously. Target-state users drain outstanding keeps before verification, prefill, release or reset.
The completed shared logit row is restored by an exact host word copy on that prefetched path.
The cache keep is encoded while the target verify runs, using its existing plans. It remains uncommitted until
the lane core supplies the authoritative path. Failure or a changed path drops the unused prepared buffer.
Selector scratch is bounded on the stack; only the three owned result arrays allocate. A full tree that loses
weak nodes during common pricing can offer context copies into the freed rows and price them once more.
Drafter scratch reserves 64 KiB chunks, so small context growth reuses its existing buffers.
On a single-slot server, a lone greedy lane starts its next draft at the following host step. Its target keep
can finish while the host publishes the current reply chunk, as in the serial loop. The saved request owns
its row indices and following tokens, and release or handoff cancels it. Shared, sampled and structured
requests retain their existing scheduling.

`TF_Q27_PASS_PROFILE=1` records host phases, GPU spans, command-buffer waits and commits, and forwarding-allocator
calls on the serving thread. The `q27_offer` and `q27_keep` lines show verified tree and copy rows and the kept path.
It preserves command boundaries. Leave it unset for throughput measurements.

The legacy lone shortcut handles greedy requests; sampled requests use the shared lane loop.
For bounded top-k requests, the BF16 host draw validates and selects candidates in one scan, using owned stack
scratch. The same FP64 keyed sampler applies temperature, top-p and min-p to the same ordered candidates.
Larger or unbounded cuts keep the general draw. Sampling time has its own pass-profile phase.

On Metal, M5 prompt passes request 2,048 rows when no other request is decoding; earlier chips keep the 512-row
default. The larger frame must fit the configured context and all streams beside loaded weights and the 8 GiB
margin, otherwise M5 keeps 512 rows. Startup reserves the actual prompt scratch sizes as well as stream caches.
Wide prompt frames keep separate 512-row activation scratch for small rounds, so decoding binds the small buffers.
Admission counts both banks.
`TF_QWEN27_WORKING_SET_BYTES` can lower the device working-set budget for admission checks. `TF_PROMPT_ROWS` selects another multiple of 16 from 128 to 2,048 for native serving.
Any other explicit value is refused at startup with its name, supplied text and accepted range; unset keeps the device default.
The internal model test interface can still use 16-row frames, which native shared serving does not admit.

Measured on an M5 Ultra (macOS 27) through the served API against mlx-lm 0.32.0 on the same checkpoint, raw prompts
from this repository's docs, 100 greedy tokens, prefill from the time to the first token:

| Prompt | Native prefill tok/s | mlx-lm prefill | Native decode tok/s | mlx-lm decode | Native with DFlash2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2k | 1325 | 1216 | 51.6 | 54.7 | 162-226 |
| 8k | 1269 | 1860 | 49.4 | 52.8 | 102 |
| 32k | 1171 | 1699 | 46.2 | 46.5 | 120 |

A plain one-row round is 19.5 ms on the M5 Ultra (`tf-qwen27-bench`, `QWEN27_ADVANCE`): its 321 projections read
14.1 GB in 16.2 ms, each shape at the K split it streams fastest at over every layer's matrix (`QWEN27_DISTINCT`;
a matrix called again sits in the system cache and misleads), and an undrafted one-row window is kept by its own
verify, as a prompt's rows are, rather than by a keep command buffer the host waited on (1.1 ms a token). Decode
attention scores each row's keys in 128-key chunks while the row's position is below 8,192 and 512-key chunks
from it (`attention_plan.chunkFor`, the chunk a row's node carries): at a 2k context a row's four key heads
were eight threadgroups of 512 keys on an 80-core GPU, 96 µs a layer. A row's chunks follow its own position, so
it merges the same partials as its one-row step in a chain, a tree, a window across 8,192 or beside other streams,
and drafted rows stay byte-equal to plain ones. A one-row round's
DeltaNet step is three dispatches a layer rather than five: `tf_delta_gdn_pre_step` writes each slot's next conv
window into its history as it reads it, so the commit and publication kernels go, and spreads a 128-wide head over
four simdgroups (each lane's squares still summed in order); 1.19 ms a token where 1.75 (`QWEN27_STEPCHECK` checks
the state, history and logits bytes against the general path).

## GGUF host adapter

`families/qwen27/gguf.zig` prepares the dense family's GGUF metadata and tensor identities on the host (#1920).
It accepts the observed qwen35 architecture, refuses the unproven qwen3 alias, uses core's typed views
and checks the fixed DeltaNet/attention geometry and layer schedule. Unknown computation keys, conflicting
patterns, missing tensors, wrong shapes and unsupported quantization are refused by key or tensor identity.

The observed ggml-org revision a316ea527fde32c12487be7574e2db5ac2ad2a7e has 40 metadata keys and 851 tensors.
Core's reader checks both Q4_K_M and Q8_0 header/index lists against the plan, with no missing names or shapes.
The testdata directory pins the extracted keys, tensor names/shapes and corresponding native Config input.
Host tests use those data files and need no checkpoint. Large tokenizer arrays record type/count only.

`Adapter.open` borrows the GGUF byte image and owns its index, destination names and compact affine arrays until
`deinit`. FP32 coefficient tables and group-16/32 layouts remain intact. Dense F32/F16/BF16 tensors borrow their
original bytes. GGUF matrices reverse dimension labels only; the convolution is reshaped without a transpose.
The host fixture checks every repacked value against independent source decoding for all ten core formats.
Core's documented signed-zero cancellation exception still applies; this does not extend its exactness claim.

Destination names are identities for future native loading, not ready-to-serve tensors. The `ssm_a` entry has an
explicit negative-exponential-decay role: its bytes are not relabelled as a usable logarithmic `A_log`. GDN head
ordering still needs checkpoint qualification. No coefficient is narrowed or group merged.

The final, input, post-attention, gated-linear, Q and K norm tensors carry the explicit `rms_gain` role.
Sixteen values per class from both GGUF variants match the supplied MLX BF16 gains after rounding to BF16.
Both checkpoints therefore store effective multiplicative gains here: the adapter neither adds nor subtracts one.
It preserves the GGUF F32 values, including the bits beyond the MLX BF16 representation. The paired sample fixture
checks all 96 values and the borrowed byte identities; this comparison does not qualify the remaining weights.
Existing Metal paths still need FP32 metadata and group-16 qualification, tokenizer/chat-template integration,
prepared-cache integration and real-model token/performance gates. GGUF model arguments receive a coming-later
refusal; the adapter does not enable end-to-end GGUF inference.

```sh
zig build test-qwen27-gguf-host test-gguf-host -j1 --summary all
```

## MLX

M5 tensor-unit GPUs run the lane decoder with draft trees. M1 through M4 use `row_forward` and the
packed row decoder with windows of up to 16 rows by default. Its existing 4-bit formats use `simd_qmm`,
and other supported affine formats use the general packed kernel. Both paths use the same arithmetic for serial
and drafted calls. Load-time checks determine usable window widths and shared-forward support.

The engine can share a round across requests while keeping each stream's attention, recurrent state and
sampling independent. DeltaNet commits replay the accepted path; attention commits retain only its keys.
Prompt chunks start at detected assistant-message boundaries and the second message when these are at
least 256 tokens beyond the previous chunk start, or after 2,048 tokens if no earlier boundary qualifies.
Prefix reuse resumes only at these chunk starts, so a follow-up can reuse the state before its previous
reply. The plan comes from rendered tokens; a template without detected markers uses 2,048-token chunks.

On the native pre-M5 lane loop, `TF_QWEN27_WINDOW=32` or `64` requests an experimental wider window and
`TF_QWEN27_COPIES=1` enables lane context copies. Defaults remain 16 and copies off until served qualification.
`TF_QWEN27_LANES=0` selects the legacy lone serial loop; its 16-row width and copy policy remain independent of
those lane switches. Startup logs the effective lone loop and width beside the configured lane window and copies.
The lane switch accepts only 0 or 1; the copy switch accepts only 0 or 1. Invalid settings name their variable.

## Weights other than 4-bit

The M5 lane kernels accept MLX affine 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6- and 8-bit projections in groups of 64.
The 4- and 8-bit paths read stored code tiles directly; the other widths expand their codes without changing values.
The 8-bit group-64 path also reuses the input producer's ordered FP32 group sums.
Mixed-width stacks keep separate calls where a fused projection needs one width. Examples include
`TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ2` and `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ4`.

On an M5 Ultra with 256 GiB, macOS 27.0.1 and Metal 32023.922, one plain stream measured:

| MLX affine, group 64 | Cold 2K prompt tok/s | Cold 8K prompt tok/s | 512-token decode tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4-bit | 1904.9 | 1856.9 | 47.7 |
| 8-bit | 768.5 | 760.0 | 29.3 |

These are two-process means from balanced main/candidate runs, with warm weights and pipelines,
raw token prompts, a 2,048-row prompt capacity and `--prompt-cache-gib 0`.
Revisions were `70ae7fac63274ff2eac54152031433374cb80f2f` for 4-bit and
`9ef68bd06f524d972d0e9b16ac0a49963528ed81` for 8-bit.
Main `985692e50` measured 648.5/643.1 prompt tok/s at 2K/8K for 8-bit; the byte reader and sum reuse improve
those rates by 18.5%/18.2%, retaining exact tokens and committed prompt-state bytes.
The remaining 8-bit prompt rate is 40–41% of 4-bit's, against a stored-weight byte ratio of 54.4%.
Dense projections still dominate its split-buffer profile, so weight size alone does not explain the prompt gap.
Decode here is a regression check; the two changes were measured together.

The packed row readers on Apple Silicon and the CUDA readers cover MLX affine 2/3/4/5/6/8-bit projections
with groups of 32/64/128, including mixed layers. CUDA also reads [EXL3 packs](#exl3-checkpoints-experimental).
A fused projection keeps its members separate where their bit width or group size differs. Unsupported formats
and tied embedding heads are refused from `config.json` before weight downloads and again at load; loaded
projections must also be covered by the selected decoder. `--lane-kernels on` requires M5 tensor units and
formats they read; `auto` falls back to the packed row decoder for the rest.
Lower weight precision does not guarantee faster decode or a fitting context.

`TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-8bit` serves natively with the same flags as the 4-bit checkpoint. On the same M5 Ultra
its weights take 27.5 GiB on disk against 15.0 GiB, and 38.3 GiB stays wired between requests against 25.5 GiB.
Its speeds are in the table above. For the fastest replies on a Mac, use the 4-bit checkpoint; take 8-bit when you
want the higher-precision weights.

The rest of this page describes the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Its flags, commands and paths belong to that
engine. @nood-co1, @jkuepker and @Arminova worked on its CUDA path; see [credits](../credits.md).

Experimental [packed affine formats](../quantization.md) include 8-bit and mixed layer precision.

The `qwen3_5` family combines Gated DeltaNet and full attention. The standard recipe below uses its
4-bit/group-64 checkpoint; the quantization guide lists the other affine formats it reads.

```bash
tensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --name bench
```

DFlash2 is used automatically once pulled. On MLX, `--drafter none` disables that draft model;
`--no-drafts` disables all drafts on either backend. CUDA requires DFlash2 unless `--no-drafts` is set.
The HIP engine runs no DFlash2 drafter yet: `serve --drafter` is refused before the engine opens the GPU or
loads any weights. Refusing DFlash2 does not turn off the engine's own drafts: the model's MTP head where the
checkpoint has one, and copies from the stream's own context. `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` has no MTP
head, so on HIP it drafts copies only. `--mtp-drafts 0` stops the MTP head's drafts alone; `--no-drafts` turns
both off and decodes plain.
The target verifies every proposed token against its own serial sample.

## CUDA

This section is the Python engine's (0.6.6). The native CUDA engine reads the MLX affine checkpoints, ModelOpt
NVFP4 and FP8 exports, and turboderp's EXL3 packs through the shared EXL3 module of #832; its own measurements are
not the ones below.

On CUDA the 27B serves NVFP4 and EXL3 checkpoints, and the MLX 4-bit checkpoint as the portable option: the same
files a Mac serves, and the only format two ranks read. `tensorfold serve` loads the checkpoint you name; it picks
none by itself. Use the [CUDA container setup](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/RUNBOOK.md#nvidia-gpus)
for any of them. Prompts take bf16
activations by default; what that costs against the FP8 prompt path (`--prefill-fp8`) depends on the format
([prompt precision](cuda.md#prompt-precision)):

| Checkpoint | Weights | Ranks | bf16 prompts against `--prefill-fp8` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` | NVFP4 MLP and head, FP8 attention and DeltaNet | one | not measured yet |
| `turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3` (3.00bpw) | EXL3 | one | unchanged: EXL3 prompts never took FP8 activations |
| `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit` | MLX affine 4-bit, groups of 64 | one or two | 0.73-0.82x from 2k to 128k |

Mia-AiLab publishes EXL3 packs of the model (`Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3`, `Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-2.0bpw`,
`Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-3.5bpw`) and an EXL3 DFlash2 drafter (`Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-EXL3-5.0bpw`); none
has been loaded here yet.

### NVFP4 checkpoints

The CUDA engine reads NVIDIA's ModelOpt export of the model (`nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`: NVFP4 MLP and head, FP8
attention and DeltaNet projections, bf16 embedding and gates) as it ships. The reader also takes
compressed-tensors NVFP4 and FP8 exports, checked on synthetic tensors only. Each projection is read by its tensors: NVFP4 codes with their e4m3 block scales and
FP8 bytes go to the device unchanged, and the lane matmuls turn them into exact bf16 operands (an e2m1 code times
its block scale fits bf16), so drafted replies equal `"draft": false` ones and prompts keep their bits in any
chunking. `--parallel` serves concurrent requests as on the MLX checkpoint, each reply equal to the same request
alone. One GPU: `--tp 2` stops at startup (two ranks read the MLX checkpoint), and so does `--vision` until image
input is qualified on this checkpoint.

```bash
tensorfold pull nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

Prompts take bf16 rows on a prompt GEMM that reads the stored bytes: each FP8 byte and each NVFP4 code times its
block scale is exact in bf16, summed in fp32 over the inputs, the tensor scale last. `--prefill-fp8` restores the FP8
prompt matmul (FP8 projections as stored, NVFP4 ones staged to e4m3 once a chunk, a step that rounds by 2^-4 at most,
and e4m3 activations). Decode, measured on one DGX Spark (GB10) through `tensorfold serve` against the MLX 4-bit
checkpoint on the same engine and box, alternating (MLX, NVFP4, NVFP4, MLX), 64 tokens, five seeds, medians:

| Cell | NVFP4 | MLX 4-bit | vLLM MTP=3 (NVFP4) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code, sampled | 47.1 tok/s | 57.8 tok/s | 23.4 tok/s |
| Chat, sampled | 38.2 tok/s | 50.0 tok/s | 25.4 tok/s |
| Code, greedy | 47.2 tok/s | 53.9 tok/s | 25.8 tok/s |
| Chat, greedy | 38.3 tok/s | 50.1 tok/s | 24.7 tok/s |

The table predates a fix to the FP8 lane matmul (its pipeline stages now start on 128-byte lines), which took a
12-row verify from 103 ms to 85 against the MLX checkpoint's 84, although the attention and DeltaNet weights are 8-bit
(16.3 GB read a token against 14.4). Tokens a round match (4.0-5.2). Cold prefill ran 1,834 / 1,872 / 1,779 / 1,563 /
1,240 tok/s at 2k / 8k / 16k / 32k / 64k on the FP8 prompt path (today's `--prefill-fp8`), level with the MLX
checkpoint's. The startup estimate is 62.5 GiB at the 262,144-token window.

### EXL3 checkpoints (experimental)

The CUDA engine also reads turboderp's EXL3 packs of the model (`turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3`, a branch per size,
`mul1` codebook, 6-bit head) through the shared EXL3 module ([EXL3 weights](exl3.md)) and drafts with
`z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`. One GPU: two ranks read the MLX checkpoint. Download a size by its branch, then
serve the folder:

```bash
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3', revision='3.00bpw', local_dir='qwen27b-exl3-3.00bpw')"
tensorfold pull z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
tensorfold serve qwen27b-exl3-3.00bpw --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

Verify windows use the row-invariant EXL3 linear, so drafted replies equal `"draft": false` ones; prompts use the
EXL3 prompt path (W_q decoded once a chunk, a fixed-tile GEMM), whose bits do not depend on chunking, so the
engine keeps prompt ends as it does for the MLX checkpoint. The drafter reads the target's 6-bit head over its
draft vocabulary by slicing the head's 128-column strips as stored: its logits are the target's, bit for bit.

Measured on one DGX Spark (GB10) through `tensorfold serve`, the 3.00bpw pack against the MLX 4-bit checkpoint on
the same engine and box, the [public benchmark command](README.md#measurements), medians of 15 runs a cell:

| Cell | EXL3 3.00bpw | MLX 4-bit | vLLM MTP=3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code, sampled | 83.4 tok/s | 57.5 tok/s | 23.4 tok/s |
| Chat, sampled | 44.2 tok/s | 49.7 tok/s | 25.4 tok/s |
| Code, greedy | 64.5 tok/s | 53.6 tok/s | 25.8 tok/s |
| Chat, greedy | 39.9 tok/s | 50.0 tok/s | 24.7 tok/s |

A 12-row round costs 75 ms on the pack against 84 on the MLX checkpoint (10.1 GB of weights a token against
14.4). The chat cells keep fewer drafted tokens a round (3.0-3.3 against 4.2), since DFlash2 was trained on the
unquantized model. Cold prefill runs 880-970 tok/s from 2k to 16k and 720-890 at 32k-64k, about two thirds of the
MLX checkpoint's bf16 prompts and half its `--prefill-fp8` ones. The engine and drafter take 13.2 GiB after loading;
a 64k prompt peaks at 28 GiB allocated. Other branches of the pack load through the same path; only 3.00bpw is
measured here.

### MLX 4-bit, one or two ranks

One or two ranks are supported. Pull the model and drafter on every rank, then start rank 1 before rank 0:

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --tp 2 --rank 1 --master 192.0.2.1
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --tp 2 --rank 0 --master 192.0.2.1 --name bench --host 0.0.0.0
```

The verify matmul fixes reduction order by weight shape. Tree attention reads only committed keys and the
node's own path; recurrent commits replay that path. Two-rank reductions gather fp32 partials and add in
rank order. Each rank count has its own serial reference. See the
[CUDA kernel map](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/families/qwen3_5/cuda/README.md).

### Concurrent requests

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --parallel 16 --context 8192 --name bench
```

`--parallel N` decodes up to N requests in shared rounds: each stream verifies its own DFlash2 tree in one
forward, and every reply equals the same request served alone. A new prompt prefills 1,024 tokens a round
while the other streams decode. On Metal, a reply that would end well before a long prompt goes first: the prompt
lends it at most a quarter of its own time, and `--decode-share` or `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ORDER` overrides this. States kept at message starts let prompts that share a system prompt resume
there, and each stream's caches are sized once, at admission.

On one DGX Spark, with the workload from issue #38 (48 chat requests of 3,000 to 5,100 tokens sharing a
2,900-token system prompt, up to 512 tokens each, greedy, all sent at once), TensorFold serves 161.7 tok/s at
16 in flight with a 25.4 GiB peak (nvidia-smi). vLLM with `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`, MTP=3, prefix caching
and `--max-num-seqs 16` serves 132.1 tok/s at 51.7 GiB on the same Spark. At 8 and 4 in flight TensorFold
serves 147.5 and 112.0 tok/s.
[`tools/shared_prefix_prompts.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/tools/shared_prefix_prompts.py)
(at the `v0.6.6` tag) builds the workload and
`tools/shared_prefix_load.py` sends it (`--concurrency`, `--mem` for the memory peak).

### Structured output

With `pip install 'tensorfold[grammar]'` (xgrammar), serving on one or two GPUs enforces `response_format` and the
`guided_*` fields: drafts the grammar rejects are cut and rows are masked by their paths' grammar before sampling, so
drafted, serial and concurrent replies stay equal. See [the API reference](../api.md#structured-output).

## Calibration and checks

The draft calibration metadata names public prompts. When regenerating it, start its server with
`--port 8473 --name qwen27` so the collection client reaches the named endpoint. Pass the saved full
provenance object with `--source` to
[`tools/fit_draft_calibration.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/tools/fit_draft_calibration.py)
(at the `v0.6.6` tag); retain model and drafter revisions.

Kernel tests check rows alone and in windows, tree paths and committed state. Release checks must also
compare drafted/serial, resumed/fresh and concurrent/solo requests with thinking on and off and tools.
Decode rate, prefill, concurrency and peak-memory results are TBD [release-0.3.5].

### Long-document prompt reuse

The lane cache can keep one additional state inside a final user message of at least 8,192 tokens. It leaves
at least 2,048 tokens outside the snapshot key for a different question following the same document. Qwen27
Metal chooses an existing request chunk start, so the optional prompt bank and its fallback both already
cut there. A direct caller supplying no chunk starts skips this optional state instead of guessing a cut.
Endpoint, rewind and shared states have priority within the same byte and slot caps. Retained-state occupancy
is published in `tensorfold:prompt_cache_states` and `tensorfold:prompt_cache_bytes`; restored tokens also count
in `tensorfold:prompt_tokens_cached_total`. Synthetic host checks cover the two-request pattern and exact
output. Real-model parity and TTFT for this state still need the Metal gate.
# Qwen3.8 Flash Next

The `qwen4_exp` family has Gated DeltaNet, sparse attention, MoE, hyper-connections and hashed n-gram
embeddings. Native Metal serves supported MLX affine checkpoints, including the 4-bit/group-32 MTP checkpoint.
Startup checks separate load and cold pack-construction budgets against the RAM/GPU-bounded ceiling.
A validated cached pack or a supplied pack skips construction pricing; supplied packs retain their existing source check.
The load plan counts retained raw/packed weights, both prompt planes, selectors, KV/state, configured vision and
requested storage, with the shared runtime reserve. Unused source-file padding is not retained model storage.
`info` prints the base text load and cold pack budgets separately; these are conservative plans, not measured fit results.
A 128 GB Mac may not hold the complete load even when the weight files fit.
Use a smaller quantization or raise the OS wired limit where supported; fewer streams or a shorter context reduce
additional session storage. Native Metal's `--ple-on-ssd` leaves the n-gram tables in the checkpoint and reads their
rows from SSD in batches ([Exact Fluid Subgraph Residency](fluid-subgraph-residency.md)). CUDA also serves the 4-bit
checkpoint ([Flash Next on CUDA](flash-next-cuda.md)), and HIP serves it and two oQ checkpoints on a Strix Halo iGPU
([native HIP](#native-hip-on-a-strix-halo-igpu)).

```bash
tensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP --name bench --temperature 0
```

For native serving, see the [Metal runbook](../../RUNBOOK.md#flash-next-and-paired-metal-serving).
Native Flash Next on CUDA serves the MLX 4-bit group-32 checkpoint on the built-in kernels: see
[Flash Next on CUDA](flash-next-cuda.md) ([#472](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/issues/472)).

The sections below describe the Python 0.6.6 engine, available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). Their flags, variables and paths are that engine's,
and the native binary refuses the flags it does not list in `capabilities --json`. Contributors to them are named in
[credits](../credits.md).
The MLX section uses `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`; CUDA checkpoints are listed below.

On MLX, a supported conversion without the head runs without MTP drafting. On CUDA, pass `--no-drafts`
for such a conversion; the default positive draft depth otherwise refuses the missing head.

## MLX execution

N-gram tables stay in host file mappings when the checkpoint's model files exceed 75% of the GPU's
recommended working set. `TF_NGRAM_HOST=1` forces this mode; `TF_NGRAM_HOST=0` keeps the tables in MLX.
Startup admission uses the same choice as the loader and subtracts the mapped weights, scales and biases
from the checkpoint's size. For the 4-bit checkpoint, about 29.8 GiB of its 105.4 GiB is mapped,
leaving a conservative 75.6 GiB resident-weight estimate. With that checkpoint, the Python engine selects host mode on an
M4 Max with 128 GiB, whose process budget is 89.6 GiB, including the 3 GiB process reserve.

Mapped pages still use RAM while cached. The loader prefetches them after its initial forwards; macOS
can reclaim them, and subsequent lookups may read from disk. The remaining weights must fit the MLX
budget, and the server sizes context from runtime cache and workspace needs. `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB`
can lower or raise the default budget, capped by physical RAM and the GPU's recommended working set.
For example, `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB=110` gives a 128 GiB M4 Max a 110 GiB process budget and
107 GiB for MLX. An explicit context must still fit the startup estimate; a larger budget does not
establish full-window inference or keep every mapped page resident. `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_LIMIT_GB` is the Python
engine's; the native binary does not read it.
After measuring shared rounds, the runtime releases the probes' rollback buffers before sizing prompt
memory, so those unused states do not reduce the available context.

Fused kernels handle hyper-connections, routing, experts, recurrence and sparse attention. Row-exact
projections and stable routing ties keep each verify row independent of the other rows. M5 GPUs use
the lane matmul; M1 through M4 use the per-row projection and hyper-connection kernels by default. Rejected tails
restore recurrent state, n-gram history and attention state, including incomplete pooled blocks.
The load-time row check disables drafting when windows do not reproduce serial steps.

The prefill path uses sparse selected-key attention, fused hyper-connections and n-gram lookups,
stacked DeltaNet projections and sorted expert rows. It submits bounded groups of layers to limit live
workspace. Compatible prefill matmul kernels check against MLX; unsupported paths use MLX's kernels.
`TF_FLASH_PREFILL=0` selects the reference prefill path for comparison. @quigles1977 added this prefill path in
[#29](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/29); the native `zig/kernels/metal/prefill/fn_prompt.metal` carries
its hyper-connection kernels.

Flash Next checkpoints may name the n-gram tables `shard_N` or `shards.N`.
All shards in one index must use the same spelling; the loader accepts either spelling.

Prefill and decode can round differently. The chunk planner uses detected assistant-message starts and
the second message when at least 256 tokens follow the previous chunk start, otherwise cutting after
the chunk chosen at startup: the largest of 8,192 (with tensor units), 4,096 and 2,048 tokens whose
working memory leaves room for 128K tokens of context, or the model's window if smaller. Where none
fits, the prompt path queues one layer at a time instead of two. Cold and resumed prompts use the same
rendered-token boundaries, and reuse starts only at these cuts. Templates without detected markers use
the same fixed chunks. A chunk's sorted expert rows reach MLX's gather in slices of at most 32,768
(its M5 kernel keeps row offsets in 16 bits through MLX 0.32.2). Snapshots include the prefill
path, resolved matmul route and GPU identity; changing arithmetic requires a fresh cache.

Load-time shared-forward checks compare each stream with its own call. A failed check limits forwards
to one stream, while successful checks allow the lane engine to combine requests.

## Native Metal shared sessions

The native 6-bit MTP engine uses shared target rounds with an explicit `--parallel N` above one; `--parallel auto`, the default, keeps the single-reply driver, whose lone decode is 1.0.12's (a lone request in a shared session decoded 7% slower on an M3 Ultra). Without `FLASHNEXT_SLOT_CONTEXTS`, an explicit count fixes the number of sessions, eight here:

```bash
tensorfold-native serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP \
  --context 16384 --temperature 0 --parallel 8
```

Each request holds its own recurrent state, attention cache, n-gram history and MTP cache. The scheduler packs
up to 16 target rows, including draft rows, into one layer loop. Projections and experts process those rows
together; recurrence, convolution and attention read each request's own state. Every stream's MTP drafts share one command buffer; `FZ_BATCH_MTP_SERIAL=1` restores serial drafting.
New requests join between rounds, and cancelling a request releases its slot for another request.

An explicit count that does not fit is refused, as below. Explicit `--parallel 1`, `--learn`, and the two-Mac path retain their supported driver. Shared sessions run on one Mac; `--parallel N` above one with `--speed-up` or `--learn` is refused. Use `--parallel 1` for the two-Mac link.

The ceiling is 70% of RAM, or `FLASHNEXT_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` (GB, up to the GPU's recommended working set). It covers the
server's whole footprint: the model, the sessions and the prompt cache. Left out, `--prompt-cache-gib` takes what the
sessions leave under it; a given budget must fit under the same ceiling. `--prompt-cache-over-cap` does not bypass model startup
admission or the runtime reserve.

Additional slots allocate caches for the selected context. Startup reserves their metadata and the prompt-cache
budget, then checks the physical footprint before accepting requests. A fixed slot count that does not fit is
refused; lower the count, context or prompt-cache budget. `--prompt-cache-over-cap` overrides only the prompt-cache
budget. Shared sessions draw sampled tokens with the same GPU sampler as the single-Mac `--parallel 1` path.
Each packed window uses its own seed, sampling settings and absolute token positions. The two-Mac path remains
greedy only. The model gate below must verify sampled token parity across routes, drafting and batch composition.

Shared sessions enforce structured output (`response_format`, the `guided_*` fields, `tool_choice: "required"` and a
named function; [API](../api.md#structured-output)) with `libtfgrammar` beside the binary. Before the argmax and the
draw, `fz_mask_rows` sets each constrained row's disallowed logits to -inf (`families/flashnext/grammar.zig`); the
first token is drawn on the host from the prompt's last row among the grammar's tokens, as the GPU draws it. Rounds
with no constrained stream skip the mask. The single-reply driver (`--parallel 1`, the two-Mac path) answers a
structured request with HTTP 400.

`--context` past the trained 262,144 tokens, up to 1,048,576, rotates with static YaRN x4 (transformers'
`_compute_yarn_parameters`: factor 4 over the trained window, beta 32 and 1, cos and sin scaled by 0.1 ln 4 + 1) in
every rotary kernel, attention, the indexer's queries and pooled keys and the MTP head alike, for every prompt; at
262,144 or less the plain rotary runs as before. Qwen recommends YaRN only where long prompts need it, since static
scaling can cost short texts. Only the engine's own session holds the long window; on shared sessions the others hold
262,144 tokens (`FLASHNEXT_SLOT_CONTEXTS` sets other sizes), and a request longer than that takes the long one. Past the trained window prompt chunks take fewer rows, so the prompt selector's scores keep the 2 GiB they take at
262,144. The two-Mac path refuses such a window. On an M5 Ultra (6-bit MTP checkpoint, `--parallel 2 --vision`,
1,048,576 and 262,144-token sessions and an 8 GiB prompt cache: 203.2 GiB wired, `FLASHNEXT_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=240`),
needles were found at 138,830, 553,139 and 1,032,827 prompt tokens (34 s, 169 s and 417 s to the first token, 4,038 to
2,479 tok/s), drafted replies equal `"draft": false` at 316,469 tokens, and a short request beside a 666,334-token
prompt equals its reply alone (it waits for that prompt's pass, about 205 s). One stream decodes at 137 to 216 tok/s
there, against 142 to 214 at 262,144 (`bench/ruler.py`, the qwen recipe's).

The shared host's residency set includes the engine, session caches and metadata, shared hidden rows and later
prompt snapshots. Residency uses the same validated load limit as the host, with a 2 GiB margin inside it for
growing buffers. The default stays at 70% of RAM; `FLASHNEXT_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` can raise or lower that ceiling, capped
by RAM and the GPU working set. A refused set leaves the server running without it, and `--prompt-cache-over-cap`
does not raise the residency ceiling. `FLASHNEXT_NO_RESIDENCY=1` disables the set. With a prompt cache, warm turns
keep the end of a reply as the single-request host does. Idle latency and throughput need fresh measurements.

The checkpoint gate compares shared replies with fresh legacy replies, with drafting off and on, then checks
prompt admission, cancellation, slot reuse and a restored prefix while another request remains active:

```bash
zig build tf-flashnext-batch
zig-out/bin/tf-flashnext-batch --sampling-only
python tools/zig/flashnext_batch_prompts.py MODEL_DIR /tmp/flashnext-prompts
FZ_N=128 zig-out/bin/tf-flashnext-batch MODEL_DIR /tmp/flashnext-prompts/*.json
FZ_SAMPLE=1 FZ_N=128 zig-out/bin/tf-flashnext-batch MODEL_DIR /tmp/flashnext-prompts/*.json
```

These device gates require exclusive GPU use. `--sampling-only` uses synthetic logits and checks distinct seeds,
positions and row offsets against the shared GPU-rule reference, including untouched greedy and spare rows.
`FZ_SAMPLE=1` repeats the model gate with fixed seeds per prompt. Compilation alone does not pass either gate.
For a served comparison with identical requests and settings:

```bash
zig build native
python tools/zig/flashnext_batch_serve.py zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native \
  MODEL_DIR /tmp/flashnext-prompts /tmp/flashnext-served \
  --parallel 1,4 --context 16384 --require-shared-rounds
```

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's `lib/` or `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`; prepare DIR with `git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar` (use the native build's same `--prefix` for grammar).

The served gate starts one server at a time on loopback port 52417. `default` omits `--parallel`; `auto` passes
it explicitly. Each block uses the same context and requests, including thinking on and off. It compares response
bodies, token counts and native token fingerprints with the serial reference and records wall time and peak
running and waiting requests. `--require-shared-rounds` also requires multi-stream GPU forwards in the batch log
during those requests. Running requests alone do not prove shared rounds. The default and `auto` serve on the
single-reply driver, so that gate fails for them; an explicit count that falls back to one session fails it too.

End-to-end time includes prompts. The shared-round check enables `FZ_BATCH_LOG`, so its times include logging;
omit that option for a separate timing run. Repeat into a fresh output directory with `--context 65536` or another
context that fits the checkpoint. The checkpoint gate separately checks prompt admission, cancellation and reuse.

## CUDA

On CUDA Flash Next serves NVFP4 and EXL3 checkpoints, and the MLX 4-bit checkpoint as the portable option: the same
files a Mac serves, and the only format two ranks and `--ple-on-ssd` read. `tensorfold serve` loads the checkpoint
you name; it picks none by itself. Use the [Python CUDA setup](cuda.md#python-06-cuda-families)
for the container and pinned 0.6.6 installation. Prompts
take bf16 activations by default; what that costs against the FP8 prompt path (`--prefill-fp8`) depends on the
format ([prompt precision](cuda.md#prompt-precision)):

| Checkpoint | Weights | bf16 prompts against `--prefill-fp8` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`925d7be6`), a mirror of local-inference-lab's export | NVFP4 routed experts, MXFP8 elsewhere and in the n-gram table | the next row's kernels; not timed on its own |
| `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`7c4f1bc1`) | NVFP4 routed experts, MXFP8 elsewhere | 0.94-1.03x from 2k to 64k |
| `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`7b719225`) | NVFP4 routed experts, bf16 elsewhere | unchanged: no FP8 prompt kernel |
| `turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3` (`3.05bpw_h5_ng5`) | EXL3 | unchanged: EXL3 prompts never took FP8 activations |
| `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP` | MLX affine 4-bit | unchanged: its prompts were already bf16 |

TensorFold finds Mia-AiLab's export by its `model_type` (`qwen3_8_flash_next`) and serves it like
local-inference-lab's.

### NVFP4 checkpoints

@tournierjc brought these checkpoints to the Python engine's CUDA path in
[#67](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/67). The CUDA engine reads published ModelOpt NVFP4 exports as they
ship, MTP head included, on one GPU:

```bash
tensorfold serve local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

| Checkpoint (revision) | Routed experts | DeltaNet, attention, shared expert | n-gram table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`7c4f1bc1`) | NVFP4 | MXFP8 | NVFP4 rows |
| `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`7b719225`) | NVFP4 | bf16 | FP8 rows |
| `Mia-AiLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`925d7be6`), a mirror of local-inference-lab's export | NVFP4 | MXFP8 | MXFP8 rows |

The loader reads each linear by its tensors. An NVFP4 weight is an E2M1 code times its e4m3 scale (a block of 16
inputs) times the tensor's fp32 `weight_scale_2`; an MXFP8 weight is an e4m3 byte times a power of two (a block of
32). Both products fit bf16 exactly, so decode multiplies them in bf16 MMAs, adds each block's products times its
scale in block order and applies the tensor's scale once; the K split depends on the shape alone, so drafted
windows keep serial decoding's bits. Prompts run the MXFP8 linears on bf16 rows and the stored bytes, each byte
times its power of two exact in bf16 and one fp32 sum over the inputs (`--prefill-fp8`: the FP8 prompt matmul).
Tests check the kernels against an fp64 reference built by an independent numpy dequantizer
([`src/tensorfold/cuda/nvfp4/format.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/nvfp4/format.py)
at the `v0.6.6` tag; the native engine's fp64 reference is `zig/src/core/quant/nvfp4.zig`). Both exports store their
RMSNorm weights centred (gamma - 1), and the loader
tells centred from uncentred norms by their stored values. An n-gram table's shards must share one layout, or the
load stops.

Block-scaled FP8 linears (ModelOpt `FP8_PB_WO`, the DeepSeek-style layout: e4m3 bytes and an fp32 `weight_scale_inv`
per 128x128 block) are read too, from [#126](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/126) by @jschmied, who also
ported them to the native CUDA engine (`zig/src/cuda/fp8.zig`).
Decode keeps the e4m3 bytes in the FP8 GEMM's fragment order and each (64 inputs,
column)'s block scale as fp32; the lane matmul multiplies a 64-input stage in bf16 MMAs (e4m3 fits bf16 exactly) and
adds the stage's products times its scale in stage order, so the stored weight is exact and rows stay independent of
the row count, as for the other formats. Prompts take the same lane matmul (bf16 activations, the stored bytes, fp32
sums); `--prefill-fp8` runs the FP8 prompt matmul over the same bytes with the block scales as bf16 group scales. A
projection stack that mixes block FP8 with bf16 (`in_proj_b` and `in_proj_a` beside `in_proj_qkv` and `in_proj_z`;
the indexer's projection beside q/k/v) runs each part on its own kernel into its columns. A block-FP8 `lm_head`
stays on the lane matmul with its stored bytes, for decode rows and a prompt's head rows; the draft head's rows are
dequantized and requantized to 4 bits, as for every NVFP4 checkpoint (drafts only). Checked on a local ModelOpt
export with NVFP4 experts, block-FP8 DeltaNet and attention projections, an FP8 n-gram table and NVFP4 MTP experts:
drafted replies equal `"draft": false` ones (six pairs, 2k-16k-token prompts, greedy and sampled), resumed prompts
equal fresh ones, and each reply of 2 and 4 concurrent requests equals the same request alone. On one Spark, one
request, it decodes 6-27% faster than the same weights dequantized to bf16 on the bf16 path (code 59.2 against 49.1
tok/s greedy, chat 36.6 against 34.6 greedy and 41.6 against 32.8 sampled).

The routed experts run on a grouped NVFP4 kernel that reads the step's routing plan on the GPU, so a decode graph
captured for one step's experts replays another step's. A test decodes a checkpoint whose expert picks change every
step with graphs on and off and compares the tokens; on local-inference-lab's and RadixArk's exports, replies with
the decode graphs equal replies without them.

local-inference-lab's and RadixArk's exports were served with `tensorfold serve` and checked: drafted replies equal
`"draft": false` ones (nine pairs, 2k-16k-token prompts, greedy and sampled), resumed prompts equal fresh ones, and
each reply of concurrent requests (`--parallel 4`) equals the same request alone. Mia-AiLab's mirror loads and serves
through the same code; its replies have not been checked on their own.

Not supported here:
- `--ple-on-ssd` on an NVFP4 checkpoint stops at startup: the NVFP4 exports' tables stay memory-mapped.
- `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (186 GB; bf16 linears and n-gram table) has the RadixArk layout apart
  from its bf16 table, which the loader reads, but the whole checkpoint has not been loaded or served here, so it
  is not listed as tested.

### EXL3 checkpoints (experimental)

@vcruz305 wrote this path, the shared EXL3 module and the Flash Next loader, in
[#42](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/42). The native engine serves no EXL3 pack yet; its reference decoder
is `zig/src/core/exl3_format.zig`, with a Metal projection in `zig/src/core/exl3_projection.zig`.

The CUDA engine also serves EXL3 packs of Flash Next (`quant_method: exl3`) on one GPU through the shared EXL3
module ([EXL3 weights](exl3.md)): any codebook, and a width per tensor, so mixed-K packs whose experts range from
2 to 8 bits within a layer load as they are. turboderp publishes a 3.05 bpw pack on the branch `3.05bpw_h5_ng5`.
Download that branch, then serve the folder:

```bash
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3', revision='3.05bpw_h5_ng5', local_dir='flashnext-exl3-3.05bpw')"
python -m tensorfold.cuda.exl3.inspect flashnext-exl3-3.05bpw   # bits per tensor, from the headers
tensorfold serve flashnext-exl3-3.05bpw --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

A pack maps its n-gram table from its own file and runs on one GPU: `--tp 2` and `--ple-on-ssd` are for the MLX
checkpoint, and an EXL3 pack refuses both.

- Dense projections (attention, DeltaNet, the MTP head's fc layers, the head) run on the row-invariant EXL3
  linear ([`src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/linear.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/linear.py)).
  Routed experts and the shared expert (as expert 512 of the same table) run on the grouped EXL3 expert kernel
  ([`src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/experts.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/experts.py)),
  each expert matrix at its own width. The fp32 router,
  its top-k with id tie-break, and the write-back in slot order are the MLX path's.
- The tensors a pack leaves unquantized (hyper-connection down / inject / up, DeltaNet `in_proj_a/b`, the n-gram
  key and value) run on an fp16 Triton matmul whose tiles and K split depend only on the shape. No cuBLAS.
- The packs store every centred RMSNorm weight as gamma - 1: the hyper-connection norms, q/k norms, the
  indexer's, the n-gram branch's three and the MTP head's two input norms. The loader detects this and adds 1
  in fp32. Checked tensor by tensor against the MLX checkpoint: after the offset the largest difference is
  0.031 (hyper-connection norms) and 0.004 (n-gram norms). DeltaNet's gated norm, `A_log`, `dt_bias`, the conv weights and the router equal the MLX values.
- The 128 `ple.ngram_embedding.shard_*` tensors are named `.trellis` but are not EXL3 tiles. They use
  ExLlamaV3's n-gram row codec: a row is one fp16 scale followed by 160 values of K bits in a tail-biting mul1
  trellis, and each head has an fp16 bias. The engine decodes a window's rows as ExLlamaV3's `ngram_dequant`
  does, bit for bit (tested at 2 to 8 bits). The rows stay in the checkpoint, memory-mapped.
- turboderp's pack keeps the MTP head's final mixer in `mtp_hyper_connection_mixer_patch.safetensors`,
  outside the index, and the reader loads it from there. A pack that carries the MTP layer drafts with it.
  For the draft head, the head's rows for the draft vocabulary are decoded through the EXL3 linear and
  requantized to 4-bit groups of 32. This affects only which drafts are proposed; verification uses the full
  EXL3 head.
- Prompt chunks decode each dense projection's weights once a chunk and multiply with a fixed-tile GEMM, so a
  prompt's rows do not depend on its chunking; routed experts run the grouped kernel in 1,024-row windows.

Measured on one DGX Spark (GB10) through `tensorfold serve`: the 3.05 bpw pack against the MLX 4-bit checkpoint
on the same engine and box, the [public benchmark command](README.md#measurements), medians of 10 runs a cell
(two sessions of each, alternated):

| Cell | EXL3 3.05 bpw | MLX 4-bit | vLLM MTP=3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code, sampled | 80.8 tok/s | 76.5 tok/s | 42.4 tok/s |
| Chat, sampled | 59.4 tok/s | 62.7 tok/s | 33.2 tok/s |
| Code, greedy | 77.7 tok/s | 74.2 tok/s | 40.9 tok/s |
| Chat, greedy | 69.2 tok/s | 72.4 tok/s | 37.6 tok/s |

Drafted replies equal `"draft": false` ones (9 of 9), resumed prompts equal fresh ones, and four concurrent
