streams equal their solo runs. Cold prefill runs 930-970 tok/s from 2k to 64k, about 0.4x the MLX checkpoint's
2,300-2,500: the routed experts decode their tiles again for every 16 rows. The pack's weights take 52 GB of GPU
memory against the MLX checkpoint's 81 GB, so on a Spark the default window is the full 262,144 tokens (57.6 GiB
allocated after loading) where the MLX checkpoint's is about 74,000; the 32.6 GB n-gram table stays in the page
cache.

#### Against ExLlamaV3 on the same pack

These comparisons were made when the path was written, on the 0.3.4.1 engine, with two packs: turboderp's
3.05 bpw and SAGE, a mixed-K 4.15 bpw pack the contributor built (2 to 8 bits a matrix; not published).

The first comparison is teacher-forced over 2,048 positions: the first 2,049 tokens of ExLlamaV3's
`eval/eval_texts`, all fed in one pass. TensorFold decodes in 64-row windows. ExLlamaV3 is the fork at 249f22a
with its mixed-K expert path. The token ids are the same for all three checkpoints, which share one
tokenizer.

| | top-1 agreement | TensorFold NLL | ExLlamaV3 NLL | TensorFold top-1 acc | ExLlamaV3 top-1 acc |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SAGE 4.15 bpw (mixed-K, 2-8 bits) | 0.954 | 1.0640 | 1.0642 | 0.718 | 0.720 |
| turboderp 3.05 bpw | 0.959 | 0.8510 | 0.8506 | 0.774 | 0.779 |
| TensorFold, MLX 4-bit (same tokens) | | 1.0574 | | 0.726 | |

The two engines' mean NLLs agree within 0.0005. The positions where they pick different tokens are close
calls. Where ExLlamaV3's top two logits are at least 0.5 apart, the engines agree on 98.8% (SAGE) and 99.1%
(3.05) of positions; at a gap of at least 1.0 they agree on 99.7%. ExLlamaV3 is no closer to itself when the
batch shape changes: rerunning the first 1,025 tokens alone, instead of as part of all 2,049, it agrees with its
own full pass on 96.4% (SAGE) and 97.2% (3.05) of positions. At the same positions TensorFold agrees with
ExLlamaV3's full pass on 95.5% and 97.0%. The per-position NLL difference has a median of 0.018 and 0.011.

On TensorFold's side, the Python engine's
[`tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py)
checks the following against the pack that
`TENSORFOLD_EXL3_FLASHNEXT` names, cut to 4 layers plus the head and the MTP head:

- a window of 1 to 128 rows gives one-row steps' logits bit for bit;
- MTP-drafted decoding gives serial decoding's tokens, eager and in CUDA graphs, greedy and sampled;
- a real layer's experts match an fp64 reference and are row-invariant.

Through `tensorfold serve` on the full packs, each reply was requested with `"draft": false` and again with
drafts. The prompts were the benchmark's two, the raw prompt as chat, and two 256-token chats, each greedy and
with seeds 1234 to 1238. On both packs, 30 of 30 replies had identical token-id SHA-256s. A drafted round
emitted 2.93 tokens on average on SAGE and 3.16 on 3.05. From a [v0.6.6](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6) checkout:

```bash
TENSORFOLD_EXL3_FLASHNEXT=flashnext-exl3-3.05bpw pytest -q tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py
```

#### Serial speed against ExLlamaV3

These are decode tokens per second after the first token, on one Spark. Each cell is one stream, 64-token replies,
and the median of seeds 1234 to 1238 after one warm-up. Every engine went through the same client:
`python tools/bench_openai.py http://127.0.0.1:PORT MODEL --tokens 64 --reps 5`. All TensorFold rows ran in
one exclusive GPU session, with every pack's page cache dropped before each server started. ExLlamaV3 ran behind a
minimal OpenAI shim around its `Generator`, serially: batch size 1, an 8,192-token cache, n-gram tables in host
RAM, no drafts. The ExLlamaV3 SAGE row comes from a second session. In that session it first failed to load
("Insufficient VRAM in split") while the previous server's pack was still in the page cache. The second session
also re-measured TensorFold on SAGE serially at 34.6 / 34.4 / 34.8 / 34.6, within 3.5% of the table.

| | Code, sampled | Chat, sampled | Code, greedy | Chat, greedy |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| ExLlamaV3, SAGE 4.15 bpw, serial | 22.3 | 22.2 | 22.3 | 22.2 |
| TensorFold, SAGE 4.15 bpw, serial | 34.3 | 34.0 | 34.5 | 33.5 |
| ExLlamaV3, turboderp 3.05 bpw, serial | 37.0 | 36.9 | 37.1 | 36.9 |
| TensorFold, turboderp 3.05 bpw, serial | 34.9 | 34.9 | 35.1 | 35.0 |
| TensorFold, MLX 4-bit, serial | 36.8 | 36.7 | 37.0 | 36.8 |

Serially on the mixed-K pack, TensorFold is 1.51-1.55x ExLlamaV3. On the uniform 3.05 bpw pack
TensorFold's serial path is 5-6% behind ExLlamaV3's, and on both EXL3 packs it is 5-9% behind its own MLX path.
With drafts on the current engine (the table above), the 3.05 bpw pack decodes 1.6-2.2x ExLlamaV3's serial speed.

### One or two ranks

Two ranks split a ModelOpt checkpoint, not the MLX one. Pull it on both and start rank 1 first:

```bash
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --tp 2 --rank 1 --master 192.0.2.1
tensorfold serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --tp 2 --rank 0 --master 192.0.2.1 --name bench --host 0.0.0.0
```

With drafts on, two ranks keep prompt states as one GPU does. On two GB10s, a chat with about 28,500 tokens of history
takes 22.5 s to reply fresh and 1.7 s resumed, and every resumed reply equals the fresh one.

### Serving

The default CUDA cap is six MTP drafts, with chains stopping below the configured confidence threshold.
`--mtp-drafts N` changes the cap; `--no-drafts` or `"draft": false` selects serial decoding.
Single-request serving uses CUDA graphs for verify windows and draft steps. Two-rank reductions add
gathered partials in rank order.

On one GPU or two ranks, `--parallel N` shares forwards across up to N requests, with a lone stream on CUDA graphs
where its weights support capture; `--parallel auto` selects one request. Pass the same N on both ranks: rank 0 sends
admissions, prompt pieces, cache growth and rounds over one TCP connection on its `--master` address, with an
ephemeral port published by the rendezvous store. Two-rank parallel requests take text without structured output;
`response_format` and `guided_*` receive HTTP 400 before generation. For prefix reuse, the single-request engine
and the concurrent decoder keep prompt
states; a follow-up prefills the reply again. A kept state stops one token before its prompt's end, so the
same prompt sent again resumes, and so does a next chat turn that renders the generation prompt's `<think>`
and newline as `<think>` and two newlines. Stream caches grow within the startup window as memory allows;
inspect the reported capacity.

With `--parallel N`, a prompt prefills inside the rounds: each round runs the live replies' windows and the next
prompt pass (up to 2,048 rows, several prompts packed) in one forward, and each layer's experts once for both. Every
reply still equals its solo run. The cost is decode speed while prompts fill: a pass of more than ~500 rows reads
most of the experts, so live replies decode at about a tenth of their usual rate during a burst's prefill (2.6-3.2
of 32-41 tok/s on one Spark) instead of stopping. `--decode-share S` sizes the passes so a round's decoding takes
that share of the pass's time: 0.25 about doubles decode during a prefill and roughly halves prompt speed. The
default, 0, keeps whole passes. The native server takes `--decode-share` as a time share instead: see [the API](../api.md).

Prompt pieces are 2,048 rows, or 4,096 while nothing decodes on a DGX Spark serving the MLX checkpoint without
`--vision`, when the admitted window leaves room (the startup log names the choice). `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS=N`
(256 to 16,384, from @MiaAI-Lab's [#238](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/238)) sets the rows instead, for
one GPU or two: the prompt buffers are sized for N rows in the startup estimate, so the window shrinks or grows to
match, and the plan above no longer applies. A round that runs beside live replies still takes at most 2,048 of them.
Replies are the same tokens at any setting; the best value depends on the machine, so measure it there.

N-gram tables are file-backed host data. On unified-memory GPUs they compete with weights and cache
allocations for RAM, so a checkpoint's GPU allocation alone does not describe its memory requirement. An explicit
`--context` that leaves them no room is reported at startup; their lookups then page from disk, a cost of about 1.3x
on prompts.

`--ple-on-ssd` and `--ssd-experts` below describe the Python engine's flags and measurements. The native binary takes both on one Mac: see [Exact Fluid Subgraph Residency](fluid-subgraph-residency.md).

`--ple-on-ssd` leaves the 29.8 GiB of n-gram tables in the checkpoint and reads each lookup's rows from SSD,
so a 128 GB Mac can hold Flash Next. It is an opt-in trade. On an M3 Ultra, replies were the same tokens,
decode was 3.5-8% slower across the four cells, prefill was unchanged, the peak footprint fell by 40 GiB
(135.1 to 95.4 GiB) and start-up halved (35.7 s to 17.8 s).

`--ssd-experts GIB` also leaves the routed experts (70.3 GiB) in the checkpoint and streams them into a GPU pool
of that many GiB; with `--ple-on-ssd` as well, a 64 GB Mac can hold Flash Next (`python -m pip install
"tensorfold[ssd]"` first: the pool's host side is a small MLX extension built on first use). The GPU hands each
MoE layer's picks to the host and waits while missing experts are read into the pool; the expert kernels are the
resident ones with only the weight address changed, so replies are the resident model's tokens.

On an M3 Ultra, each flag was held to a smaller Mac's budget and compared on the same machine:
- `--ple-on-ssd` at a 128 GB Mac's budget (89.6 GiB) peaked at 85.6 GiB. Decode was 0.91-1.03x the resident
  run and prefill 0.84-0.91x.
- Adding `--ssd-experts 24` at a 64 GB Mac's budget (44.8 GiB) peaked at 39.5 GiB. Replies were the same tokens as
  with the experts resident: 36 of 36 requests, drafted and serial. Decode ran at 36.8-42.5 tok/s against
  107.6-129.7 (0.31-0.39x), and prefill at 332-354 against 1,014-1,081 tok/s.
- A smaller budget also halves the prompt chunk, to 2,048 tokens. Prompts past that length then reply
  differently from a 256 GB Mac's run, whichever flags are set.

### KV cache

@vcruz305 added these caches and `--mtp-confidence` below to the Python engine in
[#47](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/47). The native binary refuses `--kv-dtype` and `--mtp-confidence`.

`--kv-dtype bf16` is the default. `--kv-dtype int8` and `--kv-dtype int4` store each attention layer's keys and
values as codes with one fp16 scale per 32 values, the arithmetic of ExLlamaV3's `-cq 8` and `-cq 4` (the
non-companded grid): each group of 32 is rotated by a 32-point Hadamard, its absmax is the scale, and the codes sit
on the midpoint grid. 8-bit stores `q - 128` as int8; 4-bit stores two unsigned codes a byte, low nibble first. The
query is rotated the same way and the merged attention output is rotated back, so the stored keys and values stay
rotated. Indexer keys and pooled block keys stay bf16.

A token costs 30,784 bytes in bf16, 18,304 in int8 and 11,648 in int4, counting the scales and the MTP head's own
cache: 1.68x and 2.64x smaller (the keys and values alone shrink 1.88x and 3.56x). The startup admission counts
those bytes, so an omitted `--context` admits a longer window at int8 and int4, and an explicit `--context` is
checked against the quantized cache. The dtype holds on every path: prompt chunks and decode windows, the MTP head,
`"draft": false` requests, `--parallel N` streams and their kept prompt states, and both ranks of `--tp 2`, which
refuse to start with different `--kv-dtype` values.

A quantized cache changes the output, so its replies differ from bf16's. Drafted output still equals
`"draft": false` output at the same dtype, and a resumed prompt equals a fresh one. The MLX path and the other
families refuse `--kv-dtype` before any download.

`--mtp-confidence P`, from 0 to 1, sets the probability under which a chain stops before a later draft; the CUDA
default is 0.70, for one stream and for concurrent rounds. Only Flash Next's CUDA engine has this rule, so the MLX path and the other families refuse it.

## Native HIP on a Strix Halo iGPU

The native HIP build serves Flash Next on gfx1151 (AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB unified memory) from MLX
affine checkpoints whose fused stacks each have one bit width and group size. Decode on this iGPU is bandwidth-bound and
the dense mixers (attention, Gated DeltaNet projections, hyper-connection mixers, n-gram key/value projections) dominate
each decoded token's reads, so the checkpoint choice sets both speed and quality. Three checkpoints load:

| Checkpoint (revision) | Dense mixers | Bytes per decoded token | Code / chat tok/s | MTP tokens per round (code) | KL vs bf16, prose / code | GSM8K / HumanEval / MMLU-Pro |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP` | 4-bit g32 | 4.00 GiB | 50.0 / 44.0 | 3.07 | 0.401 / 0.204 | 93.0 / 93.9 / 55.9 |
| `unigilby/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-oQ4e-HIP` (`5a0fb414`) | 8-bit g64 | 5.44 GiB | 42.0 / 36.2 | 2.61 | 0.064 / 0.013 | 94.7 / 93.9 / 69.1 |
| `unigilby/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-oQ4e-mix5-HIP` (`1b5c83a6`) | 5-bit g64 | 4.45 GiB | 51.3 / 41.4 | 3.05 | 0.096 / 0.022 | 94.3 / 93.3 / 67.6 |

The two oQ checkpoints are oMLX oQe quantizations (imatrix) with routed and shared experts at 4-bit group 32 and the MTP
head under `language_model.mtp.*`; they differ only in the dense mixers. oQ4e is the quality pick and the one to start
with. oQ4e-mix5's 5-bit dense mixers are a speed-for-quality trade you choose, not an engine default: it decodes about
22% faster on code than oQ4e and keeps MTP acceptance (3.05 tokens per round), at about 1.5x its KL (0.059 against 0.039
over both slices). A 6-bit-mixer variant reads fewer bytes than oQ4e but its MTP acceptance falls (2.44 tokens per round
on code), so it decodes no faster and is not listed. The uniform 4-bit checkpoint is the fastest on chat but the
furthest from bf16, and it costs on tasks: MMLU-Pro falls to 55.9% against oQ4e's 69.1%, and 159 of its 700 replies
there are format misses (no answer letter within 16 tokens), so weigh that before choosing it for speed.

How these were measured: TensorFold `7c068895` built with `zig build native-hip -Dhip-arch=gfx1151` (Ubuntu archive HIP
7.1, clang 21), MTP 3 drafts, `--parallel 1 --context 131072 --prompt-cache-gib 0`, `tools/bench_openai.py` decode
medians over two server starts. KL(bf16 || quant) is exact over the full 248,320-entry vocabulary, teacher-forced on
WikiText-2 raw test and HumanEval prompt plus canonical solution (31,728 scored tokens each), through mlx-vlm 0.7.10's
`qwen4_exp` model against `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` in bf16; the HIP engine does not return logprobs. That model class
does not shift norm weights at load, and the uniform 4-bit checkpoint stores its RMSNorm gains as gain + 1, so its KL is
taken after removing that offset. Task scores come from the HIP server: greedy, thinking off, GSM8K 300 zero-shot exact
match, HumanEval 164 pass@1, MMLU-Pro 700 (50 a category, a letter within 16 tokens; replies without one count as wrong,
159 of them for the uniform 4-bit checkpoint, 14 for oQ4e-mix5 and 4 for oQ4e).

```bash
zig build native-hip -Dhip=true -Dhip-arch=gfx1151 -Dhipcc=/usr/bin/hipcc -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
./zig-out/native-hip/bin/tensorfold-native serve ./Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-oQ4e-mix5-HIP \
  --parallel 1 --context 131072
```

## Draft vocabulary provenance

The Flash Next dump tool accepts `--draft-vocab default` for the shipped list,
`--draft-vocab cjk` for the opt-in CJK list, or a custom vocabulary file. The
default remains unchanged; the selected list must be a whole number of 64-ID tiles
and cannot exceed the model vocabulary.

In the Python engine, both backends read the public list in
[`src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/draft_vocab.txt`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/v0.6.6/src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/draft_vocab.txt).
The native engine embeds the same file, byte for byte, as `zig/src/families/flashnext/draft_vocab_default.txt`.
It contains 79,591 sorted IDs; MLX pads it with the lowest unused IDs to a multiple of 64 at load.
The target sampler still reads the full vocabulary, so the list affects proposals only.

The corpus is Homebrew CPython 3.14.5's standard-library `*.py` files, excluding `site-packages` and
`__pycache__`. It contains no repository or PyPI package text. Use `tokenizers==0.22.2` and
`tools/draft_vocab.py` as of the v0.6.6 tag (`git show v0.6.6:tools/draft_vocab.py`), SHA-256
`1baf0dd08669355cf9cf6e32998e5436ce8712c3ab1bffe38d369f3fa3a86b56`.
The tokenizer JSON SHA-256 is:

```text
0997f410c57a1f4e53b09e4be8f4a172d90edd9564368fb0847030937229b9f3
```

Place that tokenizer at `tokenizer.json` and copy the clean stdlib into an empty `cpython` directory,
preserving relative paths. The [Nemotron corpus-copy example](nemotron-3.5.md#draft-vocabulary-provenance)
shows the file-selection rules; change its destination to `cpython`. Then run it from a v0.6.6 checkout's root:

```bash
TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false python3 -B tools/draft_vocab.py tokenizer.json draft_vocab.txt 'cpython/**/*.py' --size 79591 --keep-below 65536 --min-count 1 --added-tokens
```

The generator retains all IDs below 65,536 and tokenizer-added IDs, then adds corpus IDs by frequency
and fills remaining places with the lowest unused IDs. It skips empty, unreadable and oversized files.
Expected output SHA-256:

```text
88d5b483a849ae9245b78b69f41f11cdfc8b5c024f0786c1c8196263857cc93e
```

Check this hash before adopting a rebuild; a different stdlib distribution can change the corpus.
The current list replaces the older list whose PyPI corpus was not reproducible.

## Measurements

Use the [public benchmark command](README.md#measurements) with the server above; omit tensor-parallel
flags for one rank. The client supplies fixed public prompts, 64-token replies and seeds 1234 through
1238. Historical rates measured with the earlier draft list do not qualify the current list.

Use a separately pinned public long-context fixture when measuring prefill and reuse. Check fresh versus
resumed prompts across sparse-attention transitions and template changes, as well as drafted versus
serial output. Decode, cold/resumed latency, concurrent throughput and peak memory are
TBD [release-0.3.5].

## Image input on CUDA

@shantanugoel added image input to the Python engine's Flash Next in
[#146](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/146). There, use `--vision` on one CUDA GPU with `--parallel` of at
least two. Image requests always prefill fresh; text prefix caching remains available. See the
[image recipe](flash-next-vision.md) for tower weights, memory admission, EXL3 sidecar conversion and verification.
The native binary's CUDA engine takes `--vision` too, experimental, through the Qwen-VL tower that Qwen's CUDA family
runs (see [Flash Next on CUDA](flash-next-cuda.md)).

The maintained Metal DeltaNet window body in decode/fn_gdn.metal takes up to 16 rows with each row's own convolution, Q/K norms and gates. The recurrence keeps its per-row arithmetic across window widths. FZ_GDN_REPLAY=0 stores each row's state; FZ_GDN_REPLAY=1 keeps one state per layer and replays the previous window's accepted rows from its saved K, V, norms and gates before the next window. Qwen4 specializations retain this body and declare their own head geometry, gate and exact weight storage.
# Qwen4 dense native preparation

The `qwen4` and `qwen4_text` adapters prepare a dense version of the related Flash Next architecture.
No released Qwen4-27B checkpoint was available for this preparation.
The supplied kernel notes establish supported shapes, not the complete model configuration.
The synthetic Metal and CUDA device gates below pass; a real checkpoint remains unchecked.

Config admission requires explicit hidden, vocabulary, layer, MLP, HC, GDN, QSA, RoPE and PLE geometry.
It accepts `linear_attention`, `indexed_attention` and the `full_attention` spelling for indexed layers.
It refuses MoE, vision, unknown fields and an undeclared positive MTP head by field name.
Copy proposals use the shared lane core; they do not imply a checkpoint MTP head exists.
Native kernels currently require hidden size divisible by 256, GDN head dimensions 128, convolution length 4,
attention head dimension 256 and index dimension 128.
Each stream window admits at most 16 rows and a shared batch at most 128 rows.
Unsupported geometry is refused before device allocation.

The shared graph is `families/flashnext/forward_graph.zig`.
It owns HC, the GDN/QSA boundary, optional PLE and the dense or routed feed-forward boundary.
Qwen4 uses the shared projection and pointwise operators and geometry specializations of maintained mixer sources.
Existing Flash Next factories retain their fixed checkpoint dimensions and their arithmetic.
The new native adapters use the existing engine API, lane host, prompt cache and verification machinery.

Living Weights currently has a [host QSA backward and CUDA/Metal implementation plan](qwen4-living-weights.md).
That mathematical check does not enable a Qwen4 learner or qualify a device gradient.

Weights remain as stored: BF16, MLX affine 4/8-bit groups 32/64/128, ModelOpt FP8 or ModelOpt NVFP4.
Each projection keeps its own recipe, scales and bias metadata.
Activations stay BF16 and reductions stay FP32.
Small BF16/F16 vectors widen exactly to FP32; original F32 vectors retain their dtype-specific rounding policy.
HF centered norms use `1 + gamma`.
An MLX namespace must explicitly state whether its norm weights are gamma or prepared scale.
The loader validates every tensor header and PLE hash vector before uploading weights.

Synthetic host tests use an independent binary64 forward with explicit BF16 nodes.
Nonzero native-compatible fixtures exercise the actual loader, packed graph, state, cache and shared lane core
through CPU operator instruments, including every prompt cut, concurrent streams and copied proposals.
These tests establish host integration and state semantics; they do not qualify device arithmetic.
Generated native source tests and normal contract-runner Cases cover the individual operators separately.
Attention uses the shared binary64 softmax reference and its stated BF16-probability error allowance.
The maintained Metal split-softmax retains FP32 probabilities; the CUDA tensor-core path rounds P to BF16.
No cross-backend byte equality or whole-checkpoint HF fidelity is claimed from those bounds.

On a host without GPU toolchains, the shader-free checks are:

```sh
zig build test-qwen4-host test-qwen4-projection-host test-qwen4-gdn-host
zig build test-qwen4-reference-host
zig build test-qwen4-qsa-host test-qwen4-native-mixers-host
zig build test-qwen4-projection-bodies test-qwen4-cuda-bodies
```

The normal Metal and CUDA contract runners collect the new Cases.
New CUDA launch records retain pending measurements until actual compiler receipts exist for each SM.
Before advertising a released checkpoint, check its config and tensor names, run the complete backend contract,
and run fresh/drafted/concurrent/resumed/prompt-cut model comparisons with its actual tokenizer and weights.
Measure cold prefill, decode and memory on each claimed GPU; no rate or memory-fit claim is established here.

The explicit synthetic device gates generate the same nonzero safetensors through the real checkpoint writer.
They load the serving native engine and compare all 384 BF16 logits and 12 GPU greedy picks with a binary64 fixture.
Metal uses its FP32 split-softmax probability profile; CUDA retains its BF16 tensor-core probability profile.
The Metal reference declares FP32 RMS scalar and rotary scalar nodes, including its stored FP32 frequency table.
No comparison tolerance or logit mask is used. These backend profiles do not claim HF or cross-backend byte parity.
They require byte equality for five repeats, every prompt cut, saved-state resume, concurrent streams,
partial acceptance and abort/retry. The shared lane adapter also checks copied proposals against plain decoding.
A learned MTP head is not declared by this fixture and remains refused by config admission.

On a Mac with the Metal toolchain:

```sh
zig build test-qwen4-metal
```

This step compiles the production shaders at runtime and executes the GPU. It is separate from default host tests.
`zig build compile-qwen4-metal-device` emits the same executable without executing it or producing shaders.
For CUDA on a GB10, build the runner and embedded images, then run both gates:

```sh
zig build -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Dsm=121
./zig-out/bin/tf-cuda-test qwen4
zig build kernel-contract -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Dsm=121
```

`zig build compile-cuda-tests` with the same options emits the runner without installing or executing it.
The normal CUDA contract collects the Qwen4 operators and their planted controls, and resolves all four images
for the 32 new launch registrations. Resource measurements are still required; pending records must fail limits.
Synthetic device success does not qualify an unreleased checkpoint or establish cross-backend equality.

Compile the generated runtime libraries and control variants before opening a device on a Mac with the Metal toolchain:

```sh
zig build test-qwen4-metal-sources -j8
```

This uses the runtime's Metal language and math settings and opens no GPU. The explicit `test-qwen4-metal` device gate
also depends on this compiler check. `emit-qwen4-metal-sources` writes the exact source inputs under
`zig-out/qwen4-metal/` for inspection without invoking a shader compiler.

The source inventory rejects buffer indices outside Metal's 0–30 range before emission. Operator repeat controls
share a four-byte constant struct at slot 17, after GDN's production bindings through slot 16. The CPU Metal
instruments also require explicit float-to-bfloat construction, so the generated HC control stores are type-checked
without a GPU; this supplements the actual Metal compiler check.

Before the full Metal comparison, the gate runs a fresh two-token case and prints `QWEN4_NODE` values for embedding,
PLE, HC sums and boundaries, GDN projections/state/output, QSA preparation/pooling/scores/parts/output, and the head.
The same captured two rows first face the legacy BF16-probability oracle as a labelled diagnostic, then the corrected
Metal oracle. No second forward or changed input is used for that before/after comparison.
`QWEN4_FIRST_DIFFERENCE` identifies the first unequal BF16 storage node per row. FP32 reductions and recurrent state
are diagnostic raw bits beside their binary64 values; they are not asserted equal to unrounded binary64 arithmetic.
The two-row QSA range is dense, so no sparse selection result is consumed. The full 12-row gate still checks logits,
tokens and every state seam strictly. The diagnostic copies stay on the inference queue and finish before readback.
Normal native inference has no trace sink and performs no diagnostic copies or host readbacks.

Regenerate the Metal reference with:

```sh
python3 tools/zig/qwen4_reference.py --config zig/src/families/qwen4/fixtures/native-dense.json \
  --probability f32 --native-scalars
```

Add `--tokens 3,5 --nodes` for the two-row node ledger. `--probability bf16` retains the legacy normalized-weight diagnostic.

CUDA's `tf-cuda-test qwen4` also runs the queued two-row node capture before the complete exactness gate. It prints
its rotary frequency view, position base, GDN snapshots, KV keys and values, QSA partial numerators and denominators,
and all shared graph storage nodes. The CUDA oracle declares BF16 exponential weights before the PV product and a
separate denominator, matching the existing CUDA tensor-core kernel. Rounding normalized probabilities is a
labelled legacy diagnostic profile. Metal retains its existing FP32 probability profile and reference files.

Regenerate the explicit CUDA reference with:

```sh
python3 tools/zig/qwen4_reference.py --config zig/src/families/qwen4/fixtures/native-dense.json \
  --probability cuda --native-scalars
```

Add `--tokens 3,5 --nodes` for its node ledger. `test-qwen4-cuda-exact-host` executes the real CUDA probability-store
statements and merge body under a CPU instrument; its matrix products are scalar substitutes for MMA instructions.
`test-qwen4-cuda-nodes-host` checks 129 BF16 nodes exactly, records 13 FP32 diagnostics, and catches the old-profile error.
QK/PV products and denominator reductions are scalar CPU instruments, with a host exponential surrogate.
These host instruments supplement the real CUDA device gate; they do not qualify GPU instruction rounding.
# Qwen4 Living Weights: host backward and implementation plan

This is the host mathematical step for #1804. It does not enable learning in the native Qwen4 engine.
`families/qwen4/qsa_backward.zig` computes the continuous selected-attention adjoint for FP32 or FP64 arrays.
Q and upstream gradients are `[rows, heads, width]`; K/V and their adjoints are token-major
`[capacity, kv_heads, width]`. Query head `h` reads KV head `h / (heads / kv_heads)`.
The served QSA scale is 0.0625 at width 256. The host routine accepts an explicit scale for synthetic checks.

For each causal row, dense attention reads keys `0..end`. Sparse attention reads exactly the supplied unique IDs,
including any incomplete causal tail. IDs beyond `end`, duplicate IDs and empty selections are refused.
The selection is a fixed tape. No surrogate derivative is supplied for pooling, score ranking or top-k decisions.
Unselected and future K/V rows are never read and their adjoints stay zero. Shared K/V adjoints accumulate every
query-head and row use. Shape, selection, alias and input-finiteness admission precedes gradient writes.
Numeric overflow clears the output adjoints and returns an error. Inputs and the selection tape remain unchanged.

The proved attention formula is `p = softmax(scale * Q K^T)`, `O = p V` over the fixed selection:

```text
dP[j] = dot(dO, V[j])
dS[j] = p[j] * (dP[j] - sum_i p[i] dP[i])
dQ += scale * dS[j] * K[j]
dK[j] += scale * dS[j] * Q
dV[j] += p[j] * dO
```

The separate output-gate pullback takes saved forward context and sigmoid values. It uses the saved sigmoid for
the context adjoint and the ordinary sigmoid derivative for the logit adjoint. Forward cuts are straight-through
in this local mathematical model. Independent finite differences freeze each cast's offset at the base point;
they do not differentiate a discontinuous rounding function. Both cut and uncut output-gate cases are checked.

```sh
zig build test-qwen4-qsa-backward-host -j1 --summary all
```

The independent reference evaluates a dense binary64 masked loss rather than calling the backward's helpers.
Tiny cases check every Q/K/V and gated-output coordinate at three central step sizes. Directional cases use the
served 24 query heads, 4 KV heads and width 256, with 129 dense keys and 2,051 sparse keys including a three-token
tail. Tests also cover poisoned unused cache rows, shared-head accumulation, malformed tapes, aliases and repeats.
FP64 checks use `1e-8 + 1e-6 * abs(slope)`; FP32 checks use `2e-7 + 3e-5 * abs(slope)`.
These are host derivative-check limits, not new device fidelity or whole-model acceptance thresholds.

The CUDA tensor-core attention path stores BF16 probability operands; Metal's split softmax retains FP32
probabilities. This step does not model those backend-specific probability cuts, split reduction orders, Q/K
RMS/RoPE or their stored intermediates. It is not a gradient receipt for either device profile. The native forward,
its probability stores and all shader sources remain unchanged. Future backward kernels need their own contracts.

## CUDA pocket and trainer

1. Adapt the dense pocket storage and shard writer used by Qwen3.5, with a Qwen4 family descriptor keyed by its
   declared config. Preserve original tensor bytes and separate base columns from appended neurons when loading.
   Use the same serialized family/tensor/quantization description on both backends. Reject unsupported learning
   layouts before allocation; a group-32 Flash Next transpose must never be applied to group-64/128 or other formats.
2. Add hooks at the dense MLP branch before the HC writeback in the shared Flash Next layer graph. Every prompt,
   verify and decode pass must run the same hook. Keep the empty-pocket branch free of allocations, readbacks,
   synchronization and added launches. Supply per-stream untaught masks, including mixed taught/untaught batches.
3. Reuse Flash Next's HC branch/readout backward and GDN backward with explicit Qwen4 geometry and gate mode.
   Qwen4's default SiLU must not inherit Flash Next's sigmoid derivative. Make the backward mode explicit and prove
   both modes with a planted wrong-gate control before reuse, preserving Flash Next's existing mode and arithmetic.
   Add dense SwiGLU/base-weight and pocket-input gradients, the LM head/loss
   path, and optional PLE backward. Until PLE backward is present, learning on PLE configs must refuse explicitly.
4. Record Q/K norm inputs, stored rotary frequencies, V, output gates and the exact selected IDs/counts/row ends
   from the same forward. The backward must use this tape, not reselect. Implement selected softmax backward in
   FP32, accumulating shared K/V uses without lost writes. Integrate the Q/K RMS, rotary, projections and HC chain.
   Keep each sequence's cache ownership explicit; packed training sequences must not read another sequence's keys.
5. Define and test the backward convention for every probability, context and gate cut in the actual CUDA profile.
   Finite differences of the ideal formula above cannot qualify BF16 probability stores. Check local cut offsets
   and the complete computed graph, with controls that drop a cut or transpose a GQA group.

## Metal pocket and trainer

Reuse the shared family descriptor, learned-neuron layout, fitting policy and shard writer. Follow the existing
Nemotron Metal trainer's ownership and residency structure, with Qwen4 operators and its own forward tape. Device
buffers and captured metadata must survive command completion. Keep training scratch separate from served streams;
drain outstanding work before changing pocket buffers and invalidate prompt states after any successful edit.

Port the qualified CUDA backward stages as Metal operators without replacing inference with CPU work. Reuse HC,
GDN and dense projection derivatives only where layout, precision and gate mode match. Register any new operators
and their served shapes, exceptional classes, repeats/aliasing, accumulator stress and launch limits. Pending
compiler/resource records stay unmeasured until actual images are checked. Include pre-M5 and M5 implementations.

## Gates before advertising learning

Use a tiny nonzero Qwen4-shaped model to check whole trainer/serving loss and directional gradients at early rows,
layer boundaries, GDN/QSA and PLE layers. A whole-model finite-difference probe must record whether its selected
IDs change under perturbation. Selection crossings are nondifferentiable witnesses, not permission to widen the
gradient bound or silently freeze a real serving pass. The local fixed-selection check remains a separate receipt.

Test fitting, held-out recall, unrelated-fact retention, exact take-out/delete/rollback, cancellation and save failure
through the existing shared learner/server acceptance path. Round outputs exactly as they will be stored before
judging a fit. Compare the immutable base tensor bytes before/after, and reopen each backend's saved folder on the
other. Assert that untaught streams read the original model even beside taught streams.

Each affected checkpoint and profile is then run on a CUDA GPU and on pre-M5 and M5 Macs. Match binary/runtime,
model/tokenizer revisions, prompts, seeds, quantization and cache settings. Require empty-folder tokens and speed
equal to the base, drafted/plain and concurrent/solo equality, every prompt cut, resume/restart and rejection cleanup.
Measure learning time and peak host/device memory separately. No device, real-checkpoint or performance gate is
claimed by this host step; the portable layout and complete CUDA/Metal trainers remain follow-up work.

Existing owners are the MLP HC seam in `families/flashnext/forward_graph.zig:34`, the CUDA HC/GDN trainer chain in
`families/flashnext/cuda_train.zig:369`, shared GDN backward in `cuda/gdn_train.zig:299`, and Qwen4's indexed-attention
and output-gate adapters in `families/qwen4/gpu_ops.zig:169` and `families/qwen4/metal_gpu.zig:196` under `zig/src/`.
# Spark-X2.6-4B, native CUDA

This recipe covers text generation with [`XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B`](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B),
revision `66e3ae7bee54e0a523d692cb8ef841f35409807b` (model_type `spark2_5`, the same architecture as Spark-X2.5-4B),
on the CUDA engine. It was brought up on an RTX 4090 (`sm_89`) under Windows and measured again on an RTX 5090
(`sm_120`) under Linux; other CUDA GPUs are untested.

## Convert, build, serve

The release is bf16 only; the family reads MLX affine checkpoints, so convert it first (numpy, no MLX needed):

```sh
hf download XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B --revision 66e3ae7bee54e0a523d692cb8ef841f35409807b --local-dir models/spark-x2.6-4b
python tools/zig/spark25_convert.py models/spark-x2.6-4b models/spark-x2.6-4b-8bit --bits 8
zig build native install -Dsm=89 -Dstrip=true -Dnvcc="$CUDA_PATH/bin/nvcc"
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve models/spark-x2.6-4b-8bit --name spark --port 8888 --context 32768 --parallel 4
```

`--bits 4` writes a 4-bit checkpoint instead (smaller, lower fidelity). Thinking is on by default, as in the chat
template; a request sends `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}` to turn it off.

## What the family is

`zig/src/families/spark25/` follows Gemma 4's CUDA family, on the same shared operators:

- 36 layers, three sliding-window layers (window 512) to each full one, 16 query heads of 256 over 4 key heads.
- `q_k_v_proj` and the per-head `g_proj` are packed into one 6,160-row projection at load.
- RoPE on all 256 dims (theta 10,000) in sliding layers and on the first 64 (pairs d, d + 32; theta 5,000,000) in full
  ones, through `qk_rows`; no QK norm; attention scale 1/16.
- The output gate is one sigmoid a head, rounded to bf16 before the product (`tf_head_gate_rows`), and the MLP is
  `bf16(gelu_erf(gate)) * up` with PyTorch's exact GELU (`tf_gelu_erf_rows`), both new in `act_rows.cu`.
- The residual stays fp32 from the embedding on, as the reference keeps it (`norms.addRms`), with fp32 norm weights.
- Tied head, no soft-cap. Prompts reuse kept states (`snap.zig`); copy drafts come from the lane core.

The tokenizer needed `Digits` (`individual_digits`) in `core/tokenizer/steps.zig`.

## Measured (RTX 4090, 8-bit, Windows, 25 Oct 2026)

- Tokenizer: equal to the HF tokenizer's IDs on mixed English, Chinese, Japanese, code, emoji and digit text, and on
  rendered chat prompts up to 2,319 tokens.
- Greedy replies against the HF reference (transformers 4.57.1) on the same weights dequantized to bf16: 3 of 4
  prompts equal over 96 tokens, among them a 2,319-token prompt across the window, the ring and five chunks; the
  fourth equal for 137 characters, then a near tie.
- One stream: 136 tokens/s on prose, 144 on code, greedy or sampled. Four streams: 414 tokens/s in all, each reply
  equal to its solo run.
- Time to first token: 0.24 s at 2k tokens, 0.93 s at 8k, 1.93 s at 16k, 4.65 s at 29k.

## Measured (RTX 5090, 8-bit, Linux, 26 Oct 2026)

Main at 31a864f13, `zig build native -Dsm=120` (CUDA 13.3, driver 615), the 8-bit conversion above, served with
`--context 32768 --parallel 4`; the server reports 9.47 GiB for the model and 1.23 GiB a stream at the 32k window.
Decode rates are medians of three 256-token greedy replies a prompt, through the recipe harness
(`github.com/BobClawblaw/recipe-harness`, target `spark-x26-4b-5090`).

- One stream: 199 tokens/s on prose, 191 on code, 203 on JSON and 204 on a list; the same after a 28k prompt
  (199, 198, 197 and 200). Two streams: 375-389 tokens/s in all; four streams: 716-729, time to first token
  0.03-0.06 s on these short prompts.
- Exactness: 12 of 12 greedy replies beside three other streams equal their solo runs, and 12 of 12 with the lane
  core's copy drafts off equal the drafted ones.
- Prompt reading, cold, thinking off: 2,381 tokens in 0.233 s, 9,391 in 0.818 s, 18,512 in 1.704 s (10,864
  tokens/s); thinking on, 2,394 in 0.234 s, 9,350 in 0.814 s, 18,687 in 1.706 s. The plan's 30,720-token point
  tokenizes past the 32k window with this tokenizer and was refused.

## Not done

The two new kernels are under the CUDA contract (`zig/tests/cuda/contract_spark_act.zig`, its float64 ends in
`core/act_ref.zig`, a control for each kernel's rounding point) with launch records in
`core/contract/spark_cuda_records.zig`. There is no fixture-based exactness test against dumped reference rows yet,
and no drafter or structured output is served.
# Spark-X2.6-4B, native Metal

This recipe covers text generation with [`XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B`](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B),
revision `66e3ae7bee54e0a523d692cb8ef841f35409807b` (model_type `spark2_5`), on the Metal engine, served from the bf16
release as published: no conversion, nothing lost. It was brought up on an M5 Ultra (256 GB); other Macs are untested.
The CUDA side of the family is [its own page](spark-x2.6-4b-cuda.md).

## Build and serve

```sh
hf download XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B --revision 66e3ae7bee54e0a523d692cb8ef841f35409807b --local-dir models/spark-x2.6-4b
zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native
zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=PATH_TO_XGRAMMAR_v0.2.8 -Dcpu=native   # structured output
SPARK_LOAD_LIMIT_GB=64 zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve models/spark-x2.6-4b --name spark --port 8888 \
  --context 262144 --parallel 4 --prompt-cache-gib 8
```

`SPARK_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` caps weights, scratch and caches together (75% of RAM when unset). The weights take 7.7 GiB; a
stream's caches take 36 KiB a position in the nine full layers plus 270 MiB of sliding rings, so 64 GB holds four
262,144-token streams or one of 1,048,576 tokens (`--context 1048576 --parallel 1`). Thinking is on by default, as in
the chat template; a request sends `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}` to turn it off. The CUDA
page's MLX affine conversions also load (the same row and prompt kernels Gemma 4 uses); they are not needed on a Mac,
and the 8-bit one costs a mean KL of 0.0021 against the release over 1,500 positions.

## What the port is

`zig/src/families/spark25/metal_*.zig` follow Flint's Metal family and share `config.zig` with the CUDA side (a
checkpoint without a quantization table is the bf16 release; CUDA refuses it by name):

- The reference's rounding points (its PyTorch code in bf16): the residual fp32 from the embedding on, each norm
  `bf16(w * (x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)))` in fp32, RoPE in fp32 from the same inverse-frequency table as CUDA
  (all 256 dims in sliding layers, the first 64 in full ones), the head gate `bf16(att * bf16(sigmoid(g)))` and the MLP
  `bf16(bf16(gelu(g)) * u)` with an erf to under one ulp (`kernels/metal/spark25/glue.metal`).
- Projections over the release's bf16 rows: prompt chunks of up to 2,048 rows on `gemm_nax`'s tensor-unit GEMM
  (`gemm.metal`); decode windows on `sp_matvec`, a simdgroup an output row, fp32 sums rounded once as torch's bf16
  linear rounds them. `q_k_v_proj` and `g_proj` are stacked into one projection at load, gate and up into another.
- Attention: prompt chunks on the tensor units (gemma4's prompt attention, `attention_nax.metal`); decode rows on
  sdpa_vector lanes over key blocks at absolute positions, so a row's bits never depend on the rows beside it. Sliding
  layers keep a ring of the window and one chunk.
- The lane host's shared rounds, a lone stream's steps drawn on the GPU a step ahead, copy drafts, the prompt cache.

The Metal glue kernels are not registered with the kernel contract, as with the other Metal family glue.

## Measured (M5 Ultra, the bf16 release, 25 Oct 2026)

Against HF's own code (transformers 4.57.1) on the release:

- 1,500 positions teacher-forced, in 16-row windows: mean KL 0.00076 against HF in fp32, top-1 99.6%; HF's own bf16
  run is 0.00048 from the same fp32 run, top-1 99.3%. One position (a near tie, the worst on every comparison made)
  holds the maximum, 0.57; no other is above 0.05. After a 9,000-token prompt (five chunks), 64 forced steps: mean KL
  0.0005, no row above 0.006.
- Greedy replies on four chat prompts (code, prose, Chinese, a 3,547-token document), 96 tokens each: all four equal to
  HF's in fp32 (the document's ends at HF's end token after 89, every one equal).
- Windows of 16 and of 7 rows give the one-row steps' logits bit for bit after prompts of 64, 1,500, 2,600 and 4,100
  tokens (the ring wraps at 2,560).

Through the recipe harness (`--context 262144 --parallel 4`):

- `quick`: structured output 18/18 (drafted equal to plain 12/12), tools 5/5, seeded sampling 9/9, a resumed turn
  equal to the cold one (5,499 of 5,624 tokens cached, 0.065 s to the first token against 0.59 s), a 60-turn soak and
  concurrent streams each equal to the request alone, and the suite's streaming, stop, copy and max-tokens checks. Its
  multi-turn check recalled 7 of 8 facts: asked for five short lines, the model gave five and left one fact out.
- Decode: 106 tokens/s with one stream (9.5 ms a step: 7.7 GiB of weights a step, the memory bandwidth), 179-190 in
  all with two, 296-326 with four (12.8 ms a round: the weights read once for every row).
- Cold prompts: 2,350 tokens 9,438 tokens/s, 9,354 tokens 10,940, 37,174 tokens 9,058, 148,588 tokens 5,002 (29.7 s).
- Needles: a code at 10%, 50% and 90% of a 254,345-token prompt, each found (73.1-76.3 s); at 50% of a
  1,032,662-token prompt on a `--context 1048576` server, found in 1,035 s with 76% of the Mac's memory still free.

## Performance options

Each keeps the replies' bits; the numbers are the M5 Ultra's.

- **Streams (`--parallel`).** One stream decodes at 106 tokens/s, bound by reading the 7.7 GiB of weights each step.
  The weights are read once a round for every stream's row: two streams give 179-190 tokens/s in all, four 296-326
  (12.8 ms a round against 9.6), each reply equal to its run alone; the first token moves from 0.05-0.07 s to
  0.13-0.17 s at four. The row kernel holds up to 32 rows a launch.
- **Weights.** The release's bf16 is exact. The CUDA page's MLX affine conversions also load: the 8-bit one decodes at
  166 tokens/s (4.1 GiB a step) for a mean KL of 0.0021 against the release and greedy replies that part within a
  hundred tokens on two of four chats; 4-bit was not measured. Neither is needed on a Mac.
- **Context and memory (`--context`, `SPARK_LOAD_LIMIT_GB`).** 36 KiB a token in the nine full layers plus 270 MiB of
  rings a stream: 64 GB holds four 262,144-token streams or one of 1,048,576. Cold prompts run 9.4k-10.9k tokens/s to
  37k tokens, 5.0k at 149k and about 1.0k averaged over a million (the full layers' attention grows with the prompt).
- **Prompt cache (`--prompt-cache-gib`).** A resumed turn (5,499 of 5,624 tokens kept) starts in 0.065 s against
  0.59 s cold, with the same reply; kept states give way to streams that need the room.
- **Copy drafts.** On by default from the lane core, replies equal to `drafts: false`; they accepted 7-15% of their
  tokens on the harness's prompts and gave no measurable decode gain there. The family has no draft head.
- **Thinking.** On by default (the template's); it lengthens replies, not the cost a token; prompt speed with it on
  is within 1% of off.
- **Not offered.** No int8 or fp8 cache, no fast-math, no reduced-precision sums.

## Not done

No quality suite was run. No drafter is served (the family has no draft head; copy drafts come from the lane core).
Only the M5's tensor units were checked; M1-M4 Macs and smaller RAM are untested.
# Speed-up mode: one model on two Macs

Speed-up mode runs Qwen3.8 Flash Next 6-bit on two Macs joined by Thunderbolt. Each Mac holds the whole model
and does half the work of every request: prompts split their rows between the Macs, and each decode round splits
its DeltaNet heads, routed experts and vocabulary head. One Mac serves the HTTP API and the other runs every
request beside it. It needs the native Zig server (`tensorfold-native`) with the Flash Next replay engine, and
MCDMA for the Thunderbolt link. [The speed-up mode guide](../speed-up-mode.md) walks through the setup step by step,
with this build's speeds.

The server loads Flash Next straight from its checkpoint, with no recorded dump and no environment variable to set.

## What it gives

Measured on two M5 Ultra Macs (256 GB each) over one Thunderbolt 5 cable, greedy, thinking off, 256-token
replies, against the same server build on one of the Macs:

| Prompt | Time to first token, two Macs / one | Decode, two Macs / one (tok/s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1k code | 0.30 s / 0.38 s | 248 / 162 |
| 1k edit | 0.27 s / 0.38 s | 389 / 298 |
| 1k chat | 0.26 s / 0.34 s | 179 / 150 |
| 8k code | 1.19 s / 2.10 s | 200 / 154 |
| 8k edit | 1.23 s / 2.10 s | 343 / 285 |
| 8k chat | 1.27 s / 2.15 s | 185 / 146 |
| 32k code | 4.10 s / 7.16 s | 204 / 161 |
| 32k edit | 4.11 s / 7.18 s | 335 / 280 |
| 32k chat | 4.04 s / 6.94 s | 180 / 142 |

Prompts run 1.7 to 1.8 times as fast from 8k tokens (about 7,900 tokens a second at 32k). Decode gains less, 1.2
to 1.3 times, and 1.5 on 1k code: each layer still exchanges results between the Macs, and the draft head and the
window's fixed per-layer work run on both.

Both Macs produce the same reply token for token, at every draft depth. The experts give one Mac's bits: each Mac
runs every expert for half of a window's rows and they swap the results. A reply can still differ from one Mac's.
The two halves of the DeltaNet output projection are added in a different order, at the same fp32 precision.
Prompt splitting gives one Mac's bits exactly.

## What you need

- Two Apple silicon Macs, each with enough memory for the whole model. Flash Next 6-bit is 158 GB of weights, and
  each server takes 172 GB once loaded. Keep each server at or under 70% of its Mac's memory, 179 GiB on a 256 GB
  Mac. The server sizes its prompt cache to fit under that line, about 5 GiB on these Macs. A 192 GB Mac is too
  small. Put the same checkpoint on both.
- A Thunderbolt 5 cable between them with RDMA enabled, and MCDMA's fabric library (`libmcdma-fabric.dylib`) built
  on each Mac from MCDMA's `main` branch, which carries its Thunderbolt links.
- Greedy decoding (temperature 0), as the Flash Next replay engine requires.

## Settings

Each Mac gets a small JSON file naming its rank, the MCDMA library and the link to the other Mac. On the Mac that
serves (rank 0):

```json
{"rank": 0, "library": "/path/to/libmcdma-fabric.dylib",
 "links": [{"peer": 1, "device": "rdma_en4", "via": "en4/192.0.2.2", "port": 7490, "name": "speedup"}]}
```

On the other Mac (rank 1), the same with `"rank": 1`, `"peer": 0` and the first Mac's address on that cable:

```json
{"rank": 1, "library": "/path/to/libmcdma-fabric.dylib",
 "links": [{"peer": 0, "device": "rdma_en4", "via": "en4/192.0.2.1", "port": 7490, "name": "speedup"}]}
```

`device` is the Thunderbolt RDMA device, `via` the interface and the other Mac's IPv4 address on that cable (an
IPv6 link-local address works too), and `port` a UDP port both ends reserve for meeting.

With two Thunderbolt cables between the Macs, MCDMA can bond them as one link (its dual-pipe build): join the two
devices and the two `via` entries with `+`, in the same order on both Macs, and keep the next port free as well:

```json
{"rank": 0, "library": "/path/to/libmcdma-fabric.dylib",
 "links": [{"peer": 1, "device": "rdma_en4+rdma_en3", "via": "en4/192.0.2.2+en3/192.0.2.6", "port": 7490, "name": "speedup"}]}
```

On two M5 Ultras the bond nearly doubles bulk throughput (96 against 53 Gbit/s); in speed-up mode it brings the first
token about 2% sooner (up to 4% at 8k) and decode under 1% faster, since decode's exchanges are small.

## Starting it

Start both servers with the same model and flags (a flag that changes decoding, such as `--no-drafts`, goes on
both), rank 1 first or within five minutes of each other; each waits for the other before it loads. Rank 1, then
rank 0:

```bash
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve ~/models/flash-next-6bit --name flash-next \
  --speed-up rank1.json --temperature 0 --no-thinking --dashboard
```

```bash
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve ~/models/flash-next-6bit --name flash-next \
  --speed-up rank0.json --temperature 0 --no-thinking --dashboard
```

Each server runs MCDMA's thread that places arriving messages, and its own sending thread, at user-interactive
priority, so other work on either Mac does not slow the rounds. `MCDMA_FABRIC_QOS=0` leaves MCDMA's thread at the
default priority. Older versions of this recipe set `FZ_LANE=1 FZ_GDN=2`, which decode 2 to 5% slower, so leave them
out.

Run both attached to a terminal session, or allow them Local Network access in System Settings. A server started
detached over SSH can't ask for that access, so macOS drops its packets and the ranks stop with `ConnectFailed`.

Send requests to rank 0. Rank 1 refuses requests of its own and runs rank 0's as they come; a stop string or a
cancel on rank 0 ends both Macs on the same round. Stopping rank 0 ends rank 1's part; stop rank 1's server
afterwards. If the link fails, both servers end the request with an error within about ten seconds instead of hanging.

## Limits

- Flash Next 6-bit on the replay engine only, one reply at a time, greedy.
- Two Macs. A model bigger than one Mac needs pipeline mode, which this is not.
# Step-5-Preview

This recipe describes the native Zig engine on one 256 GB Mac. Step-5-Preview (`stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview`) has 92
layers of sliding and full GQA attention, a sparse CSA indexer on the full layers, 352 routed experts (8 a token),
three MTP layers and a perception-encoder image tower. StepFun ships it in FP8, which one Mac cannot hold, so this
page converts it to MLX affine weights first.

## Converting

`tools/step5_fp8_to_mlx.py` streams the FP8 checkpoint into an MLX affine one. The routed experts become 2-bit in
groups of 128, each group's range searched and refit by least squares; every other linear weight becomes 8-bit in
groups of 64, and norms, the router and the indexer's weights keep their dtype. It needs mlx and a few GiB of RAM.

```bash
python tools/step5_fp8_to_mlx.py --src ~/models/step5-preview-fp8 --out ~/models/Step-5-Preview-MLX-2bit --mtp --vision
```

The text model is 166.9 GiB; `--mtp` adds 2.5 GiB and `--vision` 3.7 GiB (bf16). `--only-mtp` and `--only-vision`
add them to a checkpoint already converted. `--layers N` writes a bring-up slice of the first N layers.

## Serving

```bash
tensorfold-native serve ~/models/Step-5-Preview-MLX-2bit --port 8888 --vision
```

Structured output (`response_format`, guided JSON, regex, choice and grammars) needs `libtfgrammar` beside the binary:
release archives ship it; from source, `zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR` with an xgrammar v0.2.8 checkout.

- **Memory.** Weights, scratch and every stream's caches stay under 75% of RAM, below the point where macOS stalls;
  `STEP5_LOAD_LIMIT_GB` sets another limit. With MTP and vision, 15.8 GiB is left for caches on a 256 GB Mac: up to
  227,025 tokens of context by default, or `--context` for less. The model supports 1M tokens; a Mac's caches reach
  what the limit leaves. A 212k-token prompt ran with free memory never below 19%.
- **Prompts** run in 2,048-row chunks on the tensor units: 917, 901, 872 and 835 tokens a second at 4k, 8k, 16k and
  32k tokens (the server's prefill time, prompt cache off). A 129k-token prompt took about 200 s and a 212k-token one
  about 376 s on the build before TensorFold 1.0.12, whose 4k-32k prompts ran 2-3% slower.
- **MTP drafts** (`--mtp` checkpoints): three chained drafts a round, verified in one window. Replies are the same as
  undrafted ones. Greedy replies of 200-400 tokens, timed with their prompt: 41.2 tokens a second on code (25.8
  undrafted), 36.6 on prose (27.0), 48.8 on math (26.9).
- **Prompt cache.** Kept states hold the full layers' keys and values to the mark, the last 512 positions of each
  sliding layer and the indexer's open region, copied on the GPU. They live in what the streams' caches leave of the
  budget and give way when a stream needs the room; `--prompt-cache-gib` caps them and `0` turns them off. Replies are
  the same with it on and off. An 11.6k-token prompt sent again took 1.8 s instead of 15.3 s; later turns of the
  chat resume there. A kept state cannot sit beside its own stream past about 110k tokens, so longer prompts are not
  kept. States sit on 2,048-token boundaries and chat-history cuts, so a new question on the same image in a new
  chat reads the image again.
- **Images** (`--vision`) follow vLLM's Step3-VL processor as of vLLM `dd944845777b`: 504-pixel crops and a
  728-pixel overview, each through the encoder on the tensor units. A 1200x800 image is 688 tokens; its first reply
  took 3.8 s with an 80-token answer.
- **Streams.** `--parallel N` serves N streams at once, each with its own caches under the same budget.
- **Idle.** Weights and scratch sit in a residency set that the idle keepalive touches with a 16-byte copy, so the
  first request after a pause is as fast as the rest (0.18-0.20 s for a one-token reply after 15 s idle).

Load takes about 40 s, including a warm-up pass so the first request does not pay the GPU's first touch.

## Checking

`tools/zig/step5_ref.py` is an MLX reference of the text model (`tools/zig/step5_check_ref.py` checks it against
StepFun's torch code), and `tools/zig/step5_vision_ref.py` runs StepFun's image tower in torch. Served numbers and the
quality suite's results for this checkpoint are in
[recipe-harness](https://github.com/BobClawblaw/recipe-harness) (target `step5-m5`).

On the 4-layer slice, a 209,814-token prompt gives the reference's top 5 next tokens in its order, logprobs within
0.02. On the full model, long-context retrieval at 212k tokens (one record's code out of 10,500) answered 2 of 3
questions right and at 129k 2 of 2; the miss, an early record, is the 2-bit model's, not the engine's.

The recipe-harness runs on this build: structured output 18/18, seeded sampling 9/9, a resumed multi-turn chat
identical to a cold one (first token 0.35 s against 3.28 s), 60/60 soak turns, tools 58/60, JSON 30/30, GSM8K 49/50,
IFEval 41/50; one stream decodes 39-51 tokens a second (prose to code) with the first token in 0.24-0.28 s.
# Ternary Bonsai 2 27B

This recipe describes the Python engine's `bonsai` family, frozen at 0.6.6 and available at the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6). The native binary has no family for this pack yet,
so `tensorfold pull` and `tensorfold info` refuse it.

Prism ML's Bonsai 2 27B is Qwen3.8-27B with ternary weights stored in a rotated basis. Its MLX pack
(`model_type: prism_hadamard_qwen35`) keeps every projection as 2-bit codes in groups of 128. The weights
are ternary, so each group's codes decode to -s, 0 or +s. The pack's `hadamard.json` names the transform
each projection's input needs: fixed ±1 signs, then a normalized Walsh-Hadamard transform over 1024-wide
blocks. The embedding stores its rows in the same basis and turns them back on lookup.

```bash
tensorfold pull prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mlx-2bit z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
tensorfold serve prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mlx-2bit
```

The `bonsai` family runs the pack on the Qwen3.8-27B lane engine:

- Every projection's rows go through a row-exact rotation kernel (the signs, then the transform, then one
  rounding to bf16) before the lane matmul. Projections that share an input rotate it once.
- A lookup dequantizes the 2-bit row and rotates it back.
- The recurrent layers' unquantized fp32 gates (`in_proj_a`, `in_proj_b`) run through a fixed-order dense
  kernel.
- Norms, convolution and state parameters are held in bf16, as in the Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint.
- The vision tower in the pack is not loaded. TensorFold serves the text model.

Only the version-1 Prism contract is read: blocks of 1024, explicit signs, grouped DeltaNet activations and
no MTP head. Any other pack is refused from its configuration files before its weights download.

## Chips

- M5 tensor-unit GPUs read the 2-bit codes through the lane kernels. Each group-128 scale and bias covers two
  groups of 64 there, and each fp16 scale rounds to bf16 once at load.
- M1 through M4 run the row decoder on the codes widened exactly to 4 bits, which takes 13.9 GiB rather than
  7.2 GiB.
- Where the widened codes don't fit beside 12 GiB for the drafter and a prompt chunk (Macs with 32 or 36 GB), the
  row decoder reads the pack's 2-bit codes and fp16 scales as stored instead, through the packed affine row kernel
  ([quantized checkpoints](../quantization.md)). A forward then takes 1.3x as long at one row and 2.1x at 16 rows
  on an M3 Ultra.
- Between the two, the first layers widen as far as the budget allows: a 36 GB Mac's default 25.2 GiB widens 60 of
  64. Outputs are exact within a server; how many layers widen depends on the memory budget, so servers with
  different budgets can differ in their bits (the startup line says how many).
- With the drafter, the model needs about 20 GiB of budget, so 16 and 24 GB Macs can't serve it.

Drafting uses Qwen3.8-27B's DFlash2 model and context copies. The target verifies every draft against
its own serial sample, so drafted output equals `"draft": false` output.

Against mlx_lm running the pack's own runtime (paired runs on the same machine, the range over two runs a chip):

| Chip | Decode, code | Decode, chat | Prompt processing |
|---|---|---|---|
| M5 Max | 3.7-5.8x | 1.7-2.2x | 1.4-1.7x (2k to 32k) |
| M3 Ultra | 2.1-2.9x (94-111 vs 38-46) | 1.3-1.7x (60-67 vs 39-46) | 1.15-1.28x (2k to 64k) |

Replies are exact on both: drafted equals serial, resumed equals fresh, and concurrent streams equal their solo
runs. On the M3 Ultra the packed 2-bit rows (a 32 GB Mac's budget) are exact too, at 40-80 tok/s.

Bonsai 2 27B is by Prism ML (Apache-2.0).
# Training a drafter

This is how a learned block drafter is trained from what the native server records, and released in the
[drafter release format](../drafter-release.md). The steps are in order. Each comes with what it gained on the one
target it has been through, so treat the numbers as Kolibri's, not as laws:

- Kolibri-1 (78B MoE, 3.5B active, FP8) on one DGX Spark, 3-10 Oct 2026, released as
  [josch15366/Kolibri-1-block-drafter](https://huggingface.co/josch15366/Kolibri-1-block-drafter). Decode speed
  against copy drafting alone, one stream, prompts no checkpoint trained on: 1.40x on SWE agent turns, 1.31x on chat
  and 1.40x on German greedy; 1.49x, 1.27x and 1.24x sampled as served; 1.10x at four streams.

Kolibri was recorded and served on a fork of the Python engine, now frozen. The native server records with
`--record` (CUDA, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning first). Nemotron is the second target, and the check of whether these steps
carry over.

Training runs outside TensorFold. Ours is in
[jschmied/qwen38-flash-next-gb10](https://github.com/jschmied/qwen38-flash-next-gb10/tree/c4d69bacb6edab1b23829f98e79c2cfd6205d329/tools/kolibri/drafter):
`probe.py` (the tap probe), `model_block.py` and `train_block.py` (the drafter and its training), `eval_block.py`
(acceptance on recordings) and `export_block.py` (the release). It reads recordings and the target's head, and
prefills text through the target with that fork's Kolibri forward. TensorFold ships no training code.

## How to use it

1. Do the steps in order. Score after each on the same fixed slices, and keep their prompts out of every training set.
2. Score on output the target generated for prompts no checkpoint trained on: per class (code or agent turns, chat,
   each language), accepted drafts per round of 3 and 4, and agreement per position.
3. Acceptance is a speed measure, never a quality one: the target verifies every draft, so a drafter cannot change a
   reply. Its quality check is the contract below.
4. When a step proves out on another target, add its result. When one loses, add it to "Don't bother".

## Record

`tensorfold serve MODEL --record DIR` writes what serving computes. Each server makes its own new folder
`DIR/<pid>-<k>`, and each stream writes `<n>.*` in it:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `.tok` | u32: the token at each committed row |
| `.pos` | u32: the row's cache position |
| `.kind` | u8: 1 for a reply's row, 0 for a prompt's |
| `.st` | the tapped rows, `row_bytes` each, as the family's `features` gives them |
| `.top` | with `logprobs`, entry j for reply token j: the best ids (u32 x k), then their logprobs (f32 x k), from the row at cache position `prompt_len - 1 + j` |
| `.json` | `rows`, `first_row`, `prompt_len`, `taps`, `row_bytes`, `dtype`, `top_k`, and `gap` if the stream stopped early |

- Record with drafts on. On Nemotron the recorded rows were byte-identical drafted, with `"draft": false` and with
  concurrent streams, and replies were identical with and without `--record`. Check both on your recording build
  before you record for days: the same prompts with and without `--record`, drafted and `"draft": false`, must give
  equal `token_sha`.
- A prompt pass records the rows it computed, from its cached prefix on. Rows a prompt pass recomputes differ from the
  decode rows of the same positions by about 1-5 % (relative L2), since the kernels differ. Both are fine to train on.
- Include the tap past the last layer (`taps` = the layer count, normed). The head reads that row, so the target's
  logits at every recorded row can be computed offline over the draft vocabulary: the head rows times that row, then
  the adapter's bias and softcap. Without it, the target's distribution comes only from `.top`, which exists for
  reply rows of requests that ask for `logprobs`.
- Disk: `row_bytes` per row. Nemotron's one tap is 5,376 bytes, so a million rows is 5.4 GB. Kolibri's three bf16
  taps were 15,360 bytes a row, so its 6.03M recorded rows held about 93 GB of tapped rows. A stream starts no files
  below 25 GiB free.
- Join the files by `.pos`, not by file order. Row i of `.tok`, `.pos`, `.kind` and `.st` is one committed row at
  cache position `.pos[i]`. A resumed prompt records from its cached prefix on, so its rows start at `first_row`, and a
  `gap` ends them early. `.top[j]` is the distribution the target computed at position `prompt_len - 1 + j`, the one
  that drew reply token j, so the row at position p pairs with `.top[p - prompt_len + 1]`. For a 36-token prompt,
  `.top[0]` belongs to position 35, a prompt row (kind 0), and the first reply row, position 36, pairs with `.top[1]`.
  A row with no entry there has no recorded distribution.
- Check every `.json` against the release you train for (`checkRecording` in `zig/src/core/drafter_release.zig`):
  the same `taps`, `row_bytes` and `dtype`. A recording with other taps cannot train that release.
- Serve with at least as many `--parallel` slots as clients, or the prompt cache misses and every agent turn records
  its whole prompt again (on Kolibri, 135 of 2.8M prompt tokens hit with 7 clients on 6 slots; 95 % with 8).
- Generation and training can't share a 128 GB machine with a ~77 GB target. Alternate them.

## The steps

1. **Probe the layers.** Fit a linear map from each layer's rows to the target's own final row k ahead (k = 1 to 3),
   on held-out conversations, and score top-1 through the target's head. Tap where the next tokens sit. On Kolibri
   that was the outputs of layers 44-48 (counted from 0) of 50, not the middle; three taps (ids 45, 48 and 50 in the
   release format) added 1.5-2 points over one. Minutes on the GPU. A family defines what its tap ids mean once, in
   `features`.
2. **Pick the draft vocabulary from the target's own output.** Count the target's top-1 tokens over its recorded
   output per class, and take the slice that covers what you serve. A token outside the slice can never be drafted,
   so coverage caps acceptance. On Kolibri a 32k slice covered German at 0.896. Widening it to every token seen
   (60,614) gave +0.075 / +0.014 / +0.037 accepted (code / chat / German) without retraining.
3. **Train on the target's distribution, not on text.** The loss is KL to the target over the draft vocabulary at
   every block position, weighted 0.8^j, with the target's tapped rows as inputs. On the same 10M tokens it gained
   about 2x what L1 state regression with cross-entropy gained, and trained 17 % faster.
4. **Get volume and variety first.** 45M tokens of broad text, regenerated by a strong model and prefilled through the
   target, generalised. About 1M rows of the target's own output, repeated, were memorised and moved nothing on unseen
   prompts.
5. **Then add the target's own served output.** Mix recordings into every batch at a fixed share: 40 % on Kolibri,
   code 0.3 / chat 0.4 / German 0.3, at most one pass over code recordings and three over chat and German. German rose
   14 % and chat 7 % on one chain drafter. When one class runs out, keep the others' shares. When all run out, code
   acceptance falls back toward the text-only level, so end a run with them.
6. **Keep every language and class in every batch.** One 26M-token batch without German cost 18 % of German
   acceptance.
7. **Draft a block, with a chain head at position 1.** A 4-layer block drafter proposing four positions in one pass,
   whose row 0 is an EAGLE-3 chain head, against a 1-layer chain drafter: accepted of 3 went from 1.38 / 1.23 / 0.95
   to 1.91 / 1.29 / 1.11. Start the chain head from a trained chain drafter.
8. **Train position 1 at a low learning rate.** Frozen, it capped the block. At the full rate it forgot its chain
   skill. At 0.1x in its own optimizer group, with loss weight 2, code went from 1.50 to 1.62 in 1,621 steps.
9. **Add a predecessor head.** Each position j >= 2 reads its predecessor token through a low-rank head (rank 256,
   identity at the start), Kolibri's argmax in training. It came with the recordings in one step, so its own share is
   not separated.
10. **Export to the release format and check it.** The release carries the target's embedding, the head rows of the
    draft vocabulary, and the target's adapter values (`embed_scale`, `tied`, `softcap`, `head_bias`) read from its
    config and forward pass. It must open with `Release.open` and pass `check` against the target the server loads.

Kolibri's final hyper-parameters, for reference: hidden 2,560, 20 heads x 128, FFN 6,144, 4 layers, block 4, a
2,048-row context window, 1,024 anchors a window, AdamW from 2e-4 down to 2e-5 (cosine) after 100 warm-up steps, a
fresh optimizer per stage, predecessor and spine rank 256, checkpoints every 2,500 steps. The release took 76,083 steps
over 213.6M tokens. On Kolibri's held-out recordings it accepts 1.937 / 1.321 / 1.130 per round of 3 (code / chat /
German), against 1.38 / 1.23 / 0.95 for the chain drafter it replaced. Those slices chose the checkpoint, so they are
development numbers, not a test set.

## Check it in TensorFold

- **Replies.** Drafted replies equal `"draft": false` ones, greedy and sampled with a seed, solo and concurrent, and a
  prompt resumed from the cache gives the reply a fresh one does: the same `token_sha`. The drafter changes how fast a
  reply comes, never which reply. Any difference is a bug in the serving path, not a weak drafter.
- **Speed.** Decode tok/s against the same build with copy drafting alone, one stream and several, on prompts no
  checkpoint trained on. The reply's `acceptance_rate` and `tokens_per_round` explain a speed change; they don't rank
  drafters on their own, because a round's cost depends on depth, batch and the bytes the drafter reads.
- **Format.** The release opens (`Release.open`), its adapter matches the target the server loaded (`check`), and
  every recording it was trained on matches its taps (`checkRecording`). These check the folder; they do not run the
  drafter. Nothing loads a release at serve time yet. The loader that does must run `check` first, so a release whose
  `embed_scale`, `tied`, `softcap` or `head_bias` differ from the target's is refused, not served with wrong logits.

## Don't bother

- **Loss variants past step 3.** KL, a soft-target cross-entropy and AUF tied on Kolibri.
- **A teacher-to-self schedule for the predecessor.** Under greedy acceptance a drafted predecessor survives only if
  it equals the target's argmax, so on every accepted prefix the two are the same token.
- **The data token as predecessor, and a DSpine-style spine.** Both within +-0.002 of the control. Kolibri's release
  kept the spine because it costs little.
- **More recordings of the class you have most of.** On Kolibri the scarcest class (German) bounded every pass.
  Record that one.
- **Depth 4 on a MoE target.** Slower than depth 2 on Kolibri: each extra verify row brings its own experts.

## Serving notes from Kolibri

On the GB10 a draft round costs the bytes it reads, not its launches. The bf16 block drafter was slower than the
1-layer chain and lost 17 % at four streams. With an FP8 body, an NVFP4 head slice (the same drafts, a quarter of the
bytes) and one batched pass for a round's streams, it is 1.10x at four streams. The release's `serving` field holds
those defaults (depth 2, `fp8`, `nvfp4`).

## Nemotron as the second target

Nemotron gives one tap today: the final norm's rows (`taps` = 52), which its head and its own MTP head read. Its
adapter is plain (`embed_scale` 1.0, untied, no softcap, no head bias). Its MTP head is the baseline: a learned
drafter is worth serving only if it beats MTP at the same depth on the same prompts, by decode speed with replies
unchanged. A tap probe across its layers needs `features` to give more tap ids first.
# Intel Arc (XPU): Nemotron 3.5 Lightning

Status: experimental. One checkpoint, one card class, one request at a time. Everything below was measured on the setup in
[Tested setup](#tested-setup); nothing is claimed for other cards.

The Intel GPU backend runs OpenCL C kernels compiled to SPIR-V (`ocloc`) through Level Zero, on the same loader table as the
Qwen3.8-27B XPU runner (`zig/src/xpu/ze.zig`), and has no CUDA or Metal code in its path. The token-id CLI is a separate
Linux build (`-Dxpu`); the XPU server (`zig build xpu-native`, `--backend auto`) serves Nemotron beside Qwen3.8-27B.

## Supported

| Item | State |
| --- | --- |
| Model | Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B, MLX affine 4-bit, group 64 (the checkpoint named in [nemotron-3.5.md](nemotron-3.5.md)) |
| Card | Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage, 32 GB) |
| Not supported | NVFP4 and FP8-Mamba checkpoints: refused at load with `NVFP4 checkpoints are not supported on the XPU backend yet; use the MLX 4-bit checkpoint`. They need FP4/FP8 dequantisation kernels that do not exist yet. |
| Drafts | The checkpoint's MTP head (`mtp-4bit.safetensors`) and copy drafts through the lane core, windows of up to 16 rows; `--no-drafts` or `TENSORFOLD_XPU_MTP=0` leaves the head unloaded |
| Streams | Up to `--parallel` streams a round, each on its own sequence (Mamba states, KV, head) |
| Prompt cache | Kept at 512-row prompt chunk ends and restored by device copy; `--prompt-cache-gib`, else 4 GiB within the free device memory less 2 GiB |
| Not supported | Tool-call gates, grammars and structured output |
| Sampling | Greedy uses the device argmax. A request with temperature above 0 is drawn on the host from the step's logits with the lane core's keyed sampler: temperature, `top_k`, `top_p`, `min_p` and `seed`; the draw is keyed by seed, absolute token position and candidate id. Presence and repetition penalties are not implemented. |
| Qwen3.8 | Not covered by this page. |

## Build and run

Needs Zig 0.17.0, `ocloc` and the Level Zero loader with the Intel compute runtime, on Linux with the `xe` driver.
`zig build` defaults to `-Doptimize=fast` (ReleaseFast); every number on this page was measured with it, and a debug build is much slower.

```bash
zig build -Dxpu                 # tensorfold-xpu (token-id CLI) and tf-xpu-test
zig build -Dxpu xpu-tests       # tf-xpu-<name>-test programs (checks and benchmarks)
zig build xpu-native -Dngen-include=NGEN   # zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native, the XPU server (docs/xpu/README.md)

tensorfold-xpu devices
tensorfold-xpu run MODEL --tokens-file ids.txt --max-tokens 128 --prefill 512
zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native serve MODEL --context 32768
```

`--prefill ROWS` prefills the prompt in windows of ROWS tokens (16 and up); the plain loop then decodes. `--context` defaults
to the model window capped at 32768 in `serve`; the server lists the family `nemotron_h` with format `mlx-q4g64`.

Run model programs one at a time: `tools/zig/xpu_guard.sh SECONDS COMMAND...` takes the GPU lock, refuses to start while other
processes hold more than 8 GB of device memory and stops the command only with SIGINT.
Every program applies the same rule at start: it refuses to run while other processes hold more than 8 GB of device
memory, and there is no override.

## Tested setup

Intel Arc Pro B70 Graphics (32.5 GB maximum single allocation), Linux 7.0.0 (`xe` driver), Zig 0.17.0, a local copy of the
Nemotron MLX 4-bit checkpoint (`TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit`, revision `d9d758fb83953437f7263256b0d96157e2a348b8`,
729 tensors, 17.27 GiB of weights). The commit under test is the head of the pull request.

LFM3-1.7B (`LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B-MLX-4bit`, MLX affine 4-bit, group 64) on an Intel Iris Xe laptop GPU (Gen12LP, `tgllp`, 96 EUs, no
DPAS) under WSL2 (Ubuntu 24.04, 8 GB given to WSL), Ubuntu's compute runtime 23.43.27642 and Level Zero loader 1.16, Zig 0.17.0,
`zig build xpu-native -Dxpu-device=tgllp` (DPAS off, so the server is built without the Qwen3.8-27B runner):

| Setup | Decode, c=1, `--no-drafts` | Decode, c=1, copy drafts | Decode, c=4, aggregate | TTFT, 1,024 tokens | TTFT, 8,192 tokens | Memory (`serve --context 16384`) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Iris Xe, LFM3-1.7B MLX 4-bit | 15.6 to 16.8 tok/s | 15.9 (chat) to 26.3 (prose) tok/s | 25 to 32 tok/s | 4.6 to 4.7 s | 55.4 to 55.6 s | 1.33 GB device allocation, 448 MB host resident |

Decode, c=1: two short chats (160 tokens), a 1,001-token prose prompt and a 601-token code prompt (128 tokens), greedy, three runs
each, with copy drafts (the default) and with `--no-drafts`; c=4: four concurrent 128-token completions of distinct 32-token prompts,
six runs a mode, with or without drafts; TTFT: prompts of numbered item sentences, one token generated; three runs each, through
`/v1/completions`. Copy-draft gains depend on how repetitive the text is: prose and code that repeat their own context decode at 26
and 22 tok/s, the chats, with few copies to draft, at the speed without drafts. A `/v1/chat/completions` request with the
checkpoint's chat template answers (thinking on, `finish_reason` stop).
With `--parallel N` each stream has its own sequence (about 196 MiB of KV at 16,384 tokens); a second chat turn over an
