8,037-token document resumes from the prompt cache in 0.80 s instead of 122.6 s, with the same reply.

## Measurements

Decode, 128 greedy tokens from a 5-token prompt: 5.72 ms/token, 175 tok/s (`tensorfold-xpu run`, five runs on different
commits: 173.6 to 174.8).
Prompts take the decode step's arithmetic at every chunk size (`nem_prow.cl`: each output sums in the decode's lane order;
a sub-group holds 8 rows and 8 outputs, so a weight word is unpacked once for 8 rows and an input word once for 8 outputs;
routed experts take their rows in the same order; attention runs the decode kernel per row, 16 rows a launch). Cold prompts,
`tensorfold-xpu run --prefill 512`, random token ids, 16 tokens generated:

| Prompt tokens | Prefill s | Prefill tok/s | Earlier prefill GEMMs, tok/s | Decode tok/s after it |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2,048 | 2.41 | 851 | 3,108 | 176.0 |
| 8,192 | 9.85 | 831 | 3,086 | 172.0 |
| 32,768 | 43.4 | 755 | 2,888 (11.1 s) | 164.4 |
| 131,072 | 256.5 | 511 | 2,281 | 138.8 |

The same prompts one token at a time run at about 167 tok/s, and in 16-row windows at about 215 tok/s. The 32,768-token
prompt gives the same tokens afterwards as with the earlier prefill GEMMs (digest `64a5a3409b0b`).

Through the XPU server with the MTP head loaded (`tools/zig/xpu_draft_receipt.py`, 256 tokens, two runs each): `"draft": false`
replies 173.0 to 174.3 tok/s greedy (a one-row round is the decode step); drafted greedy 157.3 (code), 167.4 (prose), 169.0
(list) and 171.8 (copy) tok/s, 0.90 to 0.99 of plain: each extra window row costs about 3.7 ms, mostly the routed experts.
Seeded (T 0.8, seed 7) replies run at about 60 tok/s, the host drawing from 131,072 logits a row.

Concurrency (`tools/zig/xpu_concurrent_receipt.py`, `--parallel 4`, 4 streams of 192 tokens, greedy and seeded): 72.0 and 73.6
tok/s aggregate against 83.8 for the same requests one after another; each stream's window is its own forward pass.

Prompt cache (`tools/zig/xpu_resume_receipt.py`, a two-turn chat over a 6,685-token document): turn 1 prefills in 8.52 s, turn 2
resumes 6,656 tokens and prefills in 0.21 s instead of 8.67 s.

Memory, measured on the 32 GB card in a host with 62.2 GiB of RAM and 24 threads (kernel 7.0.0, `tensorfold-native serve`,
KV caches and scratch allocated at load for the chosen context): device allocation counter 17.85 GB for the weights, 18.40 GB
at `--context 4096`, 19.24 GB at 131,200 and 20.11 GB at 262,144 (the native window) without the head, 19.36 GB at 32,768
with it, unchanged by the prompts that follow.
Host process: 339 MB resident after load, 355 MB at its peak after a 262,080-token prompt (VmHWM); the engine pins only its
staging buffers. Load is ready in 7 s with the checkpoint in the page cache. After SIGINT the server exits in 0.2 s with status
0 and no device memory left. The weights alone are 17.3 GiB, so this model does not fit a 16 GB card; no 16 GB claim is made.

## Accuracy

Against the CUDA reference of the same checkpoint (teacher-forced, the reference's own tokens fed):

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 4 prompts x 48 steps, top-1 | 185 of 192 (188 with the earlier per-row pair; every miss is a near tie, see below) |
| 15 prompts, 1,440 positions, plain decode | top-1 1,421 (98.7%), mean abs log-probability difference 0.0233, 95th percentile 0.109, max 0.514 (1,422, 0.0232, 0.105, 0.750 with the earlier per-row pair) |
| same, prompt in 512-row or 128-row windows | identical to plain decode: 1,421, 0.0233, 0.1085, 0.514 |

The 19 top-1 misses of the plain run are listed with both margins by `WIDE_LIST=file tools/zig/xpu_compare_wide.py plain`:
all have a reference margin (top-1 over top-2) of at most 0.375 and a gap on our side of at most 0.625 (log-probability steps at this
precision are 0.125), and 13 of the 19 are within 0.25 on both sides. The earlier outlier of the run with the per-row decode
attention (prompt 12, step 53: reference margin 1.375, ours 0.125 the other way) is gone; with the earlier per-row pair it is still there. It came from the state the single-row
kernels built over the 1,000-token prompt, not from the step's own kernels, and the model is sensitive to the order of accumulation
between its decode and prefill paths at such positions; the reference engine shows the same sensitivity (see the parity results below).
On the 4-prompt gate the new decode attention has 7 misses against 4 with the earlier per-row pair; each of the 7 has a reference margin of
at most 0.25 and our gap at most 0.375, two of them exact ties on our side (a tie goes to the lower token id, the reference's
choice differs). The greedy reply to a test prompt differs by one word between the two kernels (the digests differ); each kernel is
deterministic.

KL divergence against BF16 (llama.cpp scoring, same public corpus, 16-row windows): the full 360-chunk run (91,800 scored tokens) gave
mean KLD 0.0775, same top-1 89.84%, perplexity ratio 1.0591, measured with an earlier build. On this branch, where windows take the
decode's arithmetic, the first 64 chunks give mean KLD 0.0866 +- 0.0011 and same top-1 87.41 +- 0.26% (0.0864 and 87.24% with the
earlier matrix-engine windows).

Generation parity against TensorFold 0.6.4 on CUDA (41 prompts, 200 greedy tokens each, prompt in 512-row windows): 14 of 41
replies are identical token for token; 25 of the 27 first divergences are exact bf16 ties or within 0.25 logit, the other two
are 0.5 and 1.125. Teacher-forced on the reference's tokens, 5,098 of 5,159 positions agree (98.8%); 49 of the 61 mismatches
are ties or within 0.25. The other 12 (the same kind as wide prompt 12 step 53 above) have a reference margin of 0.375 to 2.5
where our gap is 0.125; feeding the same prompt and the reference's tokens to the CUDA engine as one prefill, its prefill path
sided with our order or tied at three of them (short3@54, qa2@34, qa4@87) and with its own decode order at four (short3@96,
short3@155, summ1@64, code3@142), which means the reference's own decode and prefill paths differ from each other by up to
about 1.5 logit at such positions. Our engine is deterministic (41 of 41 reruns identical).

Projection classes against an independent FP64 reference (`tf-xpu-nem_fp64-test`: real 4-bit codes dequantised exactly in
f64, random bf16 rows shaped like each layer's input, first and last layer of each kind, decode, 8-row window and 8- and
64-row prompt kernels separately; every class is within the test's bounds, and the window and prompt kernels give the decode
kernels' figures):

| Output | Classes | Aggregate error | Worst column (relative to that column's max) | Notes |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| bf16 | Mamba in/out, attention q/k/v/o, router gate, embed | 1.6e-3 | 3.9e-3 | at most 0.54 ulp; 99.8-100% of outputs equal the correctly rounded f64 value |
| bf16, relu2 | shared up, routed fc1 | 3.5-3.8e-3 | 1.1e-2 | 74-77% exact: the pre-activation is rounded to bf16 before squaring |
| fp32 | shared down, routed fc2, lm_head | 5e-8 to 1e-7 | 6e-7 | |

## Exactness

- Window rows: a window of up to 16 rows takes the decode step's arithmetic (the row kernels of `nem_rows.cl`: each output's lane
  sums in the decode's order, each weight read once for all the rows), so a one-row window equals the decode step bit for bit, and
  windows of 2, 3, 4, 8 and 16 rows give the same logits over 40 tokens, including a pending-then-commit case
  (`tf-xpu-nem_rows-test`).
- Prompt chunk size: a prompt cut anywhere gives the bits of the same prompt decoded one token at a time. After 640 tokens in
  chunks of 16, 17, 100, 128 and 512 rows, the Mamba conv state, SSM state and KV bytes are byte-identical to the row-by-row
  state and the next 8 decode logits are identical (`tf-xpu-nem_seam-test`); prefill in chunks of 32, 100 and 512 rows gives
  the row-by-row last-token logits (`tf-xpu-nem_prefill-test`).
- Drafts: every drafted reply's `token_sha` equals its `"draft": false` run, 8 of 8 (greedy and seeded; code, prose, list,
  copy); a server without the head gives the same seeded `token_sha`s, 4 of 4.
- Streams: 4 concurrent replies equal their solo runs, 4 of 4 in each of two rounds (greedy and seeded).
- Prompt cache: a resumed turn's `token_sha` equals the same turn with `--prompt-cache-gib 0`, greedy and seeded.
- Requests: A client that disconnects mid-stream cancels its request
  and the next request gives the same tokens as before; seeded sampling repeats exactly; SIGINT or SIGTERM during a generation ends
  the running stream after its current token with an error event (`ShuttingDown`) and `[DONE]`, answers a queued
  request with the error `the server is shutting down`, exits with status 0 within 0.2 s and leaves no device memory held.
- Host-side slot ring: forwards queued without a sync equal synced forwards (`tf-xpu-nem_slot-test`).

## Tests

`tools/zig/xpu_compare_ref.py` (forced tokens against the reference), `xpu_compare_wide.py`, `xpu_nem_needle.py`,
and the `tf-xpu-*-test` programs (`runner-all`, `nem_rows`, `nem_prefill`, `nem_slot`, `nem_seam`,
`nem_fp64`, `nem_format`, `panic`). `zig build test` passes except `direct_io: direct reads return the same bytes as buffered
reads`, which fails the same way on an unmodified upstream 1.0.2 checkout on this machine.

## Known limits

- Decode about 172 tok/s at short context, 137 tok/s at 128k and 113 tok/s at 256k; drafts do not speed it up on this MoE yet,
  and concurrent streams do not share weight reads.
- Prompts run at about 850 tok/s at 2k tokens and 511 tok/s at 128k: the decode's fp32 arithmetic on the vector units, about a
  quarter of the earlier prefill GEMMs' speed, for prompts whose bits do not depend on how they are cut.
- A shutdown during a generation ends the stream with an error event rather than a finish reason.
- Single card, single process: the 17.3 GiB of weights leave about 14 GB on a 32 GB card.
# Native request seeds

A sampled HTTP request uses its explicit `seed`, then a configured default seed, then a fresh 63-bit OS seed.
Default seeds cover injected `Server.Config.default_sampling`; no stock serve flag or generation config sets one.
An omitted or null request seed uses this fallback. Sampled defaults without a seed still draw fresh entropy.
An explicit seed keeps its existing bit conversion and sampling behavior. Greedy requests do not draw a seed.
If the secure random source fails, the request fails rather than falling back to prompt keying.

Every sampled done line appends `seed=<n>` after `ttft`, `decode`, `elapsed`, `queued` and `tok/s`.
Copy that number into the next request's `seed` field to reproduce the draw at identical sampling settings.
A fresh seed permits a different draw; it does not guarantee a different token or reply.

Native `serve --prompt-seed` restores historical prompt keying when neither request nor defaults supplies a seed:
the key comes from prompt IDs and `TENSORFOLD_SEED_SALT`. Request seeds still override configured defaults.
The standalone CLI and speech retain their prompt keying. This flag concerns the native server.

Exactness checks must use identical explicit seeds or start the native server with `--prompt-seed`.
The release-cell harness pins missing keys to 1234 and preserves every supplied key. The shared-prefix load tool
uses 1234 plus item ID by default. `bench_openai --seed-from-prompt` requires native `serve --prompt-seed`.
No output comparison or acceptance threshold is weakened by fresh default seeds.

Requested by @tpischke in #1026.
# RoCE all-gather for two ranks

One-shot all-gather between two DGX Sparks over RoCE: the GPU side of b12x's "RoCEnante" exchange (https://github.com/local-inference-lab/b12x, b12x/comm/roce, Apache License 2.0), written for two ranks. The host side (zig/src/cuda/roce.zig) owns a pinned region both GPUs and both NICs reach:

```
  recv[slot]       the peer's shard, written by the peer's NIC (2 slots of slot_bytes)
  flag[slot][hca]  the sequence the peer's NIC writes after its stripe on that HCA (128 bytes apart)
  send[slot]       this rank's shard, staged here for its NIC (2 slots)
  ctrl             {seq, nbytes of slot 0, nbytes of slot 1, error seq, missing hca}: the proxy's doorbell
```

One launch: (1) every block stages its share of the shard into send[seq & 1]; (2) the last block to stage publishes the slot's size and rings ctrl.seq after a system fence, and the proxy thread RDMA-writes the shard and then a flag per HCA stripe on the same queue pair (so a flag never lands before its stripe); (3) each block waits for every stripe's flag; (4) every block writes both shards in rank order (the layout NCCL's all-gather gives); (5) the last block to finish advances the device epoch, so a CUDA graph replays the exchange with new sequences. A wait past the spin limit poisons the exchange: later launches return at once and the host reports the error.

## Host side

Small all-gathers between two ranks as one-shot RDMA writes over RoCE: b12x's "RoCEnante" exchange (https://github.com/local-inference-lab/b12x, b12x/comm/roce, Apache License 2.0), written for two ranks: the kernel (kernels/cuda/roce_gather.cu) stages this rank's shard in pinned host memory and rings a doorbell; a proxy thread here RDMA-writes it to the peer, striped over the HCAs, each stripe followed by its sequence flag on the same queue pair; the kernel waits for the peer's flags and copies both shards out. A decode step's gathers are a few rows of partials. On two GB10s with one ConnectX-7 cable (NCCL 2.30.7, `tf-cuda-test roce-gather`, 2,000 calls back to back) this path took 10.4 us a call at 4 KiB a rank against NCCL's 12.3, 11.6 against 13.5 at 8 KiB, 17.4 against 20.5 at 32 KiB, and 17.4 against 51.5 at 64 KiB. libibverbs is opened at run time (as the driver and NCCL are): without it, or without an active HCA, the caller keeps NCCL.

## Setup and use

`tp_group.Group.openRoce` brings the path up on a two-rank group: each rank opens its HCAs, and what each brings (its region, keys, queue pairs and the largest shard it would send) crosses the group's own NCCL communicator, as does each rank's verdict after connecting. Both ranks get the path or neither does (`TF_ROCE=0` on either rank keeps NCCL). From then on `Group.allGather` sends a gather of up to the smaller rank's cap (512 KiB by default) this way and leaves larger ones to NCCL; the size alone decides, so both ranks always take the same path. A rank whose buffers are not 16-byte aligned gets `error.Misaligned` instead of falling back alone. Liveness is `tp_watch`'s, as for every group.

A failed exchange writes nothing into the gathered rows. Call `Group.check` after any synchronize whose result reads a gather: it returns the error the GPU or the proxy recorded.

`tf-cuda-test roce-gather <rank>` runs on both ranks (NCCL_COMM_ID set): every size up to the cap and past it against NCCL's all-gather, byte for byte, then each path's time a call.
# CUDA copy-source custody

Temporary uploads clone input into core-owned storage. A failed completion retains that storage until a successful
wait in its saved driver, context and stream proves completion. Destination buffers and parent CUDA objects still
need their own completion boundary. The source owner does not replace those guards.

Not every host-to-device copy goes through the owner. Qwen's kept prompt states (families/qwen3_5/cuda_reuse.zig)
restore from their own pinned snapshot with direct copies on the engine's stream. A restore marks the snapshot read
until a stream wait proves those copies done; dropping a marked snapshot waits once more and frees it if that wait
succeeds, else hands it to the quarantine (`copy_source.retainPinned`), which counts its bytes against the limit and
frees it after a later wait on that stream or its context succeeds. A failed save's buffer goes the same way.

Admission charges CPU source bytes, pinned buffer capacities and Node sizes before allocation. The process-wide
limit is 1 GiB and 4096 owners. It includes active reusable storage, quarantine, and owners inside disposal callbacks.
Driver allocator bookkeeping and event internals are outside the byte count; their owner count is bounded.
`CopySourceLimit` refuses new storage at the bound. It never frees a pending source to make room. Complete existing
work and retry, or stop submitting after an unrecoverable context failure. Limits are fixed in production.

The legacy allocator argument and Stage.gpa field remain source compatible. They do not back custody storage.
Quarantinable Node and CPU data allocations always use the core's process-lifetime page allocator. Pinned data is
owned by the driver until its completion and disposal callbacks return. Caller arenas may end after submission.

The RADIO tower owns one pixel Stage, reserved with its scratch for the largest image. Each image waits on the
previous copy's event before refilling it, so tower uploads neither allocate nor free pinned memory and never compete
for temporary-upload spares.

The graph wrappers track up to 64 simultaneous captures by driver, context, stream and capture mode across threads.
Temporary synchronous/default-stream and asynchronous uploaders refuse while a wrapper capture applies. A global
capture guards all contexts of that driver; other modes guard its saved context. A failed begin removes its scope.
A failed end keeps its guard until a successful end. Calls that bypass the graph wrappers are outside this contract.

Captured input must use stable Buffer or Stage storage owned by the graph's parent. Keep that storage through graph
and executable disposal. Mark every replay before launching it. Wait before mutating it for a later replay. After
disposing both graph objects, wait before release; failed disposal quarantines the storage. The helper cannot infer
an executable graph's reference to arbitrary host memory.

Registered busy owners remain visible throughout query, event destruction and host-release callbacks.
Driver.close waits for those callbacks, and frees every spare stage before the library goes, one a reaper parks
while close waits included. A retained nonbusy quarantine conservatively keeps the library loaded;
close must be retried after recovery. Callers serialize ordinary submissions and Driver destruction. The helper's
reaper/close tests exercise the supported concurrent disposal path, not arbitrary concurrent use of Driver.api.

The host fixtures use fake driver queues and real graph wrapper calls. CUDA behavior, GPU/model exactness, compiled
resources and performance need separate hardware qualification.
# Speech control allowlist

`tensorfold serve MODEL --allowed-controls 'sighs,laughs'` filters the `input` of
`POST /v1/audio/speech` before UTF-8, empty-input, length and prompt checks,
tokenization, and prompt-derived seeding. It does not affect chat, completions,
or the standalone generation tool. Omitting the flag leaves input byte-identical
and does not allocate a filtered copy. An empty list (`--allowed-controls ''`)
strips recognized delivery controls. Names compare after Unicode NFC normalization,
lowercasing, whitespace folding and removal of trailing `!?.…`. Empty
comma-separated entries are ignored. Names must be valid UTF-8 without square
brackets; novel descriptors remain accepted.

## Open vocabulary and public examples

The [official vLLM-Omni recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/fishaudio/drama-3)
states that there is no fixed tag list: tags are ordinary text and any short
descriptor is accepted. LIST therefore accepts novel descriptors such as
`gentle robot`; it does not reject an otherwise valid name as unknown.

| Example | Public source |
| --- | --- |
| `sighs`, `laughs` | [Drama model card, Point tags](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3#point-tags) |
| `laughing`, `whisper`, `angry`, `excited`, `pause` | [vLLM-Omni recipe, Event and emotion tags](https://recipes.vllm.ai/fishaudio/drama-3) |

`drama_cues.txt` lists only words used in tags in Fish Audio's public Drama 3
and Emotion Control docs, the Drama 3 model card and the Drama 3 technical
report. These examples are not an exhaustive list.

## Stripping rules

Listed square-bracket controls are retained with their normalized names. An
unlisted bracket is removed only if every word is in `drama_cues.txt` and at least
one word is a cue rather than a modifier. Unknown brackets, notes, nested
contextual brackets, indexes, Markdown links, quoted syntax, unclosed brackets
and brackets beyond the control scan bound are preserved.

The documented scoped tags `whisper`, `emphasis`, `soft`, `fast`, `slow`,
`stress` and `forceful` are removed case-insensitively, including inside
preserved brackets; their enclosed text stays. Other angle-bracket text stays.

Removing a control preserves the surrounding whitespace run with more line
breaks (the preceding run wins ties), and removes leading whitespace when
there is no preceding text. Whitespace elsewhere is unchanged. An input that
becomes empty is rejected by the existing speech validation.

This is a lexical filter, not a general prompt-injection or content-safety policy.
# Speech redraws

`tensorfold serve MODEL --silence-floor-dbfs F --silence-seconds S --silence-redraws N`
draws a whole `POST /v1/audio/speech` reply again when the silence guard ended it
with `silence`, up to N times (0 to 255). Omitted or 0, with the register guard
off, it never redraws, never reads `X-Deadline-S`, and leaves every reply
unchanged. Text models refuse `--silence-redraws` at startup, an explicit 0
included, and the register flags. `--silence-redraws` of 1 or more needs an
enabled silence guard; `--silence-redraw-controls` and the
[short reply](#short-replies) flags need `--silence-redraws` of 1 or more, and
`--silence-redraw-budget-s` needs it or the [register guard](#register).

## Why Drama 3 needs it

Sampled at temperature 1.0, top-k 30 and top-p 0.9, Drama 3 sometimes speaks
the first sentence and then stalls: the rest of the reply is silence or a flat
low hum until the frame cap. The seed comes from the prompt, so a stalling input
stalls on every request. On one DGX Spark with `fishaudio/drama-3`, 2 of 9
paragraph-length inputs stalled on the default prompt path and 3 of 9 with
`TF_DRAMA_PREFILL_ROWS=128`, on different inputs; a separate port of the
reference sampler stalled on 3 of 16 seeds (#1275).

With the guard below, none of 18 whole replies stalled. Each stalled input
recovered in one redraw, and every reply that had not stalled kept the same
bytes. Take it as a starting point and calibrate the floor and durations on the
voice you serve, as the sections below describe:

```sh
tensorfold serve DRAMA3_DIR --silence-floor-dbfs=-30 --silence-seconds=4 \
  --silence-mid-s=2 --silence-mid-min-voiced-s=1 \
  --silence-redraws=3 --silence-redraw-budget-s=90
```

A floor of -30 dBFS also catches the hum. Streams are not redrawn (see
[Streams](#streams)): a stalled stream ends early, with the rest of the text
unspoken.

Two more flags cut a reply that never really starts. With `--silence-onset-s S` and `--silence-onset-voiced-s V`
(both required together, and both need the floor and `--silence-seconds`; S must be above 0 and below the
silence seconds, V above 0), a reply also ends once it has stayed S seconds below the floor while having voiced
less than V seconds in total — the model cleared its throat but never began speaking. The startup line names the
rule: "or after S s below it with under V s voiced". An onset trip is a `silence` finish, redrawn like any
other.

## Seeds

Without an explicit request `seed`, redraw k (1 to N) seeds its prompt with `TENSORFOLD_SEED_SALT` plus k; the first
take keeps the stock seed, salt plus 0. Redraws are therefore deterministic. With
the same prompt, redraw k under salt s is the same draw as the first take under
salt s + k, so a sweep over salts should space compared salts more than N apart,
or N + 1 with the register guard.

An explicit request `seed` instead uses that exact integer for the first take
and seed + k modulo 2^64 for each redraw, counting both silence and register
attempts. Requested `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` remain in effect through
all redraws and control filtering; see [speech sampling](speech-sampling.md).
The seed rule does not make timing-based redraw budgets deterministic.

## Budget

A redraw starts only when t + d fits the budget, where t is the time since the
route received the request, before reading its body, and d is how long the
previous take ran. The budget is the lower of `--silence-redraw-budget-s` and the
request's `X-Deadline-S` header, each a positive finite number of seconds. With
neither, only the retry counts bound redraws. A malformed `X-Deadline-S` is an
HTTP 400 while silence redraws or the register guard are on, including streams.
The budget decides starts; a running take is not cut.
If the engine is busy, submission retries after a sleep until the latest start
that leaves room for the previous take's duration. Without a deadline or server
budget, a busy submission keeps the previous audio rather than waiting unboundedly.

## Reply

The reply is the last take that finished with audio, sent with its own
`X-Finish-Reason`. A redraw that ends `silence`, or a [short](#short-replies)
`stop`, replaces the previous take and redrawing continues; any other finish is
sent. When a redraw does not start (budget spent, engine busy) or ends without
audio, the previous take is sent. The server keeps a second PCM buffer, sized
like the first, while a reply redraws. It logs each redraw's finish reason and
why any redraw went unused.

With `--silence-redraws` above zero, every speech response carries
`X-Silence-Redraws` as a decimal integer, including zero and error replies.
It counts redraws admitted to the engine, not trips or attempted submissions;
a redraw that later fails still counts. Omission or an explicit zero leaves
the header absent.

## Controls

Without `--silence-redraw-controls`, a redraw speaks the same input. With
`--silence-redraw-controls LIST`, silence redraws speak the input, after any
`--allowed-controls` filtering, filtered by LIST under the
[speech control allowlist](speech-controls.md) grammar and stripping rules:
listed controls stay and unlisted controls are removed. An explicitly empty list
(`--silence-redraw-controls ''`) instead selects plain speech: every closed
square-bracket span and documented lowercase scoped tag is replaced by a space,
a leading `Direction:` line followed by `Line:` is removed, and Unicode
whitespace is folded and trimmed. If no such span is found, input is unchanged.
This empty-list setting reproduces the reference plain-controls redraw transform.
If the filtered input cannot be spoken, for example because nothing is left,
no redraw starts and the first take is sent. No control list is built in.
A direct register redraw keeps the current prompt; it does not apply the silence
redraw filter. If a silence redraw already filtered that prompt, the register
redraw inherits it.

## Short replies

A take can also collapse into an early `stop`: speech ends long before the text
is spoken, with no silent tail for the guard to trip on. With
`--short-reply-ratio R` and `--short-reply-chars-per-s CPS`, a whole take that
ends `stop` with less than R × chars / CPS seconds of audio is redrawn as a
silenced one is, under the same count, budget and controls. chars counts the
code points of the text the take spoke, bracketed controls included: the input
after any `--allowed-controls` filtering, or for a redraw, after any
`--silence-redraw-controls` filtering. R is above 0 and below 1. Texts of fewer
than 200 characters are never judged, since a fixed lead-in and tail dominate
their duration, and neither are `length` finishes. Neither flag has a default;
each needs the other, and without them no `stop` is redrawn.

No rate is built in: it depends on the voice, its pace and its language.
Calibrate both flags on the voice you serve:

1. Serve it as usual, without the short reply flags.
2. Send whole replies of 200 characters or more that represent your traffic,
   controls included.
3. For each reply that finished `stop` and that you heard to be complete, divide
   its characters, counted as above, by its seconds of audio: the `samples` of
   the server's reply log line divided by the sample rate in the WAV header.
4. Set CPS to the median of those rates. Each complete reply's share is
   seconds × CPS / chars; set R below the lowest share, with a margin, so that
   no complete reply would have been redrawn.
5. Check that the replies you heard cut short fall below R. If they overlap the
   complete ones, the ratio cannot tell them apart on that voice: leave the
   flags off.

Calibrate again when the served voice or the kind of text changes.

## Register

`--register-redraw-st ST --register-redraw-high PERCENT --register-high-hz HZ`
draws a whole reply once more when a phrase after the first opens far above the
others in pitch, and sends the take with the smaller jump. The three flags have
no defaults and are given together: ST above 0, PERCENT above 0 to 100, HZ 75 to
600. Without them no reply is measured.

The guard measures takes that do not trip the silence retry rule. It reads pitch every 10 ms
by normalized cross-correlation over 20 ms windows of the audio averaged down to
8 to 16 kHz. This autocorrelation detector uses Praat's published To Pitch (ac)
parameter defaults: 75 to 600 Hz, a voicing
threshold of 0.45, a silence threshold of 0.03 of the take's peak and an octave
cost of 0.01. Unvoiced runs of 0.25 s part phrases, a phrase voiced for less than
0.25 s is skipped, and a phrase's opening is the median pitch of its first 0.25 s
voiced. A phrase after the first trips when its opening is ST semitones or more
above the median opening of the other phrases and PERCENT or more of its voiced
frames lie above HZ. The take's jump is the largest such excess. Audio sampled
below 8 kHz, all-zero audio, and takes with fewer than two retained phrases are
not measured. A measured take with no qualifying jump counts as zero.
The detector is not Praat's analysis: its values can differ from Praat's.

A take that trips is drawn once more, using the next seed under the [seed rule](#seeds) after any
silence redraws, if t + d fits the budget. The redraw is sent only if it does not
end as `silence` and has a strictly smaller jump; ties retain the first take.
A `length` redraw can replace a `stop` take. An unmeasured redraw can win only
when the silence guard is enabled; with it off, the first take is retained.
An unmeasurable first take does not trip.
The log gives the jump, the redraw's finish and why a first take is retained.

A register redraw that trips silence reenters the silence retry loop with its
remaining count and the same request budget. Only after that loop ends is its
last take compared with the held register take. The held audio is never
overwritten by those retries. Exhausting silence retries does not make a
silenced take eligible for register measurement.

With the register guard configured, whole successful replies always carry
`X-Register-Trip` and `X-Register-Redraws`, each a single `0` or `1`.
Trip is latched when any measured take trips. Redraw counts engine admission,
even when the first take is retained. Streams, error replies and guard-off
replies omit both headers. Register retries do not increment `X-Silence-Redraws`.

### Calibrating on your voice

The thresholds describe a voice's pitch, so no value suits every voice. Calibrate
them on the voice you serve:

1. Serve without the register flags, keep a set of whole replies, and mark those
   with a phrase that sounds stitched in from a higher register.
2. Choose trial HZ, ST and PERCENT values and serve the same inputs and seed salts
   with the flags enabled. Calibrate against the server's own `register jump=`
   log lines, not Praat measurements.
3. Compare logged trips with the marked replies. Raise thresholds when ordinary
   phrases trip; lower them when marked high phrases do not trip. The log reports
   qualifying jumps only, so absence of a line does not establish a measured zero.
4. Repeat on held-out inputs before using the thresholds for redraw selection.

## Streams

Streams are never redrawn or measured. A stream sends each decoded prefix as the
engine publishes it, so audio may already have reached the client when a guard
trips, and replacing it would mean buffering the stream and changing its semantics.
A stream the guard ends finishes with the `silence` trailer exactly as without
redraws. With redraws enabled, its initial headers include `X-Silence-Redraws: 0`;
this is not a trailer. Its `X-Deadline-S` is validated even though streams never redraw.
# Speech sampling

`POST /v1/audio/speech` accepts these optional fields for Drama 3. Omission or
`null` keeps the existing default for that field. They apply to WAV replies,
whole PCM replies, streamed PCM and catalog voices.

| Field | Accepted JSON value | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `temperature` | A finite number at least 0, within the `f32` range. A positive value must remain positive when converted to `f32`. | `1` |
| `top_p` | A finite number greater than 0 and at most 1, still greater than 0 after conversion to `f32`. | `0.9` |
| `top_k` | An integer from 1 through 64. | `30` |
| `seed` | An integer from 0 through 18446744073709551615. | The existing hash of the prompt and `TENSORFOLD_SEED_SALT`. |

Numbers encoded as strings and booleans are refused. `top_k` and `seed` must
use integer JSON syntax: `30.0` and `1e3` are refused. Seeds are parsed as exact
64-bit unsigned integers, including values above 9007199254740991; clients
whose JSON number type loses precision must preserve the integer when encoding
the request. Invalid fields return HTTP 400 before submission to the engine.

For `temperature` and `top_p`, the JSON parser first produces an `f64` value;
the bounds above apply to that value and its conversion to `f32`. Extremely
small floating literals such as `1e-400` and `-1e-400` already become zero in
that parser, so both request temperature 0; they are refused for `top_p`.
A positive parsed value such as `1e-100` is refused if it becomes zero only
when narrowed to `f32`.

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"local-model","input":"Hello there.","temperature":0.8,"top_p":0.9,"top_k":30,"seed":42}' \
  --output speech.wav
```

The route passes these settings to the native sampler. On Metal and CUDA, `temperature`
of 0 or `top_k` of 1 selects its existing greedy path, which bypasses repetition
aware sampling (RAS). Other runtimes may handle repetition differently; matching
fields and seeds do not promise identical audio across backends or checkpoints.
The HTTP limit of 64 candidates fits both native Metal and CUDA admission.

An explicit `seed` is used exactly for the first take. If configured
[speech redraws](speech-redraws.md) admit another take, its seed is the original
seed plus the take's attempt number (1, 2, ...), wrapping modulo 2^64. This
number includes both silence and register redraws. All takes keep the requested
sampling values, including when controls are stripped or a reference prompt is
rebuilt. With no seed, the existing prompt hash and server salt plus attempt
number are unchanged. Streams keep their existing no-redraw behavior.

Seed selection is deterministic. The final take can still change if timing or
request deadlines admit a different number of redraws.

The server's `--max-frames` flag caps a reply's length in frames. A frame is 2,048 samples at 44.1 kHz (about
46 ms), so the default cap of 1,024 frames is about 48 s of audio. The flag takes an integer from 1 through 8190
("argument --max-frames: expected 1 through 8190") and Drama 3 reads it at open: the reply's cap is the flag's
value (1,024 when it's unset), clamped to what the context leaves (`--context` - 3 frames). An explicit
value must also leave prompt room — one at or above `--context` - 1 is refused ("use --max-frames <
--context - 1") — and Drama 3's `--context` itself must stay within 1025 through 8192. Other engines ignore the
flag, and video input is untouched: the vision families' frame caps are their own (see
[vision](vision.md)).

The API design references the public
[Sogni-AI/drama3-mlx generation interface](https://github.com/Sogni-AI/drama3-mlx/blob/ecc235039ccd5f982f66a6982184f57432354ab4/drama3_mlx/model.py#L79).
TensorFold's parsing and request propagation are an independent implementation;
this does not change the native sampling algorithms.
# Speed-up mode: Flash Next on two Macs

Speed-up mode serves Qwen3.8 Flash Next from two Macs at once. Each Mac holds the whole model, and every prompt chunk
and every decode round is split between them over a Thunderbolt 5 cable, with [MCDMA](https://github.com/ashhart/MCDMA)
carrying the link. One Mac, rank 0, serves the OpenAI-compatible API. The other, rank 1, runs each request beside it.

Both Macs produce the same reply, and the reply is bit-identical at every draft depth. The engine drafts a few tokens a
round and keeps only the ones the model would have produced itself. A reply can still differ from a single Mac's,
because the two halves of one projection are added in a different order at the same fp32 precision.

The server loads Flash Next straight from its checkpoint, with no dump to make and no environment variable to set.
On our two M5 Ultras, set up as below, `"draft": false` replies equalled drafted ones and both Macs gave the same reply,
idle and with 36 busy threads on the first Mac.

## What you need

- Two Apple silicon Macs, each with enough memory for the whole model. Flash Next 6-bit is 158 GB of weights. On our
  two M5 Ultra Mac Studios, 256 GB each, each Mac's server takes 172 GB once loaded. Keep each server at or under 70%
  of its Mac's memory, 179 GiB on a 256 GB Mac, so macOS and everything else keep theirs. The server sizes its prompt
  cache to fit under that line, about 5 GiB on these Macs. A 192 GB Mac is too small.
- A Thunderbolt 5 cable straight from one Mac to the other.
- macOS 26.2 or later, which ships Thunderbolt RDMA. Ours run macOS 27.0.
- Xcode with its Metal toolchain and Zig 0.17.0, to build the server.

Macs with less memory, such as 64 GB Mac minis, can't run Flash Next in this mode today, since every Mac holds the whole
model. One such Mac can serve Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B 4-bit, 17 GiB, on the Zig engine: see
[ZIG-PREVIEW.md](../ZIG-PREVIEW.md). Spreading one model's layers over several smaller Macs needs a pipeline mode, which
isn't built.

## Setup

Do steps 1 to 4 on both Macs.

### 1. Build the server

Install Zig 0.17.0 from [ziglang.org](https://ziglang.org/download/): `zig-aarch64-macos-0.17.0.tar.xz`, sha256
`b607e9b9234790a008116ae5bdb71c6243b84b9fb42a53a9e70fde41c06c536a`. The build refuses any other version.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold.git
cd TensorFold
zig build native
```

That writes `zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native`.

### 2. Download the model

```bash
hf download TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP --local-dir ~/models/flash-next-6bit
```

`hf` comes with `pip install huggingface_hub`.

### 3. Set up MCDMA

Follow MCDMA's [README](https://github.com/ashhart/MCDMA) and its
[fabric guide](https://github.com/ashhart/MCDMA/blob/main/docs/fabric.md) for Thunderbolt links between two Macs. In
short, enable RDMA from Recovery with `rdma_ctl enable` on both Macs, build the fabric library with `make -C rpc`, which
writes `build/rpc/libmcdma-fabric.dylib`, and note each Mac's address on the cable. Thunderbolt port `enN` has the RDMA
device `rdma_enN`. We run it on two M5 Ultras over Thunderbolt 5 on macOS 27.0, with one cable and with two bonded.

### 4. Write the settings files

Each Mac gets a JSON file with its rank, the MCDMA library and the link to the other Mac. On rank 0:

```json
{"rank": 0, "library": "/path/to/MCDMA/build/rpc/libmcdma-fabric.dylib",
 "links": [{"peer": 1, "device": "rdma_en4", "via": "en4/192.0.2.2", "port": 7490, "name": "speedup"}]}
```

On rank 1, the same with `"rank": 1`, `"peer": 0` and rank 0's address on that cable:

```json
{"rank": 1, "library": "/path/to/MCDMA/build/rpc/libmcdma-fabric.dylib",
 "links": [{"peer": 0, "device": "rdma_en4", "via": "en4/192.0.2.1", "port": 7490, "name": "speedup"}]}
```

`device` is the cable's RDMA device. `via` is that port's interface and the other Mac's IPv4 address on the cable, or
its IPv6 link-local address. `port` is a UDP port both Macs keep free. The addresses above are examples. Two bonded
cables are covered in the [speed-up recipe](recipes/speed-up-mode.md).

### 5. Start rank 1, then rank 0

Both Macs run the same command with their own settings file. Start rank 1 first, then rank 0 within five minutes:

```bash
zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native serve ~/models/flash-next-6bit --name flash-next \
  --speed-up rank1.json --temperature 0 --no-thinking --dashboard
```

On rank 0, pass `--speed-up rank0.json` instead, and `--host 0.0.0.0` if other machines will connect, with `--api-key`
in that case.

Run both servers attached to a terminal session, or allow `tensorfold-native` under System Settings > Privacy &
Security > Local Network. macOS asks each program for Local Network access before it can reach the other Mac. A server
started detached, for example with `nohup` over SSH after the session closes, can't ask, so macOS drops its packets and
the ranks stop with `ConnectFailed` even though `fabric-check` passes.

- Earlier versions of this guide made a dump with Python tools and set `TF_FLASHNEXT_DUMP`, `FZ_LANE=1` and
  `FZ_GDN=2`. Leave them all out. The server needs no dump, and `FZ_LANE=1 FZ_GDN=2` decode 2 to 5% slower than the
  default kernels, on one M5 Ultra and on the pair, with the same replies.
- The server runs two threads at user-interactive priority, the highest a macOS program gets: MCDMA's, which places
  each message that arrives, and its own, which sends each one. For MCDMA's thread it sets `MCDMA_FABRIC_QOS=1` unless
  you set that variable yourself. At default priority a busy Mac slows every round. With 36 busy threads on the first
  Mac, `"draft": false` replies decoded at 65 tokens a second with `MCDMA_FABRIC_QOS=0`, and at 105 by default, as fast
  as on an idle pair.
- The prompt cache keeps conversation states between requests, so the next turn of a chat reads only its new tokens.
  Rank 0's cache decides and rank 1 keeps its halves under the same names. By default each Mac gives it what 70% of
  its memory leaves past the loaded server, less 2 GiB for prompt buffers, up to 16 GiB, and logs that at start, for
  example `prompt cache: 5.2 GiB from 5.2 GiB free under the 70% cap`. `--prompt-cache-gib N` sets another size up to
  what is free and `0` turns it off. A larger size is refused with the numbers, unless you add
  `--prompt-cache-over-cap`.
- `--temperature 0` matches the engine, which decodes Flash Next greedily and refuses requests with a higher
  temperature.
- `--dashboard` serves a live page at `/dashboard`.

Flags that change decoding, such as `--no-drafts` or `--no-thinking`, go on both Macs.

### 6. Connect a client

Point any OpenAI-compatible client at `http://RANK0:8080/v1` with the model name `flash-next`, where RANK0 is rank 0's
address. Send requests only to rank 0, since rank 1 refuses its own.

## Measured speeds

On our two M5 Ultra Mac Studios, 256 GB each, one Thunderbolt 5 cable, macOS 27.0, started with the commands above.
Greedy, thinking off, 256-token replies, decode in tokens a second, the mean of two runs:

| Prompt | 1k tokens | 8k tokens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chat | 179 | 186 |
| Code | 247 | 200 |
| Edit a file | 390 | 345 |

Edits are fastest because the reply copies long runs from the prompt. The first token came 0.25-0.30 s after a 1k prompt
and 1.19-1.29 s after an 8k one. Cold prompts ran at 7.8k to 7.9k tokens a second at 32k and 64k tokens. With
`FZ_LANE=1 FZ_GDN=2` the same build decoded 2 to 5% slower in every cell, with the same tokens.
These were measured on our machines. They aren't a promise for yours.

## Known limits

- One reply at a time. Requests queue, so several clients share one stream's speed. Running several streams in each
  round is in progress.
- A cold prompt costs the same with the prompt cache on or off: 8k to 64k-token prompts' first tokens came within
  2.2% of each other on our Macs. A follow-up turn that adds about 280 tokens to a 7-10k-token conversation got its
  first token in 0.187-0.202 s.
- The first prompt of a new size compiles some kernels. A 9.9k-token prompt took 3.6 s the first time and 1.3 s after.
- A drafted request right after a `"draft": false` one decoded slower in speed-up mode: on two M5 Ultras, 103 against
  169 tokens a second on a short story, and the next request was back to speed. On one Mac this no longer happens
  ([#2237](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/2237)); we haven't rerun it on a pair since.
- When you stop rank 0, stop rank 1 too. It stops following but keeps running, and keeps a CPU core busy, until you end
  it. If a request fails partway or the link drops, restart both servers.
- Flash Next 6-bit only. We have run speed-up mode only on two M5 Ultras.
# Image input

This page describes image input in the Python engine, frozen at 0.6.6, until [The native server](#the-native-server),
which covers the native binary: it reads images for the models listed there and refuses `--vision` for other models.
Install the Python engine from the
[`v0.6.6` tag](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/tree/v0.6.6) for the rest.
Parts of it came from pull requests: GLM-5.3-Flash images by @mgoldwasser
([#101](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/101)), Flash Next images on CUDA by @shantanugoel
([#146](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/146)) from @MiaAI-Lab's patch, video by @MiaAI-Lab
([#240](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/240)), `--vision-max-images` by @edurdias
([#170](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/170)), `--vision-offload` by @barelyworkingcode
([#187](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/187)), `--vision-image-tokens` by @MiaAI-Lab
([#239](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/239)), and HTTPS image URLs and the redacted request log by @di37
([#64](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/64)). The [credits](credits.md) list them all.

The opt-in `--vision` flag accepts image and text content parts through the existing OpenAI-compatible chat API. It supports GLM-5.3-Flash on MLX and Qwen3.5/3.8 dense checkpoints on MLX and CUDA. Image features enter the existing model's prompt prefill; generated text still uses that family's normal decoder and speculative path.
The checkpoint must contain its vision tower, tokenizer, processor files and vision configuration; text-only conversions cannot recover image support from a flag. GLM-5.3-Flash uses its own GLM5-Next image processor and tower while sharing TensorFold's already-loaded language model and MTP head.
Video, audio and image generation are not supported by this adapter.
Qwen3.8 Flash Next supports images on one CUDA GPU with `--parallel` of at least two; see the
[Flash Next image recipe](recipes/flash-next-vision.md), including offline reconstruction of an EXL3 vision sidecar.

## Start a server

Install the Python engine with its optional image dependencies (from a checkout of the `v0.6.6` tag,
`python -m pip install '.[vision]'`):

```bash
python -m pip install 'tensorfold[vision] @ git+https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold.git@v0.6.6'
tensorfold serve TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit --vision
tensorfold serve TensorFold/GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-4bit-MTP --vision
```

GLM-5.3-Flash image input is currently MLX-only. CUDA uses the same flag with `--backend cuda` for supported Qwen checkpoints; their vision tower must use floating-point weights.

On a small CUDA card the resident tower and its 4 GiB workspace reserve take a large part of the startup budget. `--vision-offload` (with `--vision`, CUDA only) keeps the tower in host RAM, copies it to the GPU only while an image is encoded, and reserves 2.25 GiB instead. On one RTX 4090 with the Qwen3.8-27B EXL3 3.50bpw pack and DFlash2, the largest window with `--vision` went from 11,922 to 38,686 tokens; a 4,096-token image peaked about 1.3 GB above idle. Each image request pays the copy of the roughly 0.9 GiB tower to the GPU and back.
MLX also reads per-module quantized tower weights when the checkpoint declares their format.
The tower shares the server process and the existing language model's embeddings; it does not load a second language model.
Dense Qwen CUDA two-rank mode encodes images on rank zero and sends their features and positions to rank one.
Use the model and drafter prerequisites from the [Qwen recipe](recipes/qwen3.8-27b.md) or [GLM recipe](recipes/glm-5.3-flash.md).
GLM derivatives may retain selected BF16 attention output projections, including the MTP layer; these use the existing dense projection path alongside the quantized weights.

## Send an image

Use OpenAI `image_url` content parts in user messages, interleaved with text in the intended order:

```python
import base64
import json
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

image = base64.b64encode(Path('photo.png').read_bytes()).decode()
body = {
    'model': 'Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit',
    'messages': [{
        'role': 'user',
        'content': [
            {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Describe this image.'},
            {'type': 'image_url', 'image_url': {
                'url': 'data:image/png;base64,' + image,
                'detail': 'auto',
            }},
        ],
    }],
    'max_tokens': 128,
    'stream': False,
}
request = Request('http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions',
                  data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
                  headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'})
with urlopen(request) as response:
    print(json.load(response)['choices'][0]['message']['content'])
```

`GET /v1/models` gives the exact model ID for the running server.
Tool results (`role: "tool"`) take `image_url` parts the same way, as agents send screenshots; the model's chat
template renders them inside the tool response.
Remote image URLs are off by default, so a server other machines can reach never fetches URLs on a client's behalf.
Start the server with `--vision-urls` to accept public HTTPS URLs on port 443 that serve `image/jpeg`, `image/png` or `image/webp`; plain HTTP, other ports, private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses, file URLs and redirects to any of them are still refused.
For a local image, send a data URL as above.
`stream: true` uses the usual text completion stream.
Image output is not generated.

## Send a video

Flash Next on CUDA (`--vision`, `--parallel` of at least two) also takes `video_url` parts in user messages, as
MP4, WebM, MOV or MKV data URLs (or public HTTPS URLs with `--vision-urls`); decoding needs PyAV (`pip install av`,
part of the `vision` extra on Linux):

```json
{"role": "user", "content": [
  {"type": "video_url", "video_url": {"url": "data:video/mp4;base64,..."}},
  {"type": "text", "text": "What happens in this clip?"}]}
```

Frames are sampled as Qwen3-VL's processor does: two a second spread over the whole video, at least 4 and at most
256, each pair of frames one block that the prompt prefixes with its time (`<1.5 seconds>`). Frames are sized so a
video takes at most 768 tokens a block and 16,384 in all (`TENSORFOLD_VIDEO_TOKENS`). The tower encodes a run of
blocks of at most 16,384 patches at a time, the scratch one full-size image needs, and blocks never attend to one
another. A request takes up to two videos of 16 MiB each, 20 MiB in all, so the base64 still fits the 32 MiB
request body, and up to an hour of footage. Videos and images can share a message; the image limits count images
only.

## Limits and state

Requests accept up to four JPEG, PNG or WebP images by default. `--vision-max-images N` sets a positive
image-count limit when serving with `--vision`, on both backends:

```bash
tensorfold serve TensorFold/GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-4bit-MTP --vision --vision-max-images 8
```

The count includes **all images in the submitted message history**, including images from earlier turns
and tool results, in tool messages or sent as user image parts. Reading images one at a time can therefore
reach the limit. Once that history exceeds it, even a text-only follow-up is refused if the client resends
the images. Remove older image content from the submitted history, start a new conversation, or restart
the server with a larger count limit. The server does not discard images automatically.

A request's images share 4,096 visual tokens, so a higher count makes each image smaller: eight images get about
512 tokens each. On CUDA Qwen checkpoints (Qwen3.5/3.8 dense and Flash Next), `--vision-image-tokens N` raises
that shared budget, up to 65,536, while each image keeps at most 4,096, so one image is sized as before. The tower
encodes runs of whole images of at most 16,384 patches, the scratch one full-size image already needs; a request
that fits one run is encoded in one call, as before. The byte and pixel limits still apply, and the longer prompt
counts against the context window.

```bash
tensorfold serve Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP --parallel 2 --vision \
  --vision-max-images 50 --vision-image-tokens 16384
```

Changing the count does not change the other limits: 10 MiB encoded per image and 20 MiB total, within a 32 MiB HTTP body.
Decoded images are bounded to 8,192 pixels per dimension, 16 million pixels per image and 32 million total.
EXIF orientation is applied and transparency is composited onto white; animated and multipage inputs are refused.
Up to 16 requests decode and process images at once; more wait up to a minute, and past 128 waiting the server answers 503 so the client retries.
The request log (`TENSORFOLD_REQUEST_LOG`) records image parts as `<redacted>`.
The model processor bounds the total expanded image tokens to 4,096, with a smaller budget for `detail: low`.
That budget is shared across the images; a higher count can reduce the detail available for each image.
Those expanded tokens count toward prompt usage and the context window before model execution.
The available memory budget may impose a smaller practical image or context limit.

Image requests currently start with a fresh KV cache and do not write reusable prompt checkpoints.
This prevents identical image-placeholder token IDs from reusing another image's state; ordinary text requests retain their prefix caching.
Multi-turn image conversations work when the request includes the original image content parts, but image-prefix reuse and persisted image KV are not implemented.
For Qwen, each image request carries its own multimodal rotary positions and continuation offset, including during concurrent lane rounds. GLM uses its native KDA/NoPE attention state.

## The native server

`tensorfold-native serve` takes `--vision`, `--vision-max-images` (default 4) and `--vision-image-tokens` (default
4,096; 13,312 for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL) for engines that read images: GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.8 Flash Next, Gemma 4
[31B](recipes/gemma-4-native.md#images) and [12B](recipes/gemma-4-12b-native.md#images) and Step-5-Preview on one
Mac, GLM-5.3-Flash on [CUDA ranks](recipes/glm-5.3-flash-cuda.md#requests) and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on CUDA. Other
native engines refuse the flag at startup.
The CLI accepts explicit image budgets from 16 to 262,144 tokens; each engine still applies its own limits and memory admission.

- Images arrive as `image_url` data URLs in user messages and tool results. With `--vision-urls` (it needs
  `--vision`), a part may name a public HTTPS URL instead, fetched as 0.6.6 fetched it: port 443 without credentials
  or a fragment; every address the host resolves to public (no private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT,
  documentation, multicast or metadata address, and for IPv6 global unicast only, without 6to4 or Teredo); TLS
  verified for the host against the system's certificates, on the address that was checked; up to 3 redirects,
  each checked again; a declared `image/jpeg`, `image/png` or `image/webp`, uncompressed; 10 MB an image and 20 MB
  a request across data URLs and downloads; 10 s a download and 30 s a request's downloads. The refusals are
  0.6.6's words; a TLS failure, like any other failed connection, is "image download failed or timed out". Host
  names that aren't ASCII and IPv6 address literals are refused. Without the flag, an HTTPS URL is refused with the
  flag's name.
- PNG and JPEG are decoded to the pixels 0.6.6 decoded with Pillow 12.3 (`zig/src/core/picture/`, which d1-3B's
  pictures on CUDA use too): PNG from the PNG specification, JPEG by libjpeg-turbo 3.1.4.1's TurboJPEG library
  (`libturbojpeg`, the release Pillow 12.3 bundles) at Pillow's settings. TensorFold does not ship that library; the
  server checks it at startup with `--vision`, or when running `capabilities --json`, from the file
  `TENSORFOLD_LIBTURBOJPEG` names, else `lib/` beside the server's
  folder, beside the server, Homebrew's `jpeg-turbo` on macOS, then the system's library path. It checks the version
  libjpeg-turbo writes into the library and refuses JPEG images by name when the library is missing or another
  release; PNG images still serve. Homebrew is a search location, not a guarantee of the pinned version: a newer
  `jpeg-turbo` package is refused too. Use a separately built libjpeg-turbo 3.1.4.1 library with the override or
  beside the server; updating the package does not satisfy this exact pin.
- WebP is decoded by libwebp 1.6.0's decoder library (`libwebpdecoder`, the release Pillow 13.0.0 bundles), to the
  RGB bytes Pillow 13.0.0 gives the same file (lossy and lossless, with and without alpha, EXIF-oriented:
  `zig/tests/fixtures/picture/webp.json`, from `tools/zig/picture_webp_fixtures.py`). TensorFold does not ship it
  either; the server checks it at startup with `--vision`, or when running `capabilities --json`, from the file
  `TENSORFOLD_LIBWEBP` names, else `lib/` beside the
  server's folder, beside the server, Homebrew's `webp` on macOS, then the system's library path, and refuses WebP
  images by name when it is missing or another release (`WebPGetDecoderVersion`). Animated WebP is refused as
  animated pictures are. Other formats are refused.
- Startup warns about unusable JPEG and WebP decoders without refusing PNG or text requests. In
  `capabilities --json`, optional libraries' `found` field means the loader opened a candidate. JPEG and WebP also
  report `usable`, checked against the decoder's required exports and exact version, and a `problem` when refused.
  For other libraries, `usable` and `problem` are null and further checks remain unchecked. No pixels are decoded
  by these diagnostics. Restart after changing a codec library, because each process caches its decoder check.
- The limits and the processing are 0.6.6's: EXIF and XMP orientation, alpha composited over white, the model's
  processor's sizing (GLM5-Next's, or Gemma 4's PIL processor) and Pillow's bicubic resampler. The decoder gives 0.6.6's pixels for every picture in
  `zig/tests/fixtures/lfm2/images.json` and `zig/tests/fixtures/picture/edges.json`, except where it departs on
  purpose: a CMYK JPEG is refused, and a JPEG holding several pictures (MPO) gives its first, which 0.6.6 refused.
- Images are counted from the request's image parts. A user or tool message whose text spells the model's image
  markers (GLM's `<|image|>`, `<|begin_of_image|>`, `<|end_of_image|>`; Qwen's `<|vision_start|>`, `<|image_pad|>`,
  `<|vision_end|>`) is tokenized as ordinary text, so only the chat template's own markers, one wrapper for each image
  part, become image tokens.
- The prompt cache keys each image's placeholder rows by the image's content, so a kept state resumes the same image
  and never another one under the same placeholders. Image conversations reuse their history like text ones.

### Qwen3.8-27B

With `--vision`, the 27B loads its checkpoint's image tower (the `vision_tower.*` tensors of
`TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit`, kept in bf16) beside the language model. Without the flag nothing of the tower
loads. An image is prepared as transformers' Qwen2-VL processor prepares it: decoded as above, sized by `smart_resize`
to multiples of 32 pixels between the processor's 65,536 pixels and the image's share of `--vision-image-tokens`
(split evenly over the request's images, 1,024 pixels a token, at most 16,777,216 pixels), resized with Pillow's
bicubic, and cut into 16-pixel patches. The tower runs once an image as its request's prompt pass starts, on the GPU
in bf16 with fp32 sums. Its 2 x 2 merged rows replace the `<|image_pad|>` placeholders' embeddings. The text's
attention layers turn each image row by its row and column (M-RoPE), and the rows after an image carry the shift those
positions leave, through decoding, drafts and later turns. Text-only requests get the tokens they got without the
flag. Video parts are refused with HTTP 400.

The tower, its scratch and a request's image rows take 1.79 GiB at the default 4,096 image tokens, and the server
counts them against the 70% load limit and the prompt cache's budget. On an M3 Ultra, six test pictures got the
processor's grids, token counts and patches bit for bit, and the tower's rows came closer to transformers' float32
tower than its bf16 run does (mean row error 1.0 to 2.2% against 1.6 to 4.1%). A 1,120-token photo takes 0.6 s in the
tower there. With an image, drafted replies equal `"draft": false`, four requests at once equal each alone, a later
turn resumes past its image and equals a fresh server's reply, and DFlash2 keeps 2.6 to 3.0 tokens a round where the
same asks without the image get 2.8 to 3.4.

### Qwen3.8 Flash Next

With `--vision`, Flash Next loads its checkpoint's image tower beside the language model, one stream or several
(`--parallel`). It is the 27B's tower (the same 333 bf16 `vision_tower.*` tensors and processor) with 2,560-wide output,
run by the same code (`zig/src/core/qwen_vl/`); images are prepared as above. Its rows replace the `<|image_pad|>`
embeddings in all four of the model's hyper-connection streams, and the prompt pass turns them by interleaved M-RoPE
(sections 11, 11 and 10 over the first 64 dimensions). The positions are transformers' `get_rope_index` shifted so that
the text after the last image keeps its own slot: decoding, drafts and later tokens run as for text. Text-only requests
get the tokens they got without the flag.

- **Prompt cache:** image and video conversations resume past their images. The shift moves every position before the
  request's last image, so a kept state is named by the shift as well as the tokens and images: a later turn with the
  same images resumes, and a turn that adds an image reads its prompt again. The tower skips the images a resumed state
  already holds. Replies equal the cache off's in multi-turn image and video chats, on one stream and shared sessions.
- **Memory:** the tower and its scratch take 1.73 GiB at the default 4,096 image tokens, counted against the load limit;
  a request's rows take 20 KiB a visual token while its prompt pass runs.
- **Checks on an M5 Ultra:** five test pictures got the grids and patches of transformers' Pillow processor bit for bit;
  the tower's rows came closer to transformers' float32 `Qwen4ExpVisionModel` than its bf16 run does (mean row error 1.4
  to 3.1% against 1.8 to 5.7%). Six fixed image prompts gave drafted replies equal to `"draft": false`, the same tokens
  on one stream and on shared sessions, and the expected answers. A 441-token picture takes 53 ms in the tower.
- **Video:** `video_url` parts as described below, in the Qwen3-VL layout: each pair of frames is one image, and its
  block is `<X.Y seconds><|vision_start|>` and its `<|video_pad|>` rows then `<|vision_end|>`, inside the template's own
  `<|vision_start|>…<|vision_end|>`, as transformers 5.17's `Qwen3VLProcessor` writes it. Frames are sampled at 2 a
  second (at least 4; at most 256, where the processor allows 768), the clip's pixels kept between 65,536 and 16,777,216
  and inside the request's `--vision-video-tokens` share, and resized with torch's antialiased uint8 bicubic. On three
  test clips the served prompt was as long as the processor's (239, 387 and 8,215 tokens); a 30-second 720p clip takes
  3.2 s to its first token.

### Video on the native server

With `--vision`, GLM-5.3-Flash also reads `video_url` parts in user messages (Flash Next too, in its own layout above),
as transformers 5.19's `Glm5NextProcessor` prepares them:
- **Sampling:** 2 frames a second, deduplicated and padded to an even count, at most 256 frames.
- **Frame pairs:** each pair of frames is one image to the tower.
- **Prompt:** the template's `<|begin_of_video|><|video|><|end_of_video|>` holds one
  `<|begin_of_image|>…<|end_of_image|>T.T seconds` block a pair.
- **Budget:** a request's videos share `--vision-video-tokens` visual tokens (default 16,384; the processor's
  `max_image_tokens`). The frames are sized under it and resized with torch's antialiased uint8 bicubic.
  `--max-frames N` caps the frames a video is sampled to, from 1 through 8,190; without it the engine samples at
  most 256.

Video needs `libtfvideo`, an optional library over FFmpeg 9.0.2 (the release PyAV 19.0.1 ships). The server loads it
when the first video arrives and refuses videos by name without it:

```sh
tools/zig/build_ffmpeg.sh ~/ffmpeg-9.0.2        # static FFmpeg: H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9, MPEG-4; MP4/MOV, MKV/WebM
zig build video -Dffmpeg=$HOME/ffmpeg-9.0.2     # zig-out/native/lib/libtfvideo.dylib, beside the server
```

- **Limits (0.6.6's):** 2 videos a request, 16 MB each and 20 MB together, an hour of footage, 8192 pixels a side.
  Data URLs work, and with `--vision-urls` public HTTPS URLs too (MP4, WebM, QuickTime or Matroska; 20 s a download,
  120 s a request).
- **Too short:** a clip too short for one sampled frame (under half a second) is refused, as the processor samples
  nothing.
- **Frame counts:** a container without one (Matroska, WebM) is counted by its video packets. transformers' PyAV loader
  can't read these at all.
- **Checks:** `tools/zig/glm_video_fixtures.py` checks the patches bit for bit against the processor on frames PyAV
  decodes, over 13 clips. `tools/zig/video_served.py` checks a served model's prompt ids against the processor's.

### PDF inputs

With `--vision --vision-pdf`, user messages and tool results also accept inline PDF documents: `file` parts in
`/v1/chat/completions`, `input_file` parts in `/v1/responses`, `document` blocks in `/v1/messages`, or
`data:application/pdf;base64,...` URLs. Without `--vision-pdf`, PDF parts are refused with the flag's name. Remote URLs
(`file_url` or `document.source.type: "url"`) are refused.

- **Libraries:** rendering requires PDFium (`chromium/7725`, `libpdfium.so` on Linux, `libpdfium.dylib` on macOS,
  `pdfium.dll` on Windows) installed in `lib/` beside the server or named by `TENSORFOLD_LIBPDFIUM` (the ambient loader
  search path is not used), plus libjpeg-turbo 3.1.4.1 (`libturbojpeg`, `TENSORFOLD_LIBTURBOJPEG`). At startup with
  `--vision-pdf`, the server logs the loaded PDFium file path and its SHA-256 digest; missing libraries are reported in
  `capabilities --json`, logged at startup, and return HTTP `501` at request time.
- **Request-wide limits before rendering:** across the entire request, PDF pages and regular images share one running
  count and byte/pixel budget: at most `min(16, --vision-max-images)` PDF pages (`TENSORFOLD_MAX_PDF_PAGES` can lower
  or raise the 16-page cap up to `--vision-max-images`), `--vision-max-images` total images, 20 MiB encoded image
  bytes, and 32 megapixels. A request that would cross any of those limits is refused before rendering the page that
  would exceed them, and a page that fails to load or render is refused explicitly rather than skipped.
- **Images only, no text layer:** each page is rendered at 144 DPI (bounded to 2,048 pixels a side and 3.6 megapixels)
  and passed to the vision tower as a JPEG image (bounded by the 10 MiB per-image and 20 MiB per-request encoded byte
  limits). No PDF text layer is extracted.
- **Resource and crash isolation:** on POSIX (`Linux` and `macOS`), each PDF renders in a fresh worker process, the
  server's own executable started again (`posix_spawn` on macOS) to run only the renderer, so no framework state is
  inherited from the multithreaded server. The worker reads the PDF on its standard input and replies on its standard
  output, closes every other inherited descriptor, sets `setrlimit` CPU, core, file-size, and (on Linux) 1 GiB
  address-space growth limits before it opens PDFium, checks progressive-rendering pauses (`IFSDK_PAUSE`), and is held
  to a 10-second wall-clock deadline (`SIGKILL` on timeout) under a serializing lock so one PDF renders at a time and
  the OS reclaims PDFium's heap after each document. A worker stopped at a limit is reported as `PDF rendering exceeded
  resource limits or failed`; one killed by any other signal is reported by name, for example `the PDF render worker
  crashed (SIGSEGV)`.

### Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on CUDA

With `--vision`, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL reads images through the checkpoint's own RADIO tower and projector, run in
TensorFold's CUDA kernels (`zig/src/families/radio/`).

- **Processor:** the checkpoint's. Each image becomes one tile whose patch grid (16 pixels a patch, an even number each
  way) holds up to 13,312 patches and at least 1,024, except that a picture smaller than that sent with
  `"detail": "low"` keeps its own grid, down to 2 x 2 patches and one token. It is resized with torch's antialiased
  bicubic on float samples and normalized with CLIP's mean and deviation. The pixels equal the checkpoint processor's
  bit for bit. An image takes a quarter of its patches as tokens (at most 3,328), written between `<img>` and `</img>`.
- **Budget:** a request's images share `--vision-image-tokens`, 13,312 by default for Super VL, so up to four images
  keep the size NVIDIA's processor gives them; a smaller budget makes them smaller. Four full-size images on one GB10
  took 13,124 prompt tokens and 11.45 s to the first token.
- **Tower:** the checkpoint's bf16 weights as stored, bf16 activations and fp32 sums. Against a float32 run of the
  checkpoint's own modules on the same pixels, its rows' error equals the modules' own bf16 run's (1.2% to 1.9% a row,
  relative, on six pictures). The tower and projector take about 2.1 GiB of GPU memory beside the language model, and
  a 13,000-patch image about 0.9 s on a GB10. On two GB10s the first runs the tower; the second holds only its share
  of the experts.
- **Not read yet:** video and audio. The checkpoint's video embedder and sound encoder stay unloaded, and video and
  audio parts are refused.
- **Checks:** `tf-cuda-test radio-processor` compares the decoded pictures, the processor's pixels, its resizes and
  3,000 patch grids with the checkpoint's processor; `tf-cuda-test radio` compares the tower's and projector's rows
  with a float32 reference.

## Verification

Compare image requests with `draft: true` and `draft: false` at identical sampling settings and seed, then compare concurrent requests with their solo results.
Tests cover input validation, bounded fetching, expanded prompt accounting, cache isolation, memory admission, rotary metadata and distributed transport contracts.
Hardware qualification is separate from these tests: each backend and chip needs real image understanding, drafted/serial equality, concurrency, chunked-prefill and memory checks before a release claim.
Checkpoint metadata must describe the decoder separately from MTP: the `mlp_layer_types` list must match `num_hidden_layers` for Transformers validation. Preserve the separate MTP configuration and weights.
Image input stays experimental until the hardware matrix is complete, and makes no throughput claim.

## Native CUDA: Qwen3.5/3.8

`tensorfold-native serve <checkpoint> --vision` loads the checkpoint's vision tower beside the language model on the
Qwen CUDA engine (`families/qwen3_5/cuda_vision.zig`, kernels in `qwen_vision.cu`, its Linears on cuBLASLt). The
server prepares each image as it does on a Mac: core/picture decodes it and core/qwen_vl resizes and cuts it with the
checkpoint's processor settings, so an image's patches, grid and cache identity are the same on both backends. The
tower and the scratch of one 16,384-patch call are allocated at startup and counted as model memory, so the stream
budget never has to make room for an image. A request's images go through the tower before its prompt; their rows
replace the `<|image_pad|>` placeholders in the prompt chunks, which rotate at M-RoPE's t, h and w positions
(interleaved sections 11, 11 and 10), and the reply's rows rotate at their position plus the layout's shift, as
transformers' `get_rope_index` lays them out. Text-only requests keep their bits. One image holds at most 4,096
tokens (one tower call); `--vision-image-tokens` bounds a request's images together. JPEG needs libturbojpeg on the
machine (PNG decodes everywhere); video parts are refused.
# TensorFold Web launcher

Run `tensorfold web [ARGS...]` to open the separately installed `tensorfold-web` application.
Arguments after `web` reach the application unchanged, including its own `--help`.
The native binary needs no model or GPU to launch it.

If the application is missing, a release binary explains it and asks `Install it now with uv? [y/N]`.
Only `y` or `yes`, ignoring case and surrounding spaces, permits installation.
The installer runs `uv tool install` with one argument pinned to the binary's release tag and the `web` subdirectory.
For example, a binary built with `-Dversion=1.2.0` prints:

```sh
uv tool install "tensorfold-web @ git+https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold@v1.2.0#subdirectory=web"
```

After installation, the launcher checks PATH and then `uv tool dir --bin` for the executable.
On systems where process replacement is available it execs the application; on Windows it waits for the child.
The application's exit status is retained.

With either stdin or stdout redirected, without `uv`, or with `TENSORFOLD_WEB_NO_PROMPT=1`, the launcher prints manual
commands and exits 1. It never installs in those cases. A negative or empty answer does the same.
An already installed application starts without prompting in all of these cases.
Builds without an explicit `-Dversion` never install automatically: their printed command targets the manifest version,
which is identified as a manual suggestion rather than the development build's release tag.

The launcher sets `TENSORFOLD_BIN` to the absolute path of its own executable, replacing any inherited value.
TensorFold Web must use that path when starting TensorFold so it runs the binary the user selected.
The handoff does not add arguments to the web application's command line.

Run `zig build test-web-cli-host` for the host-only command tests.
They use temporary PATH directories and fake local executables, with no package downloads or network calls.
# XPU port: navigation guide

A map of the Intel XPU (Arc Pro B70, Xe2) backend of the Zig engine, for a developer opening it for the first time:
where each piece lives, how a request travels through it, and which contracts the tests defend. Everything here is
read from the sources; [README.md](README.md) holds the measurements, the option list and the validation
figures, and this guide does not repeat them.

The port serves one model, Qwen3.8-27B (`model_type` `qwen3_5`: 48 Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers and 16 attention
layers, the pattern being "every fourth layer is attention"), straight over **Level Zero** (loaded with `dlopen`, no
C header, no SYCL, no PyTorch). All GPU code is OpenCL C compiled offline by `ocloc`, plus GEMMs generated as ISA by
nGEN, and is embedded in the executables.

## 1. Where things are

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`zig/src/xpu/ze.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/ze.zig) | Level Zero binding: device (found by PCI id), memory, modules, kernels, in-order command lists, kernel timestamps. A missing symbol or a failed call stops everything. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/qwen27.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/qwen27.zig) | The model's shape and `Runner`, the object the host drives (prompt, step, verify, commit, slots). |
| [`zig/src/xpu/dev.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/dev.zig) | Safetensors reader (mmap), the Level Zero device wrapper (`Dev`), kernel profiling. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/load.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/load.zig) | Weights onto the device: int4 projections (MLX and GPTQ) and the layer table. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/forward.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/forward.zig) | Activations, prompt GEMM dispatch (fp16, W4A8, W4A4) and `forward`, one pass over the layers. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/runner_multi.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/runner_multi.zig) | Shared verify rounds across slots (`verifyMulti`, `keepPaths`, `stepMulti`). |
| [`zig/src/xpu/slot_states.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/slot_states.zig) | Slot state allocation and the prompt cache's snapshots (`saveSlot`, `restoreSlot`). |
| [`zig/src/xpu/drafter.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/drafter.zig) | The DFlash2 drafter: per-slot contexts, batched lattice. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/drafter_tree.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/drafter_tree.zig) | The draft tree policy (best-first search over the lattice) and `treeRound`. |
| [`zig/src/xpu/qwen27_main.zig`](../../zig/src/xpu/qwen27_main.zig) | The `xpu-qwen27` test and profiling executable. |
| [`zig/src/native/xpu.zig`](../../zig/src/native/xpu.zig) | The server's entry point for the XPU engine (`open`), the lane host's setup and the prompt cache's hooks. |
| [`zig/src/native/xpu_lanes.zig`](../../zig/src/native/xpu_lanes.zig) | The **lane host** backend (`--parallel N`): slots, shared rounds, lone driver, structured output. |
| [`zig/kernels/xpu/qwen27/*.cl`](../../zig/kernels/xpu/qwen27) | OpenCL C kernels (section 5); `glue.cl` includes `glue_attn.cl` and `glue_quant.cl`. |
| [`zig/tools/xpu/w4_ngen.cpp`](../../zig/tools/xpu/w4_ngen.cpp), `w4_prompt.hpp`, `w4a8_prompt.hpp` | nGEN generator of the prompt GEMMs (section 8). |
| [`zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py`](../../zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py) | Converter to Hadamard-rotated int4 weights (see the [recipe](RECIPE-qwen38-27b-b70.md)). |
| [`zig/build/xpu.zig`](../../zig/build/xpu.zig) | Build steps `xpu-qwen27` and `xpu-native`. |
| [`tools/xpu/`](../../tools/xpu) | Quality studies: `a8_study.py` (W4A8), `head_study.py` (the requantized output head). |
| [`tools/bench_openai.py`](../../tools/bench_openai.py), [`tools/bench_concurrent.py`](../../tools/bench_concurrent.py) | Server benches; `bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial` also checks the bit-for-bit contracts end to end. |

The port modifies no core file: it plugs into the core's lane host and its lone driver (`Lone.resumes`) as they
are; `build.zig` only adds the XPU steps.

## 2. Building

Prerequisites: Zig 0.17; the `xe` kernel driver and Intel's compute runtime (the Level Zero loader,
`libze_loader.so.1`, is opened at run time); `ocloc`, Intel's offline compiler; a C++17 compiler (`c++`); the nGEN
headers of oneDNN.

```sh
zig build xpu-native -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<path to ngen>   # zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native
zig build xpu-qwen27 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<path to ngen>   # test executable xpu-qwen27
```
