```sh
zig build grammar    -Dxgrammar=<xgrammar checkout>                         # libtfgrammar, structured output
```

Build options defined in [`zig/build/xpu.zig`](../../zig/build/xpu.zig) and
[`zig/build/grammar.zig`](../../zig/build/grammar.zig): `-Docloc=` (default `ocloc`), `-Dxpu-device=` (default `bmg`,
the `ocloc` device name), `-Dngen-include=` (default `ngen`), `-Dxgrammar=`.

What the two XPU steps do (they share the same embedded kernels):

1. Each `.cl` file is compiled by `ocloc` with `-cl-std=CL3.0 -cl-intel-256-GRF-per-thread`:
   `glue`, `decode`, `gemm` (with `-DGSZ=64`), `gemm128` (the same file with `-DGSZ=128`), `gdn` (from
   `gdn_chunk.cl`) and `drafter`.
2. `w4_ngen.cpp` is built for the host and **run at build time** to produce the nine prompt-GEMM binaries (zebin):
   `ngen_wide`, `ngen_narrow`, `ngen_wide128`, `ngen_narrow128`, `ngen_swiglu`, `ngen_swiglu128`, `ngen_a8`,
   `ngen_a8_swiglu`, `ngen_a4` (the options each gets are listed in `zig/build/xpu.zig`).
3. Everything is embedded with `@embedFile` into the `xpu_qwen27_kernels` module that `qwen27.zig` imports as `kb`.

`xpu-native` is `tensorfold-native` with the XPU engines linked in (`native/xpu.zig`).

`zig build grammar` needs a checkout of **xgrammar at the pinned tag `v0.2.8`** (with submodules; the build refuses any
other checkout) and builds `libtfgrammar` from it plus [`zig/src/grammar/tf_grammar.cc`](../../zig/src/grammar/tf_grammar.cc).
The server loads it lazily, at the first structured request, from `<server directory>/../lib/`, then from beside the
server, then from the dynamic loader's path (`zig/src/core/lanes/grammar.zig`). Without it, structured requests are
refused and everything else works.

## 3. The runner: `qwen27.zig`

### Load

`Runner.init(dir, context)`:

1. Reads the option variables (section 9) into module-level switches.
2. Looks for a file named `hadamard128` in the checkpoint directory: if present, the weights are Hadamard-rotated
   (`rot_on`) and every GEMM input is rotated where it is produced.
3. Memory-maps the safetensors shards listed in `model.safetensors.index.json`.
4. Opens the Level Zero device whose PCI id is `0xe223` (the B70), creates one in-order immediate command list, loads
   the embedded modules and creates every kernel with its work-group size.
5. Calls `load`, which picks the format from the tensors: a checkpoint with `in_proj_qkv.qweight` is **GPTQ**
   (`GS = 128`, `loadGptq`), otherwise **MLX affine** (`GS = 64`). Projections are repacked on the GPU into the GEMM
   layout (`repack`, `repack_gptq`); in the GPTQ case the output head is requantized to affine 4/64 with MLX's
   algorithm (`quantize_mlx`).
6. Allocates the activations (`Acts`) and slot 0's states.

A `Proj` is one fused projection in GEMM layout: packed words `[K/8, N]`, scales and biases `[K/gs, N]`, `N` padded
to the 256-column tile, and a `wide` flag (wide shapes use the GEMM family without K slices, narrow ones the sliced
family; see section 5). Projections are fused by stacking on N: gate|up (interleaved by blocks of 16 columns so the
prompt GEMM can apply SwiGLU in its epilogue), q|k|v, the GDN input projections.

### One forward

`forward(d, model, acts, ids, p0, mode)` runs at most `CHUNK` rows (`XPU_CHUNK`, 1 024 by default) at positions
`p0 …`. Per layer:

```
add_rmsnorm  ->  mixer_in GEMM  ->  mixer (attention or GDN)  ->  mixer_out GEMM
add_rmsnorm  ->  gate|up GEMM + SwiGLU  ->  down GEMM            (tap rows for the drafter on 5 layers)
```

then the final norm, the head GEMM, and `argmax_part` / `argmax`. What changes with the row count `T`:

| `T` | GEMM | GDN | Attention |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 or fewer (decode, verification) | decode kernels (`w4k*` family) | serial `gdn_step`, as decode does | `attn_decode` + `attn_merge` |
| more than 16 (prompt) | nGEN prompt GEMMs (`w4g_*`, `w4a8` or `w4a4`) | chunked GDN, 64 rows a chunk | `attn_prompt` |

Prompt rows use `w4a8` or `w4a4` only with the W4A8 options. Their GDN runs `gdn_prep`, `gdn_state` and `gdn_out` on
64-row chunks padded with neutral rows, and their attention is `attn_prompt8` with the int8 cache.

Below 17 rows the GDN runs serially so that a verified row equals the serial one bit for bit; that is the foundation
of the speculative-decoding contracts (section 10).

`Mode` selects the variants: `want` (no logits, last row, all rows), `stash` (keep the GDN inputs so a partial keep can
be replayed), `taps` (write the five tap rows for the drafter), `tree` (rows form a tree: a per-row table of depth and
ancestors, `TREE` in `decode.cl` and `glue.cl`) and `multi` (each row belongs to a different slot: a per-row table of
state and cache addresses, `MT`, plus per-row positions).

### Runner API

State per sequence ("slot", at most `MAX_SLOTS` = 16): the GDN state (`rec`, plus `rec_save` for the state after a
verified block), the convolution state (ping-pong pair), and the K/V cache of the 16 attention layers. `select(slot)`
makes a slot current (allocating on first use); `slotBytes()` is what one slot costs.

| Call | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `init`, `reset` | Load; start a fresh sequence in the current slot. |
| `prompt(ids, last)` | Feed prompt tokens in `CHUNK`-row forwards. With `last`, the final row's greedy token (`last`) and logits are kept. |
| `step(token)` | One serial decode token. |
| `verify(ids)` | Run a block of at most 16 rows (the pending token, then drafts as a chain); returns every row's greedy token. The state moves by all rows until `commit`. |
| `commit(keep)` | Keep the first `keep` rows: a whole block takes the state the forward wrote (`rec` and `rec_save` swap); a shorter one rebuilds the GDN and convolution states by replaying the kept rows from the stash. |
| `verifyTree(ids, parents)` / `commitPath(path)` | The same for a tree: `parents[t]` is the row below row `t`; `commitPath` keeps one root path, replays the states along it and moves the path's K/V rows to their final positions (`kv_move`). |
| `verifyMulti(wins)` | One forward for **several slots**: each `Win` is a slot's window (its pending token, then drafts, as a chain or as a tree via `parents`), 16 rows in all. Nothing moves until the keep. |
| `keepMulti(keep)` / `keepPaths(paths)` | Keep, per window, a prefix or a root path of the last `verifyMulti`. A whole chain window takes the state its forward wrote; otherwise its states are replayed from the stash. After tree windows every window replays. |
| `stepMulti(slots, tokens)` | One token for each of several slots: a `verifyMulti` of one-row windows, all kept. |
| `rowLogits(row)`, `logits()` | The logits of a row of the last verify, or of the kept last row, as fp32 on the host (for sampling). |

## 4. The drafter: `drafter.zig`

DFlash2 is a small model (5 layers, hidden size 5 120, 32 query heads and 8 key/value heads of 128) that proposes
tokens; it only changes how many are accepted, because the target verifies every token. Its bf16 weights are
quantized to affine 4/64 **at load** on the device (`quantize4`) and run on the target's int4 GEMM. It reads
`model.safetensors` in the drafter directory (its projections plus the `candidate_selector` codebooks).

- **Context.** The drafter attends the *target's hidden states* ("taps") of the committed rows, taken after target
  layers 5, 19, 33, 47 and 61 (`TAP_LAYERS`). `addTaps` pushes `n` rows through `fc`, its norm and each layer's K/V
  projection and appends them to the context. Each runner slot has its own `Ctx`: per layer, K and V in a **ring** of
  `CAP` = 2 080 positions (`WIN` + `MAXL` + 17, where `WIN` = 2 047 context rows), allocated on first use by `use(slot)` (~42 MB).
  `skip`, `restart` and `end` manage the window (a long prompt only feeds the last `WIN` rows).
- **Block and lattice.** A block of `L` rows (the pending token plus `L − 1` masks) attends the context and itself,
  not causally. Per depth the drafter keeps the top 16 candidates (`TOPK`) with their logits and a selector
  projection (rank-256 predecessor/successor codebooks). `lattice` runs one block; **`latticeMulti` runs one block per
  slot in a single batched pass** (up to `MAXS` = 16 blocks, `MAXB` = 128 rows), and `take(i)` makes block `i` the
  current one.
- **Choosing drafts.** `chain` follows the best child under the selector's score; `tree` is a best-first search
  (a small heap, policy constants `EDGE`, `NOISE`, `SCALE`, `BRANCH`) over the lattice that returns up to `nodes` drafts
  with their parents. For a sampled request it mixes in the target's keyed Gumbel noise at each position, so drafts
  follow the draws the serial reply would make.
- **`treeRound`.** One complete round for a lone stream: lattice, tree, `Runner.verifyTree`, walk the target's draws
  down the tree, `commitPath`, then `addTaps` for the kept rows. It returns the accepted tokens and the *terminal draw*
  (the next pending token).
- **`absorbMulti`.** Pushes the kept rows' taps of several slots in one pass (for a tree, only the kept path's rows).

## 5. Kernels, by file

Kernel code uses subgroups of 16, DPAS (Xe2's matrix unit) and 2D block loads. Every file states its bit-level
conventions in its header comment; read those before changing a reduction order.

| File | Kernels | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `glue.cl` | `embed`, `embed_dense` | Token embedding (MLX 4-bit table, or the GPTQ fp16 table). |
| | `add_rmsnorm`, `add_rmsnorm_dec` | Residual add, RMSNorm, fp16 output plus the per-group row sums the GEMM family needs; the `_dec` variant uses 512 work-items per row for the decode and verification shapes. Can fuse the W4A8 quantization and the Hadamard rotation. |
| | `dense_rows` | The GDN gates `a`, `b` of the GPTQ checkpoint, a small dense fp16 projection by DPAS. |
| | `gdn_pre`, `gdn_pre_rows` | GDN front end: causal convolution (kernel 4) with its state, SiLU, q/k norms, `β` and `g`. One row per group (`gdn_pre`, also the multi-slot and tree variant) or 8 rows by head (`gdn_pre_rows`, long prompt chunks). |
| | `gated_norm` | GDN back end: gated RMSNorm into the `mixer_out` input. |
| | `attn_prep`, `attn_gate`, `rot_heads` | Attention front end (RMS norms, RoPE, K/V cache write at the row's position or its slot's address) and back end (sigmoid gate); head rotation for the K/V cache studies. |
| | `swiglu`, `rowsums_ff` | SwiGLU and its row sums, and the row sums alone after the GEMM-epilogue SwiGLU. |
| | `quant_a8`, `quant_a4`, `fakequant_rows` | Activation quantization for the W4A8 / W4A4 prompt GEMMs; the study version that quantizes and dequantizes in place. |
| | `argmax_part`, `argmax`, `tap`, `conv_commit` | Greedy token (two kernels), tap rows for the drafter, convolution-state replay after a partial keep. |
| | `repack`, `repack_gptq`, `quantize_mlx` | Load-time repacking of MLX and GPTQ weights into the GEMM layout, and the MLX-algorithm requantization of the GPTQ head. |
| `decode.cl` | `gdn_step` | Serial GDN for a few rows, for decode, verification (also replay with `ROWS`, trees with `TREE`, several slots with `MT`). |
| | `attn_decode`, `attn_merge` | Attention over the cache by key slices (`SPLIT` = 32) and their ordered merge; the grid runs a slice's tree rows back to back so they share it in L2. Tree rows see their ancestors; `MT` selects each row's slot. |
| | `kv_move` | Moves a kept path's K/V rows to consecutive positions, in depth order. |
| | `attn_prompt`, `attn_prompt8` | Prompt attention: FlashAttention-2 on DPAS, causal, bf16 cache and int8 cache (Q·Kᵀ in int8 DPAS, P·V in fp16). |
| | `exl3_gemv` | EXL3 decode probe (speed measurement only; `XPU_EXL3_PROBE`). |
| `gdn_chunk.cl` | `gdn_prep`, `gdn_state`, `gdn_out` | Chunked GDN for prompts (64-token chunks on bf16 DPAS, state in fp32): per-chunk preparation, the serial state recurrence across chunks, and the output. |
| `gemm.cl` | `w4_*`, `w4n_*`, `w4s3_*`, `w4k*` | Weight-only int4 GEMM families, compiled for group 64 or 128. The retained decode/verification kernels are `w4k1_decode`, `w4k1_d64` (wide shapes) and `w4k_dsplit` (narrow); the others are earlier families and sweeps kept as references (`w4_*` is the g64 fp16-dequantization reference). `rowsum`, `rowsum_hl` and `w4s3_reduce` are helpers. |
| `drafter.cl` | `dconv`, `dprep`, `dattn`, `rowsums_rows`, `taps_in`, `to_res`, `topk_part`, `quantize4` | DFlash2: grouped two-tap dynamic convolution, q/k/v preparation with a ring cache, block attention, tap handling, top-16 of the logits rows, load-time int4 quantization. |

The GEMM families share one arithmetic contract: **the bits of a row do not depend on the number of rows, on its
position, or on the tiling**. Each row has its own accumulator and the summation order is fixed (K in slices of groups
each summed from 0, then `((t0 + t1) + t2) + t3`, then the bias by DPAS), so the decode kernels, the nGEN prompt
kernels and every split produce the same bits. This is what lets `verify`, `verifyMulti` and a plain `step` agree.

## 6. The server hosts

`native/xpu.zig` is what `tensorfold-native serve` calls. `open` refuses any `model_type` other than `qwen3_5`,
takes `--context` (32 768 when not given), builds the `Runner` and serves it through the core's lane host for any
`--parallel` value (the core removed its serial host in 1.0.9).

**Lane host (`--parallel N`).** `openLanes` creates `Lanes` (`xpu_lanes.zig`) as the backend of the core's lane
host (`engine_api.LaneHost`, [`core/lane_host.zig`](../../zig/src/core/lane_host.zig)). The number of slots is
`slotsThatFit`: the device's free memory read through Sysman once the model, the first stream's state and the drafter
are loaded (`Gpu.freeMemory`), less a 2 GiB margin and the prompt cache, divided by `slotBytes()`, plus the first
stream, at most `MAX_SLOTS`. When the margin and the cache do not fit, there is no slot and the engine refuses to
open with a message. At startup `measure()` times a verify plus keep of 1 to 16 rows on a
scratch context in the last slot (logged as `window ms by rows`); the core's depth rule uses these costs to weigh
expected tokens per millisecond (without them it drafts at most 3 rows).

`Lanes.backend()` exposes the vtable the core drives: `prefill`, `first` / `first_masked`, `queue`, `read`, `verify`,
`keep`, `draft`, `tree`, `release`. How each maps to the runner:

| Backend call | Runner / drafter calls |
|---|---|
| `prefill` | `select(slot)`, `reset`, `prompt(ids, true)` with taps on; the last row's logits kept for sampled or structured streams. A free slot is taken from the top, so slot 0 stays for the lone driver. |
| `queue` | `select(slot)`, `step(token)` (a one-token advance). |
| `verify(windows)` | `settle`, then **`verifyMulti`**: every stream's window (pending token plus drafts, as a chain or a tree) in one forward of at most 16 rows; each row is drawn with its stream's sampling at its position, or among its grammar's allowed tokens (`drawMasked`). |
| `keep(windows, paths)` | `keepPaths`, after absorbing the kept rows' taps into each stream's drafter context (`absorb`). |
| `draft(requests)` | `absorb` the kept rows not yet taken, then **one batched drafter pass** (`latticeMulti`) for all streams, then per stream a tree (`tree`) of its asked drafts, or a chain below `TREE_MIN` = 5 drafts. The result is held per slot and handed to the core by `tree`. |

`settle` exists because the core calls `keep` only to drop rows: a verify whose rows all stayed is kept lazily, at the
start of the next call.

**Lone driver and resume.** A single stream that asks for drafts does not use shared rounds. `Lanes.lone` takes it in
slot 0 and runs `alone`, a loop of `treeRound` (DFlash2 trees, sampled or greedy) that calls the host's `yield` hook
before each round; when another stream arrives it saves `cache_len` and the pending token and returns `true`, and the
lane core takes the stream over in shared rounds. When the others finish and one stream remains, the core hands it back
through `resumeLone` (the core's `Lone.resumes` and `Engine.detach`; `lone` sees `hooks.resumed`): the drafter context is restarted if it does not end at the
runner's position, and the loop continues.

**Structured output.** The lane host is created with `.structures = true`. With `libtfgrammar` available, a request
with `response_format` or `guided_*` fields gets its tokens masked: windows carry one grammar bit-mask per row; greedy
takes the allowed argmax (first on ties), sampled takes the keyed sampler over the allowed tokens (their top `k`).
`first_masked` does the same for the first token. Such a request does not use the lone driver's trees.

## 7. A request, end to end (lane host)

1. The HTTP server tokenizes and renders the chat template, then submits a stream to the core.
2. `prefill`: the stream gets a slot; the prompt runs in 1 024-row forwards (`Runner.prompt`). Taps of the last `WIN`
   rows feed the slot's drafter context.
3. `first` draws the first token from the kept logits (argmax, or the sampler at the stream's seed and position).
4. Rounds: the core asks `draft` for the streams that want drafts, builds one window per stream (pending token plus
   drafts), and calls `verify` (one forward, at most 16 rows across streams). It decides each window's accepted path
   from the drawn tokens and calls `keep`; the runner replays or swaps states and the drafters absorb the kept rows.
   A lone stream runs the same idea in `alone` with `treeRound`.
5. Tokens are committed to the stream and streamed back until a stop token or `max_tokens`.

## 8. The prompt GEMM generator: `w4_ngen.cpp`

`w4_ngen.cpp` (the command line) builds the kernels of `w4_prompt.hpp` (fp16 activations) and `w4a8_prompt.hpp`
(int8 or int4 activations), written against nGEN (oneDNN's header-only assembler for Intel GPUs). Given a hardware (`xe2` or `xe3`), a group size
(64 or 128), an output path and option words, it writes a zebin: `./w4_ngen xe2|xe3 64|128 OUT.zebin [options]`. The
options each build kernel gets are in `zig/build/xpu.zig`. The generated
GEMMs have the same arithmetic and tiling as the OpenCL reference `w4n_prompt`, hence the same bits:

- A subgroup is one SIMD16 thread over 32 rows × 32 columns; a work-group is 2 × 8 subgroups (64 × 256); the
  grid is `(GM, N / 256, packets)` so that all the columns of a packet of row tiles run before the next (A stays
  in L2).
- Per group of `GSZ`: a DPAS partial sum from 0, then `acc += part · (s · 2²⁴)` (the int4 values enter the DPAS as fp16
  subnormals) and the bias term.
- Families (kernel names in the zebin): `w4g_dpb` (wide shapes), `w4g_s4dpb` (narrow shapes: K in four slices of groups
  summed separately, `((t0 + t1) + t2) + t3`), `w4g_dpb_swiglu` (gate|up interleaved, SwiGLU in the epilogue), `w4a8`
  and `w4a8_swiglu` (int8 activations, int8 DPAS, GPTQ g128 only) and `w4a4` (int4 activations on rotated weights).
- Option words: `b3` (B over three buffers), `s4` (the sliced family), `asplit` (A read in two halves, overlapping the
  DPAS), `swiglu`, and `a8` / `a4` for the integer-activation kernels. The register map is documented in each header.
- In `w4_prompt.hpp` a subgroup's tile is two 16-column tiles (8 accumulators). A group's DPAS partial is folded into
  the accumulator by the previous group's scale while this group's DPAS run (a one-group lag), and the bias enters by
  DPAS at the end (Ahi, Alo, b × gsz). `s4` keeps `((t0 + t1) + t2) + t3` in P, `asplit` reads A in two halves of
  16 K, and `swiglu` takes gate|up interleaved by 16 columns and writes fp16(bf16(SiLU(g)·u)) as [M, N/2].

## 9. Environment variables

The server and the runner read the same variables. See [README.md](README.md) for the effect and the measured value
of the user-facing options; this table says where each is read.

| Variable | Read in | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `XPU_CHUNK` | `Runner.init` | Prompt rows per forward (1 024; a multiple of 64). |
| `XPU_TREE`, `XPU_BLOCK` | `native/xpu.zig`, `qwen27_main.zig` | Tree nodes per round (server 15; the test runner 0, i.e. chains) and drafter block rows (8). |
| `XPU_PREFILL_INT8`, `XPU_PREFILL_INT4`, `XPU_PREFILL_INT4_SITES` | `Runner.init` | W4A8 and W4A4 prompt GEMMs (local options; W4A4 needs W4A8 and rotated weights, else `Int4NeedsRotatedWeightsAndInt8`). |
| `XPU_KV_INT8` | `Runner.init` | int8 K/V cache. |
| `XPU_ATTN_PREF` | `Runner.init` | Chunk size of the prefix decode attention (`attn_pref` or `attn_pref8` for int8 K/V, `attn_tail`, `attn_merge2`); unset: `attn_decode` and `attn_merge`. |
| `XPU_PROFILE` | `Runner.init` | GPU time per kernel (timestamp events), printed by `profReport` after the prompt and the decode (test runner). |
| `XPU_DUMP_H=FILE` | `Runner.init` | Append every row's final normed hidden state (fp16) to FILE, for the quality studies. |
| `XPU_DUMP=DIR` | `Runner.init` | The first forward writes the residual stream after the embedding and after layers 0-3 (comparison with the Python port's layer reference). |
| `XPU_A8`, `XPU_A8_SITES`, `XPU_A8_ROT`, `XPU_A8_BITS`, `XPU_A8_SITES4`, `XPU_KV8` | `Runner.init` | Quantization studies (simulated quantization of GEMM inputs, rotated activations, K/V cache variants). Not for serving. |
| `XPU_CTX` | `qwen27_main.zig` | Context of the test runner (4 096). |

Test-runner-only variables (`qwen27_main.zig`): `XPU_DRAFTER=DIR` (drafted decode compared with the serial reply),
`XPU_VERIFY_TEST`, `XPU_MULTI_TEST=N`, `XPU_ROWS_PROBE`, `XPU_OVERLAP_PROBE`, `XPU_EXL3_PROBE`,
`XPU_GEMM_ZEBIN`, `XPU_A8_ZEBIN` with `XPU_A8_PROJ` (`gu`, `in`, `out`, `down`). Section 10 describes the tests.

## 10. The test runner and the correctness contracts

```sh
xpu-qwen27 MODEL ids.txt 32          # prompt token ids separated by spaces, 32 greedy tokens, timings
xpu-qwen27 MODEL --bench=4096 2      # synthetic prompt of 4 096 tokens (timing only: not real tokens)
```

It loads the model, runs the prompt, decodes `STEPS` greedy tokens serially, prints prompt and decode rates and the
token list, then runs whichever checks the environment asks for. The serial reply is the **reference** the checks
compare against.

| Contract | Checked by | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Oracle**: greedy tokens equal the fp32 torch reference of the Python port | Compare the printed `tokens:` line with the reference's | The reference (`tools/xpu-bench/integ/oracle.py` of the Python port, named in `qwen27_main.zig`) is not in this repository. |
| **Drafted == serial** | `XPU_VERIFY_TEST=1` | Blocks of 8 rows verified and committed with *perfect* drafts (the serial reply itself) and with *wrong* drafts (token 0): both replies must equal the serial one. |
| | `XPU_DRAFTER=DIR` (+ `XPU_TREE`, `XPU_BLOCK`) | Greedy decode with real DFlash2 drafts, as chains or as trees, must equal the serial reply; prints draft and verify times. |
| **Multi-stream == serial** | `XPU_MULTI_TEST=N` (N ≤ 16) | N slots, each prompted differently. Three checks against each slot's serial reply: shared one-row rounds (`stepMulti`); shared windows of 4 rows with perfect drafts on even slots and wrong ones on odd slots (`verifyMulti` + `keepMulti`); shared tree windows of 7 rows (`verifyMulti` + `keepPaths`, parents `−1 0 0 2 1 3 3`). Then the aggregate rate of shared rounds for 1 to N slots. |
| **Same bits per projection / per row** | By construction (section 5) and through the checks above | A row's result does not depend on how many rows ran with it, on its chunk, or on which kernel computed it. |
| Cost of a window | `XPU_ROWS_PROBE=1` | Forward time for 1 to 16 rows. |
| Where the time goes | `XPU_PROFILE=1` | GPU time per kernel. |

The server-level versions of the same contracts are run with
[`tools/bench_concurrent.py`](../../tools/bench_concurrent.py) `--alone --serial`: every concurrent reply's token hash
must equal the same request alone, and the alone run must equal the same request with `"draft": false`, for greedy and
sampled requests. `zig build test` covers the core.

When changing a kernel, the quickest honest check is: `xpu-qwen27` with `XPU_VERIFY_TEST=1`,
`XPU_DRAFTER=<drafter dir> XPU_TREE=15` and `XPU_MULTI_TEST=<n>` on real token ids (not `--bench`), then
`bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial` against a running server.
# Intel Arc Pro B70 (XPU) backend for the TensorFold Zig engine

**Unofficial** port: an `xpu` backend for the TensorFold Zig engine that drives an Intel Xe2 card (Arc Pro B70,
Battlemage G31, 32 GB) directly through **Level Zero**, with no PyTorch, no SYCL and no Python at run time. It serves
**Qwen3.8-27B** behind the OpenAI API of the `tensorfold-native` server, with the DFlash2 tree drafter.

## What it serves

| | |
|---|---|
| Model | Qwen3.8-27B (`model_type` `qwen3_5`: 48 GDN layers + 16 attention layers) |
| Formats | MLX affine 4-bit, group size 64 (`mlx-q4g64`); GPTQ symmetric 4-bit, group size 128 (`gptq-int4-g128`) |
| Measured checkpoints | GPTQ: [`SergiioB/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16`](https://huggingface.co/SergiioB/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16) (revision `9d189a60`), with its tokenizer as published; full recipe: [RECIPE-qwen38-27b-b70.md](RECIPE-qwen38-27b-b70.md) |
| Drafts | DFlash2 (`--drafter`), best-first tree of 15 nodes, greedy and sampled |
| Serving | several streams (`--parallel N`, 8 by default, the engine's "lanes" host): shared rounds, a lone stream runs as a DFlash2 tree (also with `--parallel 1`) |

In the GPTQ format, the layers are int4 g128 as stored. The GDN `in_proj_a/b` gates stay in dense fp16, as in the
checkpoint, and the embedding is fp16. The output head is requantized at load time to affine 4/64 with MLX's
algorithm: its accuracy is that of the checkpoint's MLX 4-bit head (same token as the fp16 head in 97.4 % of cases,
KL 3.9e-3; `tools/xpu/head_study.py`).

## Building

Prerequisites: Zig 0.17, the `xe` driver and the Intel compute runtime (Level Zero), `ocloc` (Intel's offline
compiler), a C++17 compiler and the oneDNN nGEN headers.

```sh
zig build xpu-native -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<path to ngen>   # zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native
zig build xpu-qwen27 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<path to ngen>   # xpu-qwen27 test executable
```

Device tests: `zig build xpu-qwen27-tests -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<path to ngen>`, then `zig-out/bin/tf-xpu-qwen27-means-test` (group means against FP64, no model), `zig-out/bin/tf-xpu-qwen27-seam-test MODEL` (or `TF_XPU_QWEN27=MODEL`: a prompt cut at 64, 1024 or whole gives the same logits) and `zig-out/bin/tf-xpu-qwen27-close-test MODEL` (three opens and closes give the card back); each prints `skipped:` and exits 0 without a Level Zero device or a model. Nemotron's op tests stay `zig build -Dxpu xpu-tests`.

The OpenCL C kernels are compiled by `ocloc` for `-Dxpu-device` (default `bmg`). The prompt GEMMs are generated as
ISA by nGEN at build time (`zig/tools/xpu/w4_ngen.cpp`); everything is embedded in the executable.

## Running

```sh
tensorfold-native serve MODEL --drafter DFLASH2 --parallel 8 --context 16384 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081
```

With `--parallel N` (N > 1), each stream has its own slot on the card: GDN state (2 × 151 MB, the state and its
backup for verification) and K/V cache (64 KB per token of `--context`). The number of slots is bounded by the memory
left after loading, as the device reports it (`slotsThatFit`); a stream that does not fit is refused at startup.
A lone stream that asks for drafts runs as a DFlash2 tree. As soon as another
stream arrives, the core takes it over in shared rounds: one forward for the windows of all streams (the pending
token, then either copies of the context as a chain or the stream's DFlash2 drafts: a tree from 5 drafts up, a chain
below), 16 rows at most. Each slot has its own DFlash2 context (the drafter's K/V in a ring of 2,080 positions,
~42 MB) which absorbs all of its kept rows; the drafts of all streams are proposed in a single pass of the drafter.
When the other streams finish, the one that remains goes back to a DFlash2 tree (the core's `Lone.resumes`).

Prefix cache (`--parallel N`): the core keeps the state of a slot at planned points of the prompt (multiples of 64,
since the prompt kernels compute in blocks of 64 rows from the start of a call), and a request whose prompt begins
the same way restarts from there: GDN and convolution states, K/V cache up to that point, and the stream's DFlash2
context (~0.8 GB at 9.7 k tokens). A resume gives exactly the state of a full pass cut at the same points: the same
answer, bit for bit. Budget: `--prompt-cache-gib` (2 GiB by default, reserved before the streams: 6 streams instead
of 7 in GPTQ at 16 k; `0` disables it). The core keeps nothing below 4,096 tokens. Measured on a 9.7 k-token
document: the same request replayed 6.1 → 1.2 s, the next turn of a conversation 6.1 → 1.1 s.
Prefix shared between different requests: put the common base in the **system** message (or in the tools); the
server places points at the end of the system prefix (and 512 / 2,048 tokens before it), and any request that shares
that system message restarts from there, whatever follows (measured: two other questions on the same 9.7 k-token
document in the system message, 6.1 → 1.2 s each, same answers as with an empty cache). A base placed in the user
message is reused only by the same request or by the following turns of the conversation.

Structured outputs (`response_format` JSON / `json_schema`, `guided_*` fields) with `--parallel N`: each row is
drawn among the tokens the grammar allows (argmax, or the keyed sampler over the allowed tokens). `libtfgrammar.so`
must be next to the server (`zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR`, xgrammar v0.2.8, copied into `zig-out/xpu/lib/`). A
structured request does not go through the lone stream's DFlash2 tree: ~86 tok/s against ~145 on a long JSON answer.

Options through environment variables:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `XPU_PREFILL_INT4=1` | **Local option**, with `XPU_PREFILL_INT8=1` and a rotated checkpoint (`zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py`, marker `hadamard128`): `down` input in int4 (DPAS u4 × s4), +8 % prefill at equal quality to GPTQ W4A8; `XPU_PREFILL_INT4_SITES=10` adds the mixer outputs (+12 %, perplexity +1 %). |
| `XPU_KV_INT8=1` | **Option** (the default stays bf16): K/V cache in int8 (scale per position and K/V head): half the memory, 12 streams instead of 7 at 16 k tokens, 7 instead of 3 at 32 k; perplexity unchanged (±0.04 %), DFlash2 acceptance unchanged. Answers are not bit-identical to those of the bf16 cache (15 of 24 greedy answers identical over 256 tokens, the others diverge on near-ties); the drafted == serial and multi-stream == serial contracts hold in this mode. Prompt attention `attn_prompt8`: Q·Kᵀ in int8 DPAS, P·V in fp16. |
| `XPU_ATTN_PREF=256` | **Option** (off by default; a multiple of 32 from 64 to 4096): decode attention reads the committed prefix once a round. `attn_pref` scores chunks of that many keys on bf16 DPAS for 8 (row, head) queries at a time, `attn_tail` keeps `attn_decode`'s arithmetic for a row's last keys, and `attn_merge2` merges both in key order. Answers are not bit-identical to the default path (262 of 329 greedy answers identical, the others diverge on near-ties); drafted == serial holds in this mode. Rows below position 1,040 keep the default kernels and the default tokens. With `XPU_KV_INT8=1` the prefix runs `attn_pref8`, which widens the int8 rows to bf16; tree rounds of several streams keep the default path. Receipt: [xpu-qwen27-attn-prefix](../receipts/xpu-qwen27-attn-prefix/README.md). |
| `XPU_PREFILL_INT8=1` | **Local option**: prompt GEMMs in W4A8, int8 activations per (row, group of 128), GPTQ only. Decoding stays in fp16. |
| `XPU_TREE=N` | DFlash2 tree nodes per round (15 by default; 0: a chain) |
| `XPU_BLOCK=N` | Rows of the drafter block (8) |
| `XPU_FP64_REF=1` | `xpu-qwen27` runner only: on the prompt's real activations, each int4 GEMM of layers 0, 1, 31, 63 and the head (decode on 1 and 8 rows, prompt) against FP64 references of the same int4 weights (`core/quant` MLX affine; GPTQ as affine with bias −8·scale), worst column and error over the outputs' rms (`zig/src/xpu/fp64_ref.zig`) |
| `XPU_FIDELITY=1` | `xpu-qwen27` runner only: teacher-forced top tokens of the prompt and decode paths at every position of the IDS file against the same forward with every GEMM in FP64, all differences and margins (`XPU_FIDELITY_CACHE=FILE` keeps the FP64 forward's tokens) |

## Numbers (B70 at 230 W, server `--parallel 8 --context 16384`, validation of 2026-10-13)

| | MLX g64 | GPTQ g128 | GPTQ g128 + W4A8 | Rotated RTN + W4A4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prefill 1 k / 4 k / 8 k tokens (tok/s) | 1,783 / 1,772 / 1,742 | 1,975 / 1,965 / 1,930 | 2,617 / 2,585 / 2,540 | 2,830 / 2,811 / 2,754 |
| Single stream, DFlash2 tree, code / chat, greedy | 129 / 98 | 133 / 90 | 133 / 97 | 126 / 99 |
| 2 / 4 / 8 simultaneous streams, code, greedy (aggregate) | 211 / 294 / 326 | 235 / 310 / 270 | 235 / 310 / 270 | 222 / 288 / 260 |
| 2 / 4 / 8 simultaneous streams, chat, greedy (aggregate) | 151 / 239 / 300 | 148 / 215 / 208 | 162 / 230 / 224 | 162 / 249 / 227 |
| `bench_openai` decode, 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 requests (aggregate) | 173 / 243 / 343 / 350 | 165 / 300 / 337 / 439 | 165 / 336 / 367 / 456 | 179 / 325 / 364 / 463 |

Before the per-stream DFlash2 drafts (copies only in the shared rounds), 2 / 4 / 8 code streams ran at
64 / 120 / 182 tok/s in GPTQ. Validation: `zig build test`, oracle, drafted == serial, multi-stream == serial (chains
and trees), and `bench_concurrent --alone --serial` on 1, 2, 4 and 8 streams, greedy and sampled, for the four
configurations: 64 cells all equal, no errors in the server logs.

Benches: `bench_openai.py` (prefill, decode) and `bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial` (drafts), in `tools/` on the
`main` branch of this repository. Drafted throughput depends on the text produced; the two formats do not write the
same text.

Prefill is **power-bound**: at 230 W, the card runs at ~2,180 MHz during a prompt (PL2), not at the 2,600 of pure
DPAS. The gate|up GEMM alone sustains 146 TFLOPS fp16 and ~209 TOPS in int8.

## Correctness: what is verified

- **Oracle**: the greedy tokens equal those of the Python port's fp32 torch reference (same prompt, 32 tokens), in
  MLX and in GPTQ, with and without W4A8.
- **Drafted == serial**: bit for bit, with perfect, wrong and real drafts, as chain and as tree, greedy and sampled
  (`xpu-qwen27` with `XPU_VERIFY_TEST`, and `bench_concurrent --alone --serial` on the server).
- **Several streams == one**: bit for bit, up to 16 slots, with windows of 1 and 4 rows and partial keeps
  (`XPU_MULTI_TEST`), and each concurrent answer equal to the same request run alone
  (`bench_concurrent --alone`).
- **W4A8**: perplexity on three raw texts (English, code, French) +0.04 to +0.13 %, KL ≈ 3e-3 against fp16;
  for comparison, MLX and GPTQ differ from each other by 0.06 to 0.11 in KL
  (`tools/xpu/a8_study.py`).
- **Measure on raw text**: in a chat user turn, the model (the fp32 reference included) predicts the next token
  poorly, because it is trained only on the answers. Perplexities there are meaningless.

## Code layout

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `zig/src/xpu/ze.zig` | Level Zero access: memory, modules, kernels, command lists |
| `zig/src/xpu/qwen27.zig` | The model: loading (MLX, GPTQ), layer-by-layer forward, `Runner` (`prompt`, `step`, `verify`, `verifyTree`, `commit`, `commitPath`; slots `select`, `verifyMulti`, `keepMulti`) |
| `zig/src/xpu/drafter.zig` | DFlash2: tap context, proposed block, selector, best-first tree, `treeRound` |
| `zig/src/native/xpu.zig` | The hook into the server: the "lanes" host for every `--parallel` |
| `zig/src/native/xpu_lanes.zig` | The `lanes` backend: slots, shared rounds (`verifyMulti`, `keepMulti`), lone stream as a tree (`lone`) |
| `zig/src/xpu/qwen27_main.zig` | Test executable: oracle, contracts, profiles, probes |
| `zig/kernels/xpu/qwen27/*.cl` | OpenCL C kernels: decode int4 GEMM, chunked and serial GDN, decode attention, norms, SwiGLU, int8 quantization, drafter |
| `zig/kernels/xpu/qwen27/decode.cl` (`attn_prompt`, `attn_prompt8`) | Prompt attention: FlashAttention-2 on DPAS in oneDNN's orientation (S = K·Qᵀ, one query per lane, softmax within the lane); bf16 or int8 cache |
| `zig/tools/xpu/w4_ngen.cpp`, `w4_prompt.hpp`, `w4a8_prompt.hpp` | nGEN generator of the prompt GEMMs: int4 fp16 (`w4g_dpb`, `w4g_s4dpb`, SwiGLU epilogue), W4A8 (`w4a8`) and W4A4 (`w4a4`) |
| `zig/build/xpu.zig` | Build steps |

No core file is modified: the backend uses the core's lane host and its lone driver (`Lone.resumes`) as they are;
`build.zig` only adds the XPU steps.

## Test executable

```sh
xpu-qwen27 MODEL ids.txt 32          # prompt (ids separated by spaces), 32 greedy tokens, timings
xpu-qwen27 MODEL --bench=4096 2      # synthetic prompt of 4,096 tokens (caution: does not replace real tokens)
```

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `XPU_DRAFTER=DIR`, `XPU_TREE`, `XPU_BLOCK` | drafted rounds, compared with serial |
| `XPU_VERIFY_TEST=1` | drafted == serial contract with perfect and wrong drafts |
| `XPU_MULTI_TEST=N` | multi-stream contract: N slots, shared rounds (one row, windows of 4 rows, then trees of 7 rows) == serial, and aggregate throughput |
| `XPU_ROWS_PROBE=1` | cost of a forward of 1 to 16 rows |
| `XPU_PROFILE=1` | GPU time per kernel |
| `XPU_DUMP_H=FILE` | final hidden states of each row (accuracy studies) |
| `XPU_A8=128` or `token`, `XPU_A8_SITES` | W4A8 study: simulated quantization of the prompt GEMM inputs |
| `XPU_CHUNK`, `XPU_CTX` | rows per prompt chunk (1,024), context (4,096) |
| `XPU_OVERLAP_PROBE`, `XPU_GEMM_ZEBIN`, `XPU_A8_ZEBIN` (+ `XPU_A8_PROJ`) | probes: GEMM/GDN overlap, fp16 or W4A8 GEMM in a loop |

## Limitations

- A single model: the 27B dimensions are constants (`qwen27.zig`) and some shapes are written into the kernels (GDN
  of 128, attention of 256, head ratio 6).
- On very repetitive text, where copies are enough, the drafter pass of the shared rounds costs a few percent at 4-8
  streams. No response resume yet (`decode_chunk`).
- 4-bit formats only (MLX g64, symmetric GPTQ g128). W4A8 requires GPTQ g128.
# Recipe (draft): Qwen3.8-27B on one Arc Pro B70

> **Status: draft.** This describes how our serving setup is made so that someone else can reproduce it. Items marked
> `TODO` are not recorded yet or have not been re-run from this text. Nothing here is a benchmark: numbers live in
> [README.md](README.md) (section "Numbers"), and the code map is in [NAVIGATION.md](NAVIGATION.md).

The setup serves **Qwen3.8-27B** from one Intel Arc Pro B70 (32 GB) with the XPU backend of the TensorFold Zig engine,
a **GPTQ int4 group-128** target checkpoint, and the **DFlash2** drafter. Four pieces:

| Piece | Source | Format on disk | What the engine does with it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Target model | `SergiioB/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16` (section 2), a quantization of `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` | GPTQ INT4, symmetric, group size 128, `desc_act=false`, MTP layer in BF16 | Reads the int4 words and fp16 scales as stored (`gptq-int4-g128`). |
| Tokenizer | the files shipped with that checkpoint (section 3) | `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json` | Reads the pre-tokenizer from `tokenizer.json`. |
| Drafter | `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (section 4) | BF16 | Quantized to affine int4 (groups of 64) **at load**. |
| Rotated weights (optional) | made from the base model and the target checkpoint (section 5) | GPTQ-shaped, rotated, with a `hadamard128` marker file | Faster prompts; **readable by this engine only**. |

## 1. What you need

- An Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB) with the `xe` kernel driver and Intel's compute runtime (Level Zero).
  The engine opens the device by its PCI id.
- Zig 0.17, `ocloc` (Intel's offline compiler), a C++17 compiler, and the nGEN headers of oneDNN
  (`<ngen>`: the directory that holds `ngen.hpp`).
- For structured output: a checkout of [xgrammar](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar) at tag `v0.2.8`, with submodules.
- For making checkpoints: Python with `gptqmodel` **7.3.2**, `torch`, `safetensors`, and enough memory and a GPU for
  GPTQ calibration of a 27B model. `TODO (hardware and time used for our quantization run)`.
- Disk for the base weights, the quantized copy and the drafter.

Paths below use placeholders: `<models>` is a directory for checkpoints, `<repo>` a clone of this repository.

## 2. The target checkpoint: GPTQ INT4, group 128

We serve the checkpoint published by **SergiioB**, author of the Intel Arc Pro B70 inference cookbook, at revision
`9d189a60e4c0ad7f9f47cd94bfa393ca10b3924e` (Apache-2.0, like the base model). Download it as published:

```sh
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('SergiioB/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16', revision='9d189a60e4c0ad7f9f47cd94bfa393ca10b3924e', local_dir='<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128')"
```

The rest of this section is how such a checkpoint is made, from its `quantize_config.json`, for anyone who wants to
redo it. Its author does not document the calibration set, so a redone checkpoint will not be bit-identical.

Start from the original bf16 checkpoint:

```sh
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B', local_dir='<models>/Qwen3.8-27B')"
```

Quantize it with **gptqmodel 7.3.2** and these settings:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Bits / group size | 4 / 128 |
| Symmetric | yes (the zero point is fixed at 8: the engine never reads `qzeros`) |
| `desc_act` | `false` (no `g_idx`: the engine does not read one) |
| Layers kept unquantized | the MTP layer, kept in BF16, excluded with `dynamic: {"-:.*mtp.*": {}}` |
| Hessian damping `damp_percent` | 0.05 |
| `damp_auto_increment` | 0.01 |
| `true_sequential` | on |
| `act_group_aware` | on |
| Fallback | RTN, at a threshold of 0.5 % |
| Packing | int32 words |
| Calibration dataset | `TODO (calibration dataset to be confirmed)`: not recorded; number of samples and sequence length also `TODO` |

`TODO`: the exact key names of the fallback and of the packing in gptqmodel 7.3.2's `QuantizeConfig`. Take them from
the `quantize_config.json` of the checkpoint we published once it is confirmed, and keep that file with the checkpoint.
A sketch of the call, for the keys that are certain:

```python
from gptqmodel import GPTQModel, QuantizeConfig

cfg = QuantizeConfig(
    bits=4, group_size=128, sym=True, desc_act=False,
    damp_percent=0.05, damp_auto_increment=0.01,
    true_sequential=True, act_group_aware=True,
    dynamic={"-:.*mtp.*": {}},
    # TODO: fallback (RTN, 0.5 %) and int32 packing, with their gptqmodel 7.3.2 key names
)
model = GPTQModel.load("<models>/Qwen3.8-27B", cfg)
model.quantize(calibration)          # TODO (calibration dataset to be confirmed)
model.save("<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128")
```

### What the engine requires of the checkpoint

These are the loader's expectations (`zig/src/xpu/qwen27.zig`, `loadGptq`). A mismatch stops the load with an error
rather than serving wrong output.

- A sharded safetensors checkpoint with a `model.safetensors.index.json`.
- Every quantized projection as `<name>.qweight` (int32, `[K/8, N]`) and `<name>.scales` (fp16, `[K/128, N]`). The
  engine detects the format from the presence of `in_proj_qkv.qweight`.
- Stored in **fp16** (otherwise `UnexpectedDtype` or `UnexpectedShape`): `model.embed_tokens.weight`, `lm_head.weight`
  and the GDN gates `linear_attn.in_proj_a.weight` / `in_proj_b.weight`. The small tensors (norms, convolution, `A_log`,
  `dt_bias`) may be bf16 or fp16; fp16 RMSNorm weights are taken as stored with the `gamma − 1` convention (the engine
  adds 1). Our checkpoint has them in fp16 because gptqmodel loaded the model in float16 (its `config.json` dtype) and
  wrote every unquantized tensor in that dtype (checked: `embed_tokens`, `lm_head`, `in_proj_a`, `in_proj_b` are F16).
- The output head is requantized at load to affine int4 (groups of 64) with MLX's algorithm; the embedding stays fp16.
- The MTP tensors stay in the checkpoint but the XPU engine does not read them.

## 3. The tokenizer: keep the checkpoint's files

Serve with the `tokenizer.json` and `tokenizer_config.json` shipped with the checkpoint, so that anyone who repeats this
setup gets the same token ids and the same replies. The engine reads the pre-tokenizer from `tokenizer.json`.

Known difference: these files were re-saved with `transformers` 5.14.1, whose pre-tokenizer regular expression lacks
`\p{M}`. Hindi, Thai and text with combining marks tokenize differently from the official `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` files
(for example `สวัสดีครับ`: 7 tokens instead of 3); plain French, English and code tokenize the same. Copying the official
files over them is possible, but then the token ids, and the replies on such text, differ from this recipe's.

## 4. The drafter: DFlash2

```sh
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2', local_dir='<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2')"
```

Use the BF16 weights as published. The directory must contain `model.safetensors`, including the
`candidate_selector` codebooks. The engine quantizes the projections to affine int4 (groups of 64) on the device at
load, whatever the target's format; there is no separate quantization step.

This is the repository the other backends of this project use (`zig/src/families/qwen27/dflash/config.zig`); its model
card states that it mirrors `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`.

Drafts only change how many tokens are accepted: the target verifies every token, so the drafter cannot change a reply.

## 5. Optional: rotated weights

[`zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py`](../../zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py) remakes the quantized projections of the GPTQ checkpoint
from the original bf16 weights: each weight is multiplied by a normalized Hadamard matrix of size 128 along K, then
rounded to nearest (RTN: scale `2·max|w| / 15` per group of 128, zero point 8). The GDN gates `a` / `b` are rotated too.
Other tensors (embedding, norms, convolution, head, MTP, vision) are copied from the GPTQ checkpoint, and a small marker
file named `hadamard128` is written in the output directory. The engine then rotates every GEMM input where it is
produced.

```sh
python <repo>/zig/tools/xpu/rotate_w4.py \
    <models>/Qwen3.8-27B <models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128 <models>/Qwen3.8-27B-rot rot
```

(The last argument is `rot` or `norot`; `norot` redoes the RTN quantization without the rotation, for comparison.)
The script copies the GPTQ directory's non-weight files, tokenizer included. Needs
`torch` and `safetensors`.

> **Warning: rotated checkpoints are readable by this engine only.** The weights are not the model's weights: they are
> the weights times a Hadamard matrix, and only this engine rotates the activations to match. Any other engine (vLLM,
> llama.cpp, `transformers`, another build of TensorFold) will load the files without complaint and **produce wrong
> output silently**. Do not publish a rotated checkpoint under the name of the model, label it clearly, and keep the
> `hadamard128` marker with it: without the marker this engine would also read the weights as ordinary ones.

The W4A4 prompt path (`XPU_PREFILL_INT4=1`, together with `XPU_PREFILL_INT8=1`) requires rotated weights and refuses to
start without them (`Int4NeedsRotatedWeightsAndInt8`). It and the W4A8 option are local options: see
[README.md](README.md) for what they trade.

## 6. Build and serve

```sh
cd <repo>
zig build xpu-native -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<ngen>   # zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native
zig build xpu-qwen27 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dngen-include=<ngen>   # test executable xpu-qwen27
```

`-Dxpu-device=` (default `bmg`) and `-Docloc=` (default `ocloc`) are the other options. The kernels are compiled for the
device at build time and embedded in the executables; see [NAVIGATION.md](NAVIGATION.md#2-building).

Serve:

```sh
<repo>/zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native serve <models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128 \
    --drafter <models>/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 --parallel 8 --context 16384 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081
```

- `--parallel N` gives each stream a slot on the card (a GDN state and a K/V cache of `--context` tokens). The number of
  slots is capped by the memory left after loading; the server logs the number of streams it got.
- With one active stream the engine drafts DFlash2 trees; with several it shares rounds between them, for any
  `--parallel` value.
- Environment options (`XPU_PREFILL_INT8`, `XPU_KV_INT8`, `XPU_TREE`, …) are listed in [README.md](README.md) and
  [NAVIGATION.md](NAVIGATION.md#9-environment-variables). The defaults are the validated configuration; the others are
  options.

### Structured output

`response_format` (JSON, `json_schema`) and the `guided_*` fields need the grammar library, built from xgrammar:

```sh
git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar <xgrammar>
cd <repo> && zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=<xgrammar>
```

The build checks that the checkout is at tag `v0.2.8` and produces `libtfgrammar.so`. The server looks for it in
`<server directory>/../lib/`, then next to the server, then on the loader's path, and loads it at the first structured
request: put it in `zig-out/xpu/lib/` (`zig build grammar` installs under `<prefix>/native/lib`, so a copy of
`zig-out/native/lib/libtfgrammar.so` into `zig-out/xpu/lib/` is what we
run). Without the library, structured requests are
refused and everything else works. If you redistribute the library, ship xgrammar's licence and notice with it
(Apache-2.0).

## 7. Validate

With real prompts, not synthetic ones. `ids.txt` holds the token ids of a prompt, separated by spaces, produced with the
checkpoint's tokenizer (for example with the `tokenizers` package: `Tokenizer.from_file("<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128/tokenizer.json")
.encode(text).ids`).

```sh
cd <repo>
zig build test

M=<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128
D=<models>/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
X=zig-out/bin/xpu-qwen27

$X $M ids.txt 32                                   # 32 greedy tokens: compare with the fp32 torch reference
XPU_VERIFY_TEST=1 $X $M ids.txt 32                 # drafted == serial, perfect and wrong drafts
XPU_DRAFTER=$D XPU_TREE=15 $X $M ids.txt 64        # DFlash2 trees == serial
XPU_MULTI_TEST=8 $X $M ids.txt 32                  # 8 streams in shared rounds == serial (chains and trees)
```

- **Oracle.** The greedy tokens must equal the fp32 torch reference of the Python port for the same prompt (32 tokens).
  The reference script lives with the Python port's bench tools and is not published yet. `TODO (publish it, or ship a
  recorded token list per prompt)`.
- **Drafted == serial, multi-stream == serial.** The runner prints `equal to serial: true` for each check; any `false`
  is a bug, not noise.
- **Server level**, against a running server:

```sh
python3 tools/bench_concurrent.py http://127.0.0.1:8081 <model name> --levels 1,2,4,8 --alone --serial
python3 tools/bench_openai.py http://127.0.0.1:8081 <model name>
```

`--alone` checks that every concurrent reply is token-for-token the reply of the same request alone, and `--serial`
checks the alone runs against `"draft": false`. Both greedy and sampled requests are covered by default. Run it before
and after any change to a kernel or to the quantization.

If you made rotated weights, run the same checks on that directory, and compare perplexity on raw text against the GPTQ
checkpoint with the studies in [`tools/xpu/`](../../tools/xpu). Do not measure on chat-formatted prompts: in a user turn
the model predicts the next token badly, so perplexities there mean nothing.

## 8. Results

This page does not repeat numbers. Prompt rates, single-stream and multi-stream decode rates, and the validation that
was run (oracle, drafted == serial, multi-stream == serial, the 64-cell concurrent check) are in
[README.md](README.md), sections "Numbers" and "Correctness: what is verified", with the conditions they were taken in
(power limit, `--parallel`, `--context`, text). Rates depend on the card's power limit and on the text produced; record
the engine commit, the checkpoint and drafter revisions, and the power limit with any figure you report.

## 9. Licences and attribution

The base model and the drafter are both released under the **Apache License 2.0**. A quantized or rotated checkpoint
is a modified copy of the base weights, so if you redistribute it:

- include a copy of the Apache-2.0 licence text;
- keep the upstream copyright, attribution and trademark notices, and include the contents of the upstream `NOTICE`
  file if there is one (`TODO: check the upstream repositories for a NOTICE file`);
- credit the quantized checkpoint's author: the GPTQ checkpoint is SergiioB's
  (`SergiioB/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16`);
- state that you changed the files: for example "GPTQ int4 (group 128, symmetric) quantization of `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B`
  made with gptqmodel 7.3.2; MTP layer kept in bf16", and, for rotated weights, "weights multiplied by a Hadamard
  matrix of size 128 and rounded to nearest; readable only by TensorFold's XPU engine";
- do not use the upstream names or marks to suggest that the upstream authors endorse your files.

The drafter is quantized at load and never rewritten, so serving it as published needs nothing beyond keeping its
licence with the download. TensorFold itself is Apache-2.0 (see [LICENSE](../../LICENSE) and [NOTICE](../../NOTICE)); the
xgrammar library you may build is Apache-2.0 too, with its own notice. This section is a reminder, not legal advice:
read the licence text of each upstream repository.

Intel Arc Pro B65 32 GB · llama.cpp b11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`) Vulkan · Mesa 26.2.2 · kernel 7.2.5 · Omarchy 4.0.4.
Power is GPU board power from xe hwmon only; there's no wall meter.

**Conclusion:** [recommended-settings.md](recommended-settings.md) collects the best settings for the B65 from all phases. Phase 7 adds the engine choice: Intel's llm-scaler vLLM with MTP runs Qwen3.8 27B at 1.7× llama.cpp with its own MTP for one user (llama.cpp's MTP is one flag and gives it 1.8×), exl3xpu serves 8 users at 5.5× llama.cpp, and Strata runs the 125B Flash-Next Coder at 3.6× llama.cpp's best on the same GGUF.

## Headlines so far

1. **Turn flash attention off on this build.** `-fa 0` is faster or tied on every test. Gemma's 16K prefill went from 38 to 335 tok/s (8.8×), and Muse's decode at 16K went from 11.3 to 16.8 tok/s (Phase 0.5).
2. **All three ~30B Q4 models fit 32K context in 32 GB.** Decode at 32K: Qwen3.8 27B 16.1, Muse Glimmer 28B 14.7, Gemma 4 31B QAT 12.8 tok/s (Phase 1).
3. **Time to first token for Qwen and Muse:** 1.3–1.7 s on a 512-token prompt, about 42 s on a 16K prompt (Phase 1).
4. **Gemma + llama-server: use `--ctx-checkpoints 0`.** The default context checkpoints for sliding-window models cost 25 s on a 512-token prompt. With them off, it's 1.4 s. The multi-turn cost of turning them off isn't measured yet (Phase 1 follow-up).
5. **Idle with a model loaded is about 45 W**, against 43 W with nothing loaded.
6. **SYCL with flash attention on beats Vulkan:** +21.8% decode and +31.2% prefill on average, at the same llama.cpp commit (Phase 2). That clears the +10% rule, so **SYCL with flash attention on is the default engine from here (Forge, 2026-10-13)**. The exception is Qwen at 32K, where SYCL is 5.6% slower. Unlike Vulkan, SYCL wants flash attention on.

## Packages

Release tarballs for each run (raw data, scripts as run, summaries, SHA256SUMS) are built into `dist/`, which isn't committed because everything in it is regenerated from what's here. The dashboard serves them at `/files/dist/`.
7. **On SYCL, Qwen and Muse answer 1.4–2.0× sooner, all models fit 32K in 1.5–3.3 GiB less VRAM, and server generation matches llama-bench** (Phase 1S). Gemma's first token is slower than on Vulkan with the same checkpoint fix (2.8 s vs 1.4 s on a 512-token prompt), which is still open.
8. **Gemma on SYCL needs `-b 2048 -ub 2048`:** its 16K first token drops from 58 s to 31 s, 1.6× faster than Vulkan. Checkpoints cost nothing on SYCL (Gemma diagnostic).
9. **Quality (Phase 3): Muse scores 10/10 coding, 10/10 tools and 5/5 recall, and is quickest.** Qwen and Gemma each miss one coding task by running out of tokens while thinking. Gemma passes with more room; Qwen goes round in circles (Phase 5: it does finish on its own, at 9,402 tokens). In AJ's blind writing ranking, Gemma wins (mean rank 1.6 against 2.2 for both others).
10. **The canary is clean** (all within 0.1%), and **`-ub 2048` lifts SYCL prefill for all three models** (+35–55% at 16K, decode unchanged). On Vulkan it helps Qwen (+10%) but costs Muse 36% (Phase 4).
11. **At the new default, Qwen and Muse answer a 16K prompt in about 20.5 s,** 1.4× sooner than at ub 512 and about 2× sooner than on Vulkan. Generation is unchanged and VRAM is 0.5–0.7 GB higher (server rerun after Phase 4).
12. **Phase 5:**
    - The ub 2048 baseline reproduces Phase 4 within 0.03%.
    - Gemma on SYCL has a fixed ~1.1 s floor per request, so Vulkan answers tiny prompts 0.3–0.6 s sooner; SYCL is faster from 1K tokens up.
    - Every chat setup reuses its cache, and `--ctx-checkpoints 0` was faster in all 6 model and engine pairs (Gemma on Vulkan: 124 s per turn with checkpoints on vs 5.5 s off).
    - Qwen passes c08 5/5 with thinking off, in about 300 tokens and 13 s. With thinking on it needs up to 9,650 tokens; caps only cut it short, and the samplers don't help.
13. **Phase 6:**
    - Qwen with thinking off scores 10/10 greedy and 30/30 on the Phase 3 coding set (Phase 3: 9/10), about 4× faster. That makes thinking off the Qwen coding recipe. Muse ignores the thinking-off switches: it reasoned on all 30.
    - `--ctx-checkpoints 0` makes Qwen re-read the whole chat on every regenerate or edit (9.4K tokens, 11.3 s against 0.17 s). Gemma and Muse handle regenerate and edit-last fine with checkpoints off, but every model re-reads the whole chat when an earlier turn is edited.
    - The ub 2048 canary is within 0.03% of the Phase 5 baseline.
    - Forge's decision: checkpoints stay at the default except for Gemma on Vulkan and Gemma agent loops. The Phase 5 idea of `--ctx-checkpoints 0` everywhere is withdrawn.

## Current defaults (Forge, 2026-10-13; checkpoints and thinking updated after Phase 6)
- **Engine:** llama.cpp `8bb3cf0d2` SYCL, flash attention on, `-b 2048 -ub 2048`, for all three models.
- **Context checkpoints (llama-server):** leave at the default (on) for Qwen, Muse, and Gemma in chat UIs. `--ctx-checkpoints 0` only for Gemma on Vulkan, and for Gemma append-only agent loops on SYCL (3.2 s against 6.0 s per turn in Phase 5).
- **Qwen for coding:** thinking off (`--reasoning-budget 0`). Muse has no working thinking-off switch; it runs with thinking on.
- **Canary:** `b65-phase4/canary.sh` runs at ub 2048 against `baseline_ub2048.json` (Phase 5 part A); `UB=512` still checks against the Phase 2 baseline (Phase 6 handoff).
- **Vulkan:** if used, flash attention off and ub 512.

# Running 30B-class GGUF models on Intel's Arc Pro B65: SYCL vs. Vulkan and the settings I'd use

I wanted to know what Intel's 32 GB Arc Pro B65 could actually do with local models: how quickly it reads a long prompt, how generation holds up as the conversation grows, and which settings make a difference in everyday use.

So I tested three 4-bit GGUF models on two llama.cpp backends, then followed up on the results that looked wrong. The main experiments ran on October 12–13, 2026: seven numbered phases, from 0 through 6, plus focused follow-ups.

The setup I landed on is **SYCL with flash attention on, a 2048-token micro-batch, all layers on the GPU, and a 32K context window**. Leave context checkpoints at their default for chat. For Qwen coding tasks, turn thinking off.

On this setup, Qwen and Muse reached the first token of a 16K-token prompt in about **20.5 seconds**, compared with about **42 seconds** on the Vulkan reference. Gemma took **30.8 seconds**, compared with **49.4 seconds**, with checkpoints disabled in both of those Gemma measurements.

Those results come from several experiments. Below, I've separated the backend comparison, the later tuning, and the quality checks so it's clear what each number measures.

## The setup I'd start with

With a SYCL build of llama.cpp and Intel's oneAPI runtime installed, run this from the llama.cpp checkout in Bash. Replace the model path and check that `level_zero:0` is your B65:

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force
sycl-ls

export ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0
export UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=1

./build-sycl/bin/llama-server \
  -m /absolute/path/to/model.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -c 32768 -np 1 --jinja \
  -fa on -b 2048 -ub 2048
```

Here, `-b` is the logical batch size and `-ub` is the physical micro-batch size used to process a prompt. `-np 1` sets one parallel server slot. The measurements in this article are for one request at a time.

Two changes depend on the workload:

- **Qwen for coding:** add `--reasoning-budget 0`. The confirmation run also sent `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}` in each chat-completion request.
- **Gemma in append-only agent loops:** consider `--ctx-checkpoints 0`. Keep the default for chat interfaces where you edit earlier messages.

These are settings measured on the versions below. I would recheck them after a driver or llama.cpp update.

## Hardware, software, and model files

| Component | Tested configuration |
|---|---|
| GPU | ASRock Arc Pro B65 Creator, 32 GB, 200 W board power cap |
| Host | Ryzen 7 5700X, 48 GB RAM |
| OS | Arch Linux / Omarchy 4.0.4, kernel `7.2.5-3-omarchy` |
| llama.cpp | Build 11574, commit `8bb3cf0d2`, built separately for Vulkan and SYCL |
| Vulkan | Mesa 26.2.2 |
| SYCL | oneAPI DPC++ / oneMKL 2026.0, compute-runtime `26.31.39395.13`, Level Zero 1.32.0 |
| SYCL build | `GGML_SYCL=ON`, `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON`, JIT compilation |
| PCIe | PCIe 4.0 x4 through the X570 chipset; ReBAR enabled |

An RTX 3080 drove the display. It was excluded from inference, and the benchmark scripts checked the reported GPU on every successful test.

The GGUFs came from these Hub repositories:

| Model name used below | Hub repository | Tested file |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | [lmstudio-community/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF) | `Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf` |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | [lmstudio-community/gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-GGUF) | `gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-Q4_0.gguf` |
| Muse Glimmer | [lmstudio-community/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) | `Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf` |

Muse's repository is named 30B; the measured GGUF contains about 27.85 billion parameters, which is why the findings call it 28B. Model-file hashes are recorded in [the Phase 2 SHA-256 manifest](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/b65-phase2/raw/p2-20261013-091509/models.sha256).

## How to read the results

**Prefill** is processing the input prompt. **Decode** is generating the answer, one token at a time. Both are reported in tokens per second; higher is faster.

For llama-bench, each test used its built-in warm-up followed by **five measured repeats**. The tables show **mean ± standard deviation (SD)**. For example, `100 ± 2` means an average of 100 tokens/second with a standard deviation of 2. Smaller SD means more consistent measurements within that test; it doesn't measure variation across different machines or driver versions.

The server latency tables use **time to first token (TTFT)**, measured from requests with prompt caching disabled, with the **median of three requests** reported. Lower is faster. These are separate measurements from llama-bench throughput.

The numbered phases are different experiments. They aren't the five repeats of a benchmark cell. Dry runs are excluded from the results.

## 1. Compare the backends before changing the batch size

Phase 2 used the same model files and llama.cpp commit, with `-b 2048 -ub 512`, all layers on the GPU, and F16 KV caches. It compared three configurations: Vulkan with flash attention off, SYCL with it off, and SYCL with it on.

The full matrix was three models × three configurations × seven tests: prefill at 512, 4,096, and 16,384 tokens, plus generation of 128 tokens at context depths of 0, 4K, 16K, and 32K.

### Processing a 16K-token prompt

Tokens/second, mean ± SD across five repeats:

| Model | Vulkan, FA off | SYCL, FA off | SYCL, FA on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 388.17 ± 0.035 | 571.17 ± 0.070 | 606.15 ± 0.071 |
| Gemma | 335.29 ± 0.123 | 384.63 ± 0.020 | 397.37 ± 0.016 |
| Muse | 429.73 ± 0.139 | 508.84 ± 0.041 | 608.70 ± 0.057 |

### Generating at 32K tokens of context

Tokens/second, mean ± SD across five repeats:

| Model | Vulkan, FA off | SYCL, FA off | SYCL, FA on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 16.16 ± 0.038 | 14.11 ± 0.002 | 15.26 ± 0.012 |
| Gemma | 12.84 ± 0.084 | 9.99 ± 0.116 | 16.06 ± 0.164 |
| Muse | 14.73 ± 0.062 | 15.74 ± 0.239 | 22.29 ± 0.002 |

Across the full matrix, SYCL with flash attention on improved prefill by **31.2%** and decode by **21.8%** relative to Vulkan with flash attention off. Those are arithmetic means of the percentage change in each matched cell: nine prefill cells and twelve decode cells.

| Model | Average prefill change | Average decode change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen | +49.8% | +10.4% |
| Gemma | +9.0% | +18.6% |
| Muse | +34.9% | +36.5% |

There are exceptions worth keeping visible. **Qwen's 32K decode was 5.6% slower on SYCL.** Gemma's 512-token prefill was also slightly lower: 410.75 versus 414.48 tokens/second, a 0.9% difference.

I chose one SYCL configuration, with flash attention on, rather than selecting the fastest flash-attention setting separately for every cell.

Sources: [Phase 2 findings](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase2.md), [all 63 results, including SD and board power](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/b65-phase2/raw/p2-20261013-091509/backend_compare.csv), and [the recorded environment](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/b65-phase2/raw/p2-20261013-091509/env.txt).

## 2. Flash attention depends on the backend

On SYCL, flash attention improved decode by **18.5% on average** relative to SYCL with it disabled. Gemma at 32K went from 9.99 to 16.06 tokens/second, a 61% gain.

On the Vulkan build, it went the other way. Gemma's 16K prefill was about **38 tokens/second with flash attention on**, versus **335 with it off**.

For this software stack, my starting point is **FA on for SYCL, FA off for Vulkan**. I wouldn't carry that rule to another backend or build without measuring it.

Sources: [Phase 0.5](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase05.md) and [Phase 2](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase2.md).

## 3. A larger micro-batch improves prompt processing on SYCL

After choosing the backend, I raised the SYCL micro-batch from 512 to 2048, keeping `-b 2048`. At 16K, llama-bench prefill improved by about **35–55%**, depending on the model.

The later Phase 5 baseline confirmed these results:

| Model | SYCL FA on, ub 512 — Phase 2 | SYCL FA on, ub 2048 — Phase 5 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 606.15 ± 0.071 | 824.33 ± 0.158 |
| Gemma | 397.37 ± 0.016 | 616.92 ± 0.101 |
| Muse | 608.70 ± 0.057 | 820.67 ± 0.098 |

Tokens/second, mean ± SD, five repeats. This table compares different runs; the same-run micro-batch checks are in [Phase 4](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase4.md) and [the Gemma diagnostic](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/gemma-sycl-diag.md).

The improvement carried over to llama-server:

| Model | Vulkan, ub 512 | SYCL, ub 512 | SYCL, ub 2048 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 42.22 s | 28.89 s | 20.48 s |
| Muse | 41.65 s | 28.51 s | 20.53 s |
| Gemma | 49.36 s | 58.13 s | 30.79 s |

These are **16K-prompt TTFT medians**, three requests per cell. Vulkan used FA off; SYCL used FA on. The Gemma rows used `--ctx-checkpoints 0`, including the diagnostic's ub-2048 result. The final chat recipe keeps checkpoints at their default; that exact Gemma combination wasn't measured in this TTFT table.

The larger micro-batch added **522 MiB for Qwen** and **675 MiB for Muse** to the server's recorded VRAM use at 32K. Gemma's VRAM wasn't recorded in the ub-2048 diagnostic. Qwen and Muse server generation stayed within about 2%; Gemma's generation was 5–6% slower at 4K and 16K, in exchange for the faster prefill.

On Vulkan, a larger micro-batch wasn't consistently better: Qwen gained about 10% at 16K, while Muse lost 36%. I kept the Vulkan reference at ub 512.

Sources: [Phase 4](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase4.md), [Phase 5 baseline](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase5.md), [the server rerun](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/ubserve.md), and [the Gemma diagnostic](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/gemma-sycl-diag.md).

## 4. Test regenerate and edit before disabling checkpoints

An append-only chat test made `--ctx-checkpoints 0` look like a useful default. Every setup reused its prompt cache, and every setup answered sooner with checkpoints disabled.

Then I tested regenerating a response and editing earlier messages.

With checkpoints off, **Qwen reprocessed the entire 9,413-token chat when regenerating**, taking **11.3 seconds** to the first token. With checkpoints at their default, it reprocessed four tokens and took **0.17 seconds**.

Editing an earlier turn caused a full reread in every checkpoints-off configuration. With checkpoints on, the server could reuse the prefix before the edit.

That changed the recommendation:

| Workload | Checkpoint setting I'd use |
|---|---|
| Qwen or Muse in a chat UI | Default |
| Gemma on SYCL in a chat UI | Default |
| Gemma on SYCL in an append-only agent loop | `--ctx-checkpoints 0` |
| Gemma on Vulkan | `--ctx-checkpoints 0` |

Gemma's append-only SYCL turns took **3.24 seconds with checkpoints off**, versus **5.96 seconds with them on**. On Vulkan, Gemma had a much larger checkpoint cost: its 512-token TTFT fell from about **25.3 seconds to 1.36 seconds** when checkpoints were disabled.

Sources: [the initial server follow-up](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase1.md#gemma-llama-server-rerun-p1-swa-20261013-081841), [Phase 5 append-only chat](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase5.md), and [Phase 6 regenerate/edit tests](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase6.md).

## 5. Qwen coding improved with thinking off

The quality checks were small: ten coding tasks, ten tool-calling tasks, five notes-recall tasks, and five writing prompts.

With thinking on and a 2,048-token output cap, Qwen and Gemma each passed **9/10 coding tasks**. Both failures exhausted the budget while reasoning, before returning code. Muse passed 10/10.

In Phase 6, Qwen ran the same coding tasks with thinking disabled, a 4,096-token cap, and three attempts per task: one greedy attempt and two at temperature 0.3 with fixed seeds. It passed **10/10 greedy and 30/30 overall**, with a median answer length of **130 tokens**. The greedy pass took **73 seconds**, compared with **305 seconds** in the original test.

That supports thinking off for this Qwen coding workload. The follow-up also changed the micro-batch and token cap, so the timing isn't an isolated measurement of the thinking switch. It doesn't establish a general coding score beyond these ten tasks.

Muse ignored both thinking-off controls and returned reasoning on all 30 attempts. Its 30/30 result is **with thinking on**.

If you keep thinking enabled, leave room for it. Gemma completed its failed task in 3,326 tokens; Qwen needed up to 9,650 tokens on the same task in the budget sweep. A 4K cap wasn't enough for every Qwen attempt.

Sources: [Phase 3](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase3.md), [Phase 5's token-budget sweep](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase5.md), and [Phase 6 coding confirmation](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase6.md).

## Which model I'd use

**Muse for general use and longer conversations.** In the SYCL context-depth rerun at ub 512, decode fell from 25.69 tokens/second at empty context to 22.28 at 32K. It also finished the original quality set fastest and passed all ten coding tasks.

**Qwen with thinking off for concise coding answers.** It passed every attempt in the coding follow-up. Its long-context decode is the caveat: 15.27 tokens/second at 32K in the SYCL rerun, behind Vulkan at that depth.

**Gemma for the writing I tested.** It ranked first on three of five prompts in my blind ranking. That was one rater and five prompts, with a possible presentation-order bias recorded in the findings. It's a preference from this test, not a general writing leaderboard.

All three scored **10/10 on tool calling** and **5/5 on notes recall**, so those checks didn't separate them.

Sources: [Phase 1S context-depth results](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase1s.md), [Phase 3 quality checks](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase3.md), and [Phase 6](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase6.md).

## Power and memory

SYCL decode drew about **165–199 W of GPU board power**. Muse ran close to the card's 200 W cap. Stable repeat speeds showed no obvious decline, but I didn't independently characterize throttling.

Loaded idle was roughly **43–45 W**. These readings come from the xe driver's board-energy sensor. They don't include the rest of the PC.

At 32K context, recorded server VRAM was **18,104 MiB for Qwen** and **16,755 MiB for Muse** at ub 2048. Gemma used **20,916 MiB at ub 512**; I didn't record its ub-2048 footprint. All three loaded and ran at 32K, but these aren't three memory measurements of the complete final recipe.

Sources: [Phase 2 power](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase2.md), [Phase 1S memory](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/phase1s.md), and [the ub-2048 server rerun](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/findings/ubserve.md).
