## Reproducing the build and a throughput test

The SYCL build used the following CMake settings. Install the compiler, libraries, and Intel GPU runtime first; [llama.cpp's SYCL documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/8bb3cf0d2/docs/backend/SYCL.md) covers the prerequisites. The tested Arch package versions and local build script are in [the Phase 2 kit](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/b65-phase2/README.md).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git
cd llama.cpp
git checkout 8bb3cf0d2
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force

cmake -S . -B build-sycl -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=icx -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=icpx \
  -DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build-sycl -j --target llama-bench llama-server

export ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0
export UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=1
./build-sycl/bin/llama-bench --version
./build-sycl/bin/llama-bench --list-devices
```

After confirming that the selected device is the B65, a Phase 2-style 16K prefill measurement is:

```bash
./build-sycl/bin/llama-bench \
  -m /absolute/path/to/model.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -fa 1 -b 2048 -ub 512 \
  -p 16384 -n 0 -r 5 -o jsonl
```

Change only `-ub 512` to `-ub 2048` to check the micro-batch gain. The JSONL records the model, device, build, settings, mean, SD, and individual samples. Compare the file's SHA-256 with the manifest before treating it as the same model.

For the full backend matrix, power sampling, server requests, or quality tests, use the corresponding phase scripts and recorded environments. After updates, I use [the canary](https://github.com/snowopsdev/b65-benchmarks/blob/db9c9d25dd8b318098e36e65c391c09869123ef2/b65-phase4/README.md) to check a small set of throughput measurements against the saved baseline.

## What I'd still test

The B65 ran all three of these 30B-class Q4 models at 32K context. SYCL with FA on was the stronger starting point for this stack, and the larger micro-batch made long prompts much less painful.

The remaining questions are specific:

- Why does Qwen lose to Vulkan on decode at 32K?
- Why does Gemma have a roughly 1.1-second SYCL request floor on tiny uncached prompts?
- What does a PCIe x16 slot change? The x4 link's effect wasn't measured.
- How do newer llama.cpp builds and other engines, including vLLM, compare?
- Do the coding and writing preferences hold on larger, independently scored task sets?

If you're testing an Arc card, share the exact model file, backend, build, context depth, and batch settings with your results. I'd like to compare the cases where these recommendations hold—and the ones where they change.
# Arc Pro B65: Gemma SYCL server prefill diagnostic

Run `gd-20261013-123933`, 2026-10-13, 12:39–13:05 ET. Gemma 4 31B QAT Q4_0 only. SYCL build 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`) with flash attention on, `level_zero:0` = Arc Pro B65. Kit: `b65-gemmadiag` (Forge, with local fixes listed in its README). Package: `b65-gemmadiag-gd-20261013-123933.tar.gz`.

**The question:** in Phase 1S, llama-server prefilled Gemma at about 282 tok/s while llama-bench measured about 397 tok/s. That made Gemma's 16K time to first token 58 s on SYCL, against 49 s on Vulkan. Forge's rule: if a variant brings 16K time to first token under about 45 s, it becomes Gemma's SYCL default.

## Answer: the micro-batch size
With `-b 2048 -ub 2048` (llama-server's default micro-batch is 512), Gemma's 16K time to first token is **30.8 s**:
- **47% less** than SYCL with the default micro-batch (58.2 s)
- **1.6× faster** than Vulkan with `--ctx-checkpoints 0` (49.4 s)

That clears Forge's 45 s target, so under the rule `-ub 2048` becomes Gemma's SYCL default.

| Config (SYCL, flash attention on) | 512 TTFT | 4K TTFT | 16K TTFT | Prompt tok/s (4K / 16K) | Gen tok/s (512 / 4K / 16K) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vulkan reference (FA off, `--ctx-checkpoints 0`) | 1.36 s | 11.08 s | 49.36 s | 370 / 332 | 17.57 / 16.52 / 13.64 |
| `ckpt0` (Phase 1S config) | 2.81 s | 14.14 s | 58.17 s | 290 / 282 | 21.59 / 19.92 / 17.83 |
| `default` (checkpoints on) | 2.75 s | 14.92 s | 58.57 s | 275 / 280 | 21.55 / 19.91 / 17.82 |
| **`ckpt0_ub2048`** (`-b 2048 -ub 2048`) | **2.75 s** | **7.24 s** | **30.79 s** | **567 / 533** | 21.58 / 18.72 / 16.86 |
| `ckpt0_ctx16k` (ctx 17K) | 2.81 s | 14.12 s | 58.08 s | 291 / 282 | 21.55 / 19.88 / 17.80 |
| `ckpt0_swafull_16k` (`--swa-full`, ctx 17K) | out of VRAM at load (Level Zero `OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY`) | | | | |
| `ckpt0_fa0` (FA off, local addition) | 2.66 s | 22.01 s | 91.29 s | 186 / 180 | 19.43 / 16.10 / 10.64 |

All values are the median of 3. After the first, cold request, repeat runs agree within 0.1 s, except `default` at 4K (14.92 vs 14.63 s, a 0.28 s spread). The `ckpt0` row reproduces Phase 1S within 0.1%.

llama-bench pp16384 (SYCL, FA on):

| Micro-batch | tok/s |
|---|---|
| `-ub 512` | 397.4 (Phase 2: 397.4) |
| `-ub 2048` | **617.1 (+55%)** |

## Findings
1. **Gemma's SYCL prefill is limited by the 512-token micro-batch.**
   - Raising it to 2048 speeds up prefill by 55% in llama-bench and by 89–96% in the server (290 → 567 tok/s at 4K, 282 → 533 at 16K).
   - At ub 2048 the server is about 14% below llama-bench (533 vs 617). That's the same kind of gap Qwen and Muse show at ub 512, so the extra Gemma-specific server gap is gone.
2. **Checkpoints don't cost anything on SYCL.** The default-checkpoint server is within 6% of `--ctx-checkpoints 0` at every size: −2% / +6% / +1% at 512 / 4K / 16K (58.6 vs 58.2 s at 16K). On Vulkan they added about 100 s per prompt. The flag matters for Vulkan, not SYCL.
3. **The 32K allocation isn't the cause.** At 17K context the results are identical to 32K.
4. **Flash attention has to stay on.** With it off, Gemma's SYCL server is much slower: 91 s at 16K, with generation at 10.6 tok/s.
5. **`--swa-full` doesn't fit** even at 17K context on SYCL, as at 32K on Vulkan.
6. **The trade-off for ub 2048:**
   - Generation is 5–6% slower at depth (18.72 vs 19.92 tok/s at 4K, 16.86 vs 17.83 at 16K). The 512-token generation and time to first token are unchanged, because a 513-token prompt fits in one micro-batch either way.
   - It still fits at 32K context. VRAM wasn't recorded by this kit; the compute buffer grows with ub.
   - Board power during requests is 156–177 W, against 155–162 W.
7. **Gemma on SYCL with ub 2048 vs Vulkan with the fix:** faster to first token at 4K (7.2 vs 11.1 s) and 16K (30.8 vs 49.4 s), and faster generation at every size. Vulkan is only ahead on 512-token prompts (1.4 vs 2.8 s). With this, SYCL is faster for Gemma on everything except very short prompts.

## Implications and next steps
- **Gemma's SYCL server default:** `-fa on -b 2048 -ub 2048`. `--ctx-checkpoints 0` is optional on SYCL.
- **Qwen and Muse weren't tested at ub 2048.** If their SYCL prefill also scales (Phase 2 and 1S both used ub 512), their time to first token could improve too.
- **Phase 2's prefill comparison still stands,** because both engines used the same default ub of 512. A Vulkan ub-2048 check would show whether Vulkan gains as much.
- **Gemma's short-prompt gap** (2.8 s vs 1.4 s at 512 tokens) isn't explained by micro-batch size.

> Reviewed by Forge on 2026-10-13: every number matches the raw serve.csv and llama-bench jsonl. The rep-spread exception above (`default` at 4K) was found in a recheck afterwards.
# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 0 findings

Run `20261012-140638`, 2026-10-12, started 2:06 PM ET, finished 3:30 PM ET. Package: `b65-phase0-20261012-140638.tar.gz`.

## Setup

- **GPU:** Intel Arc Pro B65, 32 GB (BMG G31, PCI ID 8086:e222). About 29.3 GB is usable; Vulkan reports the rest as driver-reserved with nothing loaded. The RTX 3080 drives the display and was excluded (`GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`, and every test's `gpu_info` was checked for the B65).
- **Host:** Ryzen 7 5700X, 48 GB RAM (46 GiB usable), CPU governor set to performance.
- **OS:** Omarchy 4.0.4 (Arch Linux, Hyprland 0.56.2), kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy. The run's `env.txt` says `omarchy=unknown` because the script read the wrong file; that's fixed for future runs.
- **Driver:** Mesa 26.2.2 (vulkan-intel, ANV) on the xe kernel driver. Cooperative-matrix acceleration (KHR_coopmat) is available.
- **Engine:** llama.cpp `llama-bench`, build 11574 (commit 8bb3cf0d2), built from source with GCC 16.2.1, Vulkan backend.
- **Bench flags:** `-ngl 99 -fa on -r 5`. Each test gets llama-bench's warmup run plus 5 measured runs, and the **mean** is reported. For the depth tests the warmup runs before the context is filled, so the first measured run is the first decode at that depth.
- **PCIe:** 4.0 x4, in a slot wired through the X570 chipset (the card supports 5.0 x16). The GPU endpoint itself reports 2.5 GT/s x1, which is an artifact of Arc's on-card PCIe switch; the real link is read at the upstream bridge. ReBAR is on, with a 32 GB BAR.
- **Power:** GPU board power only, from the xe hwmon `card` energy counter sampled at 10 Hz, averaged over the timed runs only (not model load or warmup). Board power cap: 200 W. No wall meter.

## Models

| Model | Params (llama.cpp) | Quant | File | Size | sha256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 27.32B | Q4_K_M | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf | 16.8 GB | e00082f7…e520 |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 30.70B | Q4_0 | gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-Q4_0.gguf | 17.7 GB | 6f63619c…6a7b |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | 27.85B | Q4_K_M | Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf | 16.8 GB | 4cc57c0f…f60e |

All three are from lmstudio-community: `Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF`, `gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-GGUF` and `Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF`. LM Studio doesn't keep the Hugging Face commit locally, so the commits still need to be recorded. Full hashes are in `raw/models.sha256`.

**Naming:** Muse Glimmer's release name is 30B, but llama.cpp counts 27.85B parameters. Pick one name and use it everywhere. The share cards currently say "Muse Glimmer 30B" and the draft replies say "28B".

## Results (tokens per second, mean of 5 runs)

| Model | pp512 | pp4096 | pp16384 | tg128 | tg @4k depth | tg @16k depth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 434.2 | 358.1 | 221.1 | 19.02 | 18.75 | 17.33 |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 294.8 | 111.4 ⚠ | 38.0 ⚠ | 18.45 | 16.43 | 14.26 † |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | 522.2 | 375.0 | 274.5 | 20.93 | 15.10 | 11.23 |

All 18 tests passed, and none ran out of memory. Run-to-run variation is under 1% except for Gemma's tg @4k (1.0%) and tg @16k (4.5%).

† Gemma tg @16k: the first run was 13.12 tok/s, and the next four were 14.51–14.57. The first run was the first decode at 16K depth (see Bench flags), so the 4.5% spread comes from one cold run. The reported mean of 14.26 includes it; the median is 14.52.

## Power (GPU board, average over timed runs)

| Model | Prefill (W) | Decode (W) | Decode tokens per joule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 142–149 | 167–170 | 0.104–0.112 |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 143–152 | 164–179 | 0.087–0.103 |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | 136–156 | 130–175 | 0.086–0.119 |

Idle draw with no model loaded was 43.1 W, measured over 30 s at the start of the run.

## Findings

1. **The data is clean and publishable.** Device pinning was correct, every test passed, run-to-run variation is small, and the model hashes are recorded.
2. **Decode speed is close across models at short context (18.4 to 20.9 tok/s), but the order changes at 16K.** Qwen loses only 9% from 0 to 16K context, Gemma loses 23%, and Muse loses 46%.
3. **Gemma's prefill collapses, which is likely a software problem.** Prefill drops from 295 to 38 tok/s as the prompt grows, and the pp16384 test alone took 43.3 minutes. Over the same range Qwen and Muse roughly halve (−49% and −47%). The leading hypothesis is the Vulkan flash-attention path combined with Gemma's attention layout. That's untested, so don't publish Gemma's prefill numbers until a rerun with `-fa 0` (Gemma only) confirms or rules it out.
4. **Decode reaches about 53–58% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling.** The ceiling is approximated as 608 GB/s divided by the file size: Qwen 36.2 tok/s (19.02 measured, 53%), Gemma 34.4 (18.45, 54%), Muse 36.3 (20.93, 58%). This is typical for llama.cpp on Vulkan and gives an honest "headroom" angle. Two caveats: 608 GB/s is the published spec and hasn't been measured here, and file size only approximates the bytes read per token.
5. **Registry check (decode must be at least 15 tok/s):** Qwen passes at every depth. Gemma fails at 16K (14.3). Muse is borderline at 4K (15.1) and fails at 16K (11.2). The registry measures with its own harness, not these llama-bench numbers.
6. **PCIe 4.0 x4 through the chipset:** with every layer on the GPU, it should mainly affect model load time rather than these timed tests. Its effect wasn't measured. Mention it in the methodology section.
7. **Board power stays under the 200 W cap.** At short context decode draws more than prefill (170–179 W against 136–156 W). That reverses at long context for Muse, whose decode falls to 148 W at 4K and 130 W at 16K, along with its speed.

## Gaps and next steps

- Rerun Gemma's prefill (pp512, pp4096, pp16384) with `-fa 0` as a separate run. Optionally run all three models with `-fa 0` as a control.
- Record each model's Hugging Face commit, which the registry recipes need. The repo names are listed above.
- Optional: add prefill tok/J to `report.py`. It's left blank for prefill rows by design, since the metric was defined for decode.
- Optional: warm up at each test's depth (or drop the first run) so depth tests don't include a cold first run.
- ~~Record the Omarchy version~~: it's 4.0.4, and `run.sh` now records it.
- Phase 1: serving and time-to-first-token runs, a table of which context sizes fit, and idle power with a model loaded.
- Phase 1.5: registry recipes, blocked until @0xSero answers whether llama.cpp Vulkan counts.

## Cleared for posting

- **Cleared:** decode speed for all three models (footnote Gemma's 16K value, or give the median), Qwen's full row, the power numbers, and the methodology.
- **Hold:** all of Gemma's prefill numbers (pp512, pp4096, pp16384) until the `-fa 0` rerun. These are listed in `holds.conf`, and the share cards withhold them on the server side.

# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 0.5 findings

# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 1 findings

Run `p1-20261012-180308`, 2026-10-12, started 6:03 PM ET, finished 6:52 PM ET. Package: `b65-phase1-p1-20261012-180308.tar.gz`.

## Setup
- llama.cpp build 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`), for both llama-bench and llama-server, on Vulkan. The B65 is pinned with `GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`, and the RTX 3080 is excluded.
- Mesa 26.2.2, kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy, Omarchy 4.0.4.
- Flash attention was off for every test, per Phase 0.5.
- **llama-bench:** 5 reps per test, `tg128` at depths 0, 4K, 8K, 16K and 32K.
- **llama-server:** `-ngl 99 -fa off -c 32768 -np 1`, with everything else at its defaults, including context checkpoints (default 32 per slot). Each prompt size ran 3 times with streaming on, prompt cache off and 128 tokens generated.
- **Power:** GPU board power from xe hwmon only. There's no wall meter.

## Headlines
1. **All three models fit 32K context.** None ran out of memory. VRAM held by the loaded server process at 32K was 19,095 MiB (18.6 GiB) for Qwen, 24,244 MiB (23.7 GiB) for Gemma and 18,164 MiB (17.7 GiB) for Muse; these readings come from xe fdinfo. Gemma's server log warns that its V cache is padded to 4096 because flash attention is off, which accounts for part of the gap.
2. **Decode speed at 32K:** Qwen 16.1, Muse 14.7, Gemma 12.8 tok/s. From empty context to 32K, Qwen drops 15%, Muse 30% and Gemma 33%.
3. **Time to first token for Qwen and Muse:**
   - 512-token prompt: 1.3 s and 1.7 s.
   - 4K: 9.7 s and 11.8 s.
   - 16K: 42.2 s and 41.7 s.
4. **Idle power with a model loaded is about 45 W** for all three models. With nothing loaded it was 43.1 W, measured in Phase 0 and not re-measured here, so loading a model adds about 2 W.
5. **Server decode for Qwen and Muse runs 1–8% below llama-bench at a similar depth** (0.1–1.3 tok/s). The largest gap is Qwen at 16K: 16.33 against 17.67. Gemma's server numbers are held (see 6).
6. **Gemma's slow first token is a llama-server default, and one flag fixes it** (confirmed by the 2026-10-13 rerun below).
   - **What happens:** Gemma takes 24–25 s to first token even on a 512-token prompt, and the GPU draws only 72–93 W while it waits.
   - **What the server log shows:**
     - At 4K, the first 3,581 tokens take about 8 s (431 tok/s average). The last 516 tokens then take about 100 s, in two steps of about 50 s each: 512 tokens, then the final 4.
     - At 16K the pattern is the same. The first 15,869 tokens take 46 s (345 tok/s). The last 516 take about 100 s in the same two steps.
   - **Likely cause:** that split matches llama-server's context-checkpoint logic for sliding-window-attention models. Before saving a checkpoint, it processes the last `n_ubatch + 4` tokens separately (`tools/server/server-context.cpp`). llama-bench doesn't exercise this, and Qwen and Muse don't trigger it.
   - **Rerun result:** with `--ctx-checkpoints 0`, Gemma's time to first token is 1.36 / 11.08 / 49.36 s, in line with Qwen and Muse and with llama-bench prefill. `--swa-full` ran out of VRAM at 32K context.

## Gemma llama-server rerun (`p1-swa-20261013-081841`)

Gemma only, 2026-10-13 8:18 AM ET. Same build and server flags as the Phase 1 run (`-ngl 99 -fa off -c 32768 -np 1`) plus one change per config. Each config ran 3 reps per prompt size, and the default config was rerun in the same session as a control. Package: `b65-phase1-swa-rerun-p1-swa-20261013-081841.tar.gz`.

| Config | 512 TTFT | 4K TTFT | 16K TTFT | Prompt tok/s (512 / 4K / 16K) | Gen tok/s (512 / 4K / 16K) | Board W while serving |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 baseline (defaults) | 25.25 s | 108.30 s | 146.58 s | 20 / 38 / 112 | 17.58 / 16.52 / 13.64 | 72–93 |
| Control (defaults, same session) | 25.29 s | 108.49 s | 146.75 s | 20 / 38 / 112 | 17.57 / 16.52 / 13.63 | 71–92 |
| `--ctx-checkpoints 0` | **1.36 s** | **11.08 s** | **49.36 s** | 377 / 370 / 332 | 17.57 / 16.52 / 13.64 | 155–167 |
| `--swa-full` | out of VRAM at 32K (a 1 GiB KV-cache allocation failed) | | | | | |

- **The penalty reproduces exactly.** The same-session control is within 0.2% of the Phase 1 baseline at every size.
- **Turning checkpoints off removes it:** first token arrives 18.6× faster at 512 tokens, 9.8× at 4K and 3.0× at 16K. The GPU now draws 155–167 W during requests, like the other models, instead of 70–90 W.
- **The server now matches llama-bench.** Prompt speed (377 / 370 / 332 tok/s) is within 9% of Phase 0.5 llama-bench prefill with flash attention off (413 / 379 / 335). Generation speed is unchanged, so the checkpoints only cost prompt time.
- **Trade-off (not measured):** checkpoints exist so llama-server can reuse a sliding-window model's cached conversation when the next request only partly matches the previous one, as chat turns usually do. Without them, each new turn may reprocess the whole conversation. This test ran with prompt caching off, so it doesn't measure that cost. Before recommending the flag broadly, run a multi-turn test with caching on, comparing checkpoints on and off.
- **`--swa-full` isn't an option at 32K** on this card with flash attention off. It might fit at a smaller context, but that wasn't tested; the rule is not to retry an OOM with lower settings.
- **Loaded idle:** 42.8 W (checkpoints off) and 44.8 W (control). VRAM was 24,244 MiB in both, identical to Phase 1, so checkpoints don't change resident VRAM at idle. The 2 W spread is within measurement noise; Phase 0 measured 43.1 W with nothing loaded.
- **Gemma server generation is still below llama-bench at depth:** 13.64 against 16.00 tok/s at 16K (−15%), with checkpoints on or off. Qwen is −8% and Muse −3% there. That's unexplained, but small next to the prompt-time fix.

## Registry check (decode must be at least 15 tok/s)
With flash attention off, all three models pass at 16K context (Qwen 17.7, Muse 16.8, Gemma 16.0). At 32K only Qwen passes (16.1). Muse (14.7) and Gemma (12.8) fall below the line. The registry's recall test runs at 85% of context, so whether these models pass depends on the context size each recipe declares.

## Open questions
- **Muse's server prompt speed** (prompt tokens divided by time to first token) is well below llama-bench prefill from Phase 0.5: 301 vs 540 tok/s at 512, 348 vs 483 at 4K, and 394 vs 430 at 16K. At 512 tokens, per-request overhead is part of it. The 28% gap at 4K is unexplained. Qwen's server speed is within 13% of llama-bench at every size.

## Corrections to the draft
- VRAM figures were MiB read as GB (for example 19,095 MiB is 18.6 GiB, not 19.1 GB).
- Gemma's stall is about 100 s per prompt at 4K and 16K (two ~50 s steps), not about 50 s.
- "Server decode within about 1 tok/s of llama-bench" holds for Muse, but not for Qwen at 16K (1.34 tok/s) or for Gemma (up to 2.36 tok/s).
- `--ctx-checkpoints` does exist in build 11574 (default 32).
# Arc Pro B65: Phase 1.5 findings (registry recipes)

Runs on 2026-10-14. All three models pass the six lab gates of [local-ai-registry](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry), both on our native SYCL build and in the pinned official image, and at 64K and 128K too: nine B65 recipes, in [PR #260](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/pull/260) with the card; the hardware photo is its own [PR #264](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/pull/264) (one change per PR).

- **Unblocked by the registry itself:** Phase 1.5 waited on @0xSero about llama.cpp recipes. The registry merged a llama.cpp SYCL recipe for the Arc B390 on 2026-10-10 (`a8e64af`), so llama.cpp counts.
- **Not the recipe kit's own target:** the kit's first target (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, experts in RAM) needs 68 GB free RAM and an NVMe table; this machine has 48 GB.
- **Kit:** `b65-phase15/` (see its README). Registry clone `~/src/ext/local-ai-registry-20261014`: branch `b65-arc-pro-recipes` (`9125d90` card + 32K, `3c20070` 64K/128K, rebased on upstream `c1ef238`) for PR #260 and `b65-arc-pro-photo` (`b92bf2c`) for PR #264, both pushed to the `snowopsdev` fork. `b65-pr260-backup` keeps the earlier combined branch.

## The gates
load · chat · reasoning (thinking returned separately, 17 × 23 = 391) · tools (calls `get_weather` for Paris, then uses the result) · context (finds a code planted at 85% of the window) · speed (decode ≥ 15 tok/s over the first 30 s of an uncapped answer, empty context, one user).

## Setup
- **Card:** ASRock Arc Pro B65 Creator 32 GB; Ryzen 7 5700X, PCIe 4.0 x4.
- **Settings (both runs):** 32K context, flash attention on, `-b 2048 -ub 2048`, all layers on the GPU, one slot, `--jinja`, thinking on (the reasoning gate needs it).
- **Weights:** lmstudio-community GGUFs, pinned to the commits whose files match ours byte for byte: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF `5a7da681`, gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-GGUF `12e5eae7`, Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF `c34cb737`.
- **Pre-check** (`p15pre-20261014-131018`): the registry's `gates()` unmodified, against native llama.cpp b11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`).
- **Registry run** (`p15reg-20261014-141612`): `lab.py try --on endpoint` against the official `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp` server-intel image, b11515, digest `86b37d26…` (the B390 recipe's image), started like the registry SDK does (`--device /dev/dri`), published on 127.0.0.1 only. Docker 29.7.2.

## Results
| Model | Run | Gates | Decode (tok/s) | Context prompt | Context request | Speed answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_M | native b11574 | 6/6 | 23.8 | 25,782 tokens | 41.6 s | 16,177 tokens, 770 s |
| | image b11515 | **6/6** | **23.6** | 25,782 | 36.0 s | 11,564 tokens, 545 s |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT Q4_0 | native b11574 | 6/6 | 21.8 | 25,746 | 58.0 s | 1,214 tokens, 60 s |
| | image b11515 | **6/6** | **21.4** | 25,746 | 66.9 s | 1,307 tokens, 66 s |
| Muse Glimmer 28B Q4_K_M | native b11574 | 6/6 | 25.4 | 21,127 | 161.7 s | 3,973 tokens, 160 s |
| | image b11515 | **6/6** | **25.2** | 21,127 | 42.0 s | 1,188 tokens, 48 s |

1. **Every model clears the 15 tok/s line by a wide margin** (21.4–25.2 tok/s in the image), and the image decodes within 2% of our native build.
2. **The registry's "prefill" is not prefill speed.** It divides the context prompt by the whole request time, thinking included: the recipes say Qwen 716, Muse 503, Gemma 385 tok/s, but the same Muse prompt gave 131 in the pre-check because it thought for longer before answering. For real prefill numbers use Phase 4+ ([ubserve.md](ubserve.md)).
3. **The speed gate's uncapped answer is long for Qwen:** 11.6–16.2K tokens (9–13 min) for "a detailed 600-word story". Only the first 30 s count, so it doesn't change the result; it does make Qwen's run the slowest.

## Longer contexts (`p15reg-20261014-154648`)
Same image, flags and weights; only `--ctx-size` changes (launch ids `…-64k-…`/`…-128k-…`). All six pass; the whole run took 53 min.

| Model | Context | Gates | Decode (tok/s) | Context prompt | Context request | Registry "prefill" | Speed answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

1. **Decode doesn't change with the window** (the speed gate runs on an empty context): 23.6 / 21.4 / 25.1–25.3 tok/s at 32K, 64K and 128K.

4. The 64K Muse "prefill" (204) is again thinking time: the request took longer at 64K than at 128K.
5. With these in the catalog, the B65's picks become Qwen 128K, Gemma 128K, Muse 64K. `make check` passes (SDKs agree on 317 recipes).

# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 1S findings (Phase 1 rerun on SYCL, flash attention on)

Run `p1s-20261013-111949`, 2026-10-13, 11:19–11:50 AM ET. Package: `b65-phase1s-p1s-20261013-111949.tar.gz`.
- **Results:** all 15 decode tests ok, no out-of-memory results. All three servers started at 32K context, and all 27 requests completed.
- **Stop rules:** none triggered.
- **Throttling:** none. Decode reps are flat, including Muse at 190–198 W.

## Setup
- **Engine:** llama.cpp `8bb3cf0d2` (build 11574), SYCL build from Phase 2 (oneAPI 2026.0, compute-runtime 26.31, JIT, F16), on `level_zero:0` = Arc Pro B65.
- **llama-bench:** `-fa 1`, 5 reps.
- **llama-server:** `-fa on -c 32768 -np 1`, prompt cache off, 3 reps per prompt size. Gemma ran with `--ctx-checkpoints 0`.
- **Power:** GPU board power from xe hwmon only, averaged over the timed reps.
- **Comparison baselines:**
  - Phase 1 on Vulkan with flash attention off (`p1-20261012-180308`).
  - For Gemma's server numbers, the Vulkan rerun with the same `--ctx-checkpoints 0` flag (`p1-swa-20261013-081841`).

## Results
### Decode tok/s by context depth (SYCL, flash attention on), change vs Phase 1 Vulkan

| Model | @0 | @4K | @8K | @16K | @32K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 23.67 (+24%) | 22.22 (+18%) | 20.80 (+13%) | 18.63 (+5%) | 15.27 (**−5%**) |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 22.45 (+17%) | 20.42 (+17%) | 19.77 (+17%) | 18.28 (+14%) | 16.07 (+25%) |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 25.69 (+23%) | 24.64 (+32%) | 24.32 (+35%) | 23.56 (+40%) | 22.28 (+51%) |

The values match Phase 2's SYCL flash-attention-on results within 0.2% on all 12 shared tests.

### Time to first token, llama-server (median of 3), Vulkan → SYCL

| Model | 512 tokens | 4K | 16K |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 1.31 → **0.96 s** (1.4× faster) | 9.70 → **6.94 s** (1.4×) | 42.22 → **28.89 s** (1.5×) |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 1.71 → **0.87 s** (2.0×) | 11.78 → **6.78 s** (1.7×) | 41.65 → **28.51 s** (1.5×) |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT (both with `--ctx-checkpoints 0`) | 1.36 → **2.81 s** (2.1× slower) | 11.08 → **14.13 s** (1.3× slower) | 49.36 → **58.13 s** (1.2× slower) |

### Loaded idle (30 s) and VRAM at 32K context

| Model | Board W | VRAM, SYCL | VRAM, Vulkan (Phase 1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 44.9 | 17,582 MiB | 19,095 MiB |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 44.9 | 20,916 MiB | 24,244 MiB |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 44.9 | 16,080 MiB | 18,164 MiB |

## Findings
1. **Everything fits at 32K context with room to spare.** VRAM held at 32K is 8–14% lower than on Vulkan: −1.5 GiB for Qwen, −3.3 GiB for Gemma, −2.0 GiB for Muse. The likeliest reason for Gemma's large drop is that the padded V cache Vulkan needed without flash attention is gone; that hasn't been checked in the logs.
2. **Decode gains hold up the way Phase 2 predicted.** Gains with context:
   - Muse gains more as context grows (+23% to +51%), and its 0-to-32K falloff is only −13%.
   - Gemma gains 14–25% at every depth.
   - Qwen's gain shrinks with context and turns negative at 32K: −5%, 15.27 vs 16.14 tok/s.

   Every model now decodes above 15 tok/s at 32K; Qwen is the closest, at 15.27.
3. **First word is 1.4–2.0× faster for Qwen and Muse:** under 1 s on a 512-token prompt, about 7 s at 4K and about 29 s at 16K.
4. **Gemma's first word is slower on SYCL than on Vulkan with the same checkpoint fix:** 2.8 / 14.1 / 58.1 s against 1.4 / 11.1 / 49.4 s.
   - Its server prompt speed is 182–290 tok/s, well below what llama-bench measures for Gemma on SYCL with flash attention on (397–414 tok/s).
   - On Vulkan the server matched llama-bench (370 vs 379 at 4K), so this gap is new on SYCL.
   - It's still far better than Gemma with default checkpoints (25 / 108 / 147 s).
   - The cause is unexplained; the server log shows steady processing, not the checkpoint stall.
5. **Server generation now matches llama-bench:** within 1–4% at the same depth for all three, against up to 15% below on Vulkan. Server prompt speed for Qwen and Muse is 5–16% below llama-bench prefill, about as on Vulkan.
6. **Idle with a model loaded is 44.9 W for all three,** the same as on Vulkan.
7. **Power:**
   - Decode draws 165–198 W.
   - Muse sits closest to the 200 W cap (190–198 W), but its reps don't decline, so there's no sign of throttling.
   - Server requests draw 156–195 W.

## Open
- **Gemma's server prompt speed on SYCL:** 29–56% below llama-bench. That's the opposite of Vulkan, where it matched once checkpoints were off. Possible next steps:
  - Try a larger `-ub`/`-b` on the server, to match llama-bench's batch settings.
  - Try Gemma on SYCL with flash attention off for the server only.
- **Qwen's 32K decode regression on SYCL (−5%)** is still open from Phase 2.
- **Multi-turn cache test with checkpoints off** is still open. So is the optional `GEMMA_CKPT=32` control, which wasn't run.

## Kit notes
`b65-phase1s/README.md` covers this. In short, `phase1s.sh` was built from the fixed Phase 1 script, because Forge's copy still had several Phase 1 bugs:
- `bc`, which isn't installed.
- The AMD VRAM path.
- An unlabelled energy channel.
- Invocation-average power.
- A device check on the first test only.

## Posting status
- **Cleared:** everything.
- **When posting Gemma's time to first token:** compare it with the Vulkan checkpoints-off numbers, not Phase 1's default-checkpoint numbers. The share cards already do this.

## Review of Forge's Phase 1S findings (2026-10-13)
These are checked against the run data. The tables, the time-to-first-token and decode numbers, and Gemma's server decode gap closing (17.83 vs 18.28 tok/s at 16K, against 13.6 vs 16.0 on Vulkan) are all correct. Corrections:
- **"Qwen and Muse are faster on every number that users notice."** Qwen's decode at 32K is 5% slower (15.27 vs 16.14), which the next line of Forge's own headline says.
- **"Vulkan's roughly 142–182 W" for decode.** Vulkan decode in Phase 1 drew 166–182 W. 142 W was a Phase 0 prefill number. SYCL decode draws 165–198 W.
- **"Gemma's VRAM fell to about 20.9 GB, from 24.2 GB."** Those are MiB figures read as GB. The values are 20,916 MiB (20.4 GiB), down from 24,244 MiB (23.7 GiB).
- **"Specific to Gemma in the server (sliding-window attention or checkpoint handling), not the backend."** The gap needs all three: Gemma, llama-server and SYCL. On Vulkan with the same flag, Gemma's server prefill matched llama-bench (370 vs 379 tok/s at 4K). Checkpoint handling is unlikely, since checkpoints were off (`--ctx-checkpoints 0`); the log shows steady prompt processing.

Additions:
- **Gemma, SYCL vs Vulkan (both with `--ctx-checkpoints 0`):** SYCL starts later but generates faster (21.6 / 19.9 / 17.8 tok/s against 17.6 / 16.5 / 13.6). It finishes a whole response sooner once the answer is longer than about 140 tokens on a 512-token prompt, about 300 tokens at 4K, and about 510 tokens at 16K. That's the measured version of Forge's "long output vs long prompt" recommendation.
- **Next diagnostic:** Forge's plan is to run Gemma's SYCL server at 16K three ways: checkpoints 0, default checkpoints, and `-ub 2048`. A fourth variant, the server with flash attention off for Gemma only, would show whether the SYCL flash-attention path causes the gap.
# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 2 findings (Vulkan vs SYCL)

Run `p2-20261013-091509`, 2026-10-13, 9:15–10:53 AM ET. All 63 tests ok, no out-of-memory results. Package: `b65-phase2-p2-20261013-091509.tar.gz`.

## Setup
- **Engines:** the same llama.cpp commit `8bb3cf0d2` (build 11574) built two ways:
  - Vulkan: the existing build, Mesa 26.2.2.
  - SYCL: a new build, oneAPI DPC++ 2026.0.0, oneMKL SYCL 2026.0.0, intel-compute-runtime 26.31.39395.13, level-zero-loader 1.32.0, IGC 2.40.13. JIT only, no AOT.
- **Packages:** Arch no longer ships `intel-oneapi-basekit`, so the equivalent split packages were installed. They're listed in `b65-phase2/packages.txt`.
- **Device:** the SYCL device is `level_zero:0`, "Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B65 Graphics". Every result's `gpu_info` names the B65; the RTX 3080 isn't a Level Zero device.
- **Kernel and OS:** 7.2.5-3-omarchy, Omarchy 4.0.4.
- **Tests:** llama-bench, 5 reps each:
  - pp512, pp4096, pp16384
  - tg128 at depth 0, 4K, 16K and 32K
- **Configurations:**
  - Vulkan with flash attention off (the Phase 0.5 setting).
  - SYCL with flash attention off, and with it on.
- **Power:** GPU board power from xe hwmon only, averaged over the timed reps. No wall meter. The board power cap is 200 W.

## Headline
**SYCL with flash attention on is 21.8% faster than Vulkan on decode and 31.2% faster on prefill, averaged over all three models.** That clears the plan's +10% decode rule.

**Decision (Forge, 2026-10-13):** SYCL with flash attention on is the default engine. Per the plan, Phase 1 is rerun on SYCL with flash attention on.

| SYCL setting vs Vulkan (FA off) | Decode, mean of 12 | Prefill, mean of 9 |
|---|---|---|
| **SYCL, FA on** | **+21.8%** (−5.6% to +51.3%) | **+31.2%** (−0.9% to +56.2%) |
| SYCL, FA off | +4.4% (−22.2% to +24.2%) | +27.5% (+10.5% to +48.9%) |

Per model, SYCL with FA on vs Vulkan:

| Model | Decode | Prefill |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | +10.4% | +49.8% |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | +18.6% | +9.0% |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | +36.5% | +34.9% |

## Results (tok/s, mean of 5)

| Model | Test | Vulkan FA off | SYCL FA off | SYCL FA on | Best SYCL vs Vulkan |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | pp512 | 445.55 | **663.55** | 639.96 | +49% |
| | pp4096 | 431.84 | 635.10 | **645.52** | +49% |
| | pp16384 | 388.17 | 571.17 | **606.15** | +56% |
| | tg128 | 19.08 | **23.69** | 23.68 | +24% |
| | tg128 @4K | 18.84 | 21.87 | **22.22** | +18% |
| | tg128 @16K | 17.69 | 17.79 | **18.63** | +5% |
| | tg128 @32K | **16.16** | 14.11 | 15.26 | −6% |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | pp512 | 414.48 | **468.64** | 410.75 | +13% |
| | pp4096 | 378.54 | **418.36** | 414.44 | +11% |
| | pp16384 | 335.29 | 384.63 | **397.37** | +19% |
| | tg128 | 19.16 | 22.18 | **22.45** | +17% |
| | tg128 @4K | 17.39 | 17.09 | **20.46** | +18% |
| | tg128 @16K | 16.00 | 13.37 | **18.29** | +14% |
| | tg128 @32K | 12.84 | 9.99 | **16.06** | +25% |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | pp512 | 539.92 | 688.19 | **691.22** | +28% |
| | pp4096 | 483.03 | 580.08 | **651.98** | +35% |
| | pp16384 | 429.73 | 508.84 | **608.70** | +42% |
| | tg128 | 20.94 | 25.15 | **25.66** | +23% |
| | tg128 @4K | 18.71 | 21.07 | **24.64** | +32% |
| | tg128 @16K | 16.79 | 18.41 | **23.56** | +40% |
| | tg128 @32K | 14.73 | 15.74 | **22.29** | +51% |

The "Best SYCL" column takes whichever SYCL setting is faster on each test. Against the chosen default alone (SYCL with flash attention on), prefill is lower in three places:
- Gemma pp512: −0.9%, a tie, not +13%.
- Gemma pp4096: +9.5%, not +11%.
- Qwen pp512: +44%, not +49%.

Decode is the same either way, except that Qwen at 32K is −5.6% with flash attention on and −12.7% with it off. From here on, the share cards compare SYCL with flash attention on against Vulkan.

Board W per cell is in `phase2_summary.md` and `backend_compare.csv`.

## Findings
1. **SYCL is the faster engine on this card,** as long as flash attention is on.
   - Decode at 0 context goes from 19.1–20.9 tok/s on Vulkan to 22.4–25.7 on SYCL.
   - At 32K context it goes from 12.8–16.2 to 15.3–22.3.
   - Muse gains the most (+51% at 32K).
2. **Flash attention flips between engines.**
   - On Vulkan it hurt everywhere (Phase 0.5).
   - On SYCL it helps decode by 18.5% on average, and more as context grows: Gemma +61% and Muse +42% at 32K, Qwen +8%.
   - On SYCL it barely changes prefill (+3%).
   - SYCL with flash attention off is slower than Vulkan for Gemma decode at depth (−22% at 32K), so the setting matters.
3. **There's one exception: Qwen at 32K.** SYCL is 5.6% slower than Vulkan there with flash attention on (15.26 vs 16.16), and 12.7% slower with it off. Qwen's decode advantage shrinks with depth: +24%, +18%, +5%, −6%.
   - At 16K Qwen is only +5.3%, so SYCL clears +10% at 0 and 4K context for every model, but not at 16K for Qwen.
   - Qwen's average decode gain, +10.4%, only just clears the bar.
   - **The order of falloff with context changes.** From 0 to 32K tokens of context:
     - Qwen: −15% on Vulkan, −36% on SYCL. It falls off fastest on SYCL.
     - Gemma: −33% on Vulkan, −28.5% on SYCL.
     - Muse: −30% on Vulkan, −13% on SYCL. Its falloff is gentlest on SYCL.
4. **Gemma passes the registry's 15 tok/s line at 32K on SYCL:** 16.06 tok/s, against 12.84 on Vulkan. Its falloff with context is still steep (−28.5%); the gain comes from a faster start, not a flatter curve.
5. **Decode is closer to the bandwidth ceiling.** SYCL decode at 0 context reaches about 400–430 GB/s of the published 608 GB/s (65–71%), compared with Vulkan's 53–58% in Phase 0. This uses the same approximation as Phase 0: tok/s × file size.
6. **SYCL is more efficient, and it doesn't always draw more power.**
   - Decode tokens per joule average 0.115 on SYCL with flash attention on, against 0.100 on Vulkan (+15%). Decode at 0 context improves for all three:
     - Qwen: 0.112 to 0.122
     - Gemma: 0.105 to 0.128
     - Muse: 0.119 to 0.129
   - Power with SYCL and flash attention on, compared with Vulkan:
     - Prefill: 13–33 W more for every model.
     - Qwen and Muse decode: 18–26 W more, except Qwen at 16K (+3 W) and at 32K (−11 W).
     - **Gemma decode: 4–12 W less.**
   - Overall, decode board power is 165–199 W on SYCL and 165–182 W on Vulkan.
   - Muse's SYCL decode at 0 context averaged 199.4 W against the 200 W cap, so it may be power-limited there. Throttling wasn't measured.
   - Prefill is 3.14 tok/J on SYCL with flash attention on, against 2.78 on Vulkan.
7. **The Vulkan numbers are stable.** Vulkan with flash attention off reproduces the Phase 0.5 and Phase 1 values within 0.4% on all 21 tests, so the differences come from the engine, not drift. The largest run-to-run spread is 2.1% (Muse, SYCL with flash attention off, tg @4K); everything else is under 2%.

## Checks
- **Output isn't gibberish.** Each model wrote the same 120-token answer at temperature 0 on SYCL and on Vulkan, in llama-server:
  - Qwen, SYCL flash attention off (`raw/p2-spot-20261013-091431`): output identical to Vulkan.
  - Gemma and Muse, SYCL flash attention on (`raw/p2-spot-20261013-105352`): Muse identical; Gemma coherent and the same until a small wording difference. That difference is expected, because flash attention on vs off changes the arithmetic order.
  - Qwen, SYCL flash attention on (the chosen default; `raw/p2-spot-20261013-110712`): identical to Vulkan as well. All three models are now checked on the default setting.
  - SYCL speed in these runs matched llama-bench: Qwen 23.9, Gemma 22.4, Muse 25.9 tok/s.
- **The speeds aren't absurd.** SYCL draws more power than Vulkan, not near zero.
- **Dry run:** `raw/p2-dry-20261013-091018`. Its `env.txt` recorded a device-table header instead of the SYCL version; that's fixed for the full run.

## Step 0 (Gemma llama-server)
This was answered before Phase 2 by `b65-phase1/raw/p1-swa-20261013-081841`.
- **The fix is `--ctx-checkpoints 0`:** Gemma's 512-token time to first token drops from 25.3 s to 1.36 s.
- **`--swa-full` runs out of VRAM at 32K.**
- Details are in `phase1.md`.

## Findings
1. **There's no single best model.** Muse leads on coding and speed, while Gemma leads on writing (blind). All three tie on tool calling and notes recall.
2. **All three models are strong on these tasks.**
   - All three got every tool call right, including the two prompts that should make no call.
   - All three got every notes-recall question right, with specific answers ("43.1 W", "`--ctx-checkpoints 0`", "Qwen 3.8 27B regressed at 32K").
3. **The only coding failure is the same task for two models,** c08: extract `<link rel="canonical">` with the standard library. Qwen and Gemma both used the whole 2,048-token budget thinking (8,568 and 7,692 characters of reasoning) and never wrote code. Muse thought for 2,861 characters and passed. The failures are about thinking length under the cap, not wrong code.
4. **Side check** (`raw/p3-c08check-20261013-142822`, not part of the score): c08 was re-asked alone with an 8,192-token cap.
   - **Gemma:** finished in 3,326 tokens, and its `HTMLParser` solution passes. It just needed more room.
   - **Qwen:** still hadn't answered after 8,192 tokens (372 s). Its reasoning kept listing possible hidden tests with ever more exotic Unicode spaces (`\u2008`, `\u2009`, …). No text repeats verbatim, but it's going round in circles. That's close to the handoff's "loops" stop rule, so it's flagged here rather than treated as an ordinary fail.
5. **Muse is the quickest and the most token-efficient:** 8 min for all 30 tasks and the fewest completion tokens, despite also thinking (about 37K reasoning characters overall). Qwen and Gemma spend most of their extra time on coding (305 s and 401 s, against Muse's 187 s), and c08 alone took 89 s and 100 s.
6. **All three are thinking models in this setup:** each returned separate reasoning, 36K–40K characters across the 30 tasks. Compare total time with that in mind, as the handoff notes.

## Checks
- Apart from the two c08 cases, every reply finished normally: `stop`, or `tool_calls` for tool prompts. No writing reply hit its token cap.
- The device precheck confirmed `level_zero:0` = Arc Pro B65. The run had no errors.

# Arc Pro B65 benchmark: Phase 4 findings (canary and micro-batch check)

> **Decision (Forge, 2026-10-13, after checking every number against canary.csv):**

First canary `p4-20261013-150339`, 2026-10-13, 3:03–3:41 PM ET, run with `UBCHECK=1 B65_VK_INDEX=1` and the default models (Qwen and Muse). All 20 tests ok. Package: `b65-phase4-p4-20261013-150339.tar.gz`.

- **Versions:** the same as the Phase 2 baseline. Kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy, Mesa 26.2.2, oneAPI DPC++ 2026.0, compute-runtime 26.31.39395.13, Level Zero 1.32.0, llama.cpp 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`). Nothing has been updated, so this run is also a reproducibility check.
- **Method:** llama-bench, 5 reps, `-b 2048`. Board W is averaged over the timed reps, the same method as the baseline.

## Canary: drift vs the Phase 2 baseline (SYCL, flash attention on, ub 512)

| Model | Test | Baseline | Now | Drift | Board W |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**0 flagged.** Every test is within 0.1% of the baseline, which sets the noise floor the 5% bar has to clear.

## Micro-batch check (ub 512 vs 2048)

| Model | Backend | pp4096 | pp16384 | tg128 @16K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | SYCL, FA on | 645.5 → 890.7 (**+38%**) | 605.9 → 824.2 (**+36%**) | 18.64 → 18.86 (+1.2%) |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | SYCL, FA on | 652.1 → 906.8 (**+39%**) | 608.7 → 820.7 (**+35%**) | 23.56 → 23.44 (−0.5%) |
| Qwen 3.8 27B | Vulkan, FA off | | 388.2 → 428.7 (+10%) | |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | Vulkan, FA off | | 429.8 → 274.0 (**−36%**) | |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT (Gemma diagnostic) | SYCL, FA on | | 397.4 → 617.1 (+55%) | server decode −5% |

## Findings
1. **Nothing has drifted.** With unchanged versions, the canary reproduces Phase 2 within 0.1% on all 8 tests, so future flags will mean something.
2. **`-ub 2048` speeds up SYCL prefill for every model:** Qwen +36%, Muse +35% at 16K (Gemma +55%). Decode is unchanged (+1.2% and −0.5%). Both clear the handoff's rule (more than +10% prefill, no more than 5% decode cost), so under that rule **ub 2048 becomes the SYCL default for all three models**.
   - Board power is 10–12 W higher during prefill at ub 2048 (about 195 W against 184 W), and prefill tokens per joule still improve by 27–29%.
3. **On Vulkan, the micro-batch effect depends on the model.** Qwen gains 10%; Muse loses 36% (430 → 274 tok/s), with board power falling to 122 W. A recheck in a fresh process (`raw/p4-recheck-20261013-154203`, same model file) reproduced it: 272.0 vs 429.7 tok/s, five reps each within 1 tok/s. It's a Vulkan-path behaviour for Muse at that batch size, not noise. Keep Vulkan at the default ub 512.
4. **SYCL's prefill lead over Vulkan grows with ub 2048.** At 16K, each engine at its best setting: Qwen 824 vs 429 tok/s (1.9×, both at ub 2048) and Muse 821 vs 430 (1.9×, Vulkan at ub 512).

## Notes on this run
- **The summary was finalized by hand.** I edited `canary.sh` (adding a `vk_index` line to `env.txt`) while the run was going. Bash reads scripts incrementally, so the edit broke the script's last lines after all 20 tests had completed. `canary_summary.md` and `done` were then written by running `compare4.py` and touching `done` by hand (`NOTE-finalized-by-hand.txt`). No measurement was affected. Lesson: never edit a kit script while a run is using it.
- **`compare4.py` fix:** tests without a baseline, such as pp4096 from the micro-batch check, were listed as "+0.0% ok" in the drift table. They're now left out of it and appear only in the micro-batch table.

## Next
- **Decided:** ub 2048 is the SYCL default for all three; the canary and `baseline.json` stay at ub 512. Qwen and Muse server time to first token at ub 2048 hasn't been measured yet; llama-bench predicts about 35% faster prefill.
- **The Muse Vulkan ub 2048 drop** is a candidate llama.cpp Vulkan issue, if Vulkan stays relevant.
- **Routine:** run `./canary.sh` (about 10 minutes) after any Mesa, kernel, oneAPI, llama.cpp or LM Studio update.

- **Versions:** unchanged since Phase 2. Kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy, Mesa 26.2.2, oneAPI DPC++ 2026.0, compute-runtime 26.31.39395.13, llama.cpp 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`).

- **Kit:** Forge's, with the local fixes listed in `b65-phase5/README.md`.

Comparing its ub 2048 rows to the new file needs a small `compare4.py` change, which is left for Forge's next kit.

## B. Gemma on short prompts: time to first token

Gemma 4 31B on llama-server, `--ctx-checkpoints 0`. Median of 5. "Cold" means the cache was off; "warm" means the identical prompt was sent again.

| Prompt | SYCL ub 512 | SYCL ub 2048 | SYCL ub 2048 `--no-warmup` | Vulkan ub 512 (FA off) | SYCL minus Vulkan |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 tokens | 1.09 s | 1.09 s | 1.09 s | 0.72 s | +0.37 s |
| 64 | 1.13 s | 1.13 s | 1.13 s | 0.54 s | +0.60 s |
| 256 | 1.38 s | 1.38 s | 1.38 s | 1.08 s | +0.30 s |
| 1,024 | 3.79 s | **2.46 s** | 2.46 s | 2.65 s | −0.19 s |
| 4,096 | 14.54 s | **7.72 s** | 7.72 s | 11.05 s | −3.34 s |

1. **SYCL has a floor of about 1.1 s per request for Gemma, even for 16 tokens.** Vulkan answers tiny prompts 0.3–0.6 s sooner.
   - From 1,024 tokens up, SYCL at ub 2048 is faster, and at 4,096 tokens it's 3.3 s faster.
   - Under Forge's reading rule this is a per-request overhead, so the note is "Vulkan for tiny Gemma prompts". In practice the gap is under 0.6 s.
2. **Neither micro-batch size nor warm-up is the cause.**
   - ub 512, ub 2048 and `--no-warmup` give the same time, to the millisecond, up to 256 tokens. A prompt that small fits in one micro-batch either way.
   - ub 2048 only helps from 1,024 tokens up: 3.79 → 2.46 s, and 14.5 → 7.7 s at 4,096.
3. **Only the first request after a server starts is slower:** about 1.52 s at 16 tokens on all three SYCL configs (`--no-warmup` included), then 1.09 s from the second request on. The medians include that first request; with 5 reps it doesn't move the median.
4. **Warm cache (identical prompt resent):**
   - **SYCL:** it reuses the cache at every size (0.11–0.65 s; only 1–5 tokens reprocessed).
   - **Vulkan (`--ctx-checkpoints 0`):** it reprocesses the whole prompt at 16–1,024 tokens (warm = cold), and only reuses the cache at 4,096 tokens (0.07 s). The kit doesn't show why.

## C. Multi-turn chat: cache reuse and context checkpoints

An 8-turn chat adds about 1.5K tokens per turn, reaching about 12.5K tokens. The table gives the median time to first token for turns 2–8.
- **SYCL:** ub 2048, flash attention on.
- **Vulkan:** ub 512, flash attention off.
- SYCL vs Vulkan isn't a same-micro-batch comparison here; checkpoints on vs off is.

| Model | Engine | Checkpoints on (default) | Checkpoints off (`--ctx-checkpoints 0`) | Tokens reprocessed per turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | SYCL | 2.38 s | **2.00 s** | 1,533 both |
| | Vulkan | 4.34 s | **3.92 s** | 1,533 both |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | SYCL | 5.96 s (5.3–10.3) | **3.24 s** | ~1,570 both |
| | Vulkan | **124.4 s** | **5.48 s** | ~1,566 both |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | SYCL | 2.90 s | **2.37 s** | ~1,620; off: 3,178 once at turn 2 |
| | Vulkan | 7.75 s | **4.48 s** | ~1,620; off: 3,178 once at turn 2 |

1. **Every setup reuses its cache.** After turn 2, each turn reprocesses only the new turn (about 1.5–1.6K tokens), with checkpoints on or off, on both engines. Under Forge's reading rule ("both configs reprocess about 1.5K per turn"), **the setting doesn't matter for cache reuse on SYCL**, and "turn checkpoints off and you lose the cache" can be dropped from the docs.
2. **Muse with checkpoints off has one exception:** at turn 2 it reprocesses the whole chat once (3,178 tokens, on both engines), then reuses the cache for turns 3–8.
3. **Checkpoints off was faster in all 6 model and engine pairs,** by 0.4 s (Qwen) to 2.7 s (Gemma on SYCL) per turn. Gemma on Vulkan is the outlier:
   - With checkpoints on, every turn took 124–127 s (turn 1: 98 s), against 4.8–5.8 s with them off.
   - Each turn processed only the ~1,566 new tokens, so the time isn't spent re-reading the chat.
   - This is the same order of cost as the Phase 1 finding (about 25 s at 512 tokens, about 100 s per prompt in the rerun).
4. **Decode speed doesn't depend on the setting** (within 0.4 tok/s in every pair).
5. **Caveat:** this test only appends turns. Checkpoints exist for cases where the prompt changes earlier in the conversation, such as regenerating, editing or stripped reasoning. Those weren't tested.

## D. Qwen on the c08 coding task: budgets, samplers, thinking off

5 tries per setting.
- **Try 1** is greedy (temperature 0).
- **Tries 2–5** use temperature 0.3 with fixed seeds, except Qwen's own sampler (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20).
- **Server:** SYCL, ub 2048.

| Setting | Passed | Hit the cap | Tokens per try | Median time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Thinking, 4K cap | 2/5 | 3 | 4,096 / 4,096 / 2,188 / 3,379 / 4,096 | 180 s |
| Thinking, 8K cap | 3/5 | 2 | 8,192 / 8,192 / 2,188 / 3,379 / 6,036 | 269 s |
| Thinking, 16K cap | **5/5** | 0 | 9,402 / 9,650 / 2,188 / 3,379 / 6,036 | 269 s |
| 8K + presence penalty 1.5 | 3/5 | 2 | 7,443 / 4,564 / 8,192 / 8,192 / 5,323 | 339 s |
| 8K + Qwen's sampler | 3/5 | 2 | 8,192 / 4,799 / 3,148 / 8,192 / 6,328 | 283 s |
| **Thinking off** | **5/5** | 0 | 615 / 322 / 253 / 295 / 283 | **12.7 s** |

1. **Thinking off is the recipe.** It's the only setting that passes 5/5 in a few hundred tokens: a median of 295 tokens and 12.7 s, against 6,036 tokens and 269 s for the 16K cap. Under Forge's rule, the recipe is **"thinking off for coding tasks"** (`--reasoning-budget 0`, or `enable_thinking: false`).
2. **The token caps only cut answers short.** Because the seeds are fixed, the 4K, 8K and 16K rows are the same 5 answers stopped at different caps.
   - Wherever a try wasn't cut off, it's identical to the token across caps (tries 3–5 at 2,188, 3,379 and 6,036).
   - Uncut, Qwen needs 2,188–9,650 tokens on this task, so 4K passes 2 tries and 8K passes 3.
   - A cap doesn't make Qwen think less; it just stops it.
3. **The samplers don't help.** A presence penalty of 1.5 and Qwen's recommended sampler each pass 3/5 at the 8K cap, the same as the plain 8K cap, with similar token counts.
4. **Correction to Phase 3:** Qwen's greedy answer on c08 isn't a loop. It ends on its own at 9,402 tokens (431 s) and passes. Phase 3 stopped it at 2,048 tokens, and the side check at 8,192 tokens. The reasoning does go round in circles, but it terminates.
5. **Caveat:** thinking off was tested on this one task only. Whether it costs quality on the other coding tasks hasn't been measured.

## Corrections to the dry-run reading

The dry run (1 try and 2 turns) was summarized to AJ before the full run. Three of those statements were wrong:
- **"Muse with checkpoints off re-reads the whole chat every turn":** wrong. It does it once, at turn 2. The dry run only had turn 2.
- **"Keep checkpoints on for chat":** wrong. Every setup reuses its cache, and checkpoints off was faster in all six pairs.
- **"Gemma on Vulkan with checkpoints shows the old re-read penalty":** the 124 s per turn is real, but it isn't a re-read. Only the new ~1,566 tokens are processed.

## Open, for Forge

The canary, C and D were settled in Phase 6 ([phase6.md](phase6.md)): the canary is wired, `--ctx-checkpoints 0` is withdrawn as a default for every model, and thinking off holds for Qwen across all 10 coding tasks.

- **The canary:** wire `baseline_ub2048.json` into `compare4.py` for the ub 2048 rows (A passed the 3% rule).
- **C, checkpoint setting:** whether to make `--ctx-checkpoints 0` the default for all three models on SYCL. It was faster in every pair here, but only append-only chats were tested.
- **D, Qwen recipe:** thinking off for coding; a rerun of Phase 3 coding with thinking off would show whether quality holds.
- **B, Gemma's floor:** the ~1.1 s floor on SYCL is a fixed cost per request. Why Vulkan with `--ctx-checkpoints 0` doesn't reuse the cache for identical prompts under 4K tokens is unexplained.

- **Versions:** unchanged since Phase 2. Kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy, Mesa 26.2.2, oneAPI 2026.0, compute-runtime 26.31.39395.13, llama.cpp 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`).
- **Builds:** SYCL `level_zero:0`, and the pinned Vulkan build with `GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`.

## A. Coding with thinking off: Phase 3's 10 tasks, 3 tries each

The server ran with `--reasoning-budget 0` and `enable_thinking: false`.
- **Tries:** 1 is greedy; 2–3 use temperature 0.3 with fixed seeds.
- **Token cap:** 4,096.
- **Server:** SYCL, ub 2048.

| Model | Greedy | All tries | Median tokens per answer | Time, 30 tries | Thinking actually off? | Phase 3 (thinking on, 2K cap, greedy) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | **10/10** | **30/30** | 130 | 203 s | yes: 0 reasoning characters in 30 of 30 | 9/10 (c08 hit the cap), median 555 tokens, 305 s for 10 |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 10/10 | 30/30 | 440 | 531 s | **no: it reasoned on 30 of 30** (44,887 characters) | 10/10, median 442 tokens, 187 s for 10 |

1. **Qwen with thinking off passes everything.**
   - It scores 10/10 greedy and 30/30 over all tries, including c08, the task it ran out of tokens on in Phase 3. Here c08 takes 254–280 tokens and 11–12 s.
   - Under Forge's rule (at least 9/10 greedy and 27/30 overall), **"thinking off for coding" becomes the Qwen recipe.**
   - The greedy pass takes 73 s for all 10 tasks, against 305 s in Phase 3, about 4× faster.
2. **Muse can't be switched to thinking off this way.**
   - **The evidence:** it returned separate reasoning on all 30 tries. Its greedy answers match Phase 3 token for token (c01 205 tokens, c02 571), and so does the total time (187.6 s against 187.5 s).
   - **Neither switch works:** not `--reasoning-budget 0`, not `enable_thinking: false`.
   - **What its row measures:** Muse with thinking on and a 4K cap, which passes 30/30. It doesn't show Muse with thinking off.
   - **Qwen's template does have the switch:** its GGUF chat template contains `enable_thinking`. In the header of Muse's GGUF I found neither `enable_thinking` nor an embedded chat template.

## B. Regenerate and edit, checkpoints on vs off

A 6-turn chat of about 9.4–9.5K tokens, followed by five steps. Each cell shows tokens reprocessed and time to first token.
- **SYCL:** ub 2048, flash attention on.
- **Vulkan:** ub 512, flash attention off.

The edits change the question at the end of a user message: "main risk" becomes "main opportunity" or "biggest win". That's why editing the last message only needs about 14 tokens when the cache can roll back, and editing turn 3 has to redo everything after the edit point (about 6.2K).

| Model | Engine | Checkpoints | Regenerate | Edit last message | Edit turn 3 | Back to original |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | SYCL | on | 1 · 0.41 s | 14 · 1.7 s | 6,236 · 15.3 s | 6,236 · 18.5 s |
| | SYCL | off | 1 · 0.09 s | 14 · 1.2 s | **9,362 · 18.0 s** | **9,362 · 18.3 s** |
| | Vulkan | on | 1 · **49.4 s** | 14 · **99.1 s** | 5,204 · **135.5 s** | 5,204 · **135.4 s** |
| | Vulkan | off | 1 · 0.09 s | 14 · 0.8 s | **9,362 · 78.4 s** | **9,362 · 78.5 s** |
| Qwen 3.8 27B | SYCL | on | 4 · 0.17 s | 1,531 · 2.2 s | 6,250 · 10.1 s | 1,531 · 3.2 s |
| | SYCL | off | **9,413 · 11.3 s** | **9,413 · 11.3 s** | **9,413 · 11.5 s** | **9,413 · 11.7 s** |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | SYCL | on | 1 · 0.26 s | 8 · 0.40 s | 6,292 · 9.6 s | 9 · 0.72 s |
| | SYCL | off | 1 · 0.20 s | 8 · 0.33 s | **9,502 · 11.7 s** | **9,502 · 11.7 s** |

Regenerating a second time gave the same result as the first in every setup.

1. **Checkpoints off isn't safe as a default for every model. It breaks Qwen.**
   - With checkpoints off, Qwen re-reads the entire chat on every regenerate and every edit: 9,413 tokens and 11.3 s, against 4 tokens and 0.17 s with them on.
   - This is the control model in Forge's plan, and in Phase 5's append-only test it looked fine. The server log doesn't say why it can't roll back.
2. **Gemma and Muse with checkpoints off handle regenerate and edit-last fine.** They reprocess 1–14 tokens, and are slightly faster than with checkpoints on.
   - Under Forge's Gemma rule (whole context on regen or edit-last with checkpoints off, but not with them on), Gemma doesn't trigger "keep checkpoints on". For Gemma alone, `--ctx-checkpoints 0` would be safe.
3. **Earlier edits cost more with checkpoints off, for every model.**
   - **With checkpoints off:** editing turn 3 re-reads the whole chat in all 4 setups (9.4–9.5K tokens).
   - **With checkpoints on:** it re-reads only from the edit point (5.2–6.3K tokens).
   - **Going back to the original chat:**
     - **Muse:** with checkpoints on, it restores the original from a checkpoint, 9 tokens and 0.7 s against 11.7 s.
     - **Qwen:** with checkpoints on, it reprocesses one turn.
     - **Gemma:** reprocesses from the edit point either way.
4. **Gemma on Vulkan with checkpoints on stays the outlier:**
   - **Cost per request:** 49 s even when only 1 token is reprocessed, and 99–135 s otherwise.
   - **Checkpoints off is faster for every step there,** even when it re-reads the whole chat (78 s against 135 s for the early edit).
5. **What this means for the defaults** (Forge's call):
   - **Qwen:** keep checkpoints on (the default).
   - **Gemma on SYCL and Muse:** off is fine for regenerate and edit-last. It costs 2–3 s more on edits to earlier turns, and Muse loses its fast way back to the original chat.
   - **Gemma on Vulkan:** off is much faster in every case.
   - **So:** `--ctx-checkpoints 0` can't be a default for every model.

## C. Canary at ub 2048 against the Phase 5 baseline

All 8 tests (Qwen and Muse; prefill 512 and 16K; decode at 0 and at 16K) are within 0.03% of `baseline_ub2048.json`: Qwen 640.00 / 824.13 / 23.69 / 18.86 and Muse 690.87 / 820.72 / 25.64 / 23.44 tok/s. Nothing has drifted, so the new canary is ready.
- **Routine canary:** `b65-phase4/canary.sh`. Its main rows now default to `UB=2048` and compare with `baseline_ub2048.json`; `UB=512` uses the original baseline. See `b65-phase4/README.md`.
- **Board W:** the Phase 6 Part C kit doesn't record it (tok/s only). The routine canary does.

## Open, for Forge
- **Checkpoint defaults per model.** Qwen keeps them on. Gemma on Vulkan wants them off. Gemma on SYCL and Muse depend on whether early edits matter (off costs a full re-read there).
- **Muse thinking off.** Its template doesn't respond to `enable_thinking` or `--reasoning-budget 0`. If a no-thinking Muse is wanted, it needs a different switch (for example a system-prompt convention, if the model has one). That would be a new test.

---
## Forge review (checked against the raw CSVs)

The summary tables match `A_coding.csv`, `B_regen.csv` and `C_canary.csv`. I re-counted part A: Qwen passes 30/30 with 0 reasoning characters, and Muse passes 30/30 with reasoning on all 30 tries (44,887 characters). The local fix that adds Phase 3's system message is correct, since my kit had left it out.

**Final decisions**
1. **Qwen recipe:** thinking off for coding (`--reasoning-budget 0`). It scores 10/10 greedy and 30/30 overall, with a median of 130 tokens and about 4× less time than Phase 3. This is confirmed across 10 tasks, not just one.
2. **Muse:** no thinking-off switch was found. Its 30/30 is with thinking on and a 4K cap, and it already uses a similar number of tokens to its Phase 3 run. A Muse thinking-off test isn't worth a phase unless the model card documents a switch.
3. **Checkpoint defaults, per model:**
   - **Qwen:** checkpoints **on** (the default). With them off, every regenerate and edit re-reads the whole chat (9.4K tokens, 11.3 s, against 0.17 s with them on). My best guess is that Qwen 3.8 keeps a recurrent or hybrid state that can't rewind even one token without a checkpoint, but the log doesn't confirm that.
   - **Muse:** checkpoints **on**. Turning them off gains under 0.1 s, and loses fast edits to early turns and the fast return to the original chat (0.7 s against 11.7 s).
   - **Gemma on SYCL:** checkpoints **on** for chat UIs, where edits to early turns are cheaper (15.3 s against 18.0 s). Use `--ctx-checkpoints 0` for append-only agent loops, which Phase 5 measured at 3.2 s against 6.0 s per turn.
   - **Gemma on Vulkan:** checkpoints **off**, which is faster at every step (49–135 s with them on).
   - **Rule:** leave checkpoints at the default, except for Gemma on Vulkan and Gemma agent loops. The Phase 5 suggestion that `--ctx-checkpoints 0` could be a default everywhere is withdrawn.
4. **Canary:** all 8 tests are within 0.03% of the baseline. `b65-phase4/canary.sh` with `UB=2048` is now the routine check, and the fix your agent made to the Vulkan loop (it now uses `VUB`) is right.

The B65 benchmark plan is complete. Phase 1.5, which re-checks the registry recipes, is still blocked on @0xSero. The round 2 blind writing ranks are still waiting on AJ.
# Arc Pro B65: Phase 7 findings (other engines: Intel llm-scaler vLLM, exl3xpu, Strata)

The question: is llama.cpp SYCL still the best way to run the B65? We used one OpenAI-API client (`b65-phase7/oai_bench.py`) and the same tests on every engine, on 2026-10-22.

**Runs:**
