**Versions and setup:**
- **Host and card:** kernel 7.2.8-9-omarchy, the B65 at `0000:06:00.0` (`card0`, `renderD129`). `renderD128` is the 3080, which nothing here touches.
- **llama.cpp:** b11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`), SYCL.
- **Intel llm-scaler:** `intel/llm-scaler-vllm:1.5` (`sha256:52218ad8…`), with vLLM `0.26.1.dev0+g568afb3a1` and torch 2.12 XPU.
- **exl3xpu:** `ghcr.io/0xsero/exl3xpu@sha256:21412bdd…` (exl3xpu 0.1.0, built on the same vLLM).
- **Strata:** `011c9e6` (2026-10-21), its SYCL port built AOT for `bmg-g31` in its `strata-sycl-dev` image.

**Weights:**
- **Qwen3.8-27B:** BF16 at `1d4bf0f2`, for the vLLM parts. The llama.cpp baseline uses the Q4_K_M GGUF from Phases 0–6.
- **EXL3 4.00 bpw:** `turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3@113cf7ab`.
- **Flash-Next Coder IQ1_M:** `ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF@5348543e`, the revision Strata pins.

## How everything was measured

The same client was used for every engine. Every number is timed from the stream on the client, so no engine's own timings are trusted over another's.
- **speed:** one request at a time, with prompts of 512, 4K, 16K and 32K tokens, 256 generated, 1 warmup and 3 reps, reporting medians.
  - **Prompts:** windows of this repo's markdown, cut to exact length with the model's own `tokenizer.json`. Each rep starts at a different offset, and prefix caching is off on every vLLM engine.
  - **Track A:** `/v1/completions` with `ignore_eos`.
  - **Track B:** Strata has neither, so it uses a chat request ("continue this document"), and llama.cpp gets the identical request.
- **conc:** 1, 2, 4 and 8 requests released together, each a 512-token prompt with 256 tokens out. Reports the aggregate tok/s. Track A only, since Strata serves one request at a time.
- **coding:** Phase 5's 10 tasks × 3 tries, with thinking off and Phase 5's system message. The pass rate is the quality gate. **Decode on these answers is the honest single-user number**: speculative decoding (MTP) depends on the text, and code is the real use. The `ignore_eos` markdown continuations in *speed* flatter it at 32K.
- **Power and VRAM:**
  - **Power:** board power from the xe `card` energy counter.
  - **VRAM:** the peak resident VRAM of the server's processes (xe fdinfo), read inside the container for Docker engines.
  - **Caveat:** vLLM claims `--gpu-memory-utilization` of the card up front, so its VRAM is a setting, not a need.

## Track A: Qwen3.8 27B, 4-bit, four engines

| part | engine and settings | load | decode 512 | decode 32K | first token 32K | 8 users, total | coding pass | coding tok/s | VRAM peak (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A0 | llama.cpp SYCL, Q4_K_M, `-fa on -b 2048 -ub 2048 -c 65536 -np 8 -kvu` | 10 s | 23.1 | 15.1 | 46.5 s | 37.3 | 30/30 | **24.0** | 22.1 |
| **A0m3** | **llama.cpp SYCL, as A0 + its own MTP (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`)** | 9 s | 34.1 | 27.4 | 49.3 s | 37.4 | 30/30 | **43.1** | 25.8 (A0mk3) |
| A0mk2 / A0mk3 / A0mk4 / A0mk5 / A0mk6 | llama.cpp + MTP k = 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 6, coding only | 9–42 s | | | | | 30 of 30 each | 39.0 / 42.2 / 39.8 / 38.5 / 35.0 | 24.7 / 25.8 / 27.0 / 28.2 / 29.3 |
| A1 | Intel vLLM, `sym_int4`, **eager** (as shipped: graphs crash) | 189 s | 19.3 | 17.9 | 26.6 s | 139.2 | 30/30 | 19.8 | 29.7 |
| A1g | Intel vLLM, `sym_int4`, **graphs** (patched) | 354 s | 28.2 | 25.9 | 26.5 s | 151.9 | 30/30 | 25.1 | 27.3 |
| A3 | Intel vLLM, `sym_int4` + MTP k=3, eager | 197 s | 41.5 | 54.5 | 27.5 s | 194.3 | 30/30 | 58.5 | 30.2 |
| A3g | Intel vLLM, `sym_int4` + MTP k=3, graphs (patched) | 464 s | 45.3 | 57.4 | 27.4 s | 197.0 | 30/30 | 63.3 | 27.7 |
| A4 | exl3xpu, EXL3 4 bpw + MTP k=3, fp8 KV (0xSero's B70 config) | 369 s | 42.0 | 44.6 | **18.5 s** | **207.5** | 30/30 | 51.1 | 31.7 |
| A2 | Intel vLLM, `fp8` | 183 s | 18.3 | – | – | – | crashed | – | 31.8 |
| A2b | Intel vLLM, `fp8`, 512-token chunks | – | – | – | – | – | no fit | – | – |
| A3k2 / A3g / A3k4 / A3k5 / A3k6 | Intel vLLM, graphs (patched), MTP k = 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 6, coding only | 328 / 464 / 318 / 327 / 332 s | | | | | 30 / 30 / 30 / 29 / 30 of 30 | 58.5 / 63.3 / 68.7 / **74.3** / 71.8 | 27.6 |
| **A5** | **Intel vLLM, `sym_int4` + MTP k=5, graphs (patched)** | 367 s | 45.2 | 51.6 | 27.5 s | 136.8 | **29/30** | **74.2** | 27.7 |

Medians of 3. Decode is in tok/s. "8 users" is the aggregate tok/s of 8 requests released together.

1. **Intel's own container, with MTP and graphs, is the fastest single-user setup on the B65.**
   - **The numbers:** 74.2 tok/s while writing code with MTP k=5 (A5), against **43.1 for llama.cpp with its own MTP (1.7×)** and 24.0 for llama.cpp without it (3.1×). It passed 29/30 against 30/30; the miss is one sampled try, and the greedy try passed.
   - **The fair comparison is MTP against MTP.** The first version of this write-up compared A5 with plain llama.cpp (3.1×). This llama.cpp build has its own MTP (`draft-mtp`), and the Q4_K_M GGUF carries the model's `nextn` layer, so A0m3 is the like-for-like baseline.
   - **At Intel's documented k=3 (A3g):** 63.3 tok/s and 30/30.
   - **MTP is most of that:** it gives 2.5–3× over the same engine without it (A1g 25.1). MTP is the model's own multi-token-prediction head, used for speculative decoding.
   - **Graphs add 8%** at k=3 (58.5 → 63.3).
2. **llama.cpp's own MTP is one flag and nearly doubles its single-user speed.**
   - **On code:** 24.0 → 43.1 tok/s (1.8×) at k=3, still 30/30. On markdown continuation 23.1 → 34.1 at 512 and 15.1 → 27.4 at 32K. Load time is unchanged (9 s), and VRAM rises by about 3.7 GiB.
   - **Draft length:** k=3 is best on code (39.0 / 42.2 / 39.8 / 38.5 / 35.0 for k=2–6; the k=3 repeat gave 42.2 against 43.1 in the full run). vLLM's MTP peaks later (k=5) and higher.
   - **Several users: no help.** 37.4 tok/s total at 8 requests against 37.3 without it, and lower at 4 (23.6 against 39.1). Turn it on for one user, not for a shared server.
   - **Prompt reading: unchanged.** A 32K prompt starts in 49.3 s against 46.5 s.
3. **Intel's vLLM as shipped is slower than llama.cpp without MTP.** A1 decodes at 19.3–19.8 tok/s against 23–24.
   - **Why:** graph mode never loads with `sym_int4` in llm-scaler 1.5 (below). Eager mode, which Intel's README uses anyway (`--enforce-eager`), costs **46%** of decode at 512 (19.3 → 28.2).
   - **Patched:** with the two-line patch (`b65-phase7/patches/sym_int4.py`), plain 4-bit vLLM beats llama.cpp's decode by 22% at 512 and 72% at 32K.
4. **Reading prompts:**
   - **vLLM vs llama.cpp:** vLLM reads them about 2× faster, 1,230–1,450 against 450–770 tok/s. A 32K prompt answers in 26.5 s against 46.5 s.
   - **exl3xpu is fastest:** its int8 prefill linears and oneDNN attention reach 1,775–2,150 tok/s, so a 32K prompt starts in 18.5 s.
5. **Several users: vLLM keeps scaling, llama.cpp doesn't.**
   - **llama.cpp** peaks at about 4 requests (39.1 tok/s total) and drops at 8 (37.3).
   - **vLLM** reaches 139–197 at 8 (**4–5×**), and exl3xpu reaches 207.5.
   - **Per-stream speed holds:** A1g's per-stream decode at 8 users (22.3) is about llama.cpp's single-user speed.
6. **exl3xpu (0xSero) is second for one user, and first for long prompts and many users.**
   - **Speed:** 51.1 tok/s on code.
   - **Download:** a 16 GB EXL3 download against 56 GB of BF16 for Intel's online quantization.
   - **Context:** fp8 KV, so its config fits 256K context.
   - **Single-user deficit:** its MTP drafts from an EXL3-quantized head, while Intel's quantizes the BF16 head on load. That is a likely reason for the gap, not measured here.
   - **Against its B70 number:** its registry recipe quotes 63–77 tok/s at C1 on a B70 (thinking on, its own prompts). On the B65, with our client, it does 42–45 on markdown and 51.1 on code.
7. **fp8 doesn't fit a 32 GB card for a 27B model.**
   - **Memory:** 27.6 GiB of weights leaves about 2 GiB.
   - **A2:** it loaded at 8K context, answered 512-token prompts (18.3 tok/s), then ran out of GPU memory on the first 4K prompt and died.
   - **A2b:** with 512-token prefill chunks it ran out of memory while allocating its KV cache. The coding suite got nothing from either.
8. **Power and efficiency:**
   - **Power:** the vLLM engines draw the same 160–195 W as llama.cpp.
   - **Energy per token:** on a 4K prompt, A3g makes 48.6 tok/s at 174 W against 22.2 at 187 W, about **2.4× the tokens per joule**.
9. **Load times:** llama.cpp loads in 10 s. Intel's vLLM takes 3–8 minutes (online quantization of 56 GB of BF16, then graph capture), and exl3xpu about 6.

**MTP draft length (k): 5 is best on code.**
- **The sweep:** each extra draft token adds about 5 tok/s up to k=5 (58.5 → 63.3 → 68.7 → 74.3), then k=6 drops to 71.8.
- **Quality holds:** speculative decoding doesn't change what the model would have written. The one miss at k=5 is task c08 on a sampled try (temperature 0.3), and the greedy try passed.
- **A5** is k=5 run through the whole suite: 29/30 (the same sampled c08 miss) at **74.2 tok/s**, 1.7× llama.cpp with its own MTP (3.1× without). Markdown decode and prompt reading match k=3. **For several users k=5 is worse:** 136.8 tok/s at 8 requests against 197.0 for k=3, because drafts that get rejected cost compute when requests are batched. So k=5 is the setting for one user, and k=3 for a shared server.

## Track B: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Coder (125B MoE, IQ1_M), Strata vs llama.cpp on the same GGUF

Strata only runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (a 125B MoE with 256 experts in the Coder release), so this track compares engines on that model.
- **The file:** ISTA-DASLab's Coder IQ1_M GGUF (2 shards, 58.4 GB) for both engines.
- **Context:** 40,960 for both, so the 32K prompt fits.
- **Strata:** the setup's own config, minus `--ple-io ram` (below): 4,096-token prompt chunks, int8 KV, a 2 GiB VRAM reserve, experts streamed into VRAM.
- **llama.cpp:** the flags Strata's docs use for their own llama.cpp comparison:
  - `-ngl 999 --override-tensor per_layer_token_embd=CPU`: every layer on the card except shard 2's 28.8 GB n-gram table, which stays mmapped from the SSD
  - `-fa on`, q8_0 KV
  - `SYCL_CACHE_PERSISTENT=0`
- **Speed test:** chat mode with a "continue this document" request, because Strata has no `/v1/completions`. Every row here generated the full 256 tokens.

| part | engine | load | decode 512 | decode 32K | prefill 4K–32K | first token 32K | coding pass | coding tok/s | board W | VRAM peak (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B3 | llama.cpp SYCL | 93 s | 18.7 | 14.4 | 400–428 | 81.9 s | 27/30 | 19.4 | 121–150 | 28.9 |
| B3n | llama.cpp SYCL + n-gram drafts (`--spec-type ngram-mod`) | 72 s | 19.0 | 24.7 | 402–425 | 81.7 s | 27/30 | 20.5 | 123–153 | 29.8 |
| B2 | Strata, no MTP (`--spec 2`, suffix drafts only) | 97 s | 37.9 | 40.9 | 941–1,022 | 32.9 s | 26/30 | 38.6 | 138–153 | 28.5 |
| **B1** | **Strata, MTP drafts (setup's default `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`)** | 50 s | 49.9 | 55.0 | 945–1,023 | 32.9 s | 26/30 | **73.7** | 144–154 | 29.6 |

1. **Strata runs a 125B MoE on one B65 at 73.7 tok/s writing code, 3.6× llama.cpp at its best on the same file (20.5 with n-gram drafts; 19.4 without, 3.8×).**
   - **llama.cpp can't use MTP here:** this GGUF has no `nextn` layer (Strata ships its MTP head separately). Its n-gram drafts (`ngram-mod`, the `--spec-default`) barely help: 19.4 → 20.5 on code, 27/30 both.
   - **Without its MTP layer** it still decodes at 38–41 tok/s, about 2× llama.cpp without drafts. That run still drafts from Strata's suffix cache, which this pack can't turn off, so it isn't a drafts-off number. Prompt reading, which no drafting touches, is the clean sign that the engine itself is faster.
   - **Prompt reading:** about 2.4× faster, 941–1,023 against 400–428 tok/s. A 32K prompt starts in 33 s against 82 s.
2. **Quality is the same on both engines.**
   - **Strata:** both Strata runs miss task c08 on every try, plus one sampled c02.
   - **llama.cpp:** misses c08 on every try.
   - **The rest:** everything else passes on both. The c08 miss belongs to the model at this quant, not to an engine.
3. **Strata's B70 claim holds on the B65.**
   - **Decode:** its docs report 70–78 tok/s for greedy engine runs on a B70, and through the API we measured 73.7 on code.
   - **Prefill:** its docs say 790 tok/s at 2K, and we measured 945–1,023 at 4K–32K with a newer engine.
   - **llama.cpp on this model** is slower here than on the B70 (18.7–19.4 against 23–25).
4. **Strata's AOT build for `bmg-g31` (the B70's chip) runs on the B65 unchanged, and its answers pass.** The coding gate is what would catch a broken AOT build.
5. **Limits:**
   - **One request at a time** in this setup. Strata has an opt-in `--parallel N` that wasn't tested here.
   - **One model family.**
   - **Built from source:** a 13 GB dev image.
   - **No pictures on Intel by default:** its docs report that a picture reset the B70.

## What broke, and the fixes

1. **Intel's vLLM container died at start on this host (`ze_fd_manager.cpp: fill_device_fds`).**
   - **Cause:** even with one GPU, vLLM's `all_reduce` initialises oneCCL, which opens every render node listed in `/dev/dri/by-path`. The host's directory also lists the 3080's nodes, which aren't in the container.
   - **Intel's single-GPU example:** it maps `renderD128`, which on this host is the 3080.
   - **Fix:** map only the B65's `card0` and `renderD129`, and mount a by-path directory holding only the B65's two links (`phase7.sh`, `BYPATH`).
2. **Graph mode never loads with `--quantization sym_int4` in llm-scaler 1.5.**
   - **Cause:** `sym_int4.py`'s `apply()` calls `logger.info_once(...)` inside the region torch.compile traces, and dynamo rejects it (`gb0291`).
   - **Fix:** `patches/sym_int4.py` turns those two calls into no-ops. Nothing else changes, and the result is +46% decode and identical pass rates.
3. **fp8 doesn't fit** (above). Also, when its engine died during KV allocation, vLLM's API server stayed up and never became healthy. The runner now treats "Engine core initialization failed" in the log as a failed load.
4. **Strata's pinned GGUF was replaced upstream.**
   - **What changed:** ISTA-DASLab replaced the Coder IQ1_M shard 1 on 2026-10-19 ("updated expert-pruned model"), and Strata `011c9e6` still pins the 2026-09-29 file and its expert profile.
   - **Fix:** we downloaded the pinned revision (`5348543e`), and both sha256s match Strata's.
5. **Strata's setup took this 46 GB PC for one with 1024 GB of RAM.**
   - **Cause:** the Intel wrapper's placeholder RAM value reached the rule that keeps the 29 GB n-gram table in RAM (`--ple-io ram`).
   - **Fix:** the runner drops that flag, so the table stays on the SSD, as in Strata's own B70 numbers.
6. **Strata's native IQ pack refuses `--spec 0`** ("needs --native SHARD1, --spec T (T >= 2)"), so drafting can't be fully off. "No MTP" is the closest equivalent: `--spec 2` without the MTP layer, leaving only the suffix drafter, which Strata's docs measured at about 9% acceptance on the B70.
7. **Our runner's own bug:** the first B1/B2 attempt passed a config path relative to the run folder after `cd`-ing into Strata's checkout, and failed in 5 s. It was fixed and re-run.

## Settings that win (Qwen3.8 27B, one B65)

- **One user, fastest: Intel llm-scaler vLLM 1.5,** 74.2 tok/s writing code, with:
  - `--quantization sym_int4`
  - MTP (`--speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_5_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":5}'`). For a server shared by several users, use `3`.
  - graphs on: the `sym_int4.py` patch, and no `--enforce-eager`
  - `--max-model-len 40960 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9`
  - devices: only the B65's two nodes plus a filtered by-path
- **Long prompts and many users:** exl3xpu, 0xSero's image and config, unchanged.
- **Simplest:** llama.cpp SYCL with the Phase 0–6 recipe plus `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3` for one user. It loads in 10 s, runs any GGUF, and writes code at 43 tok/s (24 without MTP). Leave MTP off for a shared server.

Full commands are in [recommended-settings.md](recommended-settings.md#phase-7-other-engines).
# Arc Pro B65: Phase 8 findings (TensorFold's XPU engine)

The question: does [TensorFold](https://tensorfold.dev)'s unofficial Intel XPU port beat Intel llm-scaler vLLM (Phase 7's A5, the setting `b65-llm` serves) for Qwen3.8-27B on the B65? Run on 2026-11-02 with the Phase 7 client (`b65-phase7/oai_bench.py`) and an agent-shaped long-context test (`b65-phase8/longctx.py`).

**Setup:**
- **Engine:** [ashhart/TensorFold](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold) at `16d95cc`. Built from source with Zig 0.17.0, the host's `ocloc`, and the nGEN headers from oneDNN's `third_party/ngen`, following [the B70 recipe](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/main/docs/xpu/RECIPE-qwen38-27b-b70.md).
- **Weights:** SergiioB's `Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-Int4-sym-G128-MTP-BF16` at `9d189a6`, plus the `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` drafter at `50307d4`, about 23 GB in all.
- **Fewer Xe-cores than the B70:** the port was written for the B70 (32 GB), but the B65 has the same memory and the same `bmg` kernel target.
- **One patch:** the engine opens only PCI id `0xe223` (the B70). [`xpu-device-id.patch`](../b65-phase8/xpu-device-id.patch) adds an `XPU_DEVICE_ID` override, and the runs use `XPU_DEVICE_ID=e222`. Nothing else changed.
- **Correctness on the B65:** all of the engine's own checks pass.
  - Drafted output equals serial output, with both perfect and wrong drafts.
  - DFlash2 trees equal serial output.
  - 8 streams in shared rounds equal serial output.
  - 32 greedy tokens give sensible code.
- **Load:** 33 s, against 5–8 min for vLLM, which quantizes on load.

**Runs (`b65-phase8/results/`):**

| run | server | what |
|---|---|---|
| `tf-20261102-133335` | `--parallel 8 --context 16384` (7 streams fit), bf16 KV | Phase 7 speed, concurrency and coding suites |
| `tf-20261102-133335-80k` | `--parallel 2 --context 81920` (1 stream fits), bf16 KV | speed at 16K, 32K and 64K |
| `tf-20261102-133335-80k-kv8` | as above + `XPU_KV_INT8=1 --prompt-cache-gib 1` (2 streams fit) | speed from 512 to 64K |
| `longctx-tf.json`, `longctx-vllm.json` | TensorFold 80K kv8 vs `b65-llm` (vLLM A5, 80K) | real Zig source as context, then a coding request; greedy, thinking off, 512 tokens |

## Results

| test | TensorFold | Intel vLLM A5 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coding suite, decode tok/s on answers | **157.5** (30/30) | 74.2 (29/30) | **2.1×** |
| Decode, 512-token prompt (markdown, `oai_bench speed`) | 79.0 | 45.2 | 1.7× |
| Decode, 32K prompt (markdown) | 22 | 51.6 | **0.43×** |
| Prompt reading, 32K cold (first token) | 28.6 s | 27.5 s | same |
| 8 users at once, total tok/s (512-token prompts) | 168.9 | 136.8 (k=5); 197.0 (k=3) | between the two |

**Agent-shaped test:** code as context, then a coding answer. The figures are decode tok/s, as the median of 2 reps.

| context | 512 | 8K | 16K | 32K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TensorFold | **150.7** | **93.4** | 65.6 | 43.3 |
| Intel vLLM A5 | 69.4 | 77.9 | **76.7** | **68.8** |

- **TensorFold is about 2× faster on short contexts,** with the biggest margin on code, where DFlash2 trees accept about 7 tokens a round.
- **Its decode falls with context; vLLM's barely moves.** The lines cross near 14K tokens.
- **The int8 KV cache does not help with that.** It decodes at the same speed as bf16 at every length. So the slowdown is attention compute, not cache bandwidth. Its gain is capacity: 2 streams of 80K instead of 1.
- **Coding agents in T3 usually run with 15–40K tokens of context,** which is where vLLM is ahead.
- **Prompt reading (first-token time):** both read a cold prompt at about 1,150–1,350 tok/s. In the long-context test each size's first rep begins with the previous size's prompt. vLLM's prefix cache reused that part, at 7.5 s for 16K against 13.0 s. TensorFold's cache keeps state only at the points it plans, so it missed.

## Prefill option: `XPU_PREFILL_INT8=1`

Run on 2026-11-03 with `b65-phase8/prefill_int8.sh` (`results/prefill-20261103-172116`): one fresh server per mode (`--parallel 1 --context 81920`), cold prompts, 3 reps, then the coding suite. No GPU resets were logged.

| prompt | 512 | 4K | 8K | 16K | 32K | 64K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| default (fp16), tok/s | 1,269 | 1,357 | 1,330 | 1,264 | 1,144 | 949 |
| **int8, tok/s** | **1,605** | **1,730** | **1,686** | **1,583** | **1,399** | **1,118** |
| gain | +26% | +28% | +27% | +25% | +22% | +18% |
| first token, default → int8 | 0.4 → 0.3 s | 3.0 → 2.4 s | 6.2 → 4.9 s | 13.0 → 10.4 s | 28.6 → 23.4 s | 69.0 → 58.6 s |

- **Against the other engines:** int8 now beats Intel vLLM's cold prefill (2.4 s vs 3.0 s at 4K, 23.4 s vs 27.5 s at 32K). exl3xpu is still faster (1.9 s and 18.5 s). The B70's published gain at 4K is +33%, against +28% here.
- **Decode doesn't change.** The coding suite gives 157.3 tok/s (30/30) against 157.2 (30/30), and decode still falls with context, so the 14K crossover with vLLM stands.
- **Correctness:** with int8 on, drafted output equals serial, DFlash2 trees equal serial and 8 shared streams equal serial. The first 32 greedy tokens match default mode.
- **Answers are not always identical to default mode.** 27 of the 30 coding replies had the same hash; 3 differed, and all 30 passed. The prompt is computed at lower precision, so expect occasional differences on near-ties.
- **Not tested:** rotated weights with `XPU_PREFILL_INT4=1`, the B70's fastest prefill. They need a second ~19 GB copy of the model, and the disk had 13 GB free.

## Problems

- **One GPU hang.** At the end of the 80K bf16 session, after the 64K prompts, a compute job timed out. The kernel logged `Engine reset: engine_class=ccs … Timedout job … in tensorfold-nati`, and the engine exited with `a command list did not drain (Level Zero 0x70000001)`. The card recovered, and the next sessions were clean. It happened once in four sessions, too few to call it a pattern.
- **VRAM is held for a few seconds after the process exits.** A vLLM start right after TensorFold stopped saw only 6.2 of 31.9 GiB free and failed. `b65-llm`'s restart picked it up 30 s later. Wait about 10 s between engines.
- **No grammar library by default.** Structured output and `tool_choice: required` need `libtfgrammar.so`, built from xgrammar v0.2.8. Plain tool calls work without it: `get_weather` returned a correct `tool_calls` reply. Reasoning comes back as `reasoning_content`, where vLLM uses `reasoning`.
- **Not on the community board.** tensorfold.dev's `tensorfold benchmark` and its leaderboard cover Apple silicon and NVIDIA only, so these figures can't be submitted there.

## Verdict

- **Keep Intel vLLM (A5) for T3.** Coding agents carry long contexts, and vLLM holds 69–78 tok/s from 512 to 32K tokens. It also keeps 80K context with prefix caching.
- **TensorFold is the better engine for short-context work:** chat, one-off code generation, and many users with short prompts. On the B65 it decodes code at **2.1×** vLLM's speed and loads in 33 s.
- **To try it as a second server,** stop `b65-llm` first; only one 27B engine fits on the card. Then run:

```sh
XPU_PREFILL_INT8=1 XPU_DEVICE_ID=e222 ~/src/TensorFold/zig-out/xpu/bin/tensorfold-native serve ~/models/Qwen3.8-27B-GPTQ-g128 \
  --drafter ~/models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 --parallel 8 --context 16384 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 --name qwen
```

- **Worth revisiting** if upstream speeds up long-context decode on XPU, or if a DFlash2-style drafter comes to vLLM.
# Arc Pro B65 32 GB: recommended settings (Phases 0–7)

This is the conclusion of Phases 0–6 (2026-10-12 to 2026-10-13). Each line names the phase it comes from; the numbers are in the linked findings.
- **Scope:** three ~30B Q4 models (Qwen 3.8 27B Q4_K_M, Gemma 4 31B QAT Q4_0, Muse Glimmer 28B Q4_K_M) on llama.cpp.
- **Versions:** llama.cpp build 11574 (`8bb3cf0d2`), oneAPI 2026.0, compute-runtime 26.31.39395.13, Mesa 26.2.2, kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy.
- **After an update:** these settings are measured on these versions only. After any update, run the canary (`b65-phase4/canary.sh`, about 10 minutes) before trusting them.

**Share cards:** the Conclusion tab on the share page (`/share#sum`) has six cards, each in wide (X) and tall format, with captions. The cards are drawn from the run data:
- the recipe without numbers, and the recipe with its evidence
- time to first token on a 16K prompt
- generation speed out to 32K
- five settings that cost you
- which model for what

A seventh card, `sum-banner`, is a fixed 5:2 header for the X article; it shows the card under test (ASRock Arc Pro B65 Creator) from ASRock's product photo on the Amazon listing, with the background removed (`charts/assets/`). PNG exports are in `charts/conclusion/`. An article version for X and LinkedIn is in [article-b65-settings.md](article-b65-settings.md).

## The short answer

**llama.cpp SYCL, flash attention on, `-b 2048 -ub 2048`, all layers on the GPU, 32K context.** Leave context checkpoints at their default, and turn Qwen's thinking off for coding.

```bash
set +u; source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force; set -u
export ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0 UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=1
llama-server -m <model.gguf> -ngl 99 -c 32768 -np 1 --jinja -fa on -b 2048 -ub 2048
#   Qwen, coding:                add --reasoning-budget 0
#   Gemma, append-only agents:   add --ctx-checkpoints 0
```

## Why each setting

| Setting | Recommendation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Engine | **SYCL** (oneAPI, Level Zero), not Vulkan | +21.8% decode and +31.2% prefill on average at the same commit; more efficient (decode 0.115 against 0.100 tok/J) ([Phase 2](phase2.md)). Answers 1.4–2.0× sooner at 512 tokens for Qwen and Muse, and uses 1.5–3.3 GiB less VRAM at 32K ([1S](phase1s.md)). |
| Flash attention | **On** with SYCL (off with Vulkan) | On SYCL it adds 18.5% to decode on average, up to +61% for Gemma at 32K. Gemma's server with it off: 91 s to first token at 16K ([Phase 2](phase2.md), [diag](gemma-sycl-diag.md)). On Vulkan it's the reverse: it cut Gemma's 16K prefill to 38 tok/s ([0.5](phase05.md)). |
| Micro-batch | **`-b 2048 -ub 2048`** on SYCL (512 on Vulkan) | +35–55% prefill at 16K, decode within 1.2%. 16K first token: Qwen 28.9 → 20.5 s, Muse 28.5 → 20.5 s, Gemma 58.1 → 30.8 s. Costs 0.5–0.7 GB VRAM ([Phase 4](phase4.md), [server rerun](ubserve.md)). On Vulkan, ub 2048 costs Muse 36%. |
| Context | **32K fits all three** | Every model decodes above 15 tok/s at 32K on SYCL ([1S](phase1s.md)). `--swa-full` doesn't fit for Gemma, at 32K or at 17K ([1](phase1.md), [diag](gemma-sycl-diag.md)). |
| Context checkpoints | **Default (on)**, with two exceptions | With them off, Qwen re-reads the whole chat on every regenerate or edit (9.4K tokens, 11.3 s against 0.17 s). Every model re-reads it when an earlier turn is edited ([Phase 6](phase6.md)). Exceptions: `--ctx-checkpoints 0` for Gemma append-only agent loops on SYCL (3.2 s against 6.0 s per turn, [Phase 5](phase5.md)), and for Gemma on Vulkan, always. |
| Thinking | **Off for Qwen coding** (`--reasoning-budget 0`); **on** for Muse | Qwen with thinking off: 10/10 greedy and 30/30, median 130 tokens, about 4× faster than with thinking on (9/10). Muse ignores both switches ([Phase 6](phase6.md)). |
| Token budget with thinking on | **At least 4K** for coding | At a 2K cap, Qwen and Gemma each failed one task while still thinking. Gemma passes with room (3,326 tokens); Qwen needs up to 9,650 ([Phase 3](phase3.md), [Phase 5](phase5.md)). |

## What you get, per model (SYCL, flash attention on, ub 2048)

| | Qwen 3.8 27B | Muse Glimmer 28B | Gemma 4 31B QAT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Decode, empty context → 32K (tok/s) | 23.7 → 15.3 | 25.7 → 22.3 | 22.5 → 16.1 |
| Time to first token, 512 / 4K / 16K prompt | 0.96 / 4.87 / 20.5 s | 0.87 / 4.77 / 20.5 s | 2.75 / 7.24 / 30.8 s |
| Server generation, 512 / 4K / 16K prompt (tok/s) | 23.3 / 22.4 / 18.8 | 25.4 / 24.0 / 23.0 | 21.6 / 18.7 / 16.9 |
| VRAM held at 32K context | 18,104 MiB | 16,755 MiB | 20,916 MiB (ub 512; not recorded at ub 2048) |
| Quality, Phase 3 (coding / tools / recall) | 9 / 10 / 5; 10/10 coding with thinking off | **10 / 10 / 5**, fastest overall | 9 / 10 / 5; **best writing** (blind rank 1.6) |

Sources:
- **Decode:** [Phase 1S](phase1s.md), llama-bench at ub 512; ub 2048 changes decode by ≤1.2% ([Phase 4](phase4.md)).
- **Time to first token and generation:** [the server rerun](ubserve.md) and [the Gemma diagnostic](gemma-sycl-diag.md).
- **Quality:** [Phase 3](phase3.md) and [Phase 6](phase6.md).

## Which model for what
- **Long context or general use: Muse.** It loses only 13% decode from empty to 32K context, has the fastest decode and the smallest VRAM, and scored best on Phase 3's coding set.
- **Coding with quick answers: Qwen with thinking off.** It scored 30/30, and a typical answer is about 130 tokens and a few seconds. Watch its decode at 32K: 15.3 tok/s, the one place SYCL loses to Vulkan (−5%).
- **Writing: Gemma.** It ranked first on 3 of 5 prompts in AJ's blind ranking (one rater, five prompts). It's the slowest to first token and the largest in VRAM. Its SYCL floor of about 1.1 s per request makes tiny prompts 0.3–0.6 s slower than on Vulkan ([Phase 5](phase5.md)).
- **Tool calling and notes recall:** all three scored 10/10 and 5/5. These don't separate the models.

## If you have to use Vulkan
Use flash attention off, ub 512, and `--ctx-checkpoints 0` for Gemma.
- **Gemma with default checkpoints** takes 25 s on a 512-token prompt and about 124 s per chat turn ([Phase 1](phase1.md), [Phase 5](phase5.md)).
- **Expect** about 18% slower decode (SYCL is +21.8%) and roughly half the 16K prefill of SYCL at ub 2048 (Qwen 388 vs 824, Gemma 335 vs 617 tok/s).

## Power
- **Decode:** 165–199 W of GPU board power against a 200 W cap. Muse sits at 190–199 W with no sign of throttling ([Phase 2](phase2.md), [1S](phase1s.md)).
- **Idle:** about 45 W with a model loaded, and 43 W empty.
- All figures are board power, not wall power.

## In the registry
All three models pass local-ai-registry's six lab gates on these settings at 32K, 64K and 128K, in the official server-intel image (21.4–25.3 tok/s; decode doesn't change with the window, and all three fit 128K in 32 GB). Submitted as [PR #260](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/pull/260), with the card photo in [PR #264](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/pull/264) ([Phase 1.5](phase15.md)).

## Phase 7: other engines

[Phase 7](phase7.md), 2026-10-22/23, tested Intel's own vLLM container, 0xSero's exl3xpu image and Strata against the llama.cpp recipe above. We used one client and the same tests, and the honest single-user number is decode while writing code.
- **For Qwen3.8 27B, the fastest single-user setup on the B65 is Intel's llm-scaler vLLM with MTP.** It runs 74.2 tok/s writing code against 43.1 on llama.cpp with its own MTP (24.0 without), passing 29/30 against 30/30. Two changes are needed: map only the B65 into the container, and patch two log calls so graph mode loads.
- **Many users or long prompts:** exl3xpu. 8 requests reach 207.5 tok/s total (llama.cpp: 37.3), and a 32K prompt starts in 18.5 s (llama.cpp: 46.5 s).
- **llama.cpp stays the simple default:** any GGUF and a 10 s load. For one user, add its own MTP:
  - **The flags:** `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3` on top of the recipe above, with a GGUF that carries the model's `nextn` layer (lmstudio-community's Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M does).
  - **The gain:** 24.0 → 43.1 tok/s on code, still 30/30, and about 3.7 GiB more VRAM. k=3 beat k=2, 4, 5 and 6.
  - **Several users:** leave it off. It gives nothing at 8 requests (37.4 vs 37.3 tok/s) and costs at 4.

```bash
# the B65 only: its two nodes, and a by-path dir that lists only them (oneCCL opens every node listed there)
mkdir -p b65-by-path && ln -sfn ../card0 b65-by-path/pci-0000:06:00.0-card && ln -sfn ../renderD129 b65-by-path/pci-0000:06:00.0-render
docker run -d --name qwen --device /dev/dri/card0 --device /dev/dri/renderD129 -v "$PWD/b65-by-path:/dev/dri/by-path:ro" \
  --group-add "$(getent group render | cut -d: -f3)" --group-add "$(getent group video | cut -d: -f3)" --shm-size 32g -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  -v ~/models/Qwen3.8-27B:/llm/models/Qwen3.8-27B:ro \
  -v "$PWD/b65-phase7/patches/sym_int4.py:/opt/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/sym_int4.py:ro" \
  -e VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn --entrypoint vllm intel/llm-scaler-vllm:1.5 \
  serve /llm/models/Qwen3.8-27B --served-model-name qwen --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --dtype float16 --trust-remote-code \
  --language-model-only --quantization sym_int4 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --max-model-len 40960 --max-num-seqs 8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_5_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":5}'
```

- **Device names:** `card0` and `renderD129` are this host's B65. Check yours with `ls -l /dev/dri/by-path`.
- **Loading:** it loads in 5–8 minutes (online 4-bit quantization of the 56 GB BF16 checkpoint, then graph capture).
- **MTP draft length:** `num_speculative_tokens` 5 is best for one user (k = 2/3/4/5/6: 58.5 / 63.3 / 68.7 / 74.3 / 71.8 tok/s on code). For a shared server use 3: at 8 requests k=3 gives 197 tok/s total and k=5 gives 137.
- **Don't use:** `--quantization fp8`, which doesn't fit 32 GB with a 27B model, or `--enforce-eager`, which costs 46% of decode.
- **Thinking:** off for coding (`chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}`), as in Phase 6.
- **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Coder (125B MoE) on one card: Strata.** It runs 73.7 tok/s writing code against 20.5 for llama.cpp on the same IQ1_M GGUF (with n-gram drafts; that GGUF has no MTP layer for llama.cpp), and reads prompts about 2.5× faster. Build its SYCL engine with `AOT=bmg-g31`, use the GGUF revision it pins, and drop `--ple-io ram` on a PC under 64 GB of RAM ([phase7.md](phase7.md)).

## Not covered
- **Muse with thinking off:** no working switch was found.
- **Qwen's 32K regression on SYCL:** untested against SYCL tuning variables.
- **Gemma's ~1.1 s request floor on SYCL:** unexplained.
- **The PCIe link:** the card sits in a 4.0 x4 chipset slot, and its effect wasn't measured (it should mainly affect load time).
- **Quality sets:** small and self-made. They're sanity checks, not leaderboards.
# Arc Pro B65: llama-server at the new SYCL default (-b 2048 -ub 2048)

Run `us-20261013-161926`, 2026-10-13, 4:19–4:28 PM ET. Qwen and Muse. Package: `b65-ubserve-us-20261013-161926.tar.gz`.
- **Method:** the same as Phase 1S. llama-server on SYCL with flash attention on, 32K context, prompt cache off; prompts of 512, 4K and 16K tokens, 3 reps each, median reported; 30 s of loaded idle plus VRAM. Only `-b 2048 -ub 2048` changes.
- **Gemma's ub 2048 numbers** come from the Gemma diagnostic (`gd-20261013-123933`, `ckpt0_ub2048`).
- **Why:** Forge's Phase 4 decision made ub 2048 the SYCL default for all three models, but its llama-server effect had only been measured for Gemma.

## Time to first token (median of 3)

| Model | Prompt | Vulkan (Phase 1) | SYCL ub 512 (Phase 1S) | **SYCL ub 2048** | Change vs ub 512 | Prompt tok/s | Gen tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 512 | 1.31 s | 0.96 s | **0.96 s** | same | 536 → 536 | 23.36 → 23.34 |
| | 4K | 9.70 s | 6.94 s | **4.87 s** | 1.43× faster | 591 → 843 | 22.08 → 22.41 |
| | 16K | 42.22 s | 28.89 s | **20.48 s** | 1.41× faster | 568 → 801 | 18.54 → 18.78 |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 512 | 1.71 s | 0.87 s | **0.87 s** | same | 592 → 593 | 25.43 → 25.44 |
| | 4K | 11.78 s | 6.78 s | **4.77 s** | 1.42× faster | 605 → 861 | 24.52 → 24.02 |
| | 16K | 41.65 s | 28.51 s | **20.53 s** | 1.39× faster | 576 → 800 | 23.42 → 22.97 |
| Gemma 4 31B QAT | 512 | 1.36 s* | 2.81 s | **2.75 s** | same | 182 → 187 | 21.58 → 21.58 |
| | 4K | 11.08 s* | 14.13 s | **7.24 s** | 1.95× faster | 290 → 567 | 19.92 → 18.72 |
| | 16K | 49.36 s* | 58.13 s | **30.79 s** | 1.89× faster | 282 → 533 | 17.83 → 16.86 |

\* Gemma's Vulkan reference is the `--ctx-checkpoints 0` rerun.

| Loaded idle (30 s) and VRAM at 32K | Idle W | VRAM ub 512 → ub 2048 |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 42.9 | 17,582 → 18,104 MiB (+522) |
| Muse Glimmer 28B | 44.8 | 16,080 → 16,755 MiB (+675) |

## Findings
1. **The llama-bench gain carries over to serving.** Qwen and Muse reach their first token 1.4× sooner at 4K and 16K. Server prefill goes from about 570–605 to 800–861 tok/s, close to llama-bench at ub 2048 (Qwen 824, Muse 821 at 16K).
2. **Against Phase 1 on Vulkan,** a 16K-token prompt now gets its first token about **2.0× sooner** for Qwen and Muse (42 s → 20.5 s), and **1.6× sooner** for Gemma (49 s → 31 s).
3. **Short prompts don't change.** 512 tokens fit in one micro-batch either way. Gemma's 512-token gap against Vulkan (2.8 s vs 1.4 s) remains; Phase 5 Part B looks into it.
4. **The costs are small:**
   - Generation is within 2% for Qwen and Muse (Muse −1.9% at 16K, Qwen +1.3%). Gemma's is 5–6% slower.
   - VRAM at 32K is 0.5–0.7 GB higher.
   - Loaded idle is unchanged (43–45 W).
